title: Thai  Central Bank : Recent Baht Weakness Still In Line With Regional Units
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Thailand stands ready to intervene in the foreign exchange market in case there is any excessive volatility in the movement of the baht, but so far the local unit has been moving in line with regional currencies, Deputy Governor Atchana Waiquamdee said Monday.

She said the recent baht weakness is caused by portfolio outflows as well as dollar buying by importers and gold traders.

The bank will consider the impact of the softer baht on inflation, Atchana said, but she didn't elaborate.

Investors unwinding their positions in Thai stocks sent the benchmark stock market index down 7.8% by midday Monday, and this helped push up the U.S. dollar to THB31.08-THB31.10 from THB30.85 in late Asian trade Friday.

-By Bangkok Bureau, Dow Jones Newswires; 662-690-4200; djnews.bangkok@dowjones.com [ 26-09-11 0603GMT ]

title: Thai  Central Bank : Have Not  Intervened  In  FX  Market
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Thailand's Deputy Governor Atchana Waiquamdee said Friday that the bank has not intervened in the foreign exchange market to curb volatility of the local unit.

The bank is not worrying about the baht's recent weakness as it is still moving in line with regional currencies, Atchana told reporters.

The U.S. dollar was higher late Friday at THB30.85 from THB30.71-THB30.72 late Thursday in Asia on portfolio outflows after hefty falls in Thai shares. The pair was off a THB30.88 session high, with local dealers suspecting that the central bank may have stepped in to sell dollars.

-By Bangkok Bureau, Dow Jones Newswires; 662-690-4200; djnews.bangkok@dowjones.com [ 23-09-11 1046GMT ]

title: Flight From Risk Thrashes Emerging-Market  Currencies , Debt
text:
-Global economic anxieties pummel emerging-market assets

-Host of central banks suspected of intervening as their currencies tumble

-South Africa, the Czech Republic hold policy rates steady


 
   Cynthia Lin 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market assets fell under severe pressure Thursday as fears about the euro-zone credit crisis and global economic slowdown hit a boiling point despite the Federal Reserve's latest stimulus plan.

U.S. central bankers confirmed market expectations Wednesday, announcing that it will implement what most market participants call "Operation Twist," by buying longer-dated Treasurys and selling shorter-dated ones. The central bank's decision did little to allay mounting fears about the sputtering global economy, sparking an exodus out of risky assets and into the refuge of U.S. government debt.

As Treasury yields plummeted, the risk premium investors demand to hold what they perceive as riskier emerging-market debt increased. This spread as reflected on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global, or Embig, was 32 basis points wider to 449 basis points above Treasurys. In price terms, the index lost 1.49%. The Latin America regional sub-index lost 1.69% in price as its spread blew out 34 basis points to 5.14% over Treasurys.

Emerging-market currencies also took a beating across the board as the U.S. dollar soared, led by notable declines in the Mexican peso, Chilean peso and Korean won.

A slew central banks in Asia--including Korea, Taiwan and Thailand--were suspected to have intervened in the foreign exchange markets to lend support to their currencies. The Korean won was a notable underperformer in its region, weakening to KRW1,181.1 a dollar from KRW1,148.6--now the weakest since last September, according to CQG.

In Brazil, the country's central bank announced midday and quickly implemented an auction of $2.7 billion in foreign-exchange swap contracts to rein in the depreciating real. The battered Brazilian currency opened at 1.92 reais to the dollar, weakening sharply to BRL1.94 at one point. On the Embig, Brazil's risk premium increased 29 basis points to 285 basis points, losing 0.97% in price.

Such efforts come in stark contrast to moves these central banks conducted just months ago, when many complained that their currencies were strengthening too quickly and hurting exporters at home. Earlier in the year, these assets showed impressive resilience even when the situation in advanced nations began to crumble. But the rout since the start of September shows that these regions are still inextricably linked to the developed world.

"The emerging-market space is interesting because it held and held and held," said Michael Mata, portfolio manager at ING's global bond fund, "but, in the end, there's no way to decouple from 50% of global GDP." Mata's team believes there's still more room from emerging-market currencies to fall as these nations' policymakers cut rates and reduce the interest-rate differential that made their currencies so appealing.

These days, inflation and other issues that come with red-hot economic growth is taking a back seat, with fears of a double-dip recession and the intensifying euro-zone credit crisis dominating investors' fears. The latest economic reports Thursday show the euro zone's composite purchase manufacturing index falling into the sub-50 contraction territory for the first time since 2009, while China's PMI sank deeper in the contraction range to 49.4 from 49.9.

South Africa's central bank decided to keep its policy rate at 5.5%, caught in a dilemma of slowing growth and rising inflation. The South African rand weakened to ZAR8.2963 a dollar from ZAR8.2530, which Reserve Bank Governor Gill Marcus acknowledged is putting the country's goal of keeping inflation under 6% at risk.

Monetary authorities of the Czech Republic also convened Thursday and decided to keep rates steady a record-low 0.75%. Central and Eastern European currencies have been rattled this month give their ties to the neighboring euro zone.

By Cynthia Lin; Dow Jones Newswires; 212-416-4403; cynthia.lin@dowjones.com

title: WORLD  FOREX : Asian  Currencies  Scale New Heights On US Debt Woes
text:
-- U.S. dollar swoons against Asian currencies

-- Asia FX gains prompt Korea and Thailand intervention for a second straight day

-- Singapore dollar, Malaysian ringgit at long-term highs


 
   By Martin Vaughan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian currencies soared to new highs against the dollar Wednesday, as investors showed the greenback no mercy on increasing expectations the U.S. will lose its triple-A credit rating.

The U.S. currency fell to Y77.78, its lowest since the post World War II-low of Y76.25 marked in March. Japan Finance Minister Yoshihiko Noda reiterated that he will continue to closely monitor the market.

Central banks in Thailand and South Korea for a second straight day intervened to keep their currencies from rising too quickly and damaging their export-dependent economies.

Wednesday's gains extended a months-long trend of investors piling into Asian currencies and out of currencies like the dollar and euro, which are burdened by seemingly intractable fiscal problems.

"Now more than ever, Asia is seen as a region where there are strong fundamentals," said Thomas Harr, head of Asian FX strategy at Standard Chartered Bank.

"These flows coming into Asia are safe-haven flows; they are increasing even though you could say that risk appetite is not very strong," he said.

The U.S. dollar hit an all-time low against the Singapore dollar, breaching the key psychological barrier of S$1.2000 to hit S$1.1992 before rebounding gently. The Malaysian ringgit was at its strongest in 14 years, as the greenback sank to MYR2.9350 from MYR2.9535 late Tuesday in Asia.

Dollar selling lifted the Indonesian rupiah to a seven-year high. A dealer said Bank Indonesia may be checking prices in the market but there was no evidence of intervention.

Many market observers expect the U.S. to be hit by a ratings downgrade even if the White House and Congress agree on a deal to raise borrowing limits by Tuesday, a deal which for the moment remains elusive. Wednesday's dollar losses are in part front-running that expected downgrade, Harr said.

The threat of central bank intervention tempered investor enthusiasm in some markets. "With the central bank present, punters are pushing the baht up with caution," said a Bangkok dealer.

The Aussie dollar, already riding high on the U.S. debt woes, hit a fresh 30-year high at $1.1062 after a stronger-than-expected consumer inflation reading. The Aussie was trading around $1.1055 at 0450 GMT, up from $1.0951 as Asian trading got underway.

The euro climbed to a three-week high at $1.4537 earlier in the day but eased back to $1.4520 at 0450 GMT. The common currency was at Y113.01, unchanged from New York trade. The dollar was at Y77.82 from Y77.89.

title: CORRECT: Asia Central Banks  Intervene  To Curb  Currency  Gains As Dollar Slides
text:
("Asia Central Banks Intervene To Curb Currency Gains As Dollar Slides," at 0839 GMT, misstated the level at which the Bank of Korea was suspected of intervening in the fourth paragraph. The correct version follows:)

-- Central banks in South Korea, Thailand and the Philippines intervene to slow gains in their currencies

-- U.S. debt ceiling impasse propels Asian currencies upward

-- Philippines' Purisima says U.S. debt imbroglio speeds the dollar's decline

By Martin Vaughan

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Several Asian central banks were seen intervening in currency markets Tuesday, as the U.S. political stalemate on increasing the government borrowing cap caused the dollar to tumble against regional currencies.

Philippines Secretary of Finance Cesar Purisima said U.S. failure to reach a debt deal is causing a "loss of confidence" in the dollar and could "accelerate the search for an alternate reserve currency."

Purisima said U.S. leaders are "missing the point" and are endangering the dollar's preeminent status, used as the default currency across the globe in trade and finance.

The Bank of Korea was suspected of buying around $300 million in an attempt to slow the won's rise, said traders in Seoul. The bank may have been trying to defend the psychological level of KRW1,050 to the dollar, the traders said.

The Philippine central bank was estimated to have bought as much as $200 million at various levels as the peso climbed to its highest mark in three years. The dollar hit a low of PHP42.22.

Bangkok dealers said the Bank of Thailand also engaged in mild dollar buying to curb the baht's rise, as the greenback slipped to THB29.68, its lowest since November 2010.

"The idea that we're seeing intervention is a consistent theme across Asian currencies right now," said Robert Rennie, chief currency strategist at Westpac Institutional Bank.

After notching substantial gains in the first four months of the year, the riskier currencies of emerging Asia had been hemmed in recently by fears surrounding sovereign debt in the euro-zone periphery. Those fears were to some extent calmed by the announcement last week of a second bailout for Greece, setting the stage for Asian currencies to strengthen.

Asian currencies were further boosted Tuesday as the dollar sank on comments from President Barack Obama and House Speaker John Boehner which revealed that any deal to cut spending and raise the U.S. debt ceiling remains far off. U.S. officials have said they have only until Aug. 2 to raise borrowing limits or risk missing debt servicing payments.

-By Martin Vaughan; +65 6415 4033; martin.vaughan@dowjones.com

-Alex Frangos in Hong Kong, Jieun Shin in Seoul, Phisanu Phromchanya in Bangkok and Rhea Sandique-Carlos in Manila contributed to this article [ 26-07-11 0930GMT ]

title: EM ASIA  FX -Sing dlr, won rally on Greek deal;  intervention  caps
text:
* Sing dlr at record on models, leveraged names; MAS spotted

* S.Korea estimated to have bought $500 mln-$1 bln to defend 1,050/dlr

* Ringgit up on lack of intervention

(Updates text, prices)

By Jongwoo Cheon

SINGAPORE, July 22 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar rose to a new record and the South Korean won hit a near three-year peak on Friday as a European package to rescue Greece led investors to buy emerging Asian currencies, despite intervention by Asian authorities and technical signs being overbought.

On Thursday, euro zone leaders agreed on a second rescue package for Greece, alleviated worries about contagion risks, which have put a brake on the regions forex markets.

Investors say they are waiting to see if U.S. politicians cobble together an agreement to avoid default, but the currencies are likely to keep their bullish trend, analysts said.

If Washington fails to reach an agreement before the Aug. 2 deadline, that may dampen risk appetite again, but that will also push down the dollar, which will eventually support the regional units, some added.

"With EUR risk in the background at least in the near term, speculative players are back looking to go short USD/Asia pairs. Asian currencies have broken fresh highs... I think it continues to push emerging Asian currencies higher," said Westpaccurrency strategist Jonathan Cavenagh in Singapore.

Emerging Asian currencies rose for the week as concerns over the debt crisis in the two developed markets eased.

The Philippine peso and the Malaysian ringgit were the best performers during the week, gaining 1.3 percent and 1.1 percent, according to Reuters calculations.

Technically, some currencies look overbought and some dealers and analysts said there could be a correction if the U.S. politicians fail to agree a debt deal.

"Every Asian country is long U.S. assets and if U.S. get downgraded, that will be a mayhem," said a Kuala Lumpur-based dealer.

The 14-day Relative Strength Index (RSI) for the USD/THB hit a three-month low of 28, suggesting the pair is headed higher in the short-term, and the baht could weaken from current levels.

The RSI of the Singapore dollar and Korean won are also hovering around the threshold of 30, indicating weakness ahead for the Asian units.

Central banks of Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan and Thailand were spotted buying greenbacks, dealers said. South Korean authorities were also spotted buying dollars, they added.

Market players expect the regional policymakers to keep intervening to slow their gains.

"The pace of appreciation is too strong and the swing is not driven by fundamentals," said Saktiandi Supaat, head of FX Research at Maybank in Singapore.

SINGAPORE DOLLAR

Model funds, leveraged names and proprietary accounts pushed up the Singapore dollar to a record high of 1.2086 per the greenback.

Earlier, agent banks had been spotted buying the U.S. dollars at 1.2100 but lowering the bids to 1.2090 in heavy intervention, dealers said.

But the city-state currency is expected to break through 1.20 level eventually as the central bank raised inflation forecast on Thursday and on views that the country would allow gradual appreciation.

WON

Seoul's foreign exchange authorities intervened to keep the won weaker than 1,050 per dollar, dealers said.

The South Korean currency earlier rose to 1,050.0, the highest since late August 2008, on demand from offshore real money funds and exporters.

Foreign investors also turned to net buyers of local stocks

, ending an eight-session selling spree.

As the won threatened to break the level, the authorities stepped in the market and pushed it weaker minutes before the local market ended, dealers said.

Dealers speculated authorities had bought $500 million-$1 billion against the won.

Still, the authorities are unlikely to keep defending certain levels, given the country's fight against inflation, dealers said.

"Today they showed strong determination to defend 1,050. But it does not mean 'don't touch the level ever'," said a foreign bank dealer in Seoul.

"Today's intervention suggest 'don't touch the level in a single day," he added.

If dollar/won breaches 1,050, it may head to 1,046, around a falling trend line which starts from November last year.

BAHT

The baht rose on strong demand from proprietary accounts and leveraged funds.

But the central bank was spotted buying dollars from 29.84 per dollar level all the way down, dealers said.

The Thai currency, which had been pressured by the country's politics, has outperformed its Asian peers since the July 3 general election outcome eased political uncertainty.

But Barclays Capital saw short-term corrections in the baht, saying its recent gains are seen excessive and advised investors to position for it.

Bank of Thailand is expected to keep intervening to slow down the baht's appreciation and Thailand's trade balance is likely to turn to deficit more often on strong oil prices, Barclays said.

"We recommend positioning for a near-term reversal of recent THB gains by buying the 1m USD/THB forward at 29.94/USD, targeting 30.35/USD," it said in a note.

RINGGIT

The ringgit gained on heavy demand from proprietary accounts, model funds and exporters.

Some covered dollar-short positions taking profits, but a lack of the central bank's intervention provided more support to the Malaysian currency.

title: Bank Of  Thailand  Gov:  Central Bank  Hasn't  Intervened  In  FX  Market Recently
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Thailand hasn't intervened in the currency market recently, and the baht's recent weakness is the result of concerns over debt problems in Europe, Gov. Prasarn Trairatvorakul said Monday.

"We've tried to be neutral as the baht's depreciation will push oil prices higher," he told reporters.

The U.S. dollar late Monday was at THB30.42, up from THB30.28-THB30.29 late Friday in Asia.

He added that he isn't worried about possible capital outflows as most of the funds that have flowed in so far this year were destined for the Thai bond market.

title: INTERVIEW: Thai Finance Minister: Dollar To Keep Falling In Long-Term
text:
By James Hookway, Leigh Murray and Almar Latour

BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The U.S. dollar is expected to continue heading south over the long term as countries can't escape their economic fundamentals, Thai Finance Minister Korn Chatikavanij said Friday.

The U.S. can only repay its massive debt by allowing depreciation of dollar, Korn told The Wall Street Journal and Dow Jones Newswires.

"I see no way of repaying it other than through devaluation. Hopefully it will be gradual, but one can never predict that."

He said the Bank of Thailand has been intervening in the foreign exchange market, both buying and selling the U.S. dollar, and it will continue to intervene in the market to limit any excessive currency volatility.

However, he said there is no need for the central bank to fight the trend and that there is no evidence of any "hot money" behind the baht's recent strength.

"So far they (the Bank of Thailand) have been able to manage excess volatility," Korn said.

He said Thai exporters have been extremely resilient to the baht's strength, though they need any appreciation to be gradual.

"Exporters detest volatility the most," Korn said.

The minister called on Thai exporters to diversify their trade settlement currencies, into yuan, yen or other units, to match their trading counterparties in order to reduce dependency on the U.S. dollar, which is on the descent.

He noted that the adoption of the Chinese yuan in international trade and investment has been happening faster than expected.

On the other hand, Korn said the strong baht will likely attract more investments for value-added projects than those seeking the cheapest production base and low labor costs.

Potential further increases in global oil prices are considered the biggest threat to Thailand's economy, as they will fuel inflationary pressures, he said.

Higher oil and commodity prices are key factors pushing up production costs and inflation. However, the global food crisis could provide an obvious opportunity for Thailand as a food producing country.

Korn said the government's proposed minimum wage hike won't put upward pressure on inflation, which is driven more by external factors.

The Democrat Party-led government has been floating the idea of raising minimum wage by another 25% in two years in a bid to increase the purchasing power of low income earners. The proposal comes ahead of general elections in the country, which could take place by late June or early July.

Korn said the poll result will likely to be a close race between the ruling Democrat Party and the Puea Thai Party, backed by fugitive ex-Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra.

-By James Hookway, Leigh Murray and Almar Latour, +66 2690 4200; leigh.murray@dowjones.com [ 29-04-11 1037GMT ]

title: UPDATE: Asian Shares Mostly Higher; Fed Stance Buoys Risk Appetite
text:
(Adds information, quotes, updates/adds market levels)

By Shri Navaratnam and Puja Rajeev

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian stock markets were mostly higher Thursday, while the U.S. dollar fell across the board, as the U.S. Federal Reserve's commitment to retain its ultra-easy monetary policy buoyed sentiment and drove riskier currencies up.

The ongoing earnings season also played a big hand in Tokyo, Seoul and Sydney markets.

Japan's Nikkei Stock Average was up 1.3%, Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was 0.4% higher, South Korea's Kospi Composite was off 0.1%, Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index tacked on 0.5% and China's Shanghai Composite was off 0.1%.

Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were up 34 points in screen trade.

Wall Street's surge Wednesday bolstered regional sentiment, after the Federal Open Market Committee signaled the end of its controversial $600 billion bond buying program as planned, and Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke said the central bank would keep interest rates accommodative. He said there was no specific time frame to hike interest rates.

"The comments from Bernanke are very bullish for equity markets, via a weak U.S. dollar, U.S. earnings and commodity prices," said RBS Morgans investment adviser Chris MacDonald in Sydney.

The news spurred risk appetite, pushing stocks, gold and oil prices higher. Risk-sensitive currencies surged, with the euro and Asian currencies tapping multi-year highs against the U.S. dollar. Central banks in Korea, Thailand and Malaysia intervened to weaken their currencies in an effort to protect their export-led economies.

Gold bulls took a breather after earlier driving spot gold to a record high $1,530.30 a troy ounce; the yellow metal was recently fetching $1,526.90, down 40 cents from its New York settlement Wednesday. Oil prices remained bid, with June Nymex crude oil futures up 48 cents at $113.24 per barrel on Globex, off its 31-month high of $113.70 tapped in early trade.

In Tokyo, strong earnings offset concerns over grim March industrial production data.

Industrial production dropped a record 15.3% in March, but Japanese manufacturers expect their output to rise 3.9% on-month in April and increase 2.7% in May.

"The market seems to be reacting more favorably to earnings than we had anticipated (and) expectations are growing that Japan will display its underlying strength through speedy recovery efforts," said Cosmo Securities equity strategist Toshikazu Horiuchi.

Kyocera rose 2.6% after reporting strong fiscal fourth-quarter earnings and Advantest jumped 5.2% after posting a sharply narrower loss in its fiscal fourth quarter.

Sony extended its losses on news Wednesday that its online video game network had been hacked; the stock fell 3.1%.

A handful of profit warnings and a strong Australian dollar tempered gains in Sydney. The Australian dollar hit a new 29-year high of US$1.0903 in early trade, pressuring currency sensitive stocks such as Westfield Group and Bluescope Steel, which fell 0.7%, and 2.6%, respectively.

Goodman Fielder and Whitehaven were hit by profit warnings, falling 8.6% and 3.1% respectively.

In China, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index gave up morning gains. The reversal was triggered by sharp losses for the country's foreign currency denominated B shares, which were hurt by a weaker U.S. dollar and lingering concerns over China's launch of an international board.

"The B share market was designed to attract foreign investors and the international board will definitely attract many of the B share's target investors," said Duan Junfang at Dongfang Securities.

The Shanghai B Share Subindex was down 4.1%. Wuhan Iron & Steel was down 0.6% and Poly Real Estate Group fell 0.5%.

The Seoul market turned lower as investors booked profits in heavyweight technology and construction stocks. Still, a few other stocks rose on earnings-linked news.

LG Electronics tacked on 3.8%, buoyed by expectations of a firm turnaround in second-quarter earnings after the tech giant Wednesday reported an unexpected first-quarter loss. Hynix Semiconductor rose 2.5% after the world's second-largest producer of computer memory chips gave an upbeat outlook, and topped market expectations for its first quarter net profit, which fell 66% from a year earlier.

Among other markets, New Zealand's NZX-50 was 0.4% higher, Singapore's Straits Times Index gained 0.5%, Malaysia's KLCI rose 0.3%, Taiwan's Taiex fell 0.2%, Indonesian shares edged up 0.3% and Philippine shares slipped 0.5%. India's Sensex fell 0.1% and Thailand's SET was flat.

The U.S. dollar continued to suffer against its major rivals after slipping sharply on Wednesday. Emmanuel Ng, currency economist at OCBC Bank, said: "Dollar weakness is looking pervasive, while risk appetite remains strong."

The single currency is at $1.4862 against the dollar, its highest level since December 2009, from $1.4788 late in New York on Wednesday. It was at Y121.59 against the yen, from Y121.44. The dollar was buying Y81.81, compared with Y82.17.

Taking advantage of the greenback's woes, Asian currencies soared. In addition to the Australian dollar's fresh 29-year highs, the Singapore dollar hit a record S$1.2276 high against the US dollar and the Korean won rocketed to a fresh 32-month high at KRW1,071.90.

Japanese government bond futures were up 0.05 at 139.99 points, after the Bank of Japan left its unsecured overnight call loan rate target unchanged in a range of 0.0%-0.1%, as expected, and finalized a lending facility to help sustain money flow following the March 11 earthquake.

title: News Highlights: Top Economic Stories Of The Day
text:
ASIA OUTPUT GROWTH MAY BE CUT BY UP TO 1.5 PERCENTAGE POINTS IN 2011 - ADB 

The Asian Development Bank warned Tuesday that Asian output growth could be cut by up to 1.5 percentage points if recent global food and oil price rises persist for the rest of the year, with the soaring cost of food threatening to push millions of people in the region into "extreme poverty."


 
ECB'S TRICHET SEES SOME RISK OF SECOND-ROUND EFFECTS - REPORT 

European Central Bank President Jean-Claude Trichet highlighted the risks of second-round effects and said officials should be on alert against such inflation materializing, Finnish newspapers Helsingin Sanomat and Kauppalehti reported Tuesday.


 
ECB STARK: EURO-ZONE RESTRUCTURING COULD BE WORSE THAN LEHMAN 

A debt restructuring for euro-zone members could result in a new banking crisis and would fail to address budget and structural problems in individual countries, European Central Bank executive board member Juergen Stark said in an interview with German TV station ZDF. (published 1046 GMT)

A restructuring of Greek debt wouldn't help Greece gain needed economic strength or build up a surplus, Finnish Central Bank Governor Erkki Liikanen said in an interview published Tuesday in German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine.

By Phisanu Phromchanya

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Thailand has intervened in the foreign exchange market "at times" to curb the baht's rise, but such moves have only been to try and limit short-term volatility, Gov. Prasarn Trairatvorakul said Tuesday.

He told a seminar that the central bank's intervention in the market is not meant to resist market mechanisms.

"The BOT has intervened in the (foreign exchange) market at times at various levels to limit short-term volatility of the baht, but we are not intending to reverse the major trend," said Prasarn.

The Bank of Thailand was suspected of stepping into the market several times last week, according to local dealers, as it attempted to slow the local currency's rise. The dollar was trading at around THB29.98 to THB30.00 in morning trade Tuesday.

Prasarn said that Thailand's relatively strong economic fundamentals, along with its continuous trade surplus, are attracting capital inflows, adding that the central bank is closely monitoring the market for speculative activity.

"The size of the international capital flows has increased significantly at present because of excess global liquidity as a result of extra-accommodative monetary policies by the U.S., the European Union and Japan to stimulate their economies," he said.

Massive capital inflows could cause asset price inflation while also increasing volatility risk in case of capital flight, he said.

Among factors affecting global capital movement are the fragility of the economic recovery in the Group of Three leading industrial nations, the euro zone public debt problem, geopolitical tension in the Middle East and Africa, natural disasters, and any adjustment of U.S. monetary policy, said Prasarn.

"It would be difficult to separate 'hot money' from other types of inflows, but we are closely monitoring them and so far the level is not considered worrisome," he said.

Inflation pressures are likely to remain in the second half due to high oil and consumer goods prices while the domestic economy will maintain its recovery momentum, he said.

Thailand's consumer price index rose 3.14% in March compared with the same month a year earlier.

Meanwhile, he said any economic impact from renewed tension along the Thai-Cambodia border--which has seen several soldiers on both sides killed--will likely be limited as exports to Cambodia account for less than 1% of Thailand's total exports.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Won, rupiah down on profit-taking before Fed
text:
* Won down 0.4 pct on tighter FX control worries

* Rupiah, peso down 0.3 pct on dlr short-cover before FOMC

* Baht eases on importers' end-month dlr demand

(Updates with text, prices)

By Jongwoo Cheon

SINGAPORE, April 26 (Reuters) - The South Korean won and the Indonesian rupiah fell on Tuesday, leading declines in most regioanl currencies as investors took profits on recent rallies and awaited comments from the Federal Reserve that could determine the short-term direction of the U.S. dollar.

Emerging Asian currencies could pull back further in near term as investors still hold dollar-short positions, but their overall bullish trend remain intact, dealers and analysts said.

Regional central banks are expected to continue intervening in foreign exchange markets to slow gains in their currencies, but are unlikely to attempt to reverse their strength, they added.

"Fundamentally, we are bullish on AXJ currencies given the global recovery and widening US-AXJ rates spreads, which should drive capital inflows into the region," said Standard Chartered said in a note.

Emerging Asian currencies have seen healthy gains so far this year on inflows to the region's stocks and bonds, and on expectations of further policy tightening to contain inflation amid robust economic growth.

Standard Chartered said shorter-dated bonds in particular should benefit from FX-driven inflows. [ID:nL3E7FQ09D]

Investors are keeping an eye on the Fed's two-day meeting, which starts later in the day.

The central bank is expected to say it will stick to its plan to complete a $600 billion bond-buying programme in June, with the focus on a post-meeting news conference by Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke -- the first regularly scheduled news briefing by a Fed chief in its 97-year history.

But the dollar is seen fragile as the Fed will be in no rush to unwind its super-easy monetary policy.

WON

The won shed 0.5 percent against the dollar as offshore hedge funds and real money investors covered dollar-short positions.

Worries about possible tougher foreign exchange controls also weighed on the won as the country started inspecting foreign currency derivatives trading by four banks, including branches of two foreign banks, that government sources have said could lead to reductions in ceilings of such positions.

After the local currency market closed, two government sources said the country will likely to trim the ceilings by at least one-fifth "as widely expected". [ID:nL3E7FQ0UO]

Still, the South Korean currency found support as exporters bought it for settlements, especially around 1,085 per dollar.

"I don't see any other reasons to sell the won except position adjustments. The won may fall more on short-covering, but I don't think it will weaken past 1,090," said a local bank dealer in Seoul.

RUPIAH

The rupiah fell and filled most of a gap as investors covered dollar-short positions, but later recovered some losses as further falls are seen as limited.

Earlier, the Indonesian currency lost up to 0.8 percent to 8,690 against the dollar, a notch 8,692, the session high of 8,692 on April 1, a day before it gapped up.

The dollar/rupiah's 14-day relative strength index rose to 38.974, the highest since February 3, indicating the pair got out of an oversold territory.

The RSI had been below 30 since February 7 by the previous session except two days, as investors chased it on expectations that the country will allow more appreciation to fight inflation.

Still, the rupiah's gains is seen slow on caution over the central bank's dollar-buying intervention. IFR said local banks bought the pair on behalf of Bank Indonesia. [ID:nIFR8mdh5y]

PESO

The peso fell on fixing related dollar demand and dollar-short covers before the Fed's meeting.

The Philippine currency , however, found support around 43.34 per dollar, the 61.8 percent Fibonacci retracement level of its November-January weakening trend.

A European bank dealer in Manila said the peso is unlikely to move much, adding it will stay within recent range of 43.00-43.50.

The central bank had been seen defending 43.00 while the peso has a 50 percent retracement level of March-April strengthening trend around 43.51.

BAHT

The baht eased on end-month dollar demand from importers and investors covered dollar-short positions.

The central bank's governor said the Bank of Thailand will intervene periodically in the currency market to limit volatility over the short term, following the baht's gains. [ID:nB7E7FL04N]

But a Bangkok-based dealer said "the market still needs to sell on rallies (in dollar/baht)".

title: UPDATE: Asia Central Banks  Intervene  Again As  Currencies  Extend Rally
text:
(Adds yuan central parity fixing in paragraph 4; details on BOK interventions in paragraphs 7-8; updates levels in paragraphs 9-11)


 
   By Martin Vaughan and In-Soo Nam 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The dollar continued to sell off sharply in Asia Thursday, prompting central banks in South Korea and Malaysia to try to curb the surge in their currencies to long-term highs by intervening for the second day running.

South Korean authorities also said they will inspect foreign-exchange transactions at banks, focusing on activity in the overseas non-deliverable forward market. The move comes as heavy dollar selling by offshore players, largely via the NDF market, has pushed the Korean won to multi-month highs in recent weeks.

China fixed the yuan at another record high against the dollar, setting the tone for Asian trading where sentiment was also given a boost by upbeat U.S. economic data and a strong earnings-driven rally on Wall Street.

The People's Bank of China set the central parity rate Thursday at 6.5228, down from Wednesday's record low fixing of 6.5294.

Strategists said that in intervening in the markets, central banks around the region are trying to smooth sudden market moves, but likely won't stand in the way of the broad appreciation trend in Asian currencies.

"Asian central banks and government officials have made it very clear that they're going to use currencies to fight inflation," said Stuart Oakley, head of emerging market trading at the Royal Bank of Scotland. "They're allowing their currencies to move faster than they have before, and China is leading the way on that."

Traders said the Bank of Korea bought dollars throughout the session first at KRW1,080.00, then at KRW1,079 and KRW1,078 to cushion the dollar's slide. The greenback sank early to as low as KRW1,078.30, but ended the trading day around KRW1,080.30.

The central bank used at least one foreign bank and one local bank to execute trades, traders said. The head of BOK's foreign exchange market team declined to comment.

Bank Negara Malaysia bought dollars at MYR3.0120, and then later at MYR3.0080 and MYR3.0070 as the dollar fell to 13-year lows against the ringgit, local traders said.

The actions came as the U.S. dollar took a beating across the board, falling against the euro and other currencies. Commodity-linked currencies soared into rarely-seen territory. The Australian dollar hit a 29-year high of S$1.0771, while the U.S. dollar touched C$0.9482 against the Canadian Loonie, a level not seen since 2007.

The U.S. dollar fell to a fresh record low against the Singapore dollar, which has paced the gains in Asian currencies, reaching a low early Thursday of S$1.2342.

Traders in Thailand were on vigil against further intervention by the Thai authorities to weaken the baht, following suspected market activity Wednesday by the Bank of Thailand.

Better-than-expected U.S. housing data overnight helped to spur risk appetite Thursday as Asian equity markets opened higher.

But the main thing pushing Asian currencies higher against the U.S. dollar remains the sense that the U.S. Federal Reserve is lagging the European Central Bank and others in its willingness to tighten policy.

"We've had pretty clear signals from the majority on the [Fed's Federal Open market Committee] that they don't see any problem with keeping monetary conditions in the U.S. as loose as possible for as long as possible," said Cliff Tan, a foreign exchange strategist at Societe Generale in Hong Kong.

In contrast, Asian central banks have been tightening since last year to try to blunt higher food and fuel prices, and the ECB lifted its key policy rate earlier this month.

A stronger currency makes exports more expensive abroad, and central banks in Asia's export-oriented economies have historically intervened to soften the blow of a sharp currency rise.

Korea is brandishing various tools to curb gains in the won. It announced Thursday it would conduct "inspections" into non-deliverable forward trades at four banks. Offshore investors have taken short positions on the dollar in the forward market, pushing the won higher.

Analysts said the inspections might perturb the banks, but authorities can do little concretely to limit NDF trades, which are done beyond the jurisdiction of Korean authorities.

-By Martin Vaughan and In-Soo Nam, Dow Jones Newswires; +65 6415 4033; martin.vaughan@dowjones.com

--Min-Jeong Lee in Seoul and Kwan-por Lee in Kuala Lumpur contributed to this article. [ 21-04-11 0832GMT ]

title: DJ US Dollar To Remain Pressured Despite Singapore  Currency  Move
text:
-- Asian central banks unlikely to end dollar recycling

-- Singapore's currency move not likely to herald regional shift in policy

-- U.S. dollar set to remain under pressure By Siva Sithraputhran Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

LONDON (Dow Jones)--The U.S. dollar is set to remain under pressure over the long term because most Asian central banks are seen as being unlikely to slow the pace of greenback sales, even after Singapore signaled that it might do just that.

Asian central banks typically buy the dollar against local currencies to slow any export-denting bouts of strength, but then churn the dollars into euros, Australian dollars, and other currencies to spread the risks, so the greenback falls. This 'recycling' of reserves has been at the heart of the dollar's weakness against a range of currencies--including the euro--over recent years.

That relationship came under scrutiny Thursday after the Monetary Authority of Singapore opened up to more currency strength by raising the trading band of the Singapore dollar, initially boosting the currency to a record high against the greenback and dragging other Asian currencies higher with it. Tellingly though, the immediate reaction from Singapore's closest neighbor, Malaysia, was to intervene in the market to stem the rise of its currency--the ringgit--indicating that there is still lot of resistance to allow local currency gains.

Recycling quickly kicked in, and the U.S. dollar plunged, sinking fast against the euro, the Australian dollar, and other major currencies.

Valentin Marinov, a strategist at Citigroup in London, remains of the opinion that emerging-market currencies will be allowed to rise only gradually, maintaining that pressure on the dollar.

'This set-up could be particularly damaging for the dollar against its liquid alternatives in the G-10 world,' he said. 'We think this should continue to generate sufficient upside momentum for the euro and Australian dollar against the greenback,' he added.

Over the past few months, there have been waves of interventions by the central banks of South Korea, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia to arrest the rises of their respective currencies. By keeping their currencies from rising too fast, the central banks want to make sure their exports don't lose competitiveness.

'There is no monetary coordination in Asia, with most policymakers running mercantilist-type policies that favor their own exports via undervalued exchange rates,' Win Thin, New York-based strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman said.

Singapore has been 'more open to currency appreciation in [a] controlled way' than some regional competitors, said Ken Dickson, investment director at Standard Life Investments in Edinburgh, which manages GBP143 billion in assets worldwide.

To some extent, China too has been allowing its currency to rise very gradually as it tries to rein in inflation.

The amount of currency reserves held by Asian central banks has continued to mount, suggesting that the wider market impact of any region-wide change in policy could be huge, even if only a fraction of these reserves are moved in or out of dollars.

At the end of March, China's foreign exchange reserves surged to a record, topping $3 trillion. In Singapore, reserves have been climbing steadily since November, to reach just over $233 billion in March. That indicates that the central banks have been carrying out smoothing operations to keep their currencies within the required trading bands. Data for April will be eagerly awaited for signs that the pace of gains has moderated.

Singapore's move last week means it will be able to trim these smoothing operations, said Dickson at Standard Life.

But as other regional central banks are still loathe to let their currencies rise, the impact of Singapore's action on the U.S. dollar looks set to be drowned out. -By Siva Sithraputhran, Dow Jones Newswires; 44-20-7842-9462; siva.sithraputhran@dowjones.com.

title: WSJ: Thailand Former PM Thaksin: Will Cut Corporate Tax If Allies Win Election
text:
-Thailand former PM Thaksin says will cut corporate tax if allies win election

-Thailand's Thaksin says Thailand should adopt low-tax regime

-Thailand's Thaksin suggests less central bank intervention to slow baht rise

-Thailand's Thaksin: Stimulate local economy to generate more imports and curb baht


 
   By James Hookway 
   Of THE WALL STREET JOURNAL 
 

Thailand's ousted former leader Thaksin Shinawatra on Thursday said he will play a key role in setting economic policy if the country's main opposition party wins fresh elections planned for later this year, and that one of his first moves would be to cut corporate tax rates.

In an interview with The Wall Street Journal, the telecommunications mogul-turned-politician said Thailand's 30% corporate tax rate was uncompetitive and would be lowered if the For Thais Party backed by Thaksin and his supporters win the vote, which could be held as soon as the end of June.

"We want to reduce companies' tax costs because this will enable them to pay higher salaries," Thaksin said. "And when employees get paid more they consume more, and when they consume more, we'll collect more Value Added Tax."

Thailand's corporate tax rates are comparatively high. Elsewhere in Southeast Asia, Malaysia's corporate tax rate is 25% and Singapore's is capped at 17%. The current Thai government has also said it might consider lowering corporate tax rates.

"Definitely, when For Thais becomes the government, Thailand will become a low-tax regime because I see many countries do that quite effectively," Thaksin said.

Thaksin led Thailand from 2001 until 2006, when he was overthrown in a military coup. He now lives overseas to evade imprisonment on a 2008 corruption conviction which he says was politically motivated. A pioneer of populist, pro-business politics in Thailand, he is the only Thai leader to have been re-elected but remains a divisive figure in the country.

As a potentially important economic adviser, Thaksin also said he would encourage Thailand's central bank to refrain from intervening aggressively to slow the rise of Thailand's baht currency against the dollar by buying U.S. dollars and selling Thai baht. He said the country already had "excessive" reserves of foreign currency which could be better used elsewhere.

Instead, Thaksin said he will focus on policies to strengthen the domestic economy and generate more imports to help offset the country's large trade surplus. "When imports and exports are quite close, then you'll see the baht devalue," Thaksin said. "We have to let our baht reflect our real economy."

Thailand's foreign reserves stood at $181.5 billion as of March 25.

The Thai baht was trading at 30.07 baht to the U.S. dollar in late Asian trading Thursday.

-By James Hookway, The Wall Street Journal [ 04-07-11 1231ET ]

title: UPDATE: Asia Central Banks  Intervene  As US, France Press China On Yuan
text:
-- South Korea, Malaysia, Thailand intervene to curb gains in their currencies

-- China sets yuan at a record-high against the dollar

-- U.S and France press China to let yuan rise

(Adds Thailand's intervention in the lead and paragraph 11, Korea intervention size in paragraph 4, comments by Korea finance ministry official in paragraphs 5-6, updates forex quotes.)


 
   By Arran Scott and Jieun Shin 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--South Korea, Malaysia and Thailand were seen intervening to slow the rise of their currencies Thursday, as China set the yuan at a record-high while the U.S. and France called for more exchange-rate flexibility--code for wanting Beijing to let its currency rise faster.

The developments highlighted both the reservations in Asian nations about the speed of their currencies' rise and the urgency felt in the U.S. and Europe, where governments argue a stronger yuan is essential to reducing trade imbalances that threaten global economic stability.

Asia's large trade surpluses, a major source of economic growth for the region, has put strong pressure on the local currencies to rise, which authorities have resisted by selling their currencies in foreign-exchange markets. The trade surplus of China, now the world's second-biggest economy, has soared while the U.S. has run a persistent deficit, an imbalance Washington blames in part on an artificially weak Chinese currency.

The Bank of Korea apparently bought $1 billion for won, Seoul-based traders said, citing dollar purchases near KRW1,100 in early trading and additional buy orders at KRW1,095 in the afternoon. It was the first time since March 25 that the BOK was seen intervening.

Korea's Finance Ministry, which sets the country's foreign exchange policy, is closely watching the won and will counter any one-sided moves but isn't targeting a particular level, said Kim Ik-joo, director general of the ministry's International Finance Bureau.

"Capital is flowing into the local financial system with foreigners buying a lot of local shares as they focus more on positive factors. We are closely monitoring the currency market to make sure there aren't any rapid one-sided moves," Kim said.

The dollar ended trading at KRW1,096.7, down from KRW1,104.20 late Wednesday.

Bank Negara Malaysia, similarly, sold ringgit to slow its rise, two Kuala Lumpur dealers said, spotting dollar purchases by the central bank at MYR3.0250. The U.S. currency was at MYR3.0250 in late Asian trade, down from MYR3.0255 late Wednesday.

In Singapore, some traders said there was speculation that the central bank had been in the market, but intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore couldn't immediately be confirmed.

Dealers said banks known to be MAS agents bought U.S. dollars around S$1.2617 in the morning. But the Singapore dollar faced strong upward pressure throughout the trading session, with the U.S. currency falling to a record low of S$1.2592 late in the afternoon, down from S$1.2622 late Wednesday.

Thailand's central bank was suspected of buying $100 million to $200 million around THB30.24-THB30.27, traders said. The U.S. currency was last at THB30.25.

A record-high fixing for the yuan in the morning set a bullish tone for Asian currencies. The People's Bank of China set its dollar parity at CNY6.5564, the lowest ever and down from Wednesday's fixing of CNY6.5586.

The yuan, which ended trading at CNY6.5485 to the dollar in the onshore spot market, has risen 4.2% against since June, when China effectively ended its two-year currency peg and vowed to make the yuan more flexible. Other Asian central banks watch Beijing closely, and to varying degrees have also allowed their currencies to rise against the dollar.

China appeared to be under renewed pressure Thursday to move faster on the currency front at an informal meeting of finance ministers and central bankers from the Group of 20 industrial and developing nations held in the former Chinese capital of Nanjing.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner, in prepared remarks at the meeting, argued forcefully for flexible exchange rates, calling the mismatch between fixed and floating exchange rates "the most important problem to solve in the international monetary system today."

"This asymmetry in exchange rate policies creates a lot of tension," Geithner said. "It magnifies upward pressure on those emerging market exchange rates that are allowed to move and where capital accounts are much more open. It intensifies inflation risk in those emerging economies with undervalued exchange rates. And, finally, it generates protectionist pressures."

Geithner didn't mention the yuan in his prepared remarks, but there is little doubt his message was aimed at least in part at China.

French President Nicolas Sarkozy said the global currency system in its current form has fueled growing global imbalances. The world needs to move toward a more flexible exchange rate regime, he said.

China Vice Premier Wang Qishan said Beijing will work with others toward "a more equitable global monetary system" but avoided any reference to the yuan's exchange rate.

-By Arran Scott, Dow Jones Newswires; +65-6415-4042; arran.scott@dowjones.com

--Kanga Kong in Seoul, Phisanu Phromchanya in Bangkok, Esther Fung in Beijing, Christopher Wong in Singapore, Elffie Chew in Kuala Lumpur, and Aaron Back, Nathalie Boschat, Jean Yung and Shen Hong in Nanjing contributed to this article. [ 31-03-11 1022GMT ]

BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai economy won't suffer any significant impact from Japan's earthquake and tsunami and could benefit long-term as Japanese companies might further diversify their manufacturing bases overseas, Bank of Thailand Gov. Prasarn Trairatvorakul said Tuesday.

In the short-term, Thai exporters may see increased demand as the quake-stricken country would need to import more food and goods as it recovers, Prasarn told Dow Jones Newswires in an interview. However, he added that more exports aren't expected to substantially boost Thailand's overall shipments, just over 10% of which go to Japan.

Prasarn said the bank is still assessing the impact on foreign direct investment from Japan, but is maintaining its 2011 economic growth forecast at 3.0% to 5.0%.

Japan is the largest investor in Thailand in terms of FDI, and Southeast Asia's second-largest economy has become a regional manufacturing hub for many Japanese companies, including auto giants such as Toyota Motor Corp. (7203.TO), Mazda Motor Corp. (7261.TO), Mitsubishi Motors Corp. (7211.TO), Honda Motor Co. (7267.TO), and Nissan Motor Co. (7201.TO).

Japanese investors last year applied for tax privileges for 363 projects with a total investment value of THB104.42 billion ($3.43 billion), more than any other country, according to the Board of Investment.

On the downside, Thailand's tourism industry may suffer a decline in Japanese visitors in the near-term, said Prasarn. Japan was the third-largest source of tourists for Thailand last year, according to Kasikorn Research Center.

Prasarn said the Japan disaster will likely have a limited impact on Asia's growth as Japan's economy isn't a significant contributor to regional growth, though it will likely bolster commodity prices in the short-term.

He said a spike in remittances of Japanese yen in the wake of the disaster may push the yen's value higher in the short-run, but it's expected to depreciate in the long run as economic fundamentals weaken.

Inflation remains a major threat to Thailand's economy, even though it is still at a "manageable level," Prasarn said.

Thailand's consumer price index rose 2.87% in February from a year earlier. Core CPI, which excludes volatile energy and food prices, rose 1.45% from a year earlier, still within the central bank's 0.5% to 3.0% target.

Prasarn expects price pressures to accelerate when government measures to aid the cost of living expire later this year, and said there's a fair chance core inflation will temporarily breach the 3.0% level in the fourth quarter.

He said the Monetary Policy Committee will continue its rate normalization efforts to tackle inflation and rising inflation expectations, noting that gradual rate increase is preferred over an aggressive front-load tightening of 50 basis points.

"Judging from the two previous meetings, I think the majority of members wouldn't support the jump, it's not necessary," Prasarn said.

The MPC--which has raised its benchmark rate 125 basis points since last July, including a quarter percentage point increase last week--will consider the impact from the Japan disaster at its April 20 meeting, he said.

The central bank is aiming to raise interest rates until the output gap--the difference between Thailand's actual output and full potential output--is closed, he said.

"We want to achieve a rate that should not exert any bias on either growth or inflation," he said.

Although a lengthy period of negative real interest rates could adversely affect the economy and distort market mechanisms, it's not a key determining factor for raising rates, he said.

Prasarn said Thailand's trade account is expected to swing to a surplus in February, with January's $588 million deficit likely a one-off, caused by hefty gold imports.

A trade surplus of around $4 billion to $5 billion is expected this year, he said.

On the local currency, Prasarn said the Thai baht is currently at an appropriate level and moving in line with fundamentals.

While the central bank has intervened in the market "once in awhile", there is less need this year as the baht appears to be moving in a two-way direction, said Prasarn. The dollar fell by 10.6% against the baht last year, despite hefty central bank intervention, due mainly to massive capital inflows into Asia's emerging markets.

The Bank of Thailand is planning to further relax regulations to facilitate capital outflows to better balance the movement of capital flows, he said, without elaborating.

The bank stands ready to tighten restrictions on capital inflows, although the move isn't currently needed, said Prasarn.

 SINGAPORE, March 11 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso and the Thai baht fell against the dollar on Friday, extending losses after a powerful earthquake hit northeast Japan, triggering a 10-metre tsunami prompted investors to cut positions in the riskier currencies.

 Earlier China's stronger-than-expected output data alleviated investors' concerns over the health of the world's No. 2 economy after it reported weak February figures. 

 But news of the massive quake hit the yen and other Asian currencies. 

 "That is another reason to encourage a risk-off environment," said Pin Ru Tan, emerging markets currency and rates strategist at the Royal Bank of Scotland in Singapore.

 The yen extended losses against the dollar and the euro while Nikkei futures in Singapore tumbled more than 3 percent.

 Before the earthquake, Asian currencies cut some losses as China data reassured investors that Asia would continue to grow faster than developed markets.

 "The quake will prevent investors from buying Asian currencies more although Asia looks best in the longer term," said Jeong My-young, a currency strategist of Samsung Futures in Seoul.

 The peso weakened past 43.60 per dollar where the Philippine's central bank had been spotted selling dollars to check the currency's falls.

 Investors rushed to cover dollar-short positions after the quake.

 A Manila-based dealer said he has not seen dollar-sales by the central bank yet.

 The one-month dollar/won non-deliverable forward (NDF) rose to as high as 1,130 after the earthquake.

 Earlier, the spot won eased, but found strong support from exporters' demand for settlements and as dealers and corporates were wary of officials stepping into the market to support the won around 1,130 to the dollar. 

 "Inflation is the biggest issue now and (FX authorities) will probably sell dollars even when it gets close to 1,130," said a senior foreign bank dealer in Seoul.

 Dealers say South Korean authorities entered the market in February to keep a lid on the won, which has been bouncing around in a 1,104-1,134 range so far this year.

title: MONEY MARKETS-Short Thai swaps hit new 2-1/2 year highs
text:
HONG KONG, March 3 (Reuters) - Short-dated Thai interest rate swaps climbed to fresh 2-1/2 year highs on Thursday with yields set to rise more in coming weeks as the central bank tightens policy and on expected inflows into the local money market.

* One-year Thai IRS rose to 2.70 percent, their highest since December 2008. They have risen by about 90 basis points in slightly more than a month, pushing the spread between 10-year and one-year swaps to a five-month low of 170 bps.

* The flattening of the IRS curve over the past month has been mainly driven by a surge in front-end rates, which in turn has been triggered a washout of FX swap trades caused by the Bank of Thailand's intervention.

* Along with a steady stream of hawkish comments from the central bank, traders said paying in swaps is also from "kimchi funds", or Thai funds investing in Korean assets.

* At its peak in 2009, about $14 billion, or 30 percent of the entire Korean debt market, was owned by these funds, but their share has dwindled in recent months due to narrowing rate differentials between the two economies and after Seoul slapped a 15 percent withholding tax on debt investments last year.

* A lot of these maturing investments will flow back into Thailand and exchanged into baht around the second half of the year and the improved dollar liquidity in the markets would push up the floating leg of the swap fixing which is a synthetic rate implied from FX swaps, Credit Agricole strategists said.

* The Bank of Thailand has also turned hawkish in recent months, raising its benchmark interest rate by a quarter point to 2.25 percent on Jan. 12 following a similar increase in December. Another quarter point increase is expected next week.

* Six-month Thai baht fixings have rebounded this week to 2.43 percent, holding well above the central bank's main policy rate of 2.25 percent.

title: Asian Central Banks  Intervene  As  Currencies  Rise; Yuan At Record High
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Central banks in South Korea, Malaysia and Thailand intervened in foreign-exchange markets Thursday as Asian currencies surged against the dollar on optimism about the region's economic outlook, underscored by data showing the Chinese industrial sector expanded strongly in December.

Taiwan, meanwhile, unveiled measures to buttress its banking system against rapid movements in foreign capital, the latest Asian country to introduce stricter regulations to control the risks posed by so-called "hot money" flows.

The currency moves were exagerated by thin trading conditions with many investors away for year-end holidays. But traders said an upward trend for most Asian currencies appears set to continue, with China's decision to guide the yuan to a modern record high against the dollar cementing the bullish sentiment.

"People are making a bet that growth in emerging markets will still be on an uptrend and that currencies will continue with their appreciation," said Lum Choong Kuan, head of fixed income research at CIMB Group in Kuala Lumpur. "With the debt crisis in Europe and with the U.S. still showing protracted slow growth, investors will have no other place to put their money but here."

Capital has been flooding into Asia this year, helping to finance investments in one of the world's fastest-growing regions. But the influx of foreign money has raised concerns in Asian capitals about the perils of fast-moving capital flows, given the damage the region's economies suffered during the Asian financial crisis of the late 1990s, when a previous boom ended suddenly and foreigners rushed for the exits.

Fresh data Thursday from China, the powerhouse of the Asian economy, showed manufacturing growth eased slightly in December but was still at relatively high levels. The HSBC China Manufacturing Purchasing Managers Index, a gauge of nationwide manufacturing activity, fell to 54.4 in December from 55.3 in November; any reading above 50 indicates expansion.

Hongbin Qu, HSBC's chief economist for China, said that despite the moderation in the PMI inflation remains Beijing's top policy concern, rather than economic growth.

He expects China to take further tightening measures to curb inflation--which hit 5.1% in November--including additional modest interest rate hikes. China's central bank raised interest rates Dec. 25, its second hike in less than three months.

CIMB's Lum said central banks in emerging markets are looking at tightening monetary policy next year, which means interest-rate differentials between emerging markets and the developed economies of the U.S., Europe and Japan should grow wider. That leaves Asian central banks looking for ways to control inflows of capital chasing higher returns.

In Kuala Lumpur, traders said Malaysia's central bank was suspected of buying dollars to curb a rise in the ringgit, which hit a three-month high Thursday. Bank Negara Malaysia may have bought dollars around MYR3.0810-MYR3.0820, dealers said. The dollar was last at MYR3.0846.

Traders in Seoul said they suspected the Bank of Korea entered the market, buying more than $500 million at intervals around KRW1,135, KRW1,136, and KRW1,140. The dollar closed at KRW1,134.80, bringing the won's gains to 2.6% for the year.

In Bangkok, the dollar was last at THB30.15--down from THB30.16 late Wednesday--with suspected buying by the central bank around that level to limit the downside, two dealers said.

"I don't think the dollar/baht will move much on the final trading day of this year, especially with the central bank supporting the pair," one Bangkok-based dealer said.

In Taipei, which has been trying to temper gains in the New Taiwan dollar--a favorite among investors seeking exposure to China, given Taiwan's increasingly close economic ties to the mainland--the Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan) announced new measures to control capital flows.

Starting Saturday, local banks will have to set aside 90.00% of foreign investors' new deposits as reserves, a quantum leap from the current level of 9.775%.

The central bank also raised its benchmark interest rate by 12.5 basis points, the third hike this year as it seeks to normalize lending costs and cool a sizzling property market. Central bank Governor Perng Fai-nan said inflation will likely accelerate next year.

Also Thursday, Taiwan's financial regulator also said it will inspect banks' use of foreign funds to determine whether there has been speculative trading in the local currency. Earlier Thursday, the Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan) said it had found "unusual" trading strategies at a small number of banks.

"Over the past few days, a small number of authorized foreign-exchange banks have targeted specific times of the day to sell off large quantities of foreign exchange," the central bank said in a statement.

"Our inquiry has revealed that the funding for these transactions originates exclusively from the inward remittance made by certain foreign investors," the bank said, adding that it "asked the authorities concerned to probe into the final beneficiaries behind these foreign investors."

The central bank didn't name the banks in question or give details on the timing of the trades.

It's not unusual for Asian central banks to intervene in foreign exchange markets when volatility in their currencies rises. Many have taken regulatory steps in recent months to try to slow capital inflows and make their banking systems more resilient to movements in foreign funds.

On Wednesday, Indonesia's central bank said it would increase the amount of reserves commercial banks must hold at the central bank against foreign currency deposits, among others steps. Also Wednesday, South Korea said it would announce lower ceilings on banks' foreign-exchange forward positions in January.

For many countries, the main consideration has been to make sure their currencies don't rise so much that they hurt export industries. Still, stronger currencies would reduce the cost of imports, tempering inflationary pressures that are on the rise regionally on surging commodities prices. For that reason, many economists expect authorities to permit their currencies to rise further.

An official at the People's Bank of China Thursday echoed that sentiment, saying that a small, gradual appreciation in the yuan presents more benefits to the Chinese economy than costs.

In an article in the Financial News, Sheng Songcheng, director of the PBOC's Statistics and Analysis Department, said the yuan's rise against the dollar since the exchange rate was made more flexible has had only a small impact on employment and growth. At the same time, Sheng wrote, the yuan's gradual rise has cut import costs, reduced inflationary pressures and prompted Chinese companies to become more competitive.

The yuan has appreciated 3.4% since June 19, when China pledged to increase the currency's trading flexibility, effectively ending a two-year-long peg to the dollar.

The State Council, or China's Cabinet, has the final say on major policies such as yuan reform. But Sheng's article, which featured prominently in the central bank-run newspaper, may reflect growing confidence that Beijing can allow the yuan to rise further without severe consequences.

The dollar fell to a record low against the yuan Thursday after the PBOC, which tightly controls the currency, set the dollar/yuan parity rate at an all-time low of 6.6229, down from Wednesday's rate of 6.6247. It marked the eighth straight session that the central bank has set the parity rate lower.

In the over-the-counter market, the dollar was at CNY6.6008 around 0830 GMT, down from Wednesday's close of CNY6.6212. The dollar traded Thursday between CNY6.6000--the lowest intraday level since the yuan began regularly trading in 1994--and CNY6.6232.

The impact of yuan demand from bank customers was exaggerated by the thin year-end trading, one Shanghai-based trader at a local bank said.

"The market is rather one-sided right now," he said. "The yuan's gain today is definitely bigger than what people had anticipated."

Elsewhere, the U.S. currency also fell against its major rivals, as U.S. Treasury bond yields fell overnight following strong demand at a seven-year auction, again exaggerated by a thin market. The dollar slipped to a seven-week low of Y81.28 and a fresh all-time low of CHF0.9418.

The dollar also was weaker against its Australian and New Zealand counterparts: The Australian dollar surged to a fresh post-float high of $1.0197, and the Kiwi dollar rose to a high of $0.7691.

Many participants "dumped quite a few (U.S.) dollars," said Satoshi Tate, senior vice president of the forex division at Mizuho Corporate Bank.

-By Arran Scott, Dow Jones Newswires; +65-6415-4042; arran.scott@dowjones.com

BANGKOK (Dow Jones Newswires)--The Bank of Thailand wants to equip itself with various policy tools to ensure economic stability without hindering growth prospects, with a tax on foreign-exchange transactions one potential tool, BOT Gov. Prasarn Trairatvorakul said Wednesday.

"The best thing for us is to have a variety of policy tools and then be able to use a mixture of them in good proportion, hopefully with good timing too," Prasarn said in a group interview.

Referring to the tax on FX transactions, known as a "Tobin Tax," he said, "in our tool kit, it's one of the components."

If needed, the Tobin Tax could be introduced by emergency decree, requiring approval only from the Ministry of Finance and Cabinet, not the lengthy parliamentary process needed to draft legislation, Prasarn said.

With many countries in Asia facing similar problems from surging capital inflows, Prasarn said central bankers have talked of potential cooperation in curbing flows.

"If the situation called for it, if conditions called for it, there could be cooperation" among central banks to control inflows, he said.

BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Thailand wants to equip itself with various policy tools to ensure economic stability without hindering growth prospects, with a tax on foreign-exchange transactions one possibility, Governor Prasarn Trairatvorakul said Wednesday.

With many countries in Asia facing similar problems from surging capital inflows, Prasarn said central bankers have talked of potential cooperation.

"If the situation called for it, if conditions called for it, there could be cooperation" among central banks to control inflows, he said.

Given the bearish trend of the dollar and the U.S. economic outlook, the Bank of Thailand has been trimming the proportion of dollar assets in its reserves, and its reserve management team is seeking other types of assets that offer better yields and can cover the cost of the bank's liabilities, Prasarn said.

"That exercise has been started for sometime, not just by us but by everybody," the governor said.

The Thai central bank wants to increase yuan-denominated assets in its foreign reserves, but Prasarn said the Chinese government allows only a limited amount of qualified investors to invest in yuan, also known as renminbi.

It depends on "how proactively, how fast the Chinese government wants the renminbi to play a role in the international market," he said. "There's no sign they intend to do it in the near future, but in the medium term, in the longer term, that may be possible."

Members of the BOT's Monetary Policy Committee have made clear that they want to raise interest rates from the current abnormally low level, but the timing is important and the committee will weigh all relevant factors, Prasarn said. He gave no hints about the direction of monetary policy at the upcoming meeting Dec. 1.

Thailand's policy interest rate of 1.75% is quite low by regional standards, Prasarn said. But he noted that with massive inflows of capital from the West, partly inspired by U.S. quantitative easing moves, any rate hike would attract even more money and would be "like giving out benefits to undeserved investors."

"The MPC will look at these matters. We tend to take into account many facets of economic information," Prasarn said.

Most economists expect the central bank to once again stand pat next week, as recent data show growth slowing, while the baht is still showing a firmer tone and inflation remains manageable.

The MPC kept rates on hold at its last meeting in October amid mounting worries over the baht's rapid rise, after hiking by 25 basis points in each of its two previous meetings.

Prasarn said he sees no immediate threat of surging prices but said core inflation may still reach the upper end of the BOT's 0.5%-3.0% target range sometime next year.

He said any impact on inflation from recent floods--the country's worst in decades--will likely last for only three or four months.

The BOT is always on alert for asset bubbles forming, but despite economic growth of 9.3% in the first nine months of the year and massive capital inflows, the bank doesn't see any yet, Prasarn said.

The central bank recently tightened restrictions on housing loans worth THB10 million or less, a move which it says was a cautionary signal to the market about potential bubbles.

Prasarn said Thailand's economy has grown above trend in the first three quarters of the year and he expects the growth rate in the fourth quarter and next year to fall bcak to the country's normal trend of 3%-5%.

With export growth slowing, domestic demand is expected to play a larger role in economic growth, he said.

title: MONEY MARKETS-Thai swap rates fall as bond selloff spooks
text:
* Foreign selling in Thai bonds may trigger dollar shortage

 * Swaps decline may slow if Bank of Thailand adds dollars

 * Korea swaps ease after interest rate increase

 By Saikat Chatterjee

 HONG KONG, Nov 16 (Reuters) - Thai one-year swap rates fell to a five-month low on Tuesday on growing fears that foreign investors dumping their local bonds would trigger a shortage of dollars so close to the year end.

 Capital controls in Thailand and other Asian countries, have made offshore investors cautious on local markets. Foreign demand for Thai debt has cooled considerably since Bangkok reimposed a 15 percent withholding tax on offshore purchases on Oct. 13.

 As foreigners liquidate their positions and switch to dollars from baht, traders were concerned a scramble for dollars might push down the Thai currency in the forwards market and further weigh on swaps, since the floating leg of such contracts are determined by forwards. <THBFIX>.

 "Inflows have slowed to about 50 percent of what they used to be before the withholding taxes and people are taking profits on the long end fearing that liquidity would dry up before the year end," said a senior rates trader at a foreign bank in Bangkok.

 One-year swap contracts dropped by two basis points (bps) to 1.34 percent -- its lowest in late June -- taking its fall by 11 bps since last Friday as offshore receiving in swaps also took out some paid positions by local banks.

 Six month fixings were at 1.02 percent on Tuesday compared to 1.23 percent on Friday pressuring swap rates lower.

 Other traders said these concerns were overblown, pointing to the central bank's forward baht commitment book which has grown in recent weeks indicating it was still a net supplier of dollars in the forward market.

 They expect the Bank of Thailand, the country's central bank, to intervene in the currency markets to alleviate the dollar funding shortage if the bond selling by foreigners intensifies, in sharp contrast to the Philippines's central bank which artificially engineered a dollar shortage in its market earlier this month to break the peso's rally.

 Foreigners have sold a cumulative net 6 billion baht of bonds over the last week, latest data from the Thai bond market association showed and these selling pressures have exacerberated big price movements at a time when banks are winding down trading activities and client flows have slowed.

 In the cash market, 10-year yields <#THBMK=> extended their rise by six bps to 3.80 percent and five year yields popped above the 3 percent level -- a first in nearly three months as profit taking continued on the belly and the far end of the curve.

 In Seoul, swap rates eased after the central bank increased interest rates as widely expected by 25 bps, cooling speculation that the won's gains would draw the central bank's attention away from inflationary pressures. [ID:nTOE6AF01X]

 One-year contracts <KRWIRS> edged lower by three bps to 3.13 percent, moving further away from a three-month peak hit on Monday.

 In dollar funding markets, three month dollar rates in Singapore fell to 0.29 percent from 0.29112 percent on Monday, suggesting that LIBOR might be fixed lower later in the day.  (Editing by Kevin Plumberg)
