                               SHAREHOLDER UPDATE 
                            RELEASED 26 October 2010 
 
The financial markets in Asia continue to improve. However there remain a number 
of risks that could increase volatility in the medium term and impede growth. 
 
Symphony International Holdings Limited's ("SIHL" or the "Company") Net Asset 
Value ("NAV") increased from US$347,677,450 to US$410,190,151 between 30 June 
2010 and 30 September 2010, or from US$1.0278 to US$1.1981 per share. This 
increase is largely attributable to improving market valuations of our listed 
investments and appreciation of currencies in Singapore and Thailand, where 
SIHL's portfolio companies predominantly operate. SIHL's NAV per share increase 
of 16.6% in 3Q10 compared favorably with select indices such as MSCI AC World, 
MSCI AC Asia and MSCI Singapore, which increased by 13.8%, 10.3% and 8.1%, 
respectively. MSCI Thailand performed better in 3Q10 with an increase of 22.7%. 
 
PORTFOLIO SUMMARY 
 
SIHL's NAV was US$410.19 million at 30 September 2010 and consisted of 
investments in the following segments: 
 
Healthcare: US$43.41 million (10.6% of NAV) 
Hospitality: US$116.48 million (28.4% of NAV) 
Lifestyle: US$11.18 million (2.7% of NAV) 
Lifestyle / Real estate: US$123.88 million (30.2% of NAV) 
Temporary investments: US$115.25 million (28.1% of NAV). Temporary investments 
include cash and equivalents and are net of accounts receivable and payable 
 
SIHL's NAV performed better than selected indices since SIHL's initial public 
offering in August 2007 through 30 September 2010. SIHL NAV has outperformed the 
MSCI AC World, MSCI AC Asia, MSCI Thailand and MSCI Singapore indices by 51.9%, 
46.8%, 4.5% and 38.2%, respectively (Source: MSCI Inc., Company analysis). 
 
SIHL's share price at 30 September 2010 was US$0.68 representing a 43.2% 
discount to NAV. 
 
SIHL's NAV at 30 September 2010 consisted of listed investments (38.9% of NAV), 
unlisted investments (33.0% of NAV) and temporary investments (28.1% of NAV). 
Temporary investments include cash and equivalents and are net of accounts 
receivable and payable 
 
 
OVERVIEW 
 
SIHL's listed investments accounted for 38.9% of NAV at 30 September 2010, down 
from 53.7% at 30 June 2010 primarily due to the sale of shares of Parkway 
Holdings Limited ("Parkway"). On a per share basis, the value of SIHL's listed 
investments stood at US$0.466. Unlisted investments (including property) 
comprised a further 33.0% of SIHL's NAV (or US$0.395 per share), with the 
remaining 28.1% of NAV (or US$0.337 per share) being temporary investments. 
 
The Parkway exit during 3Q10 was SIHL's first realization and was made in 
response to a General Offer from Khazanah Nasional Berhad (the Malaysian 
government's investment vehicle) to privatize the company. This followed a 
bidding war for the company, which resulted in an exit price representing a 29% 
premium to the average price over a 6-month period prior to the initial offer. 
SIHL's investment in Parkway generated a 21.6% annualised return and a gain of 
US$26.6 million. 
 
Following the Parkway exit SIHL now has more than US$115 million temporary 
investments. Management continues to evaluate opportunities to deploy these 
funds in its areas of deal focus. 
 
SIHL's share price continued to trade at a discount to NAV during 3Q10. At 30 
September 2010, SIHL's share price was US$0.68, representing a discount to NAV 
of 43.2%. 
 
There has been an improvement in financial markets on account of a more 
favourable outlook for the global economy as fears over a 'double-dip' 
recession, credit worthiness of sovereign debt and fiscal sustainability abate. 
The International Monetary Fund ("IMF") announced the world economy expanded at 
an annual rate of about 5.25% during the first half of 2010 in its October 2010 
World Economic Outlook update, compared with an estimate of 5.00% in July. This 
growth was driven by a strong rebound in industrial production and trade on 
account of a surge in inventory and fixed investments. Asian economies in 
particular have been beneficiaries of the improved economic environment with 
output expanding above pre-crisis levels. The IMF estimates Emerging Asia 
(excludes developed Asian countries that include Japan, Australia and New 
Zealand) will grow at 9.2% in 2010 compared with 2.7% for developed economies. 
 
Despite a general consensus that the recovery is well on track, underlying risks 
remain elevated, particularly in developed economies. The US and Europe are 
expected to experience relatively sluggish growth compared with emerging and 
developing economies due to high unemployment, continued balance sheet 
reparation and large budget deficits. Under a renewed stress scenario, 
refinancing of sovereign and bank debt could be difficult given the diminished 
capability of many developed economies to use liquidity buffers to restore 
confidence. The stronger investor sentiment towards faster growing emerging and 
developing economies has led to strong capital inflows, particularly in Asia. 
 
There has been a strong appreciation in currencies and asset prices in most 
Asian countries. The relatively stronger economic position of Asian economies 
and expected long term interest rate differential compared with developed 
economies has attracted substantial capital. Thailand and Singapore, where 
SIHL's portfolio companies predominantly operate, have seen their currencies 
strengthen by 10.11% and 4.75% against the US dollar in the first three quarters 
of 2010. With strong capital inflows and robust domestic demand, there is 
concern that asset price bubbles are emerging. 
 
Export dependent Asian economies are looking to balance the negative impact of 
rising currencies while on the other hand managing inflationary pressures. 
Countries including Thailand, South Korea, China and the Philippines have 
intervened to slow currencies appreciating, either through capital controls or 
increasing foreign currency reserves. Where there has been previously clear 
policies of removing accommodative monetary policy to reduce inflationary 
pressures, it appears that central banks of Asian economies have paused in 
raising interest rates to hinder currencies from strengthening further. 
 
We remain optimistic on the outlook for Asian economies, such as Singapore and 
Thailand, but there remain potential risks that could increase volatility in 
financial markets and hinder growth. The balancing of capital inflows, 
appreciating currencies and inflationary pressures in Asia will be a key concern 
in 2011. 
 
 
PORTFOLIO DEVELOPMENTS 
Note: Portfolio companies are listed in the descending order of the total funds 
invested or committed. 
 
Minuet Ltd is a joint venture between SIHL and an established Thai partner for 
the development of a branded life-style residential and recreational development 
in Bangkok, Thailand. SIHL has a direct 49% interest in the venture, the maximum 
allowable under current regulations, but will be responsible for the design, 
development and execution of the project. 
 
Update: Advanced discussions with luxury resort operator Amanresorts to build 
the the first Aman club and villas are ongoing. 
 
The value of Minuet Ltd at 30 September 2010 was US$98.4 million based on an 
independent third party valuation at 30 June 2010. The change in value from 
US$91.7mn at 30 June 2010 is predominantly due to an appreciation in the value 
of the Thai Baht. 
 
 
Minor International Pcl ("MINT") is one of the largest hospitality and 
restaurant companies in the Asia Pacific region with 31 hotels and resorts 
totaling over 3,560 rooms under prominent brands such as the Four Seasons, 
Marriott, Anantara and others in Thailand, Vietnam, Maldives and South Africa. 
MINT also owns and operates 1,123 restaurants under The Pizza Company, 
Swensen's, Sizzler, Dairy Queen, Burger King, Thai Express and The Coffee Club. 
 
Following the restructuring / merger with the Minor Corporation Public Company 
Limited ("MINOR"), MINT's operations also include contract manufacturing and an 
international lifestyle consumer brand distribution business in Thailand 
focusing on fashion, cosmetics through retail, wholesale and direct marketing 
channels under brands that include Esprit, Bossini, Red Earth, Bloom, and 
Zwilling Henckels amongst others. 
 
Update: MINT's revenue and net income increased by 16.6% and 7.9%, respectively, 
in 1H10 year-over-year. The increase was primarily driven by a strong 
performance in 1Q10 from its hotel operations, continued growth of the 
restaurant business and contributions from the consolidation of Minor 
Corporation Pcl ("MINOR") businesses. 
 
MINT's hotel operations in Bangkok were particularly hard hit by the political 
unrest during the second quarter. Businesses located where the demonstrations 
were held effectively closed for two months. The Four Season's hotel in Bangkok 
had an occupancy rate of about 11% in 2Q10. 
 
The restaurant business continued to perform well driven by stronger same store 
sales and new equity and franchised outlets. Total system sales grew by 8% in 
1H10 and EBITDA margins increased from 15% to 16%. 
 
MINT successfully placed a 5-year debenture that was upsized 
from THB2 billion to THB2.5 billion on strong demand. The debenture carried a 
3.98% coupon and is rated 'A' by TRIS. The debenture was placed to refinance 
existing debt and provide additional liquidity. 
 
The management of MINT are targeting earnings growth of 20% per annum through 
acquisitions outside of Thailand, additional hotel and restaurant management 
agreements and sales of existing property inventory valued at THB6 billion. 
 
 
 
Parkway Life Real Estate Investment Trust ("P-REIT") invests in income 
generating healthcare-related properties in the Asia-Pacific region including

the buildings of Parkway's three Singapore hospitals, which are leased back to

Update: PREIT's gross revenue and property income increased by 15.3% and 14.5%

The strong growth is attributable to the full impact of eight properties

PREIT announced that for the fourth year of lease term for the Singapore

The outlook for PREIT continues to be positive given its substantial debt

Update: SG Land continues to generate stable performance from rental income on

SG Land was valued at fair value based on an independent third party valuation

title: EM ASIA  FX -Singapore dollar dips; consolidation before Bernanke
text:
* Sing dollar dips on US dollar short-covering

* Eyes on Bernanke, U.S. report on China FX

* Intervention from Thailand spotted

By Cheon Jong-woo

SEOUL, Oct 15 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar edged down against the dollar on Friday as investors covered dollar-short positions and dealers spotted Thai central bank intervention.

Asian currencies overall showed some consolidation with the South Korean won erasing most of its earlier losses before a speech by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke later in the day.

Bernanke's comments are unlikely to change expectations of further easing by the Fed to help fuel the world's top economy, which have helped lift Asian currencies.

"It is not a time for Bernanke to give another signal. He will confirm the Fed's existing stance, which will continue to support Asia," said Kim Jae-eun, an economist at Hyundai Securities in Seoul.

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> rose, recovering from suspected central bank intervention.

Market players are also keeping an eye on the U.S. Treasury Department's comments on China's currency practices later in the day. Before the report, spot yuan <CNY=CFXS> hit its highest the dollar since its landmark revaluation in July 2005. [ID:nTOE69E01X]

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> <SGD=D3> fell slightly against the U.S. dollar as investors covered U.S. dollar-short positions in thin trading before the weekend.

title: Thai PM: No Plan To Move To Exchange-Rate Targeting
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Thailand won't target a specific exchange rate for the baht even as the strength of the local currency, which is trading at a 13-year high, is hurting the country's vital export industry, Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva said in an interview Wednesday.

Abhisit said that the government instead would focus on helping sectors in the economy that are affected by the strong baht by providing better hedging tools for them through local policy banks.

"We'd rather target those affected sectors--maybe provide some help in terms of their ability to hedge currency risks better rather than trying to intervene in the market," Abhisit said in a joint interview with The Wall Street Journal and Dow Jones Newswires. "We don't think we should move to some kind of exchange-rate targeting."

Abhisit reiterated that any intervention by the Bank of Thailand, the country's central bank, is meant to stem excess currency volatility rather than achieve a particular level for the baht. The dollar fell below THB30 Tuesday for the first time since July 1997.

Abhisit said Thailand's robust economy, including gross domestic product growth of around 8% this year, export growth of around 30% and a healthy current account surplus, point to a stronger baht even as Thai exporters are complaining about their ability to maintain their competitiveness.

Referring to global efforts to tame the foreign-exchange market as countries around the world struggle to hold their soaring currencies down in what has come to be termed as a currency war, Abhisit said that any realignment of currency levels must look at economic fundamentals first. He called on the Group of 20 world's largest economies, or G-20, to reach some kind of coordination on the currency front.

Speaking of China's move toward a more flexible exchange rate for the yuan, he said the movement in the Chinese currency since June when China dropped the yuan's almost two-year de facto peg to the dollar hasn't been as great as expected.

"People may have exaggerated how much can be achieved" through a more flexible yuan, he said without elaborating.

Turning to the domestic political scene, Abhisit said that recent violence wasn't conducive to a climate of reconciliation that must be achieved before a national election is held.

Thai investigators Wednesday said they found evidence of additional bomb-making materials at the site of a blast that killed four people at a suburban Bangkok apartment building a day earlier, heightening fears that opposition Red Shirt activists are stockpiling explosives to stage violent attacks.

Thailand's government had just extended for three months on Tuesday a long-running state of emergency banning political activity in the capital, citing the continuing threat from bombing campaigns. A series of explosions have rattled Bangkok since the military put down a mammoth antigovernment demonstration in the city in May.

Some 91 people were killed in clashes between security forces and the Red Shirt protesters, who were demanding new elections and campaigning for the return of ousted populist leader Thaksin Shinawatra. Thaksin was overthrown in a military coup four years ago and is now living overseas to escape imprisonment on a corruption conviction--a charge he denies and calls politically motivated.

Abhisit's military-backed government, whose term ends at the end of 2011, has so far resisted calls for early elections. Abhisit didn't rule out the possibility of the elections taking place before the end of the current term, but he stressed that political stability must be achieved first.

"A democratic election has to be free and peaceful," he said. "I don't want to win in a bloody election. I'd rather lose in a peaceful one."

Turning to the controversial case of alleged Russian arms dealer Viktor Bout, whose extradition to the U.S. has created tensions between the three countries, the prime minister said Thailand hopes officials in the U.S. and Russia can come to an agreement.

"We don't want to upset our relations with either the U.S. or Russia," Abhisit said.

"We'd rather the two parties will talk to each other rather than make demands from us."

title: UPDATE: Thai MOF Ready To Support  Central Bank  In Managing Baht
text:
(Adds more comments from minister and background)

BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Thailand's Finance Minister Korn Chatikavanij said Monday that the ministry is ready to support the Bank of Thailand's actions in managing the baht's volatility.

He reiterated that a decision to intervene in the foreign exchange market to curb the baht's pace of appreciation rests solely with the central bank.

Korn said that the global foreign exchange situation will be among key issues to be discussed at the upcoming G-20 meeting in November, which could result in guidance on sustaining stability among global currencies.

He added that Japan's attempt to curb the rise of yen has proven to be ineffective because it did so alone.

"Thailand is a small country. The result (of intervention by the Bank of Thailand) won't be different," he told reporters.

He said a solution to the foreign exchange issue needs the cooperation of various countries.

Japan intervened in currency markets in mid-September, buying dollars against the yen for the first time in six years to stem the yen's rise after it hit a 15-year high against the greenback.

The baht has risen more than 9% in the year-to-date against the dollar in the wake of fund inflows across Asia. The dollar was at THB30.16-THB30.18 early Monday, compared with THB30.20 late Friday.

title: Asian Central Banks Keep Up  Intervention  As Dollar Weakens
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The central banks of South Korea, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia were suspected of intervening in forex exchange markets Wednesday to contain gains in their currencies, but analysts say the continued weakness of the U.S. dollar means Asian units should extend their rallies.

The wave of intervention, which has continued across the region for most of this year, hasn't been strong enough to reverse the strengthening trend in Asian currencies, as many policymakers are allowing their currencies to rise slowly to limit imported inflation.

That stance was reinforced after China, the top trading partner for key Asian countries, said in June it would let the yuan strengthen against the dollar -- meaning that other Asian countries can maintain their export competitiveness against China even if their currencies rise a bit.

On Wednesday the Thai baht and the Malaysian ringgit hit their highest levels since the 1997 Asian currency crisis, while the Singapore dollar rose to an all-time high.

In a note to investors, Standard Chartered analysts said global dollar weakness, closely tied to market expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve may launch another round of quantitative easing by boosting purchases of U.S. securities, is likely to keep Asian and other emerging market currencies in strong demand. In recent days, the central banks of countries ranging from Russia to Colombia have been suspected of intervening in forex markets because of dollar weakness.

"The prospect of another round of quantitative easing by the Fed in the fourth quarter of 2010 should be seen as broadly negative for the dollar," StanChart said.

Intervention Wednesday was particularly significant in Indonesia, which has attracted a surge of inflows thanks to its solid economic performance and high interest rates.

Jakarta-based traders said the central bank was suspected of buying around $50 million at IDR8,950 in early trade, and then an unspecified amount at IDR8,945. Neither move managed to send the rupiah lower, however, and the dollar last traded at IDR8,935.

"The dollar is still under pressure against the rupiah, as investors' appetite for riskier assets is improving," one dealer in Singapore said.

Intervention by Bank Indonesia has continued for the past two years, but is now likely at its highest volume ever. Bank Indonesia's forex reserves rose 9% in the first three weeks of September, a huge amount even by East Asian standards, mostly due to dollar-buying in forex markets.

The Bank of Thailand and Monetary Authority of Singapore also were suspected of early intervention moves Wednesday. In Bangkok, traders said the BOT was spotted intervening at THB30.50 against the dollar, but the baht rose further and last traded at THB30.46.

In Singapore, the MAS managed to weaken the local dollar slightly after it soared to an all-time high at S$1.3152 against the greenback. The Singapore dollar last traded at S$1.3170.

Seoul traders said intervention by the Bank of Korea was relatively mild, as the Korean won is still some distance away from two-year highs hit earlier this year. The dollar last traded at KRW1,141, having fallen as low as KRW1,139 earlier in the day.

title: SE Asia Stocks-Indonesia at record high, Bangkok recovers
text:
* Thai central bank comments on baht policy soothe fears

* Inflows push Indonesia to record high

* Singapore recovers, around 2-year highs

By Viparat Jantraprap

BANGKOK, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Thai stocks ended flat on Wednesday, erasing losses after comments by the central bank that helped soothe fears about the reimposition of capital controls, and Indonesia returned from a long holiday to hit a record high.

Bank of Thailand Governor Tarisa Watanagase said the central bank would curb volatility in the baht but saw no need to alter its present policy towards the currency. [ID:nSGE68E0AT]

Exporters and investors had worried that strength in the baht <THB=> would hurt Thai competitiveness, but the baht turned lower on Wednesday, in line with other Asian currencies, after news that the Bank of Japan had intervened to cap the yen's gains.

"The Bank of Thailand's comments eased earlier prevailing concerns about baht measures. Buying interest came across the board after that," said Pichai Lertsupongkij, head of sales at Thanachart Securities.

Thailand's benchmark stock index <.SETI> ended down 0.03 percent, but before the Bank of Thailand's comment it had fallen as much as 2.05 percent to its lowest level since Aug. 31, extending a 1.7 percent fall on Tuesday as investors remembered tough capital controls that caused a stock market slump in 2006.

Foreigners sold a net $8.7 million of stocks on Wednesday, smaller than the net selling of $58.9 million of the previous session, according to the stock exchange.

Telecom stocks were among the gainers, with top mobile phone operator Advanced Info Service up 1.5 percent.

National carrier Thai Airways ended down 0.7 percent, earlier plunging 9 percent to a seven-week low after it offered new stock worth $488 million at a discount of 14.5 percent to the market, cheaper than analysts had expected. [ID:nSGE68E051]

Asian stocks in general were higher, with Tokyo <.N225> rising more than 2 percent after Japan intervened in the foreign exchange market for the first time in six years to stem economic damage from the surging yen, pushing its currency sharply lower.

MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> eked out a small 0.45 percent gain by 0957 GMT.

Singapore <.FTSTI> rose 0.6 percent, reversing its loss of the previous day and hovering around two-year highs, while the Philippines <.PSI> edged up 0.13 percent to close to the record high set on Tuesday.

Malaysia <.KLSE> eased 0.1 percent ahead of a holiday on Thursday, still moving around 2-½ year high, and Vietnam <.VNI> inched down 0.06 percent.

Indonesia's benchmark stock index <.JKSE> finished 3.9 percent higher, climbing to 3,359.99 at one point, topping the previous record set on Sept. 7 before the market shut for a long holiday.

Car seller PT Astra International , the biggest firm by market capitalisation, and state lender PT Bank Mandiri , both surged to a record high, rising 6.73 percent and 7.14 percent respectively.

Edwin Sebayang, head of research at PT Bhakti Securities in Jakarta, attributed the market rally to foreign buying and Indonesia's low interest rate environment.

"On the banking and auto move, market chatter says since this morning that most people in the market expect the central bank will continue to hold rates next month, which created excitement as Astra, and the banks jumped," he said.

The Jakarta rally made the market Asia's second-best performer this year, ahead of number three the Philippines and Thailand, the fourth best.

Indonesia recorded inflows of $242.6 million on the session, the biggest daily net inflows in almost two years. Inflows rose to $1.86 billion in the year, compared with $936 million in full year 2009, Thomson Reuters data showed. (Additional reporting by Janeman Latul in Jakarta) (Editing by Alan Raybould)

title: Bank Of  Thailand Intervenes  In  FX  Market To Support Dollar -Dealers
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Thailandintervened in the foreign exchange market Wednesday to help support the U.S. dollar, though its foray into the market was no more aggressive than usual, dealers said.

The central bank's intervention helped raise the greenback to an intrasession high of THB30.85, they said.

"At first we thought the dollar/baht would have been in rangetrade, kind of biased downward. But the intervention by the BOJ (Bank of Japan) changed the direction," says one dealer, who declined to be named.

The move prompted other market players to join in on short-covering.

Officials from the Bank of Thailand weren't immediately available to comment.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Yuan jumps on fixing; baht rally capped by c.bank
text:
* Won gains with stocks as intervention fears grow

* Dollar/yuan NDFs dip, implying slower yuan rise

* Baht inches up but capped again by c.bank

By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, Sept 10 (Reuters) - The Chinese yuan jumped on Friday after the central bank surprised the market by fixing the mid-point at its highest since the landmark revaluation in 2005, while the Bank of Thailandintervened again to rein in the baht.

Asian stocks rose to a four-month high as some investors were inspired by positive U.S. and Japanese economic data to pick out bargains, with the shift to riskier assets weighing on the yen. [ID:nTOE68902E]

Trading was thinned by public holidays in Singapore, Indonesia, Malysia and the Philippines.

YUAN

The Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> gained nearly a quarter of a percent to 6.7669 per dollar after the PBOC set the mid-point at 6.7625 -- the highest since the landmark revaluation in 2005, despite the dollar's broad strength.

"The move took the market by shock. I think it's more political in nature," said an NDF trader in Hong Kong.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner will present the Obama administration's latest view of what the United States should do to press China to reform its currency practices at a hearing next week. [ID:nN09225757]

But analysts reckon the central bank may be trying to introduce two-way fluctuations in the yuan to deter market speculation.

The yuan has gained 0.8 percent since the central bank scrapped a dollar peg on June 19.

Offshore dollar/yuan non-delierable forwards <CNYNDFOR=> tumbled, with the benchmark one-year NDFs <CNY1YNDFOR=> falling to 6.6850 from 6.6950 at Thursday's close.

The implied 12-month yuan appreciation fell to 1.16 percent from 1.29 percent due to the sharply higher yuan mid-point.

BAHT

The Thai baht <THB=> inched up to 30.80 per dollar but traders suspected dollar-buying intervention by the central bank to temper its appreciation.

The baht was off a 13-year peak at 30.77 hit on Thursday.

"The baht's strength is still prompting the central bank to come in, but its job is being made relatively easy this morning by holidays in Singapore, Malaysia and some other Asian countries," said a dealer in Bangkok.

"The baht should range in 30.80-90 today, but it has room to appreciate further as long as the dollar outlook remains weak," added the dealer.

The baht has gained 8 percent against the dollar so far this year.

WON

The won <KRW=> gained a fifth of a percent to 1,164.7 per dollar, the highest since Aug 10, as local stocks rose after stronger-than-expected U.S. economic data boosted investors' tolerance for risk.

Traders were growing more cautious as the South Korean authorities, worried about the stronger won's impact on export companies, could step in and buy dollars.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Singapore dlr hits record peak; won at 1-mth high
text:
* Singapore dollar strength sparks intervention

* Thai baht at 13-year high, checked by c.bank

* Won hits 1-month high despite rates on hold

By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, Sept 9 (Reuters) - Increased fund inflows propelled the Singapore dollar to a record high on Thursday, while the South Korean won hit a one-month high despite the central bank's surprise decision to keep interest rates steady.

The U.S. dollar approached 15-year lows against the yen as traders bet that Japanese authorities are not yet ready to intervene, while the Australian dollar hit a four-month high on solid Australian jobs data. [ID:nTOE68805C]

SINGAPORE DOLLAR

The Singapore dollar <SGD=D3> hits record high of 1.3411 per U.S. dollar, buoyed by fund inflows and a broadly weaker U.S. dollar.

Traders suspected the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the central bank, intervened to buy U.S. dollars to contain the local unit's strength.

"The Singapore dollar looks to the rest of the region, and MAS is on the bid," a trader said.

The Singapore dollar, which is up 4.7 percent against the U.S. dollar this year, has been boosted by the country's solid economic growth.

Foreigners have been buying bonds and stocks, but the inflows are not as strong as elsewhere in the region, analysts say.

BAHT

The Thai baht <THB=> jumped 0.6 percent to a new 13-year high of around 30.83 per dollar, sparking fresh dollar-buying intervention by the Bank of Thailand, traders said.

Increasing capital inflows into Thai bonds and stocks in the past week have pushed the baht up 1 percent against the dollar.

"The baht dipped below 31.00 this morning and has so far risen to an intraday high of 30.83 before stabilising now at 30.87-89. Falling Thai bond yields today suggest that most of the funds are parked in local debt," a dealer at a foreign bank said.

The baht has appreciated 8.0 percent this year, the third-best Asian performer after yen and ringgit.

WON

The won hit a fresh one-month high despite the central bank's surprise decision to leave interest rates on hold.

Investors reduced dollar-long positions, helping the won strengthen to as firm as 1,166.0, the strongest since Aug 10.

title: Asia  FX Intervention : Singapore, Korea In; Japan On Standby
text:
Asian authorities stepped up the fight to curb their strong currencies Friday. Singapore intervened in the foreign-exchange market for the first time in months and Korea resumed its intervention after a two-week break, while Japan is increasingly signaling it might enter the market for the first time in six years.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore sold the Singapore dollar after it hit an all-time high, "to smooth the U.S. dollar's fall," said a person familiar with the central bank's thinking. The Bank of Korea sold won for dollars, traders said, although the greenback remained weaker on the day.

In Japan, people familiar with the matter said the government is more determined than ever to act against any unusually rapid yen rise--but would find it hard to intervene if the gains are gradual.

The developments in Asia, which is bouncing back strongly this year from the global economic downturn, highlight the difficulties policymakers face as their strengthening currencies threaten to crimp the growth in exports that is fueling the rebound.

Some Asian central banks, such as those in Taiwan and Thailand, are in the market regularly, but all of the region's interventions are aimed at merely smoothing their currencies' gains, not reversing the dollar's seemingly inexorable glide downward.

Asian currencies have been rising against the dollar this year, first as the global recovery encouraged investors to buy riskier assets and, more recently, as signs of a sharp U.S. slowdown have increased bets that the Federal Reserve will ease policy further. This decreases the attractiveness of dollar assets.

The Singapore central bank defended the greenback after it fell to a record low S$1.3425, the person told Dow Jones Newswires. The MAS, which formally targets a gradual rise in the local currency, hadn't intervened since April, despite the Singapore dollar's rise of more than 4% against the greenback so far this year.

The MAS "will continue to smooth the U.S. dollar's fall for now, but this is a regional issue with widespread weakness for the U.S. currency," the person said. The currencies of Singapore's trading partners will probably keep rising for now, in which case the MAS's role will be "to make sure that the rise is orderly."

This indicates Singapore won't fight hard against a rise in the local dollar as long as it's broadly in line with its Asian peers.

Similarly, if Japan's starts selling yen, the aim would be to curb rapid moves, not to reverse the market trend, several people familiar with the matter told Dow Jones.

"If there are no 'excessive fluctuations' in exchange rates, and if the dollar falls against the yen only gradually, it would be very difficult to act," one of the people said. "It's unthinkable that (the government) will fight back against the market trend."

The ministry views a move by the dollar of several yen a day as worryingly volatile, people familiar with currency policy have said recently.

The yen is up some 10% this year, but Tokyo is strongly signaling that if it returns to the market it won't repeat its last intervention binge, when it sold Y35 trillion over the 15 months to March 2004.

Adding to Japan's caution are the prospects that the U.S. Fed will whittle away what little interest-rate gap remains between the U.S. and Japan, as well as the fact that it would be a Herculean task to move the global foreign-exchange market, where volume is now $4 trillion a day.

Still, recent tough talk on the yen from Prime Minister Naoto Kan and Finance Minister Yoshihiko Noda is intended to show that Japan is on heightened alert against sharp market moves, the people said. Kan and Noda have both vowed "decisive" action when needed, language that in the past has denoted intervention.

"The weight carried by that word is significantly heavy," one of the people said. Another said it shows the government is "resolutely prepared" for intervention.

Korea's central bank, one of Asia's serial interveners, stepped back into the market Friday after two weeks on the sidelines, buying an estimated $300 million-$400 million as the dollar fell to around KRW1,176, Seoul traders said. But there too the aim was to slow the won's rise, not reverse it.

The dollar was at KRW1,177.6 late Friday, still well below its level of KRW1,180.5 late Thursday. The won is down for the year after falling sharply in the first half, but has rebounded more than 8% from its late-May low.

Asian currency strategies differ, of course. In Malaysia, where the ringgit has led this year's rise among developing-economy currencies with a 10% climb, there has been no recent sign of the central bank, which views the rise as reflecting solid economic fundamentals. The Bank of Thailand, by contrast, has intervened regularly to try to smooth out the baht's ascent, at 7% so far this year.

The outlier is China.

While other Asian countries are enduring strong currencies or warily attempting to temper the rise, Beijing is hardly letting the yuan budge. China ended the yuan's two year peg to the dollar in mid-June but has hardly let the local unit appreciate since then.

In fact, thanks to the central bank, the tightly controlled yuan has given up half of the modest gains it made in the first seven weeks of the new freer policy.

title: WSJA(9/3) Stronger Asian  Currencies  Stir Worry
text:
(From THE WALL STREET JOURNAL ASIA) 
   By Piyarat Setthasiriphaiboon 

Thailand and Singapore sent signals of concern Thursday about the rising value of their currencies, in the latest indication of how fluctuating foreign-exchange markets are pressuring Asian nations.

Officials in Thailand held an emergency meeting in Bangkok to discuss the baht, which last week hit a two-year high against the U.S. dollar. The Thai government is concerned about the strength of the baht and has asked the central bank to closely monitor its movement, Finance Minister Korn Chatikavanij said Thursday after the meeting.

In Singapore, a person familiar with the matter said the central bank is poised to intervene in the currency market if the Singapore dollar approaches its record high again. The U.S. dollar traded near its lowest point of the year against the Singapore dollar Thursday before regaining some ground. For the year, the U.S. dollar is down about 4.2% against the Singapore dollar.

The U.S. dollar has also fallen against other Asian currencies. Year-to-date it is down 8.7% against Malaysia's ringgit, 4.4% against Indonesia's rupiah and 3.4% against the Philippine peso as of Thursday.

The dollar is down 6.6% against the Thai baht this year.

The gains in currencies of developing Asian nations have come as investors park money in economies with strong growth prospects amid worries about the global economy. Many investors are also betting the countries will face continued pressure to raise interest rates to keep inflation under control, a move that often drives currencies higher.

Also, projections that the Federal Reserve will have to loosen policy further to stimulate growth is weighing on the U.S. currency.

Asian authorities worry that a quick rise in local currencies can be destabilizing. A stronger currency can also make a country's exports less competitive.

The U.S. dollar's fall hasn't been as extreme against other Asian currencies as it has against Japan's. The greenback is down nearly 10% this year against the yen and is trading around 15-year lows. Still, volatility over the past year has led countries such as the Philippines, Thailand and Singapore to intervene.

In Thailand, Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva called the urgent meeting Thursday with economic ministers and Bank of Thailand Gov. Tarisa Watanagase to discuss the baht's rise.

After the meeting, Mr. Korn, the finance minister, said there has been no speculation detected in the foreign-exchange market but said the Bank of Thailand already has the necessary tools to cope with such a situation should it arise.

"The government is concerned about the strong baht," the finance minister said. "[But] overall, we haven't seen that the current strong baht has caused a problem. . . . Still-growing exports reflects that exporters are still competitive."

Ms. Tarisa also played down the impact after the meeting. "The current baht situation is not worrisome. . . . Inflows so far are the short-term flows into the debt and stock markets, but it is still unclear whether it is speculation," the central-bank governor said.

Commerce Minister Porntiva Nakasai recently urged the central bank to do more to stabilize the baht, blaming its rise against the dollar for a sharp slowdown in export growth in July. On Thursday, Ms. Porntiva told reporters that the robust baht has hurt some exporters, especially in the food and agricultural sectors, but the ministry is working on measures to reduce the impact. The ministry, however, is maintaining its target for export growth of 20% this year, she said.

In Singapore, the person familiar with the matter said the Monetary Authority of Singapore is prepared to let the currency rise against the U.S. dollar in the short to medium term if the move is orderly and in line with other Asian currencies. The central bank is "on intervention watch," the person said.

This suggests intervention could be imminent for the MAS, which is thought to have stayed out of the market since April. The U.S. dollar was quoted at 1.3485 Singapore dollars in late Asian trading, up from the day's low of S$1.3454 but still close to its July 15, 2008, all-time low of S$1.3438.

In recent days the Singapore dollar has been about 2% above the midpoint of the undisclosed trade-weighted band in which the MAS guides the currency, the person said. "Anything above that will trigger action."

The central bank uses the exchange rate rather than interest rates as its main policy tool because Singapore's trade flows dwarf the island's domestic economy.

title: Thai Fin Min:  Central Bank  May Raise Rates 25 Bps This Year -CNBC
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Thailand's central bank may hike its policy interest rate by 25 basis points before the year ends to cool the domestic economy, Finance Minister Korn Chatikavanij said Monday.

"If there are signs that the global economy is going to turn negative in a significant manner, that may be reason for the Bank of Thailand maybe to have another increase and then wait and see from there on," Korn told CNBC television.

title: MONEY TALKS: Thai Govt Should Steer Clear Of Strong Baht
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai government is getting jittery about the strength of the baht. It had better get used to it.

With interest rates on an upward trajectory and capital inflows showing no signs of easing, the Thai currency is heading in only one direction: up. Don't expect a reversal anytime soon.

Commerce Minister Porntiva Nakasai on Thursday blamed the strong baht for a sharp slowdown in export growth in July. Southeast Asia's second-largest economy recorded a 20.6% on-year rise in exports to $15.56 billion in July, but it was well off the 46.3% on-year surge to a historical high of $18.04 billion in June.

Capital inflows to the bond market alone suggest the baht will remain well bid this year, keeping export growth in check. Central bank data show net capital inflow into bonds was around THB20 billion ($634.5 million) in each of June and July, and was close to THB50 billion year-to-date.

Brisk exports have been a boon for the Thai economy. Gross domestic product data for the second quarter is due for release Monday, with the median forecast of 11 economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires tipping an expansion of 7.9% on-year, from a 15-year high of 12% in the first quarter. Needless to say the still-strong economy, surging stocks and rising interest rates are luring capital into the country and driving up the currency.

The baht is up 4.8% so far this year; the dollar was recently fetching THB31.55.

Porntiva warned the U.S. dollar may drop as low as THB30.00 this year; this is possible but the more likely scenario based on recent moves is for a gradual track down toward THB31.00 as the central bank continues to intervene to limit sharp volatility, and a renewed push below that in 2011.

The minister's pleas for the Bank of Thailand to intervene more aggressively to cap the baht will likely fall on deaf ears, with the central bank repeatedly insisting the currency's been moving in line with regional peers.

Bank of Thailand Governor Tarisa Watanagase earlier this week argued that the baht wasn't too strong in the context of gains made against the dollar by regional counterparts. The governor also said the baht's strength hasn't impeded Thailand's competitiveness.

It's clear the central bank, which says it intervenes to smooth out volatility, appears averse to ramp up its efforts to reverse the trend.

The BOT would rather prefer exporters take advantage of other tools, including hedging, to cope with foreign exchange pain.

The market has already been prepared for a deceleration in export growth in the second half due to an easing need for foreign companies to increase inventories which were wound down during the global financial crisis, and a softening of demand as the pace of the economic recovery slows in some regions, particularly the U.S.

The central bank seems to know how to play its hand in the currency market. The government should stand aside.

text:
* Won, peso lead most Asian FX higher against dollar

 * Intervention seen in Korea, Thailand, the Philippines

 * Dlr/yuan NDFs off 2-week low amid policy uncertainty

 By Kevin Yao

 SINGAPORE, Aug 3 (Reuters) - The South Korean won and Philippine peso hit 11-week highs on Tuesday as upbeat U.S. factory data and European bank earnings buoyed risk-taking, but their gains were curtained by official intervention.

 Asian stocks rose to their highest in nearly three months and turned positive for the year, while the dollar hovered near a three-month low against a basket of currencies <.DXY>.

 Earnings from big European banks BNP Paribas  and HSBC  topped forecasts as bad debt fell sharply.

U.S. manufacturing grew in July for a 12th straight month, an industry report showed on Monday. Although growth slowed, it was still stronger than had been expected. [ID:nN02170396]

 WON

 The won <KRW=> gained as much as percent 1,159.9 per dollar, the highest since May 19, but later pared most gains as the authorities were spotted buying dollars, causing some investors to cover dollar-short positions.

 Still, traders expect the won <KRW=> to rise further.    "Intervention from the beginning prompt some offshore players to buy dollars, preventing the won's further gains. But it is unlikely to get back to the 1,170 levels after breaking through major resistance lines," said a foreign bank dealer.

 Another foreign bank dealer said: "It is difficult to buy the won further as the authorities may -- be able to intervene more easily once exporters deals are completed."

 Foreign investors bought a net 132.7 billion won worth of stocks on the main exchange, helping the benchmark KOSIP <.KS11> rise nearly 0.5 percent.

 PESO

 Dollar/peso NDFs fell across the curve as hedge funds and other offshore investors were seen dumping dollars, particularly in short tenors.

 "Offshore investors expect lower spot rates," said a NDF trader.

 The most liquid one-month dollar/peso NDFs <PHP1MNDFOR=> hit a 2-½   month low at 45.32 from 45.39 late on Monday, while one-month onshore forwards <PHP1M=> fell to 45.365 from 45.496.

 The onshore/offshore spread narrowed to 45 points from 106 points on Monday.

 Spot peso <PHP=> gained 0.4 percent to 45.13 to the dollar, the highest in 11 weeks, but it later pulled back to 45.20 as traders spotted dollar-buying intervention by the central bank.

 YUAN

 Dollar/yuan NDFs <CNYNDFOR=> dropped to a two-week low but later rebounded slightly as uncertainty over China's yuan policy kept markets trading within an established range.

 "People are more willing to take risk but there are still no signs China will speed up appreciation in the yuan," said a trader at an Asian bank in Hong Kong.

 He said activity remains thin and driven by trade-related hedging rather than speculation.

 One-year NDFs bounced to 6.6744 from two-week low of 6.6560 in early trade and from late-Monday's 6.6645 to price in 12-month yuan appreciation of 1.47 percent.

 The one-year NDF has fluctuated in a range of yuan appreciation between 1.3 percent and 1.9 percent since late-June.

 BAHT

 The Thai baht <THB=> gained slightly to 32.15 per dollar, with some traders seeing signs of Bank of Thailand bids for dollars at 32.18.

 "The BOT is on the bid side at around 32.18/19 but the volume is still thin. If the current trend drags on, the baht could gradually appreciate until the BOT's next policy rate review on Aug. 25 when it may raise rates again," said a dealer in Bangkok.

text:
DAEJEON, South Korea (Dow Jones)--Thai Finance Minister Korn Chatikavanij said Monday that the Bank of Thailand's policy interest rate could go up to 2% this year, depending on the country's economic growth.

"If recovery continues at this pace, it's possible, " Korn told Dow Jones Newswires on the sidelines of the "Asia 21" conference here.

The government recently upped Thailand's 2010 growth forecast to 5.5%, while others--including the International Monetary Fund--aim even higher.

Korn said an upside surprise is more likely than the opposite, as investment, exports and other sectors are likely to come in stronger than forecast. Exports in particular should grow 14%-15% this year, he said.

Separately, Korn told Reuters he would be surprised if the Bank of Thailand doesn't raise its policy rate this week. The rate stands at 1.25% ahead of the central bank's Monetary Policy Committee meeting Wednesday.

Thai inflation, which rose 0.26% on-month in June and 3.3% on-year, is "minor," Korn said: "There's no asset bubble in Thailand."

But the fact that Thailand now lags most of its neighbors in raising interest rates and taking other tightening steps may up the pressure on the central bank, he said.

"On its own it shouldn't be the reason for (a rate hike), but the fact that a number of Asian economies have increased rates probably means" the Bank of Thailand will feel pressure to follow suit, he said. The notion of being tardy "might give some discomfort to those who want rates to be raised."

Even a hike wouldn't hurt Thailand's growth prospects, Korn said. But he did identify several other risks.

"One is how the economies of trading partners perform," given the slow rebound in the U.S. and Europe. "And the second issue is related to domestic politics."

Anti-government protests this spring paralyzed Bangkok for several months until authorities launched a bloody crackdown in May. Some fear the long standoff could damage Thailand's appeal to tourists and investors.

"It's a risk," Korn said. "We won't deny" that the political unrest could have "significantly impacted" the Thai economy.

"Unless we find a way of resolving differences," the country is at risk of "repeating this conflict in the future," he said. "The global community will have no reason to have confidence in us."

Elections "almost certainly" won't be held this year, but "sometime next year," Korn said.

On currencies, Korn said the baht "fairly reflects the fundamentals of the economy." The dollar was at 32.36 baht as of 0815 GMT Monday, a gain of 3.24% for the Thai unit against the dollar this year.

While the Bank of Thailand has been known to intervene in currency markets, Korn noted that the country's exports are thriving because "our products are now competitive"--and not, by implication, because the currency is artificially held below its true value.

title: FX  ASIA: Asia Reserves Creep Up, Countries Look To Diversify
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asia's foreign exchange reserves rose 1% in June from the previous month, bouncing back after a steep drop in May, as Asian central banks bought more U.S. dollars to cap gains in local currencies.

The rise, an indication that the fast-growing region keeps attracting capital inflows despite concerns of a global economic slowdown, highlights the dilemma faced by Asian authorities as they look for ways to reduce their exposure to U.S. Treasurys--as China appears to be doing on a small scale, by stepping up its purchases of Japanese bonds.

Reserves held by 11 key Asian central banks, excluding China's, amounted to US$2.803 trillion at the end of June, up from US$2.776 trillion at the end of May, but remained just below an all-time hit in April, according to calculations by Dow Jones Newswires.

Reserve accumulation in June came as the euro remained essentially steady against the dollar--following a 7.5% drop in May--and minor reserve currencies like the yen and the British pound posted significant gains, boosting the dollar value of securities denominated in those currencies.

The yen and the pound together are estimated to account for around 8% of central bank reserves in developing countries, on average, compared with almost 30% for the euro. However, speculation over increased central bank interest in these currencies increased this week after news that China poured twice as much money into Japanese government bonds in the first four months of 2010 than its record full-year purchases in 2005.

This move underscores a willingness of some Asian countries to diversify their reserves into currencies other than the greenback and the battered euro, at a time when countries from Thailand to South Korea intervene to keep their currencies down and protect the competitive edge of their exporters. In recent years, this diversification has been done predominantly by purchasing euro-denominated securities.

Analysts say the dollar's role as paramount reserve currency remains safe, as the yen and the pound present drawbacks that should stop them from becoming major challengers, including uncertain valuation prospects since Japan is looking for a weaker currency and the U.K. faces a dire fiscal picture.

Still, a small, slow increase in yen allocations going forward is possible, said Tim Condon, chief Asian economist at ING Bank, noting that yields on U.S. Treasurys and top euro bonds have fallen towards the low levels of Japanese government bonds, removing a key obstacle that has made yen holdings unattractive for years.

"If G-3 rates remain in this sort of low level convergence, then Japanese bonds will be relatively more attractive, and holdings of Japanese bonds should rise," Condon added.

International Monetary Fund data show the yen has never accounted for more than 9% of global official reserves -- well below the 87% peak hit by the dollar in 1976, and its 61.5% share in the first quarter this year -- while the pound has been below the 5% mark since 1974.

China, which releases its reserves data on a quarterly basis, reported US$2.447 trillion in reserves at the end of March and is expected to announce second-quarter figures in the next few days.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Won, ringgit lead Asia gains; rupiah up on Moody's
text:
* Won up 2.6 pct vs dlr, biggest pct gain in 14 months

* Ringgit hits near 2-mth high

* Authorities seen intervening to check currency gains

By Cheon Jong-woo

SEOUL, June 21 (Reuters) - China's vow to allow more yuan flexibility boosted Asian currencies on Monday with the won appreciating the most in 14 months as the plan is seen bolstering demand in Asia's second-biggest economy and lifted risk appetite.

Indonesia's rupiah found further support after Moody's Investors Service raised the country's rating outlook.

Foreign exchange authorities in Asia were spotted intervening to check gains, but the currencies are expected to rise further, dealers and analysts said.

"Until we get risk off and the yuan flips above 6.83 again, Asian currencies will continue to rise," a currency dealer in Kuala Lumpur said.

Spot yuan strengthened to 6.8015 to the dollar, compared with Friday's close of 6.8262, even after the People's Bank of China set Monday's mid-point <CNY=SAEC> unchanged at 6.8275 before trading started.

On Saturday, China said it would gradually make the yuan's exchange rate more flexible, indicating it was ready to break a 23-month-old U.S. dollar peg that had come under intense fire.

The move eased tension with the West ahead of a summit of the Group of 20 countries this week, encouraging investors to snap up riskier assets.

(For more on China's currency, see [ID:nSGE65I02M])

WON

The South Korean won <KRW=> posted its biggest daily percentage gain against the dollar in nearly 14 months as China's vow to allow more yuan flexibility boosted risk appetite.

The won found further support from exporters' demand for settlements, which prompted investors to clear dollar-long positions to cut losses, although the foreign exchange authorities were spotted to curb its strength.

The currency ended local trade up 2.61 percent at 1,172.0 per dollar from Friday's domestic close <KRW=KFTC> of 1,202.6.

The percentage gain was the biggest since a 4.58 percent rise on April 30, 2009.

"Support from the yuan's news was stronger than expected. The authorities tried to curb the won's strength around the end of local trade, but the intervention was not strong enough," said a foreign bank dealer.

Seoul shares <.KS11> closed up 1.62 percent with foreign investors buying a net 293.0 billion won worth of stocks on the main exchange.

RINGGIT

The Malaysian ringgit added gains to hit a near two-month high, tracking its Asian peers after China's pledge over the weekend to allow more yuan flexibility.

The ringgit rose as much as 2.31 percent to 3.1780 per dollar, strongest since April 27.

"China's move boosts all Asian currencies. I think USD/MYR may head to this year's low of 3.17, maybe over a course of a week," says a dealer in Kuala Lumpur.

RUPIAH

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> rose as Moody's lifted the country's rating outlook to positive from stable, praising its stability and the effectiveness of its fiscal and monetary policies. [ID:nTOE65K03M]

The rupiah was up 0.91 percent to 9,005 per dollar.

The currency is expected to rise further on the brighter outlook for the economy, but market players remain cautious over intervention by the central bank to curb its strength.

"The Indonesian economy fundamentally is in good shape," said a foreign bank dealer in Jakarta. "I want to check 9,000, the last strong support, when Bank Indonesia keeps intervening to protect rapid volatility movements. If it breaks through the level, definitely rupiah will go to 8,900."

BAHT

The Thai baht <THB=> tracked stronger Asian currencies, gaining more than a third of a percent to a near-six-week high of 32.28-30 per dollar after China's move.

"The baht's tone is strong but the Bank of Thailand is actively intervening to hold it at 32.30. If the baht cannot be stabilised at this level, it might firm to as far as 32.00 later," a trader in Bangkok said.

A second trader said dollar selling pressure in early trade came mostly from foreign investors while Thai exporters held back to assess the trend. Dollar/baht was bid at 32.26 against 32.38 late on Friday. The baht has gained 3.29 percent so far this year.

YUAN

Market players are keen to sell dollar/yuan NDFs even with the slight bounce from the lows after the PBOC kept the yuan's mid-point flat, prompting some short-covering in early trade, dealers in Hong Kong said.

Large selling interest was seen on any move up in NDFs <CNYNDFOR=>, with U.S. banks and hedge funds doing the bulk of the selling for now. Trading was concentrated on the one-month and the one-year tenors, but overall volume was not too large.

"Though the pace of the selling has declined sharply from last week, people are still expecting an eventual move on the yuan in the next 1-2 weeks," said a senior NDF trader at a broker in Hong Kong.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Won, ringgit jump on EU plan, baht capped by c.bank
text:
* Massive EU, IMF emergency package revives confidence

* Won, ringgit lead Asian rally as risk appetite recovers

* Baht's strength sparks official intervention

* Dollar/yuan NDFs jump but investors cautious

By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, May 10 (Reuters) - The South Korean won and Malaysian ringgit jumped over 2 percent each on Monday after the European Union and IMF unveiled a massive $1 trillion package to help stave off a debt crisis in the euro zone.

Thailand's central bank was seen intervening in the market to slow the baht's rise.

The euro <EUR=> rallied and Asian stocks rose as investors bought back riskier assets, hopinh the emergency rescue package would stabilise world financial markets and prevent Greece's debt crisis from spreading. [ID:nSGE64802Q]

WON

The won <KRW=> closed up nearly 2.1 percent at 1,132.1 per dollar, the biggest percentage gain since April 30, 2009.

Foreign investors were not spotted buying dollars despite selling local stocks, traders said.

"Everybody is looking for dollar-short positions and the won is more likely to rise further, given the market sentiment," said a local bank dealer.

Seoul shares <.KS11> were up 1.8 percent in late trade.

Meanwhile, dollar/won NDFs <KRWNDFOR=> tumbled across tenors as investors unloaded riskier assets.

One-month NDFs fell to 1,129.1 from 1,155.9 late on Friday, when the most liquid NDFs hit a three-month high at 1,170.

"The market is awaiting details of the EU bailout plan, but generally risk is back on," says a Singapore-based NDF trader.

RINGGIT

The ringgit <MYR=> jumped to 3.2015 per dollar, rebounding sharply from six-week low on Friday.

"The ringgit is boosted by improved sentiment, which makes dollar/Asians heavy this morning," said a trader in Kuala Lumpur.

On the daily chart, the slow stochastics points to near-term gains in ringgit, which has rebounded from being oversold against the dollar.

One-month dollar/ringgit NDFs <MYR1MNDFOR=> fell to 3.1910 from 3.2725 late on Friday.

BAHT

The Thai baht <THB=> gained almost 0.7 percent to 32.11 per dollar, prompting Bank of Thailandintervention to curb and smooth its gains, dealers said.

"Its agents were spotted in the market buying dollars at around 32.23, its highest level today. The Bank of Thailand tried to smooth its volatility," said a Bangkok-based trader.

The baht has appreciated 3.4 percent against the dollar so far this year despite domestic political turbulence.

Thai Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva demanded that anti-government protesters respond by Monday to his offer of an early election, running out of patience after attacks that killed two police officers at the weekend. [ID:nSGE64901U].

YUAN

Dollar/yuan non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) tumbled, relinquishing some gains from a rally over the previous two sessions to 8-month highs.

But traders say the market remained concerned by euro zone debt problems, with little impetus for NDFs to drop further near term.

"China may still want to monitor such a complicated problem before deciding on any new policy moves," said a trader at a European bank in Shanghai.

One-year dollar/yuan NDFs <CNY1YNDFOR=> fell to 6.6680, pricing in 2.38 percent appreciation of the yuan in 12 months, compared with 6.7110 at Friday's close, or a 1.73 percent gain, and 6.7700 at Friday's high, for a rise of only 0.84 percent.

The spot yuan <CNY=CFXS> remained fixed near 6.83 per dollar, but investors expect the authorities to abandon the dollar-peg later this year to allow currency gains to help fight inflation. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

SINGAPORE, March 2 (Reuters) - The South Korean won rose on Tuesday as investors turned back to riskier assets, while the Thai baht jumped in tandem with local stocks as investors reacted positively to a court ruling on former Prime Minister Thaksin.

Asian shares rose for a third straight session, lending some support to regional currencies, although investors' sentiment remain fragile amid doubts over a quick solution to Greece's debt problems, which weighed on the euro. [IDnSGE62103Y].

Sterling fell, staying under pressure after hitting a 10-month low the previous day, while the Australian dollar slipped, giving back earlier gains made after an interest rate rise by Australia's central bank. [ID:nTOE62105A]

The Aussie had initially climbed after the Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates by 25 basis points to 4.0 percent and flagged further hikes ahead.

 The won <KRW=> gained 1 percent to 1,148.6 per dollar --
the highest in nearly a week -- as foreign investors snapped up


local stocks, but dollar/won NDFs were rangebound as offshore players remained cautious.

South Korean markets were shut on Monday for holiday.

"It seems the market is taking on some risk today, so dollar/won is sold down," said a Singapore-based trader.

Seoul shares <.KS11> rose just over 1 percent as foreigners bought a net 72.5 billion won worth of stocks.

Data showing Korean exports per working day soared to a 17-month peak in February also supported sentiment, traders said.

One-month NDFs <KRW1MNDFOR=> was confined between 1,152 and 1,162 in slow trade.

The baht rose as far as 32.72 per dollar, despite suspected official intervention to temper its strength.

"We believe the Bank of Thailand entered the market at around 32.80 but its limited efforts could not halt the rally. The baht is benefiting from more capital inflows to Thai stocks," a Bangkok-based dealer said.

A second trader also believed the central bank might have intervened, attributing baht gains to market relief that the court ruling on Friday had not triggered any violent reaction from his supporters [ID:nSGE61P02B].

But the rupiah <IDR=> bucked the firm trend in Asia.

The high-yielding unit fell half of a percent to 9,295 per dollar as some local corporates bought dollars to pay for their imports.

Most corporates had fulfiled their month-end settlements, but some had held off dollar buying in anticipation for lower dollar/rupiah, traders said.

Rupiah rose to 9,250 on Monday as investors bought the unit ahead of a government bond auction on Tuesday.

text:
* Dollar strength weighs on ringgit, baht and peso

* Charts suggest peso is near strong support

* Yuan rises further in non-deliverable forwards

By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, Dec 23 (Reuters) - The Malaysian ringgit and Thai baht fell to multi-week lows on Wednesday as the dollar held broadly firm, while the Chinese yuan inched up in offshore forwards trading to extend gains from the previous day.

The U.S. dollar rose to a two-month peak against the yen <JPY=> and stayed firm against the euro <EUR=>.

The dollar was buoyed by data showing the biggest rise in existing home sales in November in nearly three years, fuelling market speculation that the Federal Reserve may start to tighten monetary policy before either the European Central Bank or the Bank of Japan. [ID:nSGE5BM03B]

RINGGIT

The ringgit <MYR=> eased to 3.442 per dollar to match an eight-week low on Tuesday, but found support at that level from local exporter sales of dollars to take it to 3.4375.

The currency has been testing its 100-day moving average of 3.44 this week and some traders expect it to make a decisive break through the support level to reach 3.45 next month.

"We see a 70 percent chance it will reach there in January. Dollar/ringgit is being held back by exporters currently," said a Kuala Lumpur-based trader.

The ringgit has lost almost 2 percent in the past month.

One-month dollar/ringgit NDFs <MYR1MNDFOR=> edged up to 3.4366, virtually at par with the spot.

PESO

The peso <PHP=> eased to 46.59 per dollar, but the losses were mitigated by fresh remittance inflows in the run up to the Christmas and New Year holidays.

"The onshore market is still seeing remittance inflows. At the same time, most banks onshore are likely to convert earnings on foreign assets and foreign subsidiaries back into peso at year-end," said a dealer in Manila.

The peso has lost 1 percent this month.

On the daily chart, the peso has been supported by the 55-day moving average near 46.70, and the chance of testing 47, or the 38.2 percent retracement of its three-month rally from early September, looked slim, traders said.

YUAN

Dollar/yuan NDFs <CNYNDFOR=> dropped further after Tuesday's plunge, the biggest in a day this year.

One-year NDFs fell slightly to 6.644 at 0612 GMT compared with Tuesday's close of 6.6500. The one-year dropped 0.7 percent on Tuesday.

A trader said mainly U.S. names and hedge funds had sold NDFs on Tuesday. Chinese names only joined the selling late in the Asian day.

The spot yuan <CNY=CFXS> was steady at 6.8283 per dollar on Wednesday.

"I really don't think the drop yesterday was mainly because of rate-rise expectations. People often make use of this timing, when everyone steps back," said a Hong Kong-based NDF trader.

BAHT

The baht <THB=> hit a one-month low of 33.35 per dollar in thin early trade, prompting suspected intervention to support the currency by the Bank of Thailand.

"We are probably seeing the December effect as everyone tries to close year-end positions. The dollar strength is broadly supported by positive U.S. data and the baht (will) simply track Asian currencies moving in the 33.20-40 range between now and the New Year," a trader in Bangkok said. text:
* Peso leads Asia rally, rises to 2-week high

* Korean won up, renewed foreign interest in won assets

* Baht extends gains in thin trade ahead of king's birthday

By Vithoon Amorn

BANGKOK, Dec 2 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso and South Korean won led the Asian currency rally on Wednesday as investors gradually resumed buying of risky assets, with concerns easing over Dubai's debt problems that dimmed dollar's safe-haven allure and boosted the yen and gold.

But the yen <JPY=> fell 0.28 percent against a defensive dollar to 86.97, far below its 14-year high of 84.82 last week, as investors weighed steps taken by Bank of Japan on Tuesday to attack deflationary pressures that left many disappointed [ID:nT181057].

The dollar index <.DXY> fell to 74.41 from 74.46 late on Tuesday but well above its recent 15-mth low of 74.14.

PESO

The Philippine peso <PHP=> rallied 0.75 percent to a two-week high of 46.50 per dollar from a Tuesday close of 46.86, despite intervention by the central bank early in the day to curb gains.

"BSP is in the market, seen buying dollars at around 46.80-60. Volume is normal in mostly one-way trade dominated by dollar sellers," a trader in Manila said.

Dealers said the broad dollar weakness and inflows of remittances sent by Filipino workers abroad lifted the peso. They believed the central bank is pursuing a policy of trying to keep peso in a broad 46.00-49.00 range.

The central bank has been suspected of reacting to recent peso rallies by trying to restrain the currency at 46.45 and 46.25. Peso has gained about 2.17 percent so far this year.

WON

The South Korean won <KRW=> extended gains, tracking stocks and a revival in appetite for won assets. Although investors grew more cautious over possible dollar-buying intervention by the foreign exchange authorities.

Some suspected the authorities of absorbing dollars to cap the gains. The currency was quoted at 1,153.8 per dollar, compared with its domestic close <KRW=KFTC> of 1,161.1 on Tuesday.

"Foreigners are buying local stocks, supporting the won, but its gains would be limited by the authorities' smoothing operations," said a bank dealer.

The Korean Composite Stock Price Index <.KS11> closed up 1.4 percent at its highest level in a week and nearly recovered losses suffered on fears sparked by the Dubai debt woes. [ID:nSEO175445]

BAHT

The Thai baht <THB=> was among Asian currencies firming against the dollar, rising to a one-week high of 33.15 from 33.18 late on Tuesday.

"The market should be very thin today as we are in a holiday mood, which will keep the baht in a narrow range tracking bullish Asian currencies," a trader in Bangkok said.

Dealers did not detect any Bank of Thailandintervention but said the thin volume would have made it easy for the central bank to push baht back to 33.20 if it wanted to.

Thailand is celebrating King Bhumibol Adulyadej's 82nd birthday over the next two weeks. Monday is a public holiday. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: 2nd UPDATE: Asian Central Banks  Intervene  To Limit Dollar's Slide
text:
(Adds Korean intervention and updates various levels.)


 
   By David Roman 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The Philippines, Thailand, Singapore and South Korea appeared to sell their currencies Thursday, fending off the dollar's slide that threatens their export-oriented economies. But the interventions were small, reflecting a view that Asian authorities are powerless in halting a broad sell-off in the U.S. currency.

Japanese Finance Minister Hirohisa Fujii, meanwhile, expressed concern about a rapid rise in the yen, which soared to a 14-year high against the dollar. He said "now is the time to be vigilant" and repeated he would consider action against any "abnormal" moves in the exchange rate--though he didn't characterize Thursday's move as such.

Asian central banks, with the exception of Japan, have intervened in foreign exchange markets frequently in recent months trying to temper gains in the currencies driven by the swooning dollar. But officials have indicated that they can do little to turn around the trend, given the causes of the U.S. currency's weakness derive from the Federal Reserve's super-easy monetary policy.

Traders said Asian authorities would likely continue to do what they can to curb gains in their currencies, which have also benefited from the region's fast economic recovery from last year's global financial crisis.

"The (falling) dollar trend is the number one reason" that keeps Asian central banks intervening, said Sean Callow, a forex strategist with Westpac. He added that such intervention is likely to continue as long as the dollar remains under pressure.

The dollar took a heavy pounding overnight, with its value against a trade-weighted basket of six major currencies dropping to a 15-month low, and the euro surging nearly two cents, cracking above $1.51.

The Philippine central bank bought between $10 million and $50 million around PHP46.65 to the dollar, as the greenback hovered close to a one-month low against the Philippine peso, according to local traders. At 0531 GMT, the dollar was trading at PHP46.72.

In Thailand, traders said the central bank likely intervened as the dollar fell to a fresh 17-month low against the Thai baht. The dollar last traded at THB33.08, compared with THB33.17-THB33.18 late Wednesday.

"Players are well aware of the bearish tone of the dollar....The dollar-baht may slip through 33.00 near term," said one dealer, adding that the (Thai) central bank is unlikely to try and reverse the tide.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened in the foreign exchange market to support the U.S. dollar, two people familiar with the situation said. One person said the central bank intervened around S$1.3797. He added that the central bank will continue supporting the greenback if needed.

In early trading, the U.S. dollar was quoted as low as S$1.3774 and was last trading at S$1.3799.

In South Korea, the local authorities were suspected of buying an undetermined amount of dollars at around KRW1,153, a trader said. The dollar last traded at KRW1,154.

Against the yen, the dollar last traded at Y86.55, off an intra-day low of Y86.27.

Masafumi Yamamoto, a currency strategist with Royal Bank of Scotland, said Japanese authorities are now more likely to step into the market to curb the yen's rise, after the government last week announced that Japan is in deflation.

"A stronger yen will hurt Japanese stocks, which is bad for the government's approval rate," Yamamoto said. "And a stronger yen will also worsen deflation."

Yamamoto added that Japan probably needs to consult with its key trade partners, like the U.S., if it intends to make such a move.

"For now, what we will be watching is whether the government's script on the currency market will change," he said.

-By David Roman, Dow Jones Newswires, 65 6415 4045, david.roman@dowjones.com

(Piyarat Setthasiriphaiboon in Bangkok, Cris Larano in Manila, Costas Paris and P.R. Venkat in Singapore, and Takashi Nakamichi and Takashi Mochizuki in Tokyo contributed to this story.) [ 26-11-09 0545GMT ]

* Peso spot rises 0.7 pct, NDF/onshore spreads widen

* Asian currencies ride on broad dollar weakness

* Vietnam devalues dong, 1-year NDFs imply 13 pct dong fall

By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso led Asian currencies higher on Wednesday against a broadly weaker dollar, while Vietnam's central bank surprised the market by announcing its third currency devaluation since mid-2008.

The dollar fell to its lowest in seven weeks against the Japanese yen, while the Australian dollar rose after a central banker made upbeat comments on the economy. [ID:nT352975]

PESO

The peso <PHP=> gained almost 0.7 percent to 46.75 to the dolla as investors took comfort from data which showed a narrowing trade deficit in September. [ID:nMAN516448]

"The peso is getting a boost on that early news," said a Manila-based dealer, adding that offshore players could be more aggressive in selling dollars given that non-deliverable forwards have been at a discount versus onshore forwards.

Dollar/peso NDFs <PHPNDFOR=> moved lower across the curve while some traders see heavier selling at 1-year tenor.

Three-month dollar/peso NDFs eased to 47.04, implying a 0.6 percent peso fall. Meanwhile, onshore forwards with the same tenor <PHP3M=> eased to 47.183, pricing in a 0.9 percent peso fall.

title: UPDATE:Thai  Central Bank  Consistently  Intervened  In  FX  Market
text:
(Adds minister's comments about meeting with central bank regularly to discuss exchange rate situation, central bank governor's comment on baht)

BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Finance Minister Korn Chatikavanij said Friday that the Bank of Thailand has consistently intervened in the foreign exchange market in the past several months to ensure that the baht's pace of appreciation is gradual.

He told reporters that he was satisfied with the central bank's foreign exchange management in the current environment, adding that it is worthwhile to engage in intervention to support Thailand's competitiveness.

As intervention comes at a cost, it is crucial to weigh the action's worthiness and its effectiveness in shoring up the country's competitiveness, Korn said.

In order to prevent an excessive rise in baht money supply, the central bank has to sterilize the intervention by issuing massive amounts of bonds to mop up extra liquidity caused by its action in the foreign exchange market.

"When it comes to the point that the intervention isn't worth doing so anymore then we will try and figure out some other things," he said.

Korn said he meets with the Bank of Thailand at least once a week to discuss the exchange rate situation.

The central bank's governor, Tarisa Watanagase, said Friday that the baht has appreciated around 4% against the dollar so far this year, a pace that is around the midpoint of those of regional currencies.

Last week, Korn told Dow Jones Newswires that the central bank has bought $15 billion so far this year to curb the local currency's rise.
