   By Nopparat Chaichalearmmongkol 
 

BANGKOK--Thailand's central bank left interest rates unchanged Wednesday despite concerns over a slowdown in economic activity as the country mourns the death of King Bhumibol Adulyadej.

The Bank of Thailand's monetary policy committee voted unanimously to leave the one-day repurchase rate untouched at 1.5% for the 12th consecutive meeting.

The bank's decision was in line with the views of 16 economists polled by The Wall Street Journal. Most analysts played down the recent lull in activity as a short-term phenomenon that won't affect an underlying recovery in the economy, especially in exports and imports.

Following the death of the monarch on Oct. 13, the junta-installed government requested the country suspend all festive activities for one month and declared a one-year mourning period.

The bank has taken a cautious stance on policy, arguing that rates are already sufficiently supportive of the economy. The BOT is also seen wanting to maintain policy ammunition should the global economy weaken or if central bank decisions elsewhere, including a possible rate increase in the U.S., affect the local currency or capital flows.

The Thai central bank last cut rates in April 2015.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Strong yuan supports Asia  FX ; baht down on weaker growth
text:
* PBOC's yuan fixing biggest rise since Nov. 2
    * Thai Q4 q/q growth below forecast, recovery still fragile
    * Taiwan dollar near six-week high on inflows

 (Adds text, updates prices)
    By Jongwoo Cheon
    SINGAPORE, Feb 15 (Reuters) - Most emerging Asian currencies
rose on Monday after China's central bank set its daily yuan
guidance rate sharply firmer, easing concerns over risks of
devaluation, and as regional stock markets clawed back some of
their recent heavy losses.
    Thailand's baht, however, fell as quarterly
economic growth in the last three months of 2015 came in
slightly weaker than expected. 
    The yuan jumped more than 1 percent to 6.4900 per
dollar - its firmest this year - as the People's Bank of China
set its daily midpoint 0.3 percent stronger before the market
open. It was the official fixing's biggest rise since Nov. 2.
 
    The Taiwan dollar hit a near six-week high,
tracking the renminbi's strength. The Malaysian ringgit 
rose after oil prices on Friday jumped more than 10 percent.
    China's exports and imports in January fell more than
expected, but emerging Asian currencies focused more on
Beijing's stabilisation efforts for now, analysts said.
 
    In an interview over the weekend, PBOC Governor Zhou
Xiaochuan said there was no basis for the yuan to keep falling,
and China would keep it stable versus a basket of currencies
while allowing greater volatility against the U.S. dollar.
    "The weak export growth could add more speculation to CNY
weakness," said Nordea Markets' senior analyst Amy Yuan Zhuang
in Singapore, referring to the yuan.
    "But I still believe that Zhou Xiaochuan's comments during
the weekend and today's strong fixing rate helped alleviating
some of the pressure on the CNY, at least temporarily. And so
the same for Asia FX." 
    
    BAHT
    The baht slid as traders unwound bullish bets on growing
caution over possible intervention by the central bank to stem
its appreciation.
    Thailand's economy grew 0.8 percent in October-December last
year from the previous three months on a seasonally-adjusted
basis, less than the 1.0 percent in July-September and the 0.9
percent expected in a Reuters poll.
    Government bond prices fell, adding to pressure on the
currency.
    
    TAIWAN DOLLAR
    The Taiwan dollar rose as much as 1.4 percent to 33.052 per
the U.S. dollar, its strongest since Jan. 6.
    The island's currency found further support from demand from
foreign financial institutions as businesses reopened after a
week-long break for the Lunar New Year holidays.
    The central bank has not been spotted buying the U.S. Dollar
to stem strength in the Taiwan dollar yet, traders said, but
caution over intervention remained.
    
    RINGGIT
    The ringgit advanced 1 percent in thin trading as a rebound
in crude prices eased concerns over Malaysia's falling oil and
gas revenues.
    The Malaysian currency found further support from demand
against the neighbouring Singapore dollar.

title: Investors Sour on Southeast Asia's Growth Plans
text:
Governments in Southeast Asia in the past several weeks have accelerated plans to boost growth and prop up markets amid worries about the spillover of China's slowdown.

But investors aren't convinced. In August and September combined, equity outflows from Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand quickened at the fastest pace since the start of the year, according to data from EPFR Global.

In September alone, those countries announced programs that range from injecting cash into a fund used to buy stocks, to more actively intervening in currency markets. On Monday, Indonesia revealed facets of a new economic stimulus package, which will be detailed more fully in the near future.

Instead of reassuring investors, though, the moves left many skeptical about the effectiveness of stimulus.

"Boosting stock markets does not mean you boost domestic consumption and wealth," said Jalil Rasheed, investment director for Southeast Asian markets at Invesco Ltd.

The plans follow spending announcements made earlier in the year, as regional economies continue to face gloomy Chinese economic data and the prospect of higher interest rates in the U.S. 

One problem is that governments appear to be recycling old measures that didn't work well the first time.

Malaysia, for example, last month announced that it would give 20 billion ringgit ($4.6 billion) to a state-managed investment fund called ValueCap , which would buy some of the country's worst-hit stocks. Prime Minister Najib Razak also urged other quasi-independent state firms with overseas operations to cash in those investments and reinvest in Malaysia.

The move recalls 2008 when Mr. Najib, then-deputy prime minister, announced government investment in Malaysian stocks through the same fund. The investments, worth about $1 billion, helped lift the local exchange out of a seven-month malaise but failed to lead to any lasting recovery.

Meanwhile, Malaysia remains in a rut: Its economy grew 5% on year in the second quarter, the slowest pace since 2013. The country's main stock index has fallen around 7.5% since the beginning of the year and the ringgit has slumped nearly 30% against the U.S. dollar in that time.

Other investors are wary that governments may not follow through on promised economic reforms.

On Monday, Indonesia's Finance Minister Bambang Brojonegoro announced plans to offer lower interest-rate loans to labor intensive small- and medium-size businesses as part of a future economic package. Officials didn't specify how big the stimulus spending would be or other planned programs. That follows moves last month to eliminate some 89 burdensome regulations , among other measures.

But "Indonesia has been a victim of this where policies are announced and revoked, during which time much damage has been done to stock market," said Invesco's Mr. Rasheed, whose firm manages $780 billion globally.

Foreign direct investment in Indonesia fell 2% in the first half of 2015 from a year earlier and economic growth has slipped to a six-year low. Stocks are down nearly 20% this year, Asia's worst performers, while the rupiah is down 18% against the U.S. dollar.

To support the rupiah, the central bank announced last week it would begin the unusual step of intervening in the foreign-exchange forwards market, which is signaling that investors expect the currency to continue weakening. That would be in addition what appears to be regular spot-market interventions.

In Thailand, where second-quarter growth stalled to 2.8% on year and stocks are down nearly 10% this year, the government in September announced a nearly $4 billion economic stimulus package for small- and medium-size businesses ("http://www.wsj.com/articles/how-thailand-plans-to-jump-start-its-economy-1443759023"), which includes interest-free loans and cash injections.

While the current government is eager to build more infrastructure, too, Thailand's finance ministry warned in early September that it may fall significantly short of disbursement of its investment budgets for the year.

"The Thai government has a horrible track record in terms of executing spending and this new government is confirming that trend," said Angelo Corbetta, head of Asia equity at Pioneer Investments.

To be sure, governments faced with stagnant economies and deteriorating financial markets may find they have few alternatives. Weak local currencies, hit by the prospect of rising interest rates in the U.S., limit central bankers' ability to cut rates for fear of prompting more outflows, leaving government policy as the only other tool capable of boosting a weak economy, said Mr. Corbetta.

The problem is that stimulus programs artificially boost asset prices and put governments on the hook for large amounts of spending. That only sets up a market for a bigger fall at a later date, when the support is withdrawn because government coffers are weaker, investors warn.

In fact, some say they would rather weather short-term losses than see governments stretch their finances on projects that lead to deeper economic stagnation down the road, such as Andy Seaman, chief investment officer for London-based Stratton Street Capital LLP, which manages $1.1 billion.

Short-term shocks are often followed with more rapid reform and better opportunities for investment, he said.

"I'm not sure it's sensible to try and revive markets."

title: Thai Exporters Seek Relief From Strong Baht
text:
BANGKOK--Thailand's main business group urged the central bank to tamp down the country's currency, saying its strength is hurting exports as they struggle to bounce back from two years of negative growth.

The Thai baht has been relatively resilient over the past 13 months despite weak domestic growth and a political crisis that led to a military coup d'état in May.

The currency has strengthened 0.83% against the U.S. dollar since the start of this year, trading at 32.64 baht to the dollar Wednesday. Currencies of other Southeast Asian nations, including Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia, have weakened as much as 3% against the U.S. currency in 2015.

This has put Thai exporters at a disadvantage as a stronger currency makes the country's goods more expensive for buyers, Isara Vongkusolkit, chairman of the Thai Chamber of Commerce, said after meeting with officials from the Bank of Thailand.

"We have to lower our prices to be competitive with neighboring countries who export similar products," Mr. Isara said. Such a move cuts into businesses' profits.

The Bank of Thailand has likely intervened at times to keep the baht stronger to try to avert capital outflows amid concerns about an expected U.S. Federal Reserve rate increase, said Charl Kengchon, managing director at Kasikorn Research. Such a move by the Fed could spark fund outflows from emerging markets such as Thailand,where bondholdings by overseas investors total as much as 600 billion baht ($18.38 billion), added Mr. Charl.

The country's current-account surplus and large holdings of U.S. dollars have contributed to the baht's relative strength in the region.

The Thai central bank's reserves of foreign currency declined to $155.4 billion by the end of January compared with $166.8 billion in January of last year, according to the Bank of Thailand.

The baht's strength has added yet another challenge to the recovery of Thai exports. Overseas shipments, which account for about two-thirds of the country's gross domestic product, contracted 0.41% last year, compared with a 0.32% decline in 2013, the Commerce Ministry reported.

Falling agricultural prices, lower shipments of oil and declining global demand have already weighed on the outlook for exports this year amid the currency depreciation experienced by Thailand's major trade partners, including the European Union and Japan.

The strong baht "is certainly not a crisis right now, but it's something that we encourage the Bank of Thailand to look into because the impact is likely going to be long-term," said Vichai Assarasakorn, vice chairman of the Thai Chamber of Commerce, which didn't specify what it considered to be an appropriate exchange rate. The group also urged the central bank to support the use of local currencies in border trades instead of a reliance solely on the U.S. dollar, Mr. Vichai said.

Pongpen Ruengvirayudh, deputy governor of the central bank, said at a news conference after the meeting that the bank would do its best to address the concerns about the strong baht, but ruled out issuing new intervention measures.

"We will do everything with our available monetary tools to ensure that the baht isn't posing a big obstacle for exporters," she said.

Ms. Pongpen cautioned, however, that monetary policy has limitations, and foreign exchange is only one of the challenges to the country's exports. The global economic slowdown and weakening demand have already put pressure on Southeast Asian exporters, she said.

So far, the central bank hasn't noticed any sign of speculative baht trading, she said.

The Bank of Thailand has estimated exports would grow 1% this year.

title: BNP Paribas: Lower Oil Prices Mean No More BOJ Easing -- Market Talk
text:
0714 GMT [Dow Jones] Lower oil prices will keep the Bank of Japan from implementing further easing, even if lower oil prices also make its inflation target harder to achieve, says BNP Paribas economist Ryutaro Kono. The reason? The Japanese government has lowered pressure on the central bank, as more easing would cause the yen to weaken further against other major currencies. That would push imported energy prices up and squeeze consumer pocketbooks, he says. Mr. Kono expects that lower crude oil prices will help Japan's economy expand about 1.3% to 1.4% from a year earlier in real terms in the fiscal year that begins in April. (eleanor.warnock@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: TFD 
 

0706 GMT [Dow Jones] Thailand entered deflation in January for the first time in more than five years due to falling energy prices, with the headline consumer price index declining 0.4% from a year earlier. Get used to it, Nomura says. "We expect headline inflation to remain negative for several months, and core to fall with it," analyst Euben Paracuelles writes in a research note. Domestic demand is weak, while domestic spending fell 14.6% in November from a year earlier. That means inflation is here to stay for now, and the Bank of Thailand will likely cut rates by 25 basis points in March.(newley.purnell@wsj.com; Twitter: @Newley) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0705 GMT [Dow Jones] Idea Cellular (532822.BY), India's third-biggest cellphone company by the number of users is seeking a bank license from India's central bank, which would allow it to pay out cash and accept deposits. Idea Cellular's application for a banking permit follows Bharti Airtel (532454.BY), India's biggest telecom company, which applied for its own permit last week. Aditya Birla Nuvo (500303.BY) will hold 51% stake in the new payments bank while the remainder will be held by Idea, the company said. Idea has about 150 million cellphone users on its system. Idea and Aditya Birla Nuvo, both part of Aditya Birla Group, did not disclose the financial details of the deal. (krishna.jai@wsj.com; Twitter: @jaikrishna) 


 
Editor: KLH 
 

0653 GMT [Dow Jones] The Bombay Stock Exchange's banking index is the worst performing among 12 sectoral indices, trading down 1.1% after the Reserve Bank of India kept its repurchase rate unchanged at 7.75%. "Investors were hoping that there would be a rate cut but are disappointed," says Rakesh Shinde, a research analyst covering banks at Mumbai-broker Bonanza Portfolio Pvt. Ltd. The RBI had, last month, unexpectedly cut its policy rate for the first time in nearly two years to support sluggish economic growth. A rate cut would have revived credit growth which was down for the past one year, says Shinde. Also, lower rates would have helped borrowers pay back as non-performing assets are on the rise, he says. The benchmark S&P BSE Sensex is trading down 0.6%. (kenan.machado@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: KLH 
 

0650 GMT [Dow Jones] Though India won't be immune to global market volatility that may come with the end of quantitative easing, it is in a much better position to handle the situation, says Raghuram Rajan, governor of the Reserve Bank of India. "We have made important strides on at least three out of four macro variables," says Rajan. He notes that India's economic growth is rising, and inflation and the current-account deficit have fallen. Now, the government needs to announce a credible plan later this month to shrink its fiscal deficit, he says.(shefali.anand@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: KLH 
 

0638 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/THB appears supportive on the daily chart--hovering above its 200-day moving average at 32.45--but that may be due to suspected central bank intervention, a trader says. The central bank may have stepped in to suppress volatility after the baht gained sharply versus the U.S. dollar on Monday, creating a bearish technical cue that generated spillover downward momentum in USD/THB Tuesday. The dollar fell as low as 32.48 from its Monday close of 32.57 before rebounding to 32.50. Below the 200-day moving average at 32.45 lies plenty of stop-loss orders, the trader said, and the Bank of Thailandintervening to dampen currency fluctuation may be crucial in preventing another sharp spike in the baht when those stop-loss orders are triggered. (ewen.chew@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: TFD 
 

0634 GMT [Dow Jones] Reserve Bank of India tweaks rules for foreign investors buying Indian bonds, saying that in future they will be able to buy only company bonds that have a minimum residual maturity of three years. However, foreign investors will not have a lock-in and will be able to sell these bonds at any time. "We'd like to nudge people toward the longer end," says RBI Governor Raghuram Rajan at a press conference Tuesday. (shefali.anand@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: KLH 
 

0628 GMT [Dow Jones] India may not go for more big stake sales in state-run companies in the current financial year through March, says Jagannadham Thunuguntla, head of fundamental research at Karvy Stock Broking after Life Insurance Corp. of India revealed it made a large cash injection in recently concluded 10% share sale of government's equity in Coal India Ltd. (533278.BY). "Such big stake sales are one-off events. I don't see any more big stake sale happening in near future," he told the Wall Street Journal. "This also reaffirms the point that smaller share sales with good prices find more takers." On Friday, he had said there would be no dearth of investors for government stake sales this fiscal. He now says government may look at sale of smaller equity holding in government and private companies.(saurabh.chaturvedi@wsj.com; @journosaurabh) 


 
Editor: KLH 
 

0628 GMT [Dow Jones] Indonesian government's rupiah bond yields may not fall much further from the current level as bonds are already overvalued following a net $3.1 billion inflows last month, says Mandiri Sekuritas' chief debt market analyst Handy Yunianto. "In January 2015, Indonesian government's local-currency bonds recorded the highest return among Asian government's local-currency bonds," Yunianto says, adding that the return of the Indonesian government's rupiah bonds was 6.36% in January compared with the average 1.5% return booked by Asia's local currency sovereign bonds. He says the large foreign inflows last month were likely due to reallocation of some funds from Russian markets to Indonesia as well as from some eurozone nations, thanks to liquidity created by monetary easing. The inflows boosted foreign holding of rupiah sovereign bonds to a record 500 trillion rupiah--or 40% of the total outstanding amount--as of January 30, government data show. Finance Minister Bambang Brojonegoro said to The Wall Street Journal in December that the government would seek to cut the volume of government debt held by foreign funds, to insulate against the risk of large-scale capital flight. The government will do this by increasing the participation of local investors in the domestic debt market. (i-made.sentana@wsj.com) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0621 GMT [Dow Jones] South Korea's weak export and inflation data, driven by cheap oil, call for further policy-rate cuts to spur growth, says HSBC economist Ronald Man. "Weak economic activity in Korea supports our view that monetary policy remains biased towards more easing," Mr. Man says. He says he expects the Bank of Korea to cut the base rate by 0.25 percentage point to 1.75% in the first quarter and another 0.25 percentage point later in the year. Inflation remained tepid with data out Tuesday showing Korea's consumer-price index rose 0.8% on the year in January after gaining at the same pace in December. Trade data out Sunday showed Korea's exports in January fell 0.4% from a year earlier after a revised 3.6% gain in December. Lower crude prices have cut into the value of Korea's overseas shipments of oil-refinery and petrochemical products while keeping energy imports and inflation subdued. (kwanwoo.jun@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: FLS 
 

Violeta Todorova is the correct name of a senior technical analyst at Morgans in Brisbane. "Aussie Shares Could Surge to 6000 in 2H15: Technical Analyst -- Market Talk," at 0521 GMT, misstated her name as Natalia Todorova.

0612 GMT [Dow Jones] J.P. Morgan keeps an underweight rating on Coal India Ltd.(533278.BY), with an unchanged target price of INR325, after the Indian government raised $3.6 billion from a 10% stake sale in the world's biggest coal producer. "With the large stake sale behind us, we believe investor focus would now shift to the quantum of dividend (possible announcement with 3Q results next week); potential price hikes after coal block auctions are over; and more clarity on non-coal mine investment," it says. "While we see limited absolute downside, we expect Coal India to be a relative underperformer and maintain our underweight rating." It expects a dividend of INR16 a share after the stake sale, below the dividend of INR29 a share in FY14. Last year, the government, the biggest shareholder in Coal India, pushed the company for a big dividend payout as the planned stake sale couldn't go through amid opposition from Coal India's unions. This year, as the government has already raised a record $3.6 billion via the stake sale, a big dividend looks unlikely. (saurabh.chaturvedi@wsj.com; @journosaurabh)

title: Thai PM says baht's 'okay', no need for  intervention
text:
BANGKOK, Jan 27 (Reuters) - The current level of Thailand's baht currency is still appropriate so no action is needed at the moment, Prime Minister General Prayuth Chan-ocha said on Tuesday.

Prayuth told reporters that he had met with the central bank and the finance ministry last week, and "the central bank said the current baht level was okay. No need to intervene or do anything."

The baht was little changed at 32.56 against the dollar at 0740 GMT, after hitting a near three-month high of 32.48 early last week.

title: Euro To Suffer From Weaker Euro-Zone Inflows, Says Nomura -- Market Talk
text:

1208 GMT [Dow Jones]--Weaker inflows into euro-zone equities are likely to translate into a weaker euro, says Jens Nordvig at Nomura. "This is important, since strong portfolio flows have consistently supported the euro over the last 1-2 years," he says, adding that the ECB is clearly going to remain easy for very long. This is not reflected yet in rate differentials. "Hence, the euro's resilience in crosses has a lot to do with global rates still being under downward pressure," he says. (chiara.albanese@wsj.com; @chiaraalbanese)

1151 GMT [Dow Jones]--Credit market valuations are becoming less and less attractive for investors, says Giordano Lombardo, chief investment officer at Pioneer Investments. "Spread compression has continued across the whole ratings spectrum. The hunt for yield induced by central banks' zero interest rate policies has pushed the share of credit assets in household portfolios to unprecedented levels," he says. Meanwhile, liquidity in the trading market is fading. Even if investment-grade and high-yield credit retain some appeal in comparison with core government bonds, the upside potential is very limited. "Credit markets need to be handled carefully," he says. (chiara.albanese@wsj.com @chiaraalbanese)

1142 GMT [Dow Jones]--Gilts remain in the red after Tuesday's inflation data surprised to the upside (June CPI 1.9% y/y vs 1.6% expectations). This has pushed forward rate hike expectations, according to analysts at ING, who now see the first move in November. "This would also remove political concerns of waiting until early next year when election campaigning is in full swing and should keep sterling supported," says ING. The September gilt contract is 0.24 lower at 110.41 and the 10-year yields 2.631%. (nick.cawley@wsj.com)

1139 GMT [Dow Jones] Thailand isn't ready to raise rates, the central bank says. "For the time being it is deemed appropriate for Thailand to adopt a relaxed monetary policy," Bank of Thailand Gov. Prasarn Trairatvorakul says. "However, monetary policy may be adjusted...if the situation calls for it in the future." The central bank has cut its benchmark interest rate twice to 2% to shore up the economy since political unrest in November. (nopparat.chaichalearmmongkol@dowjones.com)

1124 GMT [Dow Jones] A bond backed by loans to Bulgaria's Corporate Commercial Bank, which last week had its banking licence revoked by the country's central bank, has halved in price in the last month, according to a trader. The $150 million securitized bond--Northern Lights Bulgaria BV--which was arranged by Russian bank VTB is being quoted at a cash price of around 45%-55% of face value, the trader says. The bond had been quoted at a whisker below face value as recently as June 18. "Given the size of the deal and VTB as a sole lead manager, I don't imagine there is much of this trading or anyone who is willing to take the other side given a bank wind up in Bulgaria is relatively unprecedented," the trader says. (ben.edwards@wsj.com @debtnerd)

7:17 EDT - The only focus of the Brazilian central bank at this week's meeting will be attempting to fuel the country's tepid economic activity despite inflationary pressures, says Luciano Rostagno at Mizuho Bank. Like others, it expects interest rates standing pat as part of tomorrow's policy statement. Brazil's annual inflation in June surpassed the central-bank tolerance band of up to 6.5%, but some have predicted a below-zero number for 2Q GDP. (rogerio.jelmayer@wsj.com)

1108 GMT [Dow Jones]--Thailand's central bank vows to maintain the stability of the Thai baht following calls from the military government to rein in the value of the local currency. "So far, the baht movement has not caused any problem to Thailand's trade or investment," says Prasarn Trairatvorakul, governor of the Bank of Thailand. "The BOT will stand ready to intervene if the value of the baht weakens or strengthens too much and too fast in order to prevent any impact on local economy." Since the beginning of 2014, the baht has strengthened nearly 2% against the dollar, according to the central bank. (nopparat.chaichalearmmongkol@dowjones.com)

7:03 EDT - JPMorgan's (JPM) bottom-line results haven't been impressive of late, in part on legal costs impacting earnings. That's kept shares going largely sideways the past year. The big bank's 2Q results are likely to please at least some with EPS falling much less than Wall Street anticipated as revenue dropped just 2%, not 8% as was the consensus view. "Core" loans rose 8% from a year earlier amid "record" business-banking loan originations while deposits climbed. CEO Jamie Dimon adds there were "encouraging signs" of increased business in numerous parts of JPM's operation as the quarter came to a close. A real 2H economic pickup perhaps? Say it isn't so. Shares, down 1.9% since the 1Q report, rise 1.5% premarket to $57.13. (kevin.kingsbury@wsj.com; @kevinkingsbury)

1103 GMT [Dow Jones] While the Aussie dollar is not having much luck on the topside, the U.K. clearer looks for buying interest in $0.9320 area to stem any further weakness. On the upside, the bank is looking for a return to the recent high of $0.9460 and on a break here, $0.9500. AUD now trades at $0.9374. (gary.stride@wsj.com)

1057 GMT [Dow Jones]--Banco Espirito Santo's (BES.LB) subordinated bond, which carries a coupon of 7.125% and is due in November 2018, continues to tumble on fears that holders of that paper could suffer in the wake of financial trouble at the broader group. Yields on the bonds have risen by 3.63 percentage points since Monday's close and the cost of insuring the bank's debt against default has risen by 56 basis points to 503 basis points. It now costs an average of $503,000 a year to insure $10 million of BES debt for five years. (josie.cox@wsj.com)

1054 GMT [Dow Jones] Indonesia's political situation will likely remain peaceful after the release later this month of the official results from the July 9 presidential election, says Ikrar Nusa Bhakti, political analyst with the state-controlled think tank Indonesian Institute of Science. "Historically, Indonesian presidential and legislative elections had never triggered any violence or anarchy," Mr. Bhakti says. He adds the military and police are "more prepared" to safeguard this election. Former Gen. Prabowo Subianto has said he believes he is leading the official vote count despite independent polling suggesting his rival, Jakarta Gov. Joko Widodo, is ahead. Final vote totals are scheduled to be unveiled July 22. (i-made.sentana@wsj.com)

"I see the only positive in the June inflation figure and that it wasn't negative," says Raiffeisenbank analyst Vaclav France. Looking forward there could be some increase of inflation in July but mostly thanks to the low year-ago base, Mr. France says. "The June inflation data increases the likelihood of the (Czech central bank) delaying the exit from its weak-currency regime until the end of next year," he says. But Rajiv Lall, executive chairman of the infrastructure-finance firm IDFC, says tomorrow's budget announcement, the Narendra Modi government's first, can be good for infrastructure even if it doesn't contain loads of new state spending on big projects. Lall said that the important first step the government could take to help the sector is to make it easier to get financing. That requires, among other things, recapitalizing the giant state-owned banks, which have been in a poor state largely due to earlier infrastructure-related loans that have turned toxic amid India's economic slowdown. "Existing balance-sheet issues need to be sorted out first before corporate India will return to health," Lall said. (raymond.zhong@wsj.com, Twitter: @zhonggg)

among emerging Asian currencies on Wednesday, pressured by

.

for month-end payments.
    Spot Chinese yuan flirted with fresh 18-month lows against
the dollar as investors focused on negative news from the
property sector as further evidence of a slowdown in the
economy. 
    The dollar held steady around an eight-week high
against a basket of six major currencies after data showing U.S.
durable goods sales unexpectedly rose in April and consumer
confidence perked up in May. 
    Still, analysts said the data has not prompted the U.S.
Federal Reserve to consider an early interest rate hike yet, so
emerging Asian currencies may not weaken further.
    "On a one-month time horizon, I would buy Asia. The recent
sell-off has created good entry points for long (positions),"
said Sean Yokota, head of Asia strategy at Scandinavian bank SEB
in Singapore.

Indian rupee and the yuan.
    Last week, the rupee hit an 11-month high on hopes the
recent landslide election victory of the Bharatiya Janata Party
would bring in a government willing to undertake substantial
economic reform.
    Emerging Asian currencies have benefited extensively from
monetary easing by major central banks as investors sought out
higher returns from EM assets.

since Feb. 19, tracking weakness in other Asian currencies.
    The Thai currency, however, recovered all of the losses as
the central bank was spotted intervening around the low to curb
the falls, traders said.
    Thailand's imports in April dropped 14.54 percent from a
year earlier, indicating reduced dollar demand from local
importers. 
    Factory output fell for a 13th straight month in April, and

title: Thai martial law hits baht, stocks but losses seen limited for now
text:
* Thai army declares martial law, but says not a coup               

* Baht pares losses; intervention suspected               

* Benchmark stock index slides 1 percent               

* Analysts say 'bad news' priced in  By Jongwoo Cheon and Satawasin Staporncharnchai               

SINGAPORE/BANGKOK, May 20 (Reuters) - Thai stocks and the baht currency slid on Tuesday after the army imposed martial law in a bid to restore stability after months of protests left the country without a properly functioning government.               

But analysts did not expect a significant exodus of foreign funds unless violence escalates and threatens further damage to Southeast Asia's second-largest economy.               

The army denied that it was staging a military coup and a caretaker government remained in office.               

The baht fell as much as 0.5 percent to 32.62 per dollar in early trade. It later pared most of those losses and was quoted at 32.48 as the central bank was suspected of intervening to support the currency, traders said.               

Thailand's main share index lost around 1 percent, while the five- and 10-year government bond yields   rose.               

"The near term bias is for further USD/THB strength, with 32.85/95 some initial upside targets to think about," said Jonathan Cavenagh, senior FX strategist with Westpac in Singapore, referring to the dollar/baht pair.               

The Thai currency is expected to remain an underperformer against the likes of the Malaysian ringgit and the Philippine peso, Cavenagh said.               

The economy shrank more than expected in the first quarter as anti-government protests dragged on, adding to concerns the country is sliding into recession.               

The Thai bond market has seen 51.1 billion baht ($1.6 billion) of outflows so far this year, even though foreigners have bought a combined net 19.6 billion baht in bonds, according to Thai Bond Market Association.               

In the stock market, foreign investors have sold a combined net 7.5 billion baht so far this year, according to exchange data.               

Yet, the main index is still up more than 7 percent so far this year.               

Analysts said some investors may be looking to buy Thai assets on dips.               

Thailand's government bonds have been thriving on gloomy economic and political headlines as investors line up to buy baht-oriented debt.               

"We expect interest rates will remain low, especially as the strengthening current account insulates THB from external pressures," Citigroup said in a research note, referring to the baht.               

"We continue to advise clients against being short THB. By minimizing violence, martial law could limit the impact on the critical tourism sector. The current account improvement may then outstrip potential capital outflows."               

Thailand reported a combined $8.2 billion current account surplus in the first three months of the year.               

Thai assets have already priced in the prolonged political unrest, analysts said.               

Last year, foreigners dumped a net 194.7 billion baht in Thai stocks and bond market suffered 942.0 billion baht ofoutflows.               

"Even if the bias is for equities to weaken we could still see bargain hunters support the market," Westpac's Jonathan said.

title: Thai Stocks Fall After Martial Law Declared
text:
Thai stocks fell Tuesday after the army stepped in following six months of political unrest by declaring martial law and placing soldiers onto the streets of Bangkok.

The benchmark SET index fell 1.2% with the exchange earlier forced to temporarily close its doors because troops were positioned outside. The currency initially fell, too, on worries the early-morning move by the head of the armed services might signal a potential coup, but it later climbed on suspected intervention by the central bank.

"Is this doing Thailand any favors? No, in the eyes of the world, it looks like they can't sort themselves out and their brand is definitely taking a beating," said Jalil Rasheed, investment director at Invesco, which holds assets in Thailand and is still optimistic about the long-term outlook.

"I believe the military has stepped in to expedite the process of facilitating a properly elected government and won't stay in power indefinitely," Mr. Rasheed added.

The protests in Thailand toppled Prime Minister Yingluck Shinawatra earlier this month, with the political divide characterized by mass street rallies and occasionally fatal attacks between the two main groups of protesters.

The imposition of martial law follows data Monday that showed the economy contracted in the first quarter, which analysts say could lead to a recession this year. Analysts are predicting a further cut to the central bank's core interest rate at its June meeting.

"Where financial markets go from here depends on the likelihood of blood being spilled," said ING economist Tim Condon. "Thai-on-Thai violence would be bad for Thai financial assets. The violence would have to be truly awful for financial assets outside Thailand to be affected," he added.

The losses in Thai stocks were evenly spread across the board early Tuesday. Kasikornbank PCL lost 1.2%, while telecommunications company Advanced Info Service PCL lost 1.3%.

Despite increased volatility, however, Thailand's financial markets have largely remained resilient in the face of the political tension. The baht has strengthened 0.5% against the U.S. dollar year-to-date, in line with most of its regional peers, and traded Tuesday at 32.49 per dollar, 0.4% stronger than Monday's close. The SET gained 7.6% in the January-March period, marking the third-best performance among Asian stock markets.

Some analysts hope that martial law could help prompt a resolution to the political deadlock. "The imposition of martial law is not, in itself, negative for Thailand's ratings, although clearly we are keeping the situation under close review," said Andrew Colquhoun, head of Asia-Pacific sovereign ratings at Fitch Ratings.

He said that the most important factors for ratings are whether Thailand can avoid further disorder and install a government capable of passing a budget to put back on track policies that have been derailed by the unrest. "The return of a functioning government and a lowering of the political temperature would help to restore confidence more broadly and pull the economy out of its tailspin," he said.

title: Southeast Asian Markets End Week Slightly Higher; Rupiah Pushes 4.5-Year Low
text:
Southeast Asian markets ended Friday mostly higher, with Thailand and Indonesia making strong gains in the last part of the day, while Indonesia's rupiah retreated from a 4.5-year low against the U.S. dollar on suspected intervention from the central bank.

Thailand's SET closed up 0.9%, recovering from a 0.5% fall during morning trading. Indonesia's JSX closed up 0.5%, while the Philippines' PSE Composite gained 0.6%--its fourth straight day of gains after over a week of declines triggered by the landfall of Typhoon Haiyan on Nov. 8.

Elsewhere, Vietnam's benchmark closed flat, Malaysia's KLCI added 0.3% and Singapore's FTSE Straits Times bucked the trend with a fall of 0.3%.

Central bankers in both the Philippines and Indonesia attempted to reassure investors Friday. Governor Amando Tetangco in the Philippines said that the impact of Typhoon Haiyan on the economy would be manageable and domestic growth should hit targets of this year and next without central bank intervention. The government is targeting 6.5%-7.5% growth in 2014.

Bank Indonesia governor Agus Martowardojo said that the rupiah, which is hovering near a 4.5%-year low of 12,000 against the U.S. dollar, reflected economic fundamentals despite heavy falls this year of almost 20%. He said the central bank would prioritize stabilizing the economy rather than boosting growth. There was some speculation among traders that Bank Indonesia may have intervened Friday to keep the rupiah from breaching the 12,000 mark.

Among other currencies in the region, Malaysia's ringgit strengthened 0.3% and Thailand's baht lost 0.1% against the U.S. dollar.

Thai real-estate developer Central Pattana Public Co., a volatile large-cap stock, added 2.4%, while telecoms provider Total Access Communications Public Co.--also known as DTAC--ended up 5%.

Philippine stocks continued to recover from a blip in investor sentiment following the typhoon. Telecoms provider Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co. added 2.1%, while property investor SM Investments Corporation gained 0.8%.

In Malaysia, conglomerate Genting Bhd., which has interests in casinos, power, plantations and other businesses, lost 1.4% a day after it reported third-quarter results that Kenanga Research said came in below expectations. Genting said its core net profit for the nine months to September was 1.29 billion ringgit (US$400 million). The group's earnings are expected to be better in the fourth quarter of 2013 as it is entering the busy festive year-end season, Kenanga said in a note, maintaining its "outperform" rating.

* Indonesian c.bank spotted intervening to support rupiah     * Baht down on politics; intervention suspected     * Ringgit at 2-mth low on hedge funds, speculators   (Adds text, updates prices)     By Jongwoo Cheon     SINGAPORE, Nov 27 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah hit a near five-year low on Wednesday on increasing month-end dollar demand from local companies, while most emerging Asian currencies eased in line with a weaker yen.    Thailand's baht fell on outflow pressures due to  rising political tensions at home and weaker-than-expected exports data, while the Malaysian ringgit slid to its lowest in almost two months as hedge funds sold it.     Such declines came even as the dollar broadly fell against a basket of six major currencies after weaker-than-expected U.S. consumer confidence in November.      Still, the U.S. housing market provided a more encouraging reading with permits for future home construction rising to a near 5-1/2-year high.

      "A strong dollar trend remains intact with underlying views of Fed tapering and a weaker yen supporting the trend," said Jeong My-young, Samsung Futures research head in Seoul.     "That continues to hurt Asian currencies. There will be more domestic issues such as Thailand's protests," Jeong added.     The Indian rupee, however, bucked regional weakness on corporate dollar inflows. 


    
    RUPIAH
    The rupiah lost 0.7 percent to 11,835 per dollar,
its weakest since March 2009.
    The official Jakarta Interbank Spot Dollar Rate (JISDOR)


, which the central bank introduced in May as part of a
bid to manage exchange rate fluctuations, was fixed at 11,813
rupiah per dollar, the weakest since JISDOR's introduction.
    The Indonesian currency fell in non-deliverable forwards
(NDFs) market on selling from offshore funds and leveraged
accounts, traders said.
    The rupiah's one-month NDFs also slid to
11,835 to the greenback, its weakest since Sept. 6, indicating
further depreciation.
    "At the current pace (of the rupiah's depreciation), I dare
not say no," a Jakarta-based trader when asked if the spot
rupiah would weaken past 12,000 per dollar this week.
    The central bank was spotted providing dollar liquidity to
support the rupiah in the local market, although traders
preferred to sell it.
    "The rupiah is still bearish. However, I don't want to do
prop trading from this level, but to buy dollars from exporters
and hold the positions," another trader in Jakarta said,
referring to proprietary trading.
    Due to Indonesia's current account deficit, the rupiah is
regarded as the Asian currency most vulnerable to capital
outflows once the U.S. Federal Reserve finally starts winding
down a stimulus strategy that has fuelled dollar inflows to
emerging markets.
    Indonesia's president said economic growth in the fourth
quarter was expected to be at its slowest pace in more than four
years if the Fed starts trimming its massive bond-buying
programme. 


    
    BAHT

disappointing trade data, while its downside was limited as the

Interior Ministry and forced the evacuation of four others,

government data showed.

downside pressure on Thai equities, bonds and the currency as
markets continue to price in a political risk premium,"
Scotiabank said in a client note.
    Investors were awaiting the central bank's monetary policy
meeting later in the day when the Bank of Thailand is expected
to keep its policy rate unchanged at 2.50 percent.

3.2300.

title: WSJ Blog:Would Thailand Opt for an Exchange-Rate Target?
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's Real Time Economics blog at http://blogs.wsj.com/economics)

By Michael S. Arnold

Hints that the Federal Reserve would start winding down its massive bond-buying program have sent shockwaves through Thai markets in recent months, sparking an outflow of funds that sent local stocks, bonds and the baht currency plunging.

It also sparked some unusual policy proposals -- including a call for Thailand's central bank to stop targeting inflation and focus instead on maintaining a stable exchange rate.

The Bank of Thailand uses interest rates to keep core prices within a desired range, currently set at 0.5%-3.0%. But Supavud Saicheua, executive director and head of research at Bangkok-based brokerage Phatra Securities Plc, says a monetary policy regime focused on the exchange rate would be far more effective for a relatively small, trade-dependent economy.

"They're pointing their gun in the wrong place," Mr. Saicheua said of the central bank. "It's ironic that they're so explicit about what they're trying to do with inflation but the source of instability is not inflation, it's the exchange rate. And Thailand has no policy framework to address that."

Like other developing economies, Thailand saw its currency and markets soar earlier this year as money unleashed by massive quantitative easing in the United States and Japan flowed into emerging markets. The baht was Asia's best performer for much of the year, gaining more than 7% against the U.S. dollar to a multi-year high of 28.54 on April 22 -- much to the chagrin of Thai exporters.

Then the U.S. Federal Reserve began talking of "tapering" its quantitative easing program. Within weeks the baht had given up all the year's gains and more, while Thailand's benchmark stock index fell by 18% from peak to trough. Companies that had been complaining about a strong baht now were complaining that it was too weak.

Regardless, the idea of targeting the exchange rate is likely to be a hard sell at the Bank of Thailand. Gov. Prasarn Traivoratkul told the Journal that the current framework is the most transparent, making it easier to manage inflation expectations and avoid damaging spirals in which price increases and expectations of future increases feed off each other.

In contrast, "exchange-rate targeting is the least transparent regime," he said. "Nobody can spell out what exchange rate they want because the market can front-run, the market can manipulate and attack, and sometimes you cannot defend yourself."

That's precisely what happened in 1997, when Thailand had a fixed exchange rate. Speculators who calculated the central bank didn't have enough reserves to protect the baht from sustained attack ultimately forced a devaluation of more than 50% that broke the back of Thailand's economy and forced the government into the International Monetary Fund's austere embrace. The financial crisis spread from Bangkok to the rest of Asia, wreaking havoc across the continent.

Today most Asian central banks have inflation-targeting regimes to one degree or another, though many -- including the Bank of Thailand -- will intervene to protect their currencies during periods of unusual volatility.

On one point, at least, Messrs. Prasarn and Saicheua agree: The specter of 1997 makes it highly unlikely the Bank of Thailand would ever switch back to an exchange-rate target.

That option "has been totally discredited" by the events of 1997, Mr. Saicheua said. "Inflation targeting is the nice guy with a clean image and good reputation. Exchange-rate targeting just creates a sense of horror whenever you talk about it."

title: EM ASIA  FX -Rupiah off lows on surprise rate hike; baht rebounds
text:
* Indonesia c.bank hikes benchmark rate 25 bps to 6 pct     * One-month dollar/rupiah NDFs rebound     * Thai c.bank sold dlrs to support baht last week - gov   (Adds text, updates prices)     By Jongwoo Cheon     SINGAPORE, June 13 (Reuters) - The ailing Indonesian rupiah recovered some lost ground after the central bank surprisingly hiked the benchmark rate, while most emerging Asian currencies slipped on continuing worry about a possible cut in monetary stimulus.     The Thai baht, however, rebounded as the Bank of Thailand said it intervened to limit the currency's slide last week.     The rupiah was as weak as 9,895 to the dollar until the rate hike, which strengthened it to 9,870. But in spite of the 25 basis point hike to 6.0 percent, the rupiah's spot indicated price eased 0.2 percent to 9,875 as of 0740 GMT.        Bank Indonesia's surprise hike "was a pleasantly surprise.

 I think they want to send a clear message to markets that they will act on IDR weakness," said Sean Yokota, head of Asia strategy at Scandinavian bank SEB in Singapore.     "We are waiting for the Fed on next Thursday. If Bernanke remains dovish, it can reverse the IDR's depreciation trend," Yokota said.     The Federal Reserve is scheduled to open a policy meeting  June 18 and the next day Chairman Ben Bernanke will hold media briefing, which will take place early Thursday in Asia.     The Indonesian central bank's unexpected move came two days after it surprisingly hiked its overnight deposit facility rate (FASBI) by 25 basis points to 4.25 percent to try to bolster the rupiah.      The central bank said on Wednesday it was ready to ensure large supplies of dollars and to buy government bonds in the secondary market.       Still, the rupiah is unlikely to escape from a bearish mood as investors stay concerned over the Fed tapering monetary stimulus, traders and analysts said.     One-month dollar/rupiah non-deliverable forwards  rebounded after falling on the rate hike.     "The rate hike today may not be able to stem capital outflow when markets are attempting to achieve a new equilibrium in an environment of a roll back of monetary policy easing by the Fed," said Suresh Kumar Ramanathan, head of regional interest rate and FX strategy at CIMB Investment Bank in Kuala Lumpur.     "The usual short-term reprieve - of a day or two - will allow marginal appreciation of IDR, but does not alter the view that markets have currently, that is, capital reversal to economies with stronger growth trajectory and economies with a clear signal of currency appreciation, which is the U.S. economy and the U.S. dollar," he said.     Among emerging Asian markets, Indonesia and India are the most vulnerable to capital outflows due to worries about their sizable current account deficits.

Bank of Thailand last week sold dollars to support the Thai
currency.

ensure stability in the currency.

Bangkok stocks hitting a near six-month low.

stocks in the month to June 12.

weaker stocks, while domestic importers bought the greenback for
payments.

    But investors hesitated to sell the ringgit more on caution
over possible intervention by the central bank to support the
currency.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Philippine peso, baht fall on c.banks; China PMI hits Asia  FX
text:
* Philippine c.bank seen cutting SDA rates on Thursday

 * Baht down on hedge funds selling after c.bank remarks

 * Won dips as intervention suspected - traders 

(Adds text, updates prices)

 By Jongwoo Cheon

 SINGAPORE, April 23 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso and the Thai baht fell on Tuesday as caution grew over central bank moves to stem currency appreciation, while concerns about China's weak growth hurt emerging Asian currencies.

 The peso slid on selling by offshore funds as the central bank is widely expected to cut the rate on its short-term special deposit account (SDA) facility again on Thursday in another move to temper the peso, traders said.

 "The dollar remained supported on offshore demand. Speculation of a 50 basis point (bps) or higher cut in SDA rates put pressure on the peso," said a senior Philippine bank trader in Manila.

 Last month, the central bank cut by 50 basis points to 2.5 percent the rate on all its three SDA tenors.

 Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinasis has lowered the SDA rate by a total of more than 150 basis points since July 2012 to encourage banks to lend more to consumers and discourage dollar flows that pushed the peso to become the second best performing emerging Asian currency last year.

 On April 18, it liberalised rules on foreign currency transactions on Thursday, allowing residents to invest in property abroad and offshore funds. 

 The peso was not the only emerging Asian currency to fall on caution over intervention by foreign exchange authorities.

 The baht slid after a Thailand's central bank assistant governor told Reuters on Monday that the Bank of Thailand is worried about the baht's rapid rise but is unlikely to impose "draconian" measures to rein it in. 

 The South Korean won also eased as the authorities were suspected of selling the currency to protect export competitiveness amid the yen's weakness, traders said.

 A preliminary survey showing growth in China's vast factory sector dipped in April also weighed on Asian markets, suggesting the world's second-largest economy still faces formidable global headwinds in the second quarter. 

 BAHT

 The baht slid as hedge funds reduced bullish bets on the best-performing currency after the central bank assistant governor comments.

 Paiboon Kittisrikangwan said the baht has started to move close to "a zone beyond the fundamentals" and the central bank was ready to do something if it went "way beyond" that.

 Investors grew more wary over potential intervention by the central bank, although they have not seen it in the market yet, traders said.

 "They were in the market when dollar/baht went below 28.60," said a Thai bank trader, adding the odds of intervention have increased, given the central bank's concerns.

 WON

 The won eased as the foreign exchange authorities were suspected of selling the currency, especially when it was firmer than 1,120 per dollar, traders said.

 Foreign investors continued to sell Seoul shares on worries about growth in China, which is South Korea's top export market.

 They have been net sellers in the country's main exchange for am eighth consecutive session, unloading a combined net 1.2 trillion won ($1.1 billion) during the period, according to the Korea Exchange data.

 Still, the won recovered some of losses on exporters' demand, traders said.

title: UPDATE 1-Thai c.bank not ruling out strong measures to curb robust baht
text:
* Baht has risen nearly 6 pct vs dollar this year

 * BOT satisfied with its approach on exchange rate management

 * Finance minister wants rates cut to hold currency down 

(Adds background, baht moves)

 BANGKOK, April 17 (Reuters) - The Bank of Thailand has not ruled out strong measures to halt the baht's rise but its monetary policy committee (MPC) believes the central bank has the means to address the problem if needed, according to minutes of its April meeting.

 "The MPC discussed the potential drivers of recent capital inflow and baht appreciation, including the misperception by some market participants that the Bank of Thailand had ruled out strong policy responses," the minutes published on Wednesday said.

 "The MPC, however, was satisfied that the BOT's current exchange rate management framework already entailed systematic steps of policy responses, with specific measures ready to be implemented if and when warranted by the circumstances."

 At the meeting on April 3, the monetary policy committee voted to leave the policy rate at 2.75 percent, ignoring government calls for a cut to deter "hot money" flows and reiterating it was concerned about credit growth and potential asset bubbles. 

 The baht has risen almost 6 percent against the dollar this year, by some distance the biggest rise among Asian currencies.

 The export industry has expressed concern about the baht's rise and Finance Minister Kittirat Na Ranong has repeatedly called for interest rates to be cut to diminish the allure of the currency.

 The Bank of Thailand has appeared relaxed, intervening in the market very little, if at all, and has noted that the baht was merely playing catch-up with appreciation in other currencies when the Thai economy was suffering from severe flooding and its aftermath in 2011 and 2012.

 However, on April 9 Governor Prasarn Trairatvorakul said the baht had been rising too quickly and the central bank was concerned. 

 He said it would look at the baht again after Songkran, the Thai New Year, on April 13-16. Thai financial markets were closed for that holiday on Monday and Tuesday.

 The baht is trading around 16-year highs. It hit 28.91 per dollar in early trade on Wednesday, up from levels around 28.98 on Friday before the long holiday, and then ticked down immediately after the minutes were released.

 At 0300 GMT, it was quoted at 28.95/98 per dollar.

 Most economists expect the central bank to leave its policy rate at 2.75 percent for the rest of the year. A small minority  believes a cut is possible if the global economy struggles and exports don't pick up, but most expect the next move to be an increase.

 In the minutes, the Bank of Thailand repeated its concern about risks to financial stability centred on household credit growth and "incipient signs of speculation" in the property market.

 "Inflationary pressure may edge up going forward due to supply constraints, higher labour costs and greater cost pass-through, given entrepreneurs' diminishing ability to hold down prices," it added.

 It has been less worried about inflation than some private economists and on April 12 trimmed its forecast for 2013 to 2.7 percent from 2.8 percent.

 It cut its forecast for core inflation, which excludes energy and fresh food prices, to 1.6 percent from 1.7 percent. The central bank sets interest rates with the aim of keeping core inflation in a 0.5 to 3.0 percent range.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Baht firmer, poised for best quarter in 2-1/2 years
text:
* Dollar/baht down more than 4 pct in Jan-March

* Baht on track for best quarter since July-Sept 2010

* S.Korean won slips as govt slashes forecast

(Adds comments, updates levels)

By Masayuki Kitano

SINGAPORE, March 28 (Reuters) - The Thai baht edged higher on Thursday and was on track for its best quarterly gain in 2-1/2 years as the country's upbeat economic fundamentals helped spur fund inflows into Thai equities and bonds.

Other emerging Asian currencies were mostly steady to firmer against the dollar on Thursday, although the South Korean won slipped as the country's new government sharply cut this year's growth target.

The dollar slipped about 0.2 percent to 29.25 versus the Thai baht.

With one more trading session left in the quarter, the dollar is down roughly 4.4 percent versus the Thai currency, the greenback's biggest quarterly percentage decline against the baht since the July-September quarter of 2010.

Inflows into Thai equities and bonds have helped to lift the baht, which hit a 16-year high of 29.07 on March 20.

"From the yield perspective, I think risk-adjusted yields are still fairly attractive. So that should support the baht," said Andy Ji, Asian currency strategist for Commonwealth Bank of Australia in Singapore.

When taking into account the low implied volatility of the baht, Thai bond yields hold some attraction for overseas investors, Ji said.

The macro-economic backdrop for the baht, however, seems relatively neutral at this stage, he said, adding that the baht may take a bit of a breather in the April-June quarter.

"Most of Asia is doing actually quite well so in that sense it doesn't really stand out," Ji said, adding that he expects the baht to be trading at 29.20 at the end of June.

Investors are also cautious about the potential for intervention by Thailand's central bank to stem further appreciation in the baht to help exporters. On Thursday, Thailand reported that February exports fell 5.8 percent from a year earlier.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Baht retreats on  intervention  caution; Taiwan dlr, ringgit up
text:
* Profit-taking weighs on baht after 1997 high

* Intervention has not been spotted yet - traders

* Thai importers put pressure on baht

* Taiwan dlr up on exporters; ringgit higher after Fed

(Adds text, updates prices)

By Jongwoo Cheon

SINGAPORE, March 21 (Reuters) - The Thai baht slid on Thursday as caution over intervention prompted investors to book profits after the currency strengthened in the previous session to levels last seen before the 1997 Asian financial crisis on sustained inflows.

The baht lost as much as 0.5 percent to 29.22 per dollar, underperforming other Asian currencies. Some regional units such as the Taiwan dollar and the Malaysian ringgit edged higher.

On Wednesday, the Thai currency hit 29.07, its strongest since 1997, according to Thomson Reuters data, as foreign investors poured into Thai bonds.

The central bank has not been spotted buying dollars, but local importers bought the greenback on dips for payments, traders said.

"The market is cautious and watching if there is BOT (Bank of Thailand) intervention," said a foreign bank trader, adding the baht may weaken to 29.24 on more dollar-short covering.

Technically, the baht is seen excessively bought with dollar/baht's 14-day relative strength index at 25.3, well below the threshold 30. The index has stayed below that level since March 15, indicating the pair has been oversold.

Late on Wednesday, BOT Governor Prasarn Trairatvorakul, who has argued before that the currency's rise was in line with economic fundamentals and with the trend in other regional currencies, said it was "a bit too much and fast".

Traders and analysts suspect the central bank could intervene if the market tries to take the baht below 29.00 per dollar.

The baht has been the best performing emerging Asian currency so far this year with a 4.8 percent gain against the dollar, Thomson Reuters data showed.

The appreciation came as most of its Asian peers stayed under pressure, as a weakening yen hurt the export competitiveness of other Asian countries, especially South Korea.

Thai authorities may take steps to forestall further advances by the baht as it could hinder exports, which account for some 75 percent of gross domestic product, analysts said.

"Though outright pure intervention is rather unlikely. We'd be more likely to see macro prudential measures in an effort to restrain foreign portfolio inflows," said Sacha Tihanyi, senior currency strategist for Scotiabank in Hong Kong.

Still, some analysts said a firmer baht may not hit exports as hard as feared unless the global economy falters again.

Earlier, a preliminary private survey showed growth in China's vast manufacturing sector picked up in March after dipping over the Lunar New Year holiday, pointing towards solid but not spectacular first-quarter growth.

That came as the U.S. economy continued to show signs of a recovery.

"Currency competitiveness is only one part of product competitiveness. Demand is the bigger driver, and with the U.S. economy recovering, as well as China, and emerging market demand still strong, it should still be positive for Thai exports," said BNP Paribascurrency strategist Thio Chin Loo in Singapore.

Investors were also seeking to buy the baht on dips as the currency is likely to see more capital inflows from investors seeking higher yields, traders and analysts said.

The country is also attracting more foreign direct investments and overseas money for domestic infrastructure projects, they added.

Japanese manufacturers such as car makers are stepping up investment in Thailand taking advantage of Tokyo's monetary policy easing.

"I would sell dollar/baht at 29.30 if there is no talk of intervention, because today's movement is just profit taking coupled with demand from importers, but the longer-term picture of the baht has not changed," said a Thai bank trader.

"As long as balance of payment and current account of the country still look good and there are also large investment projects by government, these are positive factors that attract offshore funds."

RINGGIT

The ringgit gained in thin trading as investors cut dollar-long positions on the Federal Reserve's decision to keep its present policy stance.

The Fed kept its aggressive policy stimulus despite improvements in the U.S. economy, pointing to still-high unemployment, fiscal headwinds out of Washington and risks from abroad.

Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke said the central bank might slow the pace of its bond buying but only after the labour market showed sustained improvement over a number of months.

But investors hesitated to chase the Malaysian currency, given sustained worries about wrangling over a bailout plan for Cyprus.

"The market has been long dollar versus ringgit. But the euro zone trouble is just causing the market to yo-yo," said a Malaysian bank trader in Kuala Lumpur.

TAIWAN DOLLAR

The Taiwan dollar edged higher from Wednesday's domestic close of 29.845 as exporters bought it around 29.800 to the U.S. dollar, traders said.

But local interbank speculators and foreign financial institutions were lined up to sell the island's currency on rallies.

Those players expected the Taiwan dollar to weaken in coming weeks, given its outperformance against some other currencies of Asian competitors in export markets.

The Taiwan dollar has lost 2.2 percent to the greenback so far this year, while the South Korean won has fallen 4.0 percent and the Japanese yen has depreciated 9.3 percent, according to Thomson Reuters data.

Investors are also wary of intervention by the central bank to maintain price competitiveness in overseas markets.

On Wednesday, the central bank was spotted intervening to push down the Taiwan dollar to close at 29.845 as usual, traders said.

In the prior session, the Taiwan dollar traded between 29.760 and 29.800 before the intervention, traders said.

title: UPDATE 2-Thai finmin wants weaker baht, lower interest rates
text:
* Says c.bank should take action on baht rise

* Repeats that he wants no special baht measures

(Adds detail, quotes)

By Kitiphong Thaichareon and Jongwoo Cheon

BANGKOK/SINGAPORE, March 21 (Reuters) - Thailand's finance minister said on Thursday both the baht and interest rates should be lower, after the currency hit a 16-year high, threatening the export-driven economy, but he repeated there would be no capital controls to curb inflows.

Thailand is one of several Asian countries struggling to contain upward pressure on their currencies, as investors laden with funds in the wake of quantitative easing (QE) moves by major central banks have poured money into high yield markets.

This year, the baht has been the best performing emerging Asian currency, strengthening 4.8 percent against the dollar, Thomson Reuters data showed.

"I want to see the baht weaker and the policy interest rate lower," Kittirat Na Ranong told a seminar. He has repeatedly called for a cut in rates to deter "hot money" but the central bank, worried about fast credit growth and the potential for higher inflation, has resisted.

On Wednesday, the baht hit 29.07, its strongest since 1997, according to Thomson Reuters data, as foreign investors poured into Thai bonds.

On Thursday, it dipped as much as 0.5 percent to 29.22 per dollar, underperforming other Asian currencies as caution over possible intervention prompted investors to book profits.

The Bank of Thailand (BOT) has not been spotted buying dollars, but local importers bought the greenback on dips for payments, traders said.

Kittirat spoke twice publicly about the baht on Thursday. In his earlier remarks, the finance minister said the central bank should take action before the baht's strength bites, although in response to a reporter's question, he said he did not believe the baht would strengthen to 27 per dollar.

Thailand has been attracting more foreign direct investments and inflows for domestic infrastructure projects.

The country has dealt carefully with inflows following a case in late 2006 when it imposed tough capital controls that made Thai shares plunge. In recent years, authorities have focused more on encouraging outflows.

NO SURPRISE MEASURE

Late on Wednesday, BOT Governor Prasarn Trairatvorakul, who has argued before that the currency's rise was in line with economic fundamentals and with the trend in other regional currencies, said it was "a bit too much and fast".

Thai authorities may take steps to forestall further advances by the baht as its strengthening could hinder exports, which account for some 75 percent of gross domestic product, analysts said.

"Though outright pure intervention is rather unlikely, we'd be more likely to see macro prudential measures in an effort to restrain foreign portfolio inflows," said Sacha Tihanyi, senior currency strategist for Scotiabank in Hong Kong.

Traders and analysts suspect the BOT could intervene if the market tries to take the baht below 29.00 per dollar.

Early on Thursday, Kittirat told reporters: "People in charge (of the baht) should take action before the baht affects employment, exports and tourism."

"Temporary measures, if introduced, will hurt confidence. So I can confirm that there will be no measure that surprises the market... It should be accepted means, such as monetary measures," he added.

Kittirat has said lower interest rates would not lead to bubbles but economists have raised concerns about the rapid rise in stock prices and property.

Despite the political pressure, the central bank's monetary policy committee left the policy rate unchanged at 2.75 percent on Feb. 20, citing strong credit growth and slightly higher inflationary pressure..

Prasarn has repeatedly said that interest rates were not the only factor, or even the main factor, attracting inflows and the central bank's main duty is to ensure economic stability.

Economists expect the central bank to hold fire for some months as the economy is growing well and inflation is contained. Its next policy review is on April 3.

title: UPDATE 1-Thai baht hits 16-yr high, sparking  intervention  talk
text:
(Adds central bank and analysts comments)

BANGKOK/SINGAPORE, March 20 (Reuters) - The Thai baht hit its highest level on Wednesday since the Asian financial crisis in 1997 and economists said the resilient economy would continue to attract foreign money, though some cautioned the central bank may have to intervene to deter speculators.

Bank of Thailand Governor Prasarn Trairatvorakul, who has argued until now that the currency's rise was in line with economic fundamentals and with the trend in other regional currencies, said on Wednesday it was "a bit too much and fast".

The baht, gaining on a day when Cypriot rejection of the terms for a European bail-out hurt other risky assets, rose as much as 0.7 percent to 29.13 per dollar and stood at 29.15 in late trade.

It has risen around 5 percent so far this year, making it Asia's best performing currency.

Technically, the currency has been seen as excessively overbought, with the dollar/baht's 14-day relative strength index at 16.6, far below the 30-threshold, but many market watchers predict further modest gains.

"We are looking at 29 baht per dollar by year-end. Foreign inflows should continue to support it in the short term," said Somchai Amornthum, a senior vice-president at Krung Thai Asset Management.

"The rise should not be tackled by interest rates because it will have a wide impact and we also have to be careful about bubbles ... What they can do is to intervene in the market, both verbally and with direct intervention," he added.

Finance Minister Kittirat Na Ranong has put pressure on the central bank to cut interest rates to deter foreign inflows but the central bank has resisted.

On Wednesday, after a meeting with the governor, Kittirat ruled out capital controls.

"We will not issue any special measure to deal with the strong baht," he told reporters, saying such moves could cause panic in the markets and undermine investor confidence. Capital controls in 2006 caused a plunge in the bourse.

The government is worried that a strong baht will hurt exports, which generally drive economic growth in Thailand.

But Kirida Bhaopichitr, country economist for Thailand at the World Bank, told a seminar on Wednesday there was no strong correlation between the currency and exports.

"Actually, Thai exports rely a lot more on global demand ... You can see that when the exchange rate appreciates... all Thai exports also increase. But for 2009, for example, although our exchange rate depreciated, exports fell," she said.

The economy grew 6.4 percent in 2012 and the National Economic and Social Development Board (NESDB), which compiles the data, forecasts 4.5 to 5.5 percent growth for this year.

DRIVEN BY FUNDAMENTALS

Gundy Cahyadi, an economist with OCBC in Singapore, also remained positive on the baht, given the potential in the economy.

"The key test will be to see if it can break the 29.00 mark - it's definitely not to be ruled out," he said.

"Certainly, the issue of speculative inflows needs to be monitored, because these tend to be destabilising. But we agree with the assessment of the central bank that the baht this year has been driven by fundamentals."

Enrico Tanuwidjaja, an economist with Royal Bank of Scotland, said he was sticking to the end-2013 forecast he made in October of 29 baht per dollar, citing "strong domestic demand and a good investment story," and adding Thailand has been a relatively underweighted market for quite a long time.

Asked about the central bank stance, he said: "I guess it's still within their comfort zone ... It's in line with regionals in terms of catching up. You can plot 2012 gains versus current levels. It's playing catch-up."

Thailand was devastated by floods in late 2011 and manufacturing was slow to recover in 2012. The baht rose just over 3 percent last year, whereas the Philippine peso rose 6.8 percent and the South Korean won 7.6 percent.

Traders said offshore funds bought the baht ahead of a bond sale on Wednesday at which the government raised 20 billion baht ($682 million).

A 6.23-year bond yielded 3.2835 percent against 3.3877 percent for a similar bond on Jan. 30.

Thai bond markets also saw inflows of about $340 million on Monday and Tuesday, according to traders. That followed a record single-day inflow of 28 billion baht ($954 million) on March 12.

Foreign flows into the stock market have been patchy since end-January but may be revived by what could be Thailand's biggest IPO, when Bangkok SkyTrain operator BTS Group Holdings Pcl raises up to $2.1 billion by listing an infrastructure fund next month.

Thailand's main stock index has surged nearly 13 percent so far this year.

Infrastructure plans are also attracting inflows. On Tuesday the cabinet approved a bill to borrow 2 trillion baht to fund infrastructure projects that are expected to fuel economic growth over the next seven years.

Prime Minister Yingluck Shinawatra said some funding might be from overseas but Kittirat said loans would be found at home.

The baht also is benefiting from Tokyo's expansionary policies, with Japanese manufacturers stepping up investment in Thailand.

In January, Toyota Motor Corp said it would invest 12 billion baht, while Honda Motor said in February it would spend more than 2 billion baht on a new assembly plant.

($1 = 29.3350 Thai baht)

text:
SINGAPORE, March 15 (Reuters) - The Thai baht rose on Friday to hover around a 28-month high on continued demand from offshore funds, but speculation of central bank intervention to curb its rise capped the upside, traders said.

The baht gained 0.3 percent to 29.55 per dollar as of 0513 GMT after hitting 29.54, according to Thomson Reuters data. The session high matched Tuesday's peak, the strongest mark since November 2010.

Traders said they have spotted central bank bids for the dollar around its lows while importers also bought the U.S. currency. But some market players dismissed the suggestion that the Bank of Thailand had intervened on the day.

Investors were generally looking to buy the baht given the continued foreign-fund inflows, traders said.

The baht has been the best performing emerging Asian currency so far this year with a 3.6 percent appreciation against the dollar, Thomson Reuters data showed, helped by offshore fund inflows to the country's stocks and bonds.

Still, traders preferred to buy the local unit on dips.

A local trader said he doubted the central bank was intervening around the current levels, adding the authorities would probably step in when the baht strengthens further to 29.50.
