title: BIS-UPDATE 1-Thai c.bank to  intervene  if baht becomes volatile
text:
(Adds quotes, background)

BASEL, Sept 7 (Reuters) - Thailand's central bank has no exchange-rate target but would intervene if the baht became very volatile, its deputy governor Atchana Waiquamdee said on Sunday.

Speaking in the Swiss city of Basel, she also said Thailand's political crisis, coupled with slowing major developed economies, would weigh on the country's growth in the second half of this year.

Investor sentiment on Thailand has been deteriorating after Prime Minister Samak Sundaravej imposed emergency rule last week which failed to lead to the eviction of thousands of protesters occupying his official compound.

The main stock index <.SETI> hit a 19-month low last week while the baht <THB=TH> hit a one-year low of 34.6 to the dollar on Friday, prompting the central bank to intervene to support the currency.

Losses were aggravated by the general investor aversion to risky emerging markets.

Asked whether Thailand would intervene in the market if the currency dropped further, Atchana told reporters: "Our exchange rate hasn't been changed. We don't have any target, for the exchange rate level, but when it's very volatile, the central bank may step in."

The political turmoil in Thailand was a risk factor but had not yet deteriorated to the point that the central bank needed to cut its growth forecast of between 4.8 and 5.8 percent for this year, she said.

"Up until now, we don't think it (political instability) is going to have an impact on our growth forecast," Atchana said.

"If it is prolonged for the next month or two, especially in the high season of tourism, it will have some impact."

The economic slowdown in G3 countries and Thai political instability would also put the brake on growth for the remainder of the year.

"Unfortunately the internal factor will become one of the negative factors that will drag on growth in the second half," she said.

Atchana said central bank officials attending the two-day meeting at the Bank for International Settlements are focused on the rising dollar at a time when data showed the U.S. economy was slowing, and Monday's gathering will discuss this issue.

"What we are talking about is the dollar gaining some strength even though the U.S. economy's statistics that (have) come out lately showed we couldn't avoid an economic slowdown in the U.S.," she said.

"However, exports in Asia (are) holding up quite well." (Reporting by Tamora Vidaillet; Writing by Natsuko Waki; Editing by Quentin Bryar)

title: UPDATE 2-Thai emergency hits baht and shares, but bonds rise
text:
* Stocks fall 2.3 percent, hit lowest since Jan 2007

* Baht hits one-year low, central bank steps in

* Government bonds seen as safe haven with inflation peaking (Updates with closing stock market prices)

By Orathai Sriring

BANGKOK, Sept 2 (Reuters) - Thai stocks hit a 19-month low and the baht touched a one-year trough on Tuesday after the prime minister imposed emergency rule, but domestic government bonds rose as local investors sought safe haven for their funds.

Shares in the tourist sector took a hit after foreigners cancelled flights when some countries issued travel warnings, although Thai Airways rallied in late trade.

The benchmark SET index <.SETI> ended down 2.3 percent at 659.51 after touching 655.62, its lowest since January 2007. The market has lost 24.7 percent since street protests began on May 25.

Thai Prime Minister Samak Sundaravej declared a state of emergency in Bangkok on Tuesday and gave the army control of public order after a man died in overnight clashes between pro- and anti-government protesters. [ID:nSP172153].

"Announcing a state of emergency is proper and timely. But if you ask me if this is the beginning of the end? No, it isn't," said Puwadol Lapudomsuk, a senior strategist at Asia Plus Securities, adding he expected a gradual fall, not panic selling.

Kosin Sripaiboon at UOB KayHian Securities felt the same.

"Selling will be coming from both sides, foreign and local investors, but I don't really think panic selling will be as bad as when the former government imposed a 30 percent capital control measure," he said, referring to the record one-day fall of 14.8 percent in reaction to capital controls in December 2006.

Bourse chief Patareeya Benjapolchai remained calm. "The circuit breaker system will work automatically if the market falls sharply to a certain point but right now everything is manageable," he said.

INTERVENTION

The baht <THB=TH> was weaker, in line with other Asian currencies, at 34.49 per dollar in late trade after hitting a one-year low of 34.52.

The Bank of Thailand said it had intervened in the market to support the currency.

"The baht had weakened rapidly this morning, so we had to take care of it. If it is volatile, we will step in," Deputy Governor Atchana Waiquamdee told reporters.

Investors in Thailand's dollar-denominated bonds have taken fright at the political crisis, with anti-government supporters occupying the prime minister's official compound, but domestic bonds continued their recent strong run.

"Political noise reduces the attractiveness of risky alternatives to safe-haven government bonds," ING analyst Tim Condon said in a report.

The 10-year domestic bond yield <TH10YT=RR> shed 5 basis points to 4.45 percent bid. It has fallen around 180 bps from a June peak as investors took the view that both inflation and interest rates have peaked.

But five-year credit default swaps (CDS) <THAILD5UA=GFI> -- the cost of protecting against a default in Thailand's dollar-denominated debt -- widened by as much as 10 bps to 150.

The CDS later tightened to 146 bps, a Hong Kong trader said, meaning it would cost investors $146,000 to protect against $10 million of sovereign debt annually for five years.

On the stock market, shares in national carrier Thai Airways bounced back to end 4.4 percent higher at 14.30 baht after hitting a record low of 13.30 baht.

The national carrier's president said passengers were cancelling due to the unrest, but the share was helped by late bargain-hunting and another drop in fuel prices, dealers said.

Airports of Thailand was down 1.3 percent at 37 baht. Several airports were closed by protests at the end of last week but have now reopened.

Among big losers, top energy firm PTT fell 4.6 percent and market leader Bangkok Bank dropped 3.4 percent. title: Emerging  FX -Asia dips further on credit worries, strong dollar
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 26 (Reuters) - The South Korean won hit a fresh four-year low in weaker Asia on Tuesday as the U.S. dollar rose against the euro due to fears of a euro zone slowdown, while renewed concerns over credit markets stoked risk aversion.

The U.S. dollar climbed towards a six-month high against the euro <EUR=> as investors waited for European data releases later in the day for evidence of the health of the euro zone economy. The dollar also neared a two-year high against the pound <GBP=D4> hit on Monday.

The South Korean won <KRW=> fell by 1 percent to 1,089.40 per dollar, its weakest since mid-November 2004, as investors increased their short won positions on growth worries, undeterred by a prospect of intervention.

"Since the market sees that government actions are now useless, everybody is on the (dollar) bid side," a trader in Seoul said.

South Korean authorities were suspected of intervening to support the local currency in recent weeks, but the won is still the biggest loser among the Asian currencies, having lost 14 percent this year.

In Malaysia, traders said the central bank was spotted selling dollars to put a floor under the ringgit <MYR=>.

The ringgit fell as low as 3.393 per dollar to hit a nine-month low against the dollar, hurt by the central bank's decision on Monday to leave rates on hold despite rising inflation.

"CPI is so high but they haven't done anything to contain the inflation while other central banks in Asia are hiking rates," said one trader in Kuala Lumpur.

"And there is the Anwar election today. A lot of event risk," he said, referring to a by-election that opposition leader Anwar Ibrahim is contesting as he seeks to return to parliament.

MORE INTERVENTION

Traders in the Philippines also suspected authorities had intervened to support the peso <PHP=>, which fell 0.8 percent to an 11-month low of 46 against the broadly stronger dollar.

"The central bank was in the market at 45.88 and 45.98 per dollar, and now they are defending 46," a trader in Manila said.

Two other traders in Manila also confirmed the intervention.

"I think there's still demand for dollars. The market would rather hold dollar than peso," a second trader said.

Analysts at Lehman Brothers said they were watching several factors to determine currency movement in the region.

"For the rest of the week the focus will mainly be on testing key central bank intervention levels, the political theatre in Malaysia and Thailand, central bank meetings in Thailand and the Philippines, and slowing growth indicators," they said in a note.

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> extended early losses and dipped 0.6 percent to 1.4263 as market players speculated the central bank may shift its monetary policy away from battling inflation towards one more supportive of growth. "There is a lot of talk that the authorities may change the policy in October," a Singapore-based trader said. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: Emerging  FX -Asia trades narrowly, supported by  intervention
text:
SINGAPORE, July 1 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies traded narrowly on Tuesday as investors warily held back following decade-high inflation rates in Thailand and South Korea, while authorities were suspected to have intervened in some currencies.

Foreign exchange authorities in Indonesia, Malaysia, India and the Philippines were suspected to have intervened to support their currencies.

South Korea's annual inflation in June rose to 5.5 percent from 4.9 percent in May, hitting its highest in almost 10 years.

Subsequently, the Korean won <KRW=> weakened to 1,048.75 per dollar, 0.3 percent lower than its previous close of 1,046 <KRW=KFTC>, while market players kept a look-out for possible dollar-selling intervention.

Earlier on, several currencies in the region were buoyed by a pullback in oil prices <CLc1>, which hit a record high above $143 per barrel on Monday, but these currencies gave up gains as oil prices rebounded to around $141 per barrel on Tuesday.

Still, the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> inched up by 0.1 percent to 9,215 against the dollar and held around those levels throughout the day.

Traders in Jakarta said the authorities had sold dollars everyday for the past few weeks to support the rupiah, and were doing the same on Tuesday.

"The government cannot subsidise our local oil, and this has caused higher inflation, so another way to (support growth) is to maintain the dollar/rupiah pairing at a cozy rate so our industries can run well," an Indonesia-based trader said.

Indonesia's annual inflation rate rose to a 21-month high of 11.03 percent in June, due largely to the lifting of fuel subsidies in the country.

The country's policy setting meeting will take place on Thursday, and Robert Prior-Wandesforde at HSBC said he expected a 25-basis-point hike in the present interest rate of 8.5 percent.

"We are expecting another quarter-point move on Thursday and a total of 125 basis points of hikes by the end of this year, taking the policy rate up to 9.75 percent," the economist said.

Thailand's consumer prices in June rose 8.9 percent from a year earlier, higher than the expected 8.5 percent polled in a Reuters survey. However, markets in Thailand were closed for a mid-year holiday.

MORE INTERVENTION CITED

The Indian rupee <INR=IN> fell to a 15-month low of 43.437 on heightened concerns over the impact of rising oil on the economy's growth. Traders said they suspected the central bank had been selling dollars early in the day.

Traders in Manila also cited intervention by the Philippine central bank to support the peso <PHP=>, which hit a 9-month low of 45.02.

"The central bank is protecting the peso around 44.99 to 45 per dollar," a trader said.

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> steadied around its previous closing levels of 3.265 per dollar, and traders said they suspected the Malaysian central bank had sold dollars to support the ringgit at 3.267-per-dollar throughout the day.

"Seems foreigners are not willing to touch this currency in the short term until political news is gone," a trader in Kuala Lumpur said.

Leader of Malaysia's revitalised opposition, Anwar Ibrahim, recently sought refuge at the Turkish embassy following sodomy accusations. The former deputy premier fled to the embassy fearing for his security. [ID:nKLR151860]

title: Emerging  FX -Asia rises on Fed rate view, mood cautious
text:
SINGAPORE, June 26 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose on Thursday after the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady and dampened expectations for an imminent rate rise, but buying interest remained fragile after recent sell-off.

The Fed held interest rates at 2 percent on Wednesday, as widely expected, and signalled it was no rush to raise them, even as it voiced greater concerns about inflation. [ID:nN25433059]

Reduced prospects of a U.S. rate rise weighed on the dollar and made higher-yielding emerging markets currencies more appealing.

The Philippine peso <PHP=> rose as far as 44.40 per dollar, up about 0.4 percent from Wednesday's close.

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose as far as 1.3643 per U.S. dollar, up a fifth of a percent from late Asian trade on Wednesday.

A Singapore-based trader said the view that the Fed was in no rush to raise rates prodded investors to buy the Singapore dollar, which is expected to trade between 1.3630 and 1.3720 for the day.

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> rose to 3.2520 per dollar, up more than 0.3 percent from late Asian trade on Wednesday.

"The risk appetite has picked up -- note rallies in stocks, tighter spreads, lower volatility and a generally softer U.S. dollar," said Thio Chin Loo, currency strategist at BNP Paribas.

The MSCI index of stocks in the Asia-Pacific region excluding Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> edged up about 0.4 percent.

Still, investors remain cautious after the recent selling of Asian currencies spurred by foreign sales of regional stocks amid inflation worries stoked by record high oil prices, and a broad rise in the dollar.

"Asian currencies are not breaking ranges yet, with oil still weighing and inflation concerns not fading," said Han Sia Yeo, currency strategist at Bank of America.

BULLISH ON TAIWAN DOLLAR

The Thai baht <THB=TH> rose a fifth of a percent to 33.50 per dollar as traders cited dollar-selling intervention by the Bank of Thailand (BoT) to support the local currency.

"They sold (dollars) from 33.60 to 33.55," said one Bangkok-based trader.

Central banks in South Korea, Thailand, the Philippines and India have in recent week sold dollars to support their currencies out of fear that their weakness would stoke inflation.

Elsewhere, the Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> rose a quarter of a percent to a one-week high at 30.30 per U.S. dollar, as the market expected the central bank to raise interest rates by at least 12.5 basis points in its drawn out campaign to curb inflation. [ID:nHKG261850]

The South Korean won <KRW=>, the region's worst performer, briefly rose to 1,033.9 per dollar.

Westpac strategist Sean Callow suggested investors should go short on the won against the dollar via non-deliverable forwards.

"The Taiwan dollar is more resilient, backed by stronger current account position and far less gloomy foreign sentiment over Taiwan stocks than Korean stocks," he said in a note.

The Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> hit a post-revaluation high at 8.8612 per dollar as policy makers are seen still favouring the steady rise in the currency to help quell inflation.

title: 2nd UPDATE: Thai  Central Bank  Ready To Hike At July Meeting
text:
(Adds Governor's comment on baht, interest rates, Vietnam's dong currency.)

By Phisanu Phromchanya

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Thailand is ready to take monetary policy action to tackle high inflation and doesn't believe a rate hike will hurt economic growth much, the central bank's governor Tarisa Watanagase said Monday.

The hawkish comments will reinforce market expectations of an interest rate hike in the near future but Tarisa ruled out calling an early meeting of the Monetary Policy Committee. It's next slated to meet on July 16.

Any increase in the policy interest rate is unlikely to have a significant impact on spending or economic growth, Tarisa told reporters.

"Our real interest rate is negative, therefore if there is any hike in the policy interest rate, any affect on spending and economic growth won't be much," she said at a hastily-called press conference.

Central bank officials last week said inflation could reach a double-digit level this year, creating worries among market participants that the bank would announce a surprise inter-meeting rate hike. The last time the Bank of Thailand changed the policy rate between meetings was after the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks in the U.S..

Thailand's benchmark interest rate has been unchanged at a growth-accommodative 3.25% since August last year to support an economy battered by the political troubles that culminated in the ouster of Thaksin Shinawatra as prime minister in a September 2006 coup.

Tarisa said financial markets have already responded to the signal sent by the last meeting of the MPC in May, when the committee warned it would tighten monetary policy if inflation continued to accelerate.

Major commercial banks raised key deposit and lending rates earlier this month while bond yields have risen sharply in anticipation that the central bank would raise the policy rate to dampen fast rising prices.

Inflation hit a decade high of 7.6% in May as record oil prices fed broad-based price increases.

The governor downplayed the chances of double-digit inflation. "It is possible that inflation may hit double digits in certain months depending on the movement in oil prices) but the chance is rather slim," she said.

The issues of whether the central bank should target headline inflation and whether it needs to change the inflation target band will be studied by a new MPC later this year, Tarisa said.

Membership of the MPC will change by the end of August following implementation of the recently passed Bank of Thailand Act

The central bank targets core inflation within a zero to 3.5% band.

On the currency front, Tarisa said the baht has become more stable lately and the central bank will continue to ensure that it moves in line with regional currencies.

Last week, the Bank of Thailand intervened in the foreign exchange market to limit the baht's depreciation and curb excessive volatility after noticing that foreign banks and offshore branches of local banks were speculating on the currency.

Tarisa said the recent baht weakness was due partly to portfolio outflows and concerns over domestic political instability.

The softer baht was in line with the regional currency trend, with Southeast Asian currencies weighed by concerns over devaluation of the Vietnam dong and lower risk appetite amid expectations that U.S. rates have already reached their bottom, she said.

 The overall decrease was led by an $6.86 billion dip in Japan's reserves, the second straight monthly decline, as higher U.S. yields cut the value of bonds in Japan's reserves while the euro's fall versus the dollar also dented the stockpile.

 South Korea's reserves fell by $2.28 billion, possibly due to the dollar-selling intervention by the authorities to prop up the won <KRW=>.

 Other central banks in the Philippines, India, Thailand and Indonesia have also intervened in the market in recent weeks to limit the declines in their currencies out of concern that further weakess could stoke inflationary risks.

 That marks a shift from Asian central banks' traditional dollar-buying intervention to keep their exchange rates competitive, resulting in the rapid build-up of their reserves.

title: WRAPUP 2-Asian central banks  intervene  to defend  currencies
text:
* Central banks defend currencies from capital outflows

* Thai central bank says speculators bet against baht

* Pressure mounts on regional currencies from strong dollar and inflation

SINGAPORE, June 10 (Reuters) - Central banks in Thailand, India and South Korea stepped into markets once again on Tuesday to defend their falling currencies from a rallying dollar and foreign capital outflows spurred by worries over inflation.

Two traders in Bangkok said the Bank of Thailand had intervened again to help the baht recover from Monday's 5-month low of 33.41 per dollar. The central bank also sold dollars on Monday.

"Intervention persists," said a trader in Bangkok. "I think they want to repel speculators."

The Bank of Thailand subsequently confirmed it had intervened to slow the baht's fall and would continue to defend the currency if it remained volatile.

Up to four foreign speculators had tried to bet against the baht, Bank of Thailand Assistant Governor Suchada Kirakul told reporters.

The baht <THB=TH> rebounded to 32.93 per dollar, up about 0.9 percent from late Asian trade on Monday. It has fallen more than 3.5 percent in the past 3 weeks.

The won <KRW=> jumped about 1 percent as two traders said the authorities were believed to be selling dollars. It hit levels as high as 1,020.9 per dollar, having at one point traded below 1,031.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was seen selling dollars around 42.92 per dollar after the currency weakened on concerns foreigners may pull out more from local stocks amid growing risk aversion.

The rupee <INR=IN> also recovered from an early low of 42.93, but stayed weaker than Monday's close of 42.87/88.

Philippine traders suspected the central bank there too had sold dollars to pull the peso <PHP=> back from 44.45 per dollar, its weakest since October.

But the currency was unable to sustain its gains, ending local trade at 44.425 per dollar.

Currencies in the region have been under pressure from rising oil and commodity prices, which have highlighted the pressures on trade and fiscal balances and raised concerns monetary authorities are behind the curve on fighting inflation.

There was further selling pressure on the regionals on Tuesday from the dollar's broad rally driven by Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke's remarks on the dangers from inflation.

"We expect this (intervention) to remain the main source of support for Asia FX in the near term, even if it may be temporary rather than a measure that will change the trend," Lehman Brothers said in a note to clients.

Lehman said there would, however, be a divergence among the Asian currencies as a worsening growth and inflation backdrop weighed on portfolio flows, with currencies such as the Singapore dollar and Taiwan dollar expected to fare better than some of the others. title: UPDATE 1-INTERVIEW-Thai cenbank in market to stem baht fall
text:
(Adds details, quotes)

BANGKOK, June 6 (Reuters) - The Bank of Thailand (BoT) intervened in the market on Friday to stem a sharp fall in the baht, and is ready to prevent any future excessive moves in the currency, Assistant Governor Suchada Kirakula said on Friday.

"The baht really weakened too fast today, but don't panic," Suchada told Reuters.

"You have to believe the central bank is taking care (of the baht) to prevent its volatility," she said, adding she expected the baht weakness to slow on Monday.

The baht <THB=TH> hit 33.10/18 to the dollar on Friday, more than a 4-month low and down from 32.87/89 on Thursday. However, it has still risen 1.7 percent against the dollar so far this year.

Suchada said the baht's recent weakness was due to dollar buying by oil importers and equities-linked capital outflows.

Foreign investors have sold 26 billion baht ($785 million) net of Thai shares so far this year due to concerns about renewed political conflict and rising inflation. They bought 55 billion net of Thai stocks in 2007.

Anti-government protests on the streets of Bangkok worried investors about a repeat of the September 2006 military coup that ousted Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra.

Suchada suggested exporters and importers should hedge and not focus on specific baht levels.

Thailand's economic fundamentals were still strong despite soaring inflation and renewed political uncertainty, she said, pointing to $2 billion in foreign direct investment in the first quarter of 2008.

"Our economic fundamentals are not bad," she said.

Suchada said the central bank would continue its current inflation-targeting policy.

Annual headline inflation surged to near a 10-year high of 7.6 percent in May, up from 6.2 percent in April, raising expectations that the central bank will raise its policy rate later this year after keeping it at 3.25 percent since July last year.

On establishing a sovereign wealth fund, Suchada said the Finance Ministry was studying the plan, but she did not expect that in the short term.

"It's probably not a hot issue now," she said without elaborating, citing the weaker baht.

Funds are popular among other emerging countries seeking ways to increase returns in growing foreign reserves. Thailand had $108.9 billion in foreign reserves and $18.8 billion in net forward positions as of May 30. ($1=33.10 Baht) (Editing by George Obulutsa and Gerrard Raven)

title: Emerging  FX -Korea won leads Asian rebound ahead of Fed
text:
SINGAPORE, March 18 (Reuters) - The South Korean won jumped on Tuesday amid suspected central bank efforts to prop up the ailing currency, leading a rebound among Asian currencies ahead of an expected Fed interest rate cut later in the day.   

The South Korean won <KRW=> rose as far as 1,008.9 per dollar, up almost 2 percent from late Asian trade on Monday, as dealers said the foreign exchange authorities may have sold some $1 billion during the morning session to support the won.   

Earlier, Deputy Finance Minister Shin Je-yoon warned against the won's sharp falls versus the dollar and vowed to take measures to smooth its volatility.   

The currency tumbled just over 3 percent in the previous session, as investors sold Asian currencies on fears of the spreading credit crisis after news of the sale of investment bank  Bear Stearns and the Fed's emergency discount-rate cut.   

"We still see negative risks for the won," said David Mann, currency strategist at Standard Chartered Bank.   

"The U.S. credit crisis is playing a role in the funding problems in Korea," he said, expecting the won to fall further to 1,032 in the near term.   

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> briefly hit 9,220 per dollar, up nearly 0.9 percent from late Asian trade on Monday.   

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose as far as 1.3785 per U.S. dollar, up nearly half of a percent from late Asian trade on Monday, as investors positioned for a hefty interest rate cut by the Federal Reserve later in the day.   

"The market expects a rate cut between 0.75 and 1 percentage point, and it's most likely they have to give in to market demand," said a trader in Singapore.   

The Fed on Sunday announced emergency measures to stem a global credit crisis, including cutting its discount rate to 3.25 percent from 3.5 percent and approving special financing to help  JPMorgan acquire the beleaguered  Bear Stearns.

The Fed is widely expected to slash its benchmark interest rate, currently at 3 percent, at its policy meeting on Tuesday.   

WIDENING RATE GAPS   

The move would further widen the interest rate differentials between the United States and Asian countries, which could in turn help spur capital inflows into the region, analysts say.   

Policy interest rates in emerging Asian countries range from 3.25 percent in Thailand to 8 percent in Indonesia.   

The Thai baht <THB=TH> gained 0.8 percent to 31.13 per dollar, its highest since August 1997, as exporters and investors sold the dollar in anticipation of the Fed's rate cut.   

"If FOMC (Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee) cuts fed funds rate tonight by 100 basis points and BOT does not cut is interest rate, it should spur capital inflows by widening the interest differential," said a Bangkok-based trader.   

Some traders cited suspected dollar-buying intervention by the Bank of Thailand (BOT) to slow the rise in the baht, the top performer in emerging Asia that has gained 8 percent this year.   

The won, the worst performer, has lost 7.7 percent this year.   

Elsewhere, the Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> fell to 7.0871 per dollar, down slightly from its post-revaluation high of 7.0815 hit on Monday.   

But analysts believe the yuan is on track to gain about 10 percent in the whole of 2008 as Beijing tries to tame inflation, which hit 8.7 percent, the highest pace in nearly 12 years.   

Premier Wen Jiabao said on Tuesday that he was confident rising prices could be controlled this year, but he conceded that the government's target of limiting annual inflation at 4.8 percent in 2008 would not be easily achieved. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0755 GMT

title: UPDATE: Thai BOT: No Unusual Inflows As Cap Controls Removed
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Bank of Thailand Governor Tarisa Watanagase said Tuesday that the central bank saw no unusual inflows following the removal of capital control measures the previous day, and she is satisfied with the results.   

"The effect of the removal of the controls isn't different from what we had expected and I'm satisfied with it," Tarisa said in a television program broadcast early Tuesday on the local Channel 9, run by the state-owned  MCOT PCL (MCOT.TH).   

After some initial volatility in government bonds, Thai markets reacted calmly to the elimination Monday of controls including a 30% withholding on short-term capital inflows and an exemption from the 30% rule for fully-hedged foreign investment in local debt.   

However, Tarisa warned that if necessary, the central bank could impose the controversial measures again.   

"We have the measure right in our pocket. It is possible that we could impose it again if we find that necessary, although we have no intention to do so for now," she said.   

Assistant Governor Suchada Kirakul admitted late Monday that the central bank stepped into the foreign exchange market to smooth the transition, but Tarisa said in the interview that no unusual capital inflows had been detected.   

The governor said the baht weakened slightly on Monday in line with regional currencies, under pressure from widespread selling in global equities.   

Exporters did not resort to panic-selling of U.S. dollars after the removal of controls, while importers have been accumulating dollars, she said.   

Traders said the dollar ended Monday at THB31.60 on the onshore market, up from THB31.50 late Friday due to aggressive intervention by the central bank. The Stock Exchange of Thailand index closed down 0.3% and bonds finished mostly flat after an initial flurry of buying. At 0341 GMT Tuesday, the dollar was at THB31.65, and the SET Index was up 0.3% at 845.00 points.   

Tarisa said some foreign funds did flow into local bonds Monday following the removal of controls.   

However, investors looking for Thai interest rates to fall didn't find anything in the governor's comments to support their hopes.   

Analysts had generally expected interest rates to drop in order to reduce pressure on the baht to appreciate, but a growing number are coming around to the view that rising inflation will limit the central bank's flexibility.   

Tarisa said Thailand's policy rate of 3.25% is already among the lowest in the region, and any decision on interest rates will be up to the Monetary Policy Committee, which will have to weigh inflation and economic risks as well as foreign exchange.   

Consumer price index inflation accelerated to a 20-month high at 5.4% on year in February on rising prices of fuel and food. The MPC meets next on April 9.

title: Thai Baht Falls On  Intervention  Despite Cap Control Removal
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The baht fell against the U.S. dollar Monday but Thailand's other markets reacted calmly to the removal of controversial controls on short-term capital inflows.   

The dollar ended the day at THB31.60 on the onshore market, up from THB31.50 late Friday, thanks to aggressive intervention on both the local and offshore markets, while the stock market closed down 0.3% and the bonds finished flat.   

Economists said markets had already factored in the end of the capital controls which was announced Friday and said the lifting of the measures wouldn't have a longer-term impact on Thailand's economy or markets either.   

"The reality is the thrust of the existing controls have already been blunted considerably and the removal is unlikely to provide any substantial economic lift,"  Goldman Sachs said.   

The end of capital controls - first imposed in December 2006 - is leading to some convergence between the onshore and offshore baht exchange rate although a rally in the baht was prevented by hectic intervention, dealers said.   

The Bank of Thailand's assistant governor Suchada Kirakul said the bank stepped into the foreign exchange market Monday to smooth the baht's intraday direction.   

In late Asian trade, the U.S. dollar was quoted offshore at THB31.55-THB31.60 versus THB31.10 late Friday.   

"The central bank seems to be the only buyer supporting the dollar both in onshore and offshore markets," a foreign exchange dealer at a foreign bank in Thailand said.   

The central bank Monday sent a circular to local banks asking them to avoid transactions that may involve currency speculation to prevent excessive baht volatility.   

"The circular wasn't helping much to calm the baht, it's the massive intervention that did the job," said a dealer at a local bank.   

The dollar is expected to be rangebound between THB31.50-THB31.70 in the near term.   

While analysts agree the two rates will eventually converge, some argue the offshore market may not disappear entirely given central bank rules that restrict baht liquidity and curb capital inflows.  JPMorgan said the central bank may now attempt to enforce a less clearly delineated two-tier foreign exchange market.   

Stock Market Looking Overseas   

Meanwhile, Thailand's main stock index closed down 0.3% at 842.92 points, off its intraday high of 849.49.   

"Sentiment was dampened by losses in external bourses. However, our performance is still considered good in relative to regional markets," said Bualuang Securities strategist Chaiyaporn Nompitakcharoen.   

"We could say that the (removal of capital control) measure did help limit our loss today."   

The SET Index is expected to move in a tight range between 840-850 points Tuesday with traders still cautious about the health of U.S. economy and its financial sector. However, optimism over the Thai government's economic stimulus package - expected to be announced Tuesday -is expected to limit any downside, he said.   

Thai government bonds rallied in early trading, dragging yields down by 15 basis points, thanks to buying from foreign investors now that their local bond investment is no longer subject to capital controls.   

"The removal of reserve requirement rules had a positive impact onthe bond market and we have seen some foreign players starting to accumulate short-term bonds," said local bond dealer.   

However, early gains were later erased as profit taking kicked in following the release of inflation data, which dimmed hopes for a quick interest rate cut. That is likely to prevent any big fall in yields going forward.   

Thailand's inflation rate rose to a 20-month high of 5.4% in February due to higher food and fuel prices. The core consumer price index, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 1.5% in February from the same month a year earlier.   

High oil prices, a healthy recovery in domestic consumption and investment and the government's expansionary fiscal policy is likely to fuel inflation in coming months too.   

"The key question now is whether fears of a strong baht would prompt the BOT (Bank of Thailand) to cut rates and how far the government would go in pressuring the BOT to cut rates. Our stance is that the BOT should not cut now and probably doesn't want to cut either," DBS said in a report Monday.   

The decision to remove the capital controls came within weeks of the formation of Thailand's first elected government since the September 2006 coup that ousted Thaksin Shinawatra as prime minister.   

During campaigning for the Dec. 23 elections, the pro-Thaksin People Power Party, which now leads a six-party coalition, vowed to abolish the controls to boost Thailand's reputation with foreign investors.

title: INSTANT VIEW 2-Thailand to lift capital controls
text:
BANGKOK, Feb 29 (Reuters) - Thailand's central bank said on Friday it would lift capital controls imposed in December 2006 to rein in the baht <THB=TH> , with effect from March 3.   

The offshore rate for the baht immediately moved closer to the onshore rate in reaction to the news.

allowed the controls to be lifted.   

For details, click [nBKT000594] [nBKT000595] [nBKT000596]   

COMMENTARY:   

USARA WILAIPICH, ECONOMIST, STANDARD CHARTERED BANK:   

"Markets are playing on a possible lifting of capital controls. A gap between offshore and onshore markets is narrowing with the expectations and people think the cutting of policy interest rateS by the Bank of Thailand is underway." KOSIN SRIPAIBOON, HEAD OF RESEARCH AT UOB KAYHIAN SECURITIES:   

"Overall, it should be positive to the country as it will attract more money inflows, but the lifting should hurt exports and imports and the central bank should have measures to help.   

"The lifting comes at a time when the government is planning to hold roadshows soon. The government wants to restore foreign investor confidence. We should see more money inflows into both stock and bond markets, as well as direct investments.   

"The index rose instantly after the Bank of Thailand planned to hold a conference, rising from 838 to go through 840 points.   

"It should lift the main index further, but just in the short term, as investors have already priced in the central bank's planned announcement."   

KONGKIAT OPASWONGKARN, CHIEF EXECUTIVE, ASIA PLUS SECURITIES:   

"Finally, the day we've been waiting for has come.   

"Like everyone else, the lifting is no surprise. The government made it clear they would lift it even before they got elected."   

"For a starter, the controls are not working. If they had really worked, the baht had to be weaker than this. Second, it's something totally opposite to the pro-growth policy of the government.   

"What's next is what the government would do with the Foreign Business Act. The stock market should react positively to this next week, but I don't think there'll be a dramatic surge."   

SEAN CALLOW, STRATEGIST, WESTPAC BANK, SINGAPORE:   

"Very much welcomed and not before time, mind you.   

"I think the relatively anti-business, anti-foreign attitude of the military-appointed government has ensured that there is no flood of foreign capital ready to pour back into Thailand.   

"But a positive step nonetheless, a win for the new government.   

"I wonder if there will be any accompanying measures to help exporters."   

CALLUM HENDERSON, HEAD OF FX STRATEGY, STANDARD CHARTERED BANK, SINGAPORE:   

"Offshore will converge towards the onshore price.   

"Details are unclear at this point, in terms of the URR and the special accounts, what has been scrapped and what is still    


there. For now the market assumes everything is gone -- that
may not necessarily be right -- and onshore baht will converge
   

to offshore baht."   

CLAUDIO PIRON, CURRENCY STRATEGIST AT JPMORGAN IN SINGAPORE:   

"The obvious move is underway - that is the convergence between offshore baht toward the onshore rate, driven by the prospect of renewed access to onshore liquidity.   

"The wider implication is that Thailand will reenter in to investable bond indices, such as  JPMorgan's GBI-EM local currency fixed income index.   

"The resultant inflows could cause the local bond curve to flatten. The Bank of Thailand can of course be expected to intervene, with FX accumulation already running at 30 percent in a year-on-year terms.   

"Also note last statement that they have alternative measures to stabilise the baht. So there may yet be a twist in the tail.   

MARKET:   

- The baht weakened in offshore trading, moving closer to the onshore levels for the currency.   

In offshore deals, the baht <THB=W> moved to 30.90 per dollar from the day's highs of 29.70 and levels near 30.05 before the announcement.   

In onshore trading, the baht <THB=TH> moved up to 31.35 from levels of 31.90 prior to the Bank of Thailand press conference.   

BACKGROUND   

- The capital controls were imposed in December 2006 to curb speculation in the baht, which rose 14 percent against the dollar that year. It rose another 7 percent in 2007 despite the controls and has risen 5 percent so far this year.   

- The controls led to the emergence of a two-tier market in the baht, one onshore <THB=TH> and one offshore <THB=W>. The baht was firmer in the offshore market.   

- The controls required in particular that 30 percent of all currency inflows without underlying business deals should be deposited with the central bank, interest free, for a year.   

- The stock exchange fell nearly 15 percent in immediate reaction to the controls, the market's biggest one-day fall, prompting the Bank of Thailand quickly to exempt equity investments. Other exemptions followed in time.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia mostly up, Singapore dollar at 11-year high
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 22 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies rose on Friday amid expectations of further U.S. interest rate cuts, with the Singapore dollar hitting an 11-year peak, the Thai baht at a 10-1/2-year high and the Taiwan dollar at a 2-1/2-year high.   

The rate outlook overshadowed more bearish news on the U.S. economy in the shape of the Philadelphia Federal Reserve's business index for February, which showed an unexpectedly deep contraction in activity.   

"Looks as though dollar weakness is outweighing risk aversion," said Sean Callow, a currency strategist at  Westpac Banking Corporation.

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose 0.3 percent to hit an 11-year high of 1.4070 per dollar, but it met some resistance there despite traders' expectations that the central bank will allow further gains in the currency to help contain inflation.   

One trader in Singapore said its rise was checked by fears of central bank intervention, although he suspected the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had not yet intervened.   

"I think MAS might be looking to intervene, just as there was some suspicion of intervention at 1.41 earlier this week," he said.   

Inflation in Singapore hit a 25-year high of 4.4 percent in December, leaving the central bank with a dilemma as it has to balance the need to control inflationary pressures with slowing economic growth.   

"Do I let the Singapore dollar run rampant to cool off imported inflation? Or do I try to weaken it to help my sagging domestic exports, which are only going to get worse with each bad print in U.S. economic numbers?" said a dealer in Singapore.   

Inflation data for January is due on Monday and analysts at DBS expect a further jump to 6.6 percent due to increased transport, food and oil costs.   

The Thai baht <THB=TH> hit a 10-1/2-year high of 32.30 per dollar in onshore trading, and traders said the central bank had been buying dollars to halt a rise fuelled by rising export receipts.   

"The reality is that the Bank of Thailand has had to intervene aggressively to counter appreciation pressure that has switched away from capital flows into current account surplus pressure," analysts at  JPMorgan said in a note.   

The currency tops the list of gainers in the region for 2008, having risen 4.2 percent so far this year.   

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> climbed as far as 31.30 per U.S. dollar, its highest since June 2005, a day after Taiwan announced higher-than-expected fourth-quarter GDP growth.   

The currency has also been helped by recent government initiatives to improve relations with China, including a proposal to allow mainland Chinese to buy property in Taiwan and for local firms to invest more in China,  UBS said in a report.

title: Unclear fate of Thai controls pushing baht higher
text:
BANGKOK, Feb 19 (Reuters) - Thailand's lack of clarity on the fate of its capital controls has fueled speculation in the baht, pushing the currency higher and threatening exports, the Thai Chamber of Commerce said on Tuesday.   

The Bank of Thailand's near daily market intervention was not working and it should take more concrete steps to rein in the baht, now at 10-year highs against the dollar, senior chamber official Chainant Ukosakul told reporters.   

"It is said the baht's rise is due to arguments among policy makers and a lack of clarity on the 30-percent measure," he said, of the measure requiring 30 percent of foreign inflows to be held at the central bank for a year, interest free.   

"That is worrying to manufacturers and fuelling speculation in the baht. Policy makers have to be clear on the issue rather than hold daily talks," Chainant said.   

Prime Minister Samak Sundaravaej said last week his government would need 2 months to review the curbs imposed in December 2006 to contain a surging baht but which tarnished Thailand's investment reputation.   

The Bank of Thailand, which for months resisted calls to remove the controls, has appealed to exporters to stop speculating in the currency, but to no avail.   

The baht, which developed into a two-tier market after capital controls were imposed, was at 32.5 against the dollar onshore <THB=TH> and at 31.7 offshore <THB=W> by 0903 GMT.   

The onshore rate has risen 3.6 percent so far this year, the highest in Asia after a 7 percent rise last year.   

The baht rose nearly 14 percent in 2006 when the controls were imposed to protect Thai exports, which account for more than 60 percent of gross domestic product.   

The measures have been gradually relaxed over the past year, but experts say a sudden lifting of the remaining curbs could trigger an influx of foreign capital flows and push the baht to 30 per dollar.   

That has fuelled calls for alternative measures such as an exit tax, Aat Pisanwanich, a director at the University of the Thai Chamber of Commerce, said.   

Chainant expected the baht to average 32.50 against the dollar this year, which would trim export growth to 4.6 percent.   

"But if the baht hits 30, exports will surely turn negative," he said.   

The Commerce Ministry expected exports to grow 10-12.5 percent this year after a 17.5 percent rise last year.   

Aat said manufacturers need a stable, slightly weaker currency, lower production costs and a recovery in domestic demand, which has plumbed record lows during two years of political strife and a bloodless 2006 coup.   

"This year foreign exchange rates will have a big impact -- bigger than oil -- on production, job cuts and production base relocation," he said, refering to speculation that some manufacturers may move elsewhere. title: FX  Asia: Clock Ticks On Baht Controls But Big Bang Unlikely
text:
By Phisanu Phromchanya   

A Dow Jones Newswires Column   

BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Removal of Thailand's controversial capital controls now appears only a matter of time but the approach is likely to be step by step, rather than a big bang, to minimize appreciation pressure on the baht.   

Investors are howling for the controls to be abolished and Thailand's new pro-investment government would be happy to oblige right away. But it also wants to avoid a messy confrontation with a reluctant central bank and nervous exporters.   

The Bank of Thailand has intervened massively over the past year to slow the baht's rise - driven by the country's gaping trade surplus - and has consistently argued its job would be even harder without the controls.   

Some analysts disagree. The requirement for 30% of short-term inflows to be held on deposit at the central bank for a year has been steadily watered down since its shock imposition in December 2006 and now has minimal effect on money flows, they say.   

"If the controls are removed I don't see foreign investors rushing in and saying: 'Thank goodness I can speculate on the baht again, we really miss that.' There are lots of other Asian currencies with far less erratic policy making and to be frank, better fundamentals too," said Sean Callow, currency strategist at Westpac Bank.   

Still, policymakers are likely to remain cautious. Following the return of democratic government, foreign money is again flowing into Thai stocks. Removal of the controls, though they hardly affect stocks directly, is expected to rehabilitate Thailand's reputation with investors and accelerate speculative inflows.   

"We view a full removal of capital controls as unlikely in an environment where the central bank is already having to lean heavily against THB strength,"  JPMorgancurrency strategist Claudio Piron said in a research note.   

"A compromise to further loosen capital controls appears likely with a promise for eventual liberalization, but appetite to restore a one-tier market on onshore and offshore USD/THB is likely to remain low."   

Hoping to stem the baht's rapid gains, the central bank imposed the 30% reserve requirement three months after the bloodless military coup that ousted prime minister Thaksin Shinawatra in September 2006. The move triggered the largest single-day fall on Thailand's stock market and was an unmitigated disaster for the country's investment reputation.   

Expectations Dashed   

The reserve requirement has been relaxed several times and only remains in place for investment in bonds, property funds and swap transactions with local banks. But use of special accounts and hedges means investments in bonds and funds can also qualify for exemption.   

With some market participants anticipating imminent removal of the controls, the offshore dollar/baht has rallied since mid-January, narrowing the spread between offshore and onshore spot rates to less than 3% now from over 10% at the beginning of this year.   

Early Thursday, the dollar was trading onshore at a new 10-year low of THB32.85 and offshore was quoted at THB32.11-THB32.19.   

Many experts estimate that dollar onshore would immediately drop to between THB32.00 and THB32.50 if the controls were removed without offsetting measures and some say it could even fall to THB31.00.   

"The removal of capital control rules would draw some foreign inflows into the bond market for speculating on the baht and enjoying the gap between local and overseas interest rates," said Vorapak Tanyawong,  JPMorgan's senior country officer for Thailand.   

If removal was done without steps such as first reducing the interest rate spread between Thailand and the U.S., the dollar would fall as much as THB1, he said.  JPMorgan currently forecasts the dollar onshore will be at THB32.50 by the end of 2008.   

Local foreign exchange dealers said most market participants have already factored in the possibility that the controls will be removed and exporters have unloaded much of their dollar holdings, fearing a spike in the baht when the capital controls are dropped.   

But expectations of immediate removal were dashed Tuesday following a meeting between new Finance Minister Surapong Suebwonglee and Bank of Thailand Governor Tarisa Watanagase.   

Surapong said he needs more information from the central bank but promised to announce a decision before the government holds a policy roadshow that's slated for March or April.   

"The signs are really there that one way or the other, the clock is ticking on the reserve requirement," said  Westpac's Callow.   

"I don't think it will take too much longer even if the Bank of Thailand resists. It was never a permanent solution. The new government has a mandate and an intention to present a friendlier face to the world," he said.   

Phased Removal   

Some analysts think removal of the controls will be a phased event that may not begin until the second half of the year and will be preceded by interest rate cuts that minimize the interest rate gap between Thailand and the U.S.   

Standard Chartered economist Usara Wilaipich expects the reserve requirement to first be lifted for investment in bonds as the government's funding requirement is set to increase.   

She said there's about a 50% probability that this will happen in the second half, giving the Bank of Thailand plenty of time to match aggressive easing by the U.S. Federal Reserve.   

Usara's second scenario, for which she sees a 40% chance, involves the reserve requirement being removed in the near future and the Bank of Thailand making an inter-meeting cut to the policy rate of at least a quarter percentage point. The bank's next policy rate meeting is slated for Feb. 27.   

By the second half of the year the Bank of Thailand may also be under less pressure to intervene aggressively as an expected pickup in domestic demand will help reduce the trade surplus.   

"We expect the Bank of Thailand to remain vigilant in the foreign exchange market, but the need to intervene significantly will be less and less once imports start to pick up," said  HSBC economist Frederic Neumann.

title: Emerging  FX -Asians fall, but Thai baht at 10-yr high
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 21 (Reuters) - Asian currencies fell on Monday, led by the South Korean won and the Malaysian ringgit, as world share markets continued to slide because of fears of a possible U.S. recession.   

The Thai baht <THB=> bucked the trend and hit a 10-year high after news on the weekend that the party backed by ousted Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra had won enough support from coalition partners to form the next government. Thai stocks also gained. Elsewhere, investors shunned risky assets after U.S. President George W. Bush's plan of temporary tax cuts and other measures worth up to $150 billion to aid the faltering economy failed to assuage fears of a downturn.   

A recent spate of dismal earnigns reports by major banks hit by write-downs linked to the subprime crisis, also added to market gloom.

"Foreign investors in the equity market are selling shares, which has continued from the start of this year. This acts as a buying pressure for the dollar," said Nam Kyu Kim, a trader at ING Singapore.

BAHT, YUAN BUCK TREND   

Buoyed by the political news, the Thai baht <THB=TH> in onshore trades matched a 10-year high hit last week at 33.00 per dollar, but a suspected central bank intervention capped any further gains.   

"I suspect that BOT (Bank of Thailand) intervened today, at 33.03 first then all the way up," said a Bangkok-based trader.   

Assistant BOT Governor Suchada Kirakul said on Monday that the baht was rising too fast due to exporters' dollar sales and capital controls were still needed.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia gains, Thailand denies policy change
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 4 (Reuters) - Asian currencies managed some light gains on Tuesday and regional stock markets also rose despite increasing market jitters about the U.S. mortgage sector.   

The U.S. dollar was supported by expectations the Federal Reserve will cut rates by as much as half a percentage point when it meets on Dec. 11, therefore providing support to the economy.   

But risk aversion was heightened, causing high-yielders such as the Aussie dollar to fall, amid mounting concerns that already tight short-term money markets will get squeezed further as the year-end approaches.   

Thai currency policy was in focus on Tuesday after a newspaper report that the central bank had shifted policy from a managed float to guiding the baht against a trade-weighted basket of currencies. The central bank denied the report.   

The currency <THB=TH>, which offshore players barely trade after last year's imposition of capital controls, stayed steady around 33.84 per dollar, showing almost no reaction to the report.   

But the report in the Nation English-language newspaper initially raised some concerns among analysts about how policy makers could possibly manage the currency within a trade-weighted basket when they already have an inflation-targeting monetary objective.   

Claudio Piron of JPMorgan Chase Bank said it seemed the baht's trade-weighted index had moved in a 4.2 percent wide band since September.   

"It is currently at the upper limit of this range. This would imply that the Bank of Thailand should be intervening now to prevent any further baht strength against currencies," he said.   

RISK APPETITE SAGS   

Other Asian currencies rallied, even though the Japanese yen <JPY=> was underpinned by an unwinding of risky carry trades funded using the low-yielding currency.   

Stock markets in most parts of Asia, barring Malaysia and Japan, were higher but just marginally. MSCI's measure of Asia Pacific stocks excluding Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> was up 0.22 percent.   

Asian high-yielders, the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> and Philippine peso <PHP=>, gained 0.6 percent each with the latter hitting a fresh 7-½ year high of 42.12 per dollar despite talk the central bank had intervened to cap its rise.   

The rupiah rose to the firmer side of 9,300 per dollar for the first time in two weeks. The South Korean won <KRW=> was steady in a 922-925 per dollar range.   

The won has been undermined by a shortage of dollar funding in Korea after the central bank's curbs during the past year to limit short-term foreign borrowings.   

Analysts say short-term funding has been scarce in several other places, such as India, China and Indonesia, and is putting downward pressure on the currency as foreign investors unwind bond and equity holdings and repatriate their dollars. "Our risk appetite index is in risk aversion, which would usually mean a sharp sell off in emerging markets," said Callum Henderson, head of currency strategy at Standard Chartered Bank.   

"The fact that is not happening yet should suggest reduced liquidity," he said.   

Interbank lending rates in sterling soared to 9-year highs on Monday as banks struggled to secure cash for the year end in markets grappling with the fallout of the U.S. subprime mortgage problems on credit. title: Thai Fin Min: Baht Mgmt Shouldn't Aim Only To Curb Oil Effect
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Thailand's Finance Minister Chalongphob Sussangkarn said Tuesday that monetary policy tools, especially the exchange rate, shouldn't be over-relied on to target heightened oil prices.   

"It is possible that the central bank is taking advantage of the baht appreciation to slow the increase of local oil prices," Chalongphob told reporters.   

"Monetary policy must be implemented for the sake of overall economic activities not just for the oil price."   

However, the central bank has closely monitored the situation to ensure adequate flexibility in the exchange rate as well, he said.   

The Bank of Thailand has persistently intervened in the foreign market recently to prevent the baht appreciating more than other regional currencies.   

Chalongphob said inflation pressures remain moderate despite record oil prices and it will take several months before core inflation reaches the top-end of the central bank's 0%-3.5% target range.   

In October, the consumer price index rose 0.9% from September and was up 2.5% from a year earlier. The core CPI, which strips out volatile fresh food and energy prices, rose 0.3% from September and rose 1.0% from a year earlier.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia retreats as stocks fall, eyes jobs data
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Sliding stocks gave investors an excuse to book profits from recent rallies in Asian currencies on Friday, while investors turned to U.S. jobs data later in the day for fresh clues on the Federal Reserve's monetary policy.   

The high-yielding Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> fell as far as 9,140 per dollar, down almost 0.6 percent from late Asian trade on Thursday to a one-week low.   

"I think the rupiah is just following other currencies that have fallen across the board," said a trader in Jakarta.   

"But there is a strong resistance for the dollar around 9,150, it needs to break that level if we want to see it higher. Otherwise it will stay around the current level," he said.   

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> fell as far as 3.35 per dollar, down nearly 0.6 percent from late Asian trade on Thursday.   

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> slipped to 1.4538 to the U.S. dollar, down almost 0.4 percent.   

The blue-chip Dow Jones industrial average <.DJI> tumbled 2.6 percent on Thursday after brokerages downgraded the two biggest U.S. banks -- Citibank and  Bank of America , sparking fears of more credit crisis fallout.   

MSCI's measure of Asia Pacific stocks excluding Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> lost 2.7 percent, a day after it hit a record high after an expected Federal Reserve interest rate cut.   

Trading was subdued as investors awaited U.S. jobs data due at 1230 GMT that could influence views on what the Federal Reserve could do at its next policy meeting in December.   

A consensus forecast of economists polled by Reuters ahead of the Labor Department's October employment report is for a modest gain of 80,000 jobs.   

Many analysts remain bullish about the underlying strength of most Asian currencies, although they caution about potential risks from negative news on the world's largest economy.   

"Our risk appetite indicator has been in risk loving territory since the time of the first Fed cut back in September," said David Mann, currency strategist at Standard Chartered Bank.   

"The question is how much sentiment is dented by the bad news from the U.S. overnight and of course how the payrolls turn out."   

REACTIVE TO STOCKS   

On Wednesday, the Fed cut its key interest rate by a quarter-point to 4.5 percent to shield the economy from risks from the credit market problems, which followed a hefty half-point rate cut on Sept. 18.   

The Fed sought to moderate expectations for further rate cuts by saying inflation risks were equal to risks to economic growth.   

Philip Wee, currency strategist at DBS Bank, said some high-flying Asian currencies were prone to correction after making steep gains since the Fed's rate cut in September.   

"I reckon the market is still committed to a weaker dollar in Asia. But in the short term, it's reactive and very sensitive to any weakness in equities," he said.   

The Philippine peso <PHP=>, another high yielder, has gained nearly 5.5 percent since Sept. 18, while the ringgit has gained about 4 percent and the Singapore dollar has risen 3.8 percent.   

Philippine markets remained closed for public holidays.   

The Thai baht <THB=TH> briefly slipped blow the 34-per-dollar level as investor sentiment took a beating from falling stocks while the central bank was suspectedly buying dollars.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia up on Fed rate cut, further gains expected
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 1 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies rose on Thursday after the Federal Reserve's expected rate cut further eroded the dollar's yield appeal, while investors awaited new data on the U.S. economy and further policy easing.   

The high-yielding Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> rose as far as 9,065 per dollar, up almost 0.4 percent from late Asian trade on Wednesday to a three-week high.   

"The dollar was sold down in non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) overnight after the Fed rate cut," said a trader in Jakarta.   

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> rose to 3.3292 per dollar, up almost a quarter of a percent from late Asian trade on Wednesday.   

The Fed cut its key interest rate by a quarter-point to 4.5 percent on Wednesday, which followed a hefty half-point cut on Sept. 18, but sought to temper expectations for further cuts by saying that inflation risks were equal to risks to growth.   

The Fed's comments prompted analysts to push back expectations for when another U.S. rate cut could come.   

In a Reuters poll after the decision, most economists at primary bond dealers said the Fed would keep rates on hold at its next meetings in December and January.   

The fed funds rate of 4.5 percent compares with central bank rates of 8.25 percent in Indonesia, 3.25 percent in Thailand and 3.5 percent in Malaysia.   

Most analysts remain bullish about the near-term prospects for most Asian currencies, even though they have already rallied since the Fed's rate cut in September.   

"The odds are that the Fed will have to ease again by another 25 basis points at their next meeting in December and most certainly over the next 9 months," said Thio Chin Loo, currency strategist at  BNP Paribas.

"That will be bullish for Asia FX whilst the dollar falls off a cliff," she said.   

The optimism was echoed by  Lehman Brothers analyst Craig Chan: "We still remain data-focused -- if the (favourable) global backdrop begins to fade off, it could spark a bit of profit-taking in the market, but overall I'm pretty constructive."   

INTERVENTION

Investors built heavy long positions in the Singapore dollar <SGD=>, the ringgit and South Korean won <KRW=> in the past two weeks as the U.S. dollar's broad weakness made investors pick low-risk Asian assets, according to a Reuters poll [ID:nSP81108].   

The Singapore dollar was little changed near 1.448 to the U.S. dollar, while the won fell to the weaker side of 900 per dollar, amid officials warning against currency speculation.   

South Korea's foreign exchange authorities were suspected of buying more than $2 billion earlier this week in an effort to limit gains in the won, according to dealers.   

The Thai baht <THB=TH> hit 33.90 per dollar, a day after it rose past the 34-per-dollar level for the first time since early August, but was checked by suspected central bank intervention.   

"I think the Bank of Thailand is trying to prevent the dollar from falling below the 33.90 support level," said a trader in Bangkok. "Otherwise, the dollar will fall to 33.80 immediately."   

The Hong Kong government said on Thursday that it had no plan to re-peg the Hong Kong dollar or widen its trading band against the U.S. dollar, despite rising capital inflows putting pressure on it to defend the peg through intervention.   

The Hong Kong dollar <HKD=> fell to a two-week low at 7.7558 per U.S. dollar, within the 7.75-7.85 band, after the central bank intervened heavily on Wednesday to curb its rises.

title: =DJ Thai MOF Says Baht, Fiscal Policies Need Harmony
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Thailand's Finance Minister Chalongphob Sussangkarn has put the central bank on notice to keep the baht under control, warning that expansionary fiscal policy will require the exchange rate to be actively managed.   

He also made a veiled call for greater cooperation between the finance ministry and the Bank of Thailand, saying that monetary and fiscal policies must work in harmony.   

'If we were to stimulate the economy by using fiscal policy, then we need to strongly manage the exchange rate. We can't simply let it move along with market forces,' Chalongphob told a Fiscal Policy Office seminar.   

Higher government spending would lead to higher interest rates, which would attract more capital inflows and cause the baht to appreciate, hurting export competitiveness and economic growth, he said.   

The army-appointed government has recently said it will accelerate major infrastructure projects in the fourth quarter to spur Thailand's sluggish economy. The government is also planning a budget deficit of THB165 billion ($4.8 billion)in the 2008 fiscal year starting October 1.   

Dealers say the Bank of Thailand has continuously intervened in the foreign exchange market in recent weeks to curb the baht's appreciation. In the onshore market, the U.S. dollar has traded in a tight range of THB34.20-THB34.30 over the past week.   

The central bank had difficulty controlling the baht in July when an influx of foreign money into the stock market propelled the unit to a fresh 10-year high against the dollar.   

Trying to ease concerns about damage to the export sector and big job losses, the government liberalized capital outflows in the hope this would stem the currency's rise.   

Chalongphob said it's important that the government's fiscal and monetary policies work in harmony. 'If both policies don't go along, then they won't be effective.'   

An amendment to public debt management law, which will soon be sent to the National Legislative Assembly, will allow the finance ministry to take a greater role in maintaining a stable exchange rate, he said.   

Once enacted, the ministry will be able to issue bonds for the purpose of debt market development, even when there is no budgetary necessity.   

The proceeds could be used to invest in domestic and offshore securities, providing another tool for management of the exchange rate, Chalongphob said.   

The government's decisions about whether to fund large infrastructure projects domestically or from overseas should also take into account the impact on the baht, which hit a 10-year high in July, he said.   

The government is also working on an amendment to the Act governing the central bank.   

It will require the central bank to submit its monetary policy framework for Cabinet approval so that the overall direction of fiscal and monetary policy is the same, the minister said. -By Phisanu Phromchanya, Dow Jones Newswires; 662 266 0744; phisanu.phromchanya@dowjones.com

title: IMF chief says Asian economies stronger than in 1997
text:
BANGKOK, July 28 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund said on Saturday it saw no immediate risks of a financial crisis for Asian economies hit in recent months by a heavy influx of global capital.   

Asian countries should employ a combination of measures to manage huge inflows of foreign funds and exploit them for accelerating their economic expansion, IMF Managing Director Rodrigo Rato said.   

"Capital inflow is certainly a worldwide phenomenon. For Asian economies, that reflects a lot of things including increased liquidity and growing attractiveness of the economies. I believe that is good news," Rato told a news conference.   

Since late last year, Thailand has struggled to discourage capital inflows which have fuelled the baht's rise to 10-year highs against the dollar and eroded its export competitiveness.   

"I don't think right now Thailand and Asia have reasons to expect any crisis. Volatility is a problem and not desirable but that doesn't necessarily bring us to a crisis," Rato said.   

"Macro-economic fundamentals are stronger now than they were 10 years ago. Exchange rate flexibility also plays a very important role and the integration of Asian economies into the world economy is stronger," he said, referring to the 1997 Asian economic crisis.   

In a speech delivered to a meeting of Asian central bankers on Saturday, Rato urged China and other Asian countries to relax their currency policies.   

"Greater exchange rate flexibility is not only in China's best interest but would allow other Asian countries to appreciate with less concern about competitiveness," he said.   

"There is also the possibility of such protectionism spinning out of control with disastrous consequences for the global economy," Rato said.   

DIFFERENT APPROACH   

China manages the value of its yuan currency, also called the renmimbi, within a narrow range that the United States and many European countries maintain does not represent its fair value given China's rising global economic might.   

Thailand imposed tough capital controls last December to try to keep foreign capital out but has since relaxed most of them after they proved ineffective in slowing the baht's gains.   

Despite active intervention and measures taken by the Bank of Thailand to stall its gains, the baht has appreciated about 7 percent against the dollar this year after rising nearly 14 percent in 2006.   

The central bank adopted a different approach last week to ease upward pressure on the currency by allowing more capital outflows, a move welcomed by the IMF chief.   

"Stronger currencies should not be seen as a danger. It makes easier monetary policy and makes it easier to keep inflation targets in check. It attracts more foreign confidence in the economies," he told reporters.   

Rato said while appreciating Thailand's reasons to resort to capital controls last year, the measures were not a solution.   

"Experiences show capital controls are more and more short-lived in terms of benefits for the country. They certainly have all the drawbacks if made to last longer," he said.   

Bank of Thailand Governor Tarisa Watanagase on Saturday asked IMF officials for advice on how to cope with adverse market volatility arising from fast flows of global capital.

title: UPDATE: Thai Fin Min Says Baht Stabilizing, BOT  Intervened
text:
(Adds comments from Finance Minister.)   

BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Thailand's Finance Minister Chalongphob Sussangkarn said Monday that the baht has been starting to soften and stabilize since last week, thanks partly to the Bank of Thailand's intervention in the foreign exchange market to limit excessive volatility.   

Earlier this month the currency hit a new 10-year high against the U.S. dollar, triggering calls for moves to protect the export sector.   

"The direction of the baht is now more in line with the current market situation," Chalongphob told reporters.   

He reiterated the government is working on new measures to stem the baht's appreciation and boost demand for dollars.   

The Ministry of Finance will propose six measures to the Cabinet on Tuesday, most of which are aimed at boosting capital outflows.   

The measures will help make it easier for the central bank to manage the exchange rate, said Chalongphob.   

"If the central bank manages it seriously, then it should be effective," he said.   

"If we are determined enough, the market will see it the way we want them to see it."   

Chalongphob was speaking after a meeting of the board of the inactive Exchange Equalization Fund.   

It was established in 1955 to maintain exchange-rate stability, with the baht fixed against a weighted basket of currencies. Thailand's Cabinet in January approved a plan to dissolve the fund, inactive since the floating of the baht in 1997.   

Despite the closure of the fund, Chalongphob said that there should be an entity, possibly an ad-hoc committee, that provides a forum for the finance ministry and central bank to discuss the management of the exchange rate.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia mostly firmer, peso jumps after rate cut
text:
SINGAPORE, July 13 (Reuters) - Rising Asian shares buoyed most regional currencies on Friday with the Philippine peso leading the pack after the central bank slashed interest rates but eased the impact by scrapping a low-interest deposit scheme.   

The peso <PHP=> steadied near 45.75 per dollar, up half a percent from Thursday's close, after suspected central bank intervention pushed it back from a day high of 45.73.   

"The central bank's rate cut yesterday seems to be taken in a positive light," a trader in Manila said. "The cut is positive for the equity market, and with the equity market strong, there is foreign interest and that causes the peso to strengthen," he said.   

The Philippine shares <.PSI> rose about 0.8 percent on Friday.   

The central bank surprised investors by cutting its key rates by 150 and 175 basis points.   

In an accompanying move, the central bank removed a tiered scheme, under which interest rates were reduced by up to 400 basis points on banks' deposits in excess of 10 billion pesos.   

Central bank governor Amando Tetangco said the combined impact of the two decisions would be neutral, but some analysts believed the moves still amounted to moderate easing.   

"While easing is bullish for the government bonds we expect a limited negative impact on the peso as strong economic fundamentals will continue to attract capital inflows to support the currency," analysts at ING said in a research note.   

Sean Callow, currency strategist at Westpac, said he believed the relaxation was compatible with the central bank's cut of its 2007 inflation forecast to 2.6-3.1 percent from 4-5 percent.   

"Markets should quickly factor in at least one rate cut in coming months," he said in a note.   

"While this will of course undermine the peso from a yield spread view, foreign equity investors already attracted to the Philippines' macro story are likely to become even more enthusiastic," he said.   

STOCKS RALLY   

MSCI's measure of Asia Pacific stocks excluding Japan climbed 1.6 percent to a record high, having risen in 11 of the past 12 sessions.   

Asian investors are more confident that the woes in the U.S. subprime mortgage market are unlikely to have any fallout on the region, given its good economic health.   

The South Korean won <KRW=> touched a fresh seven-month high at 915.20 per dollar on expectations of further interest rate rises after the central bank raised its key rate by a quarter point on Thursday.   

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=>, which has recently moved largely in tandem with the peso, rose as far as 9,010 per dollar, up about 0.4 percent from late Asia trade on Thursday.   

Asian currencies have strengthened broadly against the dollar so far this year, led by a 9.4 percent jump in the Indian rupee <INR=IN> and a 8.4 percent rise in the Thai baht <THB=TH>.   

The rupee rose moderately to 40.45 per dollar amid concerns that the central bank may intervene to cap its gains, while the Thai baht was little changed at about 33.30 per dollar.   

Thai Finance Minister Chalongphob Sussangkarn said on Friday the government would meet representatives of the private sector next week to talk about the baht's surge to 10-year highs against the dollar.   

Thailand's central bank has tried in vain to slow the baht's rise through capital controls and intervention.
