title: Thai Ctrl Bk Asks Banks To Curb Exporters' Baht Speculation
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Bank of Thailand has asked commercial banks to judiciously review exporters' requests to sell foreign currencies, in a bid to prevent speculation on the baht as the currency set a fresh 10-year high Wednesday, according to a central bank statement.   

"Recently, there is evidence that exporters have speculated on the direction of the exchange rate and accelerated their selling of foreign currencies," the statement said.   

Banks must make sure exporters provide sound reasons when they fail to deliver dollars to settle their sales orders, it said.   

"This (speculation) adds to pressure on the baht and results in a foreign exchange rate that doesn't accurately reflect Thailand's economic situation," the central bank said.   

The dollar ended in onshore trade Wednesday at THB33.35, down from THB33.48 Tuesday due to equities-related inflows and selling by exporters, traders said.   

Earlier Wednesday, the U.S. unit fell to THB33.18, its lowest level since August 1997.   

On Tuesday, Bank of Thailand governor Tarisa Watanagase said the central bank has intervened in the foreign exchange market to stem an "abnormal" rise in the baht associated with panic selling by exporters.

title: UPDATE: Thai BoT:Can't Return To Fixed  Foreign Exchange  Rate
text:
(Adds additional comments by the governor and the baht exchange rate)   

BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Bank of Thailand Governor Tarisa Watanagase said Wednesday that the country can't afford to return to a fixed exchange rate system, as she rejected calls by some exporters for drastic measures to stem the baht's rise to 10-year highs.   

"There are an enormous amount of funds out there in the global economy. To fix the exchange rate, we would need adequate foreign reserves, otherwise we wouldn't make it and that's the situation we faced 10 years ago," Tarisa said in a live interview broadcast on local television Channel 3.   

The Bank of Thailand was forced to float the baht in a move that triggered the Asian financial crisis of 1997 after spending all of its reserves in a failed defense of a fixed exchange rate mechanism.   

Since then, the central bank has used a managed float system.   

Tarisa said the central bank does not have a targeted foreign exchange rate since it largely depends on capital inflows.   

"We can't defend (the baht exchange rate) at a certain level. What we can do is prevent excessive volatility," Tarisa said.   

Tarisa said she expects upward pressure on the baht to decline in the second half of the year as exports are expected to slow while imports are tipped to rise.   

She said the recent baht's rise was due mainly to portfolio inflows into the stock market, and that the phenomenon should be only temporary.   

Later Wednesday, Tarisa told reporters that dollar selling by exporters has eased and returned to a normal level, but the baht was still under pressure to appreciate from persistent portfolio inflows.   

The governor had said Tuesday that the baht's strength was "abnormal," due to panic-selling by exporters triggered by a misunderstanding of the bank's plan to allow certain nonresidents to tap onshore baht liquidity.   

At 0707 GMT, the U.S. dollar was at THB33.29, slightly off a fresh 10-year low of THB33.18 set earlier Wednesday, after suspected intervention by the Bank of Thailand.

text:

BANGKOK, July 3 (Reuters) - Thailand's central bank sees no need to intervene on the baht despite its rise to a 10-year high onshore on Tuesday, Deputy Bank of Thailand Governor Atchana Waiquamdee told reporters.   

The baht's sharp rise against the dollar was in line with other Asian currencies, she said.   

"Overall, it is not different from regional currencies. It is still in line with regionals. We do not need to enter and act on it provided it does not overshoot or undershoot. No need to watch it every second," Atchana said.   

The baht's accelerated rise on Tuesday, after an advance the previous day, was induced partly by Thai exporters taking profit on its gains.   

The baht traded at around 34.33/35 per dollar at 0551 GMT against 34.51/53 late on Monday.   

The baht has risen onshore about 4.65 percent against the dollar so far this year after surging nearly 14 percent in 2006.

title: UPDATE 1- Thailand  still needs to  intervene  on baht - c.bank
text:
(Adds details)   

BANGKOK, May 29 (Reuters) - The Bank of Thailand still needs to intervene to stop a rising baht threatening the country's key export industries, Deputy Governor Atchana Waiquamdee said on Tuesday.   

"We need to take care of the export sector, which is our only engine at the moment, so that it can gradually adjust," she told reporters as the baht traded at its strongest level in more than nine years.   

"But intervention cannot be overdone because it will affect our balance sheet," she said.   

At 0900 GMT the baht traded at 34.59 per the dollar onshore <THB=TH>, little changed from Monday. It was at 32.85 in offshore trade <THB=W>.   

The baht has evolved into a two-tier on and offshore market since the imposition of tough capital controls in December which require 30 percent of foreign inflows to be held at the central bank, interest free, for a year.   

The central bank has intervened sporadically in a vain effort so far to curb the currency's rise.   

The baht has risen 4.3 percent against the dollar so far this year after a 14 percent rise last year.   

Atchana said an improving political picture would help to boost imports and ease upward pressure on the baht.   

A court decide will decide on Wednesday whether to disband Thailand's biggest two parties and ban their leaders from politics for breaching election laws a year ago.   

The decision could plunge the country into more political uncertainty ahead of promised elections in December.   

The central bank has cut interest rates four times this year to 3.5 percent in an effort to revive an economy expected to grow at its slowest pace this year since 2001.   

The bank has cut its 2007 economic growth forecast twice this year to a range of 3.8-4.8 percent, after 5 percent growth last year, due to sagging domestic consumption and investment since Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra was ousted in a bloodless military coup last September.

title: UPDATE 1-Thai exporter dollar sales boost baht-c.bank
text:
(Adds details)  

BANGKOK, March 14 (Reuters) - The recent rise of the Thai baht stems from continuing dollar sales by exporters and there is no need for the central bank to intervene, Bank of Thailand Governor Tarisa Watanagase said on Wednesday. "The baht remains strong because exporters continue to sell dollars," Tarisa told reporters as the baht rose towards 35 to the dollar.  

"There is no need to do anything special because it is the people in the country who sell the dollar," she said.  

Tough capital controls imposed in December, aimed at curbing the baht's rise, have spawned a two-tier onshore and offshore market for the baht.  

It was trading at 35.02/05 to the dollar onshore <THB=TH> at 0740 GMT, compared with 35.09/01 in the morning, when the BoT was thought to be buying small amounts of dollars, research firm Forecast said.  

It was traded at 32.85 offshore <THB=W>.  

Despite a series of mis-steps by the new government since a bloodless coup in September, the baht has remained strong. It rose 14 percent against the dollar last year, more than any other Asian currency, and has risen another 3 percent this year.  

The central bank would continue to monitor the baht and believed that further easing of capital controls would not affect the baht or panic the market, Tarisa said.  

It has backtracked several times on the controls. The latest was an exemption for fully hedged foreign inflows invested in mutual funds, property funds and debt markets from March 15.  

The central bank would discuss the controls with new Finance Minister Chalongphob Sussangkarn on Thursday, Tarisa said, without elaborating.  

Chalongphob is thought to favour further relaxation of the controls the central bank imposed on Dec. 18, requiring 30 percent of foreign inflows to be held in reserve with the central bank, interest free, for a year.

title: Thai govt backs BoT changes, analysts see more  intervention
text:
BANGKOK, Feb 27 (Reuters) - Thailand's military-appointed government approved changes to the law governing the Bank of Thailand on Tuesday which analysts said could trigger more currency intervention and hasten the lifting of capital controls.   

The changes, which still need parliamentary approval, would give the BoT more discretion to adjust assets kept as part of foreign reserves, government spokesman Yongyudh Maiyalarp told reporters after a cabinet meeting.   

JP Morgan said it would allow the central bank to reduce the frequency of reporting on its foreign reserve management.   

"By exonerating the central bank from reporting changes in its FX reserves, the central bank is free to intervene at will and without the concern that its losses will have to be booked under political scrutiny at year end," it said in a note to clients.   

The amendments meant the central bank would need to reassess the value of foreign reserves only once a month, Yongyudh said. The BoT currently announces changes once a week.   

Recent heavy intervention by the bank to slow the baht's rise against the dollar has pushed Thai foreign reserves to record highs in recent months, reaching $67.5 billion on Feb. 16.   

The baht rose around 14 percent against the dollar last year, the most of any Asian currency.   

The surge in foreign reserves has forced the BoT to issue more domestic baht bonds this year to mop up excess liquidity in the domestic market to avoid stoking inflation.   

The BoT reported last week that it posted a book loss of $4.9 billion in 2006, stemming largely from its intervention as the dominant dollar portion of foreign reserves depreciated in value last year.   

JP Morgan said the changes could speed up a decision to lift tough capital controls imposed on Dec. 18 to rein in the baht.   

They require foreigners bringing in funds without underlying business to put 30 percent in interest-free bank accounts supervised by the central bank for up to a year.   

The capital controls spawned a two-tier market for the baht.   

JP Morgan said the revision of the BoT law could help narrow a four percent spread between offshore and onshore baht rates.   

"Short-term FX implication is that the offshore spot USD/THB rate will move higher in the event URR restrictions are lifted and liquidity returns," it said, referring to the 30 percent unremunerative required reserves.   

The baht traded offshore at around 34.15 per dollar at 1058 GMT on Tuesday, down from 33.80 late on Monday.

title: Thai fin min: job of halting baht rise done-report
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 20 (Reuters) - Thailand had no choice but to intervene to stop the rise of the baht, a job that has now been done, the country's finance minister said in an interview published in the Singapore Straits Times newspaper on Saturday.  

Pridiyathorn Devakula, also Thailand's deputy prime minister, reiterated the threat to exports posed by the currency's rise, the original reason given for capital controls imposed on Dec. 18.  

"Exports comprise 60 percent of gross domestic product. Thailand owes its growth to exports," he told the newspaper.  

Thailand's central bank announced rules on Dec. 18 targeting short-term speculators with limits to the amount of money they could pull out of the country within a year of investing it.  

The rules were diluted the next day after a near 15 percent one-day fall in the Thai stock market forced the bank into a U-turn.  

Despite the market reaction, and strong criticism of the central bank from investors, Pridiyathorn said he had to give bank governor Tarisa Watanagase full credit for taking the strong measures necessary to curb the baht's rise, the Strait Times reported.  

The Thai minister said China's currency controls were part of the reason for having to arrest the rise of the baht.  

"If China allows its currency to appreciate, Thailand would not have to do this," he told the newspaper. Pridiyathorn also defended changes to the Foreign Business Act aimed at limiting the ability of foreign companies to control Thai firms through the use of nominees.  

He said that if a police investigation found that Singapore's state investment firm Temasek Holdings had used nominees to exert control over Shin Corp., other companies in the same boat would be forced to hurriedly sell off shares.  

"I had to prevent that nightmare," he said.  

The rules ban foreign firms from owning 50 percent or more of Thai companies, but nominees are often used to gain de facto control. Thai police are investigating whether Temasek followed this route after buying its stake in Shin Corp. from ousted former prime minister Thaksin Shinawatra.

title: RPT-PREVIEW-Thai Nov exports seen at 9-mth high despite baht
text:
(Repeating story from Dec. 27 ahead of data due at 0730 GMT)  

 * What: Bank of Thailand data on trade, manufacturing, others  

 * When: Friday Dec. 29, 2.30 p.m. (0730 GMT)  

 * Annual exports growth seen strongest in nine months  

 By Vithoon Amorn  

 BANGKOK, Dec 27 (Reuters) - Thailand's exports in November are expected to have risen at their fastest annual pace in nine months, nudging trade and current account surpluses to new highs despite rises in the baht against the dollar, analysts say.  

 Exporters saw their dollar earnings rise last month but expected smaller gains in baht terms, prompting the central bank to impose capital controls on Dec. 19 to slow Asia's fastest rising currency this year.  

 A Reuters survey of six analysts suggested the November current account surplus rose by about $1 billion from October to a record $1.88 billion.  

 The Bank of Thailand is due to release November economic data on Friday, including trade, manufacturing and money supply.  

 "Export growth will be considerably narrower in baht terms, closer to 8 percent, an indication of how exporters can indeed be squeezed as the USD-THB approached 35.0," said David Cohen, economist at Action Economics in Singapore.  

 He said the November surplus "might raise questions about the painfulness of this year's baht appreciation.  

 The baht <THB=> rose about 2 percent against the dollar in November and had gained nearly 16 percent on the year before the Bank of Thailand intervened to stop the currency from breaking the psychological barrier of 35 per dollar.  

 Foreign investors recoiled at the capital controls which triggered a 15-percent plunge on the Thai stock market last week before the measures were rescinded for equity investments.  

 The central bank said it had to act before the baht did serious damage to the country's exports, which are equivalent to 60 percent of Thailand's gross domestic product.  

 The baht was trading at 36.31 per dollar on Wednesday and was expected to remain subdued this week ahead of the New Year holidays.  

 STRONG EXPORTS  

 Analysts estimated November exports surged 21.1 percent from a year earlier, the biggest annual rise since February and topping a 20.9 percent increase in October.  

 The impressive growth in November's exports was due partly to higher auto exports to Indonesia, said analyst Nujcharin Panarode at Capital Nomura Securities.  

 Cars and auto parts are Thailand's second-biggest industrial exports after computers and electronics.  

 The Manufacturing Production Index was expected to rise 6.3 percent in November from a year earlier, up from 5.4 percent in October.  

 But some analysts questioned how long the good economic data could be sustained given signs of weaker domestic investment and consumption in the past few months.  

"On the whole, the November economic data should continue pointing to fundamental weakness. I believe the December data will likely be worse than November," said Leslie Khoo at Forecast Pte in Singapore.  

 BOT data showed annual private investment growth easing to 1.0 percent in October from average growth of 1.5 percent in the third quarter.  

 Inflation data for December is due to be released at around 2 p.m. (0700 GMT) on Jan. 3.

The impressive growth in November's exports was due partly to higher auto exports to Indonesia, said analyst Nujcharin Panarode at Capital Nomura Securities.  

Cars and auto parts are Thailand's second-biggest industrial exports after computers and electronics.  

The Manufacturing Production Index was expected to rise 6.3 percent in November from a year earlier, up from 5.4 percent in October.  

But some analysts questioned how long the good economic data could be sustained given signs of weaker domestic investment and consumption in the past few months.  

"On the whole, the November economic data should continue pointing to fundamental weakness. I believe the December data will likely be worse than November," said Leslie Khoo at Forecast Pte in Singapore.  

BOT data showed annual private investment growth easing to 1.0 percent in October from average growth of 1.5 percent in the third quarter.

title: Thai Fin Min: Cap Inflow Rules Are A Short-Term Measure
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Thailand's imposition of a 30% reserve withholding on many capital inflows is meant to be a short-term measure to reduce volatility in the baht, which was at nine-year highs and heading higher before the move was introduced, Finance Minister Pridiyathorn Devakula said Friday.  

However, any decision to revoke the measure would be up to the central bank, Pridiyathorn told Dow Jones Newswires and the Associated Press in an interview. [ 22-12-06 1148GMT ]  

"This (withholding requirement for capital inflows) is a short-term measure. It's fully within the authority of the Bank of Thailand governor (to ease or revoke the measure). With approval of the monetary policy committee, they can change it at any time. They have the liberty and flexibility to correct (adjust it to market conditions) it at any time," Pridiyathorn said.  

Asked what criteria the central bank would use to decide when to revoke the withholding requirement, the finance minister said it would happen when the objectives had been achieved and the baht was moving back into line with the currencies of regional trading partners.  

"It's not the level of the baht, it's the level of appreciation (in the baht). If currencies of our (export) competitors appreciate more or less at the same level as ours, I don't think we would need this measure any more," Pridiyathorn said.  

He said it would be a great help if China allowed its currency to rise against the dollar, so that other country's with more flexible exchange rate regimes wouldn't have to shoulder so much of the burden of the dollar's necessary adjustment to the huge U.S. trade and budget deficits.  

"It would help a lot (if China revalued the yuan), but it would depend on the degree of revaluation," Pridiyathorn said.  

Speculative investors who have been targeting Thailand will likely shift towards other countries with even more flexible exchange rates, he said.  

There are many ways that those countries can try to mitigate the effects of the overwhelming flows, but they may be looking at Thailand's measures, he said.  

The baht had reached a level prior to the initial imposition of the measures Tuesday where Thailand's export competitiveness was being affected, he said.  

Early Monday, the baht hit a nine-year high of THB35.06 to the dollar, up 17% since the beginning of the year.  

The central bank had to act because, prior to the withholding requirement, capital inflows were so huge that intervention wasn't enough, Pridiyathorn said.  

Bank of Thailand came up with a new set of measures Dec. 4, under which short-term trading of debt was banned and restrictions on foreign exchange swaps and loans between onshore and offshore institutions were tightened, but they proved to be ineffective, he said.  

Net capital inflows in the first week of December tripled relative to the already high levels seen in November and earlier in the year, as investors ramped up their one-way bets on a rising baht and falling interest rates.  

So the central bank had to impose severe measures, Pridiyathorn said.  

The finance minister and the central bank said separately earlier Friday that they were satisfied with the easing in the baht, which closed the Asian session Friday at THB36.44 to the dollar, almost flat from THB36.43 Thursday.  

Implementation of the measures didn't go smoothly.  

The Stock Exchange of Thailand index lost 15% Tuesday, more than on any other single day in its history, as foreigners sold a net THB25 billion worth of shares, according to the bourse.  

Pridiyathorn and central bank officials met with market participants to work out a way to separate equities-related inflows from other inflows and exempt them from the withholding, and the changes were announced the same evening.  

"We switched it very fast because we care about foreign investors," the finance minister said.  

Bank of Thailand has allowed onshore institutions to set up special nonresident accounts for securities, which are exempt from withholding, but the funds in the accounts can be used only for trading in equities.  

Inflows related to foreign direct investment, property, tourism, education, medical, transportation, diplomatic and myriad other areas are also exempt from the withholding, but documentation must be supplied to onshore institutions as evidence for transactions worth more than $20,000.  

However, offshore financial institutions are still reluctant to trade in foreign exchange with onshore institutions due to the burden of documentation, and many equities analysts are still predicting sluggish inflows and possibly heavy outflows in the months to come due to the perceived unpredictability of Thailand's regulators.  

Pridiyathorn said the policy was crystal clear.  

"The policy is still there and clear. It is intended to reduce capital inflows that put pressure on the baht (beyond those applied to the currencies of regional trading partners)," he said.  

"The ones who don't believe in our policy just sold and didn't buy back, and they made losses. Of course they are upset, and when they are upset they will criticize anything," Pridiyathorn said.  

"Once we get rid of these measures (when the currency is back in balance), I think the whole world will understand," he said.  

Long-term investors would also have been upset if the central bank did nothing, he said.  

"Exports are a key contributor to economic growth and the stock exchange. If exports are affected, we don't think investors will like it. If we did nothing and the baht kept rising, we might see exports drop for the first time in history," he said. Since the capital inflow measures are helping to save the baht, exports won't be hurt, and economic growth can be sustained, he said.  

The ministry's forecast for gross domestic product growth will remain at 4.5%-5% next year, compared with an estimated 5% this year, he said.  

"If there was no intervention and the baht kept rising, we would have to revise the GDP growth estimate downward," Pridiyathorn said.  

Meanwhile, inflows intended for investment in Thai debt instruments are still subject to the 30% withholding.  

The minister said that Thailand's current account is currently in surplus, indicating that savings are greater than investment, so foreign inflows won't be needed in the bond market for a while. While the measures are intended to be temporary, the central bank's high foreign reserves - at $64.7 billion as of Dec. 15 - mean that it will be able to keep the measures in place for as long as necessary, he said.  

Government bonds suffered heavy losses initially, but central bank buying calmed the market, and local corporate and interbank demand are sufficient to absorb moderate supply. The bid on the benchmark 10-year bond due July 2016 closed Friday unchanged from the previous day at 5.10%, and up from 4.87% Monday. Bank of Thailand has said that most of the hot money in debt instruments is in short-term commercial paper and bills of exchange.  

-By Phisanu Phromchanya, Dow Jones Newswires; 662-266-0744; phisanu.phromchanya@dowjones.com [ 22-12-06 1345GMT ]

title: Thai baht fumble has long-term costs - S&P
text:
BANGKOK, Dec 21 (Reuters) - Thailand's fumbled baht controls could trigger a further pull-out of foreign money and hurt domestic investment by driving up financing costs, ratings agency Standard & Poor's said on Thursday.  

"Foreign investors will now be far more wary of investing in Thai financial markets," S&P credit analyst Kim Eng Tan said in a report two days after a bungled intervention to halt the rise of the baht sparked a huge share sell-off.  

"This will lead to higher funding costs in the Kingdom, with negative implications for the prices of debt and equity assets," Tan said.  

International investors slammed the measures, which were abruptly lifted for stock investments after the Thai bourse fell nearly 15 percent on Tuesday, its sharpest one-day loss in 16 years.  

The benchmark stock index <.SETI> was down 2.66 percent at 0433 on Thursday after an 11.2 percent rebound on Wednesday.  

S&P said the currency controls appeared to have put a brake on the baht, which fell to a one-month low against the dollar on Thursday as investors continued to dump the currency.  

But it noted "such success brings long-term costs".  

Domestic investment could become costlier if planned government spending led to a return of current account deficits, the report said.  

"This is because deficits would increase Thailand's reliance on foreign financing," it said.  

The interim government appointed after a bloodless Sept. 19 coup ousted Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra plans to boost public spending next year to keep the economy humming ahead of promised elections in late 2007.  

The surprise baht controls and later policy U-turn also tarnished the central bank's reputation in the eyes of foreign investors, S&P said.  

"The Bank of Thailand has gained itself a reputation -- however undeserved -- as an interventionist, one that administers abrupt and inconsistent policy actions," the report said.

title: Thai Mkts Make Partial Recovery On Baht Rule's Revision
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Thai markets stabilized Wednesday in a partial recovery following the central bank's decision to exempt stock and foreign direct investment inflows from the harsh reserve requirement it had placed on most capital inflows the previous day.  

The Stock Exchange of Thailand index closed 11.2% higher at 691.55 points, after panic selling pushed it down almost 15% to 622.14 at Tuesday's close.  

Many analysts said the botched implementation of rules designed to limit speculative pressures which have driven the baht to nine year highs have shattered foreign investors confidence, and will lead to sluggishness in Thai shares for a long time to come.  

The move came shortly after international fund managers had raised their weightings on Thai stocks, deeming that political tensions had eased in the wake of September's military coup that overthrew Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra.  

ABN Amro said in a report Wednesday that it has cut the recommended weighting of Thai shares in its Asia Ex-Japan portfolio to 1.5% from 2.5%, citing its view that uncertainty related to potential policy changes and elections due late next year will limit foreign inflows in the coming year.  

But Bank of Thailand Governor Tarisa Watanagase told reporters Wednesday that there were no signs yet that funds from the massive selling of Thai shares were flowing out of the country.  

And some fund managers said that although the event was unsettling, it didn't change the outlook for the companies whose shares they owned.  

"It is not an impressive sign of the thinking of the Thai government. But we are not changing Thailand's weighting in our portfolios," as fundamentals of Thai companies remain the same, said fund manager Hugh Young of Aberdeen Asset Management Asia Ltd.  

Tarisa said that due to the changes exempting equities-related inflows from the reserve requirement, the baht wouldn't fall as much as had earlier been expected.  

The dollar closed onshore trading at THB35.800, down from 35.915 at the Asian close Tuesday, but still up from a nine-year low early Monday at THB35.060.  

Deputy Finance Minister Sommai Phasee told reporters he expects the U.S. dollar to eventually settle around THB36-THB37.  

But Tarisa said Tuesday that the baht would eventually start to rise again due to broad dollar weakness in foreign exchange markets, even if the central bank's efforts to eliminate speculative forces allow the Thai currency to drop back in line with its regional trading partners.  

The surging baht had prompted the central bank to require as of Tuesday that onshore banks withhold for one year 30% of capital inflows that aren't trade- or services-related or those that aren't a repatriation of Thai residents' investments abroad.  

As of Wednesday, inflows to stocks and foreign direct investments were also exempted.  

For inflows still subject to the reserve, investors can request the entire amount withheld back after one year, or two-thirds of the amount withheld back in less than a year, resulting in an effective tax of 10% on the total initial investment.  

As inflows into bonds and other debt instruments are still subject to the withholding, Thailand's government bond market only stabilized Wednesday due to central bank intervention.  

Dealers said Bank of Thailand bought issues with terms of 10 years or more from primary dealers, calming a market that otherwise would have seen another day of losses in adjustment to a likely halt in speculative foreign demand.  

The bid yield of the benchmark 10-year bond due July 2016 ended at 5.11%, after rising 33 basis points to 5.20% on Tuesday.  

Thailand's credit default swap spreads also recovered, narrowing to 25-to-30 basis points after widening sharply to 30-35 basis points on Tuesday.  


 
   Speculative Flows From Debt To Shares A Problem 
   

Finance Minister Pridiyathorn Devakula told The Wall Street Journal Asia on Wednesday that after the revision in the rules exempting equities-related inflows from the withholding requirement, the problem was to find a way to prevent speculative foreign money previously flowing into the debt market from moving into stocks.  

Tarisa said the central bank may re-impose a THB300 million limit on total deposits by a single nonresident in onshore accounts, which was removed Tuesday so that foreigners selling shares could leave their funds in the country.  

Suchart Sakkankosone, director of Exchange Control and Credits Department, said Wednesday that the central bank will announce "in one or two days" a plan to create a type of account through which nonresidents can buy and sell Thai shares.  

Funds in foreigners' special equities-related accounts won't be allowed to shift into bonds or other assets, SET President Patareeya Benjapolchai said at a separate news conference Wednesday.  

Suchart said that when the accounts restricted to equities trading are created, the central bank will restore the THB300 million limit on general nonresident accounts, but it hasn't been decided whether a limit will be imposed on the equities accounts.  

Meanwhile, Tarisa rejected calls from many economists to scrap the attempts to control inflows via regulations and solve the problem by cutting interest rates instead.  

"We shouldn't use interest rates to solve the foreign exchange problem. The monetary policy committee has decided that now isn't the time for a rate cut," she said.  

Many economists expect the MPC to make a slight downward adjustment by setting its new benchmark, the one-day repurchase market rate, at 4.75% when it meets in January, after leaving the current 14-day benchmark rate at 5% when it met on Dec. 13.  

But some economists believe Bank of Thailand may wait for the U.S. to lead the way before cutting the new one-day benchmark, because of its emphasis on inflation-targeting.  

Tarisa said the reason the central bank wouldn't use interest rates to manage the baht was that there is still a risk of higher inflation and the economy is growing at a reasonable pace.  

Cutting interest rates would also only attract more speculative inflows to debt instruments, which see capital gains when interest rates fall, and possibly to other markets if lower interest rates stimulated the economy, she said.  

Inflation risks come from oil price instability and the tendency of the Ministry of Commerce to look for items to remove from the list of products controlled prices, Tarisa said.  

A ministry official said that the next meeting of the price committee is expected to be held in January, at which revisions to the list of controlled prices will be considered.  

-By Tom Fox, Dow Jones Newswires; 662-266-0744; tom.fox@dowjones.com  

(Supunnabul Suwannakij, Phisanu Phromchanya and Rattaphol Onsanit contributed to this story) [ 20-12-06 1001GMT ]

title: UPDATE 1-Thai baht jumps, hits nine-year high
text:
(Updates with details, analyst comment)  

 SINGAPORE, Dec 12 (Reuters) - The Thai baht <THB=>, Asia's best performing currency, jumped nearly 0.6 percent against the dollar in early trade on Tuesday and hit its strongest level in more than nine years.  

 At 0224 GMT, the baht was quoted at 35.34 per dollar, extending its gains after strengthening beyond its previous high of 35.46 per dollar set in December 1998 and hitting its strongest level since early October 1997.  

 Dealers at a major Thai commercial bank in Bangkok confirmed the currency movement, but declined to comment further.  

 Christy Tan, currency analyst at Bank of America in Singapore, said markets were betting on a decision from the Bank of Thailand to keep interest rates unchanged on Wednesday, which would underpin the Thai currency.  

  "Intervention is possible, but that will only slow the baht's rises and is unlikely to reverse the trend," she said.  

 The Thai central bank meets on Wednesday to review its monetary policy, but 8 of 9 analysts surveyed by Reuters predicted the central bank would leave its 14-day repurchase rate unchanged at 5.0 percent.  

 The baht has gained 16 percent so far this year, despite Bank of Thailand intervention and new anti-speculation measures announced last week.  

 But Thai exporters have complained about the rise in the baht, worried it will crimp revenues and make their goods less competitive.  

 The latest Reuters poll on positioning in Asian currencies suggests investors stepped up long positions in the Thai baht and remained bullish on the South Korean won and Singapore dollar.  

 Asian currencies fell on Monday thanks to a global rebound in the dollar and protracted concerns about central bankintervention, but most analysts remain bullish about their near-term outlook, citing the region's solid economic fundamentals.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia up, Thai baht rally sparks  intervention
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 12 (Reuters) - The Bank of Thailand bought dollars on Tuesday to rein in the baht as Asia's best performing currency hit its highest since the Asian financial crisis, while other regional currencies followed its firm tone.  

 The baht <THB=> retreated to 35.32 per dollar after reaching 35.23, its strongest since October 1997, strengthening beyond its previous high of 35.46 per dollar set in December 1998.  

 Assistant governor at Bank of Thailand, Suchada Kirakul, told reporters that the central bank had intervened, buying dollars to try to slow the rise of the baht.  

 But she said the bank would take time to consider whether fresh measures were needed to deter foreign speculation in the baht after it imposed curbs last week to block access by foreign speculators through domestic bond and debt paper transactions.  

 A dealer at Bangkok Bank said he expected the central bank to impose new curbs to target currency speculation in the baht to prevent the currency from breaching the key 35-per-dollar level.  

 "A break below 35.00 could herald more selling, although we expect the BOT to guard this level religiously," said Thio Chin Loo, currency analyst at BNP Paribas.  

 Christy Tan, currency analyst at Bank of America in Singapore, said markets were betting on a decision from the Bank of Thailand to keep interest rates unchanged on Wednesday, which would underpin the Thai currency.  

 The Thai central bank meets on Wednesday to review its monetary policy, but 8 of 9 analysts surveyed by Reuters predicted the central bank would leave its 14-day repurchase rate unchanged at 5.0 percent.  

 The baht has gained around 16.6 percent so far this year, prompting worries among local exporters that the currency's rise could crimp their revenues and make their goods less competitive.  

 OPTIMISTIC  

 Most analysts and dealers remain optimistic about the near-term outlook on Asian currencies as capital flows into the region and trade surpluses persist, despite a wave of verbal and actual intervention by central banks to cap currency strength.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Asst Chief: Inflation Downtrend To Continue
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Bank of Thailand Assistant Governor Suchada Kirakul said Tuesday that inflation remains on a downward trend.  

The increase in consumer price index inflation in November to 3.5% on year from 2.8% in the previous month was due mainly to heavy flooding, she said.  

"Both CPI and core inflation are on a declining trend," Suchada said.  

Core inflation - based on the CPI but excluding volatile fresh food and energy prices - was up 1.7% on year, compared with 1.8% in October.  

However, comments last week from central bank Governor Tarisa Watanagase indicated that the Bank of Thailand will wait until next year to lower interest rates.  

The central bank is expected to leave its 14-day repurchase target rate unchanged at 5.0%, when it holds its next policy meeting Wednesday. [ 12-12-06 0733GMT ]  

Suchada also said the Thai baht is appreciating too quickly, buoyed by global dollar weakness and by capital inflows, but added that the baht's rise was also helping curb inflationary pressures.  

The baht has risen about 14% against the greenback this year, faster than the appreciation of other East Asian units, she said. But Suchada added that since the start of 2005, the baht has risen only 9.3% against the dollar, more or less in line with regional currencies.  

Importers and debtors are benefitting from the baht's strength, she said.  

The negative effect on exporters, however, is limited, since exports are more affected by the economic strength of Thailand's trading partners than with the baht's value, she said.  

For every 1% rise in the baht's value against the dollar, export growth declines 0.1 percentage point, while for every one percentage point increase in the gross domestic product growth of trade partners, export growth rises 1.44 percentage points, she said.  

Suchada said the baht's strength is also allowing Thai businesses to improve or expand production by importing new machinery at a low cost.  

At 0748 GMT, the dollar was quoted at THB35.335 - off a nine-year low of THB35.250 hit earlier in the day - following suspected intervention by the Bank of Thailand and a warning to speculators by Suchada that the central bank was still "taking care" of the baht.  

She didn't comment on whether the central bank was intervening Tuesday or whether it planned to introduce any new measures to limit short-term capital inflows.  

She said the central bank is still evaluating the effectiveness of last week's move to ban short-term trading of local bonds by nonresidents and expanded restrictions on foreign exchange swaps and loans between onshore and offshore financial institutions.  

-By Phisanu Phromchanya, Dow Jones Newswires; 662-266-0744; phisanu.phromchanya@dowjones.com

title: Thai Ctrl Bk: Baht Still Rising Too Fast
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Bank of Thailand Assistant Governor Suchada Kirakul said Tuesday that the baht is still rising too fast and the central bank will continue to "take care" of the currency, but she declined to comment on any specific forms of current or planned intervention.  

At 0633 GMT, the dollar bounced back to THB35.32 after Suchada's comments from a nine-year low of THB35.25 that it hit earlier in the day. [ 12-12-06 0636GMT ]  

"The baht has been rising too fast and it is still rising too fast," Suchada said.  

A foreign exchange dealer said it appeared that agents of the central bank might be entering the market to buy dollars and restrain the baht's rise, after sitting on their hands for the first half of the Asian day.  

But the assistant governor wouldn't comment on whether the Bank of Thailand was intervening on Tuesday.  

"We have been taking care of the baht and we are still taking care of it," she said.  

But she said there are many ways to care for the baht under the managed float system, including regulatory measures designed to reduce speculative activity.  

Suchada also declined to comment, however, on whether the Bank of Thailand was planning any further measures to tighten curbs on short-term capital inflows.  

The central bank is still evaluating the effectiveness of measures introduced last week, she said.  

The latest moves by the central bank banned short-term trading of local bonds by nonresidents, and expanded restrictions on foreign exchange swaps and loans between onshore and offshore financial institutions.

title: Dlr Falls To 9-Year Low Vs Thai Baht At THB35.43
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht rose early Tuesday to a nine-year high against the U.S. dollar, hitting THB35.43 for the first time since October 1997.  

Foreign exchange dealers said the dollar selling originated in Singapore, but the reason for the sales wasn't immediately apparent.  

There were also no signs in early trade of central bank intervention in support of the dollar.

text:
Suchada also said the Thai baht is appreciating too quickly, buoyed by global dollar weakness and by capital inflows, but added that the baht's rise was also helping curb inflationary pressures.  

The baht has risen about 14% against the greenback this year, faster than the appreciation of other East Asian units, she said. But Suchada added that since the start of 2005, the baht has risen only 9.3% against the dollar, more or less in line with regional currencies.  

Importers and debtors are benefitting from the baht's strength, she said.  

The negative effect on exporters, however, is limited, since exports are more affected by the economic strength of Thailand's trading partners than with the baht's value, she said.  

For every 1% rise in the baht's value against the dollar, export growth declines 0.1 percentage point, while for every one percentage point increase in the gross domestic product growth of trade partners, export growth rises 1.44 percentage points, she said.  

Suchada said the baht's strength is also allowing Thai businesses to improve or expand production by importing new machinery at a low cost.  

At 0748 GMT, the dollar was quoted at THB35.335 - off a nine-year low of THB35.250 hit earlier in the day - following suspected intervention by the Bank of Thailand and a warning to speculators by Suchada that the central bank was still 'taking care' of the baht.  

She didn't comment on whether the central bank was intervening Tuesday or whether it planned to introduce any new measures to limit short-term capital inflows.

title: Thai exporters feeling pain as baht soars
text:
BANGKOK, Dec 8 (Reuters) - From textiles to tuna, rice to rubber, Thai exporters are feeling the pain of a soaring baht, Asia's strongest currency, which has also tested the mettle of the new central bank governor.  

 The baht <THB=> has risen nearly 6 percent since the Sept. 19 coup that ousted Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra and 15.6 percent since January. That compares with a rise of 10 percent in the Korean won <KRW=> and 8.4 percent in the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=>.  

 Some analysts expect the baht, which was trading at 35.56 per dollar on Friday, to strengthen further in the next 3-6 months despite Bank of Thailand intervention and new anti-speculation measures announced on Monday.  

 That's grim news for exporters of footwear, foods, textiles and electronics who pay some or all of their costs in baht and earn the bulk of their income in foreign currencies, including that of the United States, Thailand's biggest trading partner.  

 Thai Union Frozen Products PCL , Asia's largest canned tuna exporter with its popular "Chicken of the Sea" brand, was the latest company to issue a profit warning, saying the strong baht would hit earnings and revenue in 2007.  

 "We have been trying to control costs, improve efficiency and boost sales to minimise the impact of the strong baht," TUF President Thiraphong Chansiri told Reuters on Thursday.  

 Last month, a coalition of food and textile exporters demanded action to stem the baht's rise or compensation from the government to offset rising costs.  

 "If the baht continues to rise, members will have to cut their production, employment and finally, shut down their operations. It will strongly affect farmers and labourers," 10 export associations said in a statement.  

 PACKING UP?  

 Commerce Minister Krirk-krai Jirapaet said on Thursday the government was considering tax breaks and other incentives to help embattled manufacturers. He gave no details.  

 The ministry also cut its 2007 export growth target to 12.5 percent due to the stronger baht from a previous estimate of 15 percent and compared to 16 percent growth in 2006.  

 Some exporters have urged the central bank to cut interest rates to stem strong capital inflows that have buoyed the baht and pushed down bond yields in recent weeks.  

 But Governor Tarisa Watanangase, facing her first major test since assuming the top post in October, has ruled out an immediate rate cut, saying that might draw more money into the country from investors expecting it to stimulate the economy.  

 Instead, the new measures to deter speculators from buying short-term debt should be given time to work, she said.  "If the rules introduced on Monday are not enough, there will be more measures," Tarisa said, without giving details.  

 Economist Supavud Saicheua of Phatra Securities, which forecast the baht would rise another two percent by the second quarter of 2007, said it remained to be seen if the new rules would work.  "If these measures fail to stem short-term inflows, the BOT will consider taxing certain short-term financial transactions," he said in a report.  

 Kasikorn Research Center, which expected the baht to touch 35.0 in the first half of 2007, said exporters could diversify their export markets, reduce dollar-denominated trade or even outsource production to other countries.  

 "They may have to consider relocating some manufacturing plants abroad where production costs are lower or will be less affected by the declining trend of the U.S. dollar," it said.  

 But exporters are not packing their bags just yet.  

 "I can't see companies shutting down operations and moving away just because of this," said Richard Han, chief executive of Hana Microelectronics PCL .  

 Han, whose firm assembles integrated circuit packages for mobile phones and hand-held computers and pays 35-40 percent of its costs in baht, said "people will have to get used to a weak dollar for a while to come."  

 "Whatever the government can do to stop speculation is desirable, but you have to try to ride it out and improve your efficiency," he said.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia steady, Thai baht slips on cenbank action
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 4 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies were steady versus the dollar on Monday as optimism from solid regional economic data was offset by concerns about official steps to cap currency gains, which hit the Thai baht <THB=>.  

Bank of Thailand Governor Tarisa Watanagase announced measures on Monday to tighten foreign exchange rules, including banning non-residents from bond repurchase deals.  

She said the central bank would take more action if its measures failed to ease pressure on the baht, which has risen about 14.5 percent against the dollar this year.[ID:nBKK283072]  

The baht fell 0.45 percent to 35.90 per dollar on Monday, backing off from Friday's eight-year high of 35.70. The central bank's moves overshadowed stronger-than-expected economic growth figures. [ID:nBKK93899]  

Most analysts are optimistic about the near-term outlook for Asian currencies following a spate of healthy economic data, including Thailand's growth data and solid trade surpluses in South Korea and Indonesia.  

"I think the near-term outlook for the Asian market is still very good," said Irene Cheung, a currency analyst at ABN AMRO.  

"Eventhough there is a slowdown in the U.S., we believe that the regional momentum from China, India, and consumption growth are going to be supporting factors for next year," she said.  

Sustained capital inflows and trade surpluses have led to renewed rallies among Asian currencies in recent weeks, sparking a wave of verbal and actual intervention by regional central banks to cap further currency appreciation.  

The latest Reuters poll on positioning in Asian currencies suggests investors stepped up long positions in the Thai baht and remained bullish on the South Korean won and Singapore dollar.  

The dollar remained under broad selling pressure after weak U.S. factory data last week reinforced expectations the Federal Reserve would cut interest rates next year.  

BAHT DEPRESSED  

A currency dealer at a major Thai bank said he did not spot any sign of market intervention from the Bank of Thailand to support the U.S. dollar on Monday despite the baht's sharp fall.  

Prior to Monday's announcement, the Bank of Thailand had been intervening both verbally and through dollar buying in recent weeks.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell nearly a fifth of a percent to 1.5455 on Monday, off a nine-year high set last week.  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> firmed as high as 32.25 per U.S. dollar, matching Friday's peak, which was the highest in about 4-½ months.  

The South Korean won <KRW=> firmed against the dollar for a fourth consecutive session on Monday, but the persistent speculation that the central bank may purchase dollars to rein in the won prevent it from rising sharply.  

The won rose as high as 926 per dollar, holding back from a nine-year high of 925 on Nov. 27.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia higher, shrug off  intervention  jitters
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 1 (Reuters) - Sustained capital inflows sent Asian currencies higher on Friday as the U.S. dollar weakened globally, with the Thai baht <THB=> leading the rally amid signs of easing market concern about central bank intervention.  

Underscoring solid fundamentals buoying most regional currencies, South Korea said on Friday the country's exports in November grew a faster-than-expected 19.8 percent to a monthly record from a year earlier, maintaining surprising strength.  

"The risk appetite is still very good and there is no sign that any growth slowdown is impacting inflows into the region at the moment, and the dollar is softer," said James Malcolm, currency strategist at Deutsche Bank.  

"So strong inflows plus a soft dollar, even with central banks intervening, means the trend remains in place," he said.  

Renewed strength in most Asian currencies in recent weeks has triggered a wave of verbal and actual intervention by regional central banks to cap further currency appreciation.  

"Looking ahead, renewed interests for short dollar positions should place dollar/Asia on track to end this week with another decline," currency strategists Claudio Piron and Yen Ping Ho at JPMorgan wrote in a research note.  

Thio Chin Loo, currency analyst at BNP Paribas, said she remained bullish about the near-term strength of Asian currencies, with the latest gains helped by dollar weakness.  

The dollar hit a 14-year low against sterling <GBP=> on Friday and a new 20-month trough versus the euro <EUR=> as the U.S. currency suffered from expectations a weakening economy will prompt the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates next year.  

BEST PERFORMERS  

The Thai baht and Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> were Friday's best performers, with the baht gaining more than two thirds of a percent to 35.71 per dollar, its strongest level in eight years.  

The Bank of Thailand has been intervening both verbally and through actual dollar buying this week, traders said.  

Callum Henderson, head of currency strategy at Standard Chartered Bank, said the baht, which has gained about 15 percent so far this year, was also supported as political uncertainty after a military coup in September eased.  

"People took another look at Thailand and said okay, inflation has peaked, growth is set to accelerate so quite a few investors who were underweight Thailand have come back in the past few months," he said.  

The latest Reuters poll on positioning in Asian currencies suggests investors stepped up long positions in the Thai baht and remained bullish on the South Korean won and Singapore dollar.  

The ringgit strengthened to about 3.5915 per dollar, up about 0.75 percent from levels traded late on Thursday. A trader said the ringgit's unusually sharp gains were largely due to technical selling of the dollar.  

The South Korean won <KRW=>, underpinned by third-quarter gross domestic product data that was revised upward, rose to as high as 927.1 per dollar, gaining moderately but still off a nine-year high this week of 925.  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> firmed as high as 32.25 per U.S. dollar, hitting its highest level in about 4-½ months, while the Singapore dollar <SGD=> briefly hit 1.5372 against the U.S. dollar, matching a nine-year high set on Thursday. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR; Change on the day at 0728 GMT

title: Emerging  FX -Asia higher despite  intervention  worries
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 30 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies rose against the dollar on Thursday, buoyed by economic fundamentals justifying their underlying strength, despite lingering market concerns about possible central bank intervention.  

But a spike in crude oil prices capped gains in Asian currencies, while traders continued to be wary of regional central banks intervening to rein in their currencies.  

Thio Chin Loo, senior currency analyst at BNP Paribas, said she remained bullish about the near-term strength of most Asian currencies because of funds flowing into Asian equity markets.  

"It looks likely a quite good picture for Asian currencies. The only ones seeing less inflows are the Philippines and Indonesia because they have been front-runners, so there is a bit of consolidation as markets move from the high-yielder to the laggard," she said.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> hit a fresh nine-year high of 1.5421 against the U.S. dollar before retreating to 1.5440, while the South Korean won <KRW=> reversed earlier losses to hit around 929 per dollar, slightly off a nine-year high this week of 925.  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> hit 32.42 per U.S. dollar, the highest level in 4-½ months as exporters tried to offload their dollar holdings.  

"Sentiment is quite firm and when you see price action on the Korean won, where everyday you get comments on currency strength, it is testiment to strength in local currencies," said Sean Callow, currency strategist at Westpac Bank.  

RUNNING AHEAD  

The Thai baht <THB=> gained about a third of a percent versus the dollar to 36 per dollar, hitting its strongest level in almost eight years.  

"The Bank of Thailand will not resist a lower dollar/baht if the broad global trend is for a lower dollar," said Philip Wee, DBS Bank currency strategist.  

But based on current euro/dollar and dollar/yen levels, the baht should be closer to 36.40 per dollar, he said. The euro <EUR=> was trading around $1.3145, having come off Wednesday's 20-month highs, while the yen weakened to 116.50 per dollar.  

"This sort of tells you why Bank of Thailand is uncomfortable that the baht strength may have run ahead of itself," he said.  

The Bank of Thailand (BOT) has been intervening both verbally and by buying dollars this week, traders said.  

The BOT said on Wednesday the baht had risen too fast and its rise was not justified by fundamentals. On Monday it had said it would ask the finance ministry to allow exporters to hold their overseas receipts for up to 15 days instead of the seven-day limit now in place.  

Shahab Jalinoos of ABN AMRO Bank said baht had risen this year on higher baht interest rates and the relative cheapness of Thai stocks. The currency has gained about 14 percent so far this year despite months of political uncertainty that culminated in a bloodless coup in September.  

The strength of the trade account, which has propelled Thailand's current account to swing into surplus in the later half of this year, was also behind the baht's rally, he said.  

"Until now, strong global demand has overwhelmed the effect of baht strength, allowing exports growth to remain solid.  

"If the data show more evidence that this is still the case, we see room for further baht gains through 36.00 towards 35.50, given that the central bank has already thrown in the towel on its ability to stop this trend," Jalinoos said in a note to clients. title: Emerging  FX - Intervention  worries cap Asian  currencies
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 27 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose on Monday as the dollar took a beating against the euro and yen, but wariness about central bank intervention to limit local currency strength dampened the bullish sentiment slightly.  

 The South Korean won <KRW=> was quoted at its highest level in more than nine years at 925 per dollar, before paring gains on suspected dollar-buying intervention by Korea's central bank.  

 The Bank of Thailand said the baht's rise had been too fast and it might allow exporters to hold dollars for up to 15 days, longer than the current 7-day limit. The baht <THB=> was capped at about 36.38 per dollar, a hair's breadth away from 7-1/2-year highs of 36.36 struck earlier this month.  

 The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> gained almost 0.7 percent to 32.62 to the U.S. dollar, its highest since mid-August, before paring some gains. The Philippine peso <PHP=> ended local trade off a fresh 4-1/2-year high at 49.60 per dollar.  

 "Dollar weakness pressure was felt first in Asia," said Mirza Baig, a currency strategist with Deutsche Bank.  

 But intervention by the regional central banks had reined the Asian currencies in, he said.  

 "Now, the G10 currencies have taken up the torch, and emerging Asia is lagging."  

 The euro hit a 20-month peak at about $1.3180 <EUR=> on electronic trading platform EBS and the dollar fell to a three-month low at 115.40 yen <JPY=> on Monday.  

 Although the dollar subsequently clawed back some ground against the majors, analysts suggested the Asian rally would continue even if they had underperformed so far.  

 "The fundamental picture continues to shift in favour of Asian currencies gaining in strength and it would be reasonable to expect local central banks to intervene," said Richard Yetsenga, a currency strategist at HSBC in Hong Kong.  

 "But Asian currencies have underperformed the move in the majors versus the dollar."  

 Expectations for further euro zone interest rate increases have bolstered the euro. The dollar, in general, has also been hurt by position adjusting and ongoing talk of central banks diversifying their foreign exchange reserves away from the U.S. currency.  

 Some traders said central bank intervention may be limited in the face of a strong dollar downtrend.  

 "They (the central banks) will come in on and off, but I don't think they will be too aggressive because dollar sentiment is very bearish," said a Singapore dollar trader.  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=>, meanwhile, retreated to 1.5515/25 per U.S. dollar, up about 0.15 percent from levels traded late on Friday but off a nine-year high hit last week at 1.5467.  

 Elsewhere, the Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> firmed to 7.8410 to the dollar, its strongest level since the July 2005 revaluation and analysts continued to expect a further pick-up in gains.  

 "Dollar/yuan is now under major pressure to move lower quickly given the influence of euro/dollar and dollar/yen," ABN AMRO currency strategist Shahab Jalinoos said in a note.

title: UPDATE 1-Strong baht may prompt easing of capital controls
text:
(Adds quotes, detail)  

 BANGKOK, Nov 23 (Reuters) - Thailand may relax its capital controls further to help ease upward pressure on the rising baht, Bank of Thailand Governor (BOT) Tarisa Watanagase said on Thursday.  

 The central bank's efforts to slow the appreciation of the baht through intervention were limited, she told a seminar.  

 The Thai private sector should manage and hedge foreign exchange risks, she said, with the baht having risen about 12.5 percent against the dollar so far this year, the fastest riser of any Asian currency.  

 "The BOT can move to prevent the baht's excessive volatility, but its intervention can be done only to an extent, especially as the dollar sustains its weakness," Tarisa said.  

 The central bank might consider easing capital controls further in the future to relieve pressure on the baht, she said without elaboration.  

 Thailand has given private institutional investors more room to invest abroad in the past year.  

 But the baht remained competitive and its hefty rise this year had not hurt Thai exports seriously, Tarisa said.  

 Thai export groups called on the central bank last week to take more action to help them cope with the steadily rising baht.  

 October Thai exports rose 20.1 percent from the same month of 2005, a robust pace sustained since the second half of this year despite the baht strength.

title: Emerging  FX -Philippine peso bucks Asian weakness
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 17 (Reuters) - Asian currencies weakened on Friday on further unwinding of positions by traders fearing more central bank intervention and on the dollar's strength despite the softness in U.S. inflation data.  

 The Thai baht <THB=> was the biggest loser, shedding nearly 0.4 percent as it hit a one-week trough of 36.60 per dollar.  

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> was the lone exception to the weakness, as a heavy bunch of export earnings forced it to rally 0.2 percent to around 49.96 per dollar.  

 "When spot failed to go above 50.20 yesterday, a lot of exporters placed orders to sell," said one Manila-based trader, referring to the peso's rally.  

 Sean Callow, Westpac Bank's currency strategist, said the peso has traditionally been driven more by flows from trade transactions.  

 "So it is less likely to participate in any knee-jerk moves that, for example, the Sing dollar and Korean won have when broad dollar sentiment changes," he said.  

 But this week's decline in the Asian currencies has raised worries about whether this is merely a result of intervention or the start of a bigger sell-off of emerging markets.  

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> lost a quarter of a percent to hit a low of 1.5633 per U.S. dollar, taking losses from 9-year highs struck this week to half a percent and prompting speculation the Monetary Authority of Singapore may have intervened, as several other central banks did this week.  

 The Bank of Thailand was suspected of intervening to rein in the baht after it hit its strongest level in nearly seven years on Tuesday. The Reserve Bank of India and the Bank of Korea were also spotted buying dollars to halt the appreciation in their respective currencies, the rupee <INR=IN> and the won <KRW=>.  

 The won was slightly weaker at 938 per dollar on the day, but strong dollar earnings for Korean shipmakers and electronics exporters had helped lift it from lows near 944 on Thursday.  

 The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> fell a quarter of a percent on Friday.  Analysts at UBS said selling of Asian currencies was spurred not just by intervention fears but by warnings from central banks in New Zealand and Japan on the heavy accumulation of carry trades.  

 The yen and Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> have been the favoured funding vehicles in Asia for carry trades, which involve borrowing low-yielding currencies to invest in high-yielding assets.  

 "The combination of these has contributed to position squaring particularly in high-yielding Asian currencies," UBS said.  


 "The high-yielding currencies -- Indonesian rupiah,
Philippine peso, Korean won, Indian rupee -- weakened
  

significantly while the lower-yielding currencies such as the
Singapore dollar and Taiwan dollar have largely remained
resilient."

title: UPDATE:Thai Exporter Assocs Call For Action Vs Baht Rise
text:
(Updates with supporting comments from finance ministry official, suspected central bank intervention Thursday)  

BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--A group of 10 Thai exporter associations Thursday issued a joint statement saying they will ask the Bank of Thailand and other related authorities act to ensure the baht doesn't appreciate at a greater pace than regional currencies.  

"We demand that they implement appropriate measures to maintain baht stability in order to maintain the country's competitiveness... The persistent rise in the baht makes us unable to compete in terms of price," the statement said. Chakkrit Parapuntakul, a spokesman for the Public Debt Management Office in the Ministry of Finance, later sought to reassure exporters by saying that as the threat of inflation has eased and that the central bank will have room to start cutting interest rates, which could lower demand for the baht.  

However, the Bank of Thailand's monetary policy committee had said at its last meeting on Oct. 18 that it remains cautious despite declining inflation. The committee left its 14-day repurchase market target rate unchanged at 5% due to the possibility of renewed volatility in global oil prices and other uncertainties.Comments Wednesday by central bank Governor Tarisa Watanagase didn't give exporters much encouragement about the possibility of help from official quarters. She said the baht's recent strength has been the result of flows into regional as well as local stock and bond markets, and that the baht has outperformed regional currencies against the dollar this year only after underperforming last year.  

The Bank of Thailand has a policy of intervening in foreign exchange markets to only reduce daily volatility and speculative activity, not to counter the effects of real trade and investment flows.  

But foreign exchange traders said agents of the central bank were suspected of buying the dollar Thursday to help prevent a fall toward Tuesday's eight-year low of THB36.38. The dollar closed in Asian trade Thursday at THB36.50, versus THB36.56 Wednesday.  

Chakkrit told reporters that there is no need for the central bank to maintain domestic interest rates at current levels because such rates would continue to attract capital inflows, resulting in a firmer baht.  

"Easier interest rates should help reduce appreciation pressure on the baht," said Chakkrit.  

The comments may not represent an official ministry position on the subject, however. Finance Minister Pridiyathorn Devakula declined to comment on the matter this week, saying he didn't appreciate interference from the ministry when he was governor, so he wasn't going to interfere himself.  

Economists said lower domestic rates probably wouldn't help to weaken the currency because such a move would bolster sentiment toward the local stock and bond markets, attracting even larger inflows.  

The baht has appreciated by around 12% against the U.S. dollar so far this year, while most regional units have risen by 3%-6%, and Chinese yuan has gained only 1%-2%, the exporters' associations said in the statement.  

If the baht continues to strengthen faster than its regional peers, the loss of competitiveness may cause members of the associations to begin reducing production, laying off staff and eventually closing businesses, it said.  

Representatives of the 10 associations, which group producers of frozen foods, chicken, shrimp, fruit and vegetables, vegetable oil, garments and other sectors, said they would soon be sending a formal statement to the central bank.  

The associations' members account for around THB680 billion ($18.6 billion) of the country's exports each year, according to the joint statement. Thailand's exports have recently hit record highs above $11 billion per month.

title: Thai Baht Ends Off 11-Wk Low; Medium-Term Bonds Lower
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht fell in Asian spot trade Monday to close just off an 11-week low after the dollar strengthened against global as well as regional currencies and due to suspected intervention by the Bank of Thailand, traders said.  

Medium-term government bond prices were lower, under pressure from rising Treasury bill yields. Dealers expect further flattening in the long end of the yield curve if a government bond auction Wednesday confirms that demand is still significantly higher than supply.  

The dollar finished at THB39.15, up from THB39.00 at the Asian close Friday, after rising to an 11-week high of THB39.18.  

Singapore players were believed to have actively chased the dollar up in the morning session to cover short positions, triggering stop-loss orders, a Bangkok-based trader said.  

"The U.S. unit was well bid as the central bank was suspected to have joined the buying spree," he said.  

The dollar was also helped by hefty cross-currency demand from Thailand-based Japanese companies, which bought the yen after purchasing the U.S. dollar with the baht to make payments on loans and repatriate earnings before the end of Japan's fiscal year on March 31.  

The dollar's rally was exaggerated by thin volumes due to the closure of many European markets for Easter Monday.  

Exporters sold heavily around THB39.10 for month-end settlements, but the amount wasn't sufficient to hold back the dollar.  

Traders gave a wide THB38.80-THB39.30 range for support and resistance overnight as the U.S. markets react to the sharp changes in the dollar's value later in the global day. [ 28-03-05 1046GMT ]  

Medium-term government bond yields edged up in a thin market under pressure from rising treasury bill yields. Most long-term bond yields were, however, unchanged or edged lower, dealers said.  

T-bill yields rose in line with auction results, which showed a drop in demand. Earlier in the day, the Bank of Thailand sold THB6 billion worth of 91-day T-bills at an average 2.095%, up from 2.061% at last week's auction. It sold another THB5 billion in 182-day T-bills at an average 2.278%, up from 2.259%.  

Funds set up recently to invest in short-term paper appeared to have completed their initial buying, and nonresident demand for T-bills may have weakened due to the baht's recent weakness against the dollar, a dealer said.  

The Thai yield curve is likely to flatten further if Wednesday's auction confirms that demand is still greater than supply in the long end, another dealer said. Investors will also be watching Tuesday's auction of short-term central bank bonds to be certain that it follows the trend set by T-bills.  

The Thai Bond Dealing Center said the average bid late Monday on the paper due December 2006 was virtually unchanged at 2.800%; the November 2009 bid edged up half a basis point to 3.806%; the August 2010 bid gained one basis point to 3.933%; the March 2012 bid was virtually unchanged at 4.185%; the May 2014 bid edged down half a basis point to 4.488%; the December 2014 bid was virtually unchanged at 4.601%; and the April 2021 bid was down half a basis point at 4.950%.  

The overnight interbank rate was quoted around 1.86%-1.89% in late trade, versus a most-active level Friday of 1.90%, dealers said. Liquidity was high as banks and clients prepared extra cash for month-end payments, but the overnight repurchase market rate came off a very low level late Friday of 1.75% to close at 1.78125%.  

Quotes for term interest rates were mixed. Dealers said the market was pausing because rates have climbing steadily in recent weeks, in line with the expected trend in official interest rates.

title: MOODY'S ASSIGNS (P)Ba1 RATING TO THAI MILITARY BANK'S JUNIOR SUBORDINATED NOTES
text:
Moody's Investor's Service has assigned a rating of (P)Ba1 to Thai Military Bank's (TMB's) proposed junior subordinated debt notes, due 2015. The rating reflects TMB's systemic importance, its improving, but still weak financial fundamentals, as well as the structure of this subordinated issue. The ratings outlook is stable.  

Note that this rating is subject to the receipt of final documentation, the terms and conditions of which have not changed in any material way from the draft documents reviewed by Moody's.  

As with many Upper Tier II capital-qualifying subordinated debt issues, TMB's junior subordinated securities include provisions that allow the borrower to defer payment of interest, under certain circumstances and prohibiting the payment of principal and interest under others. If implemented, such provisions (while not legally constituting an event of default) could result in payment terms appreciably different from senior securities. These distinctions are reflected in the two notch rating differential between TMB's Baa2 rating on senior obligations and this Ba1 rated junior subordinated debt issue.  

While, Moody's considers TMB to possess sufficient financial flexibility (supplemented as it is by regulatory support) to avoid, in most circumstances, deferring interest payments on its junior subordinated debt, the solvency conditions required by Thailand's regulators in Upper Tier II capital-qualifying debt are particularly strict.  

Specifically, the bond indenture specifies that in addition to the usual solvency requirement, "No principal or interest shall be payable in respect of the Notes ... if the Bank of Thailand has intervened in the Bank's operations by ordering a capital write down and increase."  

While Moody's expects regulatory support will ultimately benefit all creditor classes, this provision could affect the timeliness of such benefit reaching junior subordinated creditors. Theoretically, non-payment after an intervention could persist until such time as common dividends are reinstated. Having said that, Moody's pointed out that if current positive economic and bank performance trends persist, it will become progressively more unlikely that TMB would require such assistance.  

Thai Military Bank, headquartered in Bangkok, is Thailand's fifth largest bank, with over 450 branches countrywide. It had total assets of THB 669 billion (US$ 17 billion) on December 31, 2004. The Thai military's aggregate stake in TMB has declined significantly since the Asian financial crisis of 1997 and now stands at only 5.4%. The Thai Ministry of Finance is the largest shareholder with 31.2%. Singapore's DBS Bank holds 16.1%.  

Thai Military Bank's other ratings are:  

Long and short-term foreign currency deposits of Baa2 and Prime-2, respectively; Long-term foreign currency subordinated debt of Baa3; and Bank Financial Strength (BFSR) of E+. The BFSR has a positive outlook, while all debt and deposit ratings carry a stable outlook.

title: Thai Baht Ends Up On Equities Inflows, Yen; Bonds Higher
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht ended marginally higher against the dollar in Asian spot trade Tuesday, boosted by equities-related investment inflows and the U.S. currency's mild weakness against the Japanese yen, a regional trendsetter, traders said.  

The dollar's losses were limited, however, due to suspected intervention by Bank of Thailand.  

Government bond prices closed higher on demand driven by high cash liquidity.  

The dollar finished at THB38.34, down from THB38.39 at Monday's close.  

Following overnight weakness related to its weak tone against the yen, the dollar was sold off in early trade from the THB38.33 level by offshore players from Singapore. The selling, which was probably related to equities investments, forced the U.S. currency to an intraday low of THB38.30, a Bangkok-based trader said.  

The selling was met by strong support from suspected agents of the central bank.  

"The dollar was well bid at the THB38.31 level with heavy buying orders placed by some agents," the trader said.  

The U.S. currency made a late recovery after failing to break under support, but the gains were limited by its generally weak or directionless tone against the yen and other regional currencies.  

Traders expect the dollar to remain in a range of THB38.30 to THB38.40 overnight. [ 08-03-05 1042GMT ]  

Most Thai bond yields fell in anticipation of strong demand in Wednesday's government bond auction, and after high cash liquidity sharply limited the rise of yields in Tuesday's auction of short-term central bank bonds, dealers said.  

The Thai Bond Dealing Center said the average bid late Tuesday on the government bond due December 2006 fell two basis points to 2.867%, the December 2008 bid dropped one basis point to 3.518%, the November 2009 bid was off marginally at 3.919%, the August 2010 bid was down one basis point to 4.071%, and the December 2014 bid eased almost half a basis point to 4.710%, as did the December 2019 bid to 5.025%.  

Yields in Tuesday's central bank bond auction rose, but not as much as expected after last week's interest rate increase, due to demand driven by high cash levels of both banks and popular short-term funds. Last week, the central bank raised its 14-day repurchase market target rate by 25 basis points to 2.25%.  

Bank of Thailand sold at an auction Tuesday THB5 billion worth of 28-day central bank bonds at an average 1.883%, up from 1.853% at the previous auction. A THB3 billion tranche of 63-day central bank bonds was sold at an average 1.968%, up from 1.967%. Another THB10 billion of 364-day central bank bonds was sold at an average 2.568%, up from 2.552% last week.  

The overnight interbank rate was quoted late Tuesday around 1.85%, after early trade in a range of 1.95%-2%, versus the most-active level of 1.875% and a range of 1.7%-2.1% Monday, dealers said.  

The most-active level was expected to rise with the start of a new reserve period Tuesday, as cash is freed up to move to higher-yielding markets.  

It may not have risen, however, because liquidity remained very high, as reflected in the 28-day accepted yields and the overnight repurchase market rate, which closed flat at 1.75%.  

Quotes for most term interest rates edged higher again, as increases in onshore and offshore interest rates are expected to continue in the coming months.
