title: Emerging Asia  FX -Peso weak, others hold ground despite yen.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Feb 21 (Reuters) - Asian currencies shrugged off
the weakness in the Japanese yen on Monday and held their
ground, despite the increasing threat of regional central bankinterventions.
    The Philippine peso was among the only currencies to weaken
notably, because of worries that legislators might reject or
water down a proposed system of value-added tax. The peso fell
to 54.85 per dollar from opening levels around 54.70.
    The Korean won, Taiwan dollar and Singapore dollar
maintained narrow ranges even as the yen shed nearly half a
percent from Friday, driven lower by last week's weak Japanese
economic data and waning expectations of any immediate change
in China's currency regime.
 
    That led the yen-won cross rate to weaken to around 9.67
won per yen, close to two-year lows struck in overnight deals.
    "We think Korea has delinked from yen, as has the rest of
  

Asia," said one Singapore-based trader. "And, now the problem  

is that the market has been caught long yen/won and is  

scrambling to sell."  

Traders believe the South Korean authorities target the  

won's level against the yen, since the two countries export  

similar products. But for almost a month the yen has stayed  

below 10 won, the level that analysts believe is the lowest  

South Korea is comfortable with.  

The won rose to near 1,022 a dollar on Monday, within  

striking distance of last week's seven-year peak, as Korean  

stocks hit a five-year high on news a fund had invested $975  

million in Korean conglomerate LG Corp. and its unit.  

Won bulls shrugged off news of further issuance of bonds by  

the Bank of Korea, to absorb the won funds released during  

dollar-buying intervention.  

INTERVENTION WORRY  

Still, the worry of intervention weighed on currency

markets in India, Taiwan, Thailand and Korea. Thailand's and  

India's reserves data showed heavy dollar-buying intervention.  

The Taiwan dollar was held back from four-year highs beyond  

31.50 by talk the central bank had intervened heavily to cap  

the currency last week.  

Foreign portfolio investment inflows are putting upward  

pressure on the currency. Foreigners have bought close to T$100  

billion of Taiwan shares since late January and the market hit  

its highest in nine months on Monday.  

The Thai baht was in a range of 38.53 to 38.60 per dollar,  

while the Sing dollar was on the firmer side of 1.64 per  

dollar.  

Analysts said Thailand had received over $1 billion of  

foreign portfolio investments so far in 2005, more than in any  

year from 2001 to 2004.  

"The big theme at the moment is whether or not dollar  

weakness is going to resume," said John Cairns, head of  

research at IDEAglobal.com.   


 
    "The more the dollar stays here, the more people are going
to be worried about their long Asia positions," he said.
    The moves in Hong Kong forwards and Taiwan dollar
  

non-deliverable forwards also confirmed speculators were  

trimming their Asian positions, he added.

title: BC-MARKETS-ASIA- CURRENCIES -FACTBOX.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 1 (Reuters) - Asia's currency regimes are in the spotlight ahead of this weekend's Group of Seven meeting in London, which is expected to encourage China and its neighbours to let their exchange rates rise to promote a reduction in global economic imbalances.  

In general, emerging Asian economies explicitly or implicitly shadow the dollar. But the regimes vary, from the Malaysian ringgit's rigid peg to South Korea's independently floating won.  

The following summary, drawn from official sources and investment bank reports, is based on the International Monetary Fund's definitions for fixed currency pegs, managed floats with varying degrees of fluctuations, and independent floats.  

FIXED PEGS  

-  

MALAYSIAN RINGGIT  

The ringgit has been fixed at 3.8 to the dollar since September 1998. The currency used to float until a flight of capital and a collapse in its value during the 1997/98 Asian financial crisis prompted the authorities to impose capital controls and fix the ringgit.  

Markets have been abuzz with talk, denied by ministers, that the time is ripe to review the continued usefulness of the peg.  

HONG KONG DOLLAR  

The Hong Kong dollar is pegged at 7.8 per U.S. dollar as part of a Currency Board Arrangement that was created on October 17, 1983, in response to a currency crisis.  

Under the board's rules, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base has to be matched by equivalent foreign currency reserves.  

The system is asymmetric, requiring the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to guarantee the sale of U.S. dollars at a fixed rate of 7.8 Hong Kong dollars. But the HKMA is not obliged to buy dollars at that rate: in October 2003, when yuan revaluation speculation was rife, the HK dollar rose to 7.7 per dollar.  

The peg requires the HKMA to adopt U.S. monetary policy.  

The currency is fully convertible on the capital account.  

CHINESE YUAN OR RENMINBI  

China's yuan is a closely managed float that has pegged the currency in a 0.04 percent band centred on a rate of around 8.278 per dollar since the Asian crisis.  

China had followed a dual exchange rate since 1979 but unified those rates in 1994 to create a crawling yuan peg.  

The yuan appreciated from 8.7 per dollar to around 8.3 between 1994 and 1996, and continued to fluctuate around that level until the Asian crisis, when Beijing rejected advice to devalue like its neighbours and virtually fixed the currency instead.  

Beijing says the stability this created provided a platform for Asia's rapid economic recovery and is an argument for not being rushed now in the other direction into a revaluation.  

China's central bank intervenes heavily, buying and selling yuan to preserve the peg. The yuan is freely traded on the trade account but the capital account is relatively closed, except for foreign direct investment and a few lending and borrowing transactions.  

Still, companies and individuals have found ways round the capital controls and have poured "hot money" into China on speculation of a policy change that will loosen the peg and result in a stronger yuan.  

The yuan has an active non-deliverable forwards (NDF) market, an unofficial derivatives market where dollar-denominated forward contracts are used to bet on the yuan's future value.  

MANAGED FLOATS:  

-  

SINGAPORE DOLLAR  

Tweaking the currency's managed float has been the primary policy tool of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) since 1981. Economists say the float is a combination of the band, basket and crawl systems.  

The MAS conducts monetary policy by letting the Sing dollar's nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) appreciate or depreciate, either by shifting the mid-point of the undisclosed band or adjusting its width. The composition of the basket is secret, but economists say the dollar and dollar-bloc currencies make up the biggest proportion.  

Policy shifted from neutral to a tightening bias in April 2004 via a gradual appreciation of the mid-point of the NEER.  

The Sing dollar is freely convertible on the trade account and has very minimal restrictions on capital flows.  

INDIAN RUPEE  

Economists say the Reserve Bank of India uses a monitoring band for the rupee, which allows it to float within a band determined by the currencies of India's top five trading partners, adjusted for inflation levels.  

Markets believe the width of the band is five percent on either side of this neutral real effective exchange rate (REER), and the RBI intervenes if the band is breached.  

The RBI regularly publishes data on the REER base period and neutral value, but with a lag.  

The current unified exchange rate was adopted in 1993 after a balance of payments crisis led to devaluations in 1991.  

The rupee is not fully convertible on the capital account. There are still some limits on residents borrowing overseas, on residents converting local assets into foreign currency and on the access foreigners have to Indian debt markets.  

THAI BAHT  

Massive capital outflows forced Thailand to abandon the baht's peg against a basket of currencies on July 2, 1997, triggering a big devaluation against the dollar that marked the onset of the Asian financial crisis.  

Thailand adopted a managed float. Like other Asian central banks operating under similar regimes, the Bank of Thailand is averse to currency volatility and intervenes often in the market.  

Selective capital controls exist. There are strict limits on baht positions held by foreigners and offshore trading in baht is negligible.  

INDONESIAN RUPIAH  

Indonesia switched to a freely floating rupiah from a managed float in August 1997 during the Asian crisis. Several exchange controls remain.  

INDEPENDENTLY FLOATING:  

-   


KOREAN WON
  

The won was floated in December 1997 and is one of Asia's most actively traded currencies.  

The Bank of Korea runs an inflation-targeting policy, but the government dictates currency policy and keeps a watchful eye on the won's competitiveness. This occasionally leads to strains between the central bank and the finance ministry.  

Foreigners have greater access to South Korean capital markets than to most others in emerging Asia, yet there are some restrictions on offshore won trading and on local banks' positions in won. The won NDF market that has developed as a consequence is among the most liquid in Asia.  

The yen-won is a popular cross rate, traded in the belief that Seoul likes to keep the won competitive versus the yen because of the overlap between South Korean and Japanese exports.  

PHILIPPINE PESO  

The peso is allowed to trade in a wider band than most other Asian currencies and is prone to volatile swings in response to political developments. It is also sensitive to data on the Philippines' large fiscal deficit and on remittances from overseas Filipinos, a major source of foreign exchange.  

The central bank, with limited official reserves, intervenes occasionally. It also adjusts reserve requirements, and the rate at which they are remunerated, to help smooth the currency.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Won at 7-year high on share purchases.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Jan 19 (Reuters) - The South Korean won rose to
a fresh seven-year high on Wednesday, boosted by foreign
purchases of stocks, and leading Asian currencies higher as the
G7 presses Asian central banks to allow their currencies to
appreciate.
    The won, Asia's best performing currency in 2004,
strengthened half a percent to 1,030.2 per dollar, a level
where traders said state-owned banks probably intervened by
buying dollars to help keep exports competitive.
    Foreign investors were net sellers of about 21 billion won
in Korean stocks on Wednesday, but had bought a net 623 billion
won worth of shares in the previous three sessions.
    "There's equity-related buying on behalf of foreign
investors," said Sani Hamid, a currency analyst at 4CAST Ltd.
in Singapore.
  


 "Then there's the G7 calling for stronger Asian
currencies."
    China was likely to come under pressure from the Group of
Seven nations at a meeting in February to loosen its control on
the yuan and allow the currency to appreciate, analysts said. A
stronger yuan would boost other Asian currencies.
    The baht matched its 4-1/2-year high of 38.38 per dollar
with further gains held back by suspected central bankintervention to buy dollars. The Bank of Thailand left its key
14-day repo rate unchanged at 2.0 percent, as expected.
    The Taiwan dollar and the Philippine peso each gained a
third of a percent and the Singapore dollar strengthened a
fifth of a percent.
    "Everyone wants to hold a bullish position on Asian
currencies in case China does move," said Mark Cranfield, head
of treasury at Landesbank Baden-Wuerttemberg in Singapore.
 
    "Personally, I think they won't. It's too early. China
wants to fix its banking system first."
    The premiums on one-month, three-month and six-month yuan
  

non-deliverable forwards - agreements that investors use to  

bet on any change in the yuan's value in the future - have  

been pared back after surging through the fourth quarter of  

2004.  

U.S. DEFICIT  

Asian currencies held their ground even after data on  

Tuesday alleviated concerns that the United States was unable  

to attract enough foreign capital to fund its record trade  

deficit. Those concerns were responsible for the dollar's  

decline last year.  

Foreign investors pumped $81 billion into U.S. assets in  

November, hitting a five-month high and exceeding average  

forecasts of $55 billion. The surge in inflows more than  

covered a record $60.3 billion U.S. trade deficit in the same  

month.   


 
    Some analysts cautioned that the inflows were not so
impressive when compared with the same month last year.
    Inflows from abroad were $8 billion higher than November
  

2003, while the U.S. trade deficit was $21 billion wider than a  

year earlier, Ashley Davies, a strategist at UBS, said in a  

note.  

"So while the U.S. funding requirement has increased,  

portfolio investors are only grudgingly opening their wallets,"  

he said.  

With longer-term concerns about the dollar unchanged, Asian  

currencies are likely to outperform other major world  

currencies such as the euro and the Australian dollar this  

year, Standard Chartered Bank said in a report, adding that the  

Singapore dollar was its top pick in Asia.  

"We still think (Asian currencies) can appreciate further  

against the dollar in the first half and significantly against  

the euro in the second half given the strong balance of  

payments, tsunami-related aid, infrastructure spending and  

euro-overvaluation," the bank said. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: Thai c.bank sees no need to  intervene  on baht.
text:
BANGKOK, Jan 7 (Reuters) - Thailand's central bank sees no need to intervene in the currency market to curb the baht's volatility this week, Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said on Friday   

"We have not seen any unusual movement. It is quite okay and there is nothing we need to do," Pridiyathorn told reporters.   

The baht has weakened against a stronger dollar in the past few days, trading at around 39.15/18 per dollar at 0736 GMT on Friday against 38.80 late on Monday.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Chief Denies  FX Intervention  Cost $3 Bln
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula Tuesday denied that the central bank had bought as much as $3 billion since mid-October to stem the Thai baht's rally.  

"We didn't buy $3 billion. That's too much," Pridiyathorn told reporters.  

Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said earlier Tuesday that the central bank bought about $3 billion worth of dollars in recent days, without specifying an exact timeframe.  

Matichon newspaper reported Tuesday, citing a source from the Bank of Thailand, that the central bank's move to sell baht for dollars has resulted in flush liquidity in the financial system.  

The central bank's dollar buying added around THB120 billion in baht liquidity in the domestic financial market, some of which moved into the local stock market for speculative purposes, the paper said, quoting the source.  

"(When the central bank buys dollars) we always sponge up excess liquidity from the market. We won't let flush liquidity get too high," Pridiyathorn said.  

However, he acknowledged that the central bank has managed the baht in recent weeks in a bid to mitigate its pace of appreciation.  

Thailand's foreign reserves rose $3.1 billion from Oct. 15 to $48.1 billion as of Nov. 26. The central bank said much of that was due to the appreciation in dollar terms of other foreign currencies held in reserves.  

The baht has risen around 4.6% since early November.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Ascent slows as yen, won stall.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Nov 24 (Reuters) - A rally in Asian currencies
against a broadly weaker U.S. dollar slowed on Wednesday as the
threat of intervention reined in the Korean won and Japanese
yen.
    The dollar fell to record lows past $1.31 against the euro
  overnight and plumbed new lows versus other European
currencies.
    But it held its ground against the yen        as the
Japanese currency found it hard to scale an April 2000 peak
near 102.75 per dollar struck last week.
    The Korean won                   was quoted around 1,065 a
dollar, having come off a 7-year high of 1,060 on successive
sessions this week after state-run banks were seen buying
dollars aggressively.
 
    The Taiwan dollar          hit a high of 32.41 but was
still some distance away from Friday's 3-=   year peak.
    However, Reuters data showed the Singapore dollar
rose to 1.6433, a new 6-year high, and the Thai baht  was
quoted at 39.74, its highest since May.
  


    "I don't think anyone is fighting the (weak dollar) trend,"
said Philip Wee, strategist with DBS Bank.
    "The won has outdone even the yen and is too strong
relative to the region. The Koreans have a case for smoothening
the won's move."
    The won has risen nearly 5 percent this month, compared
with the yen's 2 percent, the Taiwan dollar's 3 percent and the
Singapore dollar's 1 percent gains.
    Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said on Wednesday
the Bank of Thailand had not intervened to stall the rising
baht.
    The Indonesian rupiah        and the Philippine peso
continued as regional laggards, holding steady levels.
    In Singapore, analysts differed on how much further the
  

Singapore dollar could rise before it hit the top end of the  

undisclosed trade-weighed band within which the Monetary  

Authority of Singapore guides the currency.  

DBS' Wee said his estimates showed the Singapore dollar  

would hit the top of the band, which he takes as 5 percent  

wide, when it rises to 1.6360.

title: Thailand  has not  intervened  on baht - PM.
text:
BANGKOK, Nov 24 (Reuters) - The Thai central bank has not intervened to slow the baht's recent sharp gains against the dollar and will let the Thai currency move in line with market forces, Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said on Wednesday.    

 "The Bank of Thailand has not resisted market forces. Its managed float of the baht is mostly in line with global currency trends. It has so far not affected our exports," Thaksin told reporters.

title: Thai Baht Ends At Fresh 6.5-Month High; Most Bonds Down
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht ended at its highest level in six-and-a-half months in Asian spot trade Monday, as the U.S. unit fell in global currency markets after U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said U.S. deficits will bring further weakness in the currency.  

Most Thai government bond prices fell, as Greenspan also promised in comments late Friday to continue raising interest rates. Intervention by the Bank of Thailand, however, limited losses to mostly short- and medium-term bonds.  

The dollar finished at THB39.84, down from THB40.21 at the Asian close Friday. The close was its lowest level since May 7, traders said.  

The U.S. unit crashed through pyschological resistance at THB40.00 during the New York session Friday.  

Follow-through selling by big-name investment houses finally pushed the dollar under THB39.90 late in Asian trade Monday.  

Traders said volume was very thin, but the Bank of Thailand stood aside Monday to let the baht catch up with the rise of the yen against the dollar late Friday.  

Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said Monday that the central bank will try to limit volatility and speculative activity which affect the country's trade, but that it can't really intervene against the regional foreign exchange trend.  

He said the recent strength of the baht was due to U.S. efforts to weaken the dollar. Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said earlier Monday that the central bank is monitoring the situation, but that the baht's strength is due to general dollar weakness, not speculative pressure.  

Traders expect the dollar to trade overnight in a range of THB39.75 to THB39.90. Further weakness is expected in the dollar due to the massive U.S. current account and budget deficits, but traders expect the market to pause for profit taking and to avoid provoking Asian central banks into intervention. [ 22-11-04 1050GMT ]  

Short- and medium-term government bond yields rose, tracking U.S. Treasury yields higher after Greenspan's comments on interest rates. However, buying by the Thai central bank in issues due August 2010 and March 2011 limited increases in the long end of the curve, dealers said.  

They expect yields in the short end of the yield curve to remain under pressure from rising interest rates, likely flattening the yield curve.  

Some economists have said they don't believe the Thai central bank will raise its 14-day repurchase market target rate from the current 1.75% at its next policy meeting on Dec. 15, due to expectations that economic growth will slow next year.  

But if the U.S. federal funds rate rises 25 basis points to 2.25% in mid-December, the central bank may be reluctant to let the premium over the Thai policy rate rise to 50 basis points.  

The average bid late Monday on the government bond due December 2006 rose six basis points to 2.725%; the December 2008 bid climbed five basis points to 3.613%; the November 2009 bid edged up one basis point to 4.153%; the August 2010 bid was flat at 4.274%; the October 2013 bid was flat at 4.90%; and the August 2019 bid rose one basis point to 5.35%, the Thai Bond Dealing Center said.  

The Bank of Thailand said it auctioned THB5 billion worth of 28-day treasury bills Monday at a weighted-average accepted yield of 1.595%, down from 1.619% at last week's auction, due to demand for paper maturing shortly after next month's interest rate policy meeting. In the secondary market, the average bid yield on 28-day T-bills eased to 1.600% from 1.632% late Friday, the Thai Bond Dealing Center said.  

Auction yields on 92- and 182-day T-bills rose, however, due to the rising risk of interest rate increases over the terms.  

The central bank auctioned THB5 billion in 92-day T-bills at an average 1.786%, up from 1.748% last week. The average secondary market bid edged down to 1.773% from 1.774%, however, because many investors want paper that matures early next year.  

Five billion baht worth of 182-day T-bills were auctioned at an average 2.239%, up from 2.156% last week. The secondary market bid jumped to 2.255% from 2.167% Friday.  

The secondary market bid on 364-day central bank bonds rose to 2.487% from 2.466% Friday, but dealers expect yields above 2.5% in Tuesday's auction, which will also put another THB5 billion of supply in the market.  

The most-active overnight interbank rate was likely flat around 1.70%, with banks mostly prepared for the end Monday of a biweekly cash reserve period, dealers said.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Chief: Will Try To Mitigate Baht Volatility
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Thailand's central bank will try to mitigate the volatility in the baht as an excessive currency movement may attract speculation and affect the country's trade, its governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said Monday.  

However, the Bank of Thailand can't rally intervene in the market to drive the baht against the regional foreign exchange trend.  

"We will do the best we can to reduce the impact (of baht volatility) on trade. But, we can't really intervene. We can't go against the market trend," he told reporters. [ 22-11-04 0537GMT ]  

Pridiyathorn said the baht's recent strength is mainly due to efforts by the U.S. to weaken the dollar. Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said early Monday that the baht's strength is due to a general dollar weakness, not speculation.  

At 0542, the dollar was quoted at 39.885 baht, a near seven-month low, down from THB39.90 early and THB40.07 at Friday's close in Asian spot trade. The baht has gained around 3% in the past three weeks.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Sing dlr, won hit multi-year highs.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Nov 18 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar rallied
to a 6-year high against the dollar and the South Korean won
hit a new 7-year high on Thursday as worries about the U.S.
current account deficit saw the dollar sold against most
currencies.
    Analysts said attention was focused on this weekend's
meeting in Germany of finance officials from the Group of 20
developed and developing nations, which could provide clues as
to whether Asian governments would tolerate further currency
strength.
    The Singapore dollar        traded as high as 1.6448 per
dollar, its strongest level since December 1998. It could
strengthen further because the Monetary Authority of Singapore
has a tightening bias for monetary policy, Bank of America
strategist Simon Flint said.
    The won        surged 1.5 percent to a high of 1,063.8 per
dollar, a high since November 1997.
  


 The currency has gained 7.5
percent since the start of October and 12 percent this year,
making it Asia's best performing currency against the dollar.
 
    The dollar fell to a record low against the euro        and
was at seven-and-a-half month lows against the yen on Thursday.
    "If the (G20) meeting comes out with no clear conclusions,
  

then chances are that the market could go for a sell-dollar  

mode again," said Christy Tan, currency analyst at 4CAST Ltd.  

in Singapore.   


 
    "We do see some outperformance by the Taiwan dollar and the
Sing dollar in the next few weeks."
    The Taiwan dollar          gained 0.8 percent to a new
  

three-and-half year high, helped by the broader dollar weakness  

and optimism about domestic economic growth that has driven  

Taiwan's benchmark stock index 6 percent higher this month.   


The Thai baht  and the Indian rupee          are
  

other possible gainers among Asian currencies in the coming  

weeks, provided that their central banks do not intervene, Tan  

said.  

Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said on  

Thursday that short-term foreign funds inflows had risen this  

week, but not to a worrying level that would require the  

central bank to step in.  

The baht strengthened to 40.04 per dollar. The rupee was  

little changed at 45.04 per dollar on worries about  

intervention.  

Asian central banks intervened heavily from 2002 to early  

2004 to limit currency gains against a weakening dollar,  

building up reserve holdings of more than $2.2 trillion as they  

sought to protect their export sectors.  

But Asian investors and exporters have sold the dollar  

since October on concern about the U.S. budget and trade  

deficits, and an expectation that Asian central banks would let  

their currencies strengthen to help check inflation.   


 
    Traders and investors will also watch the G20 meeting for
signals from China about a yuan revaluation, Tan said.
    European and U.S. officials have said China should let its
currency strengthen because the peg of 8.28 per dollar unfairly
benefits Chinese exporters.
    Flint expects China to let the yuan appreciate by the end
of the first quarter of 2005.
    European officials at the G20 could also bring pressure to
  

bear on counterparts from China, South Korea and Japan -  

countries that have a high trade surpluses with the U.S. - to  

let their currencies strengthen further given the euro was at  

record highs, Flint said.

title: UPDATE 1-Thai c.bank not to  intervene  on baht.
text:
BANGKOK, Nov 15 (Reuters) - Thailand's central bank made it clear on Monday it was comfortable with the baht's recent gains against the dollar and has no plans to intervene to slow its advance.   

The baht traded at around 40.29/32 per dollar at midday Monday, against 41.04 at the close on November 1.   

Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula told reporters he believed the baht was at an appropriate level as it had moved mostly in line with other Asian currencies.   

The baht had not gained against yen or euro, he said.   

"We don't have to do anything. Ours is at the right level. We should not look just at its exchange rate against the dollar, but should compare it with yen and euro," he said.   

Thai exports remained competitive despite the baht's recent steady gains, Pridiyathorn said.   

"The baht is still competitive when compared with other currencies because its real effective exchange rate has moved in the same direction as other currencies," he said.   

Thai exports rose a robust 25.4 percent during the third quarter against the same period of 2003, according to central bank data.   

Analysts said financial markets appeared to have adjusted slowly to lingering security problems in Thailand's Muslim south since 85 Muslims died at a public protest and in military custody on October 25.   

"Investors said that although sentiment has not turned clearly positive, people are getting used to the current bad news regarding the violence in the South," said research house 4Cast in Singapore.   

"With confidence gradually re-emerging, foreigners are buying Thai assets again and the downward USD trend intact, FX speculators are building up their short USD/THB positions.   

"Going forward, we expect USD/THB to hover around 40.30-40 early week before drifting south again in line with softer USD/Asia tone," 4Cast said in a note to clients.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Won retreats amid focus on policy.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Nov 10 (Reuters) - The Korean won retreated from
seven-year highs on Wednesday, ahead of rate decisions in the
United States and South Korea, as markets renewed their debate
about Seoul's currency policy.
    The won fell to 1,110 a dollar, dropping from a seven-year
peak overnight of 1,102, the highest since the Asian financial
crisis in 1997.
    Traders reported dollar-buying intervention by the Korean
authorities and that, coming just a day before a rate-setting
meeting, sparked a debate about policy intentions.
    Some analysts said Korean authorities would not let the
currency rise past 1,100 a dollar, a level they have in the
past said affects the profitability of smaller exporters.
Besides, the won has outperformed the region by rallying seven
percent this year and would now pause, analysts said.
  


    The head of the Bank of Korea's international department
Rhee Gwang-ju told Reuters on Wednesday sentiment in the
foreign exchange market had substantially tilted to one side
recently.
 
   Rhee said the central bank was watching the won's moves and
was prepared to act to balance market sentiment if necessary.
    "Many in the market are speculating that the BoK has agreed
  

to cut rates in exchange for the Ministry of Finance and  

Economics (MOFE) allowing further won strength. As such a rate  

cut would further damage perception of BoK independence from  

the government," economists at UBS said in a note to clients.   


 
    A Reuters poll showed most economists expect the Bank of
Korea to hold rates steady at record lows on Thursday.
    UBS said many market participants were speculating that the
central bank will cut rates.
    "This would confirm in their minds that the policy mix has
been shifted in favour of the domestic sector at the expense of
export competitiveness," UBS said.
    If rates were kept unchanged, the won could fall, UBS said.
    RUPIAH WEAKER
    The Indonesian rupiah fell over half a percent as markets
covered positions ahead of holidays.
    Indonesian markets are closed next week for a Muslim
festival. Several centres in the region are shut on Thursday
and Monday for festival holidays.
    "There is some covering of short dollar positions,
especially the shorter term and interbank names," said David
Simmonds, markets strategist with the Royal Bank of Scotland.
    "Also, there has definitely been more intervention talk
around in Korea, perhaps in Thailand, and probably some stepped
up physical intervention too," he said.
    Simmonds said the dollar-buying by regional authorities
seemed aimed at smoothing the appreciation of their currencies
rather than thwarting the trend.
    The U.S. dollar was slightly higher against the euro and
  

yen after European officials warned markets about the euro's  

rise and ahead of a U.S. Federal Reserve decision on rates. A  

quarter point rise in U.S. rates is widely expected and priced  

in.  

The Singapore dollar fell a quarter cent to 1.6550/60 a  

dollar. The Taiwan dollar shed about 0.4 percent, hitting 33.11

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Southeast Asians feel pressure.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 30 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were pulled
down as the Japanese yen weakened past 110 per dollar on
Monday, with Southeast Asia leading the losses.
    The Philippine peso has been hobbled by government talk of
  

 a fiscal crisis, markets are cautious on the Indonesian rupiah   

 ahead of next month's presidential vote, and a slowing economy   

 and persistent violence in Thailand's south have pushed the   

 baht to one-year lows.   

 "There's definitely a strongish dollar trend which is going   

 through, underlying all of this," Bank of America strategist   

 Sameer Goel said, pointing to the dollar's gains against the   


 
    In north Asia, a return of foreign investors to equity
markets, notably Taiwan, and easing oil prices offered support.
    Oil prices were steady above $43 a barrel, and dealers
  


expected more retracement from record highs, while stock
  


markets were flat to softer but holding onto their gains of
  


recent weeks.
  


The Indonesian rupiah softened beyond 9,360 per dollar, its
  


weakest since just before the first round of presidential
  


elections in early July.
  


In recent weeks, the market had been capped by a wariness
  


of central bank intervention around 9,300 per dollar, although
  


traders said the bank was not a buyer on Monday as the rupiah's
  


fall was not drastic.
  


The rupiah has lost more than 10 percent against the U.S.
  


dollar this year and is expected to stay under pressure ahead
  


of the September 20 presidential vote pitting incumbent
  


Megawati Sukarnoputri against market favourite Susilo Bambang
  


Yudhoyono.
  


The Philippine peso extended last week's slide to hit a
  


two-month low of 56.25 per dollar. The peso has been under
  


pressure since President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo said last week
  


that the country was suffering a fiscal crisis.
  


Goel said Arroyo's words seemed aimed at putting the need
  


for fiscal reform on the domestic political agenda to gain
  


support for her plans to bring the budget deficit under
  


control.
  


"There is a risk involved in using strong words like
  


'fiscal crisis' which obviously gets people rather worried, but
  


I still do feel there is no indication therein that they are
  


actually thinking about reneging on their debt or any such
  


drastic steps," he said.
  


Data showing Philippine GDP had risen by a stronger than
  


expected 6.2 percent in the year through the second quarter
  


offered the peso little respite.
  


The Thai baht held near last week's one-year low, but the
  


market was wary of the Bank of Thailand intervening if it
  


weakened past 41.70 per dollar.
  


The Thai Finance Ministry trimmed its 2004 growth forecast
  


to 6.5 to 7.0 percent, from 7.1 percent, due to higher oil
  


prices and slower growth in the first quarter.
  


TAIWAN FLOWS
  


The Taiwan dollar opened local trade testing resistance at
  


34.00 per dollar, a level that has held since late July.
  


However, its early strength soon disappeared and it retreated
  


past Friday's local close.
  


Similarly, the Korean won hit a peak of 1,150 per dollar,
  


its highest since July 14, but then gradually weakened with the
  


yen to end slightly softer.
  


Goel said that in the last two weeks' foreign equity flows
  


to Taiwan had picked up for the first time since the disputed
  


presidential election in March, although he cautioned it was
  


too soon to say if it was a sustained trend.
  


"In trade-weighted terms, the Taiwan dollar has been pretty
  


weak in the last few months, and I do feel that that trend
  


could turn around if the flows were to continue to come back,"
  


he said.

title: Asian central banks step in as  currencies  trip up.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, July 28 (Reuters) - Asian central banks appear
to be intervening in foreign exchange markets this week after a
three-month lull, but this time they have been buying their
currencies against a resurgent U.S. dollar, traders say.
    Central banks in India, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and
Indonesia are all suspected to have intervened as some of their
currencies hit lows for the year against the dollar this week.
    That represents a change in tack after the heavy
dollar-buying intervention they conducted through all of 2003
and the first few months of 2004, boosting their combined
foreign reserves to over $2 trillion.
 
    Traders cited dollar-selling intervention in India, where
the rupee hit a fresh one-year low of 46.35/40 on Wednesday.
    The Taiwan dollar has shed about 1.5 percent in less than
   

three weeks and on Wednesday hit 33.23, its lowest in eight   

months. Traders in Singapore said they had heard that the   

central bank offered U.S. dollars in onshore markets above   

34.20.   

Expectations of higher yields in a rebounding U.S. economy,   

weakness in technology stocks and diminishing interest in the   

once-popular Chinese yuan revaluation trade seemed to be   

driving foreign funds out of Asia, analysts said.   

But they felt that policy makers might be reacting too   

quickly, given they had been battling strength in their   

currencies for a couple of years, until April.    


 
    "Some of them are hypersensitive at this moment in time,"
said Claudio Piron, a strategist with Standard Chartered Bank.
    "And it seems to be a combination of where the currencies

are in historical terms, where they are in their trade-weighted   

baskets and also in terms of managing inflationary   

expectations."   

POLICY DILEMMA   

Piron said the Thai baht's two percent slide in two weeks   

had taken it to its lowest levels historically in   

trade-weighted terms. The baht hit 41.45, its weakest since   

August 2003, on Wednesday.   

Although Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula   

said the weak baht would not hurt the economy, traders   

suspected the authorities would sell dollars if there were   

further losses.   

Similarly, analysts said it was reasonable for the Monetary   

Authority of Singapore (MAS) to worry if the Sing dollar moved   

too far to the weaker side of the trade-weighted band it is   

managed in, particularly after the central bank announced in   

April it wanted to tighten policy by guiding the currency

higher.   

Local banks in Singapore were seen buying their currency

this week, spurring suspicion they were acting on behalf of the   

MAS.    


 
    South Korean markets have been baffled by conflicting
statements from policy makers.
    More than any country in the region, South Korea is faced
   

with the dilemma of whether to continue with a policy of   

boosting exports through a cheap currency, despite the risk of   

higher imported inflation from rising oil and commodity prices.   

"In Korea, they are getting a bit more sensitive in terms   

of price expectations and some of the inflationary pressure,"   

Piron said. "Some of the growth picture has started to fade,   

but they don't want price inflation to also deteriorate."   

Nonetheless, analysts said inflation was still benign in   

Asia and central banks might be acting to curb market   

volatility rather than signalling a shift in policy.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Denies  FX Intervention , Says Econ Resilient
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai central bank Thursday rejected market speculation that it has intervened to support the baht after last week's U.S. interest rate hike triggered talk of capital flows out of Thailand.  

The bank also said the Thai economy continues to be robust despite rising oil prices and, now, yet another outbreak of bird flu.  

Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said Bank of Thailand hasn't intervened in the currency market after the Federal Reserve hiked its federal-funds rate by 25 basis points, since capital flows and the baht have been stable.  

"We haven't done anything. Things have been stable for quite some time," Pridiyathorn told reporters.  

The U.S. Federal Open Market Committee lifted its federal-funds target rate to 1.25% from a 46-year low of 1.00%, putting it on par with Thailand's 14-day repurchase market target rate.  

The Fed action hasn't had any impact on local financial markets as the move was in line with market expectations and was already priced in, Pridiyathorn said.  

Many economists are now saying the Thai central bank will likely wait until the U.S. raises the federal-funds target by another 25 basis points before making a similar move to keep its 14-day rate on a similar footing.  

Earlier this week, Pridiyathorn said the central bank's Monetary Policy Committee will provide clear signals about its expectations for interest rate policy in the months ahead after its upcoming meeting on July 21.  

He left open the possibility of leaving the 14-day rate unchanged at the meeting, with local financial system liquidity high and core inflation still low.  

Thai Central Bank Still Bullish On Economy  

Pridiyathorn said he isn't overly concerned about the state of the Thai economy which has showed resilience against negative factors such as high oil prices and a fresh bird flu outbreak.  

Higher oil prices haven't significantly pushed up inflation, with most consumer products produced locally.  

The June CPI rose 0.2% from May and 3% over the year-ago month. Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and fresh food prices, was up 0.5% on year and flat on month.  

Pridiyathorn said Thailand's high foreign reserves, currently around $43 billion, and an expected current account surplus, will act as a cushion against any external shocks.  

Even though higher oil prices may push the country's trade balance into the red this year, the current account balance is expected to remain in surplus at least until 2006, he said.  

Pridiyathorn earlier forecast that this year's trade balance could range from a deficit of as much as $500 million to a surplus of $2 billion, compared with a surplus of $4.2 billion in 2003. He also predicted that the current account surplus will narrow to $4.5 billion to $6.0 billion from $8 billion last year.  

But Pridiyathorn was concerned about the delay in foreign direct investment, or FDI, inflows.  

Violence in southern Thailand since the first quarter of 2004, as well as competition from China and Vietnam, have delayed FDI inflows to possibly next year, the central bank chief said.  

"But it's not worrisome as long as we have a current account surplus and high reserves. If we run into a (current account) deficit, and our reserves fall, there will be a great need to have FDI," Pridiyathorn said.  

Ctrl Bk Says Bird Flu Won't Hammer Economy  

A new outbreak of avian influenza in Thailand's central provinces shouldn't have any significant impact on the economy because exports of chicken products account for only 1% of the country's total exports, the central bank governor said.  

"We already put the impact of bird flu in our economic model. It will shave no more than half a percentage point off our economic growth this year," Pridiyathorn said.  

Most major poultry buyers abroad still ban the import of raw poultry meat from Thailand, although the import of cooked products is allowed.  

Pridiyathorn also said he doesn't expect the reemergence of bird flu to have any significant negative effect on domestic consumption.  

Thailand Wednesday confirmed fresh outbreaks of the disease in the central provinces of Ayudhya and Prathum Thani.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Firmer on stocks, capped by mixed data.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, June 8 (Reuters) - Asian regional currencies
strengthened on Tuesday helped by gains in equity markets and
as oil prices stayed off last week's highs.
    However, analysts said mixed economic data from across the
region would likely keep investors from buying too
aggressively.
    The Indonesian rupiah        was the lead performer,
gaining by about a percent to hit a one-week high of 9,265 to
the dollar.
    Dealers in Singapore said the rise of the rupiah was partly
due to higher reserve requirements, funds banks have to
maintain with the central bank, which were announced last week.
Higher reserves mean banks would have less rupiah to buy
dollars.
    The U.S. dollar's recent retreat from highs against the
euro  and Japanese yen        also supported regional
currencies.
    The South Korean won            rose to its highest since
April 28, before giving up part of those gains on suspected
intervention by authorities.
  


    The Taiwan dollar          hit a one-week high. The
Singapore dollar , Thai baht  and Philippine peso
  posted modest gains.
    Thio Chin Lo, currency analyst at BNP Paribas in Singapore
said oil prices still had the potential to remain volatile
given the risk of terror attacks in the Middle East.
    "Hence, even though stock markets have started the week on
a bullish note and oil prices have eased from peaks, the
uncertain geopolitical landscape continues to leave investors
in a cautious mood," she said.
    MIXED DATA
    Analysts said mixed economic performance, as shown by
recent data releases, across the region also meant investors
might avoid taking aggressive directional bets in the
regionals.
    Data on Monday showed Taiwan's exports in May had jumped to
a record $15.71 billion, marking a surprising 39.5 percent
increase over a year earlier.
    Taiwan's consumer price index, however, declined by a
seasonally adjusted 0.33 percent in May from April due to lower
food prices.
    Data from South Korea showed output from the retail sector
shrank in the year through April, reflecting weak consumer
spending.
    James Malcolm, currency strategist at JP Morgan Chase, said
the won still had room to head as high as 1,152 to the dollar
in the near-term.
 
    But he added dollar-buying intervention by authorities had
restricted the won's rise.
    Thailand's soft gross domestic product growth data,
  


released on Monday, also came as a surprise. GDP grew 0.8
  


percent in the first quarter, the slowest in the past 10
  


quarters.
  


Michael Spencer, chief economist at Deutsche Bank in Hong
  


Kong, said in a client note that growth momentum had weakened
  


due to a sharp decline in exports and weak private consumption.
  


Wong Chee Seng, an economist at Singapore's DBS Bank, said
  


Thai growth was hurt by a contraction of the agriculture
  


sector.
  


"Even though agriculture sector accounts for less than 11
  


percent of total GDP, its repercussion on the economy should
  


not be underestimated, as around 43 percent of employment is
  


generated by this sector," he said.

title: Thai Baht Ends Up; Ctrl Bk Suspected To Have Capped Rise
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht ended stronger in Asian spot trade Thursday amid general dollar weakness, but the central bank was believed to have stepped in to help cap the local currency's rise, traders said.  

The dollar ended at 38.865 baht, down from THB38.965 at the Asian close Wednesday.  

The U.S. currency fell against most Asian and global currencies after U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said late Wednesday that U.S. interest rates are likely to remain at current lows for an extended period.  

Bank of Thailand Assistant Governor Tasna Rajatabhothi said Thursday that Greenspan's comments helped to trigger the baht's rise, but that so far its movements against the dollar were in line with those of other Asian currencies and the euro.  

The central bank is monitoring the baht's movements closely, she said, indirectly reaffirming a long-standing policy of buying dollars on weakness to prevent excessive volatility and build foreign reserves.  

A Bangkok-based dealer said it appeared that central bank buying provided strong support for the dollar Thursday at THB38.85. The central bank normally doesn't comment on day-to-day trading operations.  

The U.S. currency was likely to trade overnight in a range of THB38.80 to THB38.90, he said, but a test and a successful break of January's 42-month low of THB38.80 was likely by next week.  

Economists expect the baht to continue appreciating due to both the dollar's weakness and to strong inflows to Thailand for investment and through the current account.  

Another Bangkok-based dealer said the dollar was likely to be dropping at a very slow rate of about THB0.05 a day, due to intervention by Bank of Thailand and central banks across Asia.  

Thai government bond prices rose Thursday on Greenspan's indication that U.S. interest rates would remain low for an extended period, dealers said.  

Gains were limited, however, as prices had already risen because of uncertainty regarding the effects of the bird flu outbreak on the local economy, they said.  

Short-term securities were mostly unchanged, as the yield curve is already very steep.  

The bid yield of the government bond due October 2005 ended virtually flat at 1.40%, while the April 2010 bid was off three basis points at 3.05%, and the March 2014 bid was down two basis points at 4.64%, the Thai Bond Dealing Center said.  

Dealers expected trade to remain range-bound ahead of the weekend, and pending further developments in the local bird flu situation or any sharp movements in U.S. Treasurys.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Is Monitoring THB Strengthening-Official
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai central bank said Thursday that it is closely monitoring the strengthening of the baht against the dollar, but added that, so far, the currency has been in line with the region's currencies.  

Tasna Rajatabhothi, Bank of Thailand's assistant governor for financial markets operations, said the baht has risen in line with the general dollar weakness, following comments overnight by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.  

The chairman said the Fed is in no hurry to lift interest rates from their 45-year lows, despite a more upbeat assessment of economic growth, as inflation remains under control.  

"The baht movement is volatile following the Fed's comment on the U.S. economy. However, we're monitoring it," Tasna told reporters.  

The current volatility was also related to a joint statement issued by the Group of Seven finance chiefs last weekend, who called for greater flexibility in exchange rates, and to a response from China reiterating that it would be gradually allowing more channels for capital flows while maintaining exchange rate stability, she said.  

At 0540 GMT, the dollar was quoted at 38.865 baht, down from THB38.965 at Wednesday's Asian close.  

Bank of Thailand has a policy of intervening to stem daily volatility and build foreign reserves. Its interventions are often effective because its restrictions on the movement of baht between onshore and offshore markets has sharply limited speculative trading volumes.

title: Thai Baht Ends Up On General Dlr Weakness;Resistance Firm
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht ended slightly stronger in Asian spot trade Thursday amid widespread dollar weakness in foreign exchange markets, but gains were limited due to fears of central bank intervention and a possible avian flu outbreak, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at 39.035 baht, down from THB39.06 at Wednesday's Asian close.  

Volume was thin with many local players sidelined for the Lunar New Year, although it isn't an official holiday in Thailand.  

Dealers said that despite broad dollar weakness, there was no threat to support at THB39 due to expectations the Bank of Thailand would intervene at that level and on reports that the regional outbreak of avian flu may have spread to Thailand.  

A Japanese Agriculture Ministry official in Tokyo said the country temporarily suspended chicken meat imports from Thailand Thursday following reports that several people are being tested for the disease.  

The Thai government insisted that there have been no confirmed cases yet, and that widespread culling of poultry in the country has been to contain outbreaks of avian cholera and bronchitis.  

Thailand is among the world's top five chicken exporters, and last year shipped 540,000 metric tons of chicken valued at THB50 billion, according to the Thai Broilers Processing Exporters Association.  

It had targeted exports of 630,000 metric tons worth THB70 billion this year.  

Dealers expect the dollar to remain in a tight THB39.00-THB39.10 range Friday, with avian flu fears continuing to assist the central bank in resisting the tendency for the baht to appreciate on current account and investment flows.  

Prices of Thai government bonds ended mostly higher Thursday on fears that the avian flu outbreak could hurt related economic activity and reduce the attractiveness of stocks as an alternative investment, dealers said.  

The bourse's SET Index closed Thursday down 0.9% at 760.17 points. The agricultural sector index was off 4% at 56.79 points.  

Gains in bonds were limited, however, as economic growth and indicators remained strong, the avian flu outbreak was unconfirmed and long-term yields were considered likely to rise this year regardless.  

The bid-yield on the issue due October 2005 ended Thursday down one basis point at 1.357% and the bid on the issue due February 2008 was off four basis points at 2.334%, the Thai Bond Dealing Center said.  

The March 2014 bid dropped four basis points to 4.979%, but a last deal of 4.90% indicated that bidders were having to hit offers and that yields might be falling a little further Friday.  

Volume remained thin with many investors sidelined for the Lunar New Year holiday.  

The Finance Ministry auctioned government-guaranteed state enterprise bonds Thursday at slight premiums to the government bond yield curve, but within expectations.  

Six-year Expressway & Rapid Transit Authority bonds were sold at an accepted yield of 3.40%, three-year Government Housing Bank bonds at 1.85%, and five-year GHB bonds at 2.965%.  

Overnight interest rates were unchanged, supported by banks' preparations for extra cash demand over the holiday and the end Thursday of a biweekly reserve period and capped by excess financial system liquidity.

text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Jan 16 (Reuters) - Most Asian regional
currencies recovered from their recent lows on Friday, except
for the Singapore dollar, which fell even as economic data
delivered a bullish surprise.
    The Singapore dollar        tested 1.70 per U.S. dollar, as
the market gave a muted response to unexpectly strong exports
data for December.
    Exports, excluding oil, rose for a second straight month,
gaining 3.9 percent from November to beat analysts' forecasts
and push total 2003 exports up 15.1 percent.
    Dealers said any positive impact from the data had been
absorbed by Singapore banks, which had been buying U.S. dollars
since Friday morning, sparking fears of central bankintervention.
    "When local banks in Singapore are buying dollars
aggressively, others don't usually want to test and see who is
behind the order," said a dealer at a European bank.
  


    Overall sentiment on Asian currencies stayed depressed
because of recent moves in South Korea and Thailand to curb the
strength of the won and baht.
    South Korea imposed limits on Thursday on domestic
financial institutions' trade with the offshore non-deliverable
forward market -- a move seen aimed at curbing the won's
  rise.
 
    On the same day the Bank of Thailand declared that it had
intervened recently to stem the baht's  gains.
    Those actions have doused hopes of gains against the U.S.
  

dollar ahead of the early February Group of Seven meeting that  

is expected to discuss weakness of the U.S. dollar, the euro's  

rise to record highs and Asia's policy of keeping its  

currencies weak.  

Dealers said with U.S. markets closed on Monday and with  

Chinese New Year holidays in the region next week, most players  

prefered to square out of their short U.S. dollar positions.  

"The market is growing nervous about complaints on currency

appreciation by authorities and looked to book profits on its  

short dollar positions," said Bhanu Baweja, strategist at UBS  

in Singapore.  

The won on Friday eased to 1,188.5 per dollar, before  

recovering to 1,186.0 at the close of local trade. On Thursday  

it briefly hit 1,192.5 per dollar, its weakest in nearly two  

weeks.  

The baht traded on the weaker side of 39 per dollar before  

edging slightly stronger at 38.97. It hit a one-week low of  

39.04 on Thursday.  

The Taiwan dollar finished local trade a touch  

higher at 33.685 per U.S. dollar from Thursday's close of  

33.70, helped by exporter demand for local currency ahead of  

the Chinese New Year holidays starting next week.

title: UPDATE 1-Thai  central bank  satisfied with baht.
text:
BANGKOK, Jan 15 (Reuters) - The Thai central bank's recent intervention to slow the rise of the baht has been effective and the currency is at a satisfactory level, Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said on Thursday.   

"Our intervention the other day has been effective and it is now satisfactory. We are more happy with the level of the baht today than the other day," Pridiyathorn told reporters, referring to the baht's brief sharp advance on Tuesday.   

Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra told reporters on Tuesday he believed the baht still did not reflect Thailand's bullish economic fundamentals despite its recent rise against the dollar.   

Thaksin's remarks pushed the baht up to around 38.83 per dollar, but the currency retreated sharply later on Tuesday to 38.92 after the central bank chief said the baht was too strong.   

The baht traded at around 39.00 per dollar at 0445 GMT on Thursday.   

"The remarks should effectively put a cap to any further upside retracement on dollar/baht which this morning hit 39.04 on an overall firmer dollar," said Singapore-based research house MMS International.   

Pridiyathorn said he expected Thai economic growth to accelerate in 2004 from 6.3 percent growth projected by analysts for 2003.   

The central bank would continue its accommodative monetary policy in maintaining low Thai interest rates, he said.   

Economist Thanomsri Fongarun-rung at Phatra Securities said the central bank wanted to assure people it would continue the growth-oriented policies which have helped the economy expand rapidly.   

"It is telling people that this year is a better year and you don't need to worry about the business outlook. Interest rates will stay supportive of growth," she said.   

Pridiyathorn said Thailand would post another current account surplus this year. The central bank said in October it expected a 2003 current account surplus of $7-8 billion.   

Merrill Lynch estimates Thai housing demand will rise between 20 and 30 percent this year and that average capacity utilisation at most major industrial plants has risen to 85-90 percent from 65 percent two years ago.   

To avoid a repeat of a housing bubble seen during the run-up to the 1997/98 Asian economic crisis, the central bank has imposed measures to curb excessive supply in the property sector, Thanomsri said.   

"It will keep speculation on property shares down because people will know that the Bank of Thailand is on the case," she said. (Reporting by Kitiphong Thaichareon and Trisanat Kongkhunthian, additional reporting by Chawadee Nualkhair).

title: Asian stumble would hit global debt market - banker.
text:
BANGKOK, Nov 10 (Reuters) - The global debt market faces potentially severe disruption if Asian economies falter, forcing central banks to withdraw substantial investments in U.S. Treasuries, a senior Thai central bank official said on Monday.   

Tasna Rajatabhothi, an assistant governor at the Bank of Thailand (BOT), told reporters the concern was discussed at a bi-monthly meeting of senior central bank officials hosted by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).   

Most of a combined $1.8 trillion of foreign reserves at Asian central banks has been invested in U.S. Treasuries.   

"Should Asian economies falter in the future, it could affect every country, including the United States," Tasna said. "This is a concern voiced by some officials."   

The BOT official said recent currency interventions by some Asian countries, including China and Thailand, were another issue discussed at the meeting.   

Tasna said Chinese officials repeated Beijing's policy on the yuan, which has become a political issue in the United States, but gave no further details.   

She said Thai officials briefed the meeting on recent BOT measures to curb foreign speculation on the bullish baht, which has appreciated about eight percent against the dollar so far this year.   

The central bank has limited the amounts of baht non-residents can keep in Thai banks in its bid to discourage them from betting on a currency whose strength has been supported by the country's booming economy.   

The BOT has instructed Thai banks to report daily the baht accounts kept by foreigners who are not allowed to keep more than 300 million baht without other underlying business.

title: Emerging Asia  FX - Central bank  moves bring big falls.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Several Asian currencies
posted their biggest losses in months on Tuesday, reversing
most of the gains since the Group of Seven meeting last month
that was seen as a call on Asian countries to let their
currencies rise.
    Dealers said players scrambled to cover their short U.S.
dollar positions as central banks, almost across the region,
conducted aggressive dollar-buying intervention.
    The baht        fell about two percent to near 40 per
dollar, a two-week low, after the Bank of Thailand placed fresh
restrictions, including a limit on the amount of baht
foreigners can keep in Thai bank accounts. The moves were aimed
at curbing speculation in the currency market, BOT said.
    The Korean won            posted its biggest fall since
March, to a near one-month low of 1,169.5, amid what dealers in
Singapore suspected was sporadic dollar-buying intervention by
the Bank of Korea.
  


    The Taiwan central bank was spotted buying U.S. dollars to
push its dollar  to a near one-month low on the weaker
side of the 34 per U.S. dollar.
    The Hong Kong Monetary Authority was also in the market to
buy U.S. dollars and sell Hong Kong dollars , pushing the
spot market to around 7.75 per dollar -- its closest to the
official peg rate of 7.8 to the U.S. dollar since late
September.
 
    The region-wide swing in sentiment pulled the Singapore
dollar  to its lowest in more than three weeks.
    "The move was aided by rumours of intervention and
  

increasing concerns in the market about the post-G7 pace of  

Asian currency appreciation, and overstretched short dollar  

positions," said Bank of America's strategist Sameer Goel.  

He said the move was also partly in response to the U.S.  

dollar's rise against major currencies after European Central  

Bank President Wim Duisenberg said the G7 call last month for  

exchange rate flexibility was not directed at the euro .  

"There is still this issue of fear of floating where they  

had been scared in the aftermath of the Asian crisis," said  

Claudio Piron, strategist at Standard Chartered commenting on  

Thailand's steps to restrict capital flows.   


 
    "There is also an issue here of kind of protecting the
constituency, the exporters."
    Dealers said the move in the market has defied general
bullish expectations ahead of President George W. Bush's visit
to Asia next week and the APEC summit in Thailand.
    Traders had expected Asian central banks to intervene less,
  

given United States' persistent criticism of the foreign  

exchange policy of many Asian nations to keep their currencies

weak.   


 
    However, David Simmonds, strategist at Royal Bank of
Scotland said the weak U.S. dollar trend was still intact.
    "I think we are in a parameter shift here in terms of Asian
currencies going stronger against the U.S. dollar. That is the
trend and I don't think that's altered," he said.
    "Periodically we're going to get some pretty sharp and
unpleasant corrections and this is one of them," he said.
    Elsewhere, losses in the Philippine peso were limited by
fresh dollar remittances from overseas workers.
    Dealers said with the import season having peaked, and

baht.

bullish expectations ahead of the President George Bush's visit
to Asia, next week, and the APEC summit in Thailand.
    Traders had expected Asian central banks to intervene less,
  

given United States' persistent criticism of the foreign  

exchange policy of many Asian nations to keep their currencies

weak.  

"Even if you're bearish dollar/Asia, which I am, you have  

to except the reality that these central banks are not going to  

look the other way," said David Simmonds, strategist at Royal

"Pending a convincing pick up in domestic demand they  

(central banks) are going to remain pretty sensitive to  

exchange rate moves. That certainly does seem clear," he added.

title: UPDATE 1-Baht  intervention  could hurt economy-Thai PM.
text:
BANGKOK, Oct 10 (Reuters) - Official intervention to slow the appreciation of the Thai baht could hurt the economy, Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said on Friday.  

"Intervention that goes against market forces could put the economy at risk," he told reporters after exporters called on the government to halt the rise of the baht.  

The baht has appreciated about 10 percent against the dollar so far this year. Its sharp advance has hurt Thai exporters who asked the central bank to intervene this week.  

The Bank of Thailand (BOT) said on Friday it was monitoring increased baht funds parked by non-residents in domestic bank accounts in a bid to restrain foreign speculation in the currency.  

BOT deputy governor Thirachai Phuvanatnaranubala told reporters that total outstanding short-term baht funds kept by foreigners in local bank accounts had risen to about 45 billion baht from 10-15 billion baht last month.  

Thaksin said his government could not respond to all requests from different economic sectors on the baht issue.  

"We are carefully monitoring it and appreciate their problems, but we cannot oblige every request. The Bank of Thailand has the main responsibility while the government occasionally offers its advice," he said.  

Thaksin said while the authorities would try to maintain the baht's stability, Thai exporters should try to adjust to its recent fluctuations.  

The baht traded at around 39.18/22 at 0842 GMT on Friday, against 39.22 late on Thursday and 43.08 at the end of 2002.

title: Thai Baht Ends Up On Moody's; Off 39-Month Intraday High
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht strengthened further in Asia Friday, hitting a fresh 39-month intraday high, as players continued to sell dollars following news Thursday that Moody's Investor Service may upgrade Thailand's sovereign credit rating.  

However, the dollar was pulled off its lows on concerns of possible intervention by the Bank of Thailand and the late recovery in the dollar/yen. The Japanese currency is a regional trendsetter.  

The dollar closed at 39.51 baht, off an intraday low of THB39.49, and down from THB39.65 at the end of the Asian spot session Thursday.  

The dollar opened at an intraday high of THB39.58 but gradually lost ground on the prospect of an upgrade.  

"The Moody's revision continued to weigh on dollar sentiment. The news seemed to have made the central bank increasingly reluctant to intervene now, as it doesn't want the baht to resist its bullish trend," said a Bangkok-based trader.  

Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said in the afternoon that the baht's appreciation was due to the possibility of a ratings upgrade by Moody's and Thailand's strong economic fundamentals.  

He also said there were no signs of speculation.  

The central bank has said it will only act to prevent speculative, exaggerated moves in the dollar/baht.  

After Pridiyathorn's comments the dollar hit an intraday low of THB39.49 but later regained some strength on its gains against the yen.  

Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted at Y110.43, up slightly from a low of Y110.22.  

"Despite Pridiyathorn's remark, some players still were concerned the central bank may step in because it isn't likely to allow the greenback to give up the key THB39.50 easily," another trader said.  

Traders expect the dollar to find support at THB39.30 Monday and be capped on the upside at THB39.70, subject to volatility in the yen.  

Prices of Thai government bonds ended sharply lower Friday due to rising concerns about upcoming supply of various government and central bank debt securities, traders said.  

A local newspaper reported Friday that the Ministry of Finance plans to issue THB30 billion in seven-year savings bonds to institutional investors in early December. The issue is to be part of a planned THB200 billion of various types of government bonds to be offered in the fiscal year that began Oct. 1 to help refinance the debt of the state Financial Institutions Development Fund.  

Meanwhile, dealers said the central bank has informed local banks that it plans to sell THB50 billion of three-month promissory notes soon, probably next week.  

The news came on top of issues announced earlier this week of THB30 billion worth of regular government bonds in the current quarter, and THB42 billion in treasury bills in October.  

"There is lots of supply coming to the market, while demand has dried up due to a shift of funds to the more active stock market," a local bank dealer said.  

The central bank stepped in during the morning session to buy medium and long-term bonds in a bid to calm the market, but the losses continued, dealers said.  

The rise in yields was especially apparent in long-term bonds, but bid-offer spreads remained wide and movement was exaggerated in thin volume, dealers said.  

The government bond due November 2011 closed in a bid-offer range of 3.25%-3.35%, up from a previous close of 3.20%, they said. The issue due December 2008 ended at 2.23%-2.20% versus 2.13%.  

Overnight interest rates ended flat, as the central bank continued to borrow as needed to support rates against the weight of excess financial system liquidity.

title: UPDATE 1-Slow baht rise won't hurt 04 growth-Thai minister.
text:
BANGKOK, Oct 2 (Reuters) - A gradual strengthening of the baht will not hurt Thailand's gross domestic product growth next year, Finance Minister Suchart Jaovisidha said on Thursday. "If the baht continues to rise slowly, I don't see any down side of that," Suchart told reporters when asked if the rising baht would hurt exports and economic growth next year.  

"But if it jumped abruptly to 37 or 38 per dollar, we would be in trouble, he said.  

The baht, Asia's best performing currency, has appreciated around nine percent against the dollar so far this year. By 0511 GMT, the baht was traded at 39.50/39.62, up from its Wednesday close of 39.83

Commerce Minister Adisai Bodharamik also said on Wednesday that even if the baht strengthened to 38-39 per dollar by next year, exports would still be competitive.  

Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula insisted on Thursday the central bank did not need to intervene to weaken the baht since it rose "only slightly".

Late on Thursday morning, Moody's Investor Services placed Thailand's foreign currency ratings on review for possible upgrade, citing the strength of the economy.

title: Asian  Currencies  Up Late; Upbeat Economic Outlook
text:
MANILA (Dow Jones)--Asian currencies were mostly higher late Wednesday against the U.S. dollar, rising on the back of an upbeat outlook for the Japanese economy and for most of the rest of Asia.  

Currency watchers said the recent call by the Group of Seven industrialized countries for greater foreign exchange flexibility continued to hold sway in the market, highlighted by the efforts of some monetary authorities in the region to weaken their currencies.  

"This is still a follow-through of the whole G7 call," said Jimmy Koh, currency strategist at UOB in Singapore. "I think generally, post-G7 meeting, everybody is of the view that Asian currencies will have to make adjustments after the line in the sand for the dollar-yen was washed away."  

The Bank of Japan's quarterly tankan survey Wednesday showed business managers grew more upbeat about business conditions in the three months to September, but Bank of Japan intervention fears pressured the yen lower.  

Koh said efforts by the BOJ to prop up the U.S. dollar has been ineffective and is "only subsidizing the long yen entry level."  

At 0915 GMT, the dollar stood around Y111.17, higher than Y110.93 late Tuesday in Tokyo.  

With China and Hong Kong closed for a holiday, Southeast Asian currencies took center stage. The Thai baht climbed as the market focused on strong economic prospects even as participants stayed wary of central bank intervention.  

Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said the baht's recent strength against the dollar was caused by exports growing faster than imports, while debt repayment has slowed due to the sharp fall in outstanding foreign debt since the 1997 financial crisis.  

Late Wednesday, the dollar was quoted around THB39.82, below Tuesday's close of THB39.99.  

The Indonesian rupiah continued to bask in the credit ratings upgrade the country received from Moody's Investors Service which cited Tuesday increased reserves, lower external debt, and an improving trend in government debt ratios for its latest action.  

The dollar was quoted around 8,380 rupiah, down from IDR8,410 in the previous session.  

Bank of Indonesia Deputy Governor Bunbunan Hutapea said that aside from Moody's upgrade, the rupiah is also getting a boost from improving macroeconomic conditions such as falling inflation and the global weakness of the U.S. dollar.  

In Manila, the peso shadowed its neighboring currencies and rose to a one-month high against the dollar, closing at PHP54.78 despite the Moody's revision of its outlook to negative for the country's foreign currency rating. The dollar closed at PHP54.87 Tuesday.  

Philip Wee, market strategist at DBS Bank, said a stronger move by Asian currencies is possible once U.S. jobs data due later this week show a further increase in unemployment.  

He said weaker jobs data will likely fuel public sentiment in the U.S. to pressure China to widen the yuan band, if not to devalue the Chinese currency.  

In Singapore, currency traders refused to take major positions ahead of the policy announcement that the Monetary Authority of Singapore is scheduled to make next week.  

As such, the Singapore dollar was a tad stronger late Wednesday, with the U.S. dollar trading at S$1.7282. The U.S. dollar stood at S$1.7290 late Tuesday in Asia.  

Meantime, the South Korean won ended weaker on suspected government intervention, offsetting the boost from the heavy selling of the U.S. unit by local exporters.  

The dollar closed at KRW1,151.9, up from Tuesday's close of KRW1,150.1.  

"It was the government versus exporters. It was suspected that the government bought about $500 million via foreign banks to digest the dollar (supply) from the exporters," said a dealer at a foreign bank.  

In Taiwan, the local currency ended down on central bank intervention and the weaker yen.  

The U.S. dollar closed at NT$33.810, up from NT$33.780 Tuesday. Dealings were valued at US$687 million, down from US$977 million in the previous session.  

"The central bank is supporting (the U.S. dollar), while the Taiwan dollar is also tracking the yen," said a dealer at a local bank. She declined to estimate the extent of the central bank's U.S. purchases Wednesday.
