title: Thai Ctrl Bk Gov: Strong Baht May Slow Exports Slightly
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said Wednesday that the baht's recent strength against the dollar was caused by exports outgrowing imports, while debt repayment has slowed due to the sharp decrease in outstanding foreign debt since the 1997 financial crisis.  

"The baht may strengthen a little bit further, but wait until imports catch up with exports and the current account balances, then the baht will stabilize," Pridiyathorn said.  

Pridiyathorn acknowledged that the strong baht may slow exports "a bit" but said there was "nothing wrong with a strong baht" as long as exports were outpacing imports.  

He reiterated that the central bank won't oppose the market trend and is only trying to limit the day-to-day volatility through recent measures introduced to limit speculative inflows. He said the central bank is only monitoring the currency's movement in the foreign exchange market and hasn't been intervening.  

"The Bank of Thailand regards the current appreciation of the baht as a natural occurrence of a recovering economy," he told a business luncheon.  

However, he warned that the central bank will monitor the ongoing rally in the stock market for any signs of an asset price bubble and will act if necessary.  

"So far, we haven't seen any bad signs. If we see, rest assured that we'll take action," he said.  

The Stock Exchange of Thailand's main index has risen 63% so far this year, hitting a six-year high recently. Trading volume has also hit record levels in recent weeks, prompting regulatory authorities to warn they would take action against short-term speculators by banning margin lending or net settlement in certain stocks.  

Pridiyathorn expressed confidence that there is scope for the economy to improve further on the strong growth so far this year once the global economy improves and private investment kicks in to complement export growth and consumer demand as economic growth drivers.  

"The challenge is to translate current growth into a sustainable momentum... and ensure that capacity utilization will increase and private capital investment will gain a strong footing," he said.  

He said until this happens, monetary policy will remain accommodative, indicating that the low interest rate environment will be maintained next year.  

He noted there were already signs that private investment, which has so far lagged growth in exports and private consumption, has been picking up steam, having risen to 16% of gross domestic product from 11% in 1999.  

"Barring any major distractions to the economy from abroad, I expect private investment to come to the limelight soon," he said.  

Going forward, Pridiyathorn said he saw three challenges for the central bank: balancing the country's external reliance with domestic strength, ensuring the recovery of commercial bank credit growth and dealing with risks brought about by globalization.  

He expressed confidence that the lingering problem of nonperforming loans in the financial system would be tackled following the central bank's proposal to the finance ministry to transfer nonperforming assets that had been used as collateral, from the commercial banks to state-owned asset management agencies and speed up their liquidation. This plan could become effective early next year, if it's approved by the government, he said.  

Pridiyathorn said the central bank will also monitor an increase in household debt but noted that, at 27% of gross domestic product, it was still low compared with other countries in the region.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk: Baht Up On Dlr Weakness; No  Intervention
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said Thursday that the baht's recent strength was mainly due to general dollar weakness, and that the central bank hasn't intervened in the foreign exchange market.  

He told reporters that the dollar has weakened around 4% against the yen and the euro since Sept. 19, while the baht has risen only about 1.5% against the dollar.  

"The baht is still competitive, moving in line with most Asian currencies," he said.  

On Monday, the dollar fell to a 38-month low of 39.910 baht as currency markets put the Group of Seven's weekend endorsement of flexible exchange rates to the test.  

At 0550 GMT, the dollar was at THB40.095, marginally up from THB40.075 early Thursday, tracking a mild consolidation in the yen.  

"It's clear that there is no speculation in the market now," Prididyathorn said.  

The absence of speculation is apparently due to subsiding short-term inflows in the foreign exchange market following a new central bank rule.  

The Bank of Thailand earlier this month imposed a limit of THB50 million on baht imports by nonresidents for short-term loans to local financial institutions that aren't connected to trade or investment.  

The central bank's Deputy Governor Thirachai Phuvanatnaranubala said Wednesday that liquidity in the foreign exchange market that isn't linked to trade or investment has dropped dramatically to $30 million from $200 million last week and around $2.4 billion before the central bank limit was imposed.

text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Sept 25 (Reuters) - Asian currencies spent most
of Thursday in slightly softer ranges, shy of this week's highs
and watching the Japanese yen ease after threats of
intervention.
    The yen        weakened past 112 per dollar after Japan's
top financial diplomat Zembei Mizoguchi and others said Japan
was prepared to intervene if necessary.
    Other central banks in the region also seemed uncomfortable
with the rises in their currencies that have followed the Group
of Seven's call for more flexible exchange rates on the
weekend.
 
    Asian stock markets were lower, under the influence of the
decline in the Nikkei average .
    The Thai baht        stayed around 40.10 per dollar, the
  

Korean won found its gains capped at its three-year high of  

1,150 and the Singapore dollar moved in a 1.7330-1.7345  

range, having come off Monday's three-month high of 1.7230.   

Thailand's central bank said on Thursday it had not
intervened in the past 10 days.
    Other central banks appeared to be following the Thai
  

example of controls on short-term flows, amid signs they had  

tried to moderate the inflow of foreign capital being raised by  

domestic institutions without directly buying dollars.  

Corporates in Taiwan said the central bank was trying to  

ease the upward pressure on the Taiwan dollar by  

regulating the conversion of overseas bond and share issues.  

A source in the South Korean finance ministry said the  

government was in talks with domestic issuers of dollar bonds  

on the need for the issues, as well as the timing and size.  

On Wednesday, Korean authorities said they might act   


against the rising won             which was hurting
  

exports, and revealed plans to issue more of the bonds they use  

to sterilise the liquidity generated by intervention.  

Earlier in the week, an Indian government official said  

petrochemicals maker Reliance Industries Ltd's proposal to  

borrow $500 million overseas would not be approved because the  

government wanted to discourage firms from raising foreign  

debt.  

"Asian central banks have put up a robust performance in  

the face of dollar weakness/yen strength, and we expect that  

lines in the sand are being formed more robustly in Asia than  

in Japan," strategists at National Australia Bank said in a  

note.   


 
    They said key levels were 1.7250 for the Singapore dollar,
40.00 for the baht, and 1,150 for won.
    And, with China refusing to bow to demands to make the yuan
  

flexible or let it appreciate, authorities in Japan and in rest  

of Asia will have an excuse to rein in currency appreciation,  

they said.  

"Fundamentally, and in line with the policy prescriptions  

of Asian central banks, we believe that there will be very  

robust support for U.S. dollar/Asian regionals going forward,"  

NAB's report said.  

Elsewhere, the Philippine peso remained near its  

lows for the week, hitting 55.19 per dollar, with persisting  

concerns about the overshoot in the fiscal deficit in August.  

A poll also showed sliding approval rating and public trust  

for President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, with support for her  

slipping to a low of 41 percent.

text:
BANGKOK, Sept 25 (Reuters) - Thailand's central bank said on Thursday it did not intervene on the baht in the past 10 days because it saw no speculation on the currency. "We clearly see no speculation on the baht in the past 10 days and we don't need to waste our intervention effort," Bank of Thailand governor Pridiyathorn Devakula told reporters.  

At 0530 GMT, the baht was trading at 40.08/40.10 compared with 40.06 on Wednesday.  

Pridiyathorn told reporters the baht was at an "appropriate" level as it had risen by 1.5 percent recently while Euro and yen had strengthened by four percent.  

The government has said it will not fight the rise of the baht because the currency was appreciating due to economic fundamentals with the Thai economy expected to grow more than six percent this year.  

But it has said it will fight speculators and the central bank has introduced some measures to discourage them.  

The baht rose to a three-year high on Monday at around 39.90, then fell gradually in line with the Japanese yen, pushed down by fears of intervention by the Bank of Japan.

title: Thai Baht Ends Steady; Early Fall Recouped On Higher Yen
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht ended steady against the dollar Tuesday, pulled off its early lows on the yen's gains, traders said.  

Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra's bullish comments on the baht also weighed on sentiment toward the dollar, they said.  

The dollar ended at 39.985 baht, compared with THB39.98 at the Asian close Monday.  

Dollar short-covering by offshore players in the morning helped the dollar to claw up to an intraday high of THB40.14 from its 38-month low Monday.  

Some traders also suspected the Bank of Thailand intervened to slow the baht's appreciation.  

However, the dollar resumed its downward course as market players sold the currency as it slipped against the yen, the regional trendsetter.  

"Despite the suspected intervention by the Bank of Thailand, players still based their decision on the dollar's recent general weakness," said a trader.  

Late in Asia the dollar was at Y111.15 against the yen compared with Y120 early in the session and around Y111 late in Asia Monday.  

The dollar has come under immense pressure since the Group of Seven finance ministers called for exchange rate flexibility over the weekend.  

The dollar went down to its intraday low of THB39.95 after Thaksin said the baht could rise further, if it's supported by economic fundamentals, adding that the baht's recent appreciation was in line with the regional trend.  

In a sign of support for the G7 statement, Thaksin also agreed that governments and central banks shouldn't intervene regularly in the foreign exchange market, and should let the exchange rate move "naturally" as long as it wasn't too volatile.  

Dealers expect the dollar to open in Asia Wednesday in a range of THB39.80 to THB40.20, subject to volatility in the yen.  

Prices of long-term Thai government bonds ended lower Tuesday, tracking losses overnight in U.S. Treasurys, dealers said.  

Losses in the issue due November 2011 were exaggerated, however, by positioning in thin trade ahead of an auction reopening the issue Wednesday, a dealer at a foreign bank said.  

The yield on the November 2011 issue ended at 3.18%, up from 3.09% at Monday's close, the Thai Bond Dealing Center said in its daily report.  

"The November 2011 yield is well above the curve. Some players seemed to be pushing it up so they can buy the bond cheaply at tomorrow's (Wednesday's) auction," the dealer said.  

The yield on the government bond due March 2011 finished more in line with the yield curve at 2.92%, compared with an average bid/offer range of around 2.88%/2.835% in active trade Monday.  

Short-term issues closed unchanged or down only slightly, as they received continued support from demand driven by high financial system liquidity.  

The government bond due December 2006 closed at 1.525%, up just a tad from a previous close of 1.52%.  

Dealers expect the market to trade in a fairly tight range pending details of the government's issuance plans for the year beginning Oct. 1.  

An auction Tuesday of THB3 billion worth of 364-day central bank bonds resulted in a weighted-average accepted yield of around 1.218%, up from 1.206% last week.  

Accepted yields were a little higher than secondary market levels, reflecting uncertainty over the direction of yields pending information on upcoming supply and tightness in overnight liquidity. The secondary market was unaffected, however, as the tightness was only temporary and the uncertainty has largely been factored in to prices.  

Overnight interest rates fell back to normal levels by the close Tuesday, after rising temporarily on demand for baht associated with dollar weakness at the end of a biweekly cash reserve period for local banks on Monday, dealers said.

title: Asian  Currencies  Soar On G7; Ctrl Bks Fail To Curb Gains
text:
KUALA LUMPUR (Dow Jones)--Despite central bank intervention, Asian currencies surged Monday after Group of Seven finance ministers made an unprecedented call for increased flexibility in currency regimes to address global economic imbalances.  

Several Asian currencies soared to multi-month highs against the U.S. dollar, while the forward discount on the dollar-China yuan pair steepened to record levels during the day.  

The G7 communique at the weekend didn't target any country, addressing its message to "major countries or economic areas."  

Nevertheless, currency traders immediately turned to the yen and other more freely-traded Asian currencies, interpreting that remark as confirming the end of Washington's "strong dollar" policy of the late 1990s and conversely, the start of stronger Asian currencies.  

"The (G7) statement is a bit of a watershed. It explicitly said they want more flexibility in exchange rates," said BNP Paribas Senior Currency Analyst Thio Chin Loo.  

"The market thinks it (G7) is pointing towards Asia where there is the greatest trade imbalances with the U.S.," Thio added.  

As a result, the dollar plunged to a 33-month low versus the yen in Asia Monday, and a 34-month low against the Korean won. The dollar was also sharply weaker against the Singapore dollar - at a near three-month low - and reached a 13-month low against the Taiwan dollar. Stock markets across the region, meanwhile, fell as investors fretted over what stronger currencies mean for corporate profits.  


 
   Korea Bought Dlrs; China Says Policy Stance Unchanged 
   

Even jawboning from the Bank of Korea did nothing to stop dollar sales versus the won.  

"The recent trend in the market is not appropriate given Korea's economic fundamentals and we hope to see balance restored in the market on its own," said a high-ranking official at the Korean central bank.  

The Bank of Korea comments follow similar dollar-supportive remarks from the Ministry of Finance and Economy earlier Monday. The ministry followed through on its verbal intervention by buying dollars via state-run banks, according to dealers.  

The dollar fell to as low as KRW1,150 intraday Monday, tracking the dollar-yen's sharp fall, and ended at a 34-month low of KRW1,151.2, versus Friday's close of KRW1,168. The yen-won cross was at 10.2620 late Monday, from Friday's 10.2501.  

The dollar sank in the market for forward delivery against the yuan, which can be used in place of the spot market to make bets on the yuan's long-term direction. The dollar's one-year discount steepened to a record 2400 points at one stage, implying expectations of the dollar falling to 8.0374 yuan over the next 12 months, a nearly 3% drop from the tight spot range that Beijing now allows around CNY8.277.  

These expectations linger even though Chinese authorities insist nothing has changed post-G7.  

China's position on its current forex regime remains unchanged from the firm support for that policy expressed by People's Bank of China Governor Zhou Xiaochuan earlier this month, a central bank spokeswoman said Monday.  

Separately, a State Administration of Foreign Exchange spokesman said, "We will continue to keep the renminbi (or yuan) exchange rate basically stable."  

"The NDFs imply the yuan is under intense pressure," BNP Paribas' Thio said.  

"But China's (forex) stance should stay for another one or two years," she added.  


 
   Taiwan Central Bank Supplied NT$ 
   

Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.805, its lowest level since Aug. 14, 2002, versus Friday's close of NT$34.058. Dealings were valued at US$1.412 billion, the highest volume since May 30, 2002, compared with Friday's US$779 million.  

Players in the non-deliverable forward market dumped the U.S. dollar, while the Taiwan central bank was "supplying Taiwan dollar unlimitedly" to absorb dollar offers, said a local bank trader.  

The dollar slid to as low as 1.7295 Singapore dollars, its lowest level in almost three months. But by the end of the local session, the dollar was well off its early lows due to concerns Singapore's central bank may intervene and a possible easing of local monetary policy next month.  

United Overseas Bank said in a research report, "Over the next few days, U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar direction will be totally dependent on U.S. dollar-yen's outlook and whether the Bank of Japan will show up (to buy dollars)."  

Late Monday, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7322, down sharply from S$1.7490 late in Asia Friday.  

Against the Thai baht, the dollar reached a 38-month low of THB39.93 and was at THB40.05 late Monday, versus late Friday's THB40.51. No Bank of Thailand intervention was spotted though dealers said any baht sales by the authorities would likely have been easily absorbed.  

The dollar ended at 55.07 pesos Monday, down from Friday's close of PHP55.165, largely in tandem with regional markets and the dollar-yen pair. The market shrugged off the Philippine central bank's as-expected decision to keep rates unchanged.  

The Indonesian rupiah was barely traded as markets were shut for a religious holiday. Traders expect the rupiah to strengthen against the dollar Tuesday as the Indonesian unit catches up with the rises in its regional counterparts.

    SINGAPORE, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were caught
between a number of conflicting factors on Monday, including
weak U.S. data, falling north Asian stock markets and Europe's
fresh criticism of the region's currency policies.
    The yen        remained steady with Japanese markets closed
for a holiday. The euro  was under slight pressure after
Swedish voters decided not to join the single currency, but the
U.S. dollar continued to be undermined by Friday's weak retail
and consumer confidence data.
    The Thai baht        was among the few currencies to rise,
recovering from a sharp fall after the central bank last week
imposed short-term capital controls to curb speculation.
    Chinese non-deliverable forwards (NDF) showed a rising
premium on the yuan after Europe's top financial officials
again urged China and Japan to share the burden of the U.S.
current account adjustment.
  


 There were specific calls for China
to shift from a virtually fixed dollar peg to managing the yuan
against a basket of currencies.
    The one-year yuan NDF premium           hit 1,900,

  at around 8.09 in a year, compared to the narrow
8.2760/8.2800 band it is managed in.
    James Malcolm, currency strategist at JP Morgan, said the
debate over Asia's weak currencies and policies would surely
heat up heading into the Group of Seven meeting on the weekend,
and it was likely regional currency intervention would
moderate.

title: UPDATE 1-Thai  foreign exchange  curb seen delaying baht rally.
text:
BANGKOK, Sept 12 (Reuters) - Efforts by Thailand to curb inflows of hot foreign money to speculate on the baht have sent Asia's most bullish currency into retreat, but the impact may be short-lived, analysts said on Friday.  

The central Bank of Thailand (BOT) told domestic banks on Thursday to stop accepting short-term offshore baht from non-residents anticipating further gains in the currency.  

That triggered a baht sell-off early on Friday to a low of around 41.04 per U.S. dollar from 40.44 late on Thursday. The baht later recovered to 40.75 by 1020 GMT.  

Deputy BOT governor Thirachai Phuvanatnaranubala said the weaker baht on Friday reflected economic fundamentals and he was happy with its orderly retreat after the bank's move.  

"The baht has weakened slightly," he told reporters. "Its orderly adjustment is not necessarily a problem."  

"The baht, at this level, largely reflects Thai fundamentals. Our management of the currency does not have any specific target for it."  

The baht has gained around 5.3 percent versus the U.S. dollar so far in 2003, driven by strong economic growth seen at around six percent this year and a high current account surplus.  

HOT STOCKS  

The gain has attracted foreign investors, who have also targeted a booming Thai share market up 59 percent this year.  

The new restriction means non-residents would not be permitted to keep more than 50 million offshore baht in Thailand for periods of less than three months without normal underlying business.  

Last week, the central bank prohibited domestic banks from lending securities to offshore players in what it said was a precautionary move to limit future short selling of the baht.  

The central bank has intervened frequently in recent months to slow the baht's rise but foreign exchange dealers said they expected the currency to breach the key psychological level of 40 baht per U.S. dollar.  

With Thailand running a current account surplus of around six percent of GDP, UBS forex strategist Bhanu Baweja said he saw the baht at 40.50 over three months and at 39 baht in 12 months.  

"We believe the measure will change nothing in the trend of the THB/USD, and consider any weakness in the THB as temporary," he said in a commentary on Friday.  

A currency dealer at the Bank of Ayudhya said he also saw no lasting impact from the central bank actions.  

"It should have some short-term weakening effect, but with a heavy flow of funds into the Thai stock market, we will probably see it back to around 40.25 a month from now," he said.  

SPECULATION THE TARGET  

Thirachai said the average daily amount of offshore baht on the foreign exchange market, mostly hot money betting on the currency rising, surged to around $2.1 billion this month from an average $1.5 billion during May-August and $900 million early this year.  

He said the BOT was not trying to stop a baht appreciation driven by strong domestic growth, just speculation.  

"We control only short-term imports of offshore baht without underlying business, but do not restrict imports of dollars and other currencies irrespective of how short their maturity," Thirachai said on radio.  

"In managing our exchange rate, we will not try to move a big trunk with a small stick," he said.  

The International Monetary Fund urged Asian countries on Thursday to adopt more flexible exchange rates. The fund said it would be helpful for countries with managed-float currencies, like Thailand, to intervene less in the market.  

Since July, the Thai central bank has relaxed exchange controls to allow domestic institutions to invest up to $2.4 billion in foreign debt instruments, a move aimed at helping absorb a huge surplus of funds.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Baht drops on new cenbank rules.
text:
By Vidya Ranganthan
    SINGAPORE, Sept 12 (Reuters) - The Thai baht fell sharply
on Friday morning after the central bank sought to limit
speculative investors chasing it higher by capping the amount
of short-term funds non-residents could park in the country.
    That, and anxiety over dollar-buying intervention by Japan,
put a floor under the U.S. dollar in Asia, as it also recovered
against the euro after the second anniversary of the September
11 attacks passed uneventfully.
    "Asian currencies remain bid. But central banks either
through direct intervention or through regulation, as in
Thailand, are going to seek to have their currencies
competitively realigned," said Michael Jansen, markets
strategist with National Australia Bank, Sydney.
    The baht        dropped over one percent from Thursday's
levels to the weaker side of 41 per dollar in morning deals.
The baht had been testing 14-month highs of 40.20, a break of
which would have taken it to three-year highs.
  


    Late on Thursday, the Bank of Thailand said banks could not
accept more than 50 million baht from non-residents seeking to
park funds in the country for less than three months. It said
it wanted to curtail speculative inflows betting on baht
strength.
    "The new restriction reflects more on ongoing BOT efforts
to manage short-term capital flows to curb currency volatility
than on conscious efforts to manage baht strength," James
Malcolm, currency strategist at JP Morgan, said in a note.
    Last week, the Bank of Thailand banned local banks from
lending securities to offshore players, describing the measure
as a defence against speculative attacks on the baht in the
future.
    YEN INFLUENCE
    The Singapore dollar        fell early, along with the
baht, to the weaker side of 1.75 but later pared some of that
loss.
    The steady yen        was the main influence for the rest
of Asia, keeping the Taiwan dollar from firming despite the
recovery in stock markets, which attracts foreign investment.
Markets in Korea were closed for holidays. They reopen on
Monday.

yen down to 118 or even 119 per dollar over the next couple of
weeks.

the yen is weakening there will be a form of competitive

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Sing dlr slips as SARS confirmed.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Sept 9 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar slipped
late on Tuesday after the government confirmed the world's
first case of the deadly SARS virus since the World Health
Organisation declared a global outbreak over in July.
    The Singapore dollar        slipped past $1.7570 per U.S.
dollar in late trade after the Ministry of Health said a
27-year old man had tested positive for the Severe Acute
Respiratory Syndrome virus, but it remained clear of Monday's
lows.
    Before the confirmation, the Singapore dollar had rebounded
about three-quarters of a cent after falling to a one-month low
of 1.7618 in New York trade on initial reports of the SARS
case.
    "The impact on price action was very much muted. I don't
see much speculative flows as such," said a dealer at a foreign
bank in Singapore.
    Analysts said if it was an isolated case, which the
government said it was, any impact on the Singapore dollar
would be brief.
  


 SARS killed over 800 people in a global
outbreak, including 33 in Singapore, and savaged Asian
economies earlier this year.
    BAHT RALLIES
    Elsewhere, the Thai baht        hit a 14-month high, and
dealers in Bangkok suspected the Bank of Thailand had
intervened through local banks to cap the rise when it hit
40.43 per U.S. dollar, its strongest since July 2002.
    Dealers said the intervention was not as aggressive as
previous bouts, and that had left the market looking for more
gains.
    David Simmonds, currency strategist at Royal Bank of
Scotland in Singapore, said Thailand's economic outperformance
should allow authorities to be comfortable with some currency
strength.
    "It would be unrealistic to expect Thailand to stand
completely out of the way of appreciation, one has to be a
little bit wary. But by and large, I do think we are seeing a
catch up to fundamentals here," he added.
    A senior dealer at a local bank in Thailand said players
were targetting 40.25 as the next level to test. However, he
said he had heard some state enterprises were looking to buy
dollars around those levels.
   The South Korean won                   rose to a two-week
high of 1,168.0 per dollar, helped by equity inflows. The Bank
of Korea policy meeting left interest rates steady, and the
central bank governor voiced concern that an anticipated
recovery was yet to appear.
    Dealers in Singapore cited intervention by the central bank
as the won rose through 1,170. Seoul's currency market is
closed from Wednesday to Friday for Chosuk holidays.

in the Senate looking into the business dealings of President
Gloria Macapagal Arroyo's husband.

title: APEC Supports Bond Mkt Cooperation Despite  FX  Divisions
text:
PHUKET, Thailand -(Dow Jones)- Asia Pacific finance ministers Friday agreed to promote a more integrated regional bond market that will eventually lead to cross-border issues, even as they rebuffed calls to remove protective mechanisms in their exchange rate regimes. 

 In a joint statement issued at the end of a two-day meeting of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, finance ministers said they will work together to achieve well-developed bond markets. 

 "We acknowledged that further cooperation is necessary to attain domestic and regional conditions which are essential to facilitate cross-border bond market activities," the ministers said in the statement. 

 They also expressed support for an initiative by Thailand, Japan and South Korea to issue new products - such as long-term, local-currency denominated debt instruments, derivatives and asset-backed securities - to be traded within the region. 

 Integration of the regional bond market was highlighted as a key part of the APEC talks agenda by the Thai hosts, but was overshadowed by a lengthy debate over appropriate exchange rate policies. 

 The 21 APEC ministers ended their meeting accepting a U.S.-inspired call for gradual currency-policy reform but offered no specifics on how they might pick up the pace. 

 But without a clear commitment toward currency flexibility, it's uncertain how an integrated regional bond market could take off. 

 Thailand itself said it's dropped plans to issue baht-denominated bonds offshore and will only offer carefully regulated onshore bonds to nonresident investors to avoid arming potential currency speculators with baht assets. 

 Like other central banks in the region, Bank of Thailand has been regularly intervening in the foreign exchange market to stem exchange rate volatility, effectively slowing the pace of the baht's appreciation. 

 Such interventions have boosted regional central bank reserves, which at more than $1 trillion equal almost half of the world's total. 

 U.S. Treasury Secretary John Snow, who campaigned to get APEC members to commit to a process of greater exchange rate flexibility during the two days, said market interventions should be kept to a minimum. 

 "The management of currencies at unnatural rates distorts markets, tending toward beggar-thy-neighbor policies, and encourages protectionism," Snow said. 

 In June, 11 central banks from the Asia Pacific region agreed to pool a small portion of their reserves to set up an Asian Bond Fund that will invest in regional bonds, in a bid to maintain Asian savings within the region. 

 The $1-billion fund will initially invest in dollar-denominated sovereign and quasi-sovereign bonds, and possibly in local currency bonds at a later stage. 

 Market participants believe the issuance of local currency bonds for cross-border trading in the region is still a long way off as several technical hurdles must be overcome, such as tax and settlement barriers. 

 APEC ministers said they will promote the development of securitization and credit guarantee markets that will enhance the efficiency of regional bond markets, but fell short of outlining specific steps to facilitate cross-border trading. 

 -By Jenny Paris, Dow Jones Newswires; 661-929 4817; jenny.paris@dowjones.com

title: Thai PM: APEC Mins Discuss Need For Floating  Currencies
text:
PHUKET, Thailand -(Dow Jones)- Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said Thursday that Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation finance ministers talks centered on the need to promote free-float exchange rate regimes in the region, but there was no mention of China's rigid currency peg. 

 "We talked about currencies' flexibility but not the yuan in particular," Thaksin said. 

 He said he didn't expect China to float the yuan any time soon but noted such a move would benefit the Thai economy's competitiveness in the region. 

 "They (China) will have to look for the right timing" for freeing their exchange rate, he said. 

 China is resisting pressure from the U.S. and Japan to loosen its grip on the yuan, which is tightly pegged to the dollar. U.S. manufacturers, who are losing their markets to cheap Chinese goods, argue the strict exchange rate regime keeps the yuan undervalued and have been pushing for a revaluation. 

 U.S. Treasury Secretary John Snow said Thursday upon his arrival here that a brighter outlook for economic growth and relatively tranquil markets make now a good time for Asian governments to wean themselves from reliance on capital controls and currency intervention. 

 But he acknowledged his message will be a tough sell. Although much attention has been paid to China's allegedly undervalued currency, several important trading nations in the region intervene heavily to prevent their currencies from appreciating and making exports less competitive. 

 Earlier this week, Thailand's central bank, which has been regularly intervening in the foreign exchange market to stem the baht's appreciation against the dollar, banned the lending of securities offshore in a bid to restrict the inflow of speculative funds that were driving the currency higher.

title: Thailand's turn to lead Asian  currencies  again?
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 3 (Reuters) - The Thai baht has come full circle.  

Six years after a de facto devaluation of the currency sparked the Asian financial crisis, Thailand appears to be front-running a campaign to ease capital controls in Asia and tolerate currency gains.  

At a 13-month high of 40.83 against the dollar on Wednesday, the baht replaced the Indonesian rupiah as Asia's best performing tradeable currency this year.  

It has risen 5.5 percent nominally this year and more than 4 percent in trade-weighted terms since July.  

An upgrade of Thailand's ratings by Fitch vindicated the rally, which has been backed by the country's improving domestic and external growth.  

Within the country, Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra seemed to be winning the familiar war of words between the government, which forecasts the baht in a range of 39 to 40 by the end of the year, and the central bank, which wants slower moves.  

Bank of Thailand Deputy Governor Thirachai Phuvanatnaranubala on Wednesday urged the countries of the Asia-Pacific region to follow the Thai example and ease capital controls.  

"Maybe the first crack in the dam of Asian intervention against currency strength is being seen in Thailand," said David Simmonds, markets strategist with the Royal Bank of Scotland.  

Seen in the context of Thaksin's role in piloting the Asian regional bond fund, which was launched in June, it all fits into place, analysts said.  

"Thailand is pushing its political agenda in terms of leading Asia through the Asian bond fund," said James Malcolm, currency strategist with JP Morgan.  

"They need to be seen as moving ahead of other people on the currency, because it is so undervalued and its fair value is probably near 37-38."  

MYSTIFYING MOVE  

Analysts say the government forecasts for the baht to rise to 39 per dollar will be right, even if that does not happen as soon as the end of the year.  

Thailand recently exited an IMF loan programme, after repaying the debt two years in advance, and the baht's rise has not been disrupted by rate cuts in June and by a move to allow domestic institutions to invest heavily overseas.  

The attractiveness of the stock market , which has been drawing a torrent of foreign investment, the rising exports to China and the rebound in tourism after the outbreak of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) all bode well for the baht, analysts at Standard Chartered Bank said in a note.  

Implied volatility on baht options has been rising along with rumours that the Bank of Thailand has been intervening aggressively and seeking ways to rein in the appreciation.  

Markets were confused on Tuesday by a central bank announcement that it had banned local banks from lending securities to offshore players.  

The baht retreated, in a knee-jerk reaction, before markets realised such a ban is traditionally a currency defence mechanism aimed at preventing foreigners from short-selling securities to bet on a currency falling.  

Analysts said markets were misreading the measure, which probably was aimed at developing Thailand's repo segment.  

"This means the offshore markets cannot have access to the Thai repo market and cannot park their money onshore through repos," said Sameer Goel, markets strategist at Bank of America.  

"It is irrelevant to the forex market and it does not make that much of a difference because one can still go short dollar/baht and lend the baht onshore via the swap market."

title: Thai Ctrl Bk: Doesn't Need To  Intervene  In  FX  Mkt
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula reiterated Tuesday that the central bank hasn't been intervening recently to curb the baht's strength against the dollar because there's no immediate need to do so. 

 "Why would we have to intervene?" Pridiyathorn asked reporters rhetorically. He said he hadn't consulted with the department responsible for financial market operations yet Tuesday, however. 

Central bank and government officials have said repeatedly in recent days that investment inflows were attracted naturally to a growing economy, which is why the baht has been strengthening. 

 But while government officials have advertised the baht's uptrend as confirmation of confidence in the economy and their policies, the central bank has stressed that it is monitoring speculative flows and is prepared to act if necessary. 

 Dealers have said suspected agents of the central bank have been supporting the dollar at low points in recent days but not chasing it higher. Pridiyathorn sometimes says that buying dollars for reserves or to stem excessive volatility driven by speculation doesn't constitute intervention. 

 At 0258 GMT, the dollar was quoted at 41.025 baht, down from a late morning high of THB41.050, but remaining in an expected range of THB40.900, a 13-month low, to THB41.100. 

 Dealers said the dollar ran up from around the low in early trade when heavy importer buying of euros triggered dollar short-covering. Baht holders still buy dollars first before snapping up euros. 

 The afternoon easing in the dollar wasn't a result of the central bank comments, a dealer at a foreign bank said. 

 "Once the short-dollar positions were covered, and investors saw the dollar fail to move higher, they begin to sell again," the dealer said. 

 The U.S. currency is expected to move gradually lower amid broad dollar weakness and strong Thai economic data. 

 Bank of Thailand is expected to continue to buy dollars on weakness and to closely monitor speculative activity, intervening lightly at key dollar support points whenever the baht appreciates more quickly than other regional currencies. 

 Meanwhile, Atchana Waiquamdee, senior director of the central bank's domestic economic policy department, told a Cabinet meeting Tuesday not to worry about the baht's movements, because the currency's strength reflected economic conditions and the central bank was monitoring markets closely. 

 Sansanee Nakpong, deputy government spokeswoman, told reporters after the Cabinet meeting that Atchana said core inflation - which excludes volatile food and energy prices - was at zero in August compared with last year, but this was due to excessive supply, not weak demand. 

 The current situation doesn't constitute deflation, Atchana said, which is characterized by a long period of falling consumer prices caused by weak demand. 

 In theory, if prices continued to fall, the 14-day repurchase market target rate could fall again from the current level of 1.25%, but it shouldn't have any impact on the general economic situation, Atchana said. 

 She noted that deflation is usually defined as extended subzero inflation as measured by the consumer price index, and the headline CPI was up 2.2% on year in August due to higher oil and fruit and vegetable prices. 

 The commerce ministry said Monday that core inflation was held down by falling rents as low interest rates spurred home buying.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Focus on Snow visit, baht rises.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Sept 1 (Reuters) - The Thai baht        eclipsed
its regional counterparts with a rise to 13-month highs on
Monday afternoon, as most traders focused on U.S. Secretary
John Snow's visit to Asia and likely discussions on currency
policy.
    The baht rose past 41 per dollar even as the central bank
tried to limit its gains after a bullish government forecast
for the currency.
    The baht extended a three-week long sharp rally to 40.95, a
July 2002 high, after Finance Minister Suchart Jaovisidha said
on Friday he expected it to rise to 39-40 per dollar by the end
of 2003. It was quoted at around 41.20 in late Asian trade on
Friday and has risen nearly three percent in three weeks.
    The central bank, which last week admitted it had been
intervening and said it would curb speculative flows,
intervened verbally again on Monday.
  


 Bank of Thailand Governor
Pridiyathorn Devakula said the currency market should heed only
the central bank's policy on the baht.
    In a note to clients, UBS said the yen, baht and Korean won
have appreciated by 4.9 percent, 2.5 percent and 1.8 percent
respectively in trade-weighted terms so far in this quarter.
 
    It added that there were near-term risks for a fall in some
of the regionals.
    "Given the weak state of their domestic economies, less
  

valid for Thailand, and the one sided nature of market  

positioning, the threat of intervention becomes very real for  

the short term," UBS said.  

Markets were underpricing the risk from North Korea's  

nuclear plans and the rise in valuations during the recent  

equity rallies, the note said.  

SNOW VISITS  

Other Asian currencies rose modestly but underperformed the  

yen as traders awaited word from Snow, who was in Tokyo on  

Monday.  

The yen was off Friday's three-month high of 116.15,  

but stayed on the higher side of 117, finding support after  

Japanese authorities revealed they had not intervened in  

August.  

Markets believe Snow is likely to call upon Asian  

countries, particularly China, to absorb some of the U.S.  

dollar's weakness and be more flexible about letting their  

currencies appreciate.   


 
    U.S. Treasury officials said Snow had not discussed the
revaluation of any currency at a breakfast meeting in Tokyo.
    Still, the Singapore dollar        was range-bound after
  

failing to get past 1.75 in offshore weekend deals, but the  

Taiwan dollar rose to a year high as the Taiwan stock  

market hit 15-month peaks.   


The Korean won             was slightly higher, the
  

Philippine peso struggled around the key 55 level, torn  

between persisting political worries and the government's  

warnings against currency speculation.   


 
    Month-end pressure from commercial dollar demand on the
rupiah eased, allowing it to rise past 8,500, to an 8,460 high.
    Cliff Tan, currency and interest rates strategist at
  

Citigroup, said that as markets grew confident about the  

comfort of Japanese authorities with the yen's rally, Asian  

currencies would follow it higher.  

"I think some of the Asian currencies have a bit to catch  

up with the yen, so this underperformance may not last for the  

week," Tan said.  

Lehman Brothers said the Snow visit was unlikely to  

dramatically alter the intervention habits of Asian  

policymakers.  

"But, with the backdrop for Asian capital markets  

significantly improved, Asian policymakers should be  

increasingly more sympathetic if Treasury Secretary Snow  

expressed a preference for less interventionist policies," it  

said in a note sent on Monday and written last week.  

"We don't expect huge revelations in next week's round of  

FX policy sound bytes but we'd view the Asia visit as a modest  

upside risk to our long-standing bullish Asian currency view."

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Pressured by Korea talks,  intervention  fears.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Aug 29 (Reuters) - Barring the Taiwan dollar,
most Asian currencies disregarded a rising Japanese yen on
Friday and were either steady to lower.
    As the yen reached a six-week high against the dollar,
after Japanese data showed improving industrial output and the
Nikkei rose, the Taiwan dollar neared its highest in a year.
    The Korean won suffered from worries as six-nation talks in
China over North Korea's nuclear crisis ended inconclusively,
with the delegates agreeing to meet again in October and
Pyongyang highly critical of the U.S. stance.
 
    Worries the Bank of Korea was still intervening to contain
won appreciation also pushed the currency down against the yen.
    The Thai baht too was haunted by the fears of intervention,
forcing it to halt a three-week uptrend. The Bank of Thailand
hinted on Thursday it had been intervening.
    On Friday, Thai central bank governor,  Pridiyathorn


 Devakula, said the bank was monitoring speculative flows 

 betting on the baht's rise and would find ways to deal with 

 them. 

 "The uncertainties inherent in the (Korea) talks represent 

 one set of reasons why, though we like baht and Taiwan dollar 

 in reflecting the global reflation trade, we are more wary of 

 won," Bank of America said in their commentary. 

 "Bank of Thailand launched another salvo against 

 speculation in the currency. This makes sense in the context of 

 them wishing to limit baht appreciation as a result of 

 speculation," it said. 

 The Singapore dollar fell as it moved towards the centre of 

 the trade-weighted band authorities manage the currency in, a 

 day after the authorities announced cuts to employer 

 contributions to the country's pension system. 

 RUPIAH WEAK AFTER RATE CUTS 

 The Indonesian rupiah recovered from two-week lows towards 

 afternoon after falling under the pressure of month-end imports 

 and market expectations that falling interest rates will erode 

 its attractiveness to investors. 

 The central bank cut overnight rates on Friday, the seventh 

 time since May and said it saw no need to intervene to defend 

 the rupiah. 


 
    Vincent Low, markets strategist at Merrill Lynch, said the
rate cut ought to impact the rupiah adversely.
    But Low disagreed with some economists who suggest



Indonesia ought to be less aggressive in cutting rates and



should focus on attracting investment and building foreign



exchange reserves as it prepares to exit an IMF funding



programme.



 
    "I'm not sure about using the exchange rate as a stimulus
in a closed economy like Indonesia," Low said.
    "Interest rates are a more direct way for macro economic
objectives, and the way to build reserves is not through
intervention but by looking for alternative sources to the
IMF."     The Indonesian central bank was comfortable with some



weakness in the rupiah, which has been one of Asia's best



performers this year, and other than politics, Indonesia's



economic fundamentals were sound, he said.



Elsewhere, the Philippine peso was back on the weaker side



of 55, after having closed above that level for the first time



in 10 days on Thursday and despite the central bank's remark it



expected the peso around 54 per dollar at the end of 2003.



The country's Defence Secretary Angelo Reyes said on Friday



he was resigning in the wake of the July 27 failed mutiny, and



warned of a well-funded plot to bring down the government.



The peso had rallied over the past two days from near



record lows after a government warning and a slight monetary



tightening.



The central bank announced on Thursday after the market



closed that it was scrapping a tiered system on overnight



borrowing that discouraged banks from making larger deposits



with the central bank.

title: UPDATE 1-Thai c.bank monitors baht, seeks to slow rallies.
text:
BANGKOK, Aug 28 (Reuters) - The central Bank of Thailand (BOT) hinted on Thursday it has intervened to halt the baht's sharp gains against the dollar. 

 A bank director said the BOT was monitoring the sharp rise of the baht closely in a bid to try to keep it from getting too strong against the dollar. 

 "The central bank is now closely monitoring the baht," Chakramon Phasukvanich told reporters. The baht "has been appreciating, but it has not gained to the extent that it could have," he said without elaboration. 

 The baht rose 0.33 percent against the dollar overnight and has risen about 4.65 percent against the greenback so far this year. 

 Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra conceded on Thursday that the central bank could probably do little to stem the baht's hefty gains in the past week, saying he believed its rallies reflected the quickly growing domestic economy. 

 "The Bank of Thailand's current manage-float policy is designed for keeping the baht stable," Thaksin told reporters. 

 "But it is clear that our economy is very strong which convinces people that the baht will remain strong, a fact that is hard to resist." 

 Analysts said Thaksin's comments did not help central bank efforts to slow baht's rise, which could hurt Thai exports. 

 "BOT is said to have come in via direct onshore to control damage from PM Thaksin's comments: the pair recovers from 41.09 low to 41.14," MMS International in Singapore said in a research note. 

 "The BOT is now letting the market know it shouldn't get too ahead of itself." 

 The baht traded at around 41.17 per dollar at 0719 GMT on Thursday after firming to around 41.09 shortly after Thaksin's comments. 

 Another senior central bank official said on Thursday the baht was still competitive with other Asian currencies despite its recent hefty rise against the dollar.

title: Thai Baht Ends Up; Off High As Importers,Oil Cos Buy Dlrs
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended slightly higher against the dollar Tuesday on optimism the buoyant local economy would continue to strengthen, but dollar buying by oil companies and importers capped its gains. 

 The U.S. currency closed at 41.37 baht at the end of the Asian session, down from THB41.40 at the Asian close Monday - but off an overnight low of THB41.29. 

 The baht surged to a one-year high of THB41.34 against the dollar Monday, boosted by Friday's rating upgrades of top Thai banks by Moody's Investors Service, as well as a stronger yen. 

 Analysts believe rating agencies are poised to upgrade Thailand's credit ranking, which would further drive gains for the baht. Some forecast a 6% rise by year-end to THB39 to the dollar. 

 They say Thailand is well-positioned to benefit from an expected recovery in the U.S. economy and - to some extent - Japanese consumption, which would continue to lure big foreign investors to the Southeast Asian nation. 

 The dollar opened around THB41.30-THB41.35. Demand from importers and oil companies pushed it to an intraday high of THB41.42 around midday. The weaker yen also helped support the U.S. unit. 

 But Japanese unit recovered its footing subsequently - lifting the baht to a firmer close. 

 Meanwhile Thailand's central bank said it hasn't intervened in the foreign exchange market, but is monitoring the movements closely. 

 "The baht is quite stable moving in a range of THB41.38 baht to THB41.41 to the dollar. The central bank hasn't intervened in the foreign exchange market, but we're keeping an eye on movements," Tasna Rajatabhothi, assistant governor for financial market operations at the central bank, told reporters. 

 Dealers expected the dollar open between THB41.20 and THB41.50 Wednesday, subject to the movements of the yen, a regional trendsetter. 

 Thai government bonds ended slightly lower Tuesday, tracking overnight weakness in U.S. Treasurys, traders said. 

 Some mutual funds also reduced their holdings of government bonds because of market volatility to park their money in higher-yielding assets such as corporate bonds, they added. 

 After rallying in the first half of the year on strong liquidity in the financial system, Thai bonds have languished since August. 

 Market players are worried that demand for Thai debt will fall after the central bank Wednesday said it approved $2.45 billion of investment in overseas securities by local big investors such as life insurance firms, mutual funds and provident funds. 

 Concerns over a higher supply of state enterprise bonds next month also hurt sentiment. 

 The yield on the government bond due December 2008 finished up a tad at 2.02%, compared with 2.00% at the last close, according to the Thai Bond Dealing Center. 

 The issue due November 2011 ended at 2.75%, compared with Monday's close of 2.70%. 

 Money market interest rates ended little changed, as central bank support in the repurchase market helped limit the weight of excess financial system liquidity partially stemming from the baht's strength.

central bank was readying to intervene, but other Asian
currencies were pulled higher after the yen hit a one-month
high against the dollar.
    Data confirming the South Korea economy was in recession in
the first half of the year was ignored by the won
 , which was pushed to seven-month highs by foreign
investors more interested in an expected second half rebound.
    In Taiwan, another economy which has reported negative
second quarter GDP growth, the local dollar  rose to
11-month highs, despite the efforts of the central bank, as
exporters sold the U.S. dollar.
    Financial markets in the Philippines, where the peso has
been slumping towards record lows, were closed for a local
holiday. Trade would resume on Monday. The peso ended
Thursday's local session at 55.265 per dollar, a record closing
low.



    MAS CHECKS
    The Singapore rose to a high of 1.7329 per U.S. dollar in
offshore trade, its highest since June 20, but had fallen back
about one cent by late morning.
 
    Dealers said early calls by the Monetary Authority of
Singapore to check rates with some banks caused the pull back.
    That also made players in other Southeast Asian currencies
wary of the risk of intervention by authorities sensitive to
protecting export competitiveness.
    Currency gains also counter the easier monetary policy
stances many central banks have adopted this year.
    Craig Chan, an analyst at Forecast Ltd, said the Singapore
dollar has gained on a trade-weighted basis recently, and that
was why the market believed the risk of intervention was high.
    "It's a policy that continues to be implemented by all
central banks in the region," he said.
    "Any policy tightening through currency gains is



particularly of concern here in Singapore, where the government



has only recently announced some cost cutting measures," he



said, referring to the planned cut in pension contributions



made by employers.



However, Chan said central banks across the region might



only be able to hold back the gains temporarily, given the



pressure from equity-related inflows and a build up of



structural plays targetting strong growth in Asia amid a global



recovery.



BAHT WARY



The Thai baht  was around a one-month high, but



players were wary of pushing through the 41.45 per dollar level



because they feared central bank intervention beyond there.



The baht stalled three times at an 11-month high of 41.40



in June, largely because of suspected Bank of Thailand

intervention.



BOT Deputy Governor Thirachai Phuvanatnaranubala said on



Thursday the additional easing of foreign exchange controls



this week should reduce the cost of the central bank's efforts



to slow the baht's gains through intervention.



He said Bank of Thailand's decision to let domestic fund



managers invest in offshore debt instruments abroad was likely



to be followed by other central banks in the region.



Analysts said the announcement was designed to ease upward



pressure on the baht, which has risen by over four percent



against the dollar since April.



However, David Simmonds, strategist at Royal Bank of



Scotland in Singapore, said the impact on the baht would only



be temporary.



"I don't see a constant outflow in debt issues, once the



limits are met that flow will cease," he said. CURRENCIES VS

title: Thai  FX  easing curbs baht  intervention  pressure.
text:
BANGKOK, Aug 21 (Reuters) - Thailand's central bank said on Thursday its additional easing on foreign exchange controls this week should reduce the cost of its efforts to slow the baht's gains through market intervention. 

 Deputy central bank governor Thirachai Phuvanatnaranubala said the Bank of Thailand (BOT) decision to let domestic fund managers invest in more offshore debt instruments abroad was likely to be followed by other central banks in the region. 

 "I think this is a trend to be seen in Asia as it reduces the burden for a central bank to buy dollars in the market which go into national reserves," he told reporters. 

 "It is now the turn of private investors to buy dollars, thus reducing the burden on the central bank," Thirachai said. 

 The BOT on Wednesday raised, to $2.45 billion from $500 million, the combined amount of offshore debt paper Thai funds and institutions can buy abroad. 

 Analysts said the announcement was designed to ease upward pressure on the baht, which has risen about 3.6 percent against the dollar so far this year. 

 Thirachai declined to say whether the central bank would accept any further demand from Thai fund managers to invest offshore, saying it would need to satisfy itself that any additional approvals would not affect the Thai bond market. 

 Bond dealers said the BOT move sent yields of medium and long-term government bonds up 10-20 basis points on Wednesday. Some expect further yield steepening in the next few days.

title: Thai  FX , bond markets jolted by easing.
text:
BANGKOK, Aug 21 (Reuters) - Thailand's decision to let its fund managers invest more in offshore debt instruments has jolted the bond market, pushing up yields and forcing companies to rethink borrowering plans. 

 The central Bank of Thailand (BOT) raised, to $2.45 billion from $500 million, the combined amount of offshore debt paper Thai funds and institutions can buy. 

 Analysts said Wednesday's announcement was designed to ease upward pressure on the baht, which has risen about 3.6 percent against the dollar so far this year. 

 A dealer at Barclays Capital Securities (Thailand) said the BOT announcement reflected a desire to make intervention less necessary to slow the baht's rallies. 

 "It seems too focused on achieving its FX objective without duly considering the impact on bond and capital markets," said the dealer who did not want to be identified. 

 The dealer said a key uncertainty was whether the BOT would continue to raise the offshore investment limit much further from here if requested to do so by fund managers. 

 Bond dealers said the BOT's move sent yields of medium and long-term government bonds up 10 to 20 basis points on Wednesday. Some expect further yield curve steepening in the next few days. 

 "It hits long-term yields. When the bank announced the original $500 million ceiling in July, yields shot up for three days. This sharply higher amount should push up yields for a few days," said Pannarat Bhanpato of MFC Asset Management. 

 The yield of seven-year government bond  was 2.33 percent on Thursday, up 16 basis points from Tuesday. 

 VOLATILITY 

 The BOT said it approved the increase because it had underestimated demand for investment in offshore debt securities. It said the higher outflow was not expected to affect domestic economic stability. 

 Market volatility and higher yields after the central bank's decision prompted Thailand's largest finance firm, National Finance PCL (NFS.BK), to delay a planned four-billion-baht ($96.1 million) seven-year bond issue indefinitely. 

 Dealers said at least some of the 10 other Thai companies, planning to issue a total of about 45 billion baht of bonds in August and September, would probably also hold off. 

 Those which might be affected include a three billion baht issue of six-year bonds by Quality Houses PCL (QH.BK), a four-billion-baht, five-year secured amortising bond issue by Sahaviriya Steel Industries PCL (SSI.BK) and an issue of up to nine billion baht of secured, amortising bonds by mobile phone operator Total Access Communication PCL (TACC.SI). 

 "The market sell-off, higher yields and a general shift to stocks from bonds make it harder for pending issuers to go ahead with their plans. They are seeing the chance of locking low long-term coupons slip away," a fund manager said. 

 Analyst Saichon Fuvivattanakankun at the Bangkok Bond Dealers Centre said recent steepening of Thai long bond yield curve had trimmed average daily bond market turnover to eight billion baht this week from 12 billion baht in July. ($1 = 41.62 baht).

A corrected story follows


 By Vidya Ranganathan 

 SINGAPORE, Aug 15 (Reuters) - The Philippine peso hit a five month low on Friday, one day after a court ordered a year-long suspension of central bank officials including Governor Rafael Buenaventura over the closure of a commercial bank in 2000. 

 Security worries ahead of Indonesia's National Day on Sunday and in the wake of the arrest of Muslim militant leader Hambali kept regional sentiment cautious. 

 The peso  fell as far as 55.10 per dollar, stopping short of a March low of 55.16, with some traders suspecting the central bank had sold dollars at that level. The central bank had not intervened on the breach of the pivotal 55 per dollar level. 

 "The peso is the exception to the strengthening trend in Asian currencies," said Thio Chin Loo, currency strategist with BNP Paribas. 

 "The court ruling is causing some investor confidence erosion. It throws open questions about policy continuity and leadership succession issues and that's negative for the peso." 

 The ruling cannot take effect until all appeals were exhausted, and the central bank said the officials would remain in their jobs while the legal process played out. 

 Other Asian currencies rallied, supported by rising stock markets and some more improvement in economic data in the United States. The dollar steadied in Asian trade after weakening in response to the major power outages in the United States. 


The Singapore dollar  rose past 1.75 per dollar to its strongest level
since July 28, while the Thai baht        was boosted when the central
bank said the baht was not too strong.



The baht hit a one-month high of 41.58 per dollar. In June and July the
Bank of Thailand intervened to prevent the baht rising beyond 41.40 per
baht.



Singapore's Straits Times index  closed down slightly on Friday, ending
a run of seven stronger closes. On Thursday, the STI hit a 13-month
high.



Korean markets were closed for the Liberation Day holiday.



RUPIAH WARY



The Indonesian rupiah  was stronger than Thursday, but traders were
wary of pushing the rupiah higher ahead of National Day celebrations on
the long holiday weekend.



Security risks were pushed to the fore after the capture in Thailand of
Hambali, the suspected mastermind of the bomb blasts in Bali last
October.



"The fear of a potential terrorist strike in the upcoming National Day
celebrations is keeping the rupiah a bit defensive," Thio said.



Indonesian President Megawati Sukarnoputri made no reference to Hambali
in her speech to parliament on Friday.



But analysts said his capture would amplify the security concerns in
the region, which have been rising since a failed mutiny in the
Philippines at the end of July and last week's bomb blast in a Jakarta
hotel



"One can read the Hambali capture in two ways," said James Malcolm,
currency strategist with JP Morgan.



"It is certainly good from the medium to longer term perspective, but
it gives you ongoing concerns about security issues and terror attacks
and whether they want to protest this on National Day," he said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Waiting on Fed, Sing dlr easier.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Aug 11 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar steadied
after some early falls on Monday following a government
downgrade of the country's 2003 growth forecast, while the
Indonesian rupiah extended its recovery after last week's hotel
bombing.
    Overall, traders avoided taking aggressive positions in
Asian currencies ahead of the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy
meeting on Tuesday and key U.S. data this week.
    "With (U.S.) summer holidays starting, this is not a week
to have a strong view, not at least until we hear what the Fed
has to say," said Philip Wee, strategist at Singapore's DBS
Bank.
    Most analysts do not expect any change in U.S. rates this
week. Wee said the market would like to hear more about
economic recovery prospects and deflation risks that the Fed
had been debating since last November.
    U.S. data this week includes July retail sales on
Wednesday, and the June trade balance on Thursday.



 Friday is
busy, with July consumer prices and industrial production
reports and consumer sentiment figures for August to be
released.
    SINGAPORE GROWTH DOWNGRADED
    The Singapore dollar        eased as far as 1.7584 per U.S.
dollar in early trade, before recovering to be flat. On Friday,
it had traded at 1.7525, its highest since late July.
    Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong announced the growth
forecast downgrade to zero to one percent, from 0.5 to 2.5
percent, on Friday evening.
    Final second quarter GDP data on Monday showed the economy
had contracted by an annualised 11.4 percent from the first
quarter, largely because of the fallout from SARS. The data was
little changed from preliminary figures released last month.
    "The full year forecast was a little bit lower than the
market generally have been expecting," said David Simmonds,
strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland in Singapore.
    "That said, I am sure there's a preference on part of the
authorities here to be a little bit on the side of caution," he
said, adding the growth estimate could be revised up if
expectations of a better second half are met.
    Echoing his views, dealers said some long-term players were
spotted buying the Singapore dollar on the weaker side of
1.7580 per dollar. The yen's rise to three-week highs against
the U.S. dollar  and euro           also helped.
    Influenced by the Singapore dollar's early losses, the Thai
baht  eased a touch to 41.91 per dollar, before bouncing
back to test 41.80, a level it also tested on Friday. The baht
spent most of June and July on the stronger side of 41.80 but
found its gains blocked by Bank of Thailand intervention.
 
    Baht trade was limited ahead of Tuesday's public holiday,
dealers said.
    The Indonesian rupiah        continued to edge higher,
reclaiming ground lost after last week's bombing of a hotel in
Jakarta that saw it weaken beyond 8,700 per dollar.
    The rupiah was around 8,530 per dollar, with mostly



offshore players spotted covering short rupiah positions they



were caught holding after the central bank's dollar sales to



protect the rupiah last week.



However, dealers said there was caution about chasing the



rupiah too high given security and political concerns ahead of



Indonesia's national day on Sunday.



The Philippine peso  hit 54.89 per dollar, its lowest



in about a week, weighed down by higher corporate demand for



dollars. Dealers in Manila said a seasonal August/September



rise in imports was expected to keep the peso under pressure.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Pulled higher by rallying yen.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Aug 8 (Reuters) - Asian currencies mostly
strengthened on Friday as the Japanese yen's sharp rise against
the U.S. dollar sent players scrambling to cover their short
positions in regional plays.
    The yen        rallied as high as 118.75 per dollar in
offshore trade on Thursday tas it posted its biggest one day
rise since March. The yen held around 119 yen on Friday,
helping Asian currencies shake off some of their shock from
Tuesday's hotel bombing in Jakarta.
 
    "There is a broad U.S. dollar uncertainty back in the
market," said Philip Wee, strategist at Singapore's DBS Bank.
    "We don't expect any big FX moves, but Asian currencies in


 general should benefit on the margin from the dollar 

 uncertainty amid the debate over how the bond-to-equity 

 migration would affect the dollar." 

 The Indonesian rupiah  rose nearly half a percent to 

 8,545 per dollar, before pulling back slightly. Earlier this 

 week it had tumbled to near three-month lows on the weaker side 

 of 8,700 per dollar after the bomb attack. 

 The Singapore dollar , one of the region's most 

 liquid currency plays, strengthened to 1.7533 per U.S dollar, 

 its highest since late July. It had fallen to a three-month low 

 of 1.7668 after the Jakarta bomb attack. 

 Even the Philippine peso , dogged by worries of 

 political instability since a failed mutiny on July 27, managed 

 some gains. But it ran into selling from local corporates and 

 ended local trade a touch softer at 54.71 per dollar. 

 Wee said apart from the initial response to the bombing, 

 the rupiah's retracement from its lows had been in line with 

 recent moves in other high yielding currencies. 

 He said that showed that despite the talk of political and 

 economic woes, the rupiah would track the global dollar debate 

 as much as any other regional currency. 

 "We are placing our bets with the BI (Bank Indonesia), who 

 desires a 8200-8600 range for dollar/rupiah. It would be the 

 same in Philippines where we don't see the peso breaking 

 through central bank's defence at 55 (per dollar)," he added. 

 While central banks in Philippines and Indonesia have been 

 spotted supporting their currencies, authorities in South 

 Korea, Taiwan and Thailand have been capping any significant 

 rise. 

 WON RISE CUT SHORT 


The yen's rise helped push the Korean won



to its strongest since Monday, with equity-related foreign



inflows helping the gains. Still, the fear of intervention kept



the won's upside limited to 1,180.8 per dollar.



The Taiwan dollar  rose to a four-session high of



34.401 per U.S. dollar before worries about central bank

intervention tempered those gains.



The Thai baht  advanced to 41.87 per dollar, from



late Thursday's 41.93, aided by moves in the Sing dollar and



yen.



A strong domestic economy and sustained foreign equity



inflows have boosted the baht in recent months, but the gains



have been capped by repeated central bank intervention.



Bank of Thailand (BOT) Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said



on Thursday there was no need for the bank to intervene after



its recent easing of some foreign exchange restrictions.



James Malcolm, currency strategist at JP Morgan Chase said



the comments were unlikely to alleviate market wariness over



the central bank's tight currency management.



"It seems likely that the BOT will remain active in the



market until other central banks in the region begin to step



aside from buying dollars to keep their currencies weak."

title: Thai c.bank says won't  intervene  to stabilise baht.
text:
BANGKOK, Aug 7 (Reuters) - Thailand central bank chief Pridiyathorn Devakul said on Thursday there was no need for the bank to enter the market to stabilise the baht since its measures to balance capital inflows and outflows were working well. 

 "Our five-point measures to balance the capital flows are working well, our exchange rate is stable, so we are letting the market to decide on the currency based on demand and supply," Pridiyathorn told reporters. 

 He also said no new interest rate cuts were planned as credit growth rate in the banking system would overtake the deposit growth rate soon.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Chief:No Need To  Intervene  In  Forex  Mkt Now
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said Thursday that the central bank no longer needs to act in the foreign exchange market to stabilize the baht after its recent easing of restrictions on overseas investment helped balance capital inflows against outflows. 

 "Our recent measures work very well. They sent a clear signal to the market (about the central bank's intention to stabilize the baht)," Pridiyathorn told reporters. 

 The central bank late July issued new rules allowing institutions with huge deposits in low-yielding local accounts to seek higher returns in securities markets abroad. 

 The six categories to benefit from the new rules are: life insurance companies, the government pension fund, the social security fund, mutual funds excluding private funds, provident funds and specialized financial institutions. 

 Commercial banks aren't among the eligible institutions but they would also benefit from the tightening of domestic liquidity. 

 Pridiyathorn said capital inflows now "slightly exceed" capital outflows. 

 At 0640 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at 42.01 baht, down from THB42.08 early morning because of profit taking after the U.S. unit failed to rise above the THB42.10 level. 

 Pridiyathorn said investment will pick up when the country's industrial capacity utilization ratio - which measures the level of production capacity used - reaches 75%. Currently, the ratio is about 67%. 

 "It will take more than a year for the utilization rate to go up to that level," he said. 

 But he said he didn't expect capital inflows from new investment to put significant upward pressure on the local currency. 

 The Thai economy is going strong with exports and domestic demand acting as the two main engines of growth. 

 In the first half of the year, new loans grew 6% compared with the year-ago period, outpacing growth in deposits, which is a positive sign for the economy, Pridiyathorn said. 

 He added that Tuesday's bomb blast in Jakarta shouldn't have any major impact on Thailand's lucrative tourism industry. 

 "Thailand has no enemies and we are always well-behaved," he said.
