title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Ctrl Bk Presence Detected
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Thursday, with traders reporting the presence of at least two central banks in the markets during the session. 

 The Philippine peso's woes continued unabated and the currency closed at yet another four-month low, marking its fourth straight day of declines since Sunday's mutiny by junior army officers. 

 The dollar ended at 54.720 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP54.700 Wednesday. 

 Despite pressure on the peso, the central bank left its closely watched overnight rates unchanged at its policy-setting meeting Thursday, saying the currency's recent weakening hasn't affected the country's inflation outlook and isn't interest rate-related. 

 The Singapore dollar and the New Taiwan dollar were also weaker, while the Indonesian rupiah was flat, and the South Korean won and Thai baht were modestly stronger. 

 The currencies all kicked off the session on a weak note following the yen's overnight fall, but either narrowed or reversed losses as the yen made a mild recovery in Asia. 

 At 0945 GMT, the dollar was quoted at Y120.17, down from Y120.27 overnight in New York but up from Y119.82 late Wednesday in Tokyo. 

 Traders detected the presence of the central banks of Taiwan and Thailand in the markets. Some also suspected intervention in the South Korean won market. 

 A Singapore trader said agents of Bank of Thailand were looking to sell dollars at the 42.05-42.10 baht level. 

 He didn't think it was because the central bank is more amenable to the idea of a stronger baht. Rather, he said it was an exercise to smoothen volatility in currency movements, noting the central bank also buys dollars when the baht firms sharply. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted around 41.94 baht, down from THB41.97 late Wednesday. 

 The South Korean won reversed direction, tracking the yen's mild recovery, and aided also by dollar sales from local exporters, traders said. 

 The dollar, which opened at the intraday high of KRW1,182.0, finished at KRW1,179.7, slightly down from KRW1,180.0 Wednesday. 

 "Exporter dollar sales were heavier than expected," a dealer at the Industrial Bank of Korea said. "They must have been waiting for the dollar to pick up (to sell dollars)." 

 But investors were too cautious to test further downside for fear of attracting government intervention. Some traders in Seoul suspected the government provided limited support for the dollar indirectly during the session. 

 "It seemed that the government was in smoothing operations...absorbing some of (the) dollar sales," said a dealer at a local bank. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. unit ended at NT$34.417, up from Wednesday's NT$34.400. 

 Taipei dealers said the central bank intervened to keep the currency low in line with the yen to maintain the local dollar's competitiveness. 

 The New Taiwan dollar generally follows the yen as Taiwan and Japan compete in several export categories. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7593 late in Asia, up from S$1.7558 late Wednesday. 

 A European bank dealer in Singapore said there was a lot of activity in cross trades on the local dollar, notably against the Thai baht and the Indonesian rupiah. 

 Investors were selling the U.S. dollar/baht pair to buy the U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar pair because they see limited upside in the former, he said. 

 "This (cross trades) is probably the trades to put on in the next few sessions," he said. 

 The release of preliminary unemployment numbers for the second quarter didn't create any major market reaction, though some dealers said the data generally reflected the still-uncertain outlook for the local economy. 

 Singapore's unemployment rate was surprisingly steady in the second quarter, but a closer look at the data revealed a continued worsening of the job market, economists said. 

 The seasonally adjusted jobless rate stayed at 4.5% as of end-June, unchanged from the end of the first quarter, although more people lost their jobs as the economy shrank 4.3% because of SARS and weak global conditions. The jobless rate held steady only because of people exiting the work force and various seasonal factors. 

 The rupiah finished steady in a choppy session as dollar selling by foreign investors offset month-end dollar demand from local companies, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed unchanged at IDR8,510. 

 Earlier, dollar sales by foreign investors who had to settle their purchases of Bank Danamon shares Monday drove the U.S. unit to an intraday low of IDR8,475, dealers said. 

 The Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency sold a 20% stake in Bank Danamon to raise cash for the state budget. Almost half shares - worth around IDR1.3 trillion - were sold to foreign investors. 

 Dealers said most speculators chose to stay on the sidelines ahead of the 10-day annual convention of the nation's highest legislature, which begins Friday. 

 Some market players expect the session to be dominated by rising political tensions, although these aren't likely to threaten Megawati Sukarnoputri's presidency. 

 The market is also concerned the session could be tarnished by terrorism, recalling the bomb blast at the parliament building earlier this month.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Further rupiah losses,  intervention .
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, July 24 (Reuters) - The nose-diving Indonesian
rupiah overwhelmed Asian trading once again on Thursday morning
as traders said the central bank persisted with U.S. dollar
sales to try to stem its losses as it slumped to three-month
lows.
    The rupiah        hit 8,725 per dollar, taking its losses
in the past week to over five percent, before the central bankintervened, traders said. There was a sympathetic drop in the
Philippine peso  as fears foreign investors would flee
Asia's two highest-yielding markets en masse weighed. The
central bank there intervened verbally, predicting the peso
would soon rally.
    Other Asian currencies were inching higher, indifferent to
the U.S. dollar's fall on weak stock markets and Federal
Reserve Governor Ben Bernanke's remarks that U.S. rates could
be cut further.
   Part of Asia's muted reaction reflected market wariness
about pushing the yen  higher in case of Japanese
intervention.



    Views on the rupiah remained mixed, with some attributing
the plunge to a one-off outflow of foreign money and others
saying risks on the political and reform front and falling
interest rates were now overshadowing the bullishness on the
currency.
    Traders said the trigger for the rupiah's sharp slide was
the news earlier this week that BP Plc (BP.L) and global mining
giant Rio Tinto (RIO.L) (RIO.AX) were selling their Indonesian
coal mine joint venture to a local firm for $500 million.
    "There's nothing in terms of fundamentals that has
changed," said Ray Farris, strategist with Credit Suisse First
Boston.
    "All that has happened is that the single most crowded
trade in the region has now been flattened out. Everyone was
short the dollar/rupiah and they are all trying to get out
through a very small door at the same time."
 
    Farris said the rupiah would probably recover to about
8,400 or higher by the end of the year.
    While currently there were no takers for the rupiah other



than the central bank, the balance of payments was strong with



around two billion dollars worth of trade surplus every month



and potential capital inflows from government asset sales, he



said.



FOCUS ON POLICY CHANGES



Elsewhere, Thailand's move on Wednesday to open its capital



markets was a talking point among traders.



Shrewd central banks were coping with growing pressure to



let their currencies appreciate and cut down intervention by



encouraging foreign currency outflows through easing



regulations, analysts said.



China and Taiwan are expected to relax rules on their



capital accounts soon, India introduced rupee options, and the



Philippines is contemplating reversing some rigid rules on



hedging.



Thailand increased the amount that domestic investors could



hold in foreign bonds and extended the period exporters could



hold non-baht revenues in their foreign currency accounts.



"This is another example of how pressure on currencies to



strengthen has resulted in welcome relaxations of trade and



investment constraints," Deutsche Bank said in a note.



 
    The baht fell to a three-week low past 42 per dollar on the
news, but was slightly stronger on Thursday morning.
    "The Bank of Thailand knows that with an outperforming Thai
economy, it cannot intervene indefinitely to prevent underlying
U.S. dollar weakness against baht," DBS Bank said in a note.
    Rising stocks supported the Korean won



and the Singapore dollar  too firmed to a two-week high



closer to 1.75 as overseas players continued unwinding their



short Sing dollar positions.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Down vs dlr, outperform yen, euro.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, July 16 (Reuters) - Asian currencies weakened
against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday as investors scrambled out
of short dollar positions after U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman
Alan Greenspan sounded upbeat on the U.S. economic outlook.
    But regional currencies outperformed the yen        and
euro  against a strengthening dollar on expectations that
a U.S. upturn would benefit Asia's exporters.
    The Singapore dollar gapped down to a two-week trough of
1.7630 per U.S. dollar and the South Korean won
  fell from five-month high to a one-week low of 1,183
per dollar.
    The Thai baht        fell to 41.67 per dollar, its lowest
this week, after Tuesday's test of 41.50, where intervention
has been suspected recently.
    The dollar rose after Greenspan said the economy "could
very well be embarking on a period of extended growth." His
comments were good news for export-driven Asian economies, for
whom U.S. is the single largest market.



    "Today's currency moves back the view that Asia will
outperform yen and euro whenever recovery in the U.S. picks
up," said a dealer at a local bank.
    The Singapore rose to test one-week highs of 67.45 yen
  at 1.4824 Sing, about one yen off Tuesday's 11-month
low, and it hit a two-month high of 1.9575 per euro .
    The Korean won touched a five-month high of 9.9174 against
the yen  and a three-month high of 1,308.82 against
the euro .
    However, Bhanu Baweja currency strategist at UBS said the
move in the crosses was more based on capital flows rather than
economic fundamentals.
    "Its basically because U.S. bonds have been hit so much
that all the short positions taken against the dollar taken on
the basis of yield differential with yen and euro have been
closed out," he said.
    "The Asian currencies on the other hand never saw that kind
of flow in their fixed income assets, the broad theme still
remains the equity flows and they remain quite positive."
    Baweja said the fundamental view on Asian currencies would
turn bullish only when evidence of a big rise in U.S. capital
spending emerges, which would ensure higher Asian exports.
    BAHT WATCHES BOT
    The Thai baht, which has been a big recipient of foreign
inflows this year, weakened as some foreign funds were spotted
covering their short dollar positions, dealers in Singapore
said.
    They said the market was also wary of talk that a foreign
bank was buying dollars on behalf of Thai authorities late on
Tuesday, when the baht was testing 41.50 per dollar.
    Dealers said the Bank of Thailand had intervened in recent
weeks around 41.50 to cap baht's strength that has been driven
by the foreign investments in local stocks.
    James Malcolm, currency strategist at JP Morgan Chase in
Singapore, said in a note that the central bank had capped the
baht by buying dollars at around the 41.52-41.55 range.
    "We expect the BOT to continue to offset much of the equity
flows," he said, but added that improved global and local
growth prospects would eventually push the baht higher.
    The Philippine peso        fell to a two-week low of 53.65
per dollar, with corporates buying dollars to cover their
requirements ahead of the import season that usually starts in
early August and peaks in late September.
    The Indonesian rupiah        also hit a two-week low of
8,248, with mainly Singapore-based funds spotted buying
dollars.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Won at 5-month high, rest eye Greenspan.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, July 15 (Reuters) - The South Korean won touched
a five-month peak on Tuesday, while other Asian currencies held
on to their recent narrow ranges amid caution ahead of Federal
Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony later in the day.
    The won                   rose to 1,174.6 per dollar, its
strongest since February 5, before edging back to around 1,176
level on wariness over authorities' sensitivity to a stronger
won eroding export competitiveness.
    The won has appreciated in recent weeks on a steady flow of
foreign investment into local stocks, which clashes with an
official bias for stimulative monetary conditions in an economy
that is in recession.
    The Bank of Korea (BOK) lowered its key call rate by 25
basis point to a record low 3.75 percent last Thursday, and
authorities have been spotted intervening to limit the won's
gains.



    Early Tuesday, a parliamentary committee approved a four
trillion won increase in the limit on foreign exchange
stabilisation fund bonds -- used to stem the won's strength.
    Analysts said while the Bank of Korea will continue to curb
any excessive currency strength, it might allow the won to
strengthen against the U.S. dollar as long as it does not
outperform the yen , a major trading partner and
competitor.
    "The market is cautious and no one can guess when
authorities may choose to act, but as long as won is stable
against the yen the chances of intervention are less," said
Irene Cheung, ABN Amro's FX strategist in Singapore.
    The yen/won cross            was perched on the stronger
side of the 10 won level, shy of Monday's high of 9.97 won
where dealers in Singapore said state banks came in to pull the
won down on behalf of the central bank.
    SGD AWAITS GREENSPAN
    The Singapore dollar        held on to a narrow
1.7550-1.7562 per U.S. dollar range, little moved by a
surprisingly strong 10.9 percent seasonally adjusted monthly
rise in May retail sales.
    Thio Chin Loo, senior currency analyst at BNP Paribas said
the market was holding back ahead of Greenspan's speech, which
should provide fresh clues about the economic outlook.
 
    "Uninspiring. That's the mood of the markets right now with
everything in suspense ahead of Greenspan's speech," she said.
    She expected Greenspan to "play a balancing act" between



growth and inflation. And while he might emphasise the



prospects of an economic recovery, he also might want to calm



down the bond markets where longer dated yields have risen



sharply, she added.



The Thai baht  fell to 41.60 per dollar, before



recovering towards 41.50 as local markets resumed trade after a



long weekend. Dealers said with no major domestic data in the



week, the baht was likely to track the Singapore dollar and



other regional currencies.



As well as cutting interest rates by 50 basis points in



late June, dealers have said the Bank of Thailand has


intervened around 41.50 in recent weeks to cap the baht, which



tested an 11-month high of 41.40 per dollar on three occasions



in June.



The Philippine peso  eased to around 53.635 per



dollar, its weakest level in local trade since June 27, as



corporates sought dollars to cover their requirements ahead of



the import season that usually starts in early August.



The Indonesian rupiah  kept to the weak side of the



8,200 per dollar, but was clear of the two-week low of 8,235



set on Monday after a bomb exploded in the national



parliament.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late;Some Central Banks  Intervene
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were a mixed bag late Tuesday at the tail end of a generally lackluster session in which some central banks intervened to cap strength in their units, traders said. 

 The Singapore dollar and Philippine peso were weaker, the Indonesian rupiah and South Korean won were little changed and the New Taiwan dollar was stronger. 

 The Thai baht was firmer compared with pre-weekend levels but was lower from offshore levels Monday, when local markets were shut for a holiday. 

 Monetary authorities in Thailand, Taiwan and South Korea were those suspected of buying dollars in Tuesday's session. 

 Traders said these central banks were in the market to smooth the movements of their currencies rather than attempt to reverse the strengthening trend. 

 Strong portfolio inflows into regional stock markets are a key factor supporting Asian currencies. 

 But policy-makers in Asia are reluctant to allow their currencies to strengthen too much for fear of losing export competitiveness amid a still uncertain outlook for the global economy, especially the U.S. 

 They are also unlikely to allow their currencies to rise significantly as long as China resists pressure to revalue the yuan, analysts said. 

 Overall, Tuesday's session mirrored that of the previous day as many investors kept to the sidelines to hear what Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan has to say about the U.S. economy later in the global session. 

 Greenspan will address the House Financial Services Committee Tuesday and the Senate Banking Committee Wednesday. 

 The yen didn't provide much of a lead for its counterparts in the region as market players shrugged off early sharp gains in Tokyo share prices and the Bank of Japan's decision to keep monetary policy unchanged. 

 "There's nothing happening on the forex front," in the run-up to Greenspan's address, a European bank trader in Singapore said. 

 "There's some portfolio inflows" into regional stock markets, which are weighing on the dollar, and "the central banks are buying it (the dollar) up," he said. 

 The dollar ended at 1,176.0 against the South Korean won, a touch below Monday's KRW1,176.3, but off the intraday trough of KRW1,174.6. This was the won's sixth straight session of gains. 

 There was suspicion the government intervened to prop up the dollar when it fell to the intraday low on continued foreign buying of local shares, but traders had mixed views about this. 

 "Suspicious - but I don't think so. It was not that aggressive," a Seoul-based trader said, although a Singapore-based trader was sure the Bank of Korea was in the market. 

 Another Seoul-based trader said the dollar was also supported by news that a National Assembly committee approved a KRW4-trillion-won increase in this year's foreign exchange stabilization bond issue limit. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. unit ended at NT$34.364, slightly down from NT$34.376 Monday. 

 Dealers said demand from exporters and inflows of funds from foreign investors buying local stocks buoyed the local dollar. 

 But dollar purchases by the central bank and demand for the U.S. currency from importers tempered the local unit's rise, they said. 

 Falling volumes suggested the central bank wasn't very aggressive, a Taipei-based dealer said. Trading volume dropped for the third straight session Tuesday. 

 The Singapore dollar weakened after a listless session as investors were reluctant to take strong positions ahead of Greenspan's address. 

 The U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7553 late in the local session, up from S$1.7540 late Monday. 

 Earlier Tuesday, the Monetary Authority of Singapore said its current neutral monetary policy stance will be appropriate to keep inflation in check and support the economy for the rest of the year. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was steady as dollar demand from local importers offset selling by foreign investors buying into local stocks and bonds, dealers said. 

 The dollar ended at 8,223 rupiah, virtually unchanged from IDR8,225 Tuesday. 

 Continued capital inflows showed that foreign investors are undeterred by a small bomb blast at the Indonesian Parliament building Monday. There were no casualties in the incident. 

 "The market seemed to have fully forgotten Monday's blast," a Jakarta-based dealer with a foreign bank said. 

 The Philippine peso was weighed down by seasonal demand for the dollar from importers, and also security concerns following the escape Monday of three suspected terrorists from a Manila prison, traders said. 

 The dollar closed at 53.585 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP53.545 Monday, but off the intraday high of PHP53.635. 

 The peso trimmed some losses on news of the Supreme Court ruling in favor of the government on the disputed Swiss deposits of late president Ferdinand Marcos, traders said. 

 The Supreme Court Tuesday forfeited in favor of the government the frozen Swiss deposits, which had increased to $658.2 million early last year. 

Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said the court's ruling "would be good not only for the peso, but for the government budget as well." 

 Against the Thai baht, the dollar was quoted around THB41.54 late in Asia, up from THB41.50 in offshore trading Monday, but down from THB41.64 at Friday's local close. 

 Traders in Singapore said Bank of Thailand intervened during the session to cap the baht's strength, which came amid a rise in Thai share prices. 

 "Bank of Thailand (was) squeezing some shorts (on the dollar), but essentially, the range and volume was small and thin," a European bank trader said. 

 A trader at another bank said the monetary authority bought dollars at the THB41.52 to THB41.53 levels.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Contained, Sing waits on policy meet.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, July 9 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were a mixed
bag on Wednesday as traders speculated on policy changes in
some markets, and the threat of intervention offset the
appreciation pressure from inflows into the region's surging
stock markets.
    The Singapore dollar        bounced in a 1.7517-65 per
dollar range ahead of Thursday's monetary policy review and
second quarter growth data.
    "There seems to be a split on whether the policy
announcement will indicate a shift to an easing bias or not, so
most players avoided taking any significant positions ahead of
the event," a dealer at a local bank said.
    The Monetary Authority of Singapore does not set short-term
interest rates, instead it targets the currency in an
undisclosed trade-weighted band to manage monetary conditions.
    A poll by Reuters last week found most analysts expecting
no change in the neutral policy stance of the MAS, while a
minority saw an implicit shift to an easier bias.



    But dealers said Monday's data showing an $830 million rise
in reserves in June, had reignited speculation the central bank
had been buying dollars to keep the currency weak and may
formally announce a widening of the band on Thursday.
    Bank of America calculated the rise at $1.13 billion, after
adjusting for the euro's weakness. Still, it said risk of an
explicit or implicit shift to loosening was 25 percent at most.
    Thio Chin Loo, senior currency strategist at BNP Paribas,
said Singapore authorities might have bought dollars to counter
portfolio inflows, and maintained her view of no policy change.
    "With the second quarter likely to have been the worst
quarter of the year, it is unlikely the MAS will act behind the
curve," she said.
    Capital inflows, mainly in stocks, have increased across
Asia, putting appreciation pressure on currencies -- something
local central banks want to head off to keep exports
competitive and monetary conditions easy.
    Central banks in Thailand, the Philippines, Hong Kong and
Taiwan have eased policy since the U.S. Federal Reserve cut
rates by 25 basis points on June 25.
    KOREAN POLICY MEET
    South Korea's central bank also meets on Thursday, and
authorities there have been trying to counter won
  strength from a surge of equity-related inflows.
    The won rose to 1,178.4 per dollar, against late Tuesday's
1,180.2, but fear of intervention was seen resisting its return
to five-month highs of 1,176.2 hit on Monday.
    The Taiwan dollar          was also up, helped by a stock
market  around 12-month highs, but wary of Monday's
10-month intraday highs of 34.305 per U.S. dollar on aggressive
intervention by the central bank.
    In Thailand, some offshore funds sold the baht        down
to 41.71 per dollar. Dealers said the moves in major currencies
and fear of intervention by authorities had prompted players to
cut back on short U.S. dollar positions.
 
    The Indonesian rupiah        eased past 8,200 per dollar,
after hitting a one-month high of 8,153 on Monday.
    The Philippine peso        fell to 53.51 per dollar, its



lowest since June 30, but ended slightly higher on news that



proceeds of the government's $750 million bond issue would be



lent to state-run National Power Corp, ending its commercial



requirements for the year.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Step back, wary of central banks.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, July 8 (Reuters) - Asian currencies faltered
despite rallying stock markets on Tuesday, with most giving up
ground to a U.S. dollar that, buoyed by gains on Wall Street,
strengthened to two-month highs against the euro .
    Dealers said the dollar's rise and worries about
intervention by Asian central banks had raised doubts about
sustainability of gains in regional currencies, including the
yen , which briefly rose to two week highs around 117.60.
    Asian stock markets, impressed by Wall Street's rally,
posted more gains which would attract more foreign investment
that should boost Asian currencies -- something local central
banks want to head off so their exports stay competitive.



    "We remain sceptical whether central banks in the region
will be in a hurry to allow their currencies to appreciate in
any significant manner, given their caution on prospects for
global and regional economic recovery," said Sameer Goel,
analyst at Bank of America in Singapore.
    Central banks in Thailand, the Philippines, Hong Kong and
Taiwan have eased policy since the U.S. Federal Reserve cut
rates by 25 basis points on June 25. Monetary policy reviews
are due in South Korea and Singapore on Thursday.
    The Singapore dollar        eased towards 1.7580 per U.S.
dollar to be down about one-third of a percent on Tuesday as
the market remained anxious ahead of Thursday's policy review
by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.
    Dealers said thin volumes ahead of the review could make
price action in the Singapore dollar volatile. The MAS manages
the dollar, its main policy tool, against a trade-weighted
basket of currencies of major trade partners and competitors.
    A poll by Reuters last week found most analysts expecting
no change in the neutral policy stance of the MAS, while a
minority saw an implicit shift to an easier bias.
    The South Korean won                   posted gains as the
Korean stock market  ended at a seven-month high, but it
avoided Monday's five-month highs which had prompted
intervention that dealers estimated at about $1 billion.
    Dealers said state banks were active again late on Tuesday.
    The Taiwan dollar          was also up, helped by a stock
market  at 12-month highs, but wary of Monday's 10-month
highs after dealers spotted aggressive intervention by the
central bank just before Monday's close. Traders said the
central bank was active on Tuesday as well.
    BOT SAYS OUT OF MARKET
    Comments from the Bank of Thailand that it did not need to
intervene in the baht after last month's 50 basis point rate
cut had little impact on the market, as dealers in Bangkok
still expected rallies to be capped by authorities.
    "After the rate cut, we've seen slower capital inflows and
the baht has been stable, so there's no need for the central
bank to look after it for now," Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula
said.
    But dealers said the moves in major currencies and fear of
intervention by authorities to cap baht strength had prompted
players to cut back on short U.S. dollar positions.
 
    "They (the BOT) bought quite a large amount of dollars only

title: Thai c.bank says baht stable, not  intervening .
text:
BANGKOK, July 8 (Reuters) - Thailand's central bank said on Tuesday the baht currency had stabilised against the U.S. dollar after it cut its benchmark interest rate two weeks ago and it did not need to intervene to stabilise the currency. 

 "After the rate cut, we've seen slower capital inflows and the baht has been stable, so there's no need for the central bank to look after it for now," central bank governor Pridiyathorn Devakula told reporters. 

 AT 0624 GMT, the baht was trading at 41.62/41.65 against the dollar compared with 41.59 on Monday.

title: UPDATE 1-Thai PM Thaksin sees baht strengthening.
text:
BANGKOK, July 3 (Reuters) - Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said on Thursday he expected the baht would tend to strengthen in the future, due to continuing capital inflows that have helped push Thai shares to three-year highs. 

 "Investors see very bright prospects and investment potential. The baht has been very stable and tends to strengthen rather than weaken," Thaksin told reporters when asked why the Thai stock market was rising so rapidly. 

 The benchmark Stock Exchange of Thailand composite index has gained over 34 percent so far this year to hit 492.95 - its highest level since January 2000. At 0600 GMT, the SET index was up two percent at 487.41. 

 The baht has gained almost three percent since the end of last year and gained further following Thaksin's comments to trade around 41.765 to the dollar, its strongest level this week. 

 "The baht has strengthened following the PM's comment, but I don't think we should read too much into it because he was only commenting on the stock market performance," Simon Flint, Bank of America currency strategist, told Reuters. 

 Thailand's central bank last week cut its key interest rate by 50 basis points to 1.25 percent in a move that analysts said was designed to cap baht gains and keep exports competitive following a cut in U.S. interest rates. 

 Dealers in Bangkok said most players in the market were still wary of the central bank's sensitivity to currency strength. 

 "Thaksin's statements are mostly taken by the market as political. It's the central bank that sets the tone in the market," said a dealer at a local bank in Bangkok. 

 The Bank of Thailand repeatedly intervened last month as the baht touched 11-month highs of 41.40 per dollar. (With additional reporting by Ovais Subhani in Singapore).

title: Thai Baht Ends Up Slightly On 6th Anniversary Of Float
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended slightly stronger against the dollar in Asian trade Wednesday, the sixth anniversary of the float of the baht in the midst of the financial crisis of 1997, traders said. 

 The baht's rise was due to general weakness in the U.S. unit versus regional currencies, but the central bank was believed to have stepped in to cap the local currency's gains, they said. 

 The dollar finished at 41.925 baht, down from THB41.95 late in offshore trade Tuesday and a close of THB42.085 Monday. Thai markets were closed Tuesday for a public holiday. 

 Traders said exporters capped the dollar's intraday high at THB42.00, while the central bank held the bottom around THB41.90. 

 "It looks like the big guy doesn't want to let it slide," a trader at a foreign bank said, in a reference to suspected intervention by agents of the Bank of Thailand. 

Central bank Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said Wednesday that last week's 50-basis-point cut in the official 14-day repurchase market target rate to 1.25% had succeeded in slowing speculative short-term capital inflows, but that it would take another month or two to see the full effects. 

 The central bank has said it wants to restrain any excessive appreciation in the baht, so that volatility is muted and the country's exports remain competitive. 

 If the central bank was in the market Wednesday, it was in a much better position than it was six years ago, when it was forced to concede that it had wasted its foreign reserves in a failed defense of a fixed exchange rate mechanism which had previously kept the dollar around THB25. 

 Thailand's foreign reserves stood at a high $39.4 billion as of June 20, and any dollar buying Wednesday would have only boosted the figure. 

 Meanwhile, the dollar-baht exchange rate has been relatively stable for the past three years in a range of THB40 to THB46. 

 Most economists have projected that the dollar will continue to weaken gradually against the baht in the second half of 2003, due to a general decline expected in the dollar versus regional currencies and to inflows attracted by the relative strength of the Thai economy. 

 The central bank was expected to continue intervening to restrain the baht's appreciation and secondarily to further strengthen foreign reserves. 

 The dollar was expected to open Thursday in Asia in a range of THB41.85 to THB42.00. 

 Prices of most Thai government bond extended their rally Wednesday as yields continued to fall in adjustment to last Friday's 14-day policy rate cut, traders said. 

 Siam Commercial Bank's announcement earlier Wednesday of a 25 to 50 basis point cut in its deposit and lending rates, effective Thursday, also boosted sentiment, they added. 

 Siam Commercial's savings rate will fall to a new historic low of 0.75%, an easing that other commercial banks are expected to soon follow to avoid unwanted deposits. 

 The yield on the short-term government bond due December 2006 finished in a bid-offer range of 1.39%-1.37%, down from Monday's close of 1.41%. 

 The long-term bond due November 2012 finished at 2.22%-2.20% versus 2.25% previous close. 

 Dealers expected short- and medium-term yields to remain under pressure for the rest of the week because of high liquidity in the financial system 

 Bank of Thailand auctioned Wednesday THB1.5 billion of November 2022 bonds at an average yield of 3.5745%, slightly higher than what the market expected. However, the result had no impact on the secondary market as the issue was illiquid. 

 The overnight interbank rate settled at a new range of 1.125%-1.25% in line with the lower 14-day target rate. The 1-day repo rate had already fallen since Friday afternoon to an appropriate range capped by the 14-day rate.

as stocks recovered and foreign investors turned buyers again.



 
    The Philippine peso        and Taiwan dollar          too

countries such as Thailand and South Korea.



And, despite the threat of intervention by central banks to



keep their currencies competitive for exports, the currencies


would still gain.



Broecker said the inflows into South Korea have



overshadowed concerns of slowing growth and North Korea's

    "This is one tool to maintain some economic stability and

Yet, authorities would try to ensure the currency was



stable and competitive against currencies of countries

title: Thai Baht Ends Up A Tad; Caution Ahead OF FOMC Meeting
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended marginally higher against the U.S. dollar Tuesday, boosted by the strength of the Singapore dollar amid position-adjustment ahead of an expected cut in U.S. interest rates this week, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 41.53 baht, down slightly from THB41.57 at the Asian close Monday. 

 The U.S. unit has been trapped between THB41.45 and THB41.90 this month, with central bank buying of dollars on weakness countering equities-related inflows and strong exports. 

 The dollar-baht exchange rate pressed down near the THB41.50 level in late trade Tuesday, after the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar pushed lower, but investors remained wary of Thai central bank intervention. 

 The Bank of Thailand was suspected of heavy dollar buying below THB41.50 on several occasions recently. Central bank foreign exchange reserves rose $500 million in the week to June 13. 

 Investors were also wary of short-term volatility after the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee announced its rate decision Wednesday. 

 The dollar is expected to remain in THB41.50 to THB41.65 range Wednesday. 

 Prices of Thai government bonds ended flat or slightly higher Tuesday, with the market mostly quiet ahead of the expected cut in U.S. interest rates, dealers said. 

 Short- and medium-term securities fared slightly better than long-term paper due to buying to ease the burden of excess financial system liquidity and as a safe haven ahead of possible volatility after the expected cuts. 

 An auction of THB5 billion 364-day central bank bonds Tuesday resulted in an average yield of around 1.54%, about one basis point below Monday's secondary market yield curve as expected. 

 The yield on the government bond due December 2006 ended in a bid-offer range of 1.71%-1.69%, down from a close of 1.72% Monday, dealers said. 

 The long-term issue due November 2012 finished at 2.53%-2.51%, flat from a previous close of 2.525%. 

 Dealers said a 50-basis-point cut late Wednesday in the U.S. federal funds rate should lead to buying in Thai long-term bonds, as it would leave the market virtually certain of a cut of at least 25 basis points in the Thai 14-day repurchase market target rate, currently 1.75%. Bank of Thailand's monetary policy committee meets next on July 21. 

 Investors still expected a 25-basis-point cut in U.S. rates to lead to a matching cut in the Thai 14-day rate, but a smaller U.S. cut might leave them waiting for a look at July government and central bank auction schedules before deciding how aggressive they should be. The schedules should be issued late this week or early next week. 

 Overnight interbank rates fell to the lower end of their recent trading ranges, due to quiet trade ahead of the U.S. meeting on interest rates, but remained supported there by central bank borrowing to absorb excess liquidity in the system and defend the 14-day rate, dealers said.

title: Thai Baht Ends Slightly Higher In Thin, Pre-FOMC Trade
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht closed marginally higher against the dollar Monday after marking time for most of the day, thanks to late gains in the yen. 

 Trading was very thin as most investors sat on the sidelines ahead of the U.S. Federal Open Market Commitee's two-day meeting, starting Tuesday, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 41.57 baht, down a tad from THB41.60 at the Asian close Friday. 

 After languishing in a narrow THB41.59 to THB41.61 band for most of the local session, the dollar dropped marginally in late trade to its day's low of THB41.56 as it declined slightly against the yen. 

 "The market is very ... very thin. It seems like nobody wants to trade. I think they are waiting for the Fed's verdict," said a local bank trader. 

 Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said there's no need to intervene in the foreign exchange market now as the baht's level is satisfactory. 

 He said equity-related inflows had strengthened the baht significantly, although such inflows have subsided. 

 Foreign investors were buying large amounts of Thai shares last week, but by the end of the week, the upward momentum had dissipated more or less. Foreigners were net buyers of THB176.1 million worth of Thai shares Friday, down from THB1.53 billion Thursday. 

 The dollar is expected to move in a range of THB41.50 to THB41.65 Tuesday. Trade will likely remain thin until the FOMC meeting concludes. 

 Prices of long-term Thai government bonds ended lower Monday in thin trade on profit-taking in most issues, dealers said. 

 "Trading was quite thin, which magnified the yields' rise. Many investors were on the sidelines, looking forward to the Fed's decision on the rate cut and the July schedule for government and central bank bond auctions," said a dealer at a local bank. 

 Yields of most long-term government bonds were up around four-to-six basis points from Friday's closing levels. 

 The U.S. Federal Open Market Committee is expected to cut U.S. interest rates by 25 or 50 basis points this week. A 50-basis-point cut could lead to a faster recovery in ground given up by Thai bonds in recent profit-taking. 

 "Many investors unwound positions, waiting for good timing to build up their portfolio after the Fed's announcement," said another dealer at a foreign bank. 

 The government bond maturing June 2009 ended at 2.01% compared with 1.965% at Friday's close, the Thai Bond Dealing Center said in its daily report. The April 2010 issue finished at 2.11%, up from the previous close of 2.08%, and the November 2012 issue closed at 2.525%, up from 2.4815%. 

 Yields of short- and medium-term goverment bonds were up only about zero-to-two basis points, however, due to demand driven by high financial system liquidity. 

 The central bank sold at an auction Monday THB1 billion worth of 91-day treasury bills at an average yield of 1.3836%, down from 1.40% last week. 

 The auction result came in below the secondary market yield curve, as expected, due to heavy demand for big lots of short-term securities to help big banks cover the costs of excess deposits. 

 Overnight interbank rates remained in a tight range with support from central bank borrowing through the repurchase market to absorb excess liquidity in the system, dealers said.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late, Mkt Waits For FOMC Decision
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies traded within tight ranges late Monday amid a general reluctance to take strong positions either way ahead of the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision on interest rates later this week. 

 The Singapore dollar, Philippine peso and Indonesian rupiah were modestly weaker. The South Korean won and New Taiwan dollar were marginally stronger, and the Thai baht was little changed. 

 While the Federal Open Market Committee is widely expected to cut rates Wednesday, the market is divided as to whether it would be a 25-basis-point or 50-basis-point reduction. 

 An aggressive cut would "conjure optimism about an early recovery in Asia, and perhaps inspire those who would seek to be long SGD (Singapore dollar), and inspire confidence in THB (Thai baht), which is enjoying a generous welter of portfolio inflows," Bank of America said in a note. 

 It might also excite yield seekers anew over the high-yielding Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso, the bank added. 

 Meantime, U.S. dollar buying, mainly by local banks, kept the currency buoyed against the Singapore unit. 

 A dealer at a European bank said a drop in the city state's consumer price index for May stoked fears of deflation and kept the U.S. currency on a bid-ish tone against the local dollar. 

 Singapore's consumer prices fell 0.1% on year in May, and was down 0.6% on month, the Department of Statistics said earlier Monday. 

 Near the close of local trading hours, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7395, up from S$1.7360 Friday. 

 The European bank dealer said an increasing number of market players have been focusing on the Singapore dollar/Thai baht cross in recent weeks, fueled by expectations of a better outlook for the Thai economy compared to Singapore. 

 To that end, they have been selling the U.S. dollar against the baht and buying the U.S. dollar versus the Singapore unit. 

 As a result, the Singapore dollar/Thai baht cross has drifted to around 23.90 Monday from 24.20 about three weeks ago. This cross rate hardly moves, so such a shift may be considered significant, the dealer said. 

 The dollar was quoted around THB41.59 late in Asia, almost flat from THB41.60 Friday. 

 Earlier in the session, Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said there's no need to intervene in the foreign exchange market now as the baht's level is satisfactory. 

 "We don't need to be involved (in the market) that much now. Let the baht move naturally," Pridiyathorn told reporters. He said equity-related inflows have strengthened the baht significantly. 

 J.P. Morgan Chase Bank said Thailand's latest foreign reserves data suggested the central bank had been actively buying dollars. 

 Bank of Thailand said Friday that its foreign reserves stood at $39.9 billion at June 13, up from $39.4 billion a week earlier. 

 J.P. Morgan Chase said that given the strong momentum in foreign buying of Thai shares, it remained positive on the baht and targets the dollar to fall gradually to THB41 by the end of the third quarter of 2003. 

 Elsewhere, the South Korean won was supported by export settlements amid ample dollar supply, although concerns about central bankintervention kept the dollar from falling too much, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 1,190.2 won, a tad below Friday's KRW1,190.6. 

 Korean authorities weren't seen intervening in the market to support the U.S. unit following some aggressive moves last week, dealers said. 

 "The government did not have to intervene in the market as concerns about such action alone prevented the dollar from retreating too far," said a dealer at a local bank in Seoul. 

 Most players expect the authorities to step in if the U.S. dollar moves below KRW1,190, particularly if such a decline is perceived as being too rapid. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was on a slightly weaker footing on dollar demand from local importers ahead of the month-end, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed the local session at 8,250 rupiah, slightly up from IDR8,240 Friday. 

 The dollar's rise was capped by expectations of further capital inflows in the wake of Bank Mandiri's initial public offering of shares, which has attracted robust foreign demand. 

 The government has said it will raise the IPO size to four billion shares from three billion. The government is expected to raise around $300 million from the offering, the largest by a local company since the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis. 

 "Good news on Bank Mandiri helped curbed the dollar's rise," said a dealer with a European bank in Jakarta. 

 The Philippine peso snapped a three-day winning streak to close lower on corporate demand for the U.S. currency, traders said. 

 The dollar closed at the intraday high of 53.400 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP53.300 Friday. 

 Several banks also bought back some of the dollars they sold in previous sessions amid an ongoing debate on how much the Federal Reserve will likely cut U.S. rates. 

 Remarks by Finance Secretary Jose Isidro Camacho that the government doesn't have an immediate plan to tap the international debt market didn't have an impact on the peso. 

 The Philippine Central Bank is believed to have stayed on the sidelines throughout the session. A senior central bank official denied the monetary authority is buying dollars now, so it can sell them later to enhance the peso, in time for next month's State of Nation Address of President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo. 

 The New Taiwan dollar was supported by foreign buying of local shares. 

 The U.S. ended at NT$34.591, down a tad from Friday's NT$34.593. 

 Foreign investors bought a net NT$1.68 billion worth of shares on the Taiwan bourse Monday, according to the Taiwan Stock Exchange.

title: Thai Baht Ends Flat; Off Low On Late Onshore Dlr Selling
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended flat Wednesday after the dollar gave up early gains due to onshore selling once the U.S. currency came off highs against other Asian currencies, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 41.79 baht, unchanged from the Asian close Tuesday. 

 The U.S. currency surged to an intraday high of THB41.89 in early morning trade due mainly to demand from European banks in Bangkok, traders said. Dollar buying was also strong due to caution that the Bank of Thailand might intervene to support the U.S. unit. 

 Dealers suspected agents of the central bank were buying dollars Tuesday around THB41.70 when the U.S. unit quickly jumped above THB41.80. 

 But the dollar's gains Wednesday gradually ebbed away as local banks sold the U.S. unit in the afternoon as it slipped against Asian currencies, especially the yen, the regional trendsetter. The dollar touched an intraday low of THB41.77 in the afternoon. 

Central bank Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula told reporters Wednesday he couldn't confirm whether the central bank had been active in the foreign exchange market Tuesday. 

 Late last month, Pridiyathorn confirmed the central bank had bought dollars to slow the baht's appreciation so it would stay competitive with the currencies of Thailand's trading partners. 

 Late in Asia, the U.S. unit was quoted at Y117.72, compared with its early high of Y118.13. 

 Traders expected the U.S. unit to move within a THB41.75-THB41.90 range Thursday morning, subject to volatility in the yen. 

 Thai government bond prices ended sharply higher Wednesday, pushing yields on most issues to fresh historic lows, thanks to an overnight rally in U.S. Treasurys. Siam Commercial Bank's decision to cut its key interest rates across the board Wednesday also gave bonds a boost, traders said. 

 Bond yields dropped from the open as investors took cues from U.S. Treasurys and then fell further on news of Siam Commercial Bank's rate cut. 

 Siam, the country's fourth-largest commercial bank, will cut its deposit rates by between 25 and 50 basis points and key lending rates by 25 basis points, effective Thursday. 

 The cut is the first by a large Thai bank in what appears to be a new round of interest rate cuts driven by flush liquidity in the system, and signs of lower global interest rates. 

 The most active government bond due December 2006 closed Wednesday at 1.65%, down from 1.67% the previous day, dealers said. 

 The November 2011 bond finished at 2.24%, down from a close Wednesday of 2.34%, while the November 2012 bond dropped to 2.42% versus 2.52% at the last close. 

 Dealers said yields will likely hover around current levels for some time, while the market waits to see if the U.S. and Thai authorities will cut rates. 

 "Profit-taking can't push yields up as demand from long-term investors is still strong. The low supply and low interest rate trend still provide a firm buffer for any upside (for yields)," said a foreign bank dealer. 

 Bank of Thailand sold THB1 billion of a reopened November 2022 bond Wednesday at 3.6279%, down from 3.65% at the closing level Wednesday. 

 Overnight interbank rates were flat, despite flush liquidity in the financial system, due to the central bank's firm support for its 14-day target rate.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Dn Late;Mkt Wary Of  Intervention
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies gave up early gains to move to a weaker footing late Tuesday as market players covered short-dollar positions after selling it down earlier in the session. 

 The Singapore dollar, Thai baht, Indonesian rupiah and New Taiwan dollar drifted lower. However, the Philippine peso and South Korean won eked out modest gains. 

 The dollar's recovery against regional units during the session surprised analysts and traders, who had expected the currency to come under pressure in the wake of the management shake-up at Freddie Mac and weaker U.S. share prices. 

 Concerns about central bank intervention appeared to be a major factor that helped crimp regional currencies' gains. The central banks are keen to rein in the strength of their currencies to keep exports competitive. 

 "The dollar opened lower (versus regional units) and then people took the opportunity to cover short positions. It's a whippy, two-way market," a Singapore-based European bank trader said. 

 Singapore's latest foreign exchange reserves data seemed to give credence to speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had been supporting the U.S. dollar, analysts said. 

 The data, issued over the weekend, showed reserves rose $2.44 billion in May - the largest monthly gain in a couple of years, according to J.P. Morgan Chase Bank. 

 "While some of this reflects EUR (euro) valuation effects and interest accrual, the underlying message is of strong USD (U.S. dollar) buying by the MAS," the bank said in a research note Tuesday. 

 "It's definitely making people nervous. That's part of the reason why the dollar/Sing (Singapore unit) is well-bid today," noted Sameer Goel, a currency strategist at Bank of America. 

 Late in the local session, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7318, up from S$1.7285 late Monday. 

 Against the Thai baht, the dollar was quoted around THB41.80 late in Asia, up from THB41.69 Monday, taking a cue from its rise versus the Singapore currency. 

 Market players were also wary of provoking Thailand's central bank, especially with memories of last week's intervention still fresh in their minds. Bank of Thailand bought dollars Friday when the baht spiked to a fresh 10-month high, traders said. 

Intervention fears also caused the Indonesian rupiah to reverse early gains. The dollar recovered from an intraday trough of 8,155 rupiah to end the local session at IDR8,210, up from IDR8,195 Monday. 

 Dealers said market talk of dollar buying by central banks elsewhere in the region helped push the U.S. unit up versus the rupiah. 

 In Taiwan, U.S. dollar demand from government-controlled banks helped weaken the local unit. Several dealers said the dollar buying was likely related to purchases of military equipment. 

 The U.S. unit ended at NT$34.677, up from NT$34.662 Monday. 

 Dealers said government-controlled Farmers Bank of China bought an estimated $100 million, while International Commercial Bank of China was also busy buying U.S. dollars. 

 Over the weekend, the local language China Times newspaper quoted unidentified Defense Ministry officials as saying Taiwan will sign a deal this month to buy four decommissioned Kidd-class destroyers from the U.S. Navy for US$28.4 billion. 

 Dollar selling by foreign buyers of South Korean shares, and also exporters, pushed the won marginally higher, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at a two-and-a-half week closing low of 1,194.5 won, down from KRW1,196.7 Monday. 

 Foreign investors bought stocks for a ninth session Tuesday, ending as net buyers of KRW20.2 billion worth of shares. 

 There was also market talk that Daewoo Shipbuilding may soon be unloading some of the $255.6 million it raised last week in a Global Depositary Receipts offering. 

 "We expect they (Daewoo Shipbuilding) will sell at least $230 million," a Seoul-based dealer said. 

 However, the dollar isn't expected to slip under KRW1,190 as the government is likely to step in to support the U.S. currency at that level, dealers said. 

 The Philippine peso ended higher as exporters unloaded some of their dollar holdings when the U.S. unit began to gain ground during the session, traders said. 

 The dollar ended at PHP53.365 on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP53.380 Monday.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Ease as U.S. dollar slide pauses.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, May 28 (Reuters) - Asian currencies eased on
Wednesday as a pause in the U.S. dollar's decline against the
euro and yen prompted investors to consolidate their positions
in regional currencies.
    The Thai baht        held off Tuesday's 10-month highs,
helped by the central bank saying it had intervened recently to
stop the baht rising too fast, and the Indonesian rupiah
drifted further away from the near three-year highs it hit on
Monday.
    The Singapore dollar        and Korean won
  touched their lowest levels in about a week, and the
Taiwan dollar  touched a two-week trough.
    The Philippine peso        was at a one-month low when the
local market was closed an hour early due to a tropical storm
that has caused widespread flooding in the capital.
    Analysts said most Asian currencies, which have lost ground
in trade-weighted terms despite gains against the dollar, still
had room to appreciate.



 Given the market was long of dollars,
some profit-taking was not surprising.
    "The new mantra for most Asians is likely to be weakness on
a trade weighted basis; this may mean some strength against the
dollar," said Sameer Goel of Bank of America in Singapore.
    He added that stability against the dollar was also
important given most trade and foreign debt is denominated in
dollars, and often not hedged due to a lack of depth in local
markets.
    "Strength against the dollar does improve balance sheets,
while trade-weighted weakness protects export competitiveness.
This combination is possibly a good defence in a world of large
currency moves," he said.
    CENTRAL BANKS ACTIVE
    The central Bank of Thailand (BOT) said it had intervened
recently to stop the baht from strengthening too fast.
    "We had a lot of capital inflows recently and so we had to
manage the baht to prevent it from becoming too strong
unnaturally," governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said.
 
    The baht eased as far as 41.78 per dollar from an offshore
high of 41.55, which was its strongest since July 2002.
    At its high, the baht was 3.7 percent above its April 25
lows, driven by robust growth and capital inflows. The stock
market hit an 11-month high on Wednesday.
    Indonesia's central bank governor Burhanuddin Abdullah said



the rupiah was not overvalued despite gains of over eight

title: WRAP:Thai Ctrl Bk Confirms  Intervened  To Cap Baht's Rise
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula Wednesday confirmed the central bank had intervened in the foreign exchange market, buying dollars for baht to stem the sharp rise in the local currency. 

 Sentiment for the baht, along with most other Asian currencies, has turned bullish recently due to broad dollar weakness amid doubts over the U.S. government's will to continue with its strong-dollar policy. 

 Large amounts of capital inflows from foreign investors parking money in local stocks has also added to the baht's recent rally, prompting the central bank to act in the market, Pridiyathorn said. 

 The baht has consistently been hitting fresh multi-month highs against the dollar over the past two weeks and traded a fresh 10-month high of 41.62 to the dollar intraday Wednesday. The currency has strengthened around 3% versus the dollar since the beginning of the year. 

 At 0919 GMT, the dollar was trading at 41.67 baht, barely changed compared with THB41.68 at Tuesday's close in Asia. 

 The baht would be "unnaturally" strong if the central bank hadn't intervened, Pridiyathorn told reporters. 

 "We are monitoring the market and will try to keep it (the baht) at an appropriate level. We did our best," he told reporters. 

 However, he declined to say what amount of dollars the central bank had bought to cap the strength in the baht. 

 "The high foreign reserves and seven straight days' of gains in Thai stocks show you how much (foreign) money is flowing into Thailand," Pridiyathorn said. 

 Foreign net buying of Thai stocks so far this year has reached THB4.77 billion. Thai foreign reserves stood at $38.8 billion as of May 16, up from $38.4 billion a week earlier. 

 Traders said Pridiyathorn's remarks confirming the central bank's intervention shouldn't have any significant impact on the baht as it's simply standard practice and therefore won't surprise. 

 "The market doesn't react to the comments as we all know that the central bank has supported the dollar from time to time no matter if they say so or not," said a local bank dealer. 

 The attractive value of Thai stocks vis-a-vis other nations in the region and the country's strong economic fundamentals are probably drawing in investors' money, Pridiyathorn said. 

 The strong baht also encourages demand in the bond market as most banks have sold dollars for baht. They have to channel that huge baht liquidity into the local bond market. 

 He said the central bank is monitoring any impact that the strong baht might have on Thai exports and imports, but noted Thailand's competitiveness compared with other Asian countries has remained unchanged in the last three to four years. 

 The central bank has reiterated its managed-float policy many times. It has intervened in the market in a bid to help maintain Thailand's export competitiveness compared with other key rivals such as China. 

 Pridiyathorn said he met with Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra Tuesday and briefed him on the capital inflows that had led to the baht's strength. 

 Thaksin said Tuesday he was pleased with the baht's current level, noting that the currency would have been even stronger if the central bank hadn't been managing the exchange rate to keep it stable.

title: Thai Deputy PM:Asked Ctrl Bk To Allow THB Move Naturally
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thai Deputy Prime Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said Tuesday that he has asked the Bank of Thailand to refrain from intervening in the foreign exchange market while closely monitoring the baht's movements. 

 "The baht has strengthened because of capital inflows," Somkid told reporters. "I have asked the central bank to monitor the foreign exchange market and let the baht move naturally." 

 The central bank has admitted to "managing the exchange rate" to keep the baht stable. 

 Earlier Tuesday, Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said that the baht would have been even stronger if the central bank hadn't stepped into the market. 

 The baht hit a 10-month high against the U.S. dollar early Tuesday, at 41.63 to the dollar. At 0933 GMT, it was trading at THB41.71 to the dollar. 

 The strength of the Thai economy, with gross domestic product growth in the first quarter expected at more than 6%, has led foreign investors to shift their investments into Thailand's manufacturing sector and capital markets, said Somkid. 

 Strong export growth of more than 20% so far this year has also helped fuel Thai economic growth, he added. 

 Part of the capital inflow comes from Japanese investors, many of which are planning to move their manufacturing bases to Thailand, he said. 

 During a recent visit to Japan, Somkid said major Japanese automakers, including Mitsubishi Motors Corp. (J.MOT or 7211) and Honda Motor Co. (HMC), plan to increase their investments in Thailand to the tune of almost THB18 billion. 

 The baht is also supported by the dollar's overall weakness against regional currencies, Somkid noted. 

 Commerce Minister Adisai Bodharamik said earlier Tuesday that the dollar might soon drop to below THB40 but didn't give a specific timeframe.

title: Thai T-bill yields slip on strong baht, short supply.
text:
BANGKOK, May 26 (Reuters) - Yields on three-month and six-month Thai treasury bills slipped to two-month lows at Monday's auction as the baht currency strengthened and investors expected supply of government debt to shrink. 

 The average accepted yield for three billion baht ($71.51 million) worth of 91-day treasury bills fell to 1.534 percent from 1.551 percent in a similar auction a week ago. Demand was lower at 3.73 times the amount on offer from 4.22 times. 

 The yield for three billion baht worth of 182-day treasury bills dipped to 1.611 percent from 1.614 percent last week. Demand eased to 2.85 times the amount on offer from 3.39 times. 

 "Yields are too low. The three-month should be around 1.62 and the six-month around 1.65," said a dealer at a foreign bank. The Thai government has been cutting its debt issues because its budget position has been improving on better-than-expected revenue collection. In May, Thailand sold only 24 billion baht of treasury bills, against 40 billion baht in April. 

 Investors are expecting government debt supply to shrink further, driving yields across the curve lower. 

 Thai Prime Minster Thaksin Shinawatra said last week that Thailand would notch up a surprise budget surplus of around 40 billion baht for the current fiscal year, against an expected budget deficit of 174 billion baht. 

 Traders said the Thai baht's gain against the U.S. dollar was also boosting the appeal of Thai debt in recent weeks. The Thai baht has risen 2.9 percent against the dollar in the last month. 

 "The baht's strength is making investors want to hold more baht assets and less dollar assets," a trader at a local bank said. 

 By 0624 GMT, the Thai baht stood at 41.74 against the dollar, a high not seen since August 2002. Thailand's central bank said last week it would not intervene, saying Thai exports were still competitive at the current baht level. ($1=41.95 baht).

title: Thai c.bank says not  intervening  as baht gains.
text:
BANGKOK, May 21 (Reuters) - Thailand's central bank said on Wednesday the Thai baht  was strengthening in line with other regional currencies, adding that it would not "do anything against the markets" for now.

title: Thai Baht Ends At 8-Mo High On Equity Related Inflows
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended at an eight-month high against the dollar in Asia Wednesday driven by strong equity related inflows and stop-loss dollar selling by offshore players, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 42.22 baht, off its intraday low of THB42.18, but the U.S. unit was still trading at eight-month troughs. 

 The dollar closed at THB42.39 Tuesday. 

 The U.S. unit opened at the day's high of THB42.42 before strong dollar selling pulled the dollar down and weighed on the currency for most of the local session. 

 "There was heavy dollar selling led by Hong Kong players and also some genuine dollar selling for equity related purposes today," said a foreign bank trader. 

 Foreign investors have been buying into Thai stocks recently, purchasing a net THB1.74 billion in shares over the past two days. 

 The dollar's fall triggered stop-loss sales as the U.S. unit breached key THB42.35 support and then THB42.30 on the way through, traders said. 

 Some traders said local banks, possibly on behalf of the Bank of Thailand, have been buying dollars Wednesday, but the amount wasn't significant. 

 "I think the central bank wanted to slowdown the baht's sharp gains during the day. Their buying wasn't enough to dictate the market," said a local bank trader. 

 Dealers expect the dollar to fall further when local trade resumes Friday, pegging key support for the dollar at THB42.00. Resistance is expected at THB42.30 on any move up. 

 Thai financial markets will be closed Thursday for a public holiday. 

 Thai long-term government bond prices ended higher Wednesday, but off highs as a continuing rally on low upcoming supply and a low interest-rate environment stalled amid profit-taking ahead of Thursday's public holiday. 

 Dealer said investors will likely remain cautious Friday unless there was sharp movement in U.S. Treasurys during the Thai holiday to provide direction. 

 If any of the U.S. economic data to be issued Thursday raised expectations of a future cut in U.S. interest rates, the Thai bond rally could resume despite the usual caution ahead of the weekend, dealers said. 

 Long-term government bond yields ended just off new historic lows set in intraday trade. 

 The yield on the government bond due November 2012 ended in a bid-offer range of 2.98%-2.96%, up from 2.965%-2.955% in early trade but still down from Tuesday's close of 2.985%. 

 The issue due November 2022 was traded at 4.05%, down from an average accepted yield of 4.10% at an auction reopening the issue Tuesday and from 4.11% at Tuesday's secondary market close. 

 High financial system liquidity sustained demand in the short-end of the market, however. 

 One-year central bank bonds ended in a bid-offer range of 1.63%-1.62%, down from trades at 1.64% early Wednesday and 1.67% at the previous close. 

 Overnight money market interest rates closed flat despite inflows of baht liquidity from dollar selling due to central bank intervention. 

 Bank of Thailand borrowed baht from primary dealers through the seven-day repurchase, or repo, market term to absorb excess liquidity and to reactivate the term, which had fallen quiet Tuesday, dealers said. 

 Institutions found the seven-day repo unattractive since the rate was trapped at the same level as overnight rates, just under the central bank's 14-day repurchase market target rate of 1.75%. But primary dealers had to respond to the central bank's offers to sell securities under repurchase agreements.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Up after Fed, fear  intervention .
text:
SINGAPORE, May 7 (Reuters) - Asian currencies gathered upward momentum on Wednesday after the U.S. Federal Reserve's warning of economic weakness drove the U.S. dollar to deeper lows, but fears of intervention by local central banks restricted their gains. 

 The Singapore dollar, Korean won, Thai baht and Taiwan dollar all climbed to nearly two-month highs in morning deals, but then pared some gains. 

 The Philippine peso rose to an eight-month high of 52.0, extending its recent bull run after the country's tax agency reported tax collections in April exceeded the target, but then it also stalled. 

 "The U.S. dollar downtrend is still pretty much entrenched," said Thio Chin Loo, currency strategist with BNP Paribas. 

 "I think the central banks are watching the markets, otherwise we'd see the Asian currencies higher." 

 Traders said they suspected the Bank of Thailand had intervened. They also suspected the Philippine central bank had checked the peso around 52, and Korean authorities might have intervened to buy dollars after warning against excessive strength in the won early on Wednesday. 

 Japanese authorities also repeated their resolve to act against excessive currency moves. 

 The U.S. dollar fell to four-year lows against the euro and nearly two-month lows against the yen after the Fed left rates steady at Tuesday's meeting and warned of the risks to growth. It got some respite after U.S. Treasury Secretary John Snow reiterated support for the strong dollar policy. 

 SARS UNWOUND 

 The rise in regional currencies also reflected the unwinding of trades centred around the risk from the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) outbreak, traders said. 

 At its morning high of 1.7385/90, the Sing dollar was up three cents or two percent from Friday and had reversed the losses it incurred since mid-March, when the Iraq war began and the first local cases of SARS were detected. 

 Barclays Capital said the move might reflect a policy desire to have a neutral trade-weighted index. 

 "We believe that the Sing dollar's strength mainly reflects the MAS' desire to steer the Sing dollar back to a neutral monetary policy setting now that the SARS epidemic has been brought under control in Singapore," it said in a note. 

 BANK INDONESIA SURPRISES 

 The rupiah fluctuated between a 10-week high of 8,525 per dollar struck offshore and a low of 8,595, before ending near the highs which took its gains in two weeks to three percent. 

 But the central Bank Indonesia surprised markets with a statement hinting the gains were substantially due to short-term capital inflows seeking some of Asia's highest yielding papers. 

 "In regards to indications about the inflows of short-term funds...Bank Indonesia sees it as necessary to create a conducive climate to lure long-term funds," the bank said. It did not elaborate. 

 Traders had suspected foreign money for the privatisation of a majority stake in Bank Danamon had primarily boosted the rupiah, besides funds seeking the high yield in the country. 

 The baht's rise beyond 42.50 was fleeting. It stayed just a shade weaker than 42.50 with markets turning cautious after its 1.5 percent rise in under two weeks and amid talk the central bank was buying dollars.

title: Asian  Currencies  Dn Late;Acctg Woes,N Korea Weigh On Won
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The South Korean won recovered from a five-month intraday low to close just a touch weaker Thursday, but analysts said they expect more downside ahead stemming from a domestic accounting scandal and tensions from the communist North. 

 Most other Asian currencies headed south as the dollar rose against major rivals and commodity currencies, such as the Australian dollar and the Canadian unit. 

 The dollar was lifted to a two-and-a-half week high against the yen in Asia on a spate of rumors and reports related to Iraq and North Korea. 

 Traders said there was no evidence of central bank intervention in the region, though some suspected the Bank of Thailand might have been in the market to smooth out volatility in the dollar/baht. 

 The dollar's rise, coupled with increased concerns over North Korea's nuclear ambitions, "combined to put a better bid" on the U.S. unit across the region, said David Simmonds, senior emerging markets strategist at The Royal Bank of Scotland. 

 Concerns over the accounting scandal that erupted in South Korea earlier this week might have also had "a little bit of spillover" effect on the other currencies, he added. 

 The won ended at a fresh five-month low of 1,245.6 to the dollar, slightly weaker from KRW1,245.0 Wednesday. 

 The won had earlier slipped to a five-month intraday low of KRW1,254.5, pressured by the accounting scandal at SK Global, the country's third largest conglomerate. South Korean prosecutors recently uncovered accounting irregularities worth KRW1.55 trillion at the company. 

 The won later recovered to peak at KRW1,237.0, after Moody's Investors Service affirmed the country's A3 sovereign rating; many market players had been expecting a downgrade. 

 But the rebound was short-lived as risk factors - the SK Global issue, the North's nuclear standoff with the U.S. and a weakening economy - returned to grip the market. 

 Increased South Korea risk has prompted some foreign banks in Seoul to reduce the amount of foreign exchange swaps they do with domestic banks, but this hasn't had much of an impact on the spot exchange rate, dealers said. 

 "The foreign banks aren't absolutely going out of business with the local banks. They're just reducing their foreign exchange swaps by a little amount," said a spot dealer. 

 "We still prefer to buy (dollars) on dips," said Frank Gong, Hong Kong-based currency strategist at Bank of America. "The trend for the won is weaker. There are many risks with the economy, corporate scandals and geopolitical tensions." 

 The Thai baht fell to as low as 42.83 to the dollar earlier in the session as offshore players bought the U.S. currency. 

 Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said the central bank is closely monitoring the baht's movements. 

 He said the currency's volatility was due to market rumors about developments in the war against terrorism. 

 "There was talk that Iraqi soldiers were surrendering and that (Osama) bin Laden got arrested. It's pretty messy here," a Bangkok-based trader said, adding that the foreign exchange market is more sensitive to rumors these days. 

 Late in Asia, the baht was quoted at 42.72 to the dollar, from THB42.67 at the local close Wednesday. 

 The Singapore dollar weakened but came off lows as some foreign banks took profits on the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 Near the end of local trading hours, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7494, up from S$1.7463 late Wednesday. The intraday trading range was between S$1.7470 and S$1.7540. 

 The New Taiwan dollar tracked the yen lower to end at its weakest level in eight sessions. 

 The U.S. unit ended at NT$34.739, up from Wednesday's NT$34.721, after trading between NT$34.735 and NT$34.819. 

 The Philippine peso snapped a three-day losing streak to close stronger for the first time this week as banks took profits on the dollar, dealers said. 

 The peso finished at 54.950 to the dollar on the Philippine Dealing System, strengthening from Wednesday's record low of PHP55.099. 

 Some traders said the market was also rattled by talk late in the session that the central bank was prepared to impose stricter foreign exchange rules to zero in on potential speculators. 

 After market close, the central bank announced a set of measures aimed at curbing speculation, including tighter monitoring of banks' foreign exchange deals and limiting their overbought dollar limit to 2.5% of capital. 

 Meantime, the central bank's Monetary Board left the closely watched overnight rates unchanged, citing a still benign inflation outlook. 

 But the board warned it may shift to a tightening bias if the weak peso threatens the central bank's inflation target of 4.5%-5.5%. 

 The Indonesian rupiah ended unchanged at 8,905 to the dollar, recovering from an intraday low of IDR8,925 on suspected dollar selling by the central bank.
