title: Thai Baht Ends Higher On Early Offshore Dollar Selling
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended higher against the dollar in Asian spot trade Tuesday after early selling in the U.S. unit by foreign players prompted talk that the Bank of Thailand might have been intervening indirectly to stem the baht's slide, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 42.75 baht, down from THB42.83 at the Asian close Monday. 

 The dollar hit its intraday high of THB42.80 in the morning, but later gave up those gains on dollar selling by offshore European banks. 

 Traders said the dollar selling for baht prompted talk that European banks might have been acting on behalf of the Bank of Thailand to prevent the baht's depreciation, given the unusually heavy bids. 

 "But I don't think their demand for the baht has anything to do with the central bank, as the Finance Ministry has said the recent exchange rate is satisfactory," a Bangkok trader added. 

 "It's more likely that those banks wanted to transfer funds to local companies," he said. 

 Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said Monday that the central bank has been monitoring the baht's movements in foreign exchange markets to ensure that Thai export prices remain competitive. 

 Somkid said the baht's weakness in recent sessions has been in line with weakness in the yen, and the local currency remains at a satisfactory level against the currencies of Thailand's regional trading partners. 

 The dollar fell to its intraday low of THB42.73 in the afternoon, before recovering slightly by the close. 

 The dollar is expected to open Wednesday in a range of THB42.70-THB42.85. 

 Thai long-term government bond prices fell slightly on profit-taking after sharp gains Tuesday, but strong results in an initial auction of THB5 billion worth of central bank 364-day bonds reactivated short-term bonds, dealers said. 

 The yield on the long-term issue due November 2012 finished at 3.06%, up from a close of 3.05% Monday, the Thai Bond Dealing Center said in its daily report. 

 But the curve steepened slightly, after flattening in most sessions since the beginning of the year, on buying in the short-end sparked by results of the auction, dealers said. 

 The central bank auctioned its new bonds at an average yield of 1.54735%, further below the government bond yield curve than had been expected due to high financial system liquidity and prospects for an extended period of low interest rates. The government bond curve was at 1.57% at one year as of early Tuesday. 

 Buying in the short-end of the curve pushed the yield on the government bond due June 2004 down to end at 1.585% from a previous close of 1.60%, the bond dealing center said. 

 A money market dealer said the central bank's 14-day repurchase market target rate of 1.75% was out of line, too high for both money market interest rates and the treasury bill government bond yield curve. 

 But dealers aren't certain whether the central bank will cut the 14-day target, as it could lead to further declines in money market rates and commercial bank deposit account rates, which might attract unwanted political attention. 

 The central bank's Monetary Policy Committee next meets March 3. The committee is expected to cut the 14-day target rate only if U.S. interest rates fall further, or if Iraq-related disruptions in the global oil, trade and tourism markets begins to hurt the Thai economy. 

 Overnight money market interest rates continued to fall as liquidity prepared for public demand over the unofficial Lunar New Year holidays returned to the system, with additional downward pressure from short-term debt market yields.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late; Caution On Iraq Report
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies edged higher Monday but caution reigned ahead of a key report later in the global session by United Nations weapons inspectors that could indicate if a war against Iraq is imminent. 

 The South Korean won ended just a tad higher at a fresh-six month closing high, helped by month-end dollar sales by exporters. 

 Verbal intervention by the Ministry of Finance and Economy helped support the U.S. currency above the 1,170 won a dollar level, market players said. Some dealers also suspected the government bought dollars, but others said it was unlikely. 

 After trading between KRW1,169.5 and KRW1,172.0, the dollar ended at KRW1,170.7, down from KRW1,170.8 Friday. 

 Earlier, an official at the ministry said the recent drop in the dollar/won rate is "excessive" and the government is concerned about recent moves in the market. 

 The Singapore dollar, the New Taiwan dollar and the Thai baht were also higher. The Indonesian rupiah was steady but the Philippine peso bucked the trend and weakened as the market prepared for increased demand for dollars from oil companies. 

 Overall volume in regional currency markets was thin as fears of a U.S.-led war in Iraq kept many market players sidelined or reluctant to take strong positions. 

 Some observers also attributed the low volumes to reduced trading interest ahead of the long Chinese Lunar New Year weekend. 

 "There isn't much appetite to take major directional views," said Vincent Low, Merrill Lynch's Singapore-based head of foreign exchange and bond strategy for Asia. 

 Monday's report by the Iraq weapons inspectors to the U.N. Security Council will be followed by President George W. Bush's State of the Union address Tuesday. 

 Their comments are expected to signal if war is imminent. 

 Also Tuesday, market players will be keeping a close eye on Treasury Secretary nominee John Snow's confirmation hearing to see if he says anything about the U.S.' strong dollar policy. 

 The near-term picture remains one of a weak U.S. dollar, and Asian central banks are likely to intervene to help stem the decline, Low said. 

 But given the fact that there are structural reasons, not just a war risk premium, for the dollar's weakness, regional monetary authorities may have a dilemma in continuing to accumulate dollars aggressively, he added. 

 Still, with regional economies still in the nascent stages of recovery, their central banks are unlikely to want their currencies to appreciate too rapidly versus the dollar. 

 Low said although the broad view for the region remains one of a gradual economic recovery and a general resilience to geopolitical tension, "with Asia so leveraged to world growth," the region can't be insulated from major developments in the U.S., the world's biggest economy. 

 At 0943 GMT, the dollar was quoted around Y117.66, down from Y117.72 late Friday in New York. The dollar was at Y117.96 late Friday in Tokyo. 

 Singapore's better-than-expected industrial output data for December didn't generate much excitement in the currency market. The local dollar's strength was due to the weak outlook for the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 The dollar was quoted around S$1.7278 near the end of the local trading session, below S$1.7310 late Friday, but up from S$1.7235 - its lowest since late-2000 - in New York trading Friday. 

 Singapore's industrial production rose 19% on year in December, beating the average 8.9% forecast predicted in a Dow Jones Newswires poll. 

 Thailand's strong export data had little impact on the Thai baht, which firmed as market players unloaded dollars on fears of a war in Iraq, though the market was wary about central bank intervention, traders said. 

 Bank of Thailand has been buying dollars on weakness to build foreign reserves and limit volatility. 

 The U.S. currency finished the local trading session at 42.60 baht, down from THB42.68 Friday. 

 Earlier Monday, the Thai Commerce Ministry Monday said exports rose 5.7% to $68.9 billion in 2002, while imports rose 4.1% to $64.3 billion. 

 But the ministry said exports growth will slow to 3% to 5% this year, due to uncertainties linked to Iraq and the possibility of a slowdown in the global economy. 

 The New Taiwan dollar strengthened as fears of a war in Iraq encouraged selling of the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 Exporters and interbank players sold U.S. dollars during the day, though there were some importers who were dollar buyers. 

 Dealers said the Taiwan central bank bought small amounts of U.S. dollars to slow the local unit's rise, but the buying wasn't very aggressive. 

 After moving between NT$34.510 and NT$34.568, the dollar closed at NT$34.560, down from NT$34.575 Friday. 

 Elsewhere, the dollar ended at 53.670 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP53.590 Friday, after moving between PHP53.575 and PHP53.685. 

 The U.S. currency had opened weaker amid a lack of corporate demand, but gained strength in late trading as banks bought dollars. 

 "Nobody wanted to go short because we think the oil companies will be buying in the coming sessions and it might be a big demand," a trader with a local bank said. 

 The Philippine government last week required oil companies to maintain higher inventories to prepare for possible supply disruptions in case war erupts in Iraq. 

 In Indonesia, the dollar closed unchanged at 8,893 rupiah after trading between IDR8,887 and IDR8,895. 

 Dealers said dollar sales by local banks offset dollar purchases by offshore investors fearful of rising anti-Western sentiment arising from tensions over Iraq.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -SGD hits 6-month high, others ease.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 17 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar hit
fresh six-month highs early on Friday but other Asian
currencies were down as sentiment diverged on uncertainty over
the near-term direction of the dollar/yen.
    Dealers said the euro's climb to a three-year high against
the dollar was enough to provide room for a stronger Singapore
dollar, despite uncertainty over the yen's near-term direction.
    Singapore authorities manage the exchange rate against an
undisclosed trade-weighted basket of its major trading partners
and most analysts believe yen and euro are major components of
that basket.
    The Singapore unit firmed to around 1.7294 per U.S. dollar,
its strongest since July 22, when it saw a seven-month high of
1.7289.
 
    Dealers said players in regional currencies were bearish on
the dollar in the near term.
    But given the potential threat of intervention by Japan and


 by their own central banks to cap recent currency gains, most 

 players were reluctant to extend their short dollar positions 

 over the weekend, they added. 

 "Dollar will continue to face selling pressure as long as 

 war jitters are around," said Lee Boon Keng, treasury markets 

 strategist at DBS Bank in Singapore. 

 "But should the war start, it will remove the biggest 

 source of uncertainty plaguing the market," he added, saying 

 players should be cautious. 

 Hit by intensifying tensions over the prospect of a war 

 against Iraq, the U.S. dollar eased beyond $1.06 against the 

 euro. 

 But it bounced off fresh three-year lows hit overnight 

 against the single currency and was supported against the yen 

 amid fears of Japanese intervention to aid the dollar. 

 Japan's top financial diplomat, Zembei Mizoguchi, said the 

 finance ministry was always prepared to act as needed and was 

 watching currency moves closely. 

 C.BANK WARINESS WEIGH ON BAHT 

 Elsewhere, the Thai baht was down to around 42.70 per 

 dollar, from early offshore highs at 42.63 but not far from 

 late Thursday's 42.68. 

 Dealers in Singapore said overall sentiment was bullish on 

 the baht but players were wary of possible intervention by the 

 Bank of Thailand to protect export competitiveness. 

 Dealers said they suspected some foreign banks on behalf of 

 the central bank had pulled the baht off four-month highs of 

 42.54 per dollar hit on Tuesday. 


 
    They said most players believe the central bank may again
buy U.S. dollars around 42.50 to cap the baht's upside.
    "With the weekend approaching and with all the uncertainty,
players are covering their short dollar positions," said an
offshore baht dealer at a European bank in Singapore.
    The Philippines peso edged down to 53.55 per dollar, from
Thursday's onshore close of 53.47, in thin trade.
    Dealers in Manila said some downside peso support was
spotted at around 53.50 as players covered short peso
positions.
    The Indonesian rupiah stayed supported within its recent
8,860-8,880 range as dollar demand from local corporates
spotted through this week waned.
    The Taiwan dollar touched a fresh two-month high before
giving up those gains.
    The South Korean won stepped back from early highs, amid
caution over moves in the dollar/yen.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Soft dlr helps, rupiah heads for 4-month high.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Dec 16 (Reuters) - The buoyant Indonesian
rupiah
 strengthened towards 8,800 per dollar on Monday, a break of
which would take it to four-month peaks and far from the gloom
that surrounded it after the devastating Bali attacks in
October.
    Most other Asian currencies also firmed against a broadly
weaker dollar, the friendless Philippine peso the exception,
with the Singapore dollar and Thai baht consolidating around
their respective three-month and one-month highs.
    The rupiah rose to around 8,805 per dollar, its highest
since September 9, supported by Sunday's part sale of telco
giant PT Indosat. Singapore's ST Telemedia will pay $634
million for a 42 percent stake in the state-run telecom.
    Dealers in Jakarta said while dollar demand from some local
corporates capped the rupiah and thin conditions deterred
aggressive moves, speculation over dollar inflows from the
Indosat sale kept the currency supported.



    "Players are betting that at least 20 to 30 percent of the
Indosat proceeds will flow into the market," said a dealer at
an American bank in Jakarta.
    He said that speculation could push the dollar beyond
8,800, and might have already halted some dollar purchases from
corporates who can afford to wait for cheaper dollars.
    The rupiah is Asia's best performing currency in 2002,
rising over 17.6 percent against the dollar, backed by steady
inflows from sale of state assets and repatriation of earnings
from exports due to higher yields at home.
    It has risen by almost seven percent from a six-month low
around 9,400 per dollar reached after the October 12 bombings
in Bali which killed almost 200 people, mostly foreign
tourists.

    Elsewhere, dealers said the yen's rally through 121 per
dollar aided sentiment in regional currencies, but gains for
some were capped by wariness of possible central bankintervention to protect export competitiveness.
    Although data from Singapore and Thailand bettered
forecasts, analysts said the economic outlook was clouded by a
lacklustre recovery in the United States -- export-driven
Asia's largest market.
    "Dollar weakness will support Asia regionals, but
uncertainty surrounding the U.S. economy will at best keep most
of them within ranges we have seen in the second half (of

    Those concerns pulled the Singapore dollar off Friday's

    "Most players are booking profits on the Sing dollar to

    She said unless the Sing dollar strengthens beyond 1.7450,
most players would feel safe in betting on a short-term
retracement in the dollar.
    The market largely ignored a surprising 1.8 percent annual



rise in October retail sales, which analysts associated with a



more buoyant stock market and higher visitor arrivals for the



month rather than any improvement in domestic consumption.



With the exception of a slight blip in July, Singapore's



retail sales have been in a downward spiral all year as the



rising numbers of jobless keep a tight hold on their wallets.



The Thai baht touched fresh one-month highs at 43.18, with

product in the year to the September, despite a slowing in

The National Economic and Social Development Board said the

percent growth forecast by analysts and the 5.1 percent



year-on-year growth in the second quarter.



The agency forecast growth of 4.9 percent this year,

in 2003.



The Philippine peso bucked the regional trend to fall to



around 53.67 per dollar as demand for dollars from the offshore



non-deliverable forwards market outpaced the supply from



overseas workers repatriating earnings.



Dealers in Manila said the peso could ease further as local



corporates were hedging for a weaker currency at the start of



next year and exporters were holding onto their dollars.



The South Korean won posted its strongest close in five

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Higher Late;Won,NT$ At 2-Mo High
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies firmed as the dollar lost ground against major rivals, particularly the yen, amid concerns about a U.S.-Iraq conflict and uncertainty about the U.S. economy. 

 Regional units were also beneficiaries of the hunt for higher yields after the U.S. Federal Reserve's larger-than-expected 50 basis point rate cut last week. 

 The Korean won and the New Taiwan dollar ended the day at two month highs, while the Thai baht hit levels unseen since September. 

 The Singapore dollar was hardly dented by Trade and Industry Minister George Yeo's comments that he isn't ruling out the possibility of a double-dip recession for the city state. 

 For the most part, trading ranges were tight and there wasn't much significant position-taking ahead of a U.S. holiday Monday. 

 Market players were also waiting for Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's views on the economy when he testifies before the Joint Economic Committee of Congress Wednesday, as well as a slew of U.S. economic data to be released this week. 

 Verbal intervention by Japanese government officials failed to curb the yen's strength in Asia. Nor did weak share prices and shaky economic data; the Nikkei 225 Stock Average briefly fell below its 19-year low during the session. 

 David Simmonds, senior emerging markets strategist for Asia at The Royal Bank of Scotland, said markets remain concerned about why the Fed cut rates so sharply last week. 

 Some wonder if the decision reflects a greater worry about the economy than anticipated earlier. 

 Markets are also refocusing on Iraq after the United Nations approved resolutions that calls on the country to eliminate its weapons of mass destruction or face "serious consequences. 

 For now, though, markets are waiting to see how Iraq's response, and how the U.S. interprets that response, Simmonds said. 

 If there is conflict and oil prices jump, it would further threaten Asian economies that are already grappling with a slowdown in the U.S., he said. That should also curtail regional currencies' current strength, he added. 

 The dollar ended at 1,201.0 won, down from KRW1,207.4 Friday, and its weakest finish since Sept. 10. Intraday, it traded between KRW1,197.8 and KRW1,203.3. 

 Only demand from importers helped lift the currency back above KRW1,200 in the afternoon, traders said. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency ended at NT$34.415, up from NT$34.505 Friday, and its lowest since Sept. 13, though bids from importers and central bank intervention helped cushion the fall. 

 After the market's close, Taiwan's central bank announced a 25 basis point rate cut, a move widely expected by analysts since the Fed slashed rates last week. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. currency was quoted around S$1.7566 as of 1045 GMT, down from S$1.7615 late Friday. 

 The dollar opened at around S$1.7580 in Asia and slipped to S$1.7570 in the wake of its fall below 120 yen; it spent much of the session locked between S$1.7575 and S$1.7585. 

 Market participants said Yeo's bearish comments on the economy weren't a major surprise as most have already been expecting a weak economic performance in the second half. The government is widely expected to cut its full-year growth forecasts to 2%-3%, from 3%-4% currently. 

 Elsewhere, the dollar was quoted around 42.96 versus the Thai baht as of 1047 GMT, down from THB43.12 late Friday. 

 An Asian bank trader in Singapore said Thailand's central bankintervened via agent banks to curb the baht's rise when the dollar slipped to an intraday trough of THB42.94, it's lowest since Sept. 19. 

 "But with the U.S. holiday (Monday), nobody is taking new positions," he said. 

 Meanwhile, the Indonesian rupiah rose as offshore market players continued to liquidate long dollar positions as the probe into last month's deadly bombings in Bali progressed. 

 News that the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency sealed a pact Friday to sell a 51% stake in Bank Niaga to Malaysia's Commerce Asset-Holding Bhd. for around $114 million also lifted the market, dealers said. The deal is expected to bring capital flows into Indonesia. 

 The dollar closed at 9,145 rupiah, down from IDR9,190 Friday. 

 But the Philippine peso surrendered early gains as corporate demand for dollars emerged. 

 The U.S. currency ended at its intraday high of PHP52.960 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP52.880 Friday. 

 The dollar's closing level was different from the PHP52.910 initially posted on the system. 

 Metropolitan Bank & Trust Co., the electronic exchange's officer of the week, said the discrepancy was due to late mapping of the last transaction executed on the dealing system. 

 Some traders said the revision shouldn't stir negative reaction from market players since such incidents had happened in the past, and weren't an attempt to engineer the foreign exchange rate.

title: Thai Baht Ends Higher Vs Dlr In Thin Trade, Tracks Yen
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended at its day's high against the dollar in Asian trade Tuesday, boosted by an overnight rise in the Japanese yen, traders said. 

 The dollar ended at 43.35 baht, down from THB43.53 at the Asian close Monday. 

 After stumbling against the yen overnight, the dollar opened at THB43.41 early in Asia before steadily losing more ground during the day due to offshore dollar selling. 

 However, trading in regional markets was fairly thin, keeping the dollar/baht in a tight range. 

 "They were some dollar buying orders from oil companies, but they couldn't help cap losses much," said a trader at foreign bank. 

 Some dealers also suspected the Bank of Thailand intervened during the day to help limit the dollar's losses, citing dollar orders at THB43.34-THB43.35 by offshore banks that usually act on behalf of the central bank. 

 The bullish economic forecast by the National Economic & Social Development Board had no impact on the dollar/baht as the figures were somewhat in line with market expectations, dealers added. 

 NESDB, a state planning agency responsible for collecting production data, said Tuesday that Thailand's gross domestic product growth in the third quarter of 2002 is likely to be no less than 5.5% above the same period a year ago, supported by strong exports and local demand. 

 Growth for the full year is likely to be near the top end of a forecast range of 4% to 4.5%, possibly at 4.3%. 

 The dollar is expected to open in Asia Wednesday in a range of THB43.30-THB43.40, subject to the yen's movement overnight. 

 Thai government bond prices rose further Tuesday, on growing expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve Open Market Committee may cut interest rates at its Nov. 6 meeting, traders said. 

 Trading in the bond market was more active compared with Monday, as the Thai bourse ended its long-winning streak Tuesday, falling 1% at 353.95 points. 

 The yield on the government bond due April 2010 issue finished in a bid/offer range of 3.67%/3.66%, compared with 3.74% at Monday's close, while the March 2011 issue finished at 3.77%/3.76% versus 3.84% at the previous close. 

 Traders said mutual funds were active buyers as they speculated that yields on long-dated papers may fall further Wednesday when a new 10-year government bond is auctioned. 

 "The upcoming auction of the 10-year bond helped spiced up the market activity as it's quite a novelty," said a trader. 

 The overnight interest rate finished flat despite end-of-month demand for cash, as liquidity remains ample, and pressure from foreign exchange swap rates eased given the stronger baht. 

 The overnight rate is expected to ease when liquidity returns to the system at the start of November, dealers said.

title: Thai Baht Ends Down; Hits 6-Mo Low On Offshore Dlr Buying
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended just off a six-month low against the dollar in Asian spot trade Monday, thanks to selling by offshore players as the dollar rallied against the yen and other regional currencies, dealers said. 

 The dollar finished at 43.78 baht, off a six-month high of THB43.80 but up sharply from THB43.51 at the Asian close Friday, despite two apparent interventions by the central bank. 

 The U.S. unit was hovering at an intraday low around THB43.54 at the Asian open before a run up fueled by offshore players' adjustments to keep the baht in line with regional currencies and local oil importers' demand. 

 Oil importers bought dollars as global oil prices rose following an explosion on an oil tanker off the coast of Yemen, which sparked a jump in Brent crude futures. Higher oil prices tend to weaken the baht because the country is a net importer. 

 "The dollar's steep rise against the yen also convinced offshore players to buy the greenback. Most of the active players were European banks," a local bank trader said. 

 Apparent interventions by Bank of Thailand to limit the baht's fall failed to stem the slide, as the U.S. unit rose a rising tide against the yen, which is the regional trendsetter. 

 "A Japanese bank in Singapore, which usually acts on behalf of BOT (Bank of Thailand) bought the baht two times at THB43.62 and THB43.72. But the orders were too weak to make much difference," the trader said. 

 As the dollar convincingly pushed past initial resistance just above THB43.60, which held against several attempted breaches last week, more offshore and onshore players joined the dollar-buying binge. 

 The U.S. unit touched an intraday high of THB43.80 in late afternoon trade. 

 Dealers expected the dollar to open Tuesday in Asia between THB43.60 and THB43.90, subject to any further volatility in the yen. 

 "If the dollar-yen (exchange rate) is able to rise firmly above Y124 resistance by early Tuesday, the dollar-baht will likely open higher than THB43.80," a foreign bank trader said. 

 Prices of Thai government bonds finished steady Monday as liquidity driven buying from local banks was offset by profit-taking by some foreign banks, traders said. 

 Trade was very thin on a lack of participation from long-term investors and a dearth of fresh leads. 

 Heavy rain and flash flooding in Bangkok early Monday also hit trade as many market participants struggled to get into work, traders added. 

 The yield on the government bond due June 2009 finished in a bid-offer range of 3.21%-3.20%, compared from 3.21% at Friday's close. The yield on the government bond due April 2010 finished at 3.52%-3.51%, little changed from 3.52% previously. 

 The Bank of Thailand sold THB6 billion in 28-day and 91-day treasury bills at an auction Monday as part of the government's regular deficit financing. 

 As expected, average yields for both maturities were softer from those recorded at last week's auction thanks to easing short-term interest rates and small offering sizes, coupled with liquidity driven demand. 

 The THB1 billion 28-day T-bills were sold at 1.8700%, down from 1.90397% recorded last week, while THB5 billion 91-day T-bills were sold at 1.90194%, down from 1.93501%. 

 Thai short-term interest rates slightly eased at the end of biweekly reserve requirements Monday. However, dealers said the rates may move up at the start of a new reserve period Tuesday, coupled with weakness in the baht.

SINGAPORE, Oct 3 (Reuters) - The Taiwan dollar eased past a 

 key barrier of 35 per dollar to one-week lows and the 

 Philippine peso tested a fresh 14-month trough in early 

 Thursday trade. 

     Dealers in Singapore said the Taiwan dollar hit a one-week 

 low of 35.015, before talk of central bank intervention capped 

 its fall. 

     They said players were concerned about a potential rise in 

 outflow of dollars from Taiwan, after recent net sales of local 

 stocks by foreign investors. 

     Foreign equity funds were net sellers of T$852.7 million of 

 Taiwan stocks on Wednesday, taking net selling to around T$56.2 

 billion over the past five weeks. 

     Talk of the central bank's presence in the market also 

 helped the Philippine peso off a fresh 14-month low of 52.66 

 per dollar, hit early on, as speculation over a worsening 

 budget deficit grew. 

     Finance Secretary Jose Camacho said on Wednesday the 

 government if needed would tap local markets for funding the 

 deficit and ruled out further offshore borrowings. 

     "Peso sentiment remains very fragile...deficit rumours 

 continue to weigh and corporate dollar demand for hedging oil 

 import bills shows no sign of abating," said a JP Morgan Chase 

 research note. 

     WALL STREET CAPS DOLLAR 

     Other Asian currencies edged up as U.S. stock losses capped 

 the dollar's recent gains against the yen and euro 

     However, currency analysts saw limited upside for regional 

currencies and recommended players take advantage of the move 

 to build fresh long dollar positions. 

     South Korea's currency market was closed on Thursday for a 

 national holiday and will reopen on Friday. 

     The Korean won ended onshore trade at 1,230.4 per dollar on 

 Wednesday against Tuesday's close of 1,227.7, its first close 

 below the key 1,230 level since late June. 

     The dollar in early Asian trade touched session lows around 

 122.50 yen and 98.65 cents against the euro, weighed down by a 

 fall in the Dow Jones average of over two percent overnight. 

     Players were also reluctant to hold long dollar positions 

 ahead of U.S. unemployment data for September due on Friday. 

     Dealers said players in regional currencies, taking a cue 

 from the majors, booked profits on the dollar's recent gains. 

 They said some momentum was added to the move as stop-loss 

 dollar sell orders were triggered along the way. 

     The Singapore dollar rebounded aggressively to around 

 1.7825 in early trade after seeing the sharpest slide among the 

 regionals on Wednesday, to 3-=   month lows around 1.7925 per 

 dollar. 

     But the currency was swiftly sold down to levels around 

 1.7850 as the profit-taking faded and players took fresh long 

 dollar positions. 

     "Clearly amidst the raft of GDP downgrades from various 

 economists over the last few weeks, the market has also changed 

 its assessment of the prospects for this currency," said Bhanu 

 Baweja, currency strategist at UBS Warburg in Singapore. 

 The latest downgrade of Singapore's growth prospects for 

 2002 and 2003 came on Wednesday from Morgan Stanley, which 

 cited uncertain global recovery and slack demand. 

 Baweja said the currency can go a long way lower as the yen 

 and euro could ease down to 123 and 98.30 respectively. 

 "Dollar/Sing can appreciate to 1.8150 before the MAS (Monetary 

 Authority of Singapore) comes in to defend the currency". 

     The Thai baht ticked up to around 43.47 per dollar, off 

 Wednesday's 43.57, the lowest this week. 

     Dealers in Singapore said the baht's upmove was also 

 influenced by an easing of foreign selling of local stocks, 

 helping sentiment, and on fears of central bank intervention. 

     Dealers said authorities checked forex rates in the market 

 on Wednesday, but added that there was no evidence of actual 

 Bank of Thailand (BOT) intervention yet. 

     "Despite recent BOT support, the baht has weakened through 

 the 43.50 level already, and though moves may be gradual, we 

 maintain it will slip to 44.5 in a month's time," Baweja of UBS 

 Warburg said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Steady, suspicious of stronger yen.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 30 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were flat on Monday morning, waiting on key economic releases and political announcements from Japan but clearly unimpressed by the yen's gains. 

 Traders said Asian currencies were unmoved believing the yen's gains would be short-lived, even as the dollar lost a yen from Friday's levels of 122.64/74. 

 Some attributed that to position-squaring after the local currency fixing on Monday, the last day of the fiscal first half in Japan, coupled with hopes the cabinet reshuffle will be pro-reform for the banking sector. 

 The Bank of Japan's quarterly tankan business sentiment survey due on Tuesday also prevented the market from being overly bullish about the yen's rally. 

 "No one's doing anything about the rising yen. They think even if the cabinet reshuffle is positive, Japan would want a weaker yen," a trader with a Singapore-based desk said. 

 The uncertainty over how Japan proposed to bail out its banks has increased the focus on the cabinet reshuffle due later in day, especially the fate of top financial regulator Hakuo Yanagisawa, whose opposition to the use of public funds to shore up banks has been criticised. 

 "Another volatile week, particularly for yen. Events and economic releases this week are especially difficult to predict and we expect the market to be extremely reactive," Lee Boon Keng, DBS Bank's senior strategist said in a market commentary. 

 The Singapore dollar traded flat at 1.7775/7785 per dollar, barely changed from Friday and still close to last week's three-month low of 1.7872, while the Thai baht was little changed at 43.40/45. 

 The baht was near last week's five-month low of 43.60, where traders said the central bank had intervened last week. 

Thailand is due to release August trade data later in the day and economists expect strong export growth to help it show a surplus once again, after a deficit in July. 

 Ray Farris, strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston, said maintaining competitive exchange rates would still be a priority for Asian central banks. 

 "Over the next few months, Asian currencies will be dominated by swings in the yen and a preference by central banks to be averse to currency strength, as long as leading indicators for exports are still deteriorating," Farris said. 

 Fragile stock markets, reacting to the fall in U.S. equities for the fifth week, also put pressure on some Asian currencies. 

 The Korean won , which has been plagued by rising foreign investment outflows in recent weeks, fell to 1,228.6/9 after a firmer opening. 

 The Taiwan dollar was also weaker as its stock market fell, choosing not to follow the yen, while the Philippine peso hovered around last week's close at 52.35/45, just shy of 11-month lows beyond 52.50. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR AT 0310 GMT Change on the day

title: Asian  Currencies  Down Late On Yen;Mkt Ignores Econ Data
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies sank to multi-month lows in tandem with the yen late Monday after a top Japanese official late last week suggested massive yen selling as a way to end Japan's deflation. 

 With Japan's financial markets closed for a public holiday, thin trading volumes made it easy to move prices as stop-loss buying of dollars was triggered across-the-board. 

 Market players ignored a slew of strong economic data from the region, choosing instead to track the yen's weakness which spilt through from Friday's global session. 

 The yen began to weaken against the dollar after Japan's vice finance minister for international affairs, Haruhiko Kuroda, late Friday made his remarks about selling yen to combat deflation. 

 "It's triggered a lot of stop losses. Every currency has moved substantially (lower)" noted a senior trader at an Asian bank in Singapore. 

 However, the fundamental story hasn't changed, analysts said. 

 Concerns about the U.S. economy, ever-increasing prospects of a war against Iraq, and rising oil prices do not warrant a strong dollar outlook, they said. 

 Still, economic data from the U.S. so far, although mixed, indicates the U.S. economic recovery is on a recovery path. 

 On the other hand, there's little to inspire confidence about the Japanese economy. 

 Kuroda's comments suggests that any serious policy steps to fight deflation appears to include a weak yen scenario, and it is that which is dragging down the rest of the Asian currencies, analysts said. 

 "With an entire range of conflicting issues in the forex market, direction recently has been a bit of blur, but if at all there is any focus, it is on relative performance and on this count, the USD may enjoy precedence over other majors," UBS Warburg wrote in a note. 

 The South Korean won hit a three-month closing low against the dollar on the back of the yen's decline. 

 The dollar finished at 1,220.0 won - its strongest since June 20 - from KRW1,203.8 Friday. The U.S. currency traded between KRW1,212.0 and KRW1,220.5, breaking out of a nearly month-long trading band of between KRW1,190 and KRW1,210. 

 "Finally, it broke through its tight range," said Seung Hyun Kim, a member of the foreign exchange corporate sales team at BNP Paribas. "We were surprised at this strong upward movement (of the dollar) today. I'm not sure if this trend will continue or not." 

 However, aggressive dollar sales by exporters supported the won, and this is expected to persist for the rest of the week. "Many exporting companies want to sell dollars over KRW1,220," said a dealer. 

 In Taiwan, the local dollar closed at its weakest level since Apr. 25 in line with the yen's fall. 

 Importers bought U.S. dollars earlier in the day at around NT$34.71-NT$34.72, but buying of the local dollars by the central bank, and also exporters, helped cushion the local unit's fall. 

 However, offshore non-deliverable forward players started to cover their short U.S. dollar positions actively in the afternoon, pushing the U.S. dollar to its intraday high of NT$34.779, according to dealers. 

 The U.S. unit ended at NT$34.776, up from NT$34.410 Friday. 

 The Philippine peso closed at its lowest in 13 months, with the market jittery over mounting tensions in the Middle East, dealers said. 

 The dollar finished at PHP52.44 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP52.23 Friday, and its highest since Aug. 9, 2001. 

 A trader with a local bank said there was talk in the market that the central bank sold around $30 million to support the peso early Monday, but the central bank denied this. 

 Governor Rafael Buenaventura said the monetary authority didn't see any need to support the peso as the decline wasn't caused by speculation, but by weaker regional currencies led by the drop of the Japanese yen, and mounting tensions in the Middle East. 

 "We feel there's enough liquidity. If there's excessive volatility, we will come in," he told reporters. 

 He said the dollar is expected to slide back to just above 50 pesos near the year-end, with remittances from overseas Filipino workers expected to increase in the fourth quarter. 

 The Singapore dollar tracked the yen's weakness, briefly hitting a three-month low against the U.S. unit earlier in the session before profit-taking set it. 

 The market ignored news that the city state's retail index rose for the first time year-on-year after declining for eight straight months. 

 The index climbed 1.7% on year in July on the back of higher sales of vehicles and household equipment, the Department of Statistics said Monday. Compared with June, the index rose 6.9%. 

 The U.S. dollar opened at around S$1.7712, and rose to an intraday high of S$1.7810 at mid morning - its highest since mid-June - boosted by fresh purchase orders from European banks, a trader at a big foreign bank said. 

 Another currency dealer said: "The pair hasn't moved for quite some time. Now that the (U.S.) dollar is gaining on all its major counterparts, traders feel it's time (to see some major movements)." 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted around S$1.7806, from S$1.7641 late in Asia Friday. 

 In Indonesia, the dollar's rise against regional currencies prompted offshore players to cover short dollar positions against the rupiah, a dealer at a Jakarta-based foreign bank said. 

 Dealers said Bank Indonesia was believed to have sold dollars to help support the rupiah, but it had little impact as the amount was small and the selling was done late in the trading session. 

 Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom told reporters the central bank was monitoring the rupiah's weakening against the dollar and may intervene if necessary. 

 She attributed the rupiah's weakness mainly to lower regional currencies and uncertainty about a possible U.S.-led strike against Iraq. 

 "If the rupiah keeps falling, we may do something, including intervening," she said, but didn't say if the central bank was active in the market Monday. 

 The dollar closed at 9,065 rupiah, up from IDR8,965 Friday, after trading between IDR9,020 and IDR9,070 intraday. 

 Meanwhile, market players ignored better-than-expected second-quarter gross domestic product data from Thailand, with the Thai currency falling past the 43-level against the U.S. dollar. 

 Thailand's GDP rose 5.1% on year in the second quarter. A Dow Jones Newswires poll had earlier predicted an average 4.6% rise. 

 Chakramon Phasukavanich, secretary-general of the National Economic & Social Development Board, told a news conference the agency's 2002 GDP growth forecast has been revised to a range of 4% to 4.5%, from an earlier 3.5% to 4%, due to an improvement in exports and investment over the first quarter. 

 But it had little impact on the baht, which a trader said dipped to its lowest since May. 

 "The market is too busy following the rest of the (regional) currencies," he said, adding that there was rumor the Bank of Thailandintervened late in the session to stem the baht's decline. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted around 43.225. baht, from THB42.695 late Friday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Focus On US Factors, Iraq
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were a mixed bag late Thursday after the Sept. 11 anniversary of the terrorist attacks on the U.S. passed without incident. 

 But as in recent days, few market players took strong positions due to concerns over a possible war with Iraq, and uncertainty about the global economy. Any attack on Iraq would lead to higher oil prices, which would put a recovery under threat. 

 "People are looking for direction from the majors (currencies), U.S. growth and Iraq," said James Malcolm, foreign exchange strategist at J.P. Morgan Chase Bank in Singapore. 

 Traders said market players were focusing on U.S. President George W. Bush's speech to the U.N. later in the day for clues of a timeframe for any such attack on Iraq. 

 They are also hoping U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan will throw more light on the state of the U.S. economy when he testifies before the House Budget Committee later Thursday. 

 The New Taiwan dollar once again sank to its lowest level since late-May, closely tracking the yen's overnight losses. 

 The Philippine peso lost ground in late trading on a pickup in corporate demand for dollars. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah fell as local companies sought dollars to repay debt and fund imports. Some analysts said the rupiah was also weighed down by security threats. 

 But the South Korean won was lifted by exporters' dollar sales, while rumored central bank intervention by the Bank of Thailand helped keep the baht quite steady. 

 The Singapore dollar was volatile within a narrow range, veering between losses and gains against the U.S. currency. 

 Across the board, currencies were "like a yo-yo," a senior trader at an Asian bank in Singapore said. "The market is adjusting itself. It was slightly long dollars (previously). So there's a bit of dollar selling today," he added. 

 "Volumes are not big; nobody has come in in a big way, but it's (the market) been active." 

 The dollar ended higher against its Taiwan counterpart for the fourth straight session as foreign banks bought the U.S. unit following the yen's overnight losses. 

 The gains were partly trimmed as some of the banks reversed course and sold the dollar after it weakened against the yen later in the session. Exporters were also keen to sell the dollar after its recent gains, a dealer at a European bank said. 

 The New Taiwan dollar often tracks the yen because Taiwan and Japan compete in some export categories, and Taiwan also imports large amounts of goods from Japan. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.410 - another high since late-May - up from NT$34.395 Wednesday, after moving between NT$34.385 and NT$34.479 intraday. Dealings were valued at US$455 million, up from the previous day's US$371 million. 

 In Indonesia, the dollar rose as local companies bid for the currency to repay debt and fund imports. 

 The central bank reportedly sold small amounts of dollars at IDR8,895, but this didn't stop the U.S. unit from appreciating. 

 The dollar closed the Asian session at 8,920 rupiah, up from IDR8,890 Wednesday. 

 J.P. Morgan Chase's Malcolm said security and political concerns are also dogging the rupiah, and the already small number of players with exposure to Indonesia are unwinding short dollar positions against the rupiah. 

 In the Philippines, the currency market ignored a bomb scare at the British Embassy in Manila earlier Thursday after police found no explosives. 

 The dollar ended at 51.970 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, from PHP51.910 previously, due to relatively higher corporate demand near the close of trading, traders said. 

 Intraday, the dollar moved between PHP51.840 and PHP51.990, with volume rising to $120.45 million from $72.5 million Wednesday. 

 "Corporates are trigger-happy to buy dollars at levels below PHP51.90," said a trader with a foreign bank. 

 The peso's losses were limited by some banks unloading their excess dollar holdings. 

 Meanwhile, South Korean exporters continued their recent spree of dollar sales, helping the South Korean won stave off some of the impact of the yen's overnight fall. 

 The dollar closed at KRW1,201.4, down from KRW1,202.5 at the previous close, but the pair was confined to a tight band between KRW1,201.0 and KRW1,205.0. 

 "Frankly, this market is pretty hard to understand now because it's just stuck within a range," said a dealer in Seoul. "Nobody can find direction." 

 The dollar was choppy against its Singapore counterpart, moving up and down within a narrow trading band. Mainly, the Singapore dollar was tracking the yen's weaker tone, traders said. 

 The dollar opened lower as traders took profit following its sharp overnight gains against the yen and euro. 

 But major foreign banks then started to build fresh long dollar positions around S$1.7564. 

 As of 1027 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted around $S1.7592, from S$1.7551 late Wednesday. 

 Elsewhere, the dollar was quite steady against the Thai baht, with the central bank said to have stepped in to buy dollars at the THB42.39-THB42.40 level. 

 A trader at an Asian bank said the Bank of Thailand was rumored to have bought "quite a bit" of dollars -anything between $50 million and $100 million, he said. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted around THB42.522, from THB42.465 late Wednesday.

title: UPDATE 1-No plans to fire Thai c.bank chief - minister.
text:
BANGKOK, Aug 2 (Reuters) - Thailand's finance minister said on Friday the government had no plans to fire Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula despite complaints by Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra that the baht was too volatile. 

 Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak told reporters the government was not trying to interfere in the central bank's mandate to manage the currency. 

 Asked whether the central bank governor would be replaced, Somkid said: "No. Everything is okay. The prime minister has not criticised (the governor). All parties agree that the Bank of Thailand should be given full authority to manage the baht." 

 Thaksin reprimanded the central bank on Wednesday for not doing enough to curb the volatility of the baht, and demanded action to restrain the currency's swings. 

 The baht hit a two-year high of 40.20 to the dollar last month but has since weakened and was trading at 42.075 by 0531 GMT on Friday. 

 The central bank practices a "managed float" regime, saying it allows the baht to move in line with market forces but intervenes at times to reduce volatility. 

 Pridiyathorn said on Friday the central bank had intervened to stabilise the baht a week ago, and the currency had been steady since then. 

 "I have briefed the PM on the forex market and he is quite happy and pleased. There nothing to worry about," Pridiyathorn said. 

 Last month the currency surged after Thaksin said it would soon strengthen beyond 40 to the dollar. His comments prompted a rebuke from Pridiyathorn, who said Thaksin should refrain from commenting on central bank business. 

 In 2001, the government fired previous central bank governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul after a row over the appropriate level of interest rates. The government denied at the time that it was interfering with central bank independence. 

 The BOT has bought dollars in its bid to slow the baht appreciation in the past few weeks. The intervention has helped raise Thailand's foreign reserves to their highest level since January 1997.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Dulled by weekend,  intervention  worries.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 2 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were a mixed 

 bag in Friday trade, although a listless Japanese yen, the 

 approaching weekend and fears of intervention kept most from 

 rising much. 

     Regionals started the day firmer after weak U.S. economic 

 numbers undermined the dollar, but fears of intervention wiped 

 out gains in the Thailand baht and the Korean won 

 . 

     Traders were also unwilling to initiate positions before 

 the weekend with key U.S. unemployment numbers due later on 

 Friday, particularly after having seen two sets of dismal data

     "This is typical behaviour ahead of the weekend," Sameer 

 Goel, markets strategist with Bank of America, said.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Chief:PM No Longer Concerned Over THB Moves
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said he met with Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra Friday and explained to him the recent movements in the foreign exchange market, thereby defusing his concerns over the baht's volatility. 

 "I explained the situation to the prime minister with regard to his concerns over the high volatility of the baht," Pridiyathorn told reporters at the central bank. "The premier now understands the situation well and is no longer concerned." 

 Earlier this week, Thaksin criticized the central bank for failing to curb excess volatility in the baht in recent days, saying he would ask the central bank to manage the currency more actively. 

 The baht has strengthened this year against the dollar, gaining more than 6% in the first half as a result of the U.S. unit's weakening global trend. 

 However, the baht slipped sharply late last week and early this week following a general rebound in the dollar, a slip that prompted Thaksin's comments. 

 Pridiyathorn said he explained to Thaksin that the baht was most volatile July 25 when the yen moved sharply lower to the dollar. That was a public holiday in Thailand and the central bank therefore couldn't intervene in the market. 

 "So we entered the market one day late, Friday, and by Monday the situation was back to normal," he said. 

 Since the baht's flotation in 1997, the central bank has been pursuing a managed float exchange-rate policy, allowing the currency to move in line with the market trend but stepping in to limit excess volatility in either direction. 

 Pridiyathorn said he will also talk with exporters to explain to them how to use available risk management tools, such as forward cover and options, to minimize their exposure to exchange rate fluctuations. 

 At 0910 GMT (5:10 a.m. EDT), the dollar was trading at 42.135 baht, slightly down from THB42.155 at Thursday's close.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Traders eye Wall Street sell-off.
text:

 impact that Friday's sell-off on Wall Street will have on the 

 dollar and regional equity markets. 

     Dealers said a sell-off in Asian stocks in sympathy with

     "Wall Street fears reign. Markets around the region are

title: UPDATE 1-Thai reserves hit 5-year high on baht  intervention .
text:
BANGKOK, July 19 (Reuters) - Thailand's foreign reserves jumped by nearly two percent to a five-year high last week, official data showed on Friday, as the country's central bank bought dollars to slow a rise in the Thai currency. 

 Bank of Thailand (BOT) figures showed official foreign reserves jumped by $714 million to $37.62 billion in the week to July 12, taking the central bank's financial war-chest to its highest level since April 1997. 

 The rise reflects steady buying by the BOT of dollars and sales of the baht, which has appreciated sharply as the U.S. currency has fallen on world markets and as the Thai economy has expanded more quickly than expected this year. 

 The Thai baht hit 40.20 per dollar on July 16, its strongest level since July 2000. Since then, the baht has eased back but still stood at around 40.50 by 0930 GMT on Friday, well above its recent low of 45.87 per dollar seen almost exactly a year ago. 

 Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula confirmed this week that the central bank had intervened to try to restrain the rise in the Thai unit and limit its volatility. 

 On Friday, a central bank official attributed the $714 million rise in the reserves last week partly to intervention. 

 "The rise was partly due to dollar buying," the official, who declined to be identified, told Reuters. 

 "Part of the increase was also due to an upward mark-to-market of the value of other assets held as part of our reserves," she said, but declined to elaborate. 

 PRE-CRISIS LEVEL 

 Thailand's reserves - consisting of dollars, gold, special drawing rights with the International Monetary Fund and other foreign currencies - have risen by $4.6 billion this year and are now above their level before the Asian crisis of 1997/98. 

 The increase is partly a by-product of the Bank of Thailand's "managed float" policy for the currency, where the baht can move freely on foreign exchange markets but the Thai authorities intervene from time to time to try to reduce its volatility. 

 But the rise in reserves also reflects a desire by the government of Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra to avoid a repeat of the crisis of 1997/98, which saw the baht crash to a low of 56.9 per dollar in early 1998 from 25 per dollar a year earlier. 

 The fall of the baht - caused by more than a decade of Thai current account deficits and heavy speculative selling by hedge funds as the Thai authorities attempted to peg the baht to the dollar - triggered a pan-Asian economic crisis and regional recession. 

 Several of the ministers of the current government, including Thaksin, were members of administrations just before the crisis. 

 General Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, now defence minister, was prime minister on July 2 when the Bank of Thailand finally gave up its defence of the baht and allowed it to plummet. 

 Economists say Thaksin's administration believes a high level of foreign reserves is essential to avoid another crisis - even though the Thai economy is now much stronger than it was five years ago and has been running healthy current account surpluses. 

 The Thai economy is likely to grow by around four percent in 2002, after an expansion of 1.8 percent in 2001, analysts say. 

 The increase of almost $5 billion in foreign reserves has so far had little impact on the Thai economy, thanks partly to the sale of large volumes of Thai baht bonds. 

 "This (rise in the reserves) should have caused base money to rise 40 percent," Merrill Lynch Phatra Securities said in a note to clients this week. "But the forex intervention was sterilized by an equivalent sale of the BOT's domestic assets. Base money has been kept more or less stable at 550 billion baht."

title: Thai c.bank  intervenes  to curb baht volatility.
text:
BANGKOK, July 17 (Reuters) - Thailand's central bank said on Wednesday it entered the market to curb the volatility of the baht, which surged this week to near two-year highs versus the dollar to the dismay of some exporters and industrialists. 

 "We have entered to ease its volatility," central bank governor Pridiyathorn Devakula told a news conference. But he said this "managed float" system was not uncommon and did not mean the bank was ignoring market forces. 

 "Everybody is on the managed float regime. Nobody is on free float. On the other hand, we need to follow market forces. We can't resist them," he said. 

 The baht moved strongly higher this week after Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said the currency could soon breach 40 to the dollar. 

 It eased slightly on Wednesday, hit by talk in Singapore that foreign names were buying dollars on behalf of the central bank to slow its rise. 

 The central bank has said the baht remains competitive as its appreciation has been in line with the gains of other regional currencies against the dollar. 

 But some companies have warned the strong baht will stifle exports, one of the main engines of growth of the Thai economy. 

 Exports account for more than 55 percent of Thai gross domestic product. 

 Thaksin said earlier on Wednesday the baht should be allowed to move in line with market forces. 

 "We should not resist them," he told reporters. 

 On Tuesday the head of Thailand's largest industrial conglomerate told Reuters in an interview that the baht's strength could be damaging for Thailand. 

 Siam Cement President Chumpol NaLamlieng said exports and the agricultural sector would be hurt if the baht continued to appreciate.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Governor: Baht Now Stable; Not Worrisome
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said late Tuesday the level of the baht is now stable, despite the fact it hit a new 23-month high against the dollar Tuesday. 

 Pridiyathorn said he wasn't concerned about the current level of the baht, although he didn't comment on earlier market talk that the central bank may have intervened to stem the baht's appreciation. 

 "I am not worried about the baht and quite comfortable with it. The baht is stable now," Pridiyathorn told reporters. 

 He was relieved as the dollar regained some ground against the yen and the euro. 

 After the dollar touched an intraday low at THB40.28, it jerked up to THB40.40 in the afternoon in what traders suspect was an attempt by the central bank to cap the baht's rise. 

 However, the dollar soon resumed its slide in line with its general weakness against most Asian currencies. 

 However, Pridiyathorn said that the Thai baht was still in a managed float system, which means the central bank reserves the right to monitor and intervene in the market to shape movements in the currency. 

 "Thailand is using the managed float system. But, I didn't say we intervened in the market today," he said. 

 Pridiyathorn also noted the current baht level is still competitive for Thai exports. 

 "Nobody can predict the baht level. It will be decided by market mechanisms," he said. 

 Pridiyathorn's comment came after Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said Monday that the Thai baht would soon break below 40-baht to the dollar. 

 The market took Thaksin's comments as a green light for faster baht appreciation, pushing the dollar sharply lower and breaking 41-baht to the dollar Monday before falling to a 23-month low of THB40.295 to the dollar at the end of Asian trade Tuesday.

title: Thai Fin Min: THB Rise Not Sole Factor Hampering Exports
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thai Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said Wednesday the central bank is monitoring the Thai baht to keep it at a competitive level compared with other nation's currencies. 

 "If the Thai baht stay at a competitive level compared to other currencies. Its strength is not worrisome," Somkid told reporters. 

 He said the Thai baht's current strength isn't the only factor hampering exports and the main factor is the performance of exporters. 

 Previously, he said exporters have to improve their competitiveness in terms of cost-effectiveness, quality and productivity. 

 Thai exports showed a year-on-year contraction in the first quarter of this year, but picked up in the second quarter in line with the economic recovery of the country's trade partners. 

 At 0535 GMT (1:35 a.m. EDT), the dollar was quoted at THB41.115 baht, a fresh 22-month low, in line with its sharp fall against major currencies. 

 Thai central bank said recently that the Thai baht was still at a competitive level and had appreciated against the U.S. dollar less than other currencies had. 

 However, the Bank of Thailand warned that it may intervene if the baht started to move against regional market trends.

title: Thai Baht Hits New High On Dollar Stop-loss Selling
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht hit a new 22-month high at the close of Asian spot trade Tuesday, due to stop-loss dollar selling after the U.S. currency fell below key support, traders said. 

 The dollar ended the bumpy day at its intraday low at 41.30 baht, down from THB41.45 at Asian markets close Monday. 

 The U.S. currency opened around THB41.40 as offshore players continued to sell the dollar, taking their cue from its overnight weakness against the Japanese yen. 

 "The greenback dropped to THB41.33 in the morning, but then staged a brisk rebound to THB41.41 within 10 or 20 minutes," said a trader at a foreign bank, "A U.S. bank seemed to be behind that quick swing." 

 Traders said the move appeared to be driven by short-term speculation and didn't seem to be an intervention by the Bank of Thailand, which usually sets a bid before it starts buying. The central bank has been occasionally buying dollars to build its foreign exchange reserves and slow the baht's appreciation against the dollar. It usually acts through certain Japanese banks. 

 As the sudden demand petered out, the dollar resumed its weakening trend in the afternoon, fueled by the yen's strength on demand from European markets. 

 The dollar traded between Y118.35 and Y118.95 on the spot market Tuesday morning in Asia - near its recent nine-month low against the yen - on ongoing concerns about the accuracy of U.S. corporate accounts. 

 The U.S. unit hovered around THB41.35 in Thai afternoon trade, as the dollar-yen managed to hold above Y118.50. 

 However, volatility erupted again as the U.S. currency lost its support against the Thai unit on profit-taking by those who collected the U.S. unit earlier in the day, a trader said. 

 "The dollar's slip below THB41.35 also ignited stop-loss selling that sent it to the intraday low," he said. 

 Traders expected the U.S. unit to move between THB41.25 and THB41.40 when Asian markets open Wednesday. 

 Thai government bond prices ended higher Tuesday as institutional investors returned to buy medium to long-term papers after their recent falls, traders said. 

 The bond market has been bullish since concerns over new supply in the secondary market from the Financial Institutions Development Fund, or FIDF, disappeared. The plan is to issue savings bonds, which won't be traded on the secondary market. 

 Gains in U.S. Treasurys Monday and expectations that U.S. interest rates will stay flat this year also helped boost sentiment, traders added. 

 Goldman Sachs has pushed back its view on when it expects the next interest rate hike by the U.S. Federal Reserve to the second half of 2003 from November, citing a recent slowing in real consumer spending growth, weak equity prices and a recent Fed study suggesting that the central bank should err on the side of over-accomodation. 

 "Funds stepped in to snap up the bonds after their weakness late last week. The market sentiment is very good, so there is no reason to sell at the moment. Investors just wait for a good time to buy," a local bank trader said. 

 Yields dropped five basis points from Monday. Yields moves in the opposite direction to prices. 

 The bond maturing December 2008 closed in a bid-offer range of 4.19%-4.18% versus 4.25% at Monday's close, while the April 2014 issue finished at 4.80%-4.78%, compared with 4.85% at the previous close. 

 The Finance Ministry has sold at an auction THB1 billion of 10-year state enterprise bonds to be issued by the Expressway & Rapid Transit Authority of Thailand, or ETA, at a yield of 5.340%. 

 The ETA bond yield was quite good, as expected, offering a nine basis point premium over the government bond of the same maturity. 

 Thai one-day repurchase interest rate dropped slightly as most banks were flush with liquidity.

title: Most Asian  Currencies  Up Late; Dlr Hits Multi-Month Lows
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The dollar sank to fresh multi-month lows against most Asian currencies Wednesday as news of yet another potential accounting scandal in the U.S. fueled fears of more capital flight from U.S. markets. 

 Telecom giant WorldCom Inc. announced overnight that it had improperly booked $3.8 billion of expenses as capital expenditures over the past five quarters, obliging it to restate its earnings. 

 Adding to the pressure on the dollar in global markets were comments by President George W. Bush and Treasury Secretary Paul O'Neill seemingly endorsing a weaker U.S. currency. 

 Both spoke of the dollar's recent movements reflecting market forces. But perhaps most significant was Bush's additional reference implying that a weaker currency could help the U.S. manufacturing sector. 

 "The dollar will seek its level based upon market forces, and based on whether or not our country can rein in spending, can recover, can revitalize our manufacturing base," Bush said at a meeting of world leaders in Canada. 

 UBS Warburg said Bush's comment was "extremely bad news for the dollar as it represents a massive watering down - albeit implicitly - of the strong dollar policy." 

 Selling pressure against the dollar was so strong in Asia that aggressive foreign exchange market intervention by Japanese authorities to prop up the dollar did little to halt the currency's decline against the yen. 

 The dollar fell to a 21-month low against the Thai baht, an 18-month low against the South Korean won, a 13-month low against the New Taiwan dollar and a nine-month low against the Singapore dollar. The dollar also weakened against the Philippine peso, but strengthened against the Indonesian rupiah. 

 WorldCom's announcement, following a string of accounting scandal's starting with Enron Corp.'s collapse last year, dealt another blow to faith in U.S. asset markets. 

 Sharp declines in Nasdaq and S&P 500 stock futures in Asian trading promised heavy losses on Wall Street Wednesday. 

 "Yet another accounting scandal may make investors think twice about buying any U.S. stocks. That's bound to be bad for the dollar," Bank of America said in a research note. 

 Against the won, the dollar closed at KRW1,203.9, down from KRW1,213.7 Tuesday. It was the won's strongest showing since December 2000. 

 The Ministry of Finance and Economy's reiteration that it is "deeply concerned" about the dollar's fall versus the won had only fleeting impact on the local currency's rise. 

 The New Taiwan dollar's advance was restrained by forceful central bank intervention. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$33.622 versus NT$33.738 Tuesday. It was the local currency's strongest finish since May 2001. 

 The central bank bought an estimated US$500 million to keep a floor under the U.S. currency, dealers said. Without the intervention the U.S. dollar probably would have fallen through the NT$33.500 level, they added. 

 The Thai baht benefited from the strength of its regional peers and comments from a Bank of Thailand official Tuesday that the central bank would probably not intervene in foreign exchange markets to curb the local currency's strength. 

 Late in Asia the dollar was quoted at THB41.740, down from THB41.900 late Tuesday. It was the baht's strongest finish since September 2000. 

 The Singapore dollar took advantage of the broad U.S. dollar weakness to post its best performance since last September. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the U.S. currency was quoted at S$1.7633, down from S$1.7719 late Tuesday. 

 A report showing better-than-expected industrial output performance for Singapore in May also pressured the U.S. dollar, though the data failed to push the U.S. currency below a key support of S$1.7620. 

 The peso's gains were more muted due in part to ongoing investor concerns about the country's growing budget deficit. 

 The dollar ended at 50.35 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, down from Tuesday's PHP50.45. 

 "The peso should be trading below PHP50.00 by now if it weren't for concerns on the budget deficit and lack of dollar supply," a trader at local bank said. 

 The rupiah failed to take advantage of the dollar's broad decline as local companies bought the U.S. currency to repay foreign debt. 

 Late in Asia the dollar was quoted at IDR8,685, up from IDR8,675 late Tuesday.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Stay on high ground, data, Fed eyed.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 21 (Reuters) - Asian currencies found strength in dollar weakness on Friday but regional bulls lacked the resolve to aggressively push them, fearing central banks might act to rein them in. 

 The Thai baht was kept at 42.00 - a level unbreached since December 26, 2000 - on rumours of the Bank of Thailand's presence in the market. The central bank, however, said it had no plans to intervene. 

 The dollar hit 2-year lows against the euro and languished around its three-week trough against the yen, clouded by a gaping U.S. current account deficit and wobbly U.S. stocks. 

 Despite the Bank of Japan's remarks earlier on Friday that it did not intervene in the market following the dollar's brief jump, dealers did not rule out potential intervention later in the day, especially after the dollar/yen broke 123. 

 "Given that market will be very thin in London with the World Cup in progress, this should be an ideal time for the BoJ to intervene," said Ron Leven, currency strategist at Lehman Brothers in Tokyo. 

 "If they remain quiet into the close tonight, it will send a message that they are shifting down their level of dollar defence," he said. 

 The Singapore dollar tracked the yen higher, with the momentum picking up after it broke past the 1.7800 barrier for the first time since October 5 last year. 

 The currency was trading around 1.7702 in late trade. At current levels, the Sing dollar looks overbought against the U.S. dollar on technical charts. 

 The Indonesian rupiah pared earlier gains, dipping below 8,600 on the back of strong corporate dollar demand. 

 THAI DEBT PLAN 

 Besides fears of intervention, market sentiment in Thailand was weighed on by the government's plan to issue 300 billion baht of bonds this year to help refinance massive debts run up while bailing out banks and finance firms during Asian crisis. 

 "We are still digesting it. But on the surface, this does not look like a good fiscal discipline," said a dealer at a European bank in Singapore. 

 "The scheme also involves the central bank using reserve funds to meet liabilities. If the reserves are converted into the baht from the dollar to meet these liabilities, it could add upward pressure on the local currency when its export recovery remains fragile," he said. 

 MARKET WATCHES FED, DATA 

 Ahead of a busy week, some players found little incentive to take aggressive positions going into the weekend. 

 The U.S. Federal Reserve meets on June 25-26, with most analysts expecting the central bank to hold its key rates steady. 

 While market consensus is that the U.S. is unlikely to experience a double-dip recession, some contrarians see a good chance of that happening. 

 "There's a 40 percent chance the U.S. GDP growth could turn negative some time in the second half of this year," Stephen Roach, chief economist at Morgan Stanley, told reporters via a video conference from London on Thursday. 

 "If that were to occur, one of the bigger surprises will be that the next move of the U.S. Federal Reserve will not be to tighten interest rates, but actually cut interest rates." 

 Singapore will release May consumer prices on Monday and Taiwan is to announce its leading economic indicator on Thursday. 

 Thailand will publish its key monthly economic indicators on Friday, which include trade, industrial output and current account data.

title: Thai c.bank says has no plans to  intervene  on baht.
text:
BANGKOK, June 21 (Reuters) - Bank of Thailand (BOT) Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said on Friday the central bank would not intervene to soften the strengthening baht since the local unit was moving in line with other regional currencies. 

 "We don't have to do anything now. There is no need to be worried since it has been staying at the 42 level for quite a long time," Pridiyathorn told Reuters when asked if the central bank would intervene. 

 Bangkok dealers told Reuters early on Thursday the central bank was detected in the market supporting the dollar from 42.10, but the amount was small. The baht was trading around 42 to the dollar by 0500 GMT on Friday.

title: Emerging Asia  FX  - Stronger as dollar wobbles.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 21 (Reuters) - Asian currencies held on to 

 their strength in early trade on Friday as pressure mounted on 

 many fronts on the dollar. 

     But their appreciation were slowed somewhat by wariness of 

intervention by some central banks, which want to ensure their 

 local currencies do not move up too rapidly and threaten to 

 hurt export competitiveness. 

     Trading is expected to be lacklustre as players shift their 

 attention to the World Cup quarter-finals. England and Brazil 

 will slug it out at 0630 GMT while Germany and the United 

 States follow at 1130 GMT. 

     "People in the market seem to be talking more about the 

 World Cup than they do the dollar. I suspect the market might 

 come to a standstill in the afternoon...an unofficial half-day 

 holiday if you like," said a dealer at an Asian bank in 

 Singapore. 

     The U.S. currency sank further across the board. Against 

 the yen, it extended losses to 123.30 after senior Japanese 

 Finance Ministry official Zembei Mizoguchi said the ministry 

 did not intervene in the currency market following a sudden, 

 brief jump in the dollar. 

 The U.S. currency, which has been fighting an uphill battle 

 against other majors for a while, was pressured further by news 

 of a record U.S. trade deficit and sliding stocks. 

 Its current account deficit - the broadest measure of 

 trade and service with foreign countries - hit a record 

 $112.50 billion, up sharply from a revised estimate of $95.10 

 billion in the last quarter of 2001. 

 "I see the dollar's downtrend remaining intact in the very 

 near term. The area everyone is looking at is 122.80-123.00, 

 with the first being the last major intervention level. People 

 will be cautious when they get to those levels," said Andrew 

 Fung, head of treasury research at Rabobank in Singapore. 

 THAI BAHT TOP HEAVY 

 The Thai baht retained a firm tone, but bulls were 

 still reluctant to push it past the key 42 resistance amid talk 

 of central bank intervention on Thursday. 

 However, some argued there was no incentive for the Bank of 

Thailand to intervene at this point given the baht still looked 

 fine on its nominal effective exchange rate. 

 "But we believe there is a good chance that if the 

 dollar/baht threatens to move below 41.90 without any 

 supporting dollar/yen decline, the Bank of Thailand will start 

 to become uncomfortable," said Rabobank's Fung. 

 The Korean won -2 traded near its morning high of 

 1,219.20 on the back of the dollar's decline against the yen, 

 but its upside was limited by government comments. 

 A senior Finance Ministry official said on Friday the 

 ministry was deeply concerned about the recent volatile moves 

 in the dollar/won rate and would take action to stabilise the 

 market if necessary. 

 RUPIAH UP ON IBRA TALK 

 The Indonesian rupiah was supported by rumours that 

 the Bank Restructuring Agency (IBRA) sold dollars through local 

 banks. The currency was quoted around 8,560/8,600 at 0315 GMT. 

 Sentiment was also boosted by IBRA's comments on Thursday 

 that it hoped to reach a $5 billion 2002 revenue target from 

 asset sales by September instead of year-end as part of efforts 

 to help reduce the state budget deficit. 

 The agency was set up during the Asian financial crisis in 

 the late 1990s to manage assets taken over from troubled state 

 debtors. 

 But the rupiah's rise is likely to be curbed by corporate 

 dollar demand and the fact that the market is pretty short of 

 the dollar at the moment, dealers said. 

 The Taiwan dollar rose past the 34 to the dollar 

 threshold on the back of a firmer yen and the absence of the 

central bank in early trade. 

 The local currency traded around 33.854 - its 12-month 

 high - compared with 43.001 at the open and 34.023 at the 

 close on Thursday.
