title: Thai Baht Ends Up At 16-Mo High On Equity-Related Inflows
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended firmer against the U.S. dollar in Asian spot trade Tuesday thanks to equity-related inflows, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 42.285 baht, its weakest level since February 2001. On Monday, it ended at THB42.41. 

 The dollar's bearish tone against most key currencies also helped the baht, traders added. 

 The U.S. currency opened at THB42.40, the day's high, and had been on a downward path since as offshore players and exporters continued to unload dollars, triggered by portfolio investment-related inflows. 

 Foreign investors have been active net buyers on the Thai bourse recently. So far this month, they have bought a net THB4.01 billion worth of local stocks. 

 Moreover, the Bank of Thailand's tolerance toward the baht's recent gains also helped curb intervention jitters among market players. 

 Bank of Thailand Deputy Governor Pakorn Malakul Na Ayudhya said Tuesday that the baht's recent strength is in line with the dollar's weakness against other regional currencies. 

 He said the central bank isn't concerned by the baht's real effective exchange rate against regional and other currencies, which is in line with the general trend. The real effective exchange rate is a measure of the country's export competitiveness. 

 "This comment shows that the central bank is OK with the current baht level. That comforts most players to sell the dollar further," said a local dealer. 

 Traders expect the dollar to open Wednesday between THB42.20 and THB42.40, barring any sharp movements in the yen. 

 Thai long-term government bond prices rose slightly Tuesday on bargain hunting amid liquidity-driven demand, but failed to recover much of Monday's losses, traders said. Prices fell Monday on renewed fears of massive state-sector supply in the second half. 

 The short-term government bond due November 2004 ended in a bid-offer range of 2.45%-2.44%, down from 2.48%-2.46% at the close Monday. Bond yields and prices move in opposite directions. 

 The long-term issue due April 2010 finished at 5.03%-5.01%, down from 5.04%-5.02%. 

 Bank of Thailand has said it will announce by the end of the month detailed plans for the issuance of up to THB320 billion in bonds by the state Financial Institutions Development Fund, or FIDF. 

 Unconfirmed reports from central bank sources have said the issues will carry terms of 20 to 30 years, and that some of the total will be placed with the central bank or financial institutions. 

 The planned bonds should replace the FIDF's current short-term borrowings from financial institutions in the repurchase market. 

 The secondary bond market was expected to remain in a tight range in the near term. Any significant drop in yields before the end of the month is likely to invite sharp losses on occasional reports about the FIDF's issuance plans. 

 The finance ministry auctioned Tuesday THB1.2 billion worth of 10-year government-guaranteed bonds to be issued by the state Expressway & Rapid Transit Authority, or ETA, at an accepted yield of 5.595%. The premium over the government bond yield curve was within expectations at just under 15 basis points. 

 Thai money market interest rates were mostly flat at low levels as the financial system remained flooded with excess liquidity. 

 The overnight interbank rate slipped to 1.875% from 1.9375%, as continued dollar selling began to contribute to financial institutions' baht liquidity.

title: Thai c.bank says no need to  intervene  on baht.
text:
BANGKOK, May 21 (Reuters) - Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said on Tuesday he saw no need for the central bank to intervene on the baht and it had not entered the market. 

 Asked on the BOT had intervened, following a modest easing by the baht, he said: "The baht's easing was in line with the market. The Bank of Thailand does not need to do anything and it has not done anything." 

 The baht stood at around 42.70/74 per dollar at 0712 GMT against 42.57 at the close on Monday. The currency has been trading at its highest levels in more than a year, sparking worries among some analysts that exports could suffer.

title: Emerging  FX -Mostly firm, peso and won hit new highs.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 20 (Reuters) - Asian currencies held a 

 firmer tone early Monday while the dollar struggled to regain 

 some composure after last week's sharp falls. 

     Dealers said hopes of economic recovery and foreign inflows 

 in equity markets would push most Asian currencies higher, with 

 little or no threat of resistance expected by authorities. 

     "With Asian policy makers taking a more relaxed stance on 

 dollar weakness...the dollar continues to be re-rated 

 downwards," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, currency strategist at UBS 

 Warburg in Singapore. 

     He said last week's implicit condoning of currency strength 

 by top finance officials in Korea, Singapore and Thailand would 

 encourage players to test their new tolerance levels this week. 

     Meanwhile, the dollar struggled off an early low of 128.18 

 yen after Japan's top financial diplomat Haruhiko Kuroda 

 said there was no need for it to strengthen against the 

 greenback. 

     Senior Finance Ministry official Zembei Mizoguchi said the 

 ministry was always prepared to take action against excessive 

 moves in foreign exchange markets. 

     Those comments prompted rounds of short-covering and 

 bargain-hunting from institutional investors, providing some 

 support to the dollar. 


    The euro        held firm at around 0.9200 cents against



the dollar.



    PESO, WON HIT NEW HIGHS, RUPIAH DITHER

per dollar, backed by trade data showing a 10 percent jump in



imports in March. The data raised hopes that the economy was on

Korean won -2. It touched a 15-month high of 1,253.3

However, the Indonesian rupiah drifted slightly away



from a test of 9,000 per dollar, a level it had not breached

Dealers in Singapore said strong corporate bids for dollars



just ahead of 9,000 level prompted interbank players to cover



some of their short dollar positions.



The rupiah eased to 9,080 from an early high of 9,060 and



late Friday's 9,070. But dealers said most players expect a



breach of the 9,000 level later in the day.



SGD & BAHT FIRM UP



The Singapore dollar retested a seven-month high at



1.7930, touched on Friday, with market focus on the dollar's



losses against other major currencies.



Dealers said the Sing dollar was still supported by a



positive bias after recent economic data showed that a recovery



was in the works.



    But local corporates dollar bids around 1.7930-1.7940 was



capping gains for now.



    The Sing dollar last Friday was around 1.8000 when the


Monetary Authority of Singapore said the currency strength was



within its policy parameters.



    The Thai baht        rose to 42.60, from late Friday's



42.71, taking cue from the firmer tone in the yen and other



regionals.



    Dealers in Singapore said the market was less concerned



about Bank of Thailand intervening to cap baht's rise, but

title: UPDATE 2-Thailand says unconcerned by stronger baht.
text:
BANGKOK, May 7 (Reuters) - Thai authorities said on Tuesday they were not concerned over the strengthening baht currency, classing its recent gains as temporary and unlikely to affect exports which are key to sustaining economic recovery. 

Central bank governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said the rise in the baht to 14-month highs had not hurt exporters, and the Bank of Thailand (BOT) would not intervene to weaken the currency. 

 "The baht is not too strong. It still benefits exporters, since our (currency) has only risen by 0.5 percent, compared with other countries' that have risen by two to three percent," Pridiyathorn told reporters. 

 "Therefore I see no need of taking any action." 

 Earlier, the baht was trading at 42.82/42.86 to the dollar, up almost three percent from a high of 44.13 on January 2. By 1130 GMT it slipped to 42.88/42.92. 

 Despite Pridiyathorn's confidence, dealers said the latest foreign reserves data - showing a rise of $400 million in a week to $34.60 billion as of April 26 - suggested the central bank may have intervened lately. 

 Commerce Minister Adisai Bodharamik said earlier on Tuesday the strong baht would not hurt exports, but that he preferred to see the unit weaken. 

 "I see the current strong baht as temporary and we can handle that...but it should be around 44 baht," Adisai told reporters. 

 Adisai said later there would only be cause for concern if the baht continued to remain strong over a longer period. "If the baht continues at the current level for some time, our exports will face a tougher time as their prices will rise." 

 Analysts said the baht's strength was driven more by the direction of the dollar/yen rate than local factors. 

 "It's still a story of the dollar's weakness rather than the baht's strength," said Andrew Fung, head of treasury research at Rabobank in Singapore. 

 "Having said that, I must add the Thai economic outlook has improved, but I don't think that will be enough to stop the baht from weakening if the dollar/yen turns around," Fung said. 

 Thailand's central bank last week raised its forecast for economic growth this year to 2.5-3.5 percent from a previous projection of 2-3 percent, citing increased consumer spending and a faster global recovery. 

 But the central bank scaled down its 2002 export growth projection to 1-3 percent from 3-4 percent after exports dropped a bigger than expected 6.3 percent year-on-year in the first quarter. 

 In 2001, the economy grew 1.8 percent and exports, which account for about 55 percent of gross domestic product, slumped 6.9 percent. 

 The finance ministry and International Monetary Fund have also raised their growth forecasts this month, to 3.6 percent and 2.7 percent respectively.

title: Thai c.bank says won't  intervene  to weaken baht.
text:
BANGKOK, May 7 (Reuters) - Thai central bank governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said on Tuesday a recent rise in the baht had not hurt Thai exporters and the Bank of Thailand (BOT) would not intervene in the market to depress the currency. 

 "The baht is not too strong. It still benefits exporters since our (currency) only has risen by 0.5 percent, compared with other countries' (currencies) that have risen by two to three percent," Pridiyathorn told reporters. 

 By 0525 GMT, the Thai baht traded at 42.85/42.88 to the dollar, close to its highest level in 14 months.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Gov: Baht Is Not Too Strong
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thai central bank Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said Tuesday that the baht's recent strength against the U.S. dollar hasn't been excessive relative to the region's currencies. 

 "When the dollar is weakening like this, it's impossible that the baht wouldn't move. Baht strength is due to market mechanisms," Pridiyathorn told reporters. 

 Since the baht has moved in line with the currencies of Thailand's regional trade partners and export competitors, its current level still supports exports, he said. 

 Against the U.S. dollar, the yen has strengthened 2.5%, the Singapore dollar 2%, while the baht has risen only 0.5%, Pridiyathorn said, without indicating the exact period. 

 The U.S. dollar was quoted at THB42.83 in early afternoon trade Tuesday, down from THB42.87 at the Asian open and THB43.065 at the Asian close Friday, in line with the U.S. unit's losses against the Japanese yen. Thai markets were closed for a public holiday Monday. 

 Pridiyathorn's remarks had little effect on foreign exchange markets because the central bank is believed to have been regularly buying dollars on weakness this year to maintain foreign reserves while paying back loans from an expired International Monetary Fund rescue program. 

 The governor said previously that he doesn't consider such activity to be intervention. 

 Bank of Thailand's foreign reserves rose $400 million in the week to April 26 to $34.6 billion, although part of the increase was probably due to revaluation of yen holdings. Under Pridiyathorn, the central bank has ceased to provide explanations for movement in the country's foreign reserve levels. 

 Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said separately Tuesday that Bank of Thailand should continue to monitor the foreign exchange market, so that the baht doesn't strengthen to the point where export competitiveness is weakened. 

 Somkid said current baht levels and the recent appreciation haven't hurt exports much so far, however. 

 Earlier Tuesday, Commerce Minister Adisai Bhodaramik said a good exchange rate range for the country's exports would be between THB43 and THB44 to the dollar. 

 The baht shouldn't be too strong, but it wouldn't be a problem if it doesn't stay too strong for too long, he said. 

 Adisai doesn't have any direct influence on foreign exchange policy, but his ministry is charged with increasing exports. 

 He said Thailand's poor export performance recently was caused by slow global demand, not by the baht's strength against the dollar. 

 Thai exports were down 4.6% from the same month last year in March, according to central bank data. 

 The March performance was an improvement over the last few months, however. Exports amounted to $5.56 billion, above $5 billion for the first time since November 2001 amid signs of recovery in global demand.

title: Emerging  FX  - Ease with yen,  central bank  jitters.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 30 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies were 

 easier early on Tuesday as the yen took a breather after 

 its recent run up to multi-month highs against the dollar. 


    The only exception was the Philippine peso        which



continued its rally from Monday hitting fresh seven-month highs



around 50.60 per dollar.



    In rest of the region, with the yen easing back to levels



beyond 128 per dollar from near two-month highs of 127.65,



players feared central banks might intervene to cap any



trade-weighted exchange rate gains.



    "Asian bulls need to be aware," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin,



UBS Warburg's currency strategist in Singapore.



    Analysts say that with the export sector in most regional



economies still in early stages of recovery, the recent forex


rally could be quite near the threshold of their monetary



authorities who are concerned about export competitiveness.



The recent net sale of local stocks by foreign equity



investors in most Asian markets, part of which could end up



chasing dollars, was also likely to offset any gains from the



usual month-end dollar sales by exporters.



Mohi-uddin said central banks of Singapore and Thailand


might be the first ones to intervene in case of any sharp



gains, while equity-related dollar outflows have already



started to weigh down the Korean won and the Thai baht.



CENTRAL BANKS SCARE



The Singapore dollar eased to hit a session low of



1.8107 from late Monday's 1.8063 as the dollar recovered some



lost ground against the yen and euro .



The currencies are a major component of the trade-weighted



basket of currencies the Singapore authorities use to manage



their exchange rate.



Dealers said players were covering short dollar positions



as some suspect that Monday's dollar purchases by local banks



starting from 1.8030-1.8020 range was for the central bank.



    Those dollar purchases helped pull the Sing dollar down



from 1.8010 six-month peak hit on Monday.



    The Sing dollar has been in an upchannel since late March



when it was around 1.8500 and has gained 2.42 percent



year-to-date.



    Illustrating lingering worries over the pace of recovery,



Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said late on Monday that cost



pressures could weaken Singapore's recovery from recession and



unemployment may reach 5.5 to 6.0 percent.



Meanwhile, the Thai baht edged lower to 43.25 from



late Monday's 43.18 as offshore players squared their short



dollar positions ahead of economic data for March and revised


central bank macro targets due later on Tuesday.



    Dealers in Singapore said the market was waiting for the



Bank of Thailand's view on the export sector outlook.



    A weak exports outlook is likely to strengthen fears of


central bank intervention that has kept the baht in a narrow



43.10-43.20 range in the past several sessions. The baht has



gained over two percent year-to-date.



PESO PERKY, RUPIAH QUIET



The peso briefly edged to 50.71 session low but perked up



to around 50.63, a seven-month high hit on Monday, in response



to the central bank's bullish comments over the currency.



    The central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said he



expected the peso to strengthen to 50.50 to the dollar.



    The comment sent local players scrambling to cover their



short peso positions they had built in anticipation of violent



protests by opposition parties on the Labour Day on Wednesday.



    The Indonesian rupiah was easier at around 9,350, from late



Monday's 9,310 as the positive impact of International Monetary



Fund's approval of another $347 million loan tranche faded



away.



Dealers in Singapore said the rupiah was expected to remain



range bound especially amid thin trading interest ahead of the



Labour Day holiday on Wednesday.

title: Thai Baht Ends Up Against Dollar; Tracking Firmer Yen
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended higher against the U.S. dollar in Asian spot trade Thursday, tracking strength in the yen. But support for the dollar from local corporate demand and offshore short-dollar covering prevented the baht from matching the yen's sharp gains, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 43.225 baht, down from THB43.29 at the Asian close Wednesday. 

 The U.S. unit opened down in Bangkok from the previous close at THB43.255, after the dollar/yen slipped below Y130 overnight. 

 As the yen strengthened to under Y129 to the dollar during the Asian session, however, firm support was in turn provided to the U.S. currency at THB43.20 from local corporate demand and by squaring of short-dollar positions to take profits. 

 Some traders also suspected the Bank of Thailand had intervened in the market to prevent a sharp appreciation in the baht, which would hurt exporters. Others were skeptical though as Thursday's movements in the baht weren't out of line with the regional trend. 

 If the dollar/yen rate keeps heading south, dealers said the U.S. dollar could breach support at THB43.20 overnight. The dollar is expected to open in Asian trade Friday in a range of THB43.10 to THB43.25. 

 Thai government bond prices closed higher Thursday supported by demand due to the excess liquidity in the financial system and an improvement in global bond market sentiment on expectations that U.S. interest rates will remain stable for longer than was expected, dealers said. 

 The yield on the government bond due December 2006 ended in a bid-offer range of 3.57%-3.55%, down from a previous close of 3.5925%, dealers said. The December 2008 issue finished at in a 4.48%-4.46% range, down from 4.50% previously. 

 The Finance Ministry auctioned Thursday THB1 billion in government-guaranteed six-year state enterprise bonds to be issued May 8 by the Mass Rapid Transit Authority, or MRTA, at an accepted yield of 4.49%. 

 The yield represented a very low premium of about five basis points over the government bond yield curve as of Wednesday's close, or about eight-to-10 basis points over Thursday's closing yield curve. A low premium had been expected due to generally positive sentiment and liquidity driven demand. 

 Trade was very quiet Thursday after an initial rally. A foreign bank dealer said the pattern should be repeated Friday if U.S. bonds do well overnight. 

 If the U.S. bond market runs into profit-taking overnight, however, yields of Thai bonds will probably edge higher Friday, he said. 

 Money market interest rates ended mostly flat, and are expected to remain at these levels in the coming weeks due to excess liquidity. Money market rates should remain stable even if commercial banks cut deposit rates, as expected in the next week or so, because the central bank's 14-day repurchase market interest rate has probably bottomed already at 2%.

title: Emerging  FX  - Powered ahead by yen, eyeing Greenspan.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 17 (Reuters) - Asian currencies basked in 

 the yen's limelight in late trade on Wednesday, with strong 

 gains in local stocks providing an extra boost. 

     The Korean won stole a thunder, surging by more than a half 

 percent to close at a five-week high after investors ditched 

 the dollar to cut losses against the backdrop of robust gains 

 in both stocks and the yen. 

 The dollar came off against the euro and the yen, partly 

 because a February report showed fund managers were turning 

 more constructive toward European assets at the expense of U.S. 

 assets which some thought were looking a bit overvalued. 

     The U.S. currency was also pressured by a vague rumour that 

 Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan had resigned. 

     The Asian currencies took heart from the yen's resilience 

 in the face of Standard and Poor's downgrade of Japan which 

 suggested the market was long on the dollar, and that most 

 investors were not surprised by the move. 

 The market is waiting for Greenspan's testimony before a 

 Joint Economic Committee hearing on monetary policy and 

 economic outlook at 1400 GMT. 

 "What we have seen gradually throughout this year is that 

 Greenspan has become upbeat. It think we might see the 

 continuation of that trend," said Claudio Piron, currency

 strategist at Standard Chartered in Singapore. 

 "And if we are very lucky, there might be some hint as to 

 when he may be thinking of the timing of a possible rate hike. 

 But again, don't expect too much. He likes to keep his 

 constructive ambiguity," he said. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won closed at a five-week high of 1,318.70 to the 

 dollar against Tuesday's close of 1,325.60, riding on the back 

 of the yen and local stock gains. 

 Foreign investors bought a net of 265 billion won worth of 

 shares on the Korea Stock Exchange on Wednesday, the largest in 

 almost a month. They also bought a net 390 million won on the 

 over-the-counter Kosdaq. 

 Meanwhile, Korea's new Finance Minister Jeon Yun-churl said 

 on Wednesday the government would decide on whether to alter 

 its expansionary economic policy stance in May after it reviews 

 first quarter growth data. 

 Salomon Smith Barney says in a report that it expects 

 "significant" monetary tightening in the second half of this 

 year, beginning in June. 

 "We now see official rates rising from 4 percent to 5 

 percent by calendar year-end and to 5.5 percent 12 months hence 

 on strong economic growth and the policy constraint provided by 

 the central bank's own 2.5 percent core inflation target," it 

 said. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar rose to test the psychologically key 

 1.8300 per U.S. dollar level, as it shrugged off a slightly 

 worse than expected headline non-oil export data for March. 

 The data showed a decline of 17.3 on the year, slightly 

 worse than a Reuters poll average of a 15.3 percent drop, but 

 was better than February's 23.4 percent slide. 

     In fact, on a three-month average seasonally adjusted 

 month-on-month basis, exports were up a marginal 0.8 percent. 

     Dealers said a lack of response to the data suggests the 

 Sing dollar would continue its rise beyond the 1.8300 where 

 stop-loss dollar sale orders are bunched up. 

     They said players trying to avoid trigger of those stops 

 were bidding up dollars at session highs around 1.8312, but 

 overall firmer regional tone and a steadier yen was drawing 

 dollar sales from others at around 1.8320. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah rebounded just ahead of the psychologically key 

 9,500 level on sporadic dollar offers suggesting that some of 

 the sovereign credit ratings downgrade risk, that had pulled 

 the currency from recent highs near 9,300, might have already 

 been priced in. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said moderate commercial dollar demand 

 and talk of more dollar sell orders beyond 9,500 may limit 

 rupiah's downside for now. 

 Still most interbank players were trying to cover their 

 dollar shorts amid wariness over Standard and Poor's threat of 

 downgrading Indonesia to "selective default". 

 The rating action is expected in response to government's 

 intention to force some private lenders to share the debt 

 rescheduling burden with the Paris Club of creditor nations. 

 The government is likely to restructure $340 million in 

 syndicated loans from private lenders after securing a rework 

 of $5.4 billion it owed to bilateral creditors. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso held on its tight range around the 51 per dollar 

 level as lack of fresh trading cues made players reluctant to 

 push the currency either way. 

 Dealers in Manila said dollar bids from corporates and 

 importers capped the peso's upside at around 50.95 session 

 highs, while players were reluctant to sell it far beyond 51 

 per dollar amid a firmer regional tone, capping its downside at 

 51.025. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht edged higher as onshore players tried to catch up 

 with the currency's gains in the offshore market during the 

 Monday-Tuesday traditional New Year holidays. 

 Dealers in Bangkok said talk of central bank dollar 

 purchases through Japanese names capped the baht's upside. 

 However, it managed to rise to its three-week high of 43.25. 

 Despite the rumours, Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn 

 Devakula denied the central bank had intervened to slow the 

 baht's gains against the dollar and said the baht's current 

 level was "satisfactory."

title: Thai Baht Ends Lower On Yen Weakness In Thin Trade
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended slightly lower against the dollar in Asian spot trade Thursday, tracking the movements of the yen in lackluster trade, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 43.53 baht, up from THB43.46 at the Asian close Wednesday. 

 The U.S. currency opened at an intraday low of THB43.475, already showing the effects of the yen's early retreat back above Y131 against the dollar in early trade. A Japanese finance ministry official prompted dollar short-covering against the yen and other regional currencies by predicting that the yen's recent rally was over. 

 "The pair (dollar/baht) was range-bound in quiet trade in the morning. Market participants stayed sidelined due to the local holiday mood and an absence of fresh factors to lead the direction," said a dealer. 

 Local markets will be closed Monday and Tuesday for the traditional Thai New Year holidays. 

 Volume rose slightly in the afternoon due to local corporate demand for dollars, especially from oil companies amid the recent increases in crude oil prices linked to the violence and the threat of further instability in the Middle East. 

 Analysts said the Bank of Thailand won't intervene in the foreign exchange market unless the baht begins to strengthen against the yen, or on trade-weighted basis with a strong yen component. 

 The central bank has admitted to buying dollars on baht weakness in recent weeks, but denied Tuesday that it was in the market when the last serious test of dollar support at THB43.45 failed earlier in the day. 

 The dollar is expected to open Friday in Asia in a range of THB43.45 to THB43.60.

title: Emerging  FX  - Asian  forex  rally, inspired by yen.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 4 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies ended 

 higher on Thursday, trotting after the resilient yen which 

 continued to vex and frustrate the dollar. 

     After a day of choppy trade that saw the dollar shoot above 

 the 133 yen mark, the dollar was trading a bit lower from its 

 late New York levels. The greenback has been suffering from the 

 slings and arrows of investors disgruntled over the lack of 

 outflows from Japan that many had expected. 

 Moreover a batch of soft data from the U.S. service sector 

 and the continuing violence in the Middle East contiued to nag 

 the dollar. The market's awareness that Japan and Europe would 

 suffer more from rising oil prices - a consequence of the 

 violence - provided the dollar little comfort. 

 There were local factors behind regional currencies as 

 well. The Korean won continued to labour under foreign sales of 

 local stocks. And local corporate dollar demand thwarted the 

 Singapore dollar and Indonesian rupiah's rise. 

 As for regional monetary policy, the Korean central bank

 decided to hold rates steady - a widely expected move. And 

 sticking to its neutral stance, the Philippine central bank

 said further rate cuts were unlikely given higher oil prices. 

 The Philippine economy got a small pat on the back from 

 ratings agency Standard & Poor's which raised its outlook from 

 negative to stable. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won was once again shoved lower by investors upset over 

 another session of net selling of local stocks by foreign 

 investors. 

 Foreign investors disposed of a net 251.7 billion won worth 

 of shares on Thursday, the third straight day of selling. Even 

 though economist continue to hail Korea as one of the bright 

 spots in Asia as its economic recovery gathers pace, funds have 

 been cutting their positions in Korean shares and investing 

 elsewhere in Asia where they have less exposure. 

     However exporters' dollar sales saved the won from falling 

 much past the 1,330 level. 

     Meanwhile, the central bank's decision to keep its 

 overnight call rate as it is -- at four percent -- barely made 

 an impression in the market because it was widely expected. 

     The bank did warn of inflationary pressures, raising the 

 possibility that it might hike rates at its next month monetary 

 board meeting. 


    TAIWAN DOLLAR



    The Taiwan dollar kept to the stronger side of 35, aided by



a firmer yen and equity-related inflows.



     Dealers in Singapore said inflows related to stock



purchases by foreign investors from earlier in the week may



continue to trickle in for a few more days as the transactions



are settled and support the Taiwan dollar.



However, wariness over central bank dollar-buying


intervention and Wednesday's sales of local equities by foreign



investors made players reluctant to push the currency higher.



Foreign investors were net sellers of 309 million Taiwan



dollar worth of local stocks on Wednesday after buying a net



26.53 billion of shares in the previous 11 sessions.



SINGAPORE DOLLAR



The Singapore dollar tracked the firmer yen but ran into



dollar bids from local players near its session high of 1.8400.



Dealers said the Sing dollar's downside was checked by



foreign names spotted unwinding long dollar positions beyond



the 1.8420 level.



They said the absence of fresh news has left the market



focused on dollar/yen moves though uncertainty over yen's



near-term direction was expected to keep the dollar well-bid.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso was slightly higher tracking the yen and other



regionals. But local corporates kept a lid on its upside



keeping it away from testing the 51 per dollar level.



Merchandise export data for February showed a 6.4 percent



decline on the year, but the decline was smaller than previous



falls and raised hopes of a gradual recovery.



The market shruged off Standard & Poor's upgrade of outlook



on Philippines long-term ratings to stable from negative citing



tighter budget management.



    Dealers in Manila said the move was already factored in



after S&P announced its intention last month.



   S&P affirmed Philippines triple-'B'-plus long-term and 'A-2'



short-term local and double-'B'-plus long-term and single-'B'



short-term foreign currency sovereign credit ratings.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah climbed higher thanks to steady dollar sales



from foreign names who were eyeing investment flows into



Indonesia.



    Indonesia's telecom giant PT Telkom confirmed it had signed



a deal with Singapore Telecommunications to sell a 12.7 percent



stake in its cellular unit, Telkomsel. The stake amounts to



US$429 million in cash.



    The deal would reduce Telkom's holding in Telkomsel to 65



percent and raise SingTel's ownership to 35 percent.



    Corporate dollar bids, however, slowed the rupiah's



progress. And charts showed the rupiah's gains may soon be



capped as the currency has been consolidating around the



9,640-9,840 range so far this week.



THAI BAHT



The baht held onto its firmer tone, following the regional



trend higher.



Still, the currency was off the session's best of 43.59



because of wariness over central bank intervention. Bank of


Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said on Thursday that



he was concerned about the country's export performance and the



possible impact from the baht on trade flows.



    The central bank chief said it would act to reduce the



obstacles that were hindering trade, but he did not specify.

title: Emerging  FX  - Clouded by yen, Middle East woes.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 1 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were mostly 

 weaker in late trade on Monday as players snapped up dollars 

 against the backdrop of a weaker yen and brewing tensions in 

 the Middle East. 

     The yen dipped across the board, hurt by a disappointing 

 Japanese business "tankan" survey which showed no improvement, 

 and speculation investors were likely to buy foreign assets now 

 that the financial year was out of the way. 

     The regional currencies were also edgy due to conflict in 

 the Middle East which the market feared could jack up oil 

 prices and hurt growth prospects as well as current accounts of 

 oil-dependent Asian countries. 

     "The direct impact will be felt through the oil prices, 

 especially for those countries which are net importers of oil 

 like Japan and Korea, although you might argue the impact on 

 Japan might not be severe given its deflation," said Claudio 

 Piron, currency strategist at Standard Chartered in Singapore. 

     The Middle East tensions escalated after Israeli forces 

 stormed Ramallah, The Palestinian Authority's base, and other 

 West Bank cities at the weekend following a spate of 

 Palestinian suicide bombings. 

     Asia's oil consumption is estimated at around 21 million 

 barrels per day (bpd) while the region can produce only around 

 8.5 million bpd, leaving a production-consumption shortfall of 

 around 12.5 million bpd. 


    SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Sing dollar flirted with its multi-month lows seen last



week on the back of a weaker yen and the listless local stock



market, but its losses were capped by profit taking near



1.8480.



    Last week the local currency fell to 1.8510 -- its worst



level since January 10. Trading was subdued as Hong Kong and



London markets are closed on Monday.



    However, dealers expect the Sing dollar's downside to be



limited in the near and medium-term as charts show the currency


is trading at the lower end of its nominal effective exchange



rate (NEER) band, indicating upside risk ahead.



    The market barely reacted to money supply data released on



Saturday which showed bank credit in February dipped slightly



to S$160.73 billion from S$160.93 billion in January while M1



money supply rose to S$36.47 billion from S$35.80 billion.



    THAI BAHT



    The baht sank to the intraday low of 43.61 after the market



took the central bank chief's remarks and the recent export



data to mean the authority might be in favour of a weaker baht.



    Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula told



Reuters the bank would intervene if needed in the foreign


currency markets to stave off volatility in the local currency,



which had risen sharply in recent months.



    Meanwhile, exports fell 8.1 percent on the year in



February. The country's improving current account surplus was



due partly to a sharp decline in imports which raised doubt



about investment recovery.



    KOREAN WON         -2



    The won fell a notch from Wednesday's close of 1,325.9,



ending at 1,327.5 on importer dollar demand.



    Losses on the local share market also weighed on sentiment



towards the currency. Despite net purchases by foreign



investors during Monday's session, their sales on Friday



weighed on the currency.



    Seoul traders also said some foreign players were still



seeking to repatriate proceeds from dividend payments.



    Still, more evidence of Korea's economic rebound came in,



fuelling speculation as to whether the central bank would be



raising rates soon to temper inflationary pressures. While



exports fell in March, it was the smallest decline in a year.



Moreover, the new central bank governor Park Seung said the



economy was expected to grow by around five percent this year.



An official at the bank said it would adopt a flexible approach



to setting its rate target.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah edged higher from its day's worst level of



9,800, though corporate and foreign bank dollar bids were



worrying it.



Dealers in Jakarta said the currency opened around the



9,800 level, but was quickly rescued by across-the-board dollar



offers.



However, local corporates jumped in to buy the dollar



around the its day's low of 9,660, with foreign banks also



eagerly bidding in the dollar.



Volume was relatively heavy for this chronically thin



market, with dealers estimating some $300-$400 million changing



hands.



    "Whoever has the biggest flow is determining the market,"



said a foreign bank dealer in Bangkok.



    Indeed, there was a noticeable absence of fresh factors,



with the market impervious to political developments and



expecting Jakarta to secure a key debt rescheduling deal with



its Paris club of foreign creditors.



The government released some poor economic figures that



showed year-on-year inflation still in double digits and the



country's trade surplus falling.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar ended at 35.00, unchanged from Friday's



close as the currency shook off any jitters from the huge



earthquake that struck the island on Sunday.



    Damage from the earthquake was minimal, although five



people were killed and over 200 injured.



    The currency has been helped by healthy inflows into the



stock market. However, wariness over central bank intervention


meant it did not venture far from the 35 mark.



    Since the end of last year, the bank, which intervenes on



both sides of the market, has kept the currency around the 35



level. Taiwan is starting to emerge out of one of its worst



recessions, and the bank is doing what it can to keep the rate



stable as the island gets back on track.

title: Emerging  FX -Asian  forex  mixed, eye on yen,equities.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 1 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies were 

 mixed early on Monday as markets around the region re-opened 

 after the Easter holiday. 

     The tensions in the Middle East were haunting the market, 

 which was anxious that escalating violence in the region could 

 lead to a spike in oil prices. Most Asian countries, with the 

 exception of Indonesian and Malaysia, are net oil importers. 

     Still, players were keeping an eye on the two main driving 

 forces behind Asian currencies -- the yen and equity inflows. 

     In the bigger picture, analysts expect the regional 

currencies to do well in the long run as global growth picks 

 up. As a major exporter, Asia is expected to benefit from 

 sharpening consumer appetites. 

 Still, there was a catch - the temperamental yen. 

 "Like commodity currencies, Asian markets remain favoured 

 as trades on global growth. But with the JPY continuing to be 

 volatile, the region's currencies remain buffeted against the 

 USD," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, currency strategist at UBS 

 Warburg in Singapore in a research note. 

 He advocated sticking with currencies less exposed to the 

 yen's fickle ways - the Thai baht and Philippine peso - with 

 an eye on better entry levels for the more liquid currencies

 such as the Korean won, Taiwan dolllar and Singapore dollar. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar kept its weak tone against the U.S. dollar 

 alongside the yen, languishing near the 1.8450 level. 

 Dealers said the Sing dollar, like other regional 

currencies, was clouded by concerns over the brewing tensions 

 in the Middle East which, if escalated, would affect oil 

 prices. 

     The local currency was also weighed by equity outflows to 

 other countries in the region, they said. 

     "If the 1.8450 doesn't hold, the next target that we are 

 looking at is 1.8500," said a dealer at an Asian bank in 

 Singapore. 


    THAI BAHT



    The baht retreated below the 43.50 level, reflecting a



weaker yen which prompted interbank players, especially some



Japanese names, to cover short dollar positions.



    But its downside was underpinned by fears of central bank

intervention and some improvement in the February data.



    Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakul told Reuters



the central bank would intervene if needed in foreign exchange


markets to stave off volatility in the Thai currency, which had



risen sharply in recent months.



On the data front, current account surplus in February rose



to $989 million from $332 million in January. Its manufacturing



index also edge up by 2.4 percent on the year from a revised



1.5 percent in January.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso opened slightly firmer at 51.050 to the dollar



compared with 51.005 on Wednesday on the back of demand from



interbank players who had oversold the local currency ahead of



a long Easter holiday.



The market was thin, with only $3.5 million traded as of



0128 GMT as players waited for fresh leads after the Easter



break.



The local currency drew mild support from news of the



government eyeing a currency swap agreement with China and



South Korea to boost its dollar reserves as a precautionary



measure against potential financial market shocks.



Under the planned arrangement, the central bank may borrow



dollars in exchange for the local currency to meet urgent local



demand for the U.S. currency.



KOREAN WON -2



The won rose slightly from Friday's close of 1,325.9 thanks



to exporters' dollar sales.



Still, the market was keeping a close eye on the activity



of foreign investors in the stock market. It was anxious about



whether foreign investors would be net sellers of local shares.



Foreign flows have had the biggest influence on the currency's



direction in recent sessions.



Foreign investors sold a net 29.6 billion won worth of



Korean shares on Friday. So far on Monday, they've bought a net



9.7 billion won.



Overall, though, analysts and dealers said the won should



appreciate over time as the Korean economy steams ahead. Of all



the Asian economies, the market has been trumpeting Korea



because of its resilience during last year's slowdown and its



relative structural soundness.



    But rising oil prices could thwart the sunny outlook for



the Korean economy, which relies heavily on oil imports.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah was not far from its Friday levels of around



9,800, but dealers said players were looking to cover their



short dollar positions.



    Dealers in Jakarta said there were few new factors in the



market, with sentiment towards the rupiah still upbeat. While



the market was keen to cover their short dollar positions after



the re-emergence of local corporate dollar demand late last



week, players were likely to sell the dollar on rallies.



The market was also keeping an eye on crucial debt talks



between Jakarta and the Paris Club of official creditors later



this month.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR          The Taiwan dollar moved down a notch



from Friday's close of 35, following the softer yen.



    Sentiment towards the currency was also shaken by a strong



earthquake on the island on Sunday, which left five people dead



and 272 injured. Taiwan shares dipped on panic-selling, despite



no reports of major damage.



Still, the currency was unlikely to stray too far from the



35 level, where the central bank has kept it pinned to. The



bank has been active on both sides of the market to ensure a



stable rate while the island's economy slowly wends its way



down the road of recovery.

title: UPDATE 1-INTERVIEW-Thai  central bank  to nullify baht volatility.
text:
BANGKOK, March 29 (Reuters) - Thailand's central bank promised on Friday to intervene when needed in foreign exchange markets to iron out fluctuations in the Thai currency, which has risen about five percent against the dollar in recent months. 

 But Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula told Reuters the Bank of Thailand did not have a target level for the Thai baht, which now trades at about 43.40 per dollar, against 45.85 in the middle of last year and 25 before the Asian economic crisis began in 1997. 

 "There is a tendency for the baht to be strong and we have tried not to allow it to be too strong," Pridiyathorn said in an interview. 

 "Nobody in this world knows what level is healthy for the baht," he said. "Exchange rate is not an absolute thing, not an end in itself. It is a means to an end. It is a means for exporters to trade comfortably and conveniently." 

 Pridiyathorn said his officials entered the markets every now and then to support its policy of a "managed float" for the baht. 

 "Once in a while, we nullify, don't say intervene," he said. 

 "We manage for the glory of the country, for the convenience and comfort of exporters. We have to nullify the extra (capital) flows, the big amount of flows on certain days so it will not affect the exchange rate too much." 

 Pridiyathorn, who was a private banker, took over as governor in June 2001 after his predecessor fell out with the newly elected administration of Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, largely over interest rates. 

 CAPITAL OUTFLOWS 

 Former Governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul had cut Thailand's benchmark rate, the 14-day repurchase rate, to an historic low of 1.50 percent in an effort to stimulate the Thai economy at a time when its main trading partners were going into recession. 

 Exports account for almost 60 percent of Thailand gross national product (GDP) of around $120 billion. 

 But Thaksin's administration was alarmed by net outflows of capital in the first half of last year and the new governor quickly reversed the rate policy, pushing the 14-day repo rate up by a full percentage point to 2.50 percent despite a series of rate cuts by the United States and other major economies. 

 Since then the central bank has cut 50 basis points off the repo rate in two stages to 2.00 percent. 

 Pridiyathorn said the raising of rates last year had been necessary to bolster the country's foreign reserves and to slow capital outflows. But since then the situation had stabilised and foreign reserves had risen. 

 His aim now was to have foreign reserves at least twice the level of the country's short-term private foreign debt, which now stood at around $13 billion. Thailand's foreign reserves amounted to $33.6 billion as of March 15, Bank of Thailand data show. 

 The governor said he was satisfied with the current level of reserves and their ratio to short-term debt. 

 Pridiyathorn declined to give his views of the trend for Thai interest rates, saying the bank's Monetary Policy Committee, which he chairs, would decide on the rate "democratically" depending on the future economic environment. 

 "BIG BROTHER" 

 He said Thailand's main monetary policy "framework" would remain the bank's inflation target of between zero and 3.5 percent. Thai consumer price headline inflation was just 0.3 percent year-on-year in February. 

 "We are scared of hyper-inflation and don't want deflation." 

 He repeated previous forecasts that Thai growth was on track for two to three percent growth this year and said the bank's growth forecast would be reviewed soon. 

 Thaksin forecast last week that Thai GDP growth would be "3.5 up" percent this year, after growth of 1.8 percent in 2001. 

 Pridiyathorn said Thai exports would also recover this year and rejected suggestions by some economists that the recent strength of the baht was hurting sales of Thai products overseas. 

 Thailand saw an 8.4 percent year-on-year fall in exports in February, which pushed the dollar value of Thai exports to its lowest level in 32 months, commerce ministry figures show. 

 "Exports dropped because of world demand," he said. "It is not because of the (baht) policy. It is because of the real demand drop." 

 He said the key for the Thai economy for the rest of the year would be the performance of the United States economy. "The U.S. is the big brother - the big buyer in the world," he said. 

 Meanwhile, he would maintain a cautious policy with strong reserves and a stable currency, preparing for any "uncertainty". 

 "Buddhism says the only certain thing is uncertainty."

title: Emerging  FX  - Asian  forex  takes holiday breather.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 29 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies took 

 a breather in light, holiday trade on Friday, with many of the 

 region's major foreign exchange trading centres closed for the 

 Easter holiday. 

     The currencies whose markets were open for trade notched 

 lower, with the yen and equity flows dominating the Korean won 

 and Taiwan dollar and wariness over central bank intervention

 keeping a lid on the Thai baht's upside. 

     But trading in those market was relatively subdued. 

     Markets in Singapore and Hong Kong, as well as Manila and 

 Jakarta were closed for Good Friday. With the exception of Hong 

 Kong, they will re-open on Monday. Hong Kong reopens on 

 Tuesday. 

     In the bigger picture, analysts were trying to divine the 

 fate of the regional currencies as evidence of a healthy 

 rebound in the U.S. continued to come in and the dollar/yen 

 remained in familiar territory. 

     While recent fears of a potential rate hike in the U.S. did 

 cause Wall Street to fret about the possibility of tightening 

 liquidity -- in turn, hurting the dollar -- some analysts said 

 a rate hike would ultimately support the dollar. 

     "The implications of an earlier rate hike from the Fed and 

 a firmer growth performance in Q1 implies a steady USD against 

 Asian currencies," said BNP Paribas in a research note. 

     Rate hikes usually support a currency because they mean the 

 assets denominated in that currency would be more attractive to 

 investors. Last year, however, because of the slowing global 

 economy, the market viewed rate cuts by the Federal Reserve as 

 dollar supportive because it heightened hopes for a speedy 

 rebound. 


    KOREAN WON         -2



    The won eased a tad to 1,328.5 to the dollar at the open as



it shadowed the weaker yen. It later rebounded to 1,327.3,



still slightly weaker than Thursday.



    The currency was also hurt by dollar purchases from



importers with bids for the greenback connected to recent



equity sales knocking around in the market as well.



    However a number of factors were supporting the won.



Firstly, foreign equity net selling had reversed in recent



sessions after a hefty sell-off.



    Secondly, analysts' view that Korea was one of the most



attractive places in Asia to park money was underscored by



Moody's Investors Service's move to up the country's foreign


currency ceiling for bonds and noted by two notches on



Thursday. That decision puts Korea on par with China, Hong Kong



and Hungary.



    The ratings agency cited the country's sound fiscal



position, and praised the government's policies and reform



efforts.



    THAI BAHT



    The baht fell from Thursday's late levels of 43.44 to trade



around 43.52 to the dollar.



    Bangkok dealers said importers and corporates were looking



to for dollars in a market that was still unnerved by the Bank



of Thailand's verbal intervention on Thursday.


Central bank governor Pridiyathorn Devakula hinted that it



had been intervening to curb the baht's gains in order to



maintain export competitiveness.



    Foreign investors have been net sellers of local stocks for



the past three sessions, though they remain net buyers of 18.5



billion baht of Thai stocks so far this year.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR



    The Taiwan dollar edged lower on the back of the yen's



fall, and was back on the wrong side of 35.



    However, the currency was not expected to see any sharp



moves given the looming and likely possibility of central bank

intervention. Taiwan's central bank intervenes on both sides of



the market on a regular basis to keep the exchange rate stable.



    For the past three months, the currency has kept within a



narrow 34.88-35.167 range.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Singapore dollar mimicked the yen's losses, but to a



lesser extent given the holiday-thinned trade, to trade around



1.8431/41.



    Singapore markets are closed and will reopen on Monday.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah fell a rung or two in thin offshore trade.



    Jakarta markets were closed and will re-open on Monday. On



Thursday, the currency had given up its recent strong gains as



bargain hunters and corporates snatched up the dollar.



    The currency also fell after the Indonesian Bank



Restructuring Agency said it received around $320 million in



payment for a 30 percent stake in Bank Central Asia. Players in



the market had been betting on those inflows flooding the



market, which they have yet to do.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso was steady in minimal offshore trade. Manila



markets have been closed since Wednesday and will re-open on



Monday.

title: Thai c.bank hints it  intervening  to restrain baht.
text:
BANGKOK, March 28 (Reuters) - Thailand's central bank hinted on Thursday that it had been intervening in the foreign exchange market to hold down the Thai baht which has strengthened sharply against the dollar in recent weeks. 

 Bank of Thailand (BOT) Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula told reporters the bank had been "taking care of the baht". 

 "We've been taking care of the baht - otherwise it would be stronger," Pridiyathorn said in reply to a question about how the central bank's monetary policy could mitigate a recent decline in Thai exports. 

 Thailand posted an 8.4 percent year-on-year fall in exports in February, which pushed the dollar value of Thai products sold overseas to its lowest level in 32 months. 

 The baht stood at around 43.40 per dollar in late Asian trade on Thursday, up from a low of around 45.85 in the middle of last year.

title: Emerging  FX  - Asian  currencies  ease with yen.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 13 (Reuters) - Asian currencies eased a 

 tad early on Wednesday, dragged lower by a weaker yen. 

     Falls on Wall Street, particularly in technology stocks, 

 were also likely to vex the North Asian currencies, which were 

 already coping with the yen's stumble. 

     However, analysts noted that the extent of the regional 

currencies' falls has been muted. Indeed, with the exception of 

 the Korean won, all the currencies have gained against the 

 dollar since the start of the year. 

 Moreover while Japanese authorities have been busy trying 

 to prevent the yen from rising too far, too fast, Asian central 

 bankers have been relatively subdued about recent gains. The 

 Bank of Thailand once again said on Tuesday it would not 

intervene to temper the baht's recent rise, adding it did not 

 hurt exports. 

 "I think the region is getting comfortable right now ... 

 The U.S. is on the mend and the dollar/yen's collapse last week 

 just shows there's no danger for now of 140 or 150," said 

 Philip Wee, currency strategist at DBS Bank in Singapore. 

 The market was keeping its eye on Federal Reserve Chairman 

 Alan Greenspan's speech on Wednesday, which is the day when key 

 data on U.S. retail sales in February will also be issued. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht dawdled in a narrow 43.10-43.30 range in a dearth 

 of fresh leads from both the dollar/yen and the stock market. 

 "The baht seems to be consolidating around that band as the 

 dollar/yen and the stock market are settling into range as 

 well," said a dealer at a local bank in Bangkok. 

 Dealers said the baht was unlikely to rise above 43.00 - a 

 barrier not broken since February 2001 - any time soon unless 

 the yen strengthens towards 127 and more capital inflows enter 

 the market. 

     The onshore overnight interbank rate was steady at around 

 1.95-2.00 percent. 


    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah froze in a tight 9,925-9,985 band as the market



lacked the resolve to push it either way while awaiting news of



the winning bid for the government's sale of a majority stake



in Bank Central Asia.



    Trading was subdued, with dollar offers from foreign banks



offset by corporate dollar demand.



    The government said on Tuesday the winner of the sale would



not be announced later in the day as was previously hoped.



State Enterprises Minister Laksamana Sukardi said he hoped the



winner could be announced by later this week.



The sale of the bank is seen as a crucial test of the



government's commitment to economic reform and its willingness



to push through divestment of assets to foreigners in the face



of domestic opposition.



KOREAN WON -2



The won slipped on concerns over equity-related outflows



because of five consecutive sessions of net selling by foreign



investors.



Dealers in Singapore said repatriation of profits by some



multinational companies was also adding downside pressure on



the won. One U.S. bank was spotted buying dollars on Tuesday



for such repatriation requirements.



Foreign investors sold a net 124.8 billion won worth of



local shares on Tuesday amid talk the investment was flowing



into Japanese and other Asian assets.



Dealers said those concerns had prompted most interbank



players to build up long dollar positions. They said the won



was expected to ease into a weaker 1,315-1,323 range.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso opened a tick higher at 50.84 after settling at



50.87 on Tuesday, supported by favourable budget deficit



outlook.



On Tuesday, Budget Secretary Emilia Boncodin said the



government was expected to meet its 130 billion pesos ($2.55



billion) budget deficit target for this year.



Still, some dealers in Manila were sceptical about the



pledge, saying they would have to wait for the final figures as



public spending plans to boost the economy could push the



deficit to 52.9 billion pesos in the first quarter, or 40.6



percent of the year target.



They added the currency faced resistance around the 50.80



level where dollar orders from some manufacturing clients were



lined up. They also noted corporate demand for pesos was



lacklustre.



Overall, the currency was poised to trade above the key 51



level for the next few sessions because corporate investors



have not hedged their dollar positions and thus will pressure



the peso lower.



    "The current levels are a true blessing to them (the



corporate investors)," a Manila-based trader said.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR



    The Taiwan dollar was supported by equity-linked inflows.



    However, the pace of those inflows has moderated in the



past few sessions while a softer yen was also expected to cap



any significant upside for the currrency.



    Dealers in Singapore added few players were interested in



pushing the Taiwan dollar higher from current levels around



34.95 after the central bank's recent dollar-buying


intervention to protect export competitiveness.



    However, if the yen stays within 128-130 range, dealers



expected the risk of central bank intervention to drop.



    Foreign investors bought a net T$1.89 billion worth of



local shares taking their net buying over the past nine



sessions to T$46.59 billion.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Singapore dollar crept slightly lower, silently



shadowing the yen.



    Trading was lacklustre with few other factors in the



market, dealers said. With more activity and higher gains in



the major currencies, the market in the dollar/Sing has thinned



out.



Dealers said there were still players looking to exit long



dollar positions, which were taken above the 1.8300 level. That



meant the dollar was likely to run into stiff resistance around



1.8240/45 for now.

title: Emerging  FX  - Mostly firmer as yen recoups losses.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 12 (Reuters) - Asian currencies crept 

 higher in late trade on Tuesday after the yen clawed 

 back some gains against the dollar on the back of exporter 

 dollar sales. 

     Expectations of more inflows into regional assets also 

 supported the currencies, dealers said. 

   The Thai baht was among the star performers, nudging higher 

 on  capital inflows and comments by the central bank that it 

 saw no need to intervene to slow down its gains. 

     The yen recovered some lost ground after falling to a 

 session low of 128.88 due to losses in the stock market 

 and talk that the government plans to buy a large amount of 

 foreign bonds in fiscal 2002. 

     Most analysts are betting that the yen will resume its 

 sustained weakness after the book closing season is over by the 

 end of this month. 

     "We do not believe that strength in the yen will be 

 maintained. It is true that a global economic recovery and 

 (recent) rallying Japanese stock market are usually positive 

 for the yen. The sustainability of the strength of the stock 

 has to be questioned, however," said a JP Morgan note. 

     "It is a result of official manipulation -- including 

 government buying and short-sale restrictions -- rather than 

 optimism about restructuring," it said. 


    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah was trapped in a narrow range of 9,950-9,990



while players waited on the sidelines for news of the winning



bid for the government's sale of its majority stake in Bank



Central Asia.



    Jakarta-based dealers said trading was light, with



corporate dollar demand balanced by dollar offers from foreign



banks.



    They added the market kept its cool when the government



said the winner of the sale would not be announced later in the



day as was previously hoped. State Enterprises Minister



Laksamana Sukardi said he hoped the winner could be announced



by later this week.



    Local media had reported the possible delay, which meant



the market was prepared for this announcement, dealers said.



They also expressed confidence that the deal would go through.



    THAI BAHT        The baht strode higher, rising above the



43.15 level on the back of the firmer yen and dollar offers



from exporters who feared the baht would strengthen further.



    The currency was also bolstered by comments by the Bank of


Thailand, which reiterated on Tuesday it would not intervene in



the market to slow down the baht's recent sharp rise which it



said was in line with other regional currencies.



    Dealers say there was speculation in the market earlier



that the central bank was likely to enter the market to curb



the baht's appreciation if it rises past 43.00 where hefty



stop-loss orders from players with long dollar positions are



lining up.



    KOREAN WON         -2



    The won succumbed to foreign net sales of local stocks,



with the wobbly yen also hurting sentiment towards the


currency.



    Foreign investors were net sellers of local stocks for the



fifth consecutive session in a row, dumping a net 124.8 billion



won worth of shares.



    Analysts say with the global outlook improving, funds are



looking to park their money elsewhere. Korea benefited from a



huge inflow of foreign funds at the beginning of the year



because it is seen as one of the more stable economies in Asia.



But analysts say that also left more room for a correction in



the local stock market.



    Still, the Korean Composite Stock Price Index         has



gained nearly 22 percent since the start of the year.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR
    The Singapore dollar        pared earlier gains on profit



taking, but remained supported by the yen's rebound and hopes



for more inflows ahead.



    Dealers say despite some consolidation in the local stock



market, they expect more upside ahead on the back of economic



recovery.



    The Singapore unit, largely dependent on the yen's daily



activity, traded tightly between 1.8185-1.8210, with traders



suggesting the band was likely to stay narrow amid the dearth



of market-moving factors to trade on.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar ended slightly higher despite losses in



the local stock market and a wobbly yen, thanks to



equity-related inflows.



Foreign investors bought a net 1.89 billion Taiwan dollars



worth of local shares taking their net buying over the past



nine sessions to 46.59 billion Taiwan dollars.



    However, the stock market ended down 1.19 percent tracking



the Nasdaq's losses.



    That kept the overall tone of currency trading soft with a



session low of 34.985. Players were also reluctant to push the


currency higher after central bank's recent intervention to cap



the currency's upside.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso edged higher to end its onshore trade at 50.87 per



dollar from Monday's close at 50.99 amid talk of equity-and



investment-linked inflows.



The currency was also supported by a brighter outlook of



the fiscal position. The government said it has secured $2.8



billion this year in development assistance from international



donors.



Budget Secretary Emilia Boncodin said the government was



expected to meet its 130 billion pesos ($2.55 billion) budget



deficit target for this year.



However, front loading of public spending plans to



stimulate the economy could push the deficit to 52.9 billion



pesos in the first quarter, or 40.6 percent of the full



year-year target.



    She said the deficit was expected to taper off in the



succeeding quarters.

title: Thai c.bank chief says not  intervening  in baht.
text:
BANGKOK, March 8 (Reuters) - Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said on Friday he saw no immediate need to slow the baht's appreciation this week, saying its sharp gains had not hurt exports. 

 Pridiyathorn told reporters after the baht rallied to its strongest level against the dollar since February 2001 that the Thai currency's appreciation was not excessive. 

 Asked whether the central bank would intervene to slow baht gains, he said: "No need to do anything. It has just appreciated a little bit, not gaining that much." 

 On whether the gains would hurt exports, the governor said: "It is still competitive."

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late On Equity Inflows, Yen
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Continuing foreign equity inflows into local stock markets and the yen's gains bolstered most Asian currencies late Wednesday, dealers said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah's new found strength provided additional support to its Southeast Asian peers, although fears of intervention by the central banks in Singapore and Thailand stymied their currencies' rise. 

 The rupiah extended its climb toward IDR9,900 resistance, as interbank participants continued to sell U.S. dollars in anticipation of inflows from the Indonesian government's impending sale of its 51% stake in PT Bank Central Asia, observers said. 

 The rupiah, trading at near five-month highs, hit an intraday high of IDR9,915 before retreating to around IDR9,950 late Wednesday. The rupiah was weaker at IDR9,980 late Tuesday. 

 Improving prospects for the privatization of state-held assets in Indonesia - which would underscore the government's commitment to economic reforms - helped thrust the rupiah through the psychologically important IDR10,000 threshold Tuesday. 

 "With corporate bids for debt repayment still much on the sidelines, the rupiah looks well positioned to test IDR9,800," Bank of America said in a research report. 

 The Thai currency strengthened to an intraday high of 43.490 baht to the dollar, thanks to strong foreign equity inflows and dollar sales by U.S. funds - as they simultaneously unloaded their dollar positions against the yen, dealers said. 

 But the baht subsequently pulled back past the THB43.500 level on market suspicions that the Thai central bank had bought dollars via two of its agent banks based in Singapore to check the baht's advance, market observers said. 

 In an apparent bid to maintain the price competitiveness of Thailand's exports, the Thai central bank had been buying dollars in the last few days when the currency traded at THB43.55-THB43.60, said a dealer at a Thai bank. 

 "It's still in their practice to protect their exporters," he added. 

 At 0915 GMT (4:15 a.m. EST), the dollar was at THB43.515, lower than THB43.665 late Tuesday. 

 Against the Japanese currency, the dollar was quoted at Y131.84, below Y132.13 in New York and Y132.53 in Tokyo late Tuesday. 

 Market speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened to check the strength of the local currency Wednesday provided a floor for the U.S. dollar around S$1.8250, observers said. 

 The U.S. dollar slid to an overnight low of S$1.8222 on long-liquidation, but subsequently bounced back on suspected intervention by the MAS, some dealers said. 

 A large Singapore bank bought a "significant amount" of U.S. dollars around S$1.8260 during the Asian session Wednesday, moderating the upward pressure on the Singapore currency despite the firmer yen and local stock market gains, said a dealer at a European bank. 

 Although some dealers said the Singapore bank was buying U.S. dollars on behalf of its corporate clients, jitters about central bankintervention led some to speculate that the Singapore bank was acting at the behest of the central bank. 

 The South Korean won closed at KRW1,316.3 against the dollar, little changed compared with KRW1,316.4 Tuesday. 

 The won strengthened to an intraday high of KRW1,313.7 earlier, before retreating as foreign investors turned net sellers of South Korean shares and onshore demand for dollars emerged when the U.S. currency traded below KRW1,315 support, said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, a regional currency strategist at UBS Warburg. 

 State-run banks, like Korea Development Bank, or KDB, were snapping up dollars on behalf of corporations and oil importers, said a dealer at a European bank in Singapore. 

 Some market participants also believe that South Korea's central bank had intervened through KDB, he added. 

 Expectations that the yen will remain rangebound - as foreign exchange participants attempt to defend their currency options positions - also limited the won's upside, said Mohi-uddin. 

 Market participants this week established "double no-touch options with barriers at Y131.50 and Y135.50," the strategist said, adding that these players will protect these levels to ensure that the options won't be exercised. 

 "External factors are not that bullish for the won," said Mohi-uddin. 

 The New Taiwan dollar closed stronger on foreign equity inflows, but was off its intraday high as the central bank intervened to curb the local currency's appreciation, dealers said. 

 A Taipei-based dealer estimated that the central bank accounted for about half of Wednesday's turnover. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$35.030, slightly lower than NT$35.069 Tuesday. The New Taiwan dollar hit an intraday high of NT$34.995 Wednesday. 

 Trading volume was US$602 million, higher than US$458 million Tuesday. 


Buoyed by its regional counterparts, the Philippine peso closed at
PHP51.090 to the dollar, compared with PHP51.160 Tuesday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Down Late On Yen; Focus On G7 Mtg
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies were slightly lower late Friday, weighed by a tottering yen, dealers said. 

 However, with major currencies providing little in the way of any solid direction ahead of this weekend's meeting of central bankers and finance ministers from the Group of Seven leading industrial nations, Asian currencies were wedged within narrow ranges, dealers said. 

 Participants will be looking out for any comments regarding the yen and Japan's economic and structural reform agenda at the meeting, to be held in Ottawa. 

 At 1030 GMT (5:30 a.m. EST), the dollar was quoted at Y133.95, above Y133.56 in New York late Thursday. The dollar was at Y134.05 in Tokyo late Thursday. 

 Trading was also subdued as participants refrained from taking any major positions ahead of next week's Lunar New Year celebrations, dealers said. 

 The New Taiwan dollar grabbed the limelight as it slumped to its weakest level in more than three weeks. 

 With financial markets in Taipei closed from Monday through Thursday, continued uncertainty over the wobbly yen's fate prompted local interbank traders, importers and offshore non-deliverable forward participants to snap up the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 "As downside risks for the yen remain, many would prefer hedging their positions in U.S. dollars," said a Taipei-based dealer. 

 The New Taiwan dollar ended at NT$35.080 against the U.S. currency, weaker compared with NT$35.029 Thursday. 

 Taiwan's central bank - which had recently been buying U.S. dollars to curb the appreciation of the local currency - turned sellers of the U.S. currency Friday to check the New Taiwan dollar's decline, dealers said. 

 The Thai currency slipped to 43.925 baht to the dollar, compared with THB43.855 late Thursday, in part due to fears Bank of Thailand - the central bank - would intervene to check the strength of the local currency, dealers said. 

 "BOT was rumored to have taken $50 million off the market below THB43.90 on Thursday," Bank of America said in a research note. 

 Bank of Thailand said Friday that its foreign reserves had climbed to $34.0 billion as of Feb. 1, from $33.6 billion a week earlier. 

 The increase in reserves reinforced the market's belief that the central bank has been buying dollars to prevent the baht from strengthening excessively, amid strong foreign portfolio inflows, dealers said. 

 "The market is saying that the central bank has been buying dollars," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 In Seoul, the dollar closed at 1,320.2 won, up from Thursday's close at KRW1,318.2, bolstered by demand for the U.S. currency by importers, dealers said. 

 Dollar sales by exporters, however, capped the currency's rise, they added. 

 The Singapore dollar fell to S$1.8347 against its U.S. counterpart, compared with S$1.8326 late Thursday. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the dollar closed at 51.220 pesos, up from PHP51.185 Thursday. 

 Bucking the region's trend, the rupiah was stronger, thanks to heavy dollar sales by state banks, believed to be acting on behalf of the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency, observers said. Dollar demand by corporations, however, thwarted further gains by the rupiah, they added. 

 The dollar was at 10,250 rupiah, lower than IDR10,290 late Thursday.
