title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late; Ctrl Bk Fears Cap Gains
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Concerns that the region's monetary authorities may step in and smother the appreciation of their respective currencies moderated the gains in Asian currencies late Wednesday, even as the yen bounced past the psychologically important Y133 threshold to the dollar, market watchers said. 

 The anemic performance of U.S., and in turn regional stock markets, also offset any potential boost coming from the yen, observers said. 

 The Dow Jones Industrial Average skidded 2.5% Tuesday amid fears that U.S. companies could fall victim to accounting problems like those that caused energy trading company Enron to go bankrupt. 

 "In the last few weeks there was a tug-of-war between a strong dollar/yen and equity inflows in Asia," said Jimmy Koh, head of treasury research at Singapore's UOB Group. "Now it's the other way around." 

 Portfolio inflows into the region's stock markets had helped cushion the blow on Asian currencies dealt by the weakness in the yen and the euro in recent sessions. 

 With Asian currencies having strengthened against their major trading counterparts, the region's authorities may now be anxious about keeping their currencies competitive, analysts said. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. currency remained supported above the psychologically important S$1.8300 level, as the threat of central bank intervention loomed, observers said. 

 The U.S. dollar slipped to an intraday low of S$1.8305, but had recovered to S$1.8326 at 0840 GMT (3:40 a.m. EST). The U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.8325 late Tuesday. 

 The trade-weighted Singapore dollar is trading at the stronger end of the monetary authority's policy band, analysts said. The Monetary Authority of Singapore - which uses the currency rather than interest rates as its primary monetary policy tool - guides the local dollar within a trading band against a basket of currencies of the country's major trading partners and key competitors. 

 "The Singapore dollar has been hugging the strongest end of our estimate of the band," said Koh at UOB. "In fact, it has breached it slightly." 

 Koh estimates the upper boundary of the band at around S$1.8340, based on the assumption that the central bank has - earlier this month - narrowed the policy band to 1.5% on each side of the pivot point. 

 Although there were rumors in the last two days that the central bank had intervened to curb the strength of the Singapore dollar, some observers believe the MAS will unlikely stand in the way of a stronger currency. 

 They argue that the central bank would be wary of setting a psychological ceiling on the Singapore dollar, as the yen is widely expected to strengthen further on fund repatriation by Japanese institutional investors before the fiscal year-end in March. 

 Late Wednesday, the dollar was quoted at Y132.55, below Y133.31 late Tuesday in New York. 

 Some dealers also blamed the U.S. dollar's pullback against some of the region's currencies like the Singapore dollar and the South Korean won on long-liquidation of the U.S. currency ahead of the Federal Reserve's decision on interest rates. 

 After Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's encouraging assessment of the U.S. economy last week, markets have priced in expectations that the Fed will leave short-term interest rates unchanged when it concludes its two-day policy meeting later Wednesday. 

 Foreign equity outflows countered the upward pressure on the South Korean won from the yen's advance, dealers said. 

 Foreign investors unloaded a net KRW200.1 billion in shares Wednesday, contributing to a 3.2% plunge in the benchmark stock index, and in turn the won's slide to as low as KRW1,319.0 earlier in the day. 

 However, the yen's rebound and mounting expectations that South Korea's sovereign ratings might be upgraded - probably sooner rather than later - overwhelmed the yen's influence. 

 Reinforcing such optimism was an announcement by South Korea's Ministry of Finance and Economy Wednesday that a team of analysts from Moody's Investors Service Inc. will visit South Korea Feb. 25-28 for an annual review on the country's sovereign rating. In November, Moody's revised the outlook on South Korea's Baa2 ratings to positive from stable. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at KRW1,311.0, lower than KRW1,313.6 Tuesday. The U.S. dollar fluctuated between KRW1,310.5 and KRW1,319.0. 

 Some dealers said fears of intervention by the Bank of Korea kept the U.S. dollar buoyed above KRW1,310 support. 

 "There's a risk that if it breaks that level, people will sell the dollar down to KRW1,290," said a dealer at a European bank in Singapore. 

 Moderate intervention by Taiwan's central bank kept a rein on the local dollar's rise, dealers said. Apart from the yen, the New Taiwan dollar received a boost from heightened seasonal demand for the local currency ahead of the month-end and the Chinese New Year festivities around mid-February. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.985, down from NT$35.001 Tuesday. 

 The Thai currency was marginally firmer at 44.025 baht to the U.S. dollar, compared with THB44.040 late Tuesday. Fears of intervention by the Bank of Thailand - which dealers believe had been buying U.S. dollars in the last two days - kept the U.S. currency buoyed above THB44.000. 

 Bucking the trend in the region, the Philippine peso was slightly weaker as month-end corporate demand for U.S. dollars overpowered the support from the yen and foreign equity inflows into the local market. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at 51.22 pesos, slightly higher than PHP51.165 Tuesday. 

 The rupiah's gains Tuesday proved to be short-lived as Indonesian companies took advantage of the U.S. dollar's pullback to buy the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar was at 10,325 rupiah, higher than IDR10,295 late Tuesday. 

 The International Monetary Fund said Tuesday the economic challenges facing Indonesia are becoming more difficult as the government struggles to deliver promised reforms in the corporate and banking sectors. 

 Still, the IMF's board still agreed to excuse Indonesia's failure to satisfy a couple of conditions of its $4.5-billion IMF loan program. 

 The fund announced late Monday its approval of a $341-million loan installment for Indonesia, contributing to the brief surge in the rupiah.

title: Asian  Currencies  Up Late; Some Central Banks Check Gains
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies basked in the glow of the yen's rebound late Tuesday, although dealers believe the central banks in Taiwan, Singapore and Thailand had intervened to check the strength of their respective currencies, market watchers said. 

 In recent sessions, portfolio inflows had mitigated the pain on the New Taiwan dollar, Singapore dollar and Thai baht from the yen's slide to new 39-month lows versus the U.S. currency and the euro's weakness, analysts said. 

 Given the appreciation of these Asian currencies against their major trading counterparts, the region's central banks are probably concerned about the strength of their currency on a trade-weighted basis, they added. The authorities would need to maintain the price competitiveness of their exports. 

 The Singapore dollar was stronger at S$1.8325 against its U.S. counterpart, compared with S$1.8363 late Monday. 

 Talk that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had been bidding for U.S. dollars since Monday kept the unit buoyed above S$1.8300, even as the yen threatened to approach the Y133 psychological resistance level to the U.S. currency. 

 "Any further strength could push the Singapore dollar into more expensive area against the currencies of its trading partners," BNP Paribas said in a report. "This would run against the authority's current bias of maintaining a neutral Singapore dollar against its basket." 

 "We expect intervention to continue if portfolio-led Singapore dollar demand continues to push up the value of the local currency," the bank added. 

 At 0854 GMT, the U.S. dollar was quoted at Y133.20, below Y133.50 in New York late Monday. The dollar was at Y133.86 in Tokyo late Monday. 

 In the Thai currency market, the dollar failed to stay below 44 baht, amid talk that the Thai central bank has been buying dollars sporadically via its agent banks in Bangkok and Singapore since Monday. 

 The central bank appeared to have bought dollars when the currency traded between THB43.990 and THB44.050, dealers said. 

 "The amount should be substantial," said a dealer at an Asian bank in Singapore. "They came in a few times and they're still there." 

 In fact, dealers believe that the Bank of Thailand has been curbing the strength of the baht almost daily in the last two weeks, in an apparent bid to maintain the price competitiveness of the country's exports. 

 "We think that there has been a shift in policy thinking at the BOT from a focus on "stability" - through managing interest rate differentials and exchange rates (through the latter half of 2001) - to more conventional counter-cyclical 'growth-oriented' measures," Bank of America said in a research note. 

 "We expect the authorities to consciously guide the baht lower against its nominal effective basket, to boost exports," the bank said, adding that the dollar will likely be well supported around THB43.900 to THB43.950. 

 In Taiwan, the central bank reportedly bought U.S. dollars around NT$34.980, offsetting the pressure from the exporter U.S. dollar sales and the yen's rise, Taipei-based dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$35.001, marginally lower than NT$35.015 Monday. 

 The South Korean won closed at a two-week high, receiving an additional boost from dollar demand by foreign investors needing to settle their recent purchases of local shares, dealers said. 

 The won also gained from the unwinding of long dollar positions by foreign funds - triggered by the dollar's fall below the psychologically important KRW1,320 level - and jitters about the yen, with "dollar/yen hanging precariously above Y133," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 "Offshore players are coming in and selling dollar/won for speculative reasons as well," noted Mansoor Mohi-uddin, a regional currency strategist at UBS Warburg. 

 Remarks by international ratings agency Fitch that there is room for an upgrade in South Korea's sovereign ratings also boosted sentiment toward the won. 

 "It helped sentiment - definitely," said Mohi-uddin. 

 The dollar ended at 1,313.6 won, down 0.6% from KRW1,321.3 Monday. 

 The Indonesian rupiah received a fillip from the International Monetary Fund's approval of a loan installment of $341 million for the country and its agreement to extend a $4.5-billion loan facility by a year to the end of 2003. 

 The rupiah also received another dose of good news - that a Standard Chartered Plc. (U.STA)-led consortium appeared to be the front runner in bidding for a stake in nationalized PT Bank Central Asia (P.PCA). 

 The Indonesian currency strengthened to 10,295 rupiah to the dollar from IDR10,390 late Monday. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the dollar closed at 51.165 pesos, down from PHP51.240 Monday. 

 Financial markets are awaiting the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision on interest rates at the end of its two-day policy-setting meeting, which begins later Tuesday. 

 Markets have priced in expectations that the Fed will hold its overnight target rate steady at 1.75%, which would end a year-long streak of aggressive easing.

title: UPDATE 2-Thai reserves suggest  central bank  selling baht.
text:
BANGKOK, Jan 18 (Reuters) - The Bank of Thailand (BOT) appears to have intervened heavily in foreign exchange markets in recent weeks in an effort to depress the baht currency, judging by data from the central bank on Friday. 

 The BOT Web site (www.bot.or.th("http://www.bot.or.th/")) says Thailand's foreign reserves jumped sharply to $33.5 billion in the week to January 11, up from around $33.0 billion during the previous three weeks. 

 The central bank's net forward foreign exchange contracts to buy Thai baht were flat at $1.8 billion on January 11, unchanged from January 4. But they had fallen the previous week from $2.1 billion on December 28 and December 31. 

 Taken together, the figures suggest the bank either entered the foreign exchange market last week to sell spot baht and buy dollars or had previously unwound some of its forward market positions by committing to sell Thai baht forward. 

 It could also have taken a combination of both positions. 

 A BOT official who declined to be identified told Reuters Thailand had made no significant debt repayments last week that could have affected the figures. 

 "The changes in the reserves can be attributed to our currency dealings in spot and forward markets," she said, giving no further details. 

 Dealers said the rise in reserves probably reflected central bankintervention to slow appreciation of the baht, which is now not far off its highest level for 10 months. 

 The Thai authorities have said they aim to keep the baht stable relative to the currencies of competitor economies and officials have privately expressed some concern in recent weeks that the currency has appreciated sharply. 

 The Thai currency traded at 43.93-43.96 to the dollar at 1025 GMT on Friday, after trading between 43.80 and 43.95 on Thursday. 

 The currency has risen from a three-year low of 45.87 per dollar last July but is still nowhere near its level around 25 before the Asian currency crisis in July 1997. 

 BUILDING UP NATIONAL RESERVES 

 "My guess is the central bank entered the market to smooth out the baht's fluctuation," said Thanawat Patchimkul, head of research at DBS Vickers Securities in Bangkok. 

 "The rise in our foreign reserves does no harm. It's been a well known BOT policy to build up national reserves which, at $33.5 billion, is at a sound level." 

 Asked why the BOT would want to restrain baht gains, he said: 

 "It's not a question of where the baht should stand. I think what the BOT wants more is a stable baht that will make it easier for Thai exporters to do business." 

 The Bank of Thailand data, closely watched by financial markets for indications of the central bank's operations in the foreign exchange markets, suggest the Thai authorities may have more room to adjust local interest rates than previously thought. 

 The BOT's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) will meet on Monday to consider whether to cut its key reference 14-day repurchase rate, currently at 2.25 percent. 

 Thailand held out against the global trend towards easier monetary policy last year and surprised markets in June by raising the repo rate by a full percentage point to 2.5 percent. 

 The central bank said at the time it was worried about a possible speculative attack on the Thai currency such as the selling that forced the sharp devaluation of the baht in 1997. 

 Analysts suggest the Thai government is still worried about the risk of a possible sell-off and may delay any rate cut, at least until after the U.S. Federal Reserve makes its next move. 

 A Reuters poll of economists this week forecast the central bank will probably keep rates on hold until early March when its MPC is next due to meet. (With additional reporting by Vithoon Amorn).

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Respite From Rangebound Yen
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Wednesday as they paused for breath ahead of an expected relapse in the yen over the medium term, dealers said. 

 Except for the Singapore dollar, which continued to grab the attention of foreign funds, the rest of the region's currencies were wedged within narrow bands, with little in the way of direction from a rangebound yen. 

 Senior Japanese officials continued to try to placate their neighbors' growing anxieties over the yen's slide to three-year lows last week. Although the officials said Japanese authorities weren't attempting to guide the yen lower, they suggested that the finance ministry would tolerate a weaker currency. 

 Japanese Finance Minister Masajuro Shiokawa reiterated Wednesday that his ministry thinks foreign exchange levels should be left to the market. Analysts believe Japan has no short-term policy option but to depreciate the yen in order to revive its recession-hit economy. 

 Although market players expect a further reprieve for the region's currencies in the short term, they are likely to succumb to another bout of pressure if the yen resumes its recent fall, dealers said. But expectations of an economic rebound in Asia will mitigate the pain on the region's currencies inflicted by a wobbly yen, they added. 

 "The risk for the dollar is still on the downside in the near term," said a senior dealer at a European bank. "But dollar/Asians will find a floor if dollar/yen stays above Y130.50." 

 At 0940 GMT (4:40 a.m. EST), the dollar was quoted at Y131.48, above Y131.18 late Tuesday in New York. 

 As participants sought for further clues on the state of health of the U.S. economy, caution prevails ahead of the announcement later in the day of consumer price and industrial production data for December, business inventories for November and the Federal Reserve's Beige Book on regional economic activity. 

 The Singapore dollar stabilized around S$1.8300 against its U.S. counterpart late Wednesday after surging Tuesday, as foreign funds and local banks appeared to unwound their long U.S. dollar positions, dealers said. 

 Demand for U.S. dollars by local participants and U.S. investment banks helped the U.S. currency regain its footing, dealers said. 

 The Singapore dollar's sharp bounce over the past week also stoked fears of intervention by the local monetary authority, putting a floor under the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 Sentiment toward the Singapore dollar seemed to have also been helped by hopes that the pace of contraction in the city-state's non-oil domestic exports likely slowed in December due to improved overseas demand for electronic products, analysts said. 

 According to a Dow Jones Newswires survey of 10 economists, non-oil exports likely fell an average of 14.9% in December from a year ago, compared with contractions of 21.1% and 21.6% in November and October, respectively. 

 BNP Paribas said that, although based on technical charts, the U.S. dollar could extend its slide to as low as S$1.8070, fundamentals still point to a weaker Singapore dollar in the medium term. 

 "Inflation remains low and the risks to the economy from uncertain global developments remain," the bank said. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore said Wednesday in its macroeconomic review that it expects the island-nation's economy to continue contracting in the first half of 2002 from a year ago before rebounding into positive territory in the second half. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. currency was at S$1.8303 late Wednesday, off its morning low of around S$1.8270 and higher than S$1.8253 late Tuesday. 

 After slipping on heavy foreign equity fund outflows, the South Korean won recouped its losses to end higher. The dollar's repeated failure to break above KRW1,320 prompted local banks to dump the U.S. currency toward the market's close, dealers explained. 

 The dollar closed at 1,315.8 won, slightly lower than KRW1,316.9 Tuesday. It peaked at KRW1,319 Wednesday. 

 Foreign investors were net sellers of South Korean shares for the seventh consecutive day, with Wednesday's net sales amounting to KRW133 billion. Seoul's benchmark stock index ended 1.1% lower at a year-trough of 710.95. 

 The New Taiwan dollar had too earlier felt the pain of foreign equity fund outflows, sinking to as low as NT$35.063 against the U.S. currency Wednesday. 

 However, central bank intervention helped the New Taiwan dollar regain its footing to end little changed at NT$35.000 per U.S. dollar, dealers said. The greenback closed at NT$34.999 Tuesday. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the dollar closed at 51.280 pesos, above PHP51.255 Tuesday. 

 The market remains on guard amid persistent rumors of moves to destabilize the government ahead of the first anniversary of former President Joseph Estrada's ouster this weekend. 

 The Thai currency was steady at 43.865 baht to the dollar, compared with THB43.870 late Tuesday. 

 Participants were wary of pushing the baht higher amid fears of central bank intervention, dealers said. Dealers believe the Bank of Thailand had bought dollars in the last few sessions to curb the baht's rise, in part to maintain the price competitiveness of the country's exports. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was slightly firmer at 10,375 rupiah to the dollar, compared with IDR10,390 late Tuesday.

title: Thai Baht Ends A Tad Higher In Line With Yen's Recovery
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended a tad higher against the U.S. dollar in Asian spot trade Friday, tracking the Japanese yen's slight recovery, traders said. 

 The U.S. dollar finished at 44.03 baht, down slightly from THB44.065 at the Asian close Thursday. 

 The dollar was stuck in a very tight THB44.02-THB44.05 range in quiet intraday trade due to the relative lack of volatility in the yen, the regional trendsetter. 

 Thai exporters and debtors held back their respective dollar sell and buy orders ahead of the weekend, waiting for a clearer direction in the yen next week, traders said. 

 The market shrugged off a local newspaper report Friday in which central bank Assistant Governor Tarisa Watanagase was cited as saying that the bank has occasionally intervened in the foreign exchange market this year. 

 Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula had said late Thursday that the central bank hadn't intervened. 

 In any case, the central bank hasn't intervened against market trends, and the amount of dollars purchased by suspected agents of the central bank late last week wasn't significant, a foreign bank trader said. 

 Traders said the central bank may be buying dollars on weakness to build foreign reserves and that Pridiyathorn may not consider this to be intervention. 

 The dollar was expected to open Monday in a range of THB43.90-THB44.10, subject to any renewed volatility in the yen.

title: THAI PRESS: Ctrl Bk Admits  Intervening  In  Forex  Mkt In 02
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thailand's central bank has admitted occasionally intervening in the foreign exchange market this year, buying dollars to help stem the baht's volatility, the Nation reports, quoting the bank's Assistance Governor Tarisa Watanagase. 

 "The central bank entered into the market to prevent the baht trading from too much volatility. However, we don't need it (the baht) to move against the market trend," Tarisa was quoted as saying by the newspaper. She didn't disclose the amount of dollars bought. 

 She said after a period of weakening, the strength in the baht over the past few days was in line with movements in other regional currencies. There were no other special factors affecting the Thai baht recently. 

 Contrary to the newspaper report, Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said late Thursday that the central bank hadn't intervened in the foreign exchange market. 

 Pridiyathorn was apparently responding to market talk late last week that the central bank had bought dollars through a bank in Singapore to curb the baht's strength.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late As Yen Takes A Breather
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Thursday after clambering off their intraday lows, as expressions of concern by Japanese monetary officials over the speed of the yen's recent decline provided the beleaguered Japanese unit with some breathing space. 

 The yen's slide to as low as Y133.24 to the dollar early Thursday had cast a shadow on the other regional currencies. 

 The currencies, however, regained their footing when the yen recovered on comments by a senior official at Japan's Ministry of Finance, Zembei Mizoguchi, and subsequently Finance Minister Masajuro Shiokawa, expressing concerns over the pace of the yen's recent declines to three-year lows. 

 Their comments came at a time when Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi is on the second day of his five-nation tour of Southeast Asia - during which he risks being bombarded with complaints over Japan's weak yen policy. 

 Unlike some of their North Asian counterparts, Southeast Asian officials have remained silent despite worries that further pressures on their currencies from a slumping yen could push up the costs of servicing the region's dollar-denominated debts and dampen their economies' recovery prospects. 

 The dollar has bounced off the psychologically important Y132 level to trade around Y132.40 at 0910 GMT, lower than Y132.65 late Wednesday in New York. 

 "Dollar/yen's failure to break Y132 is a good sign," said a dealer at a European bank. "For all you know, dollar/regionals will trend back up again." 

 Indeed, the dollar remained buoyed above the psychologically important levels against Asian currencies, as participants took advantage of the U.S. unit's pullback to add on to their long U.S. dollar positions. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. currency stayed above S$1.8400, and was quoted at S$1.8436 late in the day, compared with S$1.8467 late Wednesday. 

 "The Singapore dollar has been the most correlated with the yen's movements," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, a regional currency strategist at UBS Warburg. "But it's beginning to show signs of outperforming." 

 He added that the Monetary Authority of Singapore's recent move to reinstate a narrower policy band within which it guides the trade-weighted local dollar indicates that the central bank may be less tolerant of the Singapore dollar's weakness against the U.S. currency. 

 The Philippine peso in part received a boost from investors' overwhelming response to the government's 15-year global bond issue, which was increased to $750 million from $500 million, dealers said. 

 "With the fresh borrowing, the government needs to raise less than $400 million to complete a $1.4 billion foreign financing requirement for 2002," which is needed to help it finance an estimated 130 billion-peso budget deficit this year, BNP Paribas said in a report. 

 Expectations of foreign investment inflows from the sale of shares in food conglomerate San Miguel Corp. (Q.MGL) to Japan's Kirin Brewery Ltd. (KNBWY) also bolstered the peso, dealers said. 

 The peso also found support from remittance inflows from Filipinos working overseas and the central bank's decision to leave overnight rates unchanged. 

 The dollar closed at PHP51.325 on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP51.560 Wednesday. Volume almost doubled to $125.2 million from $69.7 million Wednesday. 

 After floundering to as low as 1,318.0 won to the dollar in early trade, the South Korean currency ended at KRW1,312.3, only marginally lower than Wednesday's close of KRW1,311.9. 

 The U.S. currency hit a high of KRW1,318.0 after the dollar rose to just short of the three-year high against the yen set Wednesday. 

 Bank of Korea Governor Chon Chol-hwan said Thursday that the current level of the yen was "not too worrisome," despite his concern over the direction of the Japanese currency. 

 He added that the central bank won't intervene in the foreign exchange market unless market volatility increases "excessively." 

 The won shrugged off the Bank of Korea's as-expected decision to keep the overnight call rate unchanged in January at 4%. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency closed at NT$35.025, slightly lower than NT$35.050 Wednesday, in dealings valued at US$584.5 million. 

 To keep a rein on the appreciation of the local currency - in an apparent bid to maintain the price competitiveness of Taiwan's exports - the central bank snapped up more than US$100 million throughout the session, dealers in Taipei said. 

 The Thai currency was slightly weaker at 44.100 baht to the dollar, compared with THB44.065 late Wednesday. 

 "There are fears in the market that the central bank will be coming in to buy dollars if it falls sharply below THB44," said Mohi-uddin at UBS Warburg. Late last week and early this week, there were market suspicions that the Bank of Thailand had intervened to curb the strength of the baht as it traded past THB44. 

 The Indonesian currency was unchanged from late Wednesday's level of around 10,430 rupiah to the dollar.

    Of all the regional currencies, the Singapore dollar has

Sentiment was also boosted by news that Moody's Investors

rating to positive from stable. Standard & Poor's recently

The market shrugged off news that October's CPI recorded a

when it holds its monthly rate-setting meeting.

weakening fundamentals.



The government said on Thursday inflationary pressure was



hitting the economy hard. And as another signal of flagging



confidence in the economy, Fitch said it had changed its



outlook for Indonesia's ratings to stable from positive.



The government also continued to push ahead with its race



to dispose of assets ahead of year-end. Jakarta said it will



announce its decision about a closely-watched plan to sell a



majority stake in PT Semen Gresik to Mexico's Cemex. That plan



has so far been thwarted by provincial governments.

The baht was on the wrong side of the 44 per dollar mark



with players reluctant to push it higher on talk of possible



dollar buying intervention by the central bank.



The Bank of Thailand is due to release monthly economic



data on manufacturing, trade and current account balance and



its monetary policy committee will review key domestic interest



rates.



Dealers in Singapore said recent gains in regional

inflows were supporting the baht.



But speculation that the central bank, to protect export



competitiveness, may not allow the baht to appreciate above the

    The central bank has repeatedly said it would not cut its



benchmark 14-day repurchase rate, now at 2.5 percent.



    Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula on Thursday said an



adjustment in interest rates would not be needed unless the



economy looked to be slipping below its forecast growth range



of 1-3 percent for 2002.

The peso edged above the 52 level in light offshore trade



with local markets closed for a holiday. Manila markets will



resume trade on Monday.



Dealers in Singapore said players next week will focus on a



possible interest rate cut and rising remittances from overseas



workers may further help the peso higher.

The Taiwan dollar nudged higher on hopes of month-end



dollar sales by exporters but fears of central bank dollar



buying intervention and uncertainty ahead of Saturday



parliamentary elections was expected to limit gains.



More downward pressure on the Taiwan dollar may come from



expected equity-related outflows after foreign investors sold a

Thursday halting a five-session net buying streak.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late; Econ Angst Besieges Dlr
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies found respite late Thursday from the wobbly dollar, amid waning optimism that the U.S. recession would be brief, market watchers said. 

 The gains in most of the Asian currencies were, however, constrained by concerns that a prolonged downturn in the U.S. economy would only spell further gloom for the export-dependent region, market watchers said. Indeed, late in the day, these currencies - especially the Singapore dollar - had come off their intraday highs. 

 The U.S. Federal Reserve's pessimistic assessment of the economy in its Beige Book report added to the market's realization that the economy could only get worse, before getting better. 

 "Economic activity generally remained soft in October and the first half of November, with evidence of additional slowing in most regions outweighing signs of recovery in a few districts," the Fed's "beige book," a report on economic conditions throughout its 12 reserve districts, said. 

 The report appears to add to the likelihood Fed policy makers will trim its short-term interest-rate target, now at a 40-year low of 2%, when they meet Dec. 11. 

 "Overall, U.S. dollar sentiment has now turned a bit bearish," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 A string of benign U.S. economic data issued in recent weeks had fueled hopes that the recession there had bottomed, bolstering the dollar. But the market started reassessing its views this week, following a speech Tuesday by Federal Reserve Governor Laurence Meyer that appeared to leave the door open for more cuts, and a weak U.S. consumer confidence report. 

 "The question that the market needs to ask itself is not whether the (U.S.) recovery is real, but whether the rapid pace of the recovery that it appears to want to price in is real," DBS Bank said in a report. 

 The steep falls in U.S. stocks Wednesday - which was in part roiled by Dynegy Inc's decision to pull out of merger talks with debt-laden Enron Corp. - also cast a shadow on the dollar. 

 The U.S. currency's earlier fall against the Japanese yen and the euro worked in favor of the Singapore dollar, which briefly strengthened past S$1.8300 resistance to its U.S. counterpart earlier in the day, dealers said. 

 At 0930 GMT, the Singapore dollar was still firmer at S$1.8317 against the U.S. currency, compared with S$1.8332 late Wednesday. 

 After briefly falling below Y123 earlier, the dollar was quoted at Y123.19 late Thursday, above Y123.06 late Wednesday in New York but lower than Y123.55 late Wednesday in Tokyo. 

 The euro was at $0.8877, lower than $0.8884 late Wednesday in New York, but higher than $0.8845 in Tokyo. 

 The South Korean won recouped its earlier losses to end stronger, as exporters, capitalizing on the dollar's gains, jumped in to sell the U.S. currency at the last-minute for their month-end book balancing, dealers said. 

 The dollar finished at 1,269.0 won, down from KRW1,272.1 Wednesday. The dollar had hit an intraday high of KRW1,276.2. 

 The won felt the pain from foreign equity outflows earlier in the day, which contributed to the main stock index's 0.5% slide, dealers said. Foreign investors unloaded a net KRW126.8 billion in shares Thursday. 

 Dollar-buying by some of Hynix Semiconductor's creditor banks also dealt a blow to the won earlier in the day, Seoul-based dealers said. The banks have dollar-denominated loans extended to Hynix and must buy dollars to boost their loan-loss reserves, they added. 

 Late in the afternoon, however, with the dollar steady at KRW1,274, exporters rushed into the market and unloaded dollars. 

 As the yen came off its intraday high, short-covering in the U.S. currency and intermittent intervention by Taiwan's central bank countered the strength of the New Taiwan dollar, which was buoyed by moderate portfolio inflows and sales of the U.S. currency by exporters, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.465, marginally lower than Wednesday's close of NT$34.467. The U.S. dollar had touched an intraday low of NT$34.435. 

 The central bank will likely continue to keep the New Taiwan dollar steady ahead of Saturday's legislative election, which could herald the formation of a new coalition government. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, the peso finished slightly weaker at 52.000 pesos on month-end corporate demand for dollars, compared with PHP51.965 Wednesday. 

 With the market now focusing on the country's recovery prospects, the peso reacted with indifference to the Philippines' third-quarter economic report card - which was within expectations. 

 The Philippines' gross domestic product grew 2.9% in the third quarter, marginally higher than the government's target of 2.8% for this period. 

 The Thai currency was a touch firmer at 44.050 baht to the dollar, compared with THB44.090 late Wednesday. Lingering fears that the Thai central bank might buy dollars around THB44.000 kept a rein on the local currency's rise, dealers said. Some dealers believe the Bank of Thailand had intervened to curb the baht's strength around that level this week. 

 The Indonesian currency was stronger around 10,400 rupiah against the dollar, compared with IDR10,450 late Wednesday.

title: Thai Baht Ends Higher On Continued Cap Market Inflows
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended higher in Asian spot trade Tuesday, supported by inflows of investment funds to local capital markets, traders said. 

 The U.S. dollar was quoted in late trade Tuesday at 44.075 baht, down from THB44.15 at the Asian close Monday. 

 Offshore players have been selling dollars to invest in equity and bond markets over the past week, Bangkok dealers said. 

 Foreign net buying in Thai stocks continued Tuesday, and payment - in baht - was due Wednesday for the THB15 billion worth of bonds to be issued by local mobile phone operator Advanced Info Service. Much of the THB10 billion allotment to institutions was believed to have gone to offshore parties. 

 "Continued inflows from foreign investors have pressured the dollar against the local currency, despite its strength against other Asian currencies," a foreign bank dealer said. 

 The U.S. unit has risen in recent days against the Japanese yen and the Singapore dollar. 

 The U.S. dollar hit an intraday low of THB44.06 soon after the central bank announced Tuesday it will maintain the policy-signal 14-day repurchase market interest rate at 2.5%. 

 The decision to leave the rate unchanged was expected, but eliminated a factor which might have supported the dollar for at least the medium term. 

 Bank of Thailand said it could make its monetary policy more accomodative if the economic recovery was weaker than expected, but it said fiscal stimulus would help to keep gross domestic product growth in the forecast range of 1%-3% next year. 

 Dollar weakness was limited by local corporate demand from importers and those with foreign currency-denominated debts, dealers said. 

 Dealers expect resistance at THB44.15 Wednesday. Firm support is expected at THB44.00, underpinned by concerns over central bankintervention. 

 Bank of Thailand has a policy of intervening to stem volatility, and of accumulating dollars to maintain foreign reserves while repaying loans taken out under an expired International Monetary Fund rescue program. 

 Thai government bonds finished slightly higher Tuesday on liquidity-driven demand after the central bank's affirmation of no change in current monetary policy reduced uncertainty over the market's near-term direction. 

 The issue due October 2005 finished in a bid-offer range of 3.62%-3.60%, down from 3.66% at the close Monday. The July 2007 issue finished at 4.20%-4.18%, down from 4.215%. Yields move in the opposite direction to prices. 

 Yields should continue to edge lower Wednesday, when the first auction of new three-year and 10-year government bonds will be held. The secondary market yield curve suggested that results would be in a range of 3.2%-3.3%, and 5.2%-5.3% respectively. 

 The central bank auction will also reopen an existing government bond issue due April 2021 for THB1.5 billion. No activity was reported in the issue Tuesday, but results in Wednesday's auction should be around the most recent quotations near 6.20%. 

 Liquidity-driven demand should continue to underpin sentiment in the near term, but there wasn't a lot of room for yields to fall before persistent support levels were encountered again, dealers said. 

 Money market interest rates closed mostly flat amid ample liquidity.

title: Emerging  FX  - Weaker vs U.S. dollar on war news.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 14 (Reuters) - Asian currencies on Wednesday 

 were mostly softer against the U.S. dollar, which was boosted 

 by hopes of a speedy conclusion to the war in Afghanistan and 

 fears of Bank of Japan intervention to weaken the yen. 

     The Thai baht bucked the trend, rising on the back of 

 capital inflows linked to investment in the equity market, with 

 gains exaggerated somewhat by thin market volumes. 

     The U.S.-supported Northern Alliance captured the Afghan 

 capital of Kabul on Tuesday, causing soldiers for the ruling 

 Taliban regime to scatter. The news bolstered the U.S. 

currency, which had been hurt by the plane crash in New York on 

 Monday. 

     But the market was reluctant to push the U.S. currency too 

 far due to fears of central bank intervention. 

     There was talk of Taiwan's central bank entering the 

 market 

 to sell the U.S. dollar at 34.52 and of Bank Indonesia selling 

 the greenback to support the local currency. 

 Trading in the regional currencies was thinned by a market 

 holiday in Singapore. Financial markets in the city state will 

 reopen on Thursday. 

 Investors are awaiting U.S. retail sales numbers due out later 

 on Wednesday. 

 Economists polled by Reuters forecast a 2.7 percent 

 increase in October retail sales, with strong auto sales 

 driving gains in the headline figure after a 2.4 percent 

 decline in September. Excluding autos, retail sales are seen 

 gaining 0.2 percent after a 2.4 percent decline in September. 

 KOREAN WON 

 The won tallied up some gains thanks to the local stock 

 market's rise and renewed net buying by foreign investors. 

 Foreign equity-related flows, more so than the direction of 

 the dollar/yen, have held sway over the won in the past few 

 weeks. While Tuesday's net sales of local stocks drove the won 

 lower, signs of a pick-up in net buying by foreign investors 

 cheered the won. 

 Still, a softer yen did impede the won's rise, though the 

 market managed to shrug off news that the country's 

 unemployment had risen by an adjusted 3.5 percent in October 

 compared with 3.3 percent in September. 

 It was the first rise in eight months, with analysts and 

 officials saying the ranks of the unemployed were likely to 

 swell in coming months. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht remained well-supported by capital inflows which 

 dealers said were likely to be linked to the IPO of a local 

 state-run energy company later this week. 

 But its upside was capped by the dollar's strength against 

 other regional currencies and fears of central bank

 dollar-buying intervention to reign in its gains. 

Thailand relies heavily on exports, which account for more 

 than 50 percent of its gross domestic product, and a strong 

currency can hurt its competitiveness. 

     Baht funding costs in the offshore market were generally 

 firmer, with the one-month forward rate quoted at 6/10 satang 


per dollar.      PHILIPPINE PESO



    The peso crawled off its intraday low of 52.18 to the



dollar, thanks to rumoured central bank intervention.



    Dealers in Manila said the central bank might have sold



around $10-20 million to defend the peso below 52.10.



    The peso weakened after corporate players snapped up the



U.S. currency to cover short positions and to repay foreign



debt.



    Inflows from overseas Filipino workers had been scarce this



week, which may confirm analysts' predictions that inflows are



likely to slow this year because of the global economic



slowdown and rising unemployment.



In the bond market, rates on government securities fell by



as much as 25 basis points in the secondary market as demand



picked up due to excess liquidity in the system.



Earlier in the day, Finance Secretary Jose Camacho said he



expected the 91-day T-bill rate to remain below 10 percent for



the rest of 2001.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah rose above 10,600 after some players unwound



long dollar positions partly due to fears of central bank

intervention.



Dealers in Jakarta said the market had overbought the



dollar late last week on anticipation that a few local



companies would buy big amounts, but the demand turned out to



be lower than expected.



    Any reprieve is likely to be short-lived as there is no



lack of bad news in Indonesia.



    On the political front, the market was still jittery over



potential violence after a prominent pro-independence leader in



the troubled province of Irian Jaya was found dead over the



weekend.



Foreign investment approvals in January-September fell to



$6.05 billion from $12.25 billion last year. Investors have



been avoiding Indonesia for months due to concerns over its



political and economic instability.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar stayed within the bounds of its recent



range, and idled around the 34.50 mark in dozy trade.



For weeks, the local dollar has not ventured far from a



range of around 34.50-34.60 because of the central bank's near



daily presence. Foreign stock-related inflows, exporters'



dollar sales and even negative economic news have failed to



bump the currency out of its range.



Analysts say the central bank has been remarkably



successful at keeping the currency stable, which it is



determined to do to hold onto Taiwan's export competitiveness



while not damaging domestic sentiment.

title: Thai Baht Ends Dn Tracking Singapore Dollar In Thin Trade
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht closed lower Friday in thin trade tracking the Singapore dollar after shrugging off data that showed a robust trade surplus in August, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 44.435 baht, up from THB44.385 baht at the Asian close Thursday. 

 The U.S. unit opened at THB44.43 and quickly rose to the day's high of THB44.47 on dollar buying by offshore players after the Bank of Japan intervened in global currency markets to weaken the yen, said traders. 

 Importers looking to square positions also bought dollars, but fears of possible intervention by the Bank of Thailand in favor of the baht limited the dollar's rise and kept it in a narrow range, they added. 

 Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyarthorn Devakula indicated earlier this week that he wouldn't hesitate to intervene to limit excess volatility in the baht. 

 The central bank issued trade data for August late Friday showing that exports contracted less than expected due to strong demand for agricultural products. Exports fell 7.6% on the year while imports slumped 16% on year, leading to a trade surplus of $729 million, the biggest in 17 months. 

 However, traders don't expect the trend to be sustained as exports are seasonally strong in August and external demand is expected to weaken sharply following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in the U.S. 

 Dealers said the baht is expected to continue to trade in a tight range Monday and remain tied to movements in the yen and the Singapore dollar. Support is pegged at THB44.30 and resistance at THB44.50. 

 Thai government bond prices continued to rise Friday, supported by expectations that the Bank of Thailand may soon cut its key interest rate and hopes that the government may delay a large planned bond issue, traders said. 

 They said interbank players actively bought short-to-medium bonds on the belief that the Thai central bank will cut its key interest rates if the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee cuts its Federal Funds rate at next Tuesday's meeting. 

 Another supportive factor was the possible delay of a planned issuance of THB320 billion government-guaranteed bonds, initially scheduled for the fourth quarter to finance losses incurred by the Financial Institutions Development Fund, or FIDF. 

 Officials earlier said the bond issuance schedule depends on parliamentary approval of the Public Debt Management Bill. The current parliamentary session ends late next month. 

 "They (investors) think that if the bill fails to pass the parliament in this session, the bond issuance may be delayed to next year," a local bank trader said. 

 Yields, which move in the opposite direction of prices, on active bonds ended down by an average of seven basis points, after dipping around five basis points Thursday. 

 The most active issue, the bond maturing December 2006, closed at 5.05%, down from 5.14% at Thursday's close, according to the Thai Bond Dealing Center. 

 The June 2004 bond closed at 3.84%, from 3.91% Wednesday. 


Thai short-term money rates ended slightly higher as some banks
reserved extra money for the weekend on uncertainties over possible U.S.
retaliation after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks on the World Trade
Center and Pentagon.

title: Asian  Currencies  Lower Fri, Tracking Weaker Yen
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies were lower late Friday in line with a decline in the yen, after the Bank of Japan intervened once again in global currency markets to weaken the Japanese currency. 

 The Singapore dollar, the Korean Won, the Indonesian rupiah and the New Taiwan dollar all closed lower against the dollar, while the Philippine peso bucked the trend, getting a moderate lift from the gradual flow of remittances made by overseas Filipino workers. 

 Market activity was fairly subdued ahead of the weekend, with many traders reluctant to sell dollars due to widespread notions the BOJ will continue to boost the U.S. currency with intervention. Some traders also remained sidelined due to concerns the U.S. might launch a retaliatory strike in Afghanistan as part of its quest to punish the perpetrators of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in New York and Washington. 

 A late afternoon spurt of selling by Japanese banks and Hong Kong trading houses pushed the Singapore dollar lower. The U.S. currency touched a high for the session at S$1.7675 before ending at S$1.7662, up from S$1.7613 late Thursday. 

 "There was some selling toward S$1.77 from some large Hong Kong houses," one trader said. He added that he expects the U.S. dollar to meet firm resistance at that level in the coming sessions, with the immediate trading range likely to fall between S$1.7580 and S$1.77. 

 In Seoul, dollar demand from domestic banks and oil importers keen to take care of their dollar needs ahead of a five-day weekend pushed the won lower. Korean financial markets will be closed Monday and Tuesday for Chuseok, the Korean Thanksgiving, and on Wednesday for National Foundation Day. 

 The dollar finished at 1,309.6 won, up from Thursday's close of KRW1,306.4. 

 The tone for trading in most Asian currencies was set in Tokyo, where monetary authorities continued their relentless efforts to cap the yen's upside. The BOJ intervention appeared aimed at offsetting the effects of Japanese corporations repatriating dollar-assets to improve their balance sheets before closing their books at the Sept. 30 fiscal half year end. 

 The dollar strengthened initially against the yen following the BOJ intervention but later retreated to around Y118.90 late in the day, well off its Y119.75 high. 

 Some participants speculated that any further BOJ attempts to weaken the yen may meet with only limited success, as uncertainty in global financial markets is likely to discourage Japanese institutional investors from buying foreign assets. 

 "Given the global theme of risk aversion, it is extremely unlikely that we'll see any significant outflows of Japanese capital from October onwards," one trader said. 

 Although the BOJ was the only central bank in Asia that intervened Friday, the threat of intervention by other central banks in the region helped support some currencies. 

 The Thai baht weakened in light trade tracking the Singapore dollar, but fears of possible intervention by the Bank of Thailand limited its slide, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 44.385 baht, up from THB44.305 baht at the Asian close Thursday, after moving in a narrow range between THB44.33 to THB44.39. 

Central Bank Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula's comments Wednesday fueled speculation that the central bank remains ready to step into the market. He said the BOT would continue to prevent excess volatility in the baht's movements and would limit capital outflows. 

 Elsewhere, the Philippine peso also was supported in part on notions the central bank might intervene. 

 Although the dollar spiked early on expectations of month-end corporate requirements, thin demand and the gradual inflow from remittances made by overseas Filipino workers helped the peso gain some lost ground. 

 The dollar closed at 51.32 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP51.365 Friday and well below Friday's intraday high at PHP51.395. 

 The Indonesian rupiah also ended lower as local companies continued to buy dollars amid fears the U.S. unit could rise amid growing anti-U.S. demonstrations. The dollar closed Asian trade at 9,710 rupiah, its intraday high, up from its close Thursday at IDR9,685. 

 Around 2,000 Muslims took to the streets of Jakarta Friday to protest possible U.S. retaliatory strikes against Afghanistan. Indonesia is the world's largest Muslim country, with around 90% of its 200 million population. 

 The New Taiwan dollar ended nearly unchanged against its U.S. counterpart, coming off its earlier highs as market participants covered short U.S. dollar positions late in the session, dealers said. They also said the central bank was suspected of buying U.S. dollars to slow the local unit's rise. At 0800 GMT (4 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.549, nearly flat with Thursday's close of NT$34.548. 

 The market's focus next week will be directed toward Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee meeting, at which the U.S. central bank is increasingly expected to cut interest rates by 25-50 basis points. 

 Also, traders also will monitor how the yen reacts to release Monday morning of the Bank of Japan's quarterly tankan business sentiment survey. This will be one of the first reports to show how terrorist attacks in the U.S. on Sept. 11 affected business sentiment in Japan, a senior government official said Friday. 

 "The tankan survey will be studied very carefully," Eiji Kawade, vice minister of the Cabinet Office, said in a regular press conference. "The attacks may have heightened risk factors in various forms" in Japan's business environment, he said. 

 The Bank of Japan will be release the tankan at 2350 GMT Sunday, or 8:50 a.m. Monday JST.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Dlr Fails To Sustain Rise
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Thursday, after having recouped most of their earlier losses as the dollar remained wobbly against the yen despite the threat of intervention by Japanese authorities. 

 With little in the form of direction from the stable yen in early trading, most of the region's currencies fell under the sway of the Singapore dollar's swift decline, dealers said. 

 But the U.S. dollar failed to sustain its upward momentum, eventually succumbing to worries over the economic fallout of last week's terrorist attacks and uncertainty over the nature and extent of U.S. retaliation against the perpetrators of the assaults, dealers said. The dollar's fate is also tied to the performance of the U.S. equities market, which remains shaky. 

 "Everything should be sideways, at least between now and the end of the month," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 As the U.S. gears up for war, Islamic clerics Thursday urged terrorist suspect Osama bin Laden to voluntarily leave Afghanistan, where he and his followers have had sanctuary for five years, the Taliban news agency said. 

 The clerics' statement set no deadline for bin Laden to accept or reject the call, and it was unclear whether this would be enough to dissuade U.S. President George W. Bush from launching massive military strikes against Afghanistan. 

 Fears of central bank intervention, if not talk of actual intervention, also kept the market nervous, dealers said. 

 "Central banks galore," said the European bank dealer. 

 The Philippine peso and the Indonesian rupiah regained their footing after the central bank was suspected of having sold dollars to halt the depreciation of their respective currencies, dealers said. 

 Some dealers believed Taiwan's central bank bought U.S. dollars to prevent the local currency from strengthening with the yen. 

 There was also some talk - which many in the market played down, if not dismissed - that the authorities in Singapore and Thailand had intervened to weaken their currencies, dealers said. 

 Early in the day, the Singapore dollar floundered to S$1.7460 against its U.S. counterpart, compared with S$1.7417 late Wednesday. 

 U.S. dollar purchases by a large U.S. bank and investment houses based in Hong Kong propelled the currency, dealers said. The sharp jump fueled speculation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore had bought U.S. dollars. 

 But profit-taking subsequently led to a retreat in the U.S. currency, dealers said.

title: Thai Baht Ends Lower, Rate Cuts Help Dlr; Ctrl Bk Fears
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended lower Tuesday as the dollar found support from interest rate cuts overnight by several major central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve, dealers said. 

 The central banks' resolve to stabilize the markets and protect the global economy helped calm nerves in the foreign exchange markets. 

 As reported, the U.S. Fed cut its federal funds rate by 50 basis points. 

 The dollar finished at 44.235 baht, up from THB43.975 at Monday's Asian close. 

 Milder-than-expected losses on Wall Street also helped sentiment. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 7.1% Monday, while the Nasdaq Composite Index tumbled 6.8%. 

 Fears of possible intervention by Thailand's central bank, amid talk that it had bought the dollar below the THB44 level Monday, also gave a boost to the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 However, dealers said the dollar remains directionless due to uncertainties over the possible U.S. retaliation against the perpetrators of last week's terrorist attacks. 

 Reports that the ruling Taliban had urged Afghans to prepare for a holy war against the U.S. should it attack, also weighed on the dollar movements. 

 Dealers said the dollar is expected to trade in a range of THB44.10-THB44.40 Wednesday. 

 Thai government bonds ended barely changed as news of worldwide interest rate cuts was offset by concerns of a possible "holy war" against the U.S., traders said. 

 Yields, which move in the opposite direction to prices, fell by an average of six basis points in the morning in response to the interest rate reductions by the Federal Open Market Committee and other key central banks. 

 "But, yields started to rise later on market jitters after Taliban news," a local bank dealer said. 

 According to the Thai Bond Dealing Center's report, the most active December 2006 issue closed up at 5.38% versus 5.34% at the previous close, while the July 2007 issue closed flat at 5.48%, the report said. 


Thai overnight interbank rates ended lower after their recent sharp

 Pridiyathorn told reporters the BOT's policy was to focus on maintaining healthy foreign excahnge reserves. 

 "Interest and forex rates have been stable and have seen no major changes since the U.S. situation. We are focusing on maintaining healthy reserves to boost public confidence," he said.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk: THB Stable, Hasn't  Intervened  In  Forex  Mkt
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devekula said Friday that the baht has been stable so far, and the central bank hasn't intervened in the market. 

 "There is nothing to worry about. The baht's strength is in line with the global (currency) market," he told reporters. 

 The U.S. dollar has fallen against most currencies after the terrorist attacks in the U.S. Tuesday. 

 Pridiyathon said the central bank will monitor the currency market, especially when the U.S. stock market resumes trading, expected Monday. 

 However, he said panic selling of U.S. stocks is expected to be minimized, because the U.S. markets have been closed after the attacks, so the impact of Tuesday's events on the market when it opens is unlikely to be catastrophic. 

 He added that the recovery in European and key Asian bourses Friday after their recent declines also signaled that the impact of New York markets, when they do open, won't be that serious. 

 At Friday's Asian close, the dollar finished at 44.245 baht, down from THB44.290 at the previous close, on continued dollar selling in the aftermath of the terrorist attacks in the U.S.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk:US Events Almost No Impact On  Forex  Mkt
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said the central didn't intervene in the market Wednesday as there was almost no impact on the foreign exchange market from Tuesday's terrorist attacks in the U.S. 

 Pridiyathorn told a news conference he was comfortable with the level of the baht, noting that the dollar didn't weaken as much as had been expected following the attacks. 

 "The central bank is closely monitoring the market to ensure that liquidity in the system is sufficient," he said. 

 At 0511 GMT (1:11 a.m. EDT), the baht was trading at THB44.39 to the dollar, slightly stronger from THB44.425 at the open and THB44.80 at Tuesday's close. 

 In one of the most horrifying attacks ever against the U.S., terrorists on Tuesday morning crashed two airliners into the World Trade Center in New York. Another plane crashed into the Pentagon near Washington, collapsing one side of the building, and a fourth airliner crashed in a field 80 miles southeast of Pittsburgh. No one has yet claimed responsibility for the attacks. 

 Pridiyathorn said a total THB9 billion was injected into the system by the central bank through the repurchase market and from commercial banks with excess liquidity. 

 Traders said earlier that the central bank was injecting funds through its 2.5% policy-signal 14-day repo rate. 

 Pridiyathorn said no intervention took place in the foreign exchange or bond markets. He also called on banks to settle their baht obligations to prevent liquidity shortages. 

 Pridiyathorn said the Bank of Thailand will wait to see the wider economic impact of Tuesday's events before taking any needed actions or changing the bank's economic predictions. 

 The central bank recently revised its 2001 gross domestic product growth forecast to a range of 1.5%-2% from a 2%-3% range previously. 

 Analysts have said the Thai economy was already on the brink of recession. Second-quarter GDP data, due Monday, is expected to show either a contraction for the second consecutive quarter or very weak growth.

title: Emerging  FX  - Higher as dollar languishes.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 31 (Reuters) - Asian currencies stood firm early on Friday as falls on Wall Street and an interest rate cut by the European Central Bank badly bruised the dollar. 

 Even with poor economic news spilling out of Japan and the rest of the region, the market remained more compelled by the bearish news from the U.S. 

 The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped past the key psychological threshold of 10,000 and the Nasdaq fell past 1,800 - lows not seen since April. 

 While U.S. equity losses could drive local stock markets lower, regional currencies at best have risen slightly with the yen or remained stable at worst. 

 Dealers said while most of the action has been in the euro , the yen's resilience has made the dollar vulnerable to the Asian currencies. 

 "Logically, the Asian currencies should weaken against the euro and dollar given the fundamentals, but I'm not willing to bet on it at these levels," said a U.S. bank dealer. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar rose with the yen, breaking 1.7395 for the first time since February 27 despite local banks' agressive U.S. dollars bids. 

 Dealers said the market suspected these banks were acting on the Monetary Authority of Singapore's behalf as the authorities may be concerned about the Sing dollar's appreciation on a trade-weighted basis. 

 Analysts say with the city-state in a technical recession, the MAS was unlikely to tolerate further strength in the Sing dollar against the U.S. dollar. 

 But dealers said Hong Kong-based banks were selling dollar/Sing on the back of the yen's gains. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won eked out gains on the stronger yen, but losses on the local stock market prevented it from rising much higher. 

 Anxiety over local developments prevented the won from strengthening beyond 1,280. Local stocks fell as investors fretted over the fate of Hynix Semiconductor. 

 Creditors of the debt-laden chip maker have delayed talks on rescuing the company. 

 The market was also watching for July industrial output production due at 0300 GMT. A Reuters poll showed analysts on average expect a 0.9 percent month-on-month drop in July. 

 It reacted little to the rise in August's consumer price index of 0.5 percent from the previous month. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht climbed in line with the regional currencies with local and foreign banks unwinding their long dollar positions. 

 Bangkok dealers said the baht had hit a high so far of 44.18 against 44.29 in active trade. They added, however, the dollar should find support around 44.10, which is close to the low it hit on August 28. 

 While some in the market thought the Bank of Thailand may intervene around the 44 level given the country's tottering economic fundamentals, dealers said it was unlikely. 

 "The baht is moving in line with the regionals, and the authorities have said before they will tolerate that," said a local bank dealer in Bangkok. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah edged up in line with the regionals on wariness over intervention by the central bank, which was suspected to have sold dollars on Thursday. 

 But Singapore dealers said demand for the dollar from local corporates for debt repayment needs was high and would weigh the rupiah back down to the wrong side of 9,000. 

 The central bank had been in the market since the rupiah fell through the 9,000 mark earlier this week. 

 Finance Minister Boediono said on Thursday the government was considering a stronger exchange rate of 8,000-9,000 per dollar for the 2002 budget. A rate of 9,600 per dollar was assumed for the 2001 budget. 

 The government is expected to submit to parliament key economic assumptions for the 2002 budget in September. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso gained ground, helped by a firmer regional tone and on month-end export-related inflows. 

 Manila dealers said with a stronger yen and expected export inflows, most corporates and importers were likely to stay on the sidelines and an upward break of the 51 mark was possible. 

 The peso was just shy of the 51 mark, facing covering of short dollar positions. 

 Dealers said suspected intervention by the central bank was also detering importers from entering the market. They added low trading volume was exaggerating moves. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar was slightly firmer, tracking other regionals and the yen, but Hong Kong dealers said pressure on the U.S. dollar was light and no big deals were reported. 

 The local currency hit a high of 34.55 in morning trade against Thursday's close of 34.582. 

 Dealers had not heard of central bank intervention so far on Friday, but added the central bank may step in around 34.50. The Taiwan central bank has been spotted buying U.S. dollars to stem the local dollar's rise. 

 Analysts and dealers say the authorities are keen on maintaining export competitiveness.

title: ANALYSIS-Matching funds may not help Thai stock prices.
text:
BANGKOK, Aug 30 (Reuters) - Thai plans for using government money to lure foreign institutional investors into "matching funds" to help revive the country's flagging economy could help in the privatisation of state-owned companies, analysts say. 

 But they warn that the funds - which may initially be around $200 million - would be too small to significantly add to the momentum of an equities market that has already shown strong gains this year despite concerns over global economic slowdown. 

 Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra has recently visited several Asian countries to plug his government's proposal to match foreign investment with a 25 percent contribution. 

 Reports have suggested the Government of Singapore Investment Corp (GIC) and Brunei institutional investors could set up separate $100 million funds. Thailand says the Chinese government is also interested. 

 Details of the funds were scarce, but analysts suspect they could be used to smooth privatisation efforts for state-owned firms like the Petroleum Authority of Thailand (PTT) and Thai Airways. 

 One of the main perks for foreign investors in the funds could be first option on initial public offerings. 

 "There's a little fear with privatisations, that when they come up for bidding no-one will buy them," said Marc Lavoie, head of research at Asset Plus Management. 

 "But say if 80 percent of PTT has already been bought by Singapore or Brunei, people are going to jump in." 

 "I think the bulk of the (fund) money is aimed at privatisations or pre-privatisations. It's not an equity bailout fund, I don't think they're that stupid," he said. 

 THREE TYPES OF FUND 

 Thai officials said some funds would be for investment in the stock market and state-owned enterprises. But the emphasis would be on channelling money into cash-strapped private firms suffering from banks' ultra-cautious lending policies. 

 "The funds will be closed-ended, with a five-year limit, and there will be three investment types - portfolio in the stock market, direct investment depending on the objective of the fund, and investment for the privatisation programme," said Chaiyuth Sudthitanakorn, senior expert for fiscal and tax affairs at the Ministry of Finance. 

 "The government thinks if we invest some money into potential, then companies can run and then list. Our economy can then move, not just stick." 

 Chaiyuth said Thai contributions could be from the government pension fund, state-owned Krung Thai Bank or the finance ministry, with most of any capital gains handed over to participating foreign investors. 

 "Our objective is not for profit, but we are in the process of asking foreign investors what they propose," he said. 

 Analysts said the funds would not be large enough to have any durable effect on share prices if they were put into a stock market which has already risen 25 percent this year. 

 In Asia, only China's recently liberalised hard currency B markets have outperformed Thai stocks in 2001. 

 "A DROP IN THE BUCKET" 

 "They're talking about $100 million each from Brunei and Singapore and trying to get the Chinese interested, but this is a drop in the bucket in equities," said Asset Plus's Lavoie. 

 He added that Thailand could not copy the successful intervention by Hong Kong authorities when markets were jittery about the 1997 handover of sovereignty. 

 "It was successful (in Hong Kong) because no-one knew who was doing the buying, so everyone else piled in, and there was justification because stocks were undervalued," he said. 

 "Maybe in Thailand there's not enough value because prices are up significantly and most sectors are no longer cheap." 

 But some dealers said investing in stocks could have a positive psychological effect. 

 "The absolute amount of money won't make an iota of difference, but the momentum from a perception that the government cares about the stock market will be a good thing," said Ben Knowles, head of sales at Seamico Securities. 

 Analysts said improved investor confidence would boost domestic consumption, a key goal of the Thaksin administration. 

 "Anything you can do to push up the stock market gets people excited, and excited people spend money," said Andrew Stotz, Vice President of SG Securities. 

 "We do need alternatives to bank deposits - because there's a huge mass of liquidity of 600 billion baht ($13.52 billion) - whether it's in equities, bonds or property," he said.

title: Emerging  FX  - Gains stalled by dollar reprieve.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 17 (Reuters) - Asian currencies lost steam after recent strong gains as the yen retreated against the dollar late Friday following a series of comments by Japanese officials which sparked fears of intervention. 

 Analysts reckoned dollar weakness would continue but mostly against the euro rather than the yen as Japan's economy is too weak to withstand a strong currency. "We have set the U.S. dollar trade-weighted weakness on our currency forecasts to come primarily against the euro, not against the yen," said Adam Le Mesurier, regional economist at Goldman Sachs in Singapore, in a report. 

 "We still look for the yen to depreciate in the near-term. This combination means non-Japan Asia currencies will still need to weaken both in trade-weighted terms and also against the dollar to buffer them from a severe external shock," he said. 

 The market was also driven by local factors. The Singapore dollar lost ground after July trade data showed non-oil domestic exports (NODX) fell 24.2 percent on the year. 

 The Taiwan dollar ended easier on local media reports suggesting second quarter growth data would be worse than expected, a view that was borne out after the market's close. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar pulled back as the yen's retreat and bearish export data prompted players to buy the U.S. dollar. 

 Analysts said the worst was yet to come for non-oil exports which contracted 24.2 percent on the year in July. 

 "There has not been a definite sign of a rebound in U.S. demand or an upturn in activities in the U.S. manufacturing sector," said Syetarn Hansakul, economist at WestLB. 

 "Secondly, retained imports, which are a good leading indicator for NODX continue to decline, falling 17.6 percent year-on-year in July," she said. 

 Dealers expected the Sing dollar to find a toehold around 1.7500 if the yen stayed around 120 to the dollar. It hit a 5-= month high of 1.74 when the yen surged past 120 on Thursday. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar slipped from Thursday's close of 34.52 as dealers bought dollars after local media reported second-quarter gross domestic product fell a worse-than-expected two percent year-on-year. 

 After the local currency market closed, the statistics bureau said Q2 GDP contracted 2.35 percent, well below the average 0.30 percent contraction forecast in a Reuters poll. It was the first decline in 26 years. 

 A statistics agency official said the 2001 growth forecast had been slashed to a 0.37 percent contravction from a previous forecast of 4.02 percent growth, made in May. 

 The central bank called an impromptu news conference at 0930 GMT to announce a quarter percentage point cut in key interest rates. It has already lowered rates by 1.25 percentage points since late last year in an effort to get the economy going. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht nudged lower alongside the yen as dollar offers by onshore parties were outpaced by bids from offshore players, dealers in Bangkok and Singapore said. 

 Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said the central bank had not intervened in the market this week but would monitor the baht's movement to keep it stable. 

 The baht has gained more than 1.50 percent this week. A strong technical barrier is expected at 44.40, the 38 percent retracement of the dollar's February 2-April 9 rise. 

 Meanwhile, Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra rebuffed an IMF suggestion that Thailand should not rule out interest rate cuts, saying rates were already low enough. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso slipped past 51 to the dollar in thin trade as local corporate dollar demand emerged around 51.10. 

 Manila dealers said trading was subdued given the market's fear of more attempts by the central bank to shore up support for the peso. 

 "It's local factors that are moving the market now. The central bank has made it clear it's not a sin to sell dollars, it's a sin to buy dollars," said a local bank dealer in Manila. Government offices and state-owned firms were closed around noon due to flooding in metro Manila. A central bank official told Reuters the bank also closed most of its departments. 

 But traders said this had little impact on trade. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won closed lower on dollar buying from importers and a state bank. But it was not clear if the state bank's purchases were on behalf of clients or the central bank. 

 Its presence at around 1,280-1,282 prompted other commercial banks to cover short dollar positions, dealers said. 

 Meanwhile, data released on Friday showed the consumer confidence index fell in July after rising for six consecutive months, suggesting a poor outlook for consumption in the second half of this year. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah was quoted at 8,700/8,800 in the offshore market, with trade at a virtual standstill as Jakarta markets were closed for a public holiday. They will re-open on Monday. 

Central bank governor Sjahril Sabirin told reporters earlier in the day the rupiah was still undervalued. He added an acceptable level for the rupiah was 7,000-8,000 per dollar. 

 Analysts say the new government has to tackle the country's many economic problems effectively before the rupiah can make further headway. 

 Since President Megawati Sukarnoputri took office, the rupiah has gained around 30 percent on rising hopes the new government will begin mending the shattered economy.
