title: Emerging  FX  - Vulnerable dollar cheers market.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 15 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were buoyed by a perky yen which rose to two-month highs against a backdrop of bearish sentiment towards the U.S. dollar and repatriation of funds to Japan. 

 "Yesterday was a big coupon maturity date in the U.S. bond market and repatriation of this flow was the principal source of the yen strength," said Ron Leven, chief Asia currency strategist at Lehman Brothers in Tokyo. 

 "But it is disturbing that these funds are not being rolled over in the U.S. market, and this is indicative of a world that is in risk reduction mode," he said, referring to the greater perceived risk surrounding the dollar. 

 Local factors also featured. The Philippine central bank's recent moves to squeeze peso out of the market by raising liquidity reserve requirements continued to boost the peso. 

 The market is focused on a Federal Reserve report due later on Wednesday on industrial production in July which is likely to show the 10th straight month of contraction in manufacturing. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah was beginning to lose some of its shine, retreating below 8,500 per dollar partly on talk local banks were buying back dollars to meet foreign debt maturing in late August. 

 A central bank source told Reuters a group of commercial banks would have to pay some $1.0 billion in restructured loans maturing later this month. 

 But the rupiah's downside continued to be underpinned by lingering hopes the new government would soon be able to convince the IMF to release stalled loans and the Paris Club to reschedule its debt. 

 The statistics bureau said GDP in the second quarter grew 3.52 percent on the year and 0.18 percent on the quarter, predicting growth would pick up in the third quarter because of optimism over the new leadership. 

 Interest rates headed north after two weeks of declines, with the central bank's benchmark one-month SBI fetching 17.30 percent at Wednesday's auction from 17.13 percent last week. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso gapped up at the open to break through 51 per dollar for the first time since June 12, but dollar bids by corporates and importers pulled it off almost ten-week highs of 50.60. 

 Dealers said some interbank players were still looking to offload their stale long dollar positions on wariness over central bank moves to push the peso higher. 

 Charts showed dollar/peso heavily overbought with the 14-day relative strength index reading at 11.31. 

 The central bank has squeezed peso liquidity through hikes in banks' liquidity requirements and has also penalised banks for forex rule violations. 

 Meanwhile, the Department of Finance said spending cuts helped lower the budget deficit for January-July to 82.586 billion pesos, against a target of 93.586 billion. But revenues at 320.7 billion came in below the target of 327.7 billion. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht ran into onshore commercial demand for the dollar prompting interbank players to cover their short positions. 

 But dealers in Singapore said offshore names continued to trim back on long dollar positions, keeping the baht in a tight 44.75-44.90 range. 

 Dealers said intervention wariness was also limiting gains above the session highs, around which the Bank of Thailand intervened to cap the baht's rise in early June. 

 Charts showed the dollar overbought against the baht with a 14-day RSI reading at 11.50. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar gave up some of its gains due to fears of central bankintervention as players recognised its recent rise was excessive and not warranted by economic fundamentals. 

 The local currency rose to 1.7520 in early trade before settling into a 1.7530-1.7570 range on talk the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) was in the market to check rates. 

 Analysts said its recent gains were fuelled by U.S. dollar weakness which set off rounds of Sing dollar short covering, but the longer-term direction for the currency should be down. 

 The U.S. dollar is heavily oversold against the Sing dollar, with a 14-day RSI reading of 12.95. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar edged up, taking its cue from bullish sentiment in local stocks which ended at a five-week high. 

 But dealers in Singapore said the central bank's presence in the market kept trade subdued and within a tight range. The central bank has recently been spotted capping the Taiwan dollar's rise to keep exports competitive. 

 Players were also cautious ahead of second quarter gross domestic product data due Friday. Most analysts expect negative growth for the first time in 26 years. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won nudged up in light, offshore trade as onshore markets were closed for Liberation Day. 

 The won was expected to take its cue from the yen when local markets resume trade on Thursday. A firmer yen has helped sentiment but selling of local stocks by foreign investors has weighed on the won in recent sessions.

title: Thai Baht Ends Higher Amid US Dlr Weakness Vs Regionals
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended firmer Wednesday amid U.S. dollar weakness against regional currencies on concerns about the ailing U.S. economy and the sustainability of the strong U.S. dollar policy, dealers said. 

 The dollar finished at THB44.865, up from THB44.965 at the Asian close Wednesday. 

 Concerns over the U.S. economic downturn drove players to unwind long-dollar positions, sending the dollar to a two-month low at THB44.73 in early trade, as the baht played catch up to appreciation of other regional currencies, traders said. 

 The dollar rebounded in afternoon session to THB44.865 as offshore players bought back dollars in profit-taking, said a dealer at foreign bank based in Bangkok. 

 The dollar's low came after central bank Assistant Governor Chetthavee Charoenpitaks said there had been no unusual movement recently in the baht, which eased concern about possible intervention. 

 He said baht's recent appreciation followed movement in regional currencies, as weakness in the U.S. economy has put pressure on dollar sentiment. 

 The rebound in the dollar came as investors considered, however, that Chetthavee had declined to say at what level the central bank might intervene if the baht strengthens too much. 

 Bank of Thailand reportedly intervened in the market in June when the dollar last weakened to around THB44.70. 

 Volume was active compared with light trade during the last few days, as offshore players squared dollar positions, they said. 

 The dollar was expected to open Thursday in a range of THB44.70 to THB45, subject to the fluctuation of regional currencies, dealers said. Next support would be THB44.50. 

 Thai government bond yields closed down in moderate trade Wednesday, led by buying from newly established funds, traders said. 

 "Several new funds stepped in to buy some medium- and long-term bonds early morning to build up their portfolios, prompting other investors to follow suit," said a dealer at local bank. 

 The baht's recent strength also prompted some banks to invest in the bond market, she said. 

 Yields dropped by 10-20 basis points in early trade before late profit-taking emerged to limit gains, they said. The yields of most active issues closed down by 5-to-10 basis points. 

 The Thai Bond Dealing Center said in its daily report that the yield on the government bond due June 2004 closed at 4.660%, down from a last deal Tuesday at 4.70%, while the December 2006 issue closed at 5.79% versus 5.865%. 

 However, concerns over THB320 billion in government-guaranteed bonds to be issued in the fourth quarter by the Financial Institutions Development Fund continued to weigh on market sentiment. 

 Some investors were also waiting to see the market's reaction to auctions of government bonds, which will resume next week. 

 Money market interest rates were mostly flat, on flush liquidity. The overnight repurchase market rate was down slightly as extra cash put into circulation ahead of the recent long weekend returned to financial institutions.

title: Emerging  FX  - Out of the yen's shadow, for now.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 14 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies struck 

 an upbeat note late on Tuesday, even as the yen floundered, 

 following the Bank of Japan's surprise decision to further ease 

 ultra-loose monetary policy. 

     Dealers pegged further position unwinding, amid the 

 dollar's general weakness against other major currencies, as 

 the reason for the bout of strength in regionals. 

     The Southeast Asian currencies racked up the greatest 

 gains, though thin liquidity in the peso, rupiah, and baht 

 markets exaggerated their rises. 

     "You have to consider the open positions out there. At the 

 beginning of the year, the most obvious trade is selling 

 regional currencies and going underweight in local stocks," 

 said a senior European bank dealer in Hong Kong. 

     "So given that, the recent dollar weakness, and the summer 

 holidays -- it's clear we are in a corrective phase." 

     But he and others said a weaker dollar does not bode well 

 for Asia given the region's dependence on exports to the U.S. 

     More yen weakness was also poised to weigh on regional 

currencies as it would increase already cut-throat export 

 competition. The yen slipped after the BOJ unexpectedly 

 announced its decision to ease already loose monetary policy. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht finally caught up with the other Southeast Asian 

currencies, and broke the 45 to the dollar mark for the first 

 time since June 8. 

 Bangkok dealers said Singapore-based players kicked off the 

 long dollar unwinding, which triggered stop-loss dollar sell 

 orders around 45.20. 

 They added the baht was mainly inspired by the stronger 

 regional currencies, and the currency later gained momentum 

 when the Bank of Thailand said it did not intervene in the 

 market. The bank added the baht was stable and in line with 

 regionals. 

 The market had been bracing for the central bank to buy 

 dollars to maintain export competitiveness, and took those 

 comments to signal the bank's approval of the baht's gains. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar was quoted around 1.7582 in late 

 trade, marginally up from 1.7584 late on Monday, after choppy 

 trading. 

 Dealers said the Sing dollar was mostly tracking the yen. 

 However, dollar appetite has been dulled by the recent spate of 

 long dollar unwinding by funds that burned many players. 

 Charts showed the dollar/Sing languishing in oversold 

 territory with a 14-day relative strength index reading of 

 17.696. It has been oversold since July 24. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah was anchored within a 8,400-8,500 range after 

 sharply surging to 11-month highs around 8,225 in early trade. 

 Jakarta dealers said the sudden rise was caused by 

 interbank players liquidating their long dollar positions on 

 fears the central bank may intervene to push the rupiah higher. 

 But the market later realised there was no supply of 

 dollars from authorities and local corporates jumped in to buy 

 dollars. 

     The central bank denied it had intervened this week, but 

 dealers believed it sold up to $50 million late on Monday. 

     The rupiah has risen by about 30 percent since President 

 Megawati Sukarnoputri took office on July 23. 

     The central bank deputy governor Miranda Goeltom said she 

 was not worried by the abrupt surge. But chief economics 

 minister Dorodjatun Kuntjoro-Jakti warned earlier pace of the 

 rise could hurt the economy. 

 The IMF praised the new government's determination to 

 reforms and said a mission would visit Indonesia next week to 

 work out an early resumption of lending. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso edged higher, but was unable to hit Monday's highs 

 around 51 as dollar inflows dwindled. 

     But Manila dealers said the central bank's moves to push 

 the peso higher kept players from taking aggressive positions. 

     The central bank has raised liquidity requirements by a 

 total of four percentage points to 11 percent in recent weeks, 

 squeezing peso liquidity and last week it penalised nine banks 

 for forex rule violations. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won was off its intraday high of 1,286.7 as importers 

 covered short dollar positions ahead of a holiday and foreign 

 investors settled some of their recent sales of local stocks. 

 Players were also cautious not to push the won higher on 

 wariness of intervention after a state bank bought dollars on 

 Friday when the local currency hit two-month highs. 

     Foreign investors sold a net 201.8 billion won worth of 

 shares in the past three sessions. 

     Even though Korean stocks closed at five-week high on 

 Tuesday, foreign investors were net sellers, offloading another 

 12.6 billion won in shares.

in a dearth of fresh leads.



    Market participants were cautious ahead of Friday's release

    The currency was underpinned by local stock purchases by

    On the macro front, economists polled by Reuters expected



the island's second-quarter current account surplus to triple



to US$3.32 billion from a year ago as imports posted a larger



year-on-year decline than exports.



The central bank will issue current account data on Monday.

text:
BANGKOK, Aug 14 (Reuters) - Thai central bank governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said on Tuesday the baht was stable and moving in line with other regional currencies without Bank of Thailand intervention.

title: Thai Baht Ends Up On Strength In Other Asian  Currencies
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht rose against the U.S. dollar in Asian spot trade Tuesday, supported by strength in other regional currencies, traders said. 

 The U.S. dollar finished at 44.965 baht, down from THB45.19 in other Asian markets late Monday, and from THB45.315 at the Bangkok close Friday. 

 Thai markets were closed Monday for a public holiday. 

 It was the first time since early June that the dollar fell below THB45.00. 

 Dollar-selling on concerns about weakness in the U.S. economy triggered stop-loss selling just above THB45.00 in early trade Tuesday, but local corporate demand and fears of central bank intervention kept the dollar above support at THB44.80. 

 The dollar moved back above THB45.00 after Bank of Japan announced a surprise easing in its monetary policy, but fell below that level in the afternoon as concerns about the U.S. economy reasserted themselves. 

 Dealers said the baht has lagged behind regional currencies in their gains on the dollar recently, but it played catch up Tuesday, moving quickly when leading regional currencies rose against the dollar, but barely moving when they retreated. 

 The yen and Singapore dollar should continue to set the tone for the baht, but support for the U.S. dollar should be underpinned by local corporate demand at THB44.80. 

 Stop-loss selling easily overwhelmed local demand Tuesday, but investors haven't been aggressive in building up long-dollar positions against the baht, so there may not be as much stop-loss selling if the dollar approaches its next support levels, dealers said. 

 The dollar is expected to open Wednesday in a range of THB44.80 to THB45.05, subject to regional volatility. 

 The Bank of Thailand intervened the last time the dollar fell to the THB44.70 to THB44.80 range, giving the support level an added psychological boost.

authorities haven't been intervening in the foreign exchange market
recently, as the currency has been moving naturally in line with the
market.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Higher Late; Baht Plays Catch Up
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies maintained their firm undertone late Tuesday, showing limited reaction to the yen's pullback following Bank of Japan's surprise decision to further ease monetary policy, dealers said. 

 Concerns over Asia's tottering economies were pushed to the backburner, as position-unwinding continued to drive regional foreign exchange trading, market watchers said. The severity of the U.S. economic malaise and doubts about the prospects for an imminent recovery have caught dollar bulls off guard, they added. 

 "They want to sell off their long dollar positions in line with the shifting perception of the dollar," said Thio Chin Loo, a regional currency strategist at BNP Paribas. 

 But "dollar bullishness is not over yet," she added. 

 "The dollar should be able to rebound once the recovery in the U.S. is evident in the fourth quarter," Thio said. 

 Markets are awaiting U.S. retail sales data for July, due to be issued at 1230 GMT. 

 The median estimate of 20 economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires and CNBC is for a 0.2% decline in total sales, but for a 0.1% increase when auto-dealer sales are excluded. 

 Until the dollar breaks out of its tight range against the yen, the Japanese currency will also provide little in the way of direction for the region's foreign exchange markets, observers said. 

 In response to a sharply deteriorating global economy, the BoJ said Tuesday it is to increase outright purchases of government bonds to Y600 billion a month from Y400 billion and to increase its current account deposits target to Y6 trillion from Y5 trillion, effectively flooding the financial system with more cash. 

 At 0900 GMT, the dollar was at Y122.75, higher than the Y122.41 late Monday in New York, but lower than its intraday high of Y123.15. 

 The Thai baht finally snapped out of its recent ranges to play catch up with the current rally of its Southeast Asian peers. 

 The Thai currency surged past 45 baht per dollar for the first time since early June, as offshore participants unwound their long dollar positions, dealers said. Stop-loss dollar sales were triggered just before the dollar's break below THB45, dealers said. 

 The dollar was quoted at 44.925 baht, down from THB45.135 late Monday. 

 The baht will unlikely make much headway, as dollar demand, largely by onshore participants, is expected to emerge around THB44.80 to THB44.90, dealers said. They noted that bids from local corporates kept the dollar buoyed above THB44.80 Tuesday. 

 "The market wasn't all that long in dollars (against the baht) because they were anticipating stringent reporting rules that would curb speculative baht trading," said Thio at BNP Paribas. 

 The revised reporting requirements for foreign exchange transactions through nonresident bank accounts, unveiled last Thursday, turned out to be less stringent than earlier forms that the central bank had come up with about a month earlier. 

 The rules will go fully into effect Oct. 1, following a transition period beginning Sept. 3. 

 While fears that the Thai central bank might buy dollars below THB45 somewhat restrained the baht's advance, central bank Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said Tuesday the Bank of Thailand hasn't been intervening in the market to support the currency. 

 The Indonesian currency extended its rally to hit an 11-month high of 8,225 rupiah per dollar, enlivening the currencies of most of its Southeast Asian neighbors, dealers said. 

 The rupiah has rallied more than 30% since President Megawati Sukarnoputri took power on July 23, following the impeachment of Abdurrahman Wahid. 

 Market hopes that her strong economic team may be able to resuscitate the struggling economy, and that the International Monetary Fund will soon resume a $5 billion loan program continued to propel the rupiah, dealers said. 

 The IMF said Tuesday it will send a mission to Indonesia next week. 

 Continued dollar sales by the Indonesian central bank gave the rupiah an added boost, dealers said. 

 But corporate dollar demand and rupiah profit-taking pulled the rupiah off its intraday high, dealers said. 

 Late in the day, the dollar was at 8,455 rupiah, down from IDR8,560 late Monday. 

 The strength of the baht and the rupiah combined with concerns over the Philippine central bank's watchful supervision over the local foreign exchange market to shore up the peso to a two-month closing high, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 51.175 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, down from PHP51.210 Monday. 

 The Singapore dollar was weaker, after a day of choppy trading, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar was at S$1.7609, higher than S$1.7588 late Monday. 

 The South Korean won rose in line with the yen and as some market participants covered their short dollar positions or established long positions in the U.S. currency ahead of a local holiday Wednesday, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 1,288.5 won, up from KRW1,285.5 Monday. 

 The New Taiwan dollar received a fillip from a 1.5% rise on the local equity market, dealers said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.582, down from Monday's close of NT$34.599. 

 The central bank had bought the U.S. currency to temper the appreciation of the New Taiwan dollar, dealers said.

title: Most Asian  Currencies  Higher Late; Rupiah Continues Rally
text:
Dow Jones Newswires 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The foreign exchange market continued to cheer Megawati Sukarnoputri's rise to the Indonesian presidency as the rupiah rallied to a five month high Tuesday. 

 Although Megawati has offered few details about how she plans to turn around Indonesia's struggling economy, analysts said market players were simply hopeful she would do a better job than her predecessor, Abdurrahman Wahid. 

 The rupiah began is surge Monday when it became clear Wahid's departure was imminent. Indonesian lawmakers, who had accused Wahid of corruption and incompetence, followed through with their pledge to remove him from office and by late Monday had named Megawati as his successor. 

 The market euphoria proved contagious, fueling gains in the neighboring Singapore dollar and Thai baht for a second day in a row Tuesday. The South Korean won and New Taiwan dollar also finished stronger, although the Philippine peso was weaker. 

 The rupiah traded as high as 9,750 against the dollar during the Asian day Tuesday, its best performance since February 26 when it strengthened to IDR9,600. Late in the session the dollar was quoted at IDR9,850, down from 10,230 late Monday. 

 The market will now be closely watching to see who Megawati appoints to key cabinet positions, such as finance minister and minister for economics. 

 Near the top of the list of candidates is Lakasamana Sukardi, a well respected and former state enterprises minister who has won accolades for insisting on reform and strengthening of the judicial system. 

 Megawati must not make the mistake of choosing her cabinet based on political considerations, something Wahid was accused of, said Richard Baker, an Indonesia expert at the East-West Center in Honolulu. 


"This isn't the time for politics as usual," Baker said. He added that
"Megawati has to be given the ability to pick her people based on the
basis of competence and to develop a set of policies that realistically
meet the country's needs."

title: Thai Exporter Assocs Call For Ctrl Bk To Curb Baht Rise
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--A group of 10 Thai exporter associations Thursday issued a joint statement saying they will ask the Bank of Thailand and other related authorities act to ensure the baht doesn't appreciate at a greater pace than regional currencies.  

"We demand that they implement appropriate measures to maintain baht stability in order to maintain the country's competitiveness... The persistent rise in the baht makes us unable to compete in terms of price," the statement said.  

Representatives of the 10 associations, which group producers of frozen foods, chicken, shrimp, fruit and vegetables, vegetable oil, garments and other sectors, said they would send a formal statement to the central bank.  

The associations' members account for around THB680 billion ($18.6 billion) of the country's exports each year, according to the joint statement. Thailand's exports have recently hit record highs above $11 billion per month.  

The baht has appreciated by around 12% against the U.S. dollar so far this year, while most regional units have risen by 3%-6%, and Chinese yuan has gained only 1%-2%, the statement said.  

If the baht continues to strengthen faster than its regional peers, the loss of competitiveness may cause members of the associations to begin reducing production, laying off staff and eventually closing businesses, it said.  

The Bank of Thailand has a policy of intervening in foreign exchange markets only to reduce daily volatility and speculative activity, not to counter the effects of real trade and investment flows.  

Governor Tarisa Watanagase said Wednesday the baht's recent strength has been the result of flows into regional and local stock and bond markets.  

She said the baht has outperformed regional currencies against the dollar this year after underperforming last year.  

At 0556 GMT, the dollar was quoted at THB36.505, off a low Tuesday of THB36.38, it's lowest level since February 1999.

title: = UPDATE:Thai Exporter Assocs Call For Action Vs Baht Rise

BANGKOK, Nov 16, 2006 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

(Updates with supporting comments from finance ministry official, suspected central bank intervention Thursday)  

A group of 10 Thai exporter associations Thursday issued a joint statement saying they will ask the Bank of Thailand and other related authorities act to ensure the baht doesn't appreciate at a greater pace than regional currencies.  

"We demand that they implement appropriate measures to maintain baht stability in order to maintain the country's competitiveness... The persistent rise in the baht makes us unable to compete in terms of price," the statement said. Chakkrit Parapuntakul, a spokesman for the Public Debt Management Office in the Ministry of Finance, later sought to reassure exporters by saying that as the threat of inflation has eased and that the central bank will have room to start cutting interest rates, which could lower demand for the baht.  

However, the Bank of Thailand's monetary policy committee had said at its last meeting on Oct. 18 that it remains cautious despite declining inflation. The committee left its 14-day repurchase market target rate unchanged at 5% due to the possibility of renewed volatility in global oil prices and other uncertainties.Comments Wednesday by central bank Governor Tarisa Watanagase didn't give exporters much encouragement about the possibility of help from official quarters. She said the baht's recent strength has been the result of flows into regional as well as local stock and bond markets, and that the baht has outperformed regional currencies against the dollar this year only after underperforming last year.  

The Bank of Thailand has a policy of intervening in foreign exchange markets to only reduce daily volatility and speculative activity, not to counter the effects of real trade and investment flows.  

But foreign exchange traders said agents of the central bank were suspected of buying the dollar Thursday to help prevent a fall toward Tuesday's eight-year low of THB36.38. The dollar closed in Asian trade Thursday at THB36.50, versus THB36.56 Wednesday.  

Chakkrit told reporters that there is no need for the central bank to maintain domestic interest rates at current levels because such rates would continue to attract capital inflows, resulting in a firmer baht.  

"Easier interest rates should help reduce appreciation pressure on the baht," said Chakkrit.  

The comments may not represent an official ministry position on the subject, however. Finance Minister Pridiyathorn Devakula declined to comment on the matter this week, saying he didn't appreciate interference from the ministry when he was governor, so he wasn't going to interfere himself.  

Economists said lower domestic rates probably wouldn't help to weaken the currency because such a move would bolster sentiment toward the local stock and bond markets, attracting even larger inflows.  

The baht has appreciated by around 12% against the U.S. dollar so far this year, while most regional units have risen by 3%-6%, and Chinese yuan has gained only 1%-2%, the exporters' associations said in the statement.  

If the baht continues to strengthen faster than its regional peers, the loss of competitiveness may cause members of the associations to begin reducing production, laying off staff and eventually closing businesses, it said.  

Representatives of the 10 associations, which group producers of frozen foods, chicken, shrimp, fruit and vegetables, vegetable oil, garments and other sectors, said they would soon be sending a formal statement to the central bank.  

The associations' members account for around THB680 billion ($18.6 billion) of the country's exports each year, according to the joint statement. Thailand's exports have recently hit record highs above $11 billion per month.

title: POLL-Markets further increase Asian  FX  long positions
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 15 (Reuters) - Currency markets raised their long positions on the Singapore dollar and South Korean won and remained bullish on the Indonesian rupiah and Thai baht in the past couple of weeks, undeterred by sporadic central bank intervention, a Reuters poll shows.  

The twice-monthly survey asked 15 currency strategists to estimate how the market is positioned in four Asian currencies against the U.S. dollar.  

It measures estimates on the net long or short position in a currency on a scale of minus 3 to plus 3. A score of plus 3 indicates the market is significantly long on dollars.  

The findings of the survey conducted on Nov. 14 are as follows:  

-- SOUTH KOREAN WON <KRW=>:  

The average positioning was minus 1.33, indicating the market had increased its short dollar positions versus the won in early November, having reversed a long dollar position in the previous two weeks. The scores ranged between zero and minus 2 with one respondent saying the market was neutral.  

-- SINGAPORE DOLLAR <SGD=>:  

The average positioning was minus 1.77, suggesting the market has ratcheted up long Singapore dollar positions against the U.S. dollar. The scores ranged between minus 1 and minus 3.  

-- INDONESIAN RUPIAH <IDR=>:  

The average positioning was minus 0.63, implying the market had slightly pared its short dollar-long rupiah positions. Scores ranged from minus 2 to zero.  

-- THAI BAHT <THB=>:  

The average positioning score was minus 1.67, almost the same level of long baht positions as estimated in the Oct. 31 poll. Scores ranged from zero to minus 3.  

Several Asian currencies hit multi-month or multi-year highs versus the dollar this week, underpinned by foreign equity investment flows into Asia, softer U.S. economic data and talk that China was diversifying its estimated $1 trillion in currency reserves.  

Central banks in South Korea, India and Thailand were suspected of having intervened to check the gains in their currencies.  

"Widespread U.S. dollar underperformance, coupled with steady gains in the yuan, has supported Asian regionals on a broad basis," said Sue Trinh, a currency strategist at RBC Capital Markets.  

"We are seeing modest consolidation today after the hefty intervention especially by Bank of Korea early this week but, on a relative basis, Asia is still performing well," she said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Rally but traders wary of  intervention
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Asian currencies, led by the Japanese yen, were broadly firm against the dollar on Monday after soft U.S. economic growth numbers reinforced a view that U.S. interest rates would stay steady for a while.  

But wariness about central bank intervention to curb strength in local currencies tempered some of the gains.  

Dealers said they suspected the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had stepped into the market to buy U.S. dollars and sell Singapore dollars.  

The Bank of Thailand said its had again intervened on the baht -- which rose to a 7-year high -- although the currency had started to stabilise after inflows slowed.  

"The move in some Asian currencies has been aggressive in the past week, and generally there is no resistance to the direction of the move but the magnitude," said DBS Bank currency strategist Philip Wee. "Generally the big picture is still not changed -- everyone is still looking for a weaker dollar."  

The Thai baht <THB=> climbed to 36.66 to the U.S. dollar, its strongest level since July 1999, before pulling back slightly by late trade.  

A Bangkok trader said there was strong support for the dollar around 36.35, but the outlook still suggested further baht gains.  

"Sellers of dollars are still strong," he said. "They (the central bank) may just come in to calm the market down."  

The Singapore dollar was quoted at 1.5610/20 <SGD=> per dollar, up about a quarter of a percent, but pulling away from a nine-year peak hit in offshore trade on Friday at about 1.5580.  

A dealer said he suspected the MAS had intervened on Monday in the 1.5605 to 1.5620 per dollar area.  

FED OUTLOOK  

The U.S. economy grew at an annualised rate of 1.6 percent in the third quarter, its weakest pace in more than three years, due to a slump in the housing market, data showed on Friday.  

This set a backdrop for fresh gains in Asian currencies, which hit multi-week highs last week on foreign investment inflows, gains in the Chinese yuan and weakness in the U.S. dollar.  

The yen strengthened more than 1 percent from levels traded late on Friday to about 117.20 yen per dollar <JPY=>, while the South Korean won firmed to a one-month high at about 942.60 to the dollar <KRW=>.  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> rose about a quarter of a percent to 33.19 per U.S. dollar, its highest in just over a week.  

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> strengthened to about 3.6380 per dollar, its highest in more than three months, while the Philippine peso <PHP=> gained about a fifth of a percent to 49.73 to the U.S. dollar, its highest level in more than four years.  

"Dollar/yen weighed on dollar/peso at the open, but we are also seeing demand for pesos and some corporates are coming into the market," said a trader in Manila.  

"The central bank could come in at the 49.70 area." CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0745 GMT

title: UPDATE 1-Thai c.bank says  intervenes  on baht again
text:
BANGKOK, Oct 30 (Reuters) - The Bank of Thailand has intervened on the baht again although the currency has started to stabilize after inflows slowed, central bank Governor Tarisa Watanagase said on Monday.  

"We have still come in to take care of the baht closely. But the situation is better now after inflows have slowed," she told reporters.  

The baht <THB=> was quoted at around 36.72 per dollar at 0650 GMT, its strongest since January 2000.  

Tarisa said exporters must cope with the stronger baht although the central bank would continue to enter the market.  

"We believe exporters can adjust themselves, while the central bank will still come in as necessary to prevent the baht from being too volatile," she said.  

However, Tarisa said it was not the time to cut interest rates due to uncertainties about inflation and world oil prices.  

"It's not the time to cut rates as we are still not sure about inflation," she said.  

The central bank kept its 14-day repurchase rate unchanged at 5.0 percent for the third month in a row in October after inflation eased to its lowest in 19 months.  

The central bank did not say how long it would leave rates unchanged, but senior officials told have said oil prices and inflationary pressures would be taken into account before deciding any rate cut. Its next rate meeting is in December.  

It raised rates 13 times between August 2004 and June 2006 as policy makers worldwide tightened credit to combat inflation.

title: INTERVIEW:Baht Peaking, To Ease With Rates '07 -BankThai
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Further upside for the baht, which reached a fresh seven-year high on Friday, is limited and it will likely ease next year in line with expected lower local interest rates, according to an executive at BankThai PCL (BT.TH).  

"There is not much room for the baht to gain further as it's now very close to peaking...I believe that the baht would find strong resistance at around 36.50 and it shouldn't breach 36.00 level," Sutee Losoponkul, BankThai's executive vice president for Treasury Department, told Dow Jones Newswires in an interview.  

He said pent-up dollar demand from importers remains substantial, because they are waiting to see how far the dollar will fall, and weakness in the U.S. unit might encourage some importers and debtors to be more aggressive in building larger positions.  

The Bank of Thailand's plan to ease rules on local entities investing overseas will also prevent the baht from rising rapidly, he said.  

The dollar hit the fresh seven-year low on Friday night of THB36.65, the lowest since July 1999. It has steadily fallen from THB37.95 on Sept. 19, when a bloodless coup ousted former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra. It has fallen by just over 10% this year from THB41.025.  

Thanks to weakening inflationary pressures resulting from lower global oil prices, the central bank is expected to maintain its policy target repo 14-day rate at 5.00% for the remainder of this year to make sure inflation is tamed before starting to cut rates, said Sutee.  

"When it becomes clearer that inflation is actually on the downtrend, it will be easier for the central bank to make a rate-cut decision. Interest rates should start falling in the first or second quarter of next year, with a possible cut of around 50 basis points altogether...Lower rates should also pull baht lower," said Sutee.  

New Measures To Reduce Intervention Burden  

After using both verbal and actual intervention over the past week in a failed attempt to stop the baht from rallying, the central bank Friday stepped up its battle to slow the baht's appreciation by saying it was considering relaxing foreign investment rules for local entities.  

Acting central bank governor Tarisa Watanagase said Friday that the bank is studying possibilities and there could be relaxation on the amount of investment or the conditions of investment.  

"This measure is a good move as it would help slow down the baht's rise while at the same time allowing investment diversification by local funds...Besides, it will help lessen the intervention burden on the central bank," said Sutee.  

However, any actual impact will depend on how much the central bank relaxes its regulations, he said.  

Tarisa said Friday that the central bank bought the dollar to lift the currency as the U.S. unit had fallen too far, too fast. The comments were the first public admission of intervention by Tarisa, who was appointed by the Cabinet last week to the post and is awaiting official endorsement by Thailand's king.  

Traders suspect that the central bank has intervened several times in recent days.  

Foreign investors have been active buyers of Thai shares since the middle of this month. Their net purchases have totaled THB18.2 billion so far this month, compared with net purchases of around THB11 billion last month.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Thai baht off highs, Sing dlr supported
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Verbal intervention by the Bank of Thailand reined in the Thai baht on Wednesday after foreign investment flows boosted it to its strongest level in nearly seven years, close to 37 per dollar.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> was underpinned by flows from funds betting on Asian currency gains, pushing it to what analysts said was the top of the secret trade-weighted band within which the Monetary Authority of Singapore manages it.  

Markets in Indonesia and Malaysia were closed but other Asian currencies firmed, shrugging off the yen's weakness as foreign investment flowed into the region. The South Korean won <KRW=> rose 0.4 percent to around 955 per dollar.  

Southeast Asian stock markets have been the bigger beneficiaries of foreign investment flows, with the Hong Kong and Indonesian markets near recent highs and Singapore's Straits Times Index <.STI> hitting a record high on Wednesday.  

The yen <JPY=> remained in a 119.10-119.20 per dollar range as nervousness ahead of a Federal Reserve policy decision trapped the U.S. dollar.  

The Fed's two-day policy meeting ends on Wednesday.  

Economists expect U.S. rates to be left unchanged this week. The Fed raised rates 17 times in two years up to June, but kept them steady in August and September.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose a quarter of a percent to 1.5721 per U.S. dollar.  

"Much of the flow pressure seems to be coming from models, which presumably are rebuilding positions they had closed in the run-up to this month's policy review," said Mirza Baig, Deutsche Bank's currency strategist.  

The Singapore dollar was sought by funds that mainly use trends to trade foreign exchange since the Singapore dollar is the most liquid emerging market currency in the region, he said.  

BAHT GAINS HALTED  

The baht was quoted as high as 37.06 per dollar, its highest level since January 2000, but retreated somewhat after new Bank of Thailand Governor Tarisa Watanagase said it was rising too fast.  

The baht has gained 1.3 percent in two weeks. Some dealers had expected the baht to weaken in anticipation of a possible sale by Singapore state firm Temasek Holdings [TEM.UL] of a stake in Thailand's Shin Corp , which it bought in January from the family of ousted Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra.  

Thaksin's critics have said the agreement breached foreign ownership laws and the deal is under investigation.  

"I am sceptical about that flow rumour," said Claudio Piron, a JPMorgan Chase currency strategist.  

"We are relatively optimistic on baht partly because we feel there is some undervaluation in the assets and partly because, with the prospect of political stabilisation, we could be getting investment picking up," Piron said.  

"And foreign equity purchases have been very strong relative to the rest of the region."  

Data from the stock exchange showed net foreign portfolio inflows into Thailand have been about $389 million so far in October.  

Thailand's 242-member National Legislative Assembly, handpicked by the leaders of the military coup, met for the first time on Tuesday. The baht has now fully recovered losses made after the Sept. 19 military coup. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0831 GMT

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Steady, central banks in focus
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 5 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were largely steady on Thursday, supported by a rally in the yen, but mostly sticking to familiar ranges and waiting for fresh direction.  

Dealers said the market was reluctant to take on big positions before Friday's key U.S. jobs report, while holidays in China and South Korea added to subdued trading activity.  

The Thai baht <THB=> was steady at about 37.60 per dollar, shrugging off comments from Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula that the central bank would intervene if the baht rose too quickly.  

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> held steady at about 9,200 per dollar after Bank Indonesia delivered its fifth interest rate cut of the year, as expected.  

The key rate was lowered by half a percentage point to 10.75 percent and the central bank said there was room for further cuts.  

"The decision was priced into the market and the central bank is expected to keep cutting rates to 9.75-10 percent by year end," said a Jakarta trader.  

"Bonds continue to rally but it's not that significant for the rupiah -- the correlation between the two is not that strong anymore and most buyers of debt are local players."  

The yen rose about 0.4 percent to around 117.55 yen per dollar <JPY=> and bounced back from Wednesday's one-month lows versus the euro <EURJPY=R>.  

DBS Bank currency strategist Philip Wee said the yen was due for a relief rally, which could spill over into Asian currencies. "This has to do with falling oil prices and also an improving outlook for Japan's economy," he said.  

Oil prices have fallen sharply this week and held below $60 a barrel <CLc1> on Thursday. A pull-back in oil prices from record highs set in July is seen as positive for Asian currencies as much of the region imports the bulk of its oil needs.  

YEN IMPACT  

Wee said the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> and Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> were two Asian currencies that could benefit the most from a further recovery in the yen.  

The yen has been hurt in recent weeks as investors dump the low-yielding currency for higher-yielding ones.  

The Taiwan dollar firmed to 33.08 per U.S. dollar, off this week's nine-month lows at about 33.17, while the ringgit firmed about 0.1 percent to 3.6850 to the U.S. dollar.  

A comment by Malaysian central bank chief Zeti Akhtar Aziz on Thursday that a stronger ringgit will reinforce monetary policy helped support the currency. But she added that the authorities had other policy instruments to deal with inflation.  

The prospect of rate cuts meanwhile was in focus in the Philippines after the country's central bank said on Wednesday it will discuss the possibility of such a move at its next policy meeting in November.  

Philippine consumer prices in September rose 5.7 percent from a year ago, slowing from a 6.3 percent increase in August.  

Some traders said they suspected the Philippine central bank intervened in the market on Thursday to keep the peso on the weak side of 50 per dollar.  

"It seems like 50 is the line in the sand for now and peso upside could slow for the time being," said Dresdner Kleinwort Asia currency strategist Sabrina Jacobs.  

The peso has risen about 7 percent since late June, hitting its highest level in more than four years earlier this week.  

"The prospect of a rate cut could put some pressure on the peso short-term," said a Manila trader. "But it depends on the magnitude of the move and the medium-term outlook is still positive." CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0816 GMT

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Dep Chief: Interest Rates Not Falling Yet
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Bank of Thailand Deputy Governor Tarisa Watanagase said Tuesday that declining inflation isn't enough for the central bank to start cutting interest rates.  

"Inflation started to fall for only three months, that's not long enough to make us lower the interest rate. The interest rate is not on the downtrend yet," Tarisa told reporters. [ 03-10-06 0455GMT ]  

The central bank's Monetary Policy Committee kept its key interest rate at 5.00% at its last two meetings after raising the rate steadily since August 2004 to curb inflation.  

Tarisa said the current decline in inflation was in line with the central bank's expectations.  

"The inflation risk has fallen substantially, but we have to wait and see more," she said.  

The Ministry of Commerce said Monday that headline inflation fell again in September to a 19-month low, due mainly to lower oil prices.  

The consumer price index rose 2.7% on year in September, compared with 3.8% in August. The CPI was down 0.3% from the previous month, after rising 0.1% on month in August. The month-on-month decline was the first since November last year.  

Tarisa said headline inflation for the whole year is expected to be below 5.0%. The central bank earlier forecast the 2006 headline inflation at 5.0%-5.8%.  

Separately, Nitaya Pibulratanagit, assistant central bank governor, told reporters that the Bank of Thailand didn't intervene in the foreign exchange market Tuesday.  

"The baht strengthened slightly early in line with the dollar weakness," Nitaya said.  

Asked whether the baht strength was due party to Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula's agreement to join the Cabinet team, Nitaya said she wasn't sure about that.  

At 0505 GMT, the dollar was quoted at THB37.565, down from THB37.59 early and from THB37.615 at Monday's close in Asia.

title: Thai Baht Stabilizes After Coup; Bonds Recover
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht stabilized in Asian trade Thursday, ending well off the lows it fell to against the U.S. dollar after a sudden military coup late Tuesday, traders said.  

The baht's recovery was driven by exporters' dollar sales and portfolio inflows on optimism that the bloodless coup would bring an efficient resolution to the country's political stalemate.  

Long-term government bond prices also plummeted for a brief period after the post-coup opening but ended higher as demand from local funds returned.  

Local and foreign funds regained confidence after seeing other markets recover quickly, bond dealers said.  

The dollar ended at an intraday low of THB37.455, up from Tuesday's close of THB37.27 but recovering from a post-coup high of THB37.95.  

Financial markets were closed Wednesday on orders of the Administrative Reform Council, which led the coup to oust Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra. The closure helped to limit panic selling in the early stages of the coup.  

"The baht is in the stabilizing stage. From the limited impact in the stock market, it's clear that investors are not too panicked by the coup and not in a hurry to cash out of the country," said a dealer at a local bank.  

Many foreign investors were also believed to have participated in the bargain hunting that followed initial losses among Thai shares with solid fundamentals, foreign exchange dealers said.  

Investors shrugged off comments by Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula that the central bank hadn't intervened in the forex market, as most parties hadn't suspected that the authorities were active anyway.  

Army Commander-in-Chief and coup leader Gen. Sondhi Boonyaratkalin said Wednesday that the military would turn over power to the interim government in about two weeks, after a constitutional drafting committee is appointed. But elections under the new constitution aren't planned until October 2007.  

The initial comments were sufficient for the time being to restore confidence, but investors won't want to wait too long to know who will be in the interim government Cabinet.  

Dealers expect the dollar is expected to find immediate support at THB37.40, while resistance is pegged at THB37.60. [ 21-09-06 1049GMT ]  

Thai long-term government bond yields fell as demand from funds returned after an initial bout of panic selling.  

Yields were expected to settle around current levels pending news of fourth quarter supply, which could come at any time between now and early October.  

However, short- and medium-term yields rose under pressure from offshore and onshore foreign exchange swap rates. Swap rates were higher on heavy dollar buying after the coup, which raised demand for the baht in the Thai financial system.  

The average bid on the government bond due August 2008 rose almost three basis points to 5.084%, the July 2016 bid fell three basis points to 5.270%, and the July 2026 bid was down four basis points to end at 5.422%, according to the Web site of the Thai Bond Market Association.  

In early panic selling, the 10-year bond bid had jumped to 5.36% and the 20-year to 5.60%, dealers said.  

The most-active overnight interbank interest rate may have risen to around 4.98% from 4.95% Tuesday due to temporary tight liquidity in the financial system.  

The Bank of Thailand sold at auction for the first time Thursday THB5 billion worth of its three-day bonds, introducing a new tool for control of liquidity. The bonds will be issued and settled on Monday, two days after the auction as usual. The average yield was 4.974%. The accepted yield range was wide at 4.88%-5.00%, but bid coverage was strong at 2.44 times.  

In another sign of continuity in the market after the coup, the Ministry of Finance sold THB1 billion of three-year Government Housing Bank bonds at 5.19%, and THB1 billion of nine-year State Railway of Thailand bonds at 5.635%. Both issues are guaranteed by the ministry.

"The baht is in the stabilizing stage. From the limited impact in the stock market, it's clear that investors are not too panicked by the coup and not in a hurry to cash out of the country," said a dealer at a local bank.  

Many foreign investors were also believed to have participated in the bargain hunting that followed initial losses among Thai shares with solid fundamentals, foreign exchange dealers said.  

Investors shrugged off comments by Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula that the central bank hadn't intervened in the forex market, as most parties hadn't suspected that the authorities were active anyway.  

Army Commander-in-Chief and coup leader Gen. Sondhi Boonyaratkalin said Wednesday that the military would turn over power to the interim government in about two weeks, after a constitutional drafting committee is appointed. But elections under the new constitution aren't planned until October 2007.  

The initial comments were sufficient for the time being to restore confidence, but investors won't want to wait too long to know who will be in the interim government Cabinet.

title: WSJA(9/21) Thais Face A Tough Test, But Economy May Benefit
text:
Sep 20, 2006 (DJCS via Comtex) --  

(From THE WALL STREET JOURNAL ASIA)
   By James Hookway
  

BANGKOK -- Thailand appears set for a long and potentially difficult transition back to democracy after the military leader who ousted Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said new elections won't be held for more than a year.  

But some economic officials -- including U.S. Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson and International Monetary Fund Managing Director Rodrigo de Rato -- suggested that the coup, provided it leads quickly to a credible interim government, won't have a significant negative impact on the Thai economy. Indeed, some analysts contend that Mr. Thaksin's removal will break the political impasse that's clouded the country's business outlook during months of political turmoil.  

In Thailand's first coup in 15 years, army commander Gen. Sondhi Boonyaratkalin led a swift, bloodless revolt against Mr. Thaksin's government on Tuesday night, while the Thai premier was in New York to attend the United Nations General Assembly.  

Yesterday, a statement broadcast on national television said powerful Thai King Bhumibol Adulyadej endorsed Gen. Sondhi as head of the new interim government, a widely expected endorsement that political analysts consider essential for any Thai government to survive.  

Western governments -- including those of the U.S., European Union, Australia and New Zealand -- criticized the coup as a setback for democracy in this Southeast Asian country of 65 million that serves as a manufacturing base for many Asian, U.S. and European companies.  

But many Thais have welcomed the coup against Mr. Thaksin, a brash telecommunications billionaire who was as disliked by Bangkok's middle class for his autocratic governing style as he is adored by many poor, rural Thais. Yesterday, Thai families gathered around tanks securing government buildings and the army's Bangkok headquarters and posed for photographs. Women offered roses to troops in armored personnel carriers.  

Putting Thailand's democracy back in place will be more complicated to execute than Tuesday's coup and is likely to raise an array of questions about the future of Thai political institutions. And the longer it takes for the new regime to meet its pledge to hold new elections, the more that the patience of pro-democracy Thais with the military takeover will be tested, analysts say.  

At a news conference yesterday, Gen. Sondhi outlined his time frame for returning Thailand to civilian rule, saying he will act as temporary prime minister for just two weeks before handing over power to an interim civilian government. He didn't indicate who might head the interim administration.  

Gen. Sondhi said the new civilian government will oversee the task of drafting a new constitution to remodel the political institutions the coup leaders say Mr. Thaksin systematically eroded during his five years in power. That process could take a year, Gen. Sondhi said, adding that the military's end goal is to hold a new general election in October 2007.  

Referring to the military, Gen. Sondhi said: "We have two weeks. After two weeks, we step out."  

In the meantime, Thailand will remain under martial law until the military deems the country sufficiently stable for it be lifted, he said.  

Despite some disruption of manufacturing operations yesterday, the longer-term impact of the coup on businesses and the economy could be relatively mild, economic analysts say. "There has been very little dislocation in the Thai capital markets, no spillover into the global capital markets," said Mr. Paulson, speaking to reporters in Beijing. "It's always very regrettable when you see change take place this way in a democracy . . . but in terms of the economic impact -- and I don't mean to say an adverse development isn't possible -- but if I'm talking about the top five or six things I'm worried about today, that isn't on the list."  

Pridiyathorn Devakula, Thailand's central-bank governor, predicted the economy will improve because the military coup will pave the way for a new interim government to be set up quickly. "From an economic point of view, the result (of the coup) should be an improvement -- the economy can now move forward," he told a news conference yesterday.  

"One way to look at it is that the coup leads to a political resolution, and the economy could bounce back quickly," concurred James McCormack, Fitch Ratings' Hong Kong-based head of Asian sovereign ratings, in an interview with Dow Jones Newswires. Fitch and Standard & Poor's put the country on negative credit watch following the coup. Both agencies have a triple-B-plus long-term foreign-currency sovereign rating.  

Mr. McCormack said Fitch is standing by its forecasts for Thailand's gross-domestic-product growth this year and next of 4.3% and 4.6%, respectively. He said the forecasts have already priced in delays in government construction spending and weakening investment sentiment due to the months-long political crisis that preceded the coup. The Thai economy grew 4.5% in 2005. Mr. McCormack said the country's exports, growing at about 16% this year, would be able to help cushion economic fallout from the coup in the short term.  

The IMF's Mr. de Rato said yesterday that Thailand's economy is "fundamentally strong," noting that financial-market reactions to the coup have been limited.  

Until earlier this year, Mr. Thaksin was one of Thailand's most effective and popular prime ministers. Economists applauded his efforts to generate wealth in rural areas and his desire to improve Thailand's infrastructure so that the country can better compete with its neighbors, particularly China.  

Mr. Thaksin's Thai Rak Thai party won strong parliamentary majorities in two national elections in 2001 and 2005, and Mr. Thaksin is still popular in impoverished rural areas for his easy-credit plans and programs to provide low-cost medical care. "How is the military going to explain itself to the 16 million people who voted for Mr. Thaksin?" said Giles Ungpakorn, a political-science professor at Bangkok's Chulalongkorn University.  

But despite Mr. Thaksin's skill as a manager, reflected in the way he rose from the ranks of the police to become one of Asia's richest men as head of a telecommunications empire, his critics said he couldn't resist meddling with Thailand's democratic institutions to entrench his power.  

His perceived supporters were appointed to the courts and administrative bodies such as the election commission. Within Thailand's civil service, which is traditionally nonpartisan, support for Mr. Thaksin was often seen as a way to a better career. The Thaksin government also cracked down harshly on Thailand's freewheeling news media.  

In January, disenchantment with Mr. Thaksin among Bangkok's middle class and traditional political elite came into the open when the premier's family sold its controlling shares in Shin Corp., the telecommunications company he founded, to a group of investors led by Temasek Holdings Pte. Ltd., an investment company owned by the Singapore government. The sale brought the family $1.9 billion, and was structured so that it paid no taxes on the proceeds. Shortly after the sale was announced, tens of thousands of protesters took to the streets in a series of demonstrations, accusing Mr. Thaksin of profiting at the expense of the country.  

In response, Mr. Thaksin called a snap election for April to ease the growing pressure on him, but that plan backfired when the main opposition parties boycotted the vote. That left many seats unfilled -- making it impossible to form a parliament under Thai law, while the pace of economic growth slowed as the political crisis deepened.  

Then, in May, King Bhumibol made one of his periodic forays into politics by instructing judges to find a way out of the mess. The king has frequently intervened during moments of political crisis in Thailand, sometimes implicitly signing off on military coups, as in 1976, and sometimes nudging Thailand toward the restoration of democracy, as he did in 1992.  

The judges responded to King Bhumibol's initiative by voiding April's election and agreeing to hear accusations that Mr. Thaksin's political party had broken election rules.  

King Bhumibol is viewed by many Thais as a quasidivine figure. It is considered inappropriate for Thais to speak publicly about the king's possible role in politics, and on Monday, Mr. Thaksin denied suggestions that the king was involved in any of the recent political dramas. "One should not bring him into politics," he said.  

Nevertheless, in June Mr. Thaksin said a "charismatic person" was out to remove him from his job as prime minister. Mr. Thaksin went on to say that a mysterious figure whom he refused to name was "wielding extraconstitutional force" to push him from office.  

Most Thais assumed that to mean the king or his chief lieutenant, Gen. Prem Tinsulanonda. By appearing to attack the monarch and his supporters, Mr. Thaksin escalated the economically damaging political conflict into a contest between Thailand's royal and military traditions, and a new, more modern way of governing a rapidly industrializing country.  

King Bhumibol's advisers struck back with a show of force. Donning his military uniform, Gen. Prem toured army camps around the country warning soldiers that their loyalty is to the king, not Mr. Thaksin.  

Other people seen as close to the royal palace gave prominent speeches in recent weeks that were interpreted as critical of Mr. Thaksin's push to modernize the Thai economy and open it up to more foreign investment.  

Seizing on that sentiment, local shopkeepers across the country have petitioned the king and the government in recent weeks to block big foreign-owned hypermarkets, such as Tesco PLC of the U.K. and Carrefour SA of France, that are sprouting up across Thailand and taking away their business.  

(MORE TO FOLLOW) Dow Jones Newswires

title: UPDATE: Thai Ctrl Bk Rate Unchanged; "Too Early" For Cut
text:
(Updates with analyst comments, more central bank comments) 
   

BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Bank of Thailand left its benchmark 14-day target rate unchanged at 5.0% Wednesday, saying that despite a slowdown in the country's economic growth rate, it is too early to consider any reduction in interest rates.  

The steady policy decision was in line with expectations and underlines a shift by many central banks in Asia to focus on growth rather than inflation in setting policy.  

The central bank said in a statement that the economy is adjusting well as a slight slowdown in growth has been partially offset by a favorable export performance.  

"It's too early to talk about a declining interest rate trend now, because inflation has only been declining for a few months," Assistant Governor Atchana Waiquamdee said at a press conference.  

Oil prices have fallen somewhat, but the risk of future volatility and accompanying inflation remain, "so the current level of the policy rate was considered appropriate," the statement said.  

The baht and the country's stock and bond markets were unmoved, as the rate decision and the maintenance of a neutral policy stance were signaled by central bank comments on recent data, which have showed a softening in both economic growth and inflation.  

Standard Chartered Bank senior economist Usara Wilaipich said domestic demand remains weak as consumption and investment decisions continue to be postponed due to political uncertainty, but the central bank's neutral stance is the correct one.  

"There is no need to rush. The central bank still has time to wait for more evidence that inflation is on a (sustained) decline," Usara said.  

Economists polled recently by Dow Jones Newswires forecast on average that Bank of Thailand will start cutting its 14-day repurchase market target rate from the current level of 5.0% in the second quarter of 2007.  

"The next move in interest rates should be a cut in 2007, once inflation has clearly headed south, and we are sure the Fed is done," Usara said.  

Usara said she believes that the U.S. Federal Reserve has completed its tightening cycle, but there is a risk that U.S. fed funds rate could rise one more time from its current level of 5.25%.  

Atchana said it isn't necessary for Thailand to follow U.S. rates, but the tightening cycles have been correlated because local inflation in both countries was driven by global oil prices. An interest rate differential of 25-to-50 basis points between the two countries is too small to have a significant effect on capital flows, she said.  

Bank of Thailand has intervened in foreign-exchange markets recently to prevent the baht from outperforming other Asian currencies against the U.S. dollar, in order to maintain the competitiveness of the country's vital export sector.  

The dollar closed in Asian trade Wednesday at THB37.35, just above the six-year low of THB37.28 it set on Aug. 11.  


 
   Inflation-Adjusted Rates Back In Positive Territory 
   

Currently, however, other factors are playing a bigger role than exchange-rate management in the central bank's decision-making process on interest rates.  

Atchana said second-quarter gross domestic product growth at 4.9% on year and a seasonally-adjusted 1.0% on quarter was slightly better than the central bank expected, so growth isn't an overriding concern at the moment. In the first quarter, GDP was up 6.1% on year and 0.8% on quarter.  

"If core inflation falls further, there will be more room for the central bank to focus on economic growth," Atchana said.  

Core inflation eased to 1.9% on year in August from a peak of 2.9% in April. The monetary policy committee has an official core inflation-targeting range of zero to 3.5%.  

Thailand's headline inflation rate has fallen to 3.9% on year in August from a peak of 6.2% in May, due mainly to a rising base of comparison resulting from the elimination of a diesel price subsidy in July 2005.  

Atchana said oil prices have declined recently, but they could start to climb again if - for example - there is a terrorist attack. Therefore, the central bank can't assume that the downward trend in oil prices will continue, and the risk of higher inflation remains.  

The central bank is leaving its estimate of the average Dubai oil price this year at $71 a barrel, she said. Thailand traditionally uses Dubai oil prices as its benchmark.Early Wednesday, cash Dubai was assessed by Dow Jones Newswires at $64.72-$64.77.  

Meanwhile, analysts said a quick move to cut interest rates wouldn't remove political uncertainty, which is one of the major factors holding back growth in investment and consumption.  

Thailand has been under a caretaker government since parliament was dissolved in February. The results of elections held in April were annulled due to irregularities, and fresh polls scheduled for Oct. 15 may be delayed because a new Election Commission is still in the process of selection.  

Formation of a new government - likely late this year or early next year - is expected to release pent-up investment demand in the second and third quarter of next year, so a central bank rate cut would have a more positive effect on growth at that time.  

Bank of Thailand's long-held desire to encourage savings by pushing commercial bank deposit account interest rates above the rate of inflation was another factor supporting the decision to leave the policy rate unchanged.  

Atchana said the country's real interest rate - based on an average deposit rate adjusted for expected inflation - has finally returned to positive territory at 0.12%, from minus 0.4% at the time of the previous monetary policy committee meeting on July 19.  

Returning real deposit rates to positive territory was one of the reasons cited by the central bank for an aggressive tightening cycle in which the 14-day target rate rose 375 basis points in 13 steps over 15 meetings between August 2004 and June 2006.

title: Thai Baht Ends Up, Off High On Ctrl Bk Action; Bonds Jump
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht ended marginally stronger against the U.S. dollar Tuesday, off an early high after the central bank stepped in to help curb the baht's strength, traders said.  

Government bond prices ended sharply higher as the yield curve flattened again ahead of Wednesday's central bank Monetary Policy Committee meeting. Recent trends in economic data and related comments from the central bank make it almost certain that the MPC will retain a neutral policy stance and leave its 14-day repurchase market target rate unchanged at 5%.  

The dollar ended at THB37.34, versus THB37.36 at the Asian close Monday, after moving in a tight range between THB37.33 and THB37.38.  

Traders said the dollar opened around the day's low. Offshore players continued to unload the U.S. unit, as the dollar was weak against most key currencies.  

However, central bank agents were buying dollars late Monday and also Tuesday, helping to slow the baht's rise toward the six-year high it set last month at THB37.28 to the dollar.  

"Offshore banks, which were suspected to be central bank agents, stepped in to buy the dollar around the THB37.33-THB37.35 level during the day, helping to cap the dollar's downside. Without the central bank's action, the dollar would have fallen further," said a local bank trader.  

Bank of Thailand Assistant Governor Nitaya Pibulratanagit said the central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market Tuesday, but the amount wasn't much.  

Nitaya said the baht's strength was in line with the global weakness of the dollar, but the central bank needed to take action in a bid to reduce the effect on exporters.  

Traders said THB37.30 was likely to remain a key support for the U.S. currency Wednesday due to expectations the central bank will continue to defend that level. Stiff resistance is tipped around THB37.45 for any dollar rebound. [ 05-09-06 1006GMT ]  

Thai government bond yields fell sharply again as foreign funds optimistic about prospects for the baht added to demand from big local funds that already outstripped local supply, dealers said.  

Bank of Thailand sold at auction Tuesday THB15 billion of its 364-day bonds at an average accepted yield of 5.07786%, down from 5.17086% at last week's auction.  

Long-term yields have dropped about 20 basis points and medium-term yields about 10 basis points in the first two days of the week, already matching last week's flattening.  

The average bid on the government bond due August 2008 fell four basis points to 5.078%, the July 2016 bid was down seven basis points to 5.167%, and the July 2026 bid plunged 15 basis points to end at 5.317%, according to the Web site of the Thai Bond Market Association.  

An upward correction isn't expected because inflation is on a downward trend, but there is little further room for flattening because the Bank of Thailand is almost certain to leave its 14-day repurchase market target rate unchanged at 5% when it meets Wednesday, and cuts in the policy rate aren't expected until around the second quarter of 2007.  

The most-active overnight interbank interest rate was expected to have remained around 4.95%.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Creeping higher as oil, dollar retreat
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 29 (Reuters) - Asian currencies crept up on Tuesday, supported by a sharp overnight fall in oil prices and a retreat in the dollar before the release later in the day of minutes from the Federal Reserve's Aug. 8 meeting.  

Oil prices fell almost 3 percent on Monday as tropical storm Ernesto was expected to miss U.S. oil installations in the Gulf of Mexico.  

That provided a boost to Asian currencies, which have been hurt in recent sessions by weakness in the yen.  

Still, dealers said trade should remain subdued ahead of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) minutes, which may provide fresh clues on the U.S. interest rate outlook.  

"The fall in oil prices to about $70 provided relief to the U.S. stock market, which is welcomed by Asian counterparts," said DBS Bank currency strategist Philip Wee.  

"More importantly, the market is looking at tonight's FOMC minutes to close the perception gap between the overly bearish market and more sanguine policymakers regarding the health of the U.S. economy."  

At its August meeting, the Fed left interest rates steady after two years of tightening monetary policy to curb inflation.  

The South Korean won <KRW=> firmed a third of a percent to about 961.30 per U.S. dollar, while the Taiwan dollar <TWD=> rose to around 32.86 to the U.S. dollar, up almost 0.3 percent from Monday's five-week trough at about 32.96.  

Wee said foreign capital flows out of Korean shares were one reason why the Taiwan dollar was likely to perform better than the won.  

From a regional perspective, Taiwan's equity market has attracted the most net foreign buying in the year to date, while South Korea has seen the most foreign selling.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> firmed to 1.5750 per U.S. dollar, up from Monday's two-week low at 1.5815, while the Philippine peso <PHP=> hit a one-week high of 51.15 per dollar.  

The Thai baht <THB=> also rose to its highest in about a week, at around 37.60 per dollar.  

Dealers said the baht was bolstered by news late on Monday that GE Money, the consumer finance unit of General Electric Co. , had agreed to acquire a 25.4 percent stake in Thailand's Bank of Ayudhya Ltd. for $600 million.  

The deal would give the U.S. conglomerate a foothold in Thailand's retail banking business.  

ABN AMRO currency strategist Shahab Jalinoos said in a note that the market had been looking to push the dollar up because of political problems in Thailand and central bank intervention to hold the baht down, but the merger news "could spur a near-term correction lower back towards 37.50". title: Thai Baht Ends Tad Up On Exporters Dlr Selling; Bonds Up
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht ended marginally stronger against the U.S. dollar in Asian spot trade Friday, with exporters' dollar selling taking it off an early low, traders said.  

Government bond prices rose on continued buying by customers of commercial banks - funds and corporations.  

The dollar ended at THB37.66, down from THB37.685 at the Asian close Thursday.  

The U.S. currency opened at the day's high of THB37.73, led by offshore dollar buying in line with its broad strength overnight.  

However, it failed to sustain its gains as exporters jumped in to unload the U.S. currency. A number of local players also took profit on the dollar.  

Trading volume was moderate. Traders said most players remained on the sidelines, waiting for fresh leads and a clearer view of the Thai political situation.  

"There has been lots of news and rumors. They didn't spark buying or selling, but most investors prefer to wait and see until they know what's going on," said a local bank trader.  

A bomb was found in a car that was driven back and forth outside caretaker Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra's home Thursday, and an army lieutenant was charged with illegal possession of an explosive device. The junior officer was once a driver for army General Pallop Pinmanee, who was sacked.  

However, Pallop said Friday that the alleged assassination attempt was fabricated by the prime minister himself. Local newspapers also reported speculation that the alleged plot was an attempt by the government to divert attention from other issues ahead of general elections scheduled for Oct. 15.  

Traders expect the dollar to trade over the weekend in a range of THB37.60-THB37.75.  

Looking ahead, the dollar's downside is expected to be supported firmly at THB37.50 due to likely central bank intervention.  

Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said late Thursday the central bank will do its best to slow the baht's rise and reduce the currency's volatility. [ 25-08-06 1048GMT ]  

The Thai government bond yield curve flattened on strong demand in the long end from banks' customers - local funds and corporations - which have forced banks into the market to refill trading portfolios despite some concerns about how far yields can fall, dealers said.  

Many analysts don't expect interest rates to begin to decline until around the second quarter of next year, but the prospect of lower rates helps to make long bonds a relatively safe place to park cash while waiting for a new government to be formed late this year or early next year.  

In the secondary market, the average bid on the government bond due November 2009 was down two basis points at 5.257%, the July 2016 bid fell three basis points to 5.395%, and the July 2026 bid dropped five basis points to end at 5.683%, according to the Web site of the Thai Bond Market Association.  

Interest rate swaps were also three to six basis points lower, reflecting the decline in yields and expectations that inflation will continue to slow significantly in the second half of the year.  

The most-active overnight interbank interest rate was expected to have remained around 4.95%.
