title: Thai Baht Ends Dn, Ctrl Bk Sales Suspected; Long Bonds Up
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht ended weaker against the U.S. dollar in Asian spot trade Wednesday on suspected central bank intervention and dollar supportive comments by Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula, dealers said.  

Long-term government bond prices closed slightly higher, as the results of the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee meeting overnight supported the view that global interest rates will peak in the first half of the year. The U.S. federal funds target rate rose 25 basis points to 4.5% as expected, but the statement issued after the meeting appeared to indicate that there mightn't be a need to raise rates much further.  

The U.S. dollar ended at THB39.23, up from THB39.00 at Tuesday's Asian close.  

The dollar opened lower at THB38.905 on selling by offshore players.  

However, buying by local importers and oil companies limited the losses and pushed the U.S. unit higher, said dealers, who suspected that central bank agents were also behind the corrective rise in the dollar.  

"Short-covering was triggered after the dollar/baht breach above the 39.00 figure. The pair was boosted further in the afternoon by the central bank's comment," said a dealer at a major local bank.  

Pridiyathorn said Wednesday afternoon that the central bank is watching to make sure that the baht's foreign exchange rate doesn't affect exports, but it won't intervene as much as some exporters would like.  

"The baht's strength isn't affecting exports because we are taking care of it," Pridiyathorn said.  

There was no confirmation of Wednesday's suspected dollar buying, because the central bank doesn't comment on daily market actions.  

The governor indicated, however, that the central bank mightn't be able to satisfy exporters who want to see the baht around THB40 to the U.S. dollar.  

The central bank will try to manage the currency's float as much as it can, but too much management would cause problems, he said.  

Pridiyathorn said flows from New York into Asian markets were the reason for the baht's strength since the beginning of the year, as Thai stock prices were at attractive levels relative to earnings per share.  

Equity-linked inflows were very strong earlier this year, before easing significantly lately, he said.  

Political concerns over the controversy surrounding the sale of a stake last month in Shin Corp. by Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra's family to Singapore's Temasek Holdings are also weighing on baht sentiment, dealers said. Although the premiere's family will escape any taxation on the THB73.3 billion ($1.88 billion) deal, the Securities & Exchange Commission is investigating his adult son's reporting of share transfers in the years prior to the deal.  

Dealers expect the dollar to find next resistance at THB39.30 and immediate support at THB39.00. [ 01-02-06 1155GMT ]  

Thai long-term government bond yields declined slightly due to a lack of supply this week and on the view that global and local interest rates will peak in the first half of the year, traders said.  

There was no government bond auction Wednesday, but regular weekly offerings resume Feb. 8.  

The FOMC meeting results helped support the view that interest rates will peak soon, but short and medium-term yields were flat or little changed due to lingering uncertainty about where the U.S. fed funds rate and the local 14-day repurchase rate will peak between 4.5% and around 5%.  

The central bank is expected to raise its 14-day repurchase market target rate by 25 basis points to 4.5% at its next policy meeting on March 8.  

The Thai Bond Market Association said the average bid yield on the government bond due August 2008 was up less than half a basis point at 4.943%. The March 2012 bid was down nearly two basis points to 5.257%. The July 2013 bid was down almost two basis points to 5.324%. The July 2016 bid dropped three basis points to 5.509%, and the August 2019 bid fell two-and-a-half basis points to end at 5.689%.  

Also Wednesday, the Ministry of Finance sold at auction THB1 billion worth of six-year government-guaranteed Bangkok Mass Transit Authority bonds at an accepted yield of 5.345%. The yield was in line with expectations about 10 basis points above the government bond yield curve.  

The Thai overnight interbank most-active rate was expected to have remained unchanged at 4.14%.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Not  Intervening  As Baht Weakens -Governor
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said Tuesday the central bank isn't intervening in the foreign exchange market to make the Thai baht weaken.  

"We don't do anything in the current baht weakness. There is nothing wrong in the market. We have no need for intervention," Pridiyathorn said.  

At 0525 GMT, the dollar was at THB39.75, down from THB39.81 earlier Tuesday, but still above THB39.69 at Monday's close in Asia. [ 17-01-06 0529GMT ]  

The central bank intervened heavily in the market last week to curb the baht's sharp strength. The baht has risen around 3% so far this year, in line with the dollar's broad weakness and heavy equity-related inflows.

The capital inflow is "normal", but it has started to level off since late last week, he said.  

Foreigners still were net buyers of THB1.87 billion worth of Thai stocks Monday, but the amount of buying was lower significantly from a high of over THB15 billion seen in a single day earlier this month.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Has  Intervened  Against Baht -Dep Governor
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Bank of Thailand Deputy Governor Bandid Nijathaworn said Monday that the central bank has intervened in foreign exchange markets recently to limit the rise of the baht.  

The central bank will continue to prevent any excessive movement in the Thai currency, he said.  

"We will closely monitor the baht and we will make sure that it doesn't fluctuate too much," Bandid told a news conference after the close of markets. [ 09-01-06 0959GMT ]  

Bandid said the baht has been rising since the start of the new year due to the strength of the yen and to heavy capital inflows possibly related to portfolio adjustment by foreign investors.  

The baht's strength also tends to attract inflows, so the central bank will be monitoring markets for any increase in volatile short term flows, he said.  

Bank of Thailand will also have to continue monitoring markets to determine whether the baht's strength has affected the country's export competitiveness, but its rise hasn't exceeded those of other regional currencies, he said.  

Bandid said the baht had risen only 0.73% against the U.S. dollar since Friday, while the Japanese yen was up 1.77%, the Korean won 1.16%, the Indonesian rupiah 1.06% and the Singapore dollar 0.75%.  

The U.S. dollar was quoted at the end of the Asian trading day Monday at THB39.77, off a seven-month low of THB39.72 on buying by suspected agents of the central bank, traders said. The U.S. currency fell from THB40.05 at Friday's close and THB40.35 Thursday, after opening the year at THB41.025.  

The dollar has fallen sharply against regional currencies since U.S. data released Friday showed nonfarm payrolls up by 108,000 jobs last month, versus expectations of a rise of 215,000.  

Meanwhile, capital inflows have been supported by heavy net buying by foreign investors of THB38 billion worth of local shares on the Stock Exchange of Thailand last week.  

The SET Index rose 2% Monday to close at 762.29 points with trading volume boosted by continued foreign inflows, local analysts said.

text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said late Thursday the central bank hasn't intervened in the foreign exchange market to prevent the Thai baht from rising.  

"We let the baht move in line with the market mechanism. If we are in the market (to manage the baht), it (the baht) won't be this strong," Pridiyathorn told reporters.  

The Thai baht ended in Asian spot trade Thursday at THB40.35 against the U.S. dollar, a fresh seven-month high, due mainly to equity-related inflows and broad dollar weakness. [ 05-01-06 1038GMT ]  

Asked about the lower-than-expected consumer price index reading in December, Pridiyathorn said it was in line with the central bank's expectations.  

"We expect that the inflation in the near term will be around 6%. In the first quarter, inflation will likely be slightly over 6%, possibly in a range of 5.8%-6.2%," he said.  

The Ministry of Commerce announced Wednesday that the headline inflation rate was 5.8% on year in December, down 0.1% from the previous month, as lower food prices helped offset rising oil prices.  

Economists surveyed by Dow Jones Newswires had on average expected the CPI to rise 6.0% on year and 0.1% on month.

title: Thai Baht Ends Firmer On Broad Dlr Weakness; Bonds Up
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht ended at a fresh one-month high in Asian spot trade Thursday in hefty volume due to the dollar's generally weak tone against most regional currencies.  

A more dovish tone in the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee's policy statement this week has been taken as a signal that U.S. interest rates will soon be peaking.  

The change in the global interest rate outlook has weakened the U.S. dollar on foreign exchange markets. It also helped to trigger buying on the local bond market, where prices of government bonds rose sharply for the second consecutive day.  

The dollar closed at THB40.92, down from THB41.05 Wednesday, but off an intraday low of 40.90.  

The U.S. currency opened easier at THB40.98, tracking losses against the yen and other Asian units.  

Its fall was accelerated by stop-loss selling after its drop to below THB41.00 overnight, but buying by local corporations and suspected intervention by the Bank of Thailand helped to limit its losses.  

"Selling orders were from both onshore and offshore players this morning, some to (stop losses) and some to build up short (dollar) positions amid a steady drop in the dollar against the yen," a trader at a local bank said.  

Equities-related inflows also supported the baht. Foreign investors were net buyers of a combined THB4.73 billion of Thai stocks Tuesday and Wednesday.  

"However, there is talk that the central bank stepped in to limit the dollar's fall around THB40.90. Active buying by local corporate also helped the dollar to regain some ground in late trade," the trader said.  

The U.S. unit is expected to find firm support at THB40.85, with resistance at THB41.10.  

Sentiment toward the baht was also bolstered by the central bank's move Wednesday to raise its 14-day repurchase market target rate by 25 basis points to 4% and its promise of further policy tightening until real interest rates are positive, or above the level of inflation.  

The tone of the Bank of Thailand's policy statement was also slightly more dovish than previous ones. It raised the 14-day rate by only 25 basis points versus 50 basis points at each of the previous two meetings, citing a moderation in inflation as well as in private consumption and investment.  

In response, JPMorgan cut its forecast for the 14-day target rate by 25 basis points to a likely peak of 4.75% by the second quarter of 2006. [ 15-12-05 1109GMT ]  

Thai government bond yields closed sharply lower Thursday, as the end of uncertainty over U.S. and local policy meetings this week released pent-up demand, and on expectations that global and local interest rates could peak sooner than expected, dealers said.  

The current round of buying will rebuild thin trading portfolios and reverse some losses before the year-end closing of account books, a dealer said.  

But selling might follow in the first few weeks of the new year, as interest rates are expected to rise again in the first quarter of 2006.  

The Thai Bond Market Association said the average secondary market bid on the government bond due November 2009 fell 13 basis points to 5.300%, the March 2012 bid dropped 13 basis points to 5.570%, the December 2014 bid slid 10 basis points to 5.722%, and the December 2019 bid was down 11 basis points at 5.963%.  

The most active overnight interbank rate was expected to drop to 3.90% as liquidity returned to normal after a sharp rise to 4.10% Wednesday when the central bank's rate hike played havoc with money market flows, dealers said.  

The overnight repurchase market rate has already settled at 3.93750%, versus 3.68750% prior to the interest rate increase, indicating that the most active overnight interbank rate will likely settle in a range of 3.90%-3.95%.  

Quotes for money market interest rates with terms of six months or more eased in line with expectations that the 14-day target rate might peak sooner than expected, but the three-month Bangkok Interbank Offered Rate, or Bibor, continued to advance closer to 4.5%.

The dollar closed at THB40.92, down from THB41.05 Wednesday, but off an intraday low of 40.90.  

The U.S. currency opened easier at THB40.98, tracking losses against the yen and other Asian units.  

Its fall was accelerated by stop-loss selling after its drop to below THB41.00 overnight, but buying by local corporations and suspected intervention by the Bank of Thailand helped to limit its losses.  

'Selling orders were from both onshore and offshore players this morning, some to (stop losses) and some to build up short (dollar) positions amid a steady drop in the dollar against the yen,' a trader at a local bank said.  

Equities-related inflows also supported the baht. Foreign investors were net buyers of a combined THB4.73 billion of Thai stocks Tuesday and Wednesday.  

'However, there is talk that the central bank stepped in to limit the dollar's fall around THB40.90. Active buying by local corporate also helped the dollar to regain some ground in late trade,' the trader said.  

The U.S. unit is expected to find firm support at THB40.85, with resistance at THB41.10.  

Sentiment toward the baht was also bolstered by the central bank's move Wednesday to raise its 14-day repurchase market target rate by 25 basis points to 4% and its promise of further policy tightening until real interest rates are positive, or above the level of inflation.  

The tone of the Bank of Thailand's policy statement was also slightly more dovish than previous ones. It raised the 14-day rate by only 25 basis points versus 50 basis points at each of the previous two meetings, citing a moderation in inflation as well as in private consumption and investment.  

In response, JPMorgan cut its forecast for the 14-day target rate by 25 basis points to a likely peak of 4.75% by the second quarter of 2006.

title: Thai Baht Ends Flat In Lackluster Trade; Long Bonds Up
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht finished flat against the dollar in Asian spot trade Friday on lack of clarity over the U.S. unit's direction against regional currencies and no fresh domestic leads, dealers said.  

Long-term government bond prices resumed an upward correction of sharp losses over the past several weeks, after easing Thursday, on demand from big funds attracted by higher yields.  

The dollar closed at THB41.14, unchanged from Thursday's close. The U.S. unit moved in a tight range of THB41.12 to THB41.18 Friday.  

"The market is rather quiet today without any fresh leads. Many interbank players are now squaring their positions pending any clear trend for the dollar in the short-term," said a dealer at a local bank.  

Dealers said the dollar also stayed rangebound on fears that the central bank might intervene. The Bank of Thailand has appeared to step in on either side of the market when the exchange rate moves substantially.  

Dealers allayed fears that the uncertainty over the pending EGAT PCL IPO, Likely Thailand's largest-ever IPO, will have no impact on the baht.  

The Supreme Administrative Court will decide Tuesday whether or not to halt the IPO. Even if the court decides to stop the IPO, there shouldn't be any immediate effect on capital outflows as no substantial funds have been brought in directly for participation in the IPO. Foreign funds have adjusted existing portfolios in the local market to make room for the EGAT shares, dealers said.  

Dealers said the dollar should remain in a tight range overnight between buy orders from local oil companies around THB41.10 and sell orders from exporters anywhere above THB41.20. [ 11-11-05 1107GMT ]  

Long-term government bond yields resumed a downward correction of the sharp increases seen in recent weeks due to demand from large funds, but medium-term yields added to yesterday's mild reversal, rising under pressure from the interest rate trend, dealers said.  

The downward correction can continue in the long run as long as the big funds are still buying, but yields are likely to remain under upward pressure in the next few months as interest rates will likely still be rising.  

The Thai Bond Dealing Center said the average bid on the government bond due November 2009 edged up one basis point to 5.900%, but the March 2012 bid fell three basis points to 6.248%, the December 2014 bid was down two basis points to 6.380%, and the December 2019 bid edged down one basis point to end at 6.868%.  

Bank of Thailand said Friday the coupon rate for five-year government savings bonds to be offered to retail investors Nov. 15-24 was set at 6.25%, versus 5.25% for five-year savings bonds issued in mid-September. The coupon was set slightly higher than the five-year yield of 6.11%, extrapolated from the yield curve for regular government bonds issued to institutional investors, in line with coupon rates for previous savings bond issues.  

The most active overnight interbank rate was likely to remain at 3.68%, dealers said. The rate might come under some slight upward pressure in the middle of next week as monthly corporate tax payments are due on Nov. 16.  

Quotes for most term interest rates were higher in line with the broad trend.

title: Thai baht capped by suspected c.bank  intervention
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 21 (Reuters) - The Thai baht was little moved against the dollar on Friday and underperformed most other Asian currencies, with dealers saying they suspected Thailand's central bank had intervened in the market to cap currency gains.  

One trader in Bangkok said the Bank of Thailand was worried about a further strengthening in the baht, especially with the yen <JPY=> bouncing back from this week's two-year low against the dollar and dragging other Asian currencies with it.  

"They may have come in this morning at around 40.85 as the yen rebounded against the dollar," said the trader.  

By 0425 GMT, the baht <THB=> stood at about 40.87 against the dollar, little changed from levels seen in late Asia trade on Thursday.  

Dealers in Bangkok said they suspected the central bank was buying dollars for baht to prevent the Thai currency from breaking through the 40.80 key chart resistance level.  

A move through this level is expected to lead to a rapid strengthening in the baht to 40.50 against the dollar.  

Aggressive monetary tightening by the Bank of Thailand has boosted the baht, but analysts say the central bank does not want to see too strong a currency as this would hurt exporter competitiveness.  

The baht has strengthened about three percent from two-year lows hit against the dollar in July at about 42.20.  

Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said on Thursday the baht was trading at a normal level after its "excessive strength" in the past few weeks.  

"Other Asian currencies are losing ground, so the central bank does not want the baht to strengthen too much," said Irene Cheung, head of Asian currency strategy at ABN AMRO in Singapore.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Led higher by peso, but Korean won stumbles
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies strengthened against a broadly weak dollar on Friday, with the peso receiving an extra boost from the previous day's unexpected rise in Philippine interest rates.  

The South Korean won <KRW=><KRW=KFTC> was the exception. It weakened almost a third of a percent to a nine-month low at 1,058.8 per dollar as foreign investors continued to bail out of the local equity market.  

South Korean shares <.KS11> closed slightly higher on Friday, but foreign investors were net sellers for the 21st consecutive trading session, dumping a net 238 billion won in stocks on the day.  

In contrast to the won, the peso <PHP=> rose half a percent to about 55.40 per dollar -- a three-month high.  

Dealers said Thursday's 25 basis-point rise in Philippine interest rates and a move through key chart barriers boosted the peso.  

"The peso opened at 55.61 (per dollar) and that is due to the fact that rates were raised," said a trader in Manila. "We're looking for another hike in November or December, especially with the U.S. likely to hike rates again."  

Strong currency inflows from Filipinos working overseas together with higher interest rates were expected to bolster the peso heading into the end of the year.  

The country's top court also cleared the way this week for the government to expand a sales tax, the centre piece of fiscal reform.  

"We've been turning bullish on the peso in the last few weeks," said Philip Wee, currency analyst at DBS Bank. "Remittances are one factor and the dollar has been unable to keep rallying."  

YEN HELP  

Sentiment towards Asian currencies picked up as the yen bounced back from this week's two-year low against the dollar.  

Asian currencies, along side the yen <JPY=>, have been hurt this month by expectations that U.S. interest rates will keep rising to contain inflation.  

But the dollar succumbed to profit taking on Friday, allowing regional currencies to recover.  

"The U.S. dollar is weaker across the board, but the market is still trying to shape its opinion on U.S. growth," said BNP Paribas senior currency analyst Thio Chin Loo.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> added about a quarter of a percent to 1.6903 per dollar, moving further away from a three-month low hit on Wednesday at about 1.6990.  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> was a touch firmer at about 33.63 per U.S. dollar, above Wednesday's one-year low near 33.73, while the Indian rupee <INR=IN> recovered from this week's 11-month lows against the dollar.  

Dealers in Bangkok said they suspected the Bank of Thailand had intervened to cap the baht's gains following its decision earlier this week to raise interest rates for the eighth time since last August.  

The baht was little changed at about 40.86 per dollar <THB=> and underperforming most of its regional peers.  

A trader said the central bank was worried the baht could strengthen further, especially with the yen's rebound dragging other Asian currencies with it.  

"They may have come in this morning at around 40.85 as the yen rebounded against the dollar," the trader said.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Rupiah breaks 10,000 mark, Taiwan dlr weak
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 14 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah strengthened past the psychologically important 10,000-per-dollar mark on Wednesday on the back of improving investor confidence after monetary tightening in the past two weeks.  

The Taiwan dollar hovered close to its lowest level in at least eight years against the currency of export rival South Korea <TWDKRW=R> on expectation the central bank will prevent gains in the currency after a widely expected rate rise on Thursday aimed at stamping out inflation expectations.  

Other Asian currencies were little changed as a smaller-than-expected U.S. trade deficit for July supported the U.S. dollar.  

The rupiah <IDR=> gained almost 1 percent from late Asian trading on Tuesday and was quoted at a three-week high of 9,980 per dollar in early Asian trades.  

It gave up some of those gains by the afternoon and was bid at 10,025 per dollar at 0822 GMT.  

The currency has gained more than 17 percent since hitting a four-year low of 11,750 on Aug. 30 after the central bank moved to calm financial markets by raising its key rate by 125 basis points and requiring banks to park a greater share of deposits as reserve with the central bank in a bid to tighten money supply.  

"Foreign investors who sold the rupiah last month are trying to collect it now," said a Jakarta currency dealer.  

"It's all about the supporting news," he said referring to the rate rises and a government pledge to raise fuel prices early next month as part of a plan to cut its ballooning fuel subsidies.  

Ratings agency Fitch said on Tuesday it expected further aggressive monetary tightening in Indonesia in coming weeks.  

TAIWAN DOLLAR  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> weakened to 32.811 per dollar, trading close to last week's 10-month lows after a top central bank official warned on Tuesday that the currency was too strong compared with regional peers and did not reflect the country's deteriorating trade performance.  

The currency has already weakened 3.5 percent in the third quarter against the dollar.  

IDEAglobal said the verbal intervention by the central bank deputy governor was seen by the local market as an attempt to ward off strength in the currency in the event of a 25 basis point rise in the benchmark interest rate on Thursday.  

A Reuters poll of 13 analysts showed seven expected a 12.5 basis points rise in the key discount rate while the others forecast a 25 basis point rise.  

IDEAglobal said central bank warnings tilted the balance of expectations to a 25 basis points rise.  

"We, however, would also view the statements as testimony to the authorities' competitiveness concerns and as such would continue to expect the Taiwan dollar upside to lag its regional counterparts into early fourth quarter," IDEAglobal said in a note.  

The Thai baht traded on Wednesday close to Tuesday's three-month high against the Singapore dollar <SGDTHB=R> in the wake of the central bank's higher-than-expected 50 basis points rate increase last week -- the seventh rate rise since last August.  

IDEAglobal said the trend could reverse as Bank of Thailand intervenes to keep the baht's gains in check to support local exporters.  

Thai foreign exchange reserves rose more than $500 million in the week ended Sept. 2 indicating central bank purchases. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0801 GMT

title: Thai baht at 2-month peak, chart outlook bullish
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 11 (Reuters) - The Thai baht extended this week's gains to hit its strongest level in almost two months against the dollar on Thursday and analysts said the outlook was bullish after a break of key chart barriers.  

Equity market gains, a rally in the yen and Asian currency strength following last month's revaluation of the yuan have helped the baht rebound about three percent from more than two-year lows hit in July.  

The baht <THB=> firmed a third of a percent from late Asian trading levels on Wednesday to 40.86 per dollar, its strongest showing since mid-June.  

Analysts said the baht's gains accelerated after breaking trendline resistance on Wednesday at 41.40 per dollar.  

The baht is now flirting with chart resistance at 40.80, a support level for the currency that was broken in June.  

"As long as dollar/baht trades below 41.31, the target is for a move to 40.44," said Winston Tang, technical analyst at 4CAST in Singapore.  

A move to 40.44 per dollar would take the baht to where it traded in early June. This level provided support during the decline against the dollar.  

Tang said momentum indicators showed some signs of the baht being overbought but added these were not strong yet.  

Despite the rebound in the baht, it remains this year's worst performing Asian currency after the yen.  

Analysts said further gains in the yen, which the baht tracks closely, could push the Thai currency to 40.80 per dollar.  

The Japanese currency has rallied amid optimism about growth after weathering political upheaval this week over plans for a snap election following the government's defeat in a parliamentary vote on postal privatisation.  

"Southeast Asian currencies are taking a bit more of a cue from the yen, which has recovered after the postal vote defeat," said Thio Chin Loo, senior currency analyst at BNP Paribas. "The technical picture is bullish for the baht."  

Thailand's central bank has no plans to intervene on the stronger baht and will leave the currency to move in line with market forces, a senior bank official said late on Wednesday.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Baht hits 6-week high, Sing dlr strengthens
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 10 (Reuters) - The Thai baht hit its strongest level against the dollar in more than six weeks on Wednesday, with the return of investors to the local stock market helping it outperform other Asian currencies, which were largely steady.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> gained as much as a quarter of a percent to 1.6483 per dollar after data showing a higher-than-expected, annualised 18 percent jump in gross domestic product in the second quarter from the first.  

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> gained a fifth of a percent to 9,780 per dollar a day after the central bank surprised the market by raising a key rate by a quarter of a point to 8.75 percent in a bid to fight inflation and support the currency.  

Other Asian currencies were little changed from late Asian trading on Tuesday after the U.S. Federal Reserve's 10th consecutive rate increase and its promise to continue tightening policy helped support the dollar. The baht <THB=> added half a percent to 40.99 per dollar, its best showing since June 24. It has rebounded about 2.5 percent since it hit its weakest level for more than two years on July 8.  

Traders said share price gains and expectations that Asian currencies will strengthen following last month's revaluation of the Chinese yuan had helped the baht's recovery.  

"There has been a mini-transfer of hot money into Thailand recently. Stocks are doing well and this has lifted the baht," said a trader at a local bank in Bangkok.  

IDEAglobal.com said in a note to clients that the Bank of Thailand did not intervene to stop the baht rising. It said any further gains in the yen, which the baht tracks closely, could boost the Thai currency to 40.80 per dollar.  

SINGAPORE DOLLAR  

Khor Hoe Ee, assistant managing director of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), said the policy of allowing a gradual appreciation in the Singapore dollar was appropriate as inflation was likely to pick up in the second half.  

Khor also said that a stronger Singapore dollar, which was trading within the central bank's preferred range, would not affect the city-state's export outlook.  

IDEAglobal said that although a strong run of economic data had bolstered the central bank's strengthening bias for the Singapore dollar, the currency was already near the stronger end of MAS's preferred trading range, making it difficult for traders to push it higher.  

It said the U.S. dollar was likely to find support at 1.6475/80 Singapore dollars on Wednesday. The 1.6520 level was the first level of resistance if the Singapore dollar weakened, IDEAglobal said.  

The Singapore dollar hit a two-month high of 1.6465 per dollar on Aug. 4. It has lost 1 percent against the dollar this year, compared with a 7.8 percent depreciation in the Japanese yen <JPY=>.  

The Singaporean central bank conducts monetary policy by guiding the Singapore dollar against a basket of currencies of its major trading partners. It does not disclose the composition of the trade-weighted basket or its preferred trading range.  

"The comments from the MAS suggest it is more comfortable with the global outlook and that there is not too much implication for the currency," Philip Wee, a DBS Bank currency strategist, said. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day

title: FACTBOX-Asian  currency  regimes
text:
SINGAPORE, July 22 (Reuters) - Asia's currency regimes grabbed the spotlight after China revalued the yuan against the U.S. dollar and said it would manage it against a basket of currencies, a move which sent regional currencies higher.  

Malaysia was quick to follow China's shift on Thursday evening, scrapping its seven-year-old peg and adopting a managed float. That leaves Hong Kong as the last major economy in Asia with a peg against the U.S. dollar.  

In general, Asian economies explicitly or implicitly shadow the U.S. dollar. But the regimes vary greatly -- the Singapore dollar is floated against basket of currencies while South Korea has an independently floating won.  

The following summary, drawn from official sources and investment bank reports, is based on the International Monetary Fund's definitions for fixed currency pegs, managed floats with varying degrees of fluctuations, and independent floats.  

FIXED PEG  

--------------  

HONG KONG DOLLAR <HKD=>  

Hong Kong adjusted its linked exchange rate system in May for the first time since 1998, moving its currency to a band between 7.75 and 7.85 to the U.S. dollar from a asymmetric peg that set a floor of 7.8 per U.S. dollar.  

The initial peg was part of a Currency Board Arrangement created on October 17, 1983, in response to a currency crisis. Under the board's rules, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base has to be matched by equivalent foreign currency reserves.  

MANAGED FLOATS:  

-------------------  

CHINESE YUAN OR RENMINBI <CNY=>  

After essentially pegging the yuan near 8.28 per dollar since the Asian crisis, China on Thursday revalued it to 8.11 and tied it to an undisclosed basket of currencies of trading partners.  

The yuan will be allowed to move 0.3 percent above or below the previous day's close against the U.S. dollar, and by 1.5 percent against other currencies.  

Theoretically, the trading band allows the currency to edge higher, but China has had such flexibility since 1994 but has not used it since 1996, instead holding the yuan almost still.  

China's central bank is still expected to intervene heavily, buying and selling yuan to maintain the new currency band.  

Prior to the Thursday's move, the yuan was kept in a 0.04 percent band centred on a rate of around 8.278 per dollar.  

China had followed a dual exchange rate since 1979 but unified those rates in 1994 to create a crawling yuan peg.  

The yuan appreciated from 8.7 per dollar to around 8.3 between 1994 and 1996, and continued to fluctuate around there until the Asian crisis, when Beijing rejected advice to devalue like its neighbours and virtually fixed the currency instead.  

MALAYSIAN RINGGIT <MYR=>  

Malaysia on Thursday dropped its seven-year-old peg of 3.8 to the U.S. dollar in favour of a managed float against an undisclosed basket of currencies, moving soon after China did.  

Malaysia has said the aim of its exchange rate policy is to maintain stability with currencies of major trading partners. The currency used to float until a flight of capital and a collapse in its value during the 1997/98 Asian financial crisis prompted authorities to impose capital controls and fix the ringgit.  

SINGAPORE DOLLAR <SGD=>  

Since 1981, the Monetary Authority of Singapore conducts monetary policy by steering the Singapore dollar in an undisclosed band against an undisclosed trade-weighted basket of currencies, rather than setting an interest rate as many central banks do.  

Economists say the regime is a combination of the band, basket and crawl foreign exchange systems.  

The MAS runs policy by letting the nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) appreciate or depreciate, either by shifting the mid-point of the band or adjusting its width. Economists say the U.S. dollar and dollar-bloc currencies make up the biggest proportion of the trade-weighted basket.  

Policy shifted from neutral to a tightening bias in April 2004 via a gradual appreciation of the mid-point of the NEER.  

The Sing dollar is freely convertible on the trade account and has very minimal restrictions on capital flows.  

INDIAN RUPEE <INR=>  

Economists say the Reserve Bank of India uses a monitoring band for the rupee, which allows it to float within a band determined by the currencies of India's top five trading partners, adjusted for inflation levels.  

Markets believe the width of the band is five percent on either side of this neutral real effective exchange rate (REER), and the RBI intervenes if the band is breached.  

The RBI regularly publishes data on the REER base period and neutral value, but with a lag.  

The current unified exchange rate was adopted in 1993 after a balance of payments crisis led to devaluations in 1991.  

The rupee is not fully convertible on the capital account. There are still some limits on residents borrowing overseas, on residents converting local assets into foreign currency and on the access foreigners have to Indian debt markets.  

THAI BAHT <THB=>  

Massive capital outflows forced Thailand to abandon the baht's peg against a basket of currencies on July 2, 1997, triggering a big devaluation against the dollar that marked the onset of the Asian financial crisis.  

Thailand adopted a managed float. Like other Asian central banks operating under similar regimes, the Bank of Thailand is averse to currency volatility and intervenes often in the market.  

Selective capital controls exist. There are strict limits on baht positions held by foreigners and offshore trading in baht is negligible.  

INDONESIAN RUPIAH <IDR=>  

Indonesia switched to a freely floating rupiah from a managed float in August 1997 during the Asian crisis. Several exchange controls remain.  

Indonesia's central bank regularly intervenes in the foreign exchange market to help the rupiah, which fell more than five percent against the dollar in the first half of 2005. To stabilise the currency, the central bank has also banned sales of rupiah securities by non-residents.  

INDEPENDENTLY FLOATING:  

------------------------  

KOREAN WON <KRW=> <KRW=KFTC>  

The won was floated in December 1997 and is one of Asia's most actively traded currencies.  

The Bank of Korea runs an inflation-targeting policy, but the government dictates currency policy and keeps a watchful eye on the won's competitiveness. This occasionally leads to strains between the central bank and the finance ministry.  

Foreigners have greater access to South Korean capital markets than to most others in emerging Asia, yet there are some restrictions on offshore won trading and on local banks' positions in won.  

The won non-deliverable forward (NDF) market that has developed as a consequence is among the most liquid in Asia.  

The yen-won is a popular cross rate, traded in the belief that Seoul likes to keep the won competitive versus the yen because of the overlap between South Korean and Japanese exports.  

PHILIPPINE PESO <PHP=>  

The peso is allowed to trade in a wider band than most other Asian currencies and is prone to volatile swings in response to political developments. It is also sensitive to data on the Philippines' large fiscal deficit and on remittances from overseas Filipinos, a major source of foreign exchange.  

The central bank, with limited official reserves, intervenes occasionally. It also adjusts reserve requirements, and the rate at which they are remunerated, to help smooth the currency.

title: Thai Fin Min: Strong Yuan, Weaker Oil To Cut Deficits
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Thai Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said Friday that the revaluation of the Chinese yuan will help to cut the country's trade and current account deficits.  

"The baht has strengthened less than the yuan, so it will benefit Thai exports," Somkid told reporters.  

And with global crude oil prices declining at the same time, "the trade and current account deficits are likely to be less than forecast," he said.  

Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said recently that he expected the current account to swing to a deficit around $2.5 billion, or less than 2% of gross domestic product this year, from a surplus of $7.29 billion last year.  

Somkid said the central bank will be monitoring the baht closely to ensure that its movements aren't too volatile when local players return to the market Monday morning after a long weekend. Thai markets and financial institutions are closed Friday for a public holiday.  

However, any volatility resulting from the yuan revaluation will only be short term, he said.  

Central bank Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula told reporters separately Friday that there has been no excessive volatility so far, but the central bank has prepared measures to reduce volatility if necessary. He didn't elaborate.  

Commerce Minister Thanong Bidiya said separately Friday that it will take about two months to gauge the effects of the yuan revaluation, but that as long as the baht doesn't strengthen below THB40 to the dollar the country's exports won't be hurt.  

The dollar was quoted in offshore trading Friday at THB41.345, down from THB41.79 prior to the decision by the People's Bank of China to drop the yuan's de facto peg to the dollar in favor of a managed float against a basket of currencies. In the process, the yuan was initially revalued about 2% to CNY8.1100 to a dollar from CNY8.2765.  

Pridiyathorn said late Thursday he was pleased with the change in China's foreign exchange regime because it will help to stabilize regional currencies and facilitate trade, which will be good for everyone.  

And now that the uncertainty surrounding the yuan has eased, "the baht should be less volatile," he said.  

The baht and other regional currencies have been fluctuating in recent months as investors speculated about the timing of China's move, appreciating in anticipation of a yuan revaluation when they thought the time was near, and depreciating when it failed to arrive.  

Usara Wilaipich, an economist in Bangkok for Standard Chartered Bank, said late Thursday that the yuan regime change will probably mean the Bank of Thailand and other regional central banks may not need to intervene in foreign exchange markets as much to protect the competitiveness of their countries' exports.  

Usara said Thai exports should benefit from lower export prices in dollar terms if the baht appreciates less than the yuan and other regional currencies, but over the long term, the benefits for Thailand and other regional suppliers of China's massive export industry are less clear.  

If the Chinese economy or its export growth slows as a result of the yuan's appreciation, the fall in income for its suppliers could be a greater factor for them than the price advantage provided by more competitive foreign exchange rates.  

"Exports from (Thailand and) the region to China could slow down, and in that case, the income effect is larger than the price effect," Usara said.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk: Yuan Change Good For China, World, Baht
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Thailand's central bank governor, Pridiyathorn Devakula, said late Thursday that China's move to peg the yuan to a basket of currencies, instead of solely to the U.S. dollar, will be good for China, good for the global economy and good for the Thai baht.  

Pridiyathorn said in a press conference that he is pleased with the change because it will help to stabilize regional currencies and facilitate trade, which will be good for everyone.  

And now that the uncertainty surrounding the yuan has eased, "the baht should be less volatile," he said.  

The baht and other regional currencies have been fluctuating in recent months as investors speculated about the timing of China's move, appreciating in anticipation of a yuan revaluation when they thought the time was near, and depreciating when it failed to arrive.  

The baht strengthened by 1.27% in the two hours after the People's Bank of China said it would scrap the yuan's peg to the dollar and use a basket of currencies to manage the yuan, the central bank governor said, the dollar falling to THB41.26 from THB41.79.  

At 1450 GMT, the dollar had fallen further and was quoted at THB41.180.  

Bank of Thailand didn't interfere despite the volatility following the yuan revaluation because it was normal movement in line with strengthening Asian currencies, he said. But the central bank will continue to monitor the baht's movements closely, he added.  

Bank of Thailand has a long-standing policy of intervening to limit daily volatility and keep the Thai currency in line with regional currencies, without trying to fight market trends.  

Pridiyathorn said the central bank is prepared to handle the effects of the change in foreign exchange markets, and it shouldn't have any impact on the Thai financial system.  

Thai markets and financial institutions are closed Friday for a public holiday.  

Beijing revalued the yuan by just 2.1% to CNY8.11 to the dollar, which probably isn't enough to satisfy those in the U.S. who believe that the Chinese currency's undervaluation gives China's products an unfair advantage in global markets.  

But the size of the initial move isn't the point, Pridiyathorn said.  

"The important point is not about how much the yuan has changed, it is that China is willing to adjust and allow it's currency to tie up with other currencies," he said.  

Usara Wilaipich, an economist in Bangkok for Standard Chartered Bank, said the initial reaction to the yuan regime change will come in the form of short-term capital inflows to the region, which have already boosted the baht and other currencies.  

Beyond that, Bank of Thailand and other regional central banks may not need to intervene in foreign exchange markets as much to protect the competitiveness of their countries' exports.  

"I think it will help relax central bank pressure because the yuan revaluation will help reduce pressure. Most Asian countries previously were concerned about competitiveness in terms of trade," she said.  

Although it is unclear how much less undervalued the yuan will be, since currencies and their relative representation in the yuan basket are unknown, a stronger yuan should also improve the export competitiveness of Thailand and other Asian countries, she said.  

Looking further ahead, however, the benefits for Thailand and other regional suppliers of China's massive export industry are less clear.  

If the Chinese economy or its export growth slows as a result of the yuan's appreciation, the fall in income for its suppliers could be a greater factor for them than the price advantage provided by more competitive foreign exchange rates.  

"Exports from (Thailand and) the region to China could slow down, and in that case, the income effect is larger than the price effect," Usara said.

title: Thai Baht Ends Dn, Off 9-Mo Low; Short Bonds Dn Sharply
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht ended weaker after hitting a nine-month low against the U.S. dollar in Asian spot trade Tuesday, tracking the losses of regional currencies against a surging dollar, dealers said.  

Government bond prices drifted lower ahead of the start of a new series of weekly auctions on Wednesday, while prices of short-term central bank bonds fell sharply ahead of an increase in short-term interest rates expected later in the month.  

The dollar finished at THB41.55, up from THB41.43 at the Asian close Monday, and just off a nine-month high of THB41.57.  

Expectations that the U.S. will continue raising interest rates for now, especially if U.S. payrolls data come out as strongly as expected Friday, supported the dollar against most global currencies.  

Payrolls are expected to show a rise of 200,000 in June, much more than the 75,000 increase reported in May.  

The dollar was also helped higher against the Japanese yen, a regional trendsetter, as Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi won only a thin five-vote majority in a key vote on postal system reform. The vote cast doubts on his government's ability to push through further reforms.  

There was little fresh local news moving the baht, but sentiment has been hurt by a string of current-account deficits in the three months to May.  

One trader said it was unlikely that the Bank of Thailand was intervening in the foreign exchange market Tuesday, as the baht's move wasn't so great and it was in line with regional currencies.  

Traders expected the dollar to trade in a range of THB41.45 to THB41.60 overnight, subject to any further volatility in the dollar-yen exchange rate. [ 05-07-05 1104GMT ]  

Thai long-term government bond yields drifted higher Tuesday under pressure from a rising interest-rate trend, but most investors were sidelined ahead of the start of a new series of weekly auctions on Wednesday, dealers said.  

The auction will give indications of real levels of demand from funds and insurance companies, which are expected to be more than adequate to absorb supply in the long end of about THB4.5 billion per week.  

The Thai Bond Dealing Center said the average bid on the government bond due November 2009 bid was up 2 basis points at 3.463%. The March 2012 bid jumped almost 3 basis points to 3.859%. The December 2014 bid rose one-and-a-half basis points to 3.981%, and the August 2019 bid added one-and-a-half basis points to finish at 4.349%.  

Expectations that the central bank's 14-day repurchase market target rate could rise by 25 basis points to 2.75% as early as the next monetary policy meeting on July 20 pushed short-term yields sharply higher.  

The Bank of Thailand auctioned Tuesday THB5 billion of its 28-day bonds at an average 2.315%, up from 2.055% at last week's auction. Another THB5 billion of 63-day central bank bonds was sold at an average 2.436%, up from 2.260%, and THB15 billion of 364-day bonds at an average 2.936%, up from 2.856%.  

The most-active overnight interbank rate likely fell to 2.48% or 2.49% Tuesday, from 2.50% the previous day, as liquidity tied up for accounting purposes at the end of the first half of the year flowed back into the system, dealers said. The overnight repurchase market rate ended flat, having eased back on Monday to 2.46875% from 2.50% over the half-year end.  

Quotes for term interest rates were also mostly higher under pressure from the expected interest rate trend.

title: ANALYSIS-Won, Taiwan dlr to outshine other Asian  currencies
text:
SINGAPORE, June 17 (Reuters) - It was not that long ago when all Asian currencies looked good in the eyes of investors. Exports were booming across the region and speculation was high that China would allow the yuan to rise.   

But now, with the U.S. dollar on a roll, currency analysts say investors need to be more picky. The South Korean won and Taiwan dollar still have a lot going for them, but southeast Asian units such as the Thai baht are expected to underperform.   

"Generally, northeast Asia is more tapped into the Chinese economy, which is still showing quite a good performance," said Philip Wee, senior market strategist at DBS in Singapore.   

"Use of the northeast currencies as proxies for the yuan has been quite evident."   

Half way into the year and the dollar, helped by rising U.S interest rates, has gained over six percent against the yen and almost double that against the euro. Its gains have allowed the dollar to escape a downtrend that was in its third year.   

Asian currencies have taken a bruising as a result. The won <KRW=KFTC> hit an eight-week low and the Singapore dollar <SGD=> dropped to an eight-month trough this week.   

But analysts say regional currencies, especially those from northeast Asia, should hold their ground against the U.S. dollar from here, particularly as speculation continues that China will reform its currency regime in the months ahead.   

The yuan <CNY=CFXS> is pegged in a tight band near 8.28 per dollar and China's trading partners have urged the country to let its currency appreciate, arguing the yuan is undervalued and gives Chinese exporters an unfair advantage.   

If China allows the yuan to rise, other Asian currencies are expected to rise too and that means investors are reluctant to sell regional currencies too much.   

GOING WITH THE FLOW   

Analysts said the won and Taiwan dollar would benefit most from China speculation because of their countries' increasingly strong trade links to China.   

Trade and investment between Taiwan and China has boomed since the late 1980s. Exports to China accounted for about 20 percent of total South Korean exports in 2004, from under five percent in 1990, JP Morgan noted in a recent report.   

Speculation about what China will do with its currency has also boosted inflows of foreign capital into the region.   

India and Taiwan have seen the heaviest net foreign buying of equities in the region in the past 250 days, data released this week by Nomura International shows.   

The strength of demand for Taiwan shares has taken many analysts by surprise.   

John Cairns, head of research for Asia at IDEAglobal in Singapore, said portfolio equity inflows had been expected to slow after a recent weighting upgrade by Morgan Stanley Capital International, whose indices heavily influence share buying.   

"But the inflows have actually continued, so that is keeping the Taiwan dollar quite resilient," Cairns said.   

TRADE BARRIER   

The key factor determining which currencies will resist dollar strength and which ones will not, says JP Morgan currency strategist Claudio Piron, is each country's current account.   

Since 1998, Asia has had a large trade surplus but some countries are starting to see their surpluses either narrow or move into deficit as oil prices remain persistently high, pushing up the price of imports, while exports to China slow.   

"Southeast Asian currencies are a bit more vulnerable at this point as they are backed by narrowing trade surpluses and in some case deficits," said UBS currency strategist Bhanu Baweja.   

India's trade deficit widened to $7.21 billion in the first two months of the fiscal year to March 31, 2006. Thailand's current account recorded a deficit in March and April after a small surplus in February.   

Analysts said Thailand was on course for an annual current account deficit in 2005 and that would be the first since the Asian financial crisis.   

"Asian currencies should continue to perform quite well but the baht is our underperformer," said IDEAglobal's Cairns.   

"This is mostly because of the surplus moving into a deficit. Bank of Thailand policy is also important," he said. "They don't seem too willing to come in at the top end and support the baht."   

Asian central banks have a reputation for being heavy interveners on the currency markets, but Thailand's central bank chief said this week the baht was not too weak against the dollar.   

The baht <THB=>, Asia's worst performing currency this year after the yen, hit a seven-month low versus the dollar on Friday.   

Significant outperformance of Asian currencies against the dollar was also seen as unlikely as rising U.S. interest rates suggest investors may get better returns by holding dollars.   

The Federal Reserve's key interest rate is at 3.0 percent and expected to rise further. That compares to Singapore, where rates are just above 2.0 percent, and Taiwan, where they are just below there.

title: Thai Baht Ends Dn On Late Dlr Rally; Bonds Dn On Supply
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht hit a fresh six-month low against the dollar in Asian spot trade Wednesday as onshore firms rushed to buy the U.S. unit when as it made a late charge against regional currencies, traders said.  

Sentiment toward the baht was hurt by a report from the Ministry of Finance that, based on customs department data, Thailand recorded a trade deficit of $1.55 billion in the month of April.  

Government bond prices rose in continuing gains after the finance ministry said Tuesday afternoon that it was canceling auctions scheduled from June 1 to July 6, and reducing the amount to be sold on Wednesday.  

The dollar finished at THB40.16, up from THB40.04 at the Asian close Tuesday, just off a six-month high of THB40.17.  

The U.S. unit opened down and slid to an intraday low of THB39.96 tracking its early weakness against the Japanese yen, a regional trendsetter, amid renewed talk of a possible revaluation of the Chinese yuan.  

The Financial Times reported overnight that the U.S. had asked China through unofficial envoys to revalue its currency by 10%. But China reportedly said it would not be influenced by external pressure.  

Sentiment toward the baht soured after the customs department said exports were 13% on year in April to $8.24 billion, but imports were up 30% on year to $9.79 billion due to surging imports of oil and steel. Exports were interrupted by several holidays during the month.  

Deputy Prime Minister Somkid Jatusripitak, who also serves as finance minister, said the deficit was not a concern as the central bank holds substantial foreign exchange reserves on hands.  

The baht wasn't affected immediately, because the dollar was still testing intraday lows against the yen.  

But after players failed to take the U.S. unit into new lows for the second time Wednesday afternoon, they chased the dollar back up against the yen and most other regional currencies, sparking a buying spree in late trade against the baht.  

Local oil firms and importers bought dollars aggressively, and exporters removed their sell orders.  

Some dealers said the Bank of Thailand was intervening to cool the dollar's momentum at the Asian close.  

Technical charts suggest that after breaking strong resistance at THB40, the dollar could head toward THB40.265, and then THB40.41 in the coming weeks. Support is likely overnight at THB40.00, with major support at THB39.80. [ 25-05-05 1134GMT ]  

Thai government bond yields ended sharply lower Wednesday in continuing losses after news the previous afternoon that June auctions had been canceled, dealers said.  

Profit taking by funds took yields off lows, however, along with uncertainty over what levels of supply might be upcoming to help finance planned infrastructure projects.  

Dealers expected yields to level off around current levels pending further supply news.  

The Thai Bond Dealing Center said the two-year central bank bond traded Wednesday around 3.13%, down from 3.16% the previous day. The average bid on the government bond due December 2006 was virtually unchanged at 3.002%. The November 2009 bid fell 4 basis points to 3.523%. The March 2012 bid plunged 6 basis point to 3.900%. The December 2014 bid eased 3 basis points to 4.122%, and the December 2019 bid lost 2 basis points to end at 4.537%.  

The Bank of Thailand auctioned Wednesday THB1.5 billion of seven-year bonds due March 2012 at an average yield of 3.876%, down from 4.055% at last week's auction.  

An official from the Ministry of Finance said the remaining auctions in the schedule were canceled because the government budget will be balanced this year, and the Treasury's refinancing needs were reduced after receiving a share of the central bank's net profit for 2004. No figures were provided. A new supply schedule is likely to be announced in the first half of June, the official said.  

The overnight interbank rate was quoted late Wednesday around 2.25%, unchanged from the most-active level of the previous day. The overnight repurchase market rate also ended flat at 2.25%.  

Dealers said overnight rates will remain firm due to central bank borrowing. The Bank of Thailand supplemented its daily heavy borrowing in the regular afternoon repurchase market with light additional borrowing Wednesday in the morning bilateral repurchase market.  

Most quotes for term interest rates were unchanged because an interest-rate increase of 25 basis points likely in June or July has largely been priced in by related markets.

title: DJ Thai Baht Ends Dn On Late Dlr Rally; Bonds Dn On Supply
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht hit a fresh six-month low against the dollar in Asian spot trade Wednesday as onshore firms rushed to buy the U.S. unit when as it made a late charge against regional currencies, traders said.  

Sentiment toward the baht was hurt by a report from the Ministry of Finance that, based on customs department data, Thailand recorded a trade deficit of $1.55 billion in the month of April.  

Government bond prices rose in continuing gains after the finance ministry said Tuesday afternoon that it was canceling auctions scheduled from June 1 to July 6, and reducing the amount to be sold on Wednesday.  

The dollar finished at THB40.16, up from THB40.04 at the Asian close Tuesday, just off a six-month high of THB40.17.  

The U.S. unit opened down and slid to an intraday low of THB39.96 tracking its early weakness against the Japanese yen, a regional trendsetter, amid renewed talk of a possible revaluation of the Chinese yuan.  

The Financial Times reported overnight that the U.S. had asked China through unofficial envoys to revalue its currency by 10%. But China reportedly said it would not be influenced by external pressure.  

Sentiment toward the baht soured after the customs department said exports were 13% on year in April to $8.24 billion, but imports were up 30% on year to $9.79 billion due to surging imports of oil and steel. Exports were interrupted by several holidays during the month.  

Deputy Prime Minister Somkid Jatusripitak, who also serves as finance minister, said the deficit was not a concern as the central bank holds substantial foreign exchange reserves on hands.  

The baht wasn't affected immediately, because the dollar was still testing intraday lows against the yen.  

But after players failed to take the U.S. unit into new lows for the second time Wednesday afternoon, they chased the dollar back up against the yen and most other regional currencies, sparking a buying spree in late trade against the baht.  

Local oil firms and importers bought dollars aggressively, and exporters removed their sell orders.  

Some dealers said the Bank of Thailand was intervening to cool the dollar's momentum at the Asian close.  

Technical charts suggest that after breaking strong resistance at THB40, the dollar could head toward THB40.265, and then THB40.41 in the coming weeks. Support is likely overnight at THB40.00, with major support at THB39.80.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Chief: No  FX Intervention  For Many Weeks
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said Thursday the central bank hasn't intervened in the market to weaken the baht for many weeks, and that recent baht weakness is mainly due to the broad dollar strength.  

"If we compare the baht to the yen or euro, we still strengthen," he told reporters. [ 19-05-05 0705GMT ]  

Pridiyathorn said the central bank will continue to monitor the market closely, act to stabilize the baht if necessary, facilitate trading transactions and try to prevent any speculation amid the changing environment in the Asian foreign exchange market.  

The central bank is prepared for movements in the yuan should China revalue its currency, he said.  

"Don't worry. We already have plans for yuan movements. Whenever it moves, we will try to smooth things out, reducing the effect to trading transactions."  

He added that the central bank doesn't foresee any dollar crisis in the future but that it is prepared for any such event. The Thai economy is supported by strong domestic consumption, and could survive any dollar crisis, he said.

title: Thai Baht Ends Down On Weak Yen, Local Stocks; Bonds Up
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht fell against the U.S. dollar for an eighth consecutive day in Asian spot trade Wednesday, closing just off a 15-week low on weakness in the Japanese yen, equity-linked outflows and cross-currency demand from locally-based Japanese companies, traders said.  

Medium- and long-term government bond prices ended higher after strong auction results boosted market sentiment.  

The dollar finished at THB39.35, up from THB39.265 at the Asian close Tuesday, after rising to a 15-week high of THB39.39 in early trade.  

Traders said the U.S. unit's early gains were largely driven by its strength against the yen after Tokyo reported weaker-than-expected industrial production in February, with a 2.1% fall on month.  

Equity-related outflows also hurt the baht. Foreign investors sold a net THB1.48 billion worth of Thai shares Wednesday, after having sold a combined net THB7.0 billion in the six previous sessions.  

Thailand-based Japanese units continued to buy the yen outright in cross-currency transactions through the U.S. dollar to make payments on loans and repatriate earnings before the end of Japan's fiscal year on March 31.  

"However, the dollar's rally cooled later in the day on exporter selling and suspected intervention by the central bank," a trader said.  

Bank of Thailand Assistant Governor Nitaya Pibulratanagit said Wednesday that the baht was at an acceptable level, weakening against the dollar in line with regional currencies, but she noted the central bank has stepped into the foreign exchange market when necessary.  

Trader said some interbank players also sold to take advantage of the dollar's sharp recent gains, booking profits ahead of the release of U.S. consumer data Thursday and nonfarm payrolls data Friday, both of which could influence the dollar's direction.  

The U.S. currency is expected to retest resistance at THB39.40 overnight or Thursday, with the next resistance pegged at THB39.50. Support is expected at THB39.25. [ 30-03-05 1103GMT ]  

Most Thai government bond yields fell after an auction demonstrated that demand driven by cash liquidity still outweighs moderate supply.  

The average accepted yield for a THB1.5 billion offering of the issue due March 2012 fell to 4.1559% from 4.2205% at last week's auction. Another THB1 billion of the issue due December 2019 was sold at an average 4.8252%, down from 4.8621% last week.  

Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said Wednesday that the central bank will consider both growth and inflation when determining interest rate policy, but that 2005 gross domestic product growth will exceed 5%.  

"It's possible that that key rate will rise by 1% (100 basis points) for the whole year as we still have six meetings left for this year," Pridiyathorn said.  

The governor's comments didn't affect the bond market, however, as they were in line with expectations. The central bank's 14-day repurchase market rate is currently 2.25%. Most economists expect an increase of 25 basis points when the policy committee next meets April 20, and further increases to around 3%-3.5% by year-end.  

The Thai Bond Dealing Center said the average bid late Wednesday on the government bond due November 2009 was down two basis points to 3.768%, the March 2012 bid dropped three basis points to 4.150%, the December 2014 bid fell six basis point to 4.524% and the December 2019 bid eased one basis point to 4.821%.  

The overnight interbank rate was quoted around 1.85%, lower in late trade as usual, but the most-active level likely remained around 1.90% due to earlier deals, dealers said. Liquidity was high as banks and clients had plenty of extra cash on hand for end-month wages and payments.  

Quotes for term interest rates were mostly down slightly, following steady increases in recent weeks, due to a lack of demand to borrow baht through the foreign exchange swap market, lowering implied yields of onshore swaps, dealers said.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk: Current Level Of Baht Won't Affect Exports
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thailand's central bank said Friday that the current level of the baht won't adversely affect the country's exports. 

 Chetthavee Charoenpitaks, Bank of Thailand assistant governor for the Financial Markets Operations Group, told reporters: "The baht at 37.40 to the dollar is okay." 

 "There should be no intervention. I think in general this level shouldn't affect exports," he said. 

 At 0901 GMT (4:01 a.m. EST), the dollar was quoted around THB37.367, down slightly from THB37.400 at the close of trading in Asia Thursday. 

 Chetthavee said the authorities shouldn't intervene in the foreign exchange market because Thailand has abandoned the fixed exchange system. This means the baht has to move in line with market forces. 

 He said the recent movement of the baht in a range of two or three baht to the dollar "wasn't a great fluctuation." 

 He said investors should look at the baht with a longer term perspective. 

 "They shouldn't look at it on a day-to-day basis," he said.

title: Thai c. bank says no baht  intervention .
text:
BANGKOK, Jan 4 (Reuters) - The Bank of Thailand said on Tuesday it would not intervene in the market to influence the baht's movement despite the currency's sharp rise and it would allow it to fluctuate according to market forces. 

 "We would like to confirm that we will not intervene in the market and will let (the baht) move according to market forces. If we take any action, it would probably add to the baht's volatility, something which the central bank does not want to see," said assistant central bank governor Chetthavee Charoenpitaks. 

 The Thai baht rose to a high of 36.83 on Tuesday, from 37.40/37.50 at the end of December. 

 Chetthavee told reporters the baht's rally on Tuesday reflected market confidence in the stability of the Thai economy and a smooth rollover into the new year by the financial sector and the stock market without any computer bug problems. 

 He said the baht benefited from recent projections by the state think tank, the National Economic and Social Development Board, that Thailand's gross domestic product would expand about 4.4 percent in 2000. 

 Chetthavee said a high year-end demand for baht from both domestic and offshore markets, made through the central bank currency swap window, would not have much impact on the currency this month when market participants unwound positions made with the central bank. 

 "The central bank's net forward swap position stood at more than $4.5 billion at the end of December, up from $4.3 billion a week earlier," Chetthavee said. "The swap deals would not affect the baht as they are spread out over one to three-months maturity."

title: Emerging  FX  - Up on stock flows, authorities alert.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 4 (Reuters) - The Taiwan dollar	    shot



more than two percent higher by Tuesday afternoon, providing


 the region's best example of capital inflows translating into 

 firmer currencies in the new year. 

     Impressive performances were made by many of Asian stock 

 markets on relief the Y2K bug had been a non-event, 

 underpinning the generally buoyant mood in almost all the 

 regional currencies. 


    The speed of the rise in the yen	   , the Korean won and



the Taiwan dollar proved too much for domestic authorities,



with dealers citing a flurry of interventionist activity aimed



at tempering further upside.



    Dollar/yen bounced back above 102 after repeated rounds of



Bank of Japan intervention lifted it off earlier lows of around



101.46.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR	



    Offshore dollar sales as investors bought into a domestic



stock rally pushed the Taiwan dollar more than two and a half



percent higher despite efforts by the central bank to steady



its speedy rise.



    The local unit soared as high as 30.53 per dollar,



surpassing its recent string of 25-month highs around the



T$31.39 level.



    Taipei dealers said the government appeared more willing to



tolerate its appreciation of late due to an upturn in exports



and as presidential elections were around the corner.



    But an analyst at a U.S. bank in Singapore said the



government was likely to cap any rise above the 30.00 level.



    KOREAN WON	     -2



    Excitement over equities also fuelled sharp moves in the



won, forcing the monetary authorities to issue warnings and



then follow through with dollar buying intervention.



    But renewed efforts to put the brakes on were short-lived,



with the won swinging yet higher and ending at its strongest



level since late November 1997.



    The Ministry of Finance said a drop in exports caused by a



stronger currency would not be desirable for economic recovery



and that the monetary authorities would use various methods to



stabilise the domestic foreign exchange market.



THAI BAHT	



The Thai baht was slightly off after shooting higher in



offshore trade the previous day, but it was still trading



around its highest levels for six months.



Dealers in Thailand said the rise stemmed from optimism



over foreign capital inflows linked to corporate investment and



a surging stock market.



The Bank of Thailand said it would not intervene in the



market to influence the baht's movement despite the currency's



sharp rise and that it would allow it to fluctuate according to



market forces.



The consumer price index for 1999 rose 0.3 percent



year-on-year compared to an 8.1 percent year-on-year rise in



1998 while the wholesale price index (WPI) fell 6.5 percent.



    The WPI had risen 13.8 percent year-on-year in 1998.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The Singapore dollar gained almost half a percent despite



corrective losses in the Straits Times Index	    after



record closings over the past three sessions.



    Dealers said its upward bias was likely to continue based



on better than expected growth data for the fourth quarter of



1999 and forecasts of sound growth ahead.



    Some local analysts have said they see the STI heading



towards 2,700 points by late January from around 2,500 now and



that dollar/Sing should reach between 1.50 to 1.60 by the end



of this year.



PHILIPPINE PESO	



The peso gained as banks unloaded their dollar positions



amid fading fears of the millennium bug.



Export growth looks set to rise steadily this year due to



demand for electronic products in Asia and Europe. The



government said exports rose 19 percent year-on-year in the



first 11 months of 1999.



Finance Secretary Edgardo Espiritu said the benchmark



91-day Treasury bill rate could drop 25 basis points at next



week's auction. It was at 8.898 percent at the last auction in



1999.



He also said annual inflation in December may come in



higher than the November figure of 3.9 percent, a 12-year low,



but it should not exceed 4.5 percent.



A Reuters poll produced an average forecast of a 4.35



percent rise in December inflation. The number is due on



Wednesday.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



The rupiah was off its lows but still comfortably within



the 7,000/7,100 per dollar range in light trade.



The central bank's financial woes remained a focal point,



with dealers saying the published audit into its affairs would



be positive over the long term despite some immediate



bearishness.



The IMF said Bank Indonesia needed some recapitalisation,



but there was nothing in the critical audit which showed the



bank could not meet its daily obligations. It also said greater



transparency would strengthen BI.



A finance ministry official said the government would



unveil its next budget and the latest IMF letter of intent on



January 20.
