title: INTERVIEW - Thai c.bank says baht speculation curbed.
text:
BANGKOK, Dec 21 (Reuters) - Thailand's central bank governor said on Tuesday that "pure speculation" in the baht had now been curbed but remaining controls on baht transactions involving offshore players would still be kept. 

 Chatu Mongol Sonakul also told Reuters in a rare interview that although the baht was now relatively strong the Bank of Thailand was not propping up the currency. 

 "There's no plan to do such a thing (lifting remaining controls). We can do it when the financial stabilising system comes out with a workable system where international capital flows can be...reasonable," he said. 

 A key remaining restriction on baht transactions for foreign parties is a 50 million baht limit on non-commercial swap deals. 

 The baht was quoted at around 37.85/37.95 to the U.S. dollar on Tuesday afternoon against 41.65 late in September. 

 "We are not actually intervening at all at this particular point. It is where people expect it to be given the trade and the FDI (foreign direct investment). 

 "FDI flow has been regular although not extensive as yet. (You've got to watch) the FDI coming in and making it (the baht) too strong. Otherwise it will actually neutralise the FDI coming in in terms of the exchange effects," he said. 

 But the governor said the Bank of Thailand would not hesitate to intervene again as it did in October to prevent sharp speculative baht movements. 

 "If you look at the Asia and Pacific baht rate, it is basically the same as the onshore baht rate. So the measures were successful," Chatu Mongol said. 

 NO NEW PROBE NEEDED AT KRUNG THAI BANK 

 He also said he did not think the government needed to conduct a new probe into debt-laden state-owned Krung Thai Bank Plc, at the centre of a controversy over its bad loans and management. 

 "Krung Thai is already being supervised full-time (by the central bank)," he said. The bank's non-performing loans stood at 51 percent of all loans at end-September and it accounts for nearly 20 percent share of all loans in the Thai banking sector. 

 Critics have been raking the government and in particular Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda for the handling of the bank. 

 Chatu Mongol said Krung Thai had not performed much worse than other Thai banks and actually faced more stringent supervision from the authorities, including the central bank and other government auditors. 

 "We don't need to make Krung Thai the best Thai bank, just make it viable and fairly reasonable," he said. 

 He said he did not believe Krung Thai executives had been involved in questionable lending or fraudulent bank practices. 

 "All these cases will be very grey and some technical...involving some minor breaches of regulations. We are not going to have a case in which a guy stole a lot of money and ran away with it in a jeep," he said. 

 NON-PERFORMING LOANS STILL HIGH BUT DECLINING MONTHLY 

 Chatu Mongol said non-performing loans (NPLs) were still high, but were declining at a net rate of one percentage point per month. 

 "NPLs are coming down. Net wise, it is going down about one percentage point a month. The buying off of bank NPLs by the government also helped bring down the NPL figures," he said. 

 At end-October, there were 2.46 trillion baht (US$65 billion) of NPLs in the ailing financial system. The level of NPLs in the financial sector stood at around 43.8 percent of outstanding loans and 43.4 percent for banks alone. 

 At their peak at end May, NPLs in the whole financial sector were at 47.7 percent of total lending. 

 Chatu Mongol said the mechanism for dealing with NPLs was working well, but the authorities were still short of staff and expertise for monitoring the exact level of bank NPLs. 

 He said there was no policy conflict between himself and the finance minister as speculated recently in the local media. 

 The outspoken central bank governor also said he was keeping his options open on whether or not to enter politics. 

 "My career in politics will be based solely on whether there will be anything useful (for me) to do," he said. 

 The six-party coalition government of Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai must call an election by November but the beginnings of election fever are already starting to grip the country. 

 (US$1 = 38 baht). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1999.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk: Thai Baht Strengthens On Export Growth
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thailand's central bank governor said Wednesday that the recent strength in the baht was due to strong export growth. 

 Chatu Mongol Sonakul told reporters that exports grew by 10% on year in September. 

 Exports grew by 15% on year in August, helping Thailand to maintain a hefty trade surplus of 746 million baht. Official figures from the Bank of Thailand for September are due Friday. 

 At 0426 GMT (12:26 a.m. EDT), the dollar was at THB38.615 down from THB38.69 at Tuesday's close and much lower than highs of just below THB41.70 last month. 

 Thai exports remained strong in September because of baht weakness at that time, making locally-produced goods more competitive overseas. 

 Chatu Mongol said baht strength was also due to the unwinding of long-dollar positions in the forwards market. 

 Offshore investors had bet on further declines in the baht last month by borrowing the local currency to buy dollars, hoping to sell them later at a higher price. 

 A combination of central bank dollar selling to slow the baht's decline, and a tightening of restrictions on baht lending to offshore investors, helped stem the local currency's decline. 

 Investors subsequently unwound exposure to long-dollar positions, helping to push the baht higher. 

 Bank of Thailand's governor said the central bank hadn't intervened in the currency market recently, without elaborating.

 Chatu Mongol said a weaker baht last month had obviously boosted Thai exports. 

 Analysts expect Thai September exports to rise to about $5.0 billion, a 23-month high, from a preliminary $4.86 billion in August and $4.47 billion in September last year.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Gov/Baht -2: To Buy Baht If Prices Unstable
text:
WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--It is inappropriate to call the Thai central bank's entry into foreign exchange markets Friday an act of intervention, Bank of Thailand governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul said Tuesday. 

 Speaking on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund in Washington, Chatu Mongol told Dow Jones Newswires that recent purchases of baht were "not really" intervention because they were of a "very little" amount and aimed at containing volatility, rather than at boosting the currency. 

 "Intervention is when you decide that a certain exchange rate is not right for you and then you intervene to make it go up or down," Chatu Mongol said. "We didn't do that." 

 "We saw the baht moving up and down rather fast, so we just slowed it down a little bit. It worked very well," he said. 

 Chatu Mongol said the central bank is finding application of a new flexible inflation-targeting model - based on a combination of indicators - "rather difficult to do," and for that reason it would continue to monitor changes in "various currencies and oil prices" for measures of price stability. In that context, he indicated that the government might yet act to strengthen the baht if it weakens too much. 

 "If it seems to us that the situation is unsustainable, we might actually do something. But we are in that status at the moment," Mongkul said.

title: Baht seen falling further as debtors seek cover.
text:
BANGKOK, Sept 28 (Reuters) - The weak Thai baht is set to slide further near-term as corporate debtors, worried about yen strength, run for shelter. 

 Analysts believe that the baht's current sharp weakness is more due to poor sentiment and technical reasons rather than fundamental factors which have not changed much. 

 At 0745 GMT, the baht dropped to its lowest level since August 31, 1998 at 41.27/41.32 per dollar. It hovered around the 37 level in July but really started tumbling in September. 

 Analysts said the baht could test the 41.50-42.00 level in the coming weeks unless there was strong indication the yen would weaken further or other strong positive leads emerged. 

 The Bank of Thailand's veiled threat that it would intervene if the baht went too low might not be forceful enough to avert its imminent fall, but it could slow the pace, they said. 

 The central bank in the past prided itself on telling the market that it would not intervene and the currency should move with market forces. 

 "They (The Thai central bank) are not telling you they are not worried any more. But this does not mean that the market will not try (to sell the baht), but they will be cautious," said Alison Seng, a forex specialist at Standard and Poors' MMS. 

 "The impact of the (central bank) statement was slightly diluted by an earlier statement that the baht at 41-42 level is acceptable. This is like an invitation for the market to go short," she said. 

 Recent baht weakness was caused mostly by corporate debt repayments on fears the yen could rise further, hedging activity, dollar demand for year-end book closings, and position adjustments on Y2K computer bug worries for the year-end. 

 "Our positive view on Thailand's economic fundamentals has not changed. Debt restructuring has improved and the export sector and consequently the trade surplus remains strong," said Chan Chia Lin, head of economic research at ABN AMRO Bank in Singapore. 

 "The weakness we see now in the baht is caused by external and domestic factors. One major factor the market was talking about is debt repayment for yen-denominated loans," she said. 

 The Thai private sector's foreign debt as at the end of June was estimated at $45 billion, about 20 percent of which is believed to be yen-denominated. 

 The yen rose sharply recently, sparking speculation that it could test the key 100-yen level. Although it has calmed down a little after the latest G7 meeting, concerns still linger. 

 "Some of our corporate clients sold baht for yen to repay the debt, fearing that the currency could rise further and affect their debt servicing ability," said a senior dealer at a major U.S. bank. 

 "At the same time, more companies hedged their positions in the forward market to minimise risks. This also pressured the baht as banks which sold forward contracts have to buy dollars in the spot market. The poor sentiment seems to feed on itself." 

 The problem was exacerbated by exporters' withholding of dollars on anticipation that the baht might drop further. 

 Treasurers at several major exporting firms surveyed by Reuters said they were in no rush to sell dollars. 

 "In this kind of market, we would rather hold on to the dollar as long as it is permitted by the government," said a corporate treasurer at a major agri-business company. 

 The government gives exporters 120 days to repatriate their export revenues to Thailand and seven days to change it into local currency after that. 

 Analysts said the baht was expected to climb again from current low levels in the medium-term with Thailand's trade surplus and other positive domestic fundamentals, but it might not see the 38 per dollar level again for the rest of the year.

 potential impact of the strong yen on the global economy and

 Initial optimism over the statement soon gave way to

 concrete evidence of a change in monetary policy. 

 *** The rupiah firmed back above the 8,400 level as Jakarta 

 returned to normal after last week's bloody riots but dealers 

 said trade was thin and players cautious. 

 Student groups in the capital have vowed to protest until 

 the country's new security law - which they say will give the 

 military freer reign to crush dissent - is revoked. 

 They say the government's decision to delay its 

 implementation is insufficient and reject arguments that the 

 new law is better than the old one. 

 Jakarta dealers said the rupiah adopted a firmer tone after 

 parliament said that seven top officials, including the central 

 bank governor and finance minister, should face swift legal 

 action over the Bank Bali scandal. 

 The recent suspension of fresh loans by the International 

 Monetary Fund remained in place, though, as the IMF awaited the 

 release of an external audit on the bank. 

 The state statistics bureau said it expected September's 

 month-on-month inflation figure to be between minus 0.5 and 

 minus 0.9 percent, compared to minus 0.9 percent in August. 

 *** The Taiwan dollar pared early losses as the central 

 bank stepped in to protect it from the impact of last week's 

 earthquake, which killed some 2,100 people. 

     The central bank said damage to infrastructure and industry 

 was limited and economic recovery would be swift. 

     It said Taiwan's sound economic fundamentals would 

 stabilise the local dollar. 

     Taiwan shares fared worse, losing 2.66 percent on the first 

 trading day since the earthquake last Tuesday.

 expected more declines.

intervened in the forward market late on Friday.

 government and because of debtor-creditor agreements. 

 The central bank said on Monday that total NPLs of Thai 

 banks amounted to 46.12 percent of total credits at end-July

 8.548 percent at Monday's regular auction against 8.55 percent

 key overnight rates for now despite the currency's recent falls

title: ASIA MARKETS-Stocks sink,  currencies  calm post-G7.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 27 (Reuters) - Asian stocks remained prone 

 to jitters about U.S. asset markets on Monday while regional 

currencies gained ground after the Group of Seven meeting failed 

 to come up with measures to rein in the rising yen. 

     DOLLAR/YEN SPLUTTERS, REGIONALS HOLD FIRM 

     Analysts found little that was new in the G7 communique, 

 which said the group shared Japan's concern about the impact of 

 the rising yen and welcomed efforts by Tokyo to conduct its 

 policies accordingly. 

     Speculation the Bank of Japan might take credit easing steps 

 to counter the yen's appreciation and pave the way for 

 coordinated intervention initially boosted the dollar to 106 

 yen. 

     But its rally was short-lived and analysts said the dollar's 

 downtrend remained intact. 

     "The bearish trend of dollar/yen shows no sign of reversal. 

 We would recommend re-instating short positions at 105.90 yen 

 with a stop above the 21-day moving average at 107.50," said 

 Chin Loo Thio, strategist at Paribas. 

 Regional currencies were resilient to the yen's early falls 

 as players took profit on long dollar positions after last 

 week's big losses in the baht, peso and rupiah. 

 TAIWAN STOCKS SINK BUT DAMAGE CONTAINED - FOR NOW 

 Taiwan's stock market featured prominently as trade resumed 

 after a four-day break following last week's massive earthquake. 

     The weighted index gapped sharply lower at the open with 

 chipmakers predictably bearing the brunt of the decline. 

     But the damage was contained by buying in the construction 

 and cement sectors, and by a newly narrowed volatility limit 

 which left trade in about 85 percent of listed companies 

 suspended for the day after the first half-hour. 

 The Finance Ministry on Sunday ordered the narrowing of 

 volatility limits in its stock and futures markets to 3.5 

 percent from seven percent to avoid panic-selling. The new limit 

 remains in place until October 8. 

 But Taipei brokers said the market was set to head much 

 lower, with sell orders, mainly from local retail investors, 

 piling up after the suspension of trade. 

     Technically, the weighted index could soon test support just 

 below the 7,700 level to fill a gap created on August 16. 

     Taiwan stock futures traded on SIMEX in Singapore also made 

 hefty losses, with the key September contract gapping down 

 sharply after a three-day suspension. 

     The falls were somewhat cushioned by trading limits, though 

 these are not nearly as rigid as in Taiwan. 

     And dealers said the market could see some consolidation, as 

 the key September contract looks heavily oversold, with a 14-day 

 RSI reading of about 17. 

     THAI BAHT PERKS UP, BUT PROSPECTS POOR 

     The Thai baht firmed back to the right side of 41 per dollar 

 as players booked profit on the dollar's rise to 13-month highs 

 last week. 

     Dealers said there were also rumours that the Bank of 

Thailand had intervened in swap markets late on Friday and this 

 spurred players to reduce their long dollar positions. 

     The central bank said last Thursday that it was keeping a 

 close watch on the baht, but had found no evidence of a 

 speculative attack and did not plan to act on its weakness. 

     Analysts said the baht's rebound on Monday was likely to be 

 short-lived. 

     "We're not looking for any sudden turnaround in the baht 

 anytime soon. We're still looking for a target of 43, but that 

 is a six-month view," said Kate O'Donoghue, regional economist 

 at Barclays Capital. 

 She said any upside was likely to be limited by worries 

 about Thailand's persistently high level of non-performing 

 loans, the slow pace of bank restructuring and a deflationary 

 environment. 

 The central bank said on Monday that total NPLs of Thai 

 banks amounted to 46.12 percent of total credits at end-July 

 against 46.48 percent a month earlier.

title: EMERGING MARKET  FX -Asia up, Colombia set to drop.
text:
LONDON, Sept 27 (Reuters) - Emerging Asian currencies firmed on Monday as players sold dollars after taking a closer look at comments on the yen from the Group of Seven (G7) industrial powers. 

 Colombia's newly floated peso was expected to tumble on the first trading day after the scrapping of its old currency band, while the surging world gold price helped lift the South African rand sharply higher. 

 A weekend G7 statement expressed concern over the potential impact of the strong yen on the global economy, and triggered rumours the Bank of Japan might agree to ease credit in return for international cooperation to halt its currency's climb. 

 The dollar reached a day's high of 106 yen on that view, but on closer scrutiny players decided the G7 statement contained little concrete sign of action on the yen and the dollar slipped back to around 104. 

 "There was no agreement on coordinated intervention or policy change," said Callum Henderson, currency strategist at Citibank in London. 

 "Reassessment of that statement caused dollar/yen to fall and that provided a perfect excuse for profit-taking on long dollar positions in a number of exchange rates." 

 The volatile Indonesian rupiah showed the sharpest move against the greenback, strengthening past 8,400 in thin trade after grazing 8,900 late last week during clashes between students and security forces. 

 Jakarta was quiet after President Habibie delayed signing the controversial new security law that sparked the riots. But analysts said the calm was unlikely to last as student groups have vowed to continue their protest until the law is scrapped. 

 They said the rupiah's stronger tone owed more to last week's tough parliamentary report saying seven top officials, including the central bank governor and the finance minister, should face swift legal action over the Bank Bali scandal. 

 The Thai baht, which has led regional currency weakness over the past couple of weeks, firmed back through the key barrier of 41 to the dollar, helped by rumours in Singapore that the Bank of Thailand intervened in the forward market late last week. 

 But analysts saw further medium-term weakness as a heavy burden of non-performing loans continued to weigh on the Thai banking sector and players nervous of the millennium bug became increasingly wary of emerging Asian assets. 

 "Medium-term technicals point to 43.50 in perhaps a six-month frame," Henderson at Citibank said. 

 The Singapore dollar and Philippine peso were also significantly firmer. 

 COLOMBIA PESO'S SLIDE SEEN LIMITED 

 Colombia's peso was expected to slip when American markets opened later on Monday, after the central bank scrapped its trading band and crawling peg system on Saturday. 

 But most analysts said the slide should be limited as the currency was not drastically overvalued, and was likely to bounce back towards current levels later in the week. 

 The peso closed on Friday at 1,994.49 to the dollar, and most analysts saw it tumbling on Monday to between 2,000 and 2,200. 

 "It depends how the Americans view it, but it won't be there for long - it'll come back a bit towards the end of the week," said Mike Noone, Latin America economist at Westdeutsche Landesbank in London. 

 The move to a free float followed persistent market attacks on the band, and was announced one day after Colombia clinched an agreement with the International Monetary Fund for a $7 billion international loan package. 

 The central bank had haemorrhaged more than $400 million in reserves last week alone to try to defend the band. 

 Elsewhere, the rand firmed to hover around 6.0 to the dollar after world gold prices soared on Sunday's news that 15 European central banks had agreed to cap gold sales. The metal was fixed in London at $281.70 a troy ounce, its highest since early May, against Friday afternoon's $270. 

 Analysts said the rise had a strong emotional impact on the spot rand market, although gold accounts for less than one-fifth of South Africa's export earnings. 

 Comments by Reserve Bank Governor Tito Mboweni on the need for caution on further monetary easing after last week's prime rate cut also supported the currency, analysts added. ((Gill Tudor, London Capital Markets +44 171 542 6414, fax 583 7239, gill.tudor@reuters.com)).

title: Chatu Mongol: Phatra Thankit Action To Be Ctrl Bk's Last
text:
WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--The Thai central bank's recent intervention into the management of ailing financial concern Phatra Thanakit PCL (H.PTK) will be its last such intervention into the country's bad debt-ridden banking sector, Bank of Thailand Governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul predicted Sunday. 

 Speaking at a conference sponsored by the Institute of International Finance, Chatu Mongol said the ratio of non-performing loans at Thai banks will "come down dramatically in the next two to three months." 

 He said negotiations between creditors and debtors set to conclude in coming months will lead to a vast improvement in banks' balance sheets. 

 The improvement means "we expect Phatra Thanakit this week to be our last intervention," Chatu said. 

 The bank of Thailand announced last week a planned 4.4 billion-baht ($1=THB41.215) capital injection into Phatra Thanakit, which is wholly owned by Thai Farmers Bank PCL (H.TFB). 

 Thai Farmers Bank's planned THB24 billion rights issue has been delayed as a result of the central bank's move. 

 Under the central bank's plan, THB7 billion in performing loans will be transferred to Thai Farmers Bank, while the remaining THB40 billion in nonperforming loans will be managed by an asset management firm owned by the Thai Farmers Bank. 

 Separately, Chatu said restrictions on offshore trading in countries' currencies have proved effective in Southeast Asia. 

 While he stressed that a free floating currency regime is the best policy for the Thai baht, Chatu said such "soft capital controls" on offshore trading are "a prerequisite" to stability in Asian markets. 

 He also said that Thailand has a "contingency plan" in place for dealing with the effects of a possible devaluation in the Chinese yuan, but he declined to disclose details. 

 "The real test" of Asian currency stability "does not depend on dollars and yen. No, the real test will come if China devalues," he said. 

 "We have a contingency plan if China devalues, but I don't have enough time to talk about it, or I guess it's not such a good idea" to discuss it, he said. 

 The IIF conference took place on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.

 BANGKOK, Sept 23 (Reuters) - The baht lost almost 70 satangs against the dollar on Thursday due to huge demand for the U.S currency by Thai corporates for debt settlements. 

 The baht hit at a day-low of 41.30 to the dollar at 1118 GMT in the London market, its lowest level since hitting 41.80 on August 31 last year. 

 "The baht was surrounded by piles of sell orders," said a trader at a major European bank in Bangkok. 

 Traders said the unit could test support around 41.50 to 41.65 tonight in U.S and European trading time. 

 "I don't want to imagine where it will be after it breaks through that level. But many are looking at some where around 42.00," the dealer said. 

 Traders said they saw a few profit-taking moves in afternoon trade. 

 "But that's not strong enough to push up the Thai currency. Many players are beting on a much weaker baht," said another dealer at a local bank. 

 He forecast that the baht would hit 41.80 overnight, a level it last hit on August 31, last year. 

 The Bank of Thailand said earlier on Thursday the baht's recent weakness against the dollar was due to limited dollar supply in the money market. 

 Tasana Rachatapo, director of the central bank's banking department, told reporters exporters had been holding on to dollars due to low premiums in the forward swap market. 

 The strengthened yen had also encouraged Thai concerns that had borrowed in yen to rush to settle Japanese debts. 

 Investors also unwound the baht because of low Thai interest rates, she said. 

 Traders said they had not detected any market-intervention movement of the central bank. 

 Bank of Thailand deputy governor Kitti Patpongpibul told reporters earlier on Thursday the authorities were keeping a close watch on the baht but found no evidence of any speculative attack on the unit.

title: Thai baht breaks below 40.80 support on dlr demand.
text:
BANGKOK, Sept 23 (Reuters) - The baht broke through significant support at 40.80 to the dollar in Thursday afternoon trade on high demand for the U.S. unit. 

 Traders expect the baht to test its next support of 41.00 later in the day. 

 The baht hit 40.90, its lowest level since September 9 last year, when it traded at 41.00 to the dollar. 

 "The baht is being oversold against the dollar by local corporates with foreign-currency debts," said a dealer at a major local bank. "The unit will remain on the downside throughout afternoon trade." 

 The Bank of Thailand said on Thursday the baht's recent weakness against the dollar was due to limited dollar supply in the money market. 

 Tasana Rachatapo, director of the central bank's banking department, told reporters exporters had been holding on to dollars due to low premiums in the forward swap market. 

 The strengthened yen had also encouraged Thai concerns that had borrowed in yen to rush to settle Japanese debts. 

 Investors also unwound the baht because of low Thai interest rates, she said. 

 Tasana said investors had previously borrowed in yen and deposited the loans at Thai banks, which used to offer far higher rates than in Japan. 

 "The (interest rate) gap has recently been considerably narrower," she said. 

 Fixed deposit rates at Thai banks have fallen to about 4.00 to 4.75 percent from a peak of more than 10 percent in the middle of last year. 

 Traders said they did not see any market-intervention movement of the central bank. 

 Bank of Thailand deputy governor Kitti Patpongpibul told reporters earlier on Thursday the authority was keeping a close watch on the baht but found no evidence of any speculative attack on the unit. He said the bank did not plan to act at the moment.

 BANGKOK, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Thai baht dropped further against the dollar early on Thursday as Thai corporates and players continued to buy the U.S. currency onshore and overseas, traders said. 

 The unit hit 40.55 to the dollar in early Asian trade. Some traders said they saw the baht go as 40.60 to the greenback in the U.S. market on Wednesday night, a level it last hit on September 21 last year. 

 "There had been series of attacks on the baht that drove the currency down to 39.50 from 37.50 a few weeks ago. The recent decline to 40.50 could be another round," said a dealer at a major European bank. 

 But Satian Tantanasarit, senior vice president for Treasury at DBS Thai Danu Bank, said he believed the baht had not been speculatively attacked. 

 "I firmly believe this," he told Reuters. 

 The baht was testing first support at 40.55 to 40.60 in morning trade and the second support is seen at 40.80. Resistance is expected at 40.40. 

 "Demand for the dollar increased dramatically on the need to settle debts by Thai corporates, including a small Thai commercial bank," said the first dealer. 

 At 0314 GMT, the relative strength index (RSI) of the dollar/baht exchange rate stood at 90.508, suggesting a highly overbought dollar condition as any level beyond 70 suggests overbuying and below 30 overselling. 

 The baht was quoted at 40.57 to 40.61 to the dollar onshore. 

 There was no market intervention by the Bank of Thailand at any stage, traders said. 

 "I really think it's the time for the government to come into the market. The baht shouldn't go down any further," said a trader at a major Thai bank. 

 Arparporn Sawaengpak, deputy vice president of Nava Vickers Ballas Securities in Bangkok, expressed the view that the baht value at about 40 to 42 to the dollar was still "acceptable". 

 "The weakened baht will help exports, which are the key to an economic recovery," Arparporn said, though she admitted Thai corporates would suffer foreign exchange losses. 

 "But the current situation suggests the economic recovery might not be as bullish as we initially projected," she said. 

 Gross domestic product (GDP) growth in the second quarter of this year was also lower-than-expected at 3.5 percent year-on-year, said the National Economic and Social development Board. 

 Media reports had quoted Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda as saying the GDP could have expanded as much as eight percent year on year in the second quarter. 

 The government projects a GDP growth of four percent for this year. 

 Nava Vickers Ballas estimates a GDP growth of 2.8 percent, according to Arparporn.

title: Fin Min To Explain Thai Recovery At World Bank/IMF Meet
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Thai Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda said he will explain at the annual International Monetary Fund and World Bank meeting how the Thai government recovered to economic growth forecast at 3% to 4% this year, from a contraction of 10% last year. 

 Prior to his departure later Wednesday, Tarrin also told reporters that the meeting in Washington will focus on how to help countries which can't help themselves. 

 The minister refused to comment on the baht, which hit another 12-month low of THB40.44 to the dollar before recovering slightly at the Asian close, other than to say it was the result of market forces. No abnormal speculative activity has been spotted by the authorities, he said. 

Thailand's central bank has a policy of intervening only to damp volatility or to interrupt speculative activity, not to counter market trends. 

 Dealers and analysts have said there is high demand for dollars and yen from local corporations with foreign debts, and importers with upcoming obligations. Servicing foreign debt gets more expensive as the baht weakens, especially debt denominated in yen, as the Japanese currency has been strengthening. 

 In wide-ranging but brief comments, Tarrin said low growth in outstanding commercial bank credit was slightly misleading because corporations are turning more to the domestic bond market. He said the central bank needs data from the Securities & Exchange Commission so that combined figures can be compared. 

 The Bank of Thailand said Tuesday it will lower its 1999 commercial bank lending growth target of 4% to 7%, as it is apparent it won't be met. The central bank didn't say what the new target would be. 

 Tarrin said the baht value of outstanding credit also fluctuates with the exchange rate, because the total includes foreign currency-denominated loans from domestic branches with Bangkok International Banking Facilities, or BIBF, licences. When the baht strengthens, total lending appears to drop. For accurate comparison of lending at different periods, the total figure should be adjusted, he said.

title: Thai Baht/THB40 -3: Last Local Trade At THB40.05/Dlr
text:
At 0955 GMT, DBS Thai Danu Bank executed its last trade of the day at THB40.05 to the dollar. 

 Satian Tantanasarit, a senior vice president in the bank's treasury department, said he expects the Bank of Thailand to intervene early in Asian trade Friday if the dollar climbs to a range of THB40.25 to THB40.50. 

 "They should if they want to stem the baht's fall," he said. 

 The central bank has a policy of intervening only to damp volatility, not to fight market trends. The government said it has neither a strong-baht nor weak-baht policy, as it must balance the interests of debtors who benefit from the former against the those of exporters who prefer the latter. 

 Satian added that he expects profit-taking soon, however, on long-dollar positions set up about eight-to-nine weeks ago. The dollar has been climbing since June, when it hit this year's low of THB36.51. 

 When the profit-taking comes, whether Friday or next week, Satian said he doesn't expect investors to start building up new long-dollar positions until the U.S. currency corrects to around THB39.50. 

 The baht, the Philippine peso, and to a lesser extent, the Singapore dollar, have recently followed the Indonesian rupiah lower on contagion from violence in East Timor. 

 Dealers noted that despite stability in the rupiah Thursday, sentiment was very negative, with the president and the central bank implicated in a banking scandal, and a high probability of complications upon entry as early as this weekend of a U.N. peacekeeping force into Timor. 

 Meanwhile, foreign investors in the Thai stock market have been net sellers more often than net buyers recently, as investors appear to be locking in gains. The dealer said these investors might be reluctant to reenter the market for the remainder of the year due to the Y2K risk, he said. 

 The outlook for the Thai stock market is still positive, despite a drop of 2% Thursday in the composite SET index to 429.89 points, due to increasing signs of renewed growth in the Thai economy after two years of recession. 

 Analysts also believe that Thailand's strong trade surplus and direct investment inflows will be sufficient to balance outflows to pay down foreign debts. 

 The commerce ministry said Thursday that August exports were up 14.7% on year, while exports in the first eight months rose 3.4% on year. Official August data is due for release by the central bank at the end of September.

title: ASIA MARKETS - Ease on yen wobbles, U.S. rate fears.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 16 (Reuters) - Jitters over possible 

 Japanese intervention pressured the yen and other regional 

currencies on Thursday, as Asian stock markets bowed to fears 

 of another U.S. interest hike. 

     News that Japanese Finance Minister Kiichi Miyazawa was 

 meeting Bank of Japan governor Masaru Hayami to discuss 

 monetary policy stoked fears intervention could be imminent, 

 propping the dollar up briefly against the yen. 

     Chin Loo Thio, currency strategist at Paribas, said in a 

 daily report the dollar was technically unlikely to find a 

 bottom until September 29, the end of the first half of Japan's 

 fiscal year. 

     "Once September is over, the need for yen purchases may 

 decline as both Japanese exporters and investors complete their 

 hedges," she said. 

     RUPIAH SLIPS BACK BEYOND 8,000 

     The rupiah eased to the wrong side of the 8,000 per dollar 

 level as players maintained their wait-and-see approach to the 

 smouldering Bank Bali scandal and plans to move a U.N. peace 

 keeping force to East Timor. 

     Some dealers in Jakarta said fears the U.N.'s presence 

 could heighten animosity in the bloodied territory were 

 overwhelming relief over the impending arrival of foreign 

 troops. 

     Sentiment was also weak due to comments by the central bank

 that an audit into the Bank Bali scandal had been unfair and 

 that loan delays by the World Bank and the IMF could harm the 

 economy. 

     And central bank governor Syahril Sabirin warned that Bank 

 Indonesia could take legal action against 

 PricewaterhouseCoopers, which conducted the audit. 

     "The currency is underpinned by quite tight monetary policy 

 in Indonesia but politically, the threat is still great," said 

 Kate O'Donoghue, regional economist at Barclays Capital Asia. 

     "Volatility will be on the cards for quite some time," she 

 told Reuters Television. 

     PESO RISK RETURN SEEN WORTHY DESPITE DEFICIT 

     The peso was placed under added pressures by prospects of a 

 widening budget deficit one day after the IMF agreed to a 10 

 billion peso increase to this year's fiscal shortfall. 

 Socio-economic planning secretary Felipe Medalla said next 

 year's deficit was also likely to overshoot the 40 billion peso 

 target by about 10 billion pesos. 

 But analysts remained upbeat on the Philippines. 

 "The Philippines' chronic fiscal deficit has made them 

 develop a healthy T-bill market so we are still quite bullish 

 on the peso. The economy is suffering more from cyclical 

 problems than from structural ones," Barclays Capital's 

 O'Donoghue said. 

     "We see the peso offering value and we would certainly be 

 looking to buy it at these levels," she said. 

THAILAND RULES OUT INTERVENTION ON BAHT 

     The baht hovered near its year lows, pressured as the yen 

 came off its high, but the government said it had no plans to 

 step in. 

     Thai Deputy Finance Minister Pisit Leeahtam said current 

 baht levels were okay and the government had no plans to 

intervene. 

     "The baht should be dictated by market forces. The current 

 level of the currency is okay. There is no irregular movement 

 so far," he told reporters in Bangkok. 

     KOSPI SLIDES AMID LIQUIDITY FEARS 

     Korean stocks slid more than three percent partly due to an 

 uptick in domestic interest rates triggered by liquidity fears. 

     The benchmark three-year Treasury bond yield crossed the 

 9.5 percent mark amid fears Daewoo's financial troubles could 

 spark a run on investment companies in November, when more 

 redemptions of beneficiary certificates are to be allowed. 

     Investment trusts hold 75 percent of the 30.75 trillion won 

 ($25.8 billion) in Daewoo's bonds and commercial papers. 

     Some analysts said the direction of the KOSPI -- which has 

 yielded dollar-based year-to-date returns of over 88 percent -- 

 depends on future government handling of Daewoo's problems.

title: INTERVIEW/ Thailand 's Supachai-2:Ctrl Bk Hasn't  Intervened
text:
AUCKLAND (Dow Jones)--Thailand's deputy prime minister and commerce minister, Supachai Panitchapdi, said he isn't worried by a recent fall in the baht, and believes it will eventually settle at an export-friendly level. 

 In an interview, Supachai also said year-on-year growth in the second quarter would be around 8% or 9%, well above the original target of 1% or 2%. Export growth in 1999 is now seen at 3.5%, from around 1% previously, he said. 

 Last week, the baht fell to an 11-month low as the dollar reached THB39.730. The dollar finished Asian trading Friday at THB39.465, down marginally from THB39.485 at the close Thursday. The weakness was linked to a slide in regional currencies in reaction to turmoil in Indonesia. 

 Supachai told Dow Jones Newswires that the Bank of Thailand hasn't intervened at all in recent days and said the government will let the baht "find a new level, hopefully a level that will be helpful to export promotion from Thailand. 

 "The only thing we have to cope with is a short-term fluctuation of fund flows because of the security concern in this part of the world," he said, referring to international concern over the violence in the Indonesian province of East Timor. 

 "This won't be with us forever. It will go away one of these days and we're back to normal business," he said. 

 Supachai noted that when the baht rose in June and July to around THB35 per dollar, there was fear that the currency's strength was excessive. Now that it has fallen toward THB40, it shows that the baht is centering around a range of THB36 to THB38 per dollar. 

 "If you look at the fundamentals you shouldn't be overly worried that there is a declining trend for the baht, or an upward trend," he said. 


He said the level of reserves near US$32 billion, monthly trade
surpluses of US$500 million to US$900 million, and expected substantial
capital inflows into shares and to purchase two banks marked for sale,
were fundamentals supporting the outlook for the baht.
-
Says Need To Address Bad Loans
-



Analysts have also highlighted slow progress in restructuring
nonperforming loans within the banking system as a factor behind the
weak baht.



Supachai said the average level of nonperforming loans is around 46%
to 47% of the total lending portfolio, but there are banks with higher
levels just as there are those with lower levels.



"We have to tackle those banks (with high levels)," he said.



He said some loans can be restructured, and the central bank is
working with commercial banks to agree on the definition of some loans,
and this will lower the level of nonperforming loans. "They have to
agree how to reschedule some of these loans," he said.



However the final solution will be sales of some banks, and successful
merger of other banks.



Supachai said Thailand's letter of intent to the International
Monetary Fund has been delayed by the need for reassessment of economic
data "which is much more positive" and which changes the "background
against which we make our decisions."



He said second quarter gross domestic product should grow 8% or 9%
from original targets of 1% or 2%.



The Thai government said Friday that the letter of intent for the
coming ninth quarter of the IMF's US$17.2 billion rescue program will be
considered by the cabinet Sept. 21, and not Tuesday as previously
indicated.



Meanwhile, Supachai said he has no concern with the emerging trend of
free-trade arrangements between economies within APEC "if they serve the
purpose of reducing tariffs and don't discriminate against third
countries.



"It might seem to be distracting from the original objective of APEC,
but if the countries are pushing for more trade liberalization, and are
not jeopardizing trade with third countries they should be supported and
allowed," he said.



He said "more are being arranged, and will be arranged," noting that
Thailand is considering arrangements with South Korea and China.



Supachai said the arrangements are consistent with his original
proposal to have closer links between the Association of Southeast Asian
Nations and the Closer Economic Relationship arrangement between
Australia and New Zealand.

title: Thai Fin Min-2:No Weak Baht Policy, No Strong Baht Policy
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Thai Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanhaeminda denied Wednesday a report that he had spoken late the previous day in support of a weak baht policy. 

 "The reporter reported it wrong," Tarrin said in response to a question about the report after a speech to the Federation of Thai Industries Wednesday. 

 "Any report that I have changed policy on the baht is inaccurate," he said. 

 Tarrin and the Bank of Thailand have often reiterated that authorities intervene in foreign exchange markets only to damp volatility, not to fight market trends. 

 "If there is any unusual fluctuation of the baht, the Bank of Thailand will monitor it closely," he said. 

 He refused to say whether Wednesday's moves were unusual or not, or whether authorities were intervening. 

 A report by an international news agency on Tarrin's comments late Tuesday cited the Finance Minister as saying the government was trying to keep the baht weaker in order to increase export competitiveness. 

 The report was cited as one factor in a sharp drop in the baht to a low of THB39.43 to the dollar Wednesday, from an Asian close of THB38.875 Tuesday, although dealers said the main factor was fear of contagion from the Timor crisis. 

 Following his denial, the dollar quickly dropped from the high to less than THB39.30. 

 Tarrin said the central bank was closely monitoring trade, and that the baht was moving in line with market forces. 

 He wouldn't specify what the government might see as an appropriate range for the baht. 

 Tarrin repeated to reporters on the sidelines of the seminar Wednesday that he never said he supported a weak baht policy. 

 "We don't have a specific policy to a particularly strong baht. Neither do we have a policy to support a particularly weak baht," he said.

title: CORRECTED-Thailand does not favour strong baht-finmin Tarrin.
text:
In Sept 7 BANGKOK story headlined "Thailand does not favour strong baht-finmin Tarrin"...please read in second paragraph... "On a permanent basis to keep the baht unrealistically weak is not a correct policy because we would sell cheap and buy expensive in baht terms"...instead of "We will try to primarily keep the baht weaker in order to help exporters and as it could be a factor contributing to the (Thai) economic recovery"...(correcting quote). 

 A corrected repetition follows: 

 BANGKOK, Sept 7 (Reuters) - Thai authorities are not in favour of a strong baht because a firmer currency could have a negative impact, Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda said on Tuesday. 

 "On a permanent basis to keep the baht unrealistically weak is not a correct policy because we would sell cheap and buy expensive in baht terms," he told a social club gathering. 

 At the same time, he added: "The government has no policy to make the baht unrealistically strong." 

 Earlier on Tuesday the baht tumbled past the 39 baht per dollar level to its lowest since October 5 1998. 

 The baht was quoted sharply lower late on Tuesday at 39.15-39.20 after opening the day near 38.75-38.80 per dollar. 

 Dealers said the baht slid along with other regional currencies as investors chilled by mayhem in East Timor switched to dollars from regional Asian currencies, including the Indonesian rupiah. 

 There were no signs of intervention by the Bank of Thailand to stem the baht's fall, dealers said. 

 Tarrin also that massive non-performing loans (NPLs) carried by Thai financial institutions and recapitalisation of banks were the major economic problems faced by Thailand which sank into recession in mid-1997 but has lately shown few signs of recovery. 

 Latest data available show that Thai banks carry about 2.7 trillion baht or 47 percent of total lending. 

 The central bank classifies loans on which interest repayments have not been made for three months as NPLs. 

 "Now that everything has been stabilised I see the NPLs problems and the question of helping commercial banks raise sufficient capital as remaining major problems that require sustained solutions," he said. 

 "The NPL problem in the business sectors and insufficient capital of banks are two sides of the same coin," he added. 

 The Thai authorities had since last August to now helped banks raise their capital by about 600 billion baht, he said. 

 By doing this, the authorities had almost doubled the capital of local banks which in their whole history had built up only 700 billion baht in capital, he added. 

 Tarrin said that if NPLs could be reduced to around 25 percent of total bank lending from 47 percent now, they would reach appropriate levels conducive to sustainable Thai economic recovery. 

 "NPLs should be looked at in baht terms not in percentage terms. NPLs have stabilised in baht terms. In June they declined by 70 billion baht and we are waiting for the July figure," he said. 

 The minister said there had been progress in NPLs restructuring and to date a total of 690 billion baht in NPLs had been restructured by banks. 

 He expected that by the year-end this could reach one trillion baht. 

 On NPLs classification, he said: "The Bank of Thailand standards do not themselves cause NPLs although they may add burdens (causing provisioning burdens for commercial banks)." 

 "It would be a dream to believe that easing these standards would help solve the problem," he added.

 BANGKOK, Sept 8 (Reuters) - The baht plunged to its lowest level since October 2 last year as investors sold it along with other regional currencies on concern over political unrest in East Timor. 

 Last October 2, the baht was traded at 39.40 to the dollar. 

 Dealers said the baht, the Philippine peso and Singapore dollar, were dumped along with the Indonesian rupiah as investors wanted to minimise risk in holding South East Asian currencies. 

 "Offshore players squared positions to cut losses from the rupiah. They also sold other regional currencies with higher liquidity," said a dealer at a local bank.

title: Thai Dep Fin Min: Baht Volatile On Strong Yen, Politics
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Thai Deputy Finance Minister Pisit Leeahtam said Friday the baht's recent volatility is due to a combination of external and internal factors, notably the strength of the yen and domestic political uncertainty. 

 The dollar has stabilized in a range of THB38.70 to THB38.75 Friday, after surging from less than THB38.40 Wednesday and briefly touching an 11-month high of THB38.93 on Thursday. 

 Pisit told reporters that the Bank of Thailand didn't intervene in foreign currency markets this week because the volatility wasn't too great. 

Central Bank Governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul said earlier there was no intervention because the movement wasn't caused by speculative activity. 

 Pisit said the strength of the yen, currently below Y110 against the U.S. dollar, from above Y120 a few weeks ago, is causing global money markets to be highly sensitive. 

 Officials said earlier that the run of the dollar from below THB38.40 this week was triggered by repatriation of funds by Japanese and other foreign companies in Thailand, and dollar short-covering by some U.S. funds. 

 Pisit said political uncertainties also contributed to baht volatility this week. 

 It has been speculated that there will be a new general election within the next 12 months, before the current government under the premiership of Chuan Leekpai completes its four-year term in November 2000. 

 Most analysts believe it is unlikely that Chuan will call an election until the second quarter next year, and that coalition partners of his Democrat party will stick with the government to take part of the credit for an improving economy.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk/Baht -3: Slow Debt Workouts A Concern
text:
Chatu Mongol said investors felt insecure about domestic politics, so they didn't want to hold the baht. 

 The political opposition has been calling for Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai to dissolve the parliament and call a fresh election before his term ends in November next year. 

 Investors are also concerned about the slow restructuring of problem loans, which currently total about half of all outstanding loans in Thailand's financial system, he said. 

 Bank of Thailand has been helping the financial sector reach agreements on multi-creditor debt restructuring involving large bad loans. 

 "I don't believe that external factors have great impact on the Thai currency," Chatu Mongol said. 

 The central bank prefers the baht to move in a narrow range according to market forces, rather than to stand still, he added. The bank has said it will only intervene in the market to stem speculative attacks. 

 Bank of Thailand's governor noted Thai companies were showing more confidence in the stability of the local currency by hedging fewer of their foreign currency obligations than during the period after the de facto devaluation of the baht July 2, 1997.

title: Thailand/Reserves-3:Reserves Up Despite Rumored Dlr Sales
text:
A Bank of Thailand official said its foreign reserves rose $300 million in U.S. dollar terms during the week ended Aug. 20 due to the appreciation of other major currencies held by the central bank. 

 The Japanese yen appreciated over the period to about Y112 to the dollar from around Y115. 

 The increase came as rumors circulated that the central bank sold dollars this week to cap the U.S. currency at THB38.50, after it rose from THB36.50 two months earlier. 

 The Bank of Thailand has a policy of intervening in foreign exchange markets only to prevent volatility, not to fight market trends. 

 It also has a policy of accumulating foreign reserves. 

 The central bank said the sharp decrease in net claims on financial institutions in the week ended Aug. 20 was due to the injection of capital by the government into the state-run Krung Thai Bank PCL under its financial sector restructuring program. 

 Loans from the central bank's Financial Institutions Development Fund worth THB108 billion were converted into new shares in the bank. 

 The central bank also said the injection of capital had no impact on the monetary base because the debt was transformed into equity. 

 The decrease in the monetary base was due to a decline in deposits of financial institutions at the central bank, and a normal decrease in cash held by the public in the middle of the month.

title: Thai Dep Fin Min: Stable Baht, Reforms Helping Recovery
text:
WELLINGTON (Dow Jones)--Thailand's Deputy Finance Minister Pisit Leeahtam said the Thai government is happy with the current level of the baht, and with the central bank is working to keep a stable currency in order to sustain a pattern of emerging growth. 

 Pisit was commenting at the fringes of an Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum deputy finance officials meeting in Wellington Friday. 

 He told Dow Jones Newswires that the baht has now been stable for around 16 months, and that the government is comfortable with the THB36 to THB38 levels it has been trading in. 

 The combination of a strong yen and factors that tend to have the opposite effect - such as the prospect of a weakening in the yuan and tensions between China and Taiwan - have caused volatility recently in many Asian currencies. 

 Pisit said Thailand is willing to intervene to keep the baht from reacting violently to other influential currency moves. 

 "The central bank has a role to play in definitely trying to quell the rapid movements of the currency but they must not put rigidity into the exchange system," Pisit said. 

 "They must not try to defend the currency at a certain price (so) must allow the currency to move along with fundamentals," he said. 

 Bank of Thailand has stated that it bought dollars to damp volatility and build foreign reserves as the baht tended to strengthen in the second quarter. Since then, it reportedly sold dollars to cap the its rise at THB38.50. 

 Pisit said countries like Thailand shouldn't be complacent regarding further economic shocks. The government is working to build strong foundations through corporate governance, transparency in financial systems and organizations, and risk management, he said. 

 "All these have to be new disciplines for the private sector. In the past decade they have been a bit too complacent and lax in terms of financial discipline. They borrowed too much, they had too much foreign exchange exposure," Pisit said. 

 "For them to survive and grow in the next decade, they have to build a strong foundation and discipline, and also creating a lot more corporate etiquette," he added. 

 He said once this new structure has been created, the growth momentum now being experienced should be sustainable.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Chief -3: Exporters Will Cap Dollar's Rise
text:
The dollar's recent rise against the baht isn't a worry because local exporters are coming into the market to sell the U.S. currency at the higher levels, Chatu Mongol said. 

 He reiterated the Bank of Thailand's policy to let market forces dictate the baht's level, with the central bank only acting in the foreign exchange market to stem the activity of speculative traders. 

 "We manage the deliberate speculation," he said. "We haven't intervened (in the baht's trend) at all." 

 On Thailand's banking sector, Chatu Mongol said private banks still need about THB140 billion to THB200 billion in fresh capital to be able to absorb losses from their huge problem loans. 

 That figure is based on the assumption that problem loans, which total about half of all outstanding lending in the system, don't get any worse. Ratings agencies, which use conservative debt figures, estimate banks need over THB400 billion in fresh capital. 

 Chatu Mongol said those banks that raise capital sooner rather than later - such as Thai Farmers Bank PCL (H.TFB) which raised THB24 billion in a rights issue this month - will benefit by being in a position earlier to extend new loans and gain a greater market share. 

 "They'll be ready earlier to make a run for it when the economy gets better," he said.

title: Thailand  reiterates won't  intervene  to curb baht.
text:
BANGKOK, June 29 (Reuters) - Thai deputy finance minister, Pisit Leeatham, reiterated on Tuesday the government would not intervene to slow the baht's recent gains and would leave the currency to find its own market level. 

 He told reporters: "The authorities would be unlikely to intervene. I think it (the baht) is now suitable and should be left to find its own level." 

 The minister said Thai exports had increased at a satisfactory pace in recent months despite concerns at the commerce ministry that the sector had not been helped by a stronger baht. 

 Thai May exports rose an estimated 8.4 percent year-on-year in dollar terms, the second monthly growth posted after a contraction of 6.8 percent for the whole of 1998. 

 The baht firmed to a five-month high of about 36.55 to the dollar last week and has since stayed in the 36.65-36.85 range compared with 37.00-38.00 in the past four months. 

 Pisit's comments echoed those of central bank governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul who said on Monday that the baht was not too strong. 

 The minister said a one to two baht appreciation of the Thai currency would not make any big impact on export performance. 

 "We have seen the baht falling to 36-37 from 25-26 (to the dollar). Isn't that enough (for helping exports)?", he said, referring to the baht's pre-devaluation level before July 1997.

text:

 trading calmly ahead of the result of the FOMC meeting, a 

 get-together which has transfixed the markets for days. 

     The vast majority of analysts see a 25 basis point 

 tightening in the Fed funds target rate of 4.75 percent but 

 there has been growing speculation that more rises might be in 

 the pipeline. 

 A modest 25 basis point is unlikely to have much impact as 

 it is already factored in, but if the Fed hints at more 

 tightening to come then a U.S. asset market and dollar reaction 

 is likely. 

     Assuming 25 basis points analysts say what the Fed say

title: ASIA MARKETS - Relaxed about likely Fed move.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 29 (Reuters) - Asian markets held their 

 ground on Tuesday as the yen meandered in familiar ranges and 

 investors took a more relaxed view of a widely expected U.S. 

 rate hike. 

     Analysts said a U.S. tightening was unlikely to spark fears 

 of similar moves in Asia, where most central banks are still 

 trying to jump-start bank lending in the wake of the crisis. 

     "The central banks' key policy focus at the moment is to 

 maintain monetary policy which provides for growth rather than 

 stable exchange rate targets," said John Woods, head of 

 research at HSBC Markets in Hong Kong. 

     "Whatever the Fed does, at this juncture, that particular 

 policy isn't going to be upset," Woods told Reuters Television. 

     KOREAN OUTPUT SURGES, MARKETS UNIMPRESSED 

     South Korea had yet more proof that its economy is out of 

 the woods. 

     Industrial output jumped 21.8 percent in May, its biggest 

 year-on-year rise in more than a decade. 

     But the base effect was quite sharp, given last May's 

 eleven percent contraction in output. 

     The current account surplus also continued to shrink in 

 May, with close to a 50 percent year-on-year fall, reflecting a 

 growing hunger for imports as domestic demand recovers. 

     But the strong numbers had little impact on Korean markets, 

 as investors opted to take profit on the KOSPI's surge Monday. 

     The won also failed to make headway in a market wary of 

 further intervention but heavy with dollars from exporter 

 deals. 

     Dealers said the central bank bought dollars sporadically, 

 signalling its unease with a strengthening currency after 

 Monday's purchases of an estimated $100-$150 million. 

     TAIWAN SHARES SHINE, BUT CHART OUTLOOK UNCERTAIN 

     Taiwan shares had a stellar session, thanks to Wall 

 Street's overnight gains and a near-two percent rise in the 

 tech-heavy U.S. Nasdaq. 

     Taiwan's weighted index has broken above important 

 technical resistance at 8,410 which marks a 61.8 percent 

 retracement of the pre-crisis high to the low earlier this 

 year. 

     But on the short-term charts, the picture is less clear, 

 with a couple of gaps opening up in the past few sessions. 

     If the market drops sharply for any reason, it could still 

 pull back to fill an exhaustion gap around the 8,060 level, 

 which opened on June 17. 

     And if that downmove opens up a downside breakaway gap, it 

 will have very bearish implications for the near-term trend. 

     But for the time being, foreign flows to the stock market 

 were keeping the Taiwan dollar on firm footing, though dealers 

 were wary of pushing it too far. 

Central bank governor Perng Fai-nan said on Monday the bank 

 only defends the Taiwan dollar when "irregular or seasonal 

 factors" emerge, and its interventions do not defy economic 

 fundamentals. 

 BAHT STEADY DESPITE C.BANK ASSURANCES 

 The Thai baht was dragging its feet despite the central 

 bank's insistance that it would not intervene to influence the 

 exchange rate. 

 Bank of Thailand governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul said the 

 baht's current rate at around 36.60-36.80 per dollar was backed 

 by sound fundamentals. 

 His view was echoed by the finance ministry. But the 

 market's likely to be less than convinced after Deputy Prime 

 Minister Supachai Panitchpakdi said last week the baht's 

 strength could hurt exports if its rallies were not checked. 

 Thai stocks bucked the generally firmer trend, with bank 

 shares leading the decline after news that a proposed takeover 

 of ailing Nakornthon Bank Plc by Britain's Standard Chartered 

 Bank had been called off. 

     The BOT said it instead planned to put Nakorthon up for 

 auction.

title: FX  Asia: Thai Econ Recovery May Reverse Strong Baht
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--While the Thai baht's rally looks likely to go unchecked for a few more months, a climb to THB35 to the dollar could force the central bank into a head-to-head battle with the market, amid concern about the impact of the currency on the country's exports. 

 The baht will continue climbing as funds roll in ahead of an economic recovery expected to gather steam later this year, but most analysts see the dollar regaining ground to between THB36 and THB38 by year-end. 

 Authorities have said they find the current range of THB36.50 to THB37 to the dollar acceptable. But Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai and his Deputy Premier Supachai Panitchpakdi expressed concern last week that if the baht gets any stronger, it will choke off a recovery in export growth that just began in April, after 13 consecutive months of year-on-year contraction. 

 "A stronger baht isn't necessarily good for the recovery," said Satian Tantanasarit, senior vice president of DBS Thai Danu Bank PCL. 

 The Bank of Thailand is counting on export growth of 2.1% this year, to help meet a 1999 gross domestic product growth forecast of 1%, after two years of recession. 

 Rising capital inflows are paying no heed to the government's targets, however, and will eventually have their way. 

 "It's just a matter of time before we see a stronger baht," said Satian. 

 That was evident last Tuesday, when confirmation by an official that the Bank of Thailand continues to forswear intervention against market trends prompted forex players to sell down the dollar by THB0.30 from the previous day's close to finish at THB36.58. 

 A rising baht won't go unchecked: the central bank acts to damp volatility and accumulate foreign reserves by placing anonymous orders through agents in various markets. 

 But since its failed defense of the baht prior to the July 2, 1997, float of the currency, the central bank has never drawn any lines in the sand and dared investors to step over them. 

 Supachai doesn't have direct authority in the matter, but he, for one, wants to draw that line now. 


   THB35 May Force Central Bank To Drastic Action



"If we let the baht rise to THB35, it will be unbearable. It will hurt
the economy," said Supachai, who is also commerce minister and head of
the government's export promotion committee.



Rob Collins, executive vice president of Paribas Asia Equity, agrees
that THB35 is a critical level.



"I think if it was to strengthen to THB35, the central bank would be
forced to take serious action," he said.



Satian thinks so, too. He predicts the central bank will first step in
at THB36.50, and then force investors who are pushing the baht higher to
climb over the bank at every step.



"I think they will come into the market every five or 10 satang," he
said, adding it will take more than just a few weeks to reach THB35 (1
satang=THB0.01).



Supachai is counting on that delay, in the hope that factors will
change and ease market pressure on the baht.



"I hope that its strength will be just for a short period of time," he
said.



According to some analysts, he has reason to be optimistic.



As the economy picks up, Thailand's trade surplus should narrow. A
recovery in domestic demand would lead to higher imports.



Meanwhile, Thai companies might step up repayment of foreign debt.



"If the economy picks up and banks begin to lend again, all
non-exporting companies will want to switch back into baht debt,"
Paribas' Collins said. A weakening currency "would almost be a sign of
recovery."



An analyst at a European house in Bangkok, however, discounts the
significance of debt repayments in capital outflows.



Domestic refinancing of foreign loans can't happen unless banks resume
new lending, but institutions are reluctant to risk new lending amid a
shortage of credit-worthy clients, he said.



Armed with new legal and regulatory frameworks and facing steep
increases in loan-loss reserve requirements every six months between now
and end-2000, major banks are expected to step up workouts of
non-performing loans, which account for 47% of outstanding credit.



But resulting outflows won't be as big as expected, the European house
analyst said. "In most restructurings, the money isn't repaid - it's
swapped for equity or assets, or principal repayments are delayed."



Private-sector foreign debt has already fallen to about $50 billion
from $67 billion last year, he added. "A lot of debts have already been
paid down."



   Foreign Investment Will Rise



Arguing for the stronger side of the baht consensus range, around
THB36 to THB36.50 against the dollar by year-end, the analyst said trade
and current account surpluses will narrow, but on the other hand,
private investment inflows will tend to pick up.



Aside from hot money flowing into Thai stocks, longer-term foreign
direct investment will also increase in a recovery, offsetting a
narrowing of the current account and then some, he said.



"We are not talking about investment in new capacity, but in existing
capacity. There is a lot of talking going on, but when prices start to
rise in a recovery, you will see a lot more deals" with new foreign
partners, he said.



At the bottom line, the European house analyst's view doesn't differ
so much from that of Paribas' Collins.



Last month, Paribas lowered its year-end baht forecast to THB37 from
THB40 to the dollar, in light of the recent influx of funds. Merrill
Lynch & Co. is holding out at THB38, also recently revised down from
THB40.



Robert McMillen, joint managing director at Seamico Securities PCL,
said the dollar could end the year anywhere between THB35 and THB40,
given Thailand's vulnerability to economic trends in the world's
developed countries, which are its major export markets and creditors.



But money is going to flow into Asia because it won't be profitable to
keep it elsewhere, he said.



Global fund managers believe there is a good chance that U.S. stocks
are headed for a major correction and the Euro is on the brink of a
nose-dive. In Asia, Thailand and South Korea would be among the main
beneficiaries, McMillen said.

title: Thai c. bank says no plan to  intervene  for baht.
text:
BANGKOK, June 28 (Reuters) - Thai central bank governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul reaffirmed on Monday a policy of the Bank of Thailand not to intervene in the market to influence the baht's exchange rate. 

 Chatu Mongol told reporters he believed the baht's current rate, at about 36.60-36.80 to the dollar, was backed by sound fundamentals. He did not elaborate. 

 "I believe the baht, at its current rate, is based on right fundamentals...and on the right track...I don't think it is too strong and definitely not hurting exports," the governor said. 

 The baht rallied to its five-month high of about 36.55 to the dollar last Tuesday and had since hovered in the 36.60-36.80 range compared with 37.00-38.00 in recent months. 

 The baht was quoted at 36.83/36.93 late on Monday. 

 Deputy Prime Minister Supachai Panitchpakdi said last week the baht's strength could hurt exports if its rallies were not checked. 

 The central bank governor said his bank maintained its normal monitoring of the baht and any of its entries into the market was for meeting its normal dollar/baht swap obligations. 

 "The baht's gains simply reflect confidence of investors," he said. 

 Chatu Mongol said the Thai authorities had no plan to do to the baht what the Japanese government had done to try to slow the yen's appreciation. The Bank of Japan has intervened in the foreign exchange markets several times this month to curb the yen's rise following strong first quarter GDP data.

 dollar-yen failed to move in decisive direction as it was

 the Bank of Japan. 

     *** Thailand earned an upgrade from rating agency Fitch

intervention by the central bank. The commerce ministry said in

 movement from hurting exports. 

 The won was also supported by comments from IMF's Hubert

 market were to smooth the movement of the won, not to weaken 

 it. 

     *** Hubert Neiss, visiting Hong Kong on Thursday, also said 

 there was still more room for the rupiah to strengthen. 

     He said a stronger rupiah would not cause problems for 

 Indonesia's recovery. 

     "On the contrary, the confidence that is created by the 

 strengthening rupiah, and in turn the strengthening rupiah's 

 influence on confidence, are good for the recovery," Neiss 

 said.

 economy was growing well but he would not revise the official 

 GDP forecast of one percent expansion for this year. 

 The central bank governor has said GDP growth could exceed

 percent, but the government will maintain its conservative

title: EMERGING MARKET  FX -Asia balancing act,Europe quiet.
text:
LONDON, June 23 (Reuters) - Emerging Asian currencies kept up their balancing act on Wednesday, caught between investor bullishness and central bank concern over exports. 

 Central European currencies were quiet, with the Polish zloty tipped to test resistance at five percent above its basket parity and the Czech crown becalmed ahead of Thursday's central bank board meeting. 

 Most Asian currencies were slightly softer from late New York levels, with central banks divided on how to cope with the regionals' recent surge. 

 The Bank of Korea intervened again to buy dollar/won, and analysts said there was talk the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened to curb Singapore dollar strength. 

 But the baht hit a five-month high on Tuesday after the Bank of Thailand said it would not intervene to restrain the currency's rise. 

 "Their currencies are strengthening to the extent that some are definitely starting to impinge on export growth, or even cause export contraction," said Callum Henderson, emerging market currency strategist at Citibank in London. 

 "They seem to be trying to intervene and as a result continuing to offer the market good opportunities to sell into any rallies." 

 But he noted that Taiwan's central bank stopped intervening to damp down the Taiwan dollar a couple of weeks ago, and was now acting only to smooth out market moves. 

 "You could argue that one by one the Asian central banks have seen the writing on the wall and are giving up," he said. 

 Analysts said emerging Asian currencies were still showing little correlation with movements in dollar/yen, which firmed back through 122 in the London morning. 

 "This is largely a reflection of the strength of Asian currencies, and the underlying demand for them," analysts at Banque Paribas said in a briefing note. 

 "As authorities' confidence in the economic recovery improves, gradual currency strength will be tolerated." 

 The won was slightly weaker on the day after the Bank of Korea waded back in to buy an estimated $350 million. 

 The baht also lost some ground after rating agency Moody's slammed Thai banks, saying the sector was still in deep crisis. The Philippine peso tracked the baht lower, dealers said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah tried to press on towards 6,500 to the dollar but got stuck around 6,700 as profit-taking trimmed earlier gains, despite upbeat comments by central bank Governor Syahril Sabirin that he would be happy with a stable range of 6,000-6,500. 

 In Europe, the zloty edged up to around 4.8 percent above its basket parity from Tuesday's 4.7 percent. 

 Analysts said the currency, which has gained two percentage points against the basket in June alone, would soon test five percent amid expectations that the $1 billion privatisation of Pekao bank would bring in large foreign inflows. 

 Data showing Poland's gross domestic product grew by 1.5 percent in the first quarter of the year had no immediate impact on the currency. Analysts said the figures were close to expectations and were already discounted.

title: Thai PM says exports may suffer from stronger baht.
text:
HAT YAI, Thailand, June 23 (Reuters) - Thai Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai said on Wednesday the baht's strength reflected a return of confidence in the economy, but exports could suffer if the currency firmed too much. 

 "The baht has been steady lately, but the recent firmer tone reflects a return of confidence in the economy which is improving," he told reporters on the sidelines of an international rubber conference here. 

 The baht rallied sharply on Tuesday and hit a five month high late in the day after the Bank of Thailand said it would not intervene in the market to restrain the currency. 

 Dealers have said that the Indonesian rupiah's rally close to the 6,500 per dollar level had also helped baht sentiment. 

 The baht was quoted at around 36.60/36.65 by 0305 GMT, firmer than the 36.80-36.90 level earlier this week. Earlier on Wednesday the baht climbed as high as 36.49/36.54. 

 Dealers said the market was keeping an eye on what the central bank might do next about the baht's surge. 

 Premier Chuan said: "However, the stronger baht will affect exports and the Bank of Thailand is monitoring that closely because we are now under a managed float system." 

 "However, I don't think the Bank of Thailand will do anything to the point of distorting the market because that will create problems later," he added.

title: Thai Baht Rises On Ctrl Bk Comments, Strong Exports
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht ended up sharply against the dollar Tuesday, after a Bank of Thailand assistant governor reiterated that it will not intervene against market trends, traders said. 

 The dollar finished Tuesday at 36.58 baht (THB) down from THB36.88 at the close of trading in Bangkok Monday. 

 The central bank's Kiettisak Meecharoen told reporters that intervention would only occur if the baht moved too strongly. 

 He said the economy was showing signs of renewed strength, so the baht was naturally rising, as the baht had fallen when the economy was weak. 

 Traders said the market took this as a nod of acquiesence to a further strengthening of the Thai currency, traders said. 

 The dollar is expected to trade between THB36.50 and THB36.70 in the near term. 

 The baht is supported by renewed strength in exports, with 8.4% year-on-year growth reported from preliminary figures in May, and continued equity and direct investment inflows.

title: Thai Baht Ends Flat; Mkt Awaits Key U.S. Data
text:

title: Thai  central bank  sees baht strength as temporary.
text:
BANGKOK, May 10 (Reuters) - The governor of the Thai central bank, Chatu Mongol Sonakul, said on Monday the baht was being pushed up by flows of capital into Thailand and the currency's strength was likely to be temporary. 

 Chatu Mongol said he was not concerned by the baht's recent strength because the currency was likely to be adjusted by market mechanisms once it became too strong. 

 He said the recent inflows were mostly of capital invested in the stock market and not for foreign exchange speculation. 

 "The Bank of Thailand is not concerned about this because the baht is under the 'managed float system'," he said. 

 "When there are a lot of inflows coming in, it will strenthen temporarily. Once it becomes strong to the point that it is not attractive for investment, it will be adjusted by the market mechanism," he told reporters. 

 Under Thailand's "managed float system", the Bank of Thailand allows the baht to float freely but intervenes occasionally to try to iron out excess volatility. It does not seek to influence the overall direction of the baht. 

 The system was introduced in July 1997. 

 Chatu Mongol said the central bank saw no need to intervene in the market now as it believed in market mechanisms.
