title: FX  Asia: Tearaway Baht Poses Awkward Policy Dilemma
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Two years after the Bank of Thailand slapped controls on its capital account in an ultimately doomed attempt to avert the collapse of the baht, monetary authorities in Bangkok are facing a problem they could barely have imagined just 24 months ago. The baht is strengthening rapidly, and short of imposing fresh capital controls there is little the central bank or anybody else can do to stop it. 

 Before profit-taking set in on Thursday afternoon and trimmed its gains, the baht was trading at a 16-week high. With the U.S. currency at THB36.76, the baht was an impressive 54% above its all time low of THB56.75 to dollar, hit in January 1998. 

 The baht's rally has been fueled by a combination of trade flows and an inrush of foreign funds destined for investment in Bangkok's soaring stock market. 

 Although down from a year earlier, Thailand's trade balance was still firmly in surplus over the first quarter at $1.73 billion - a residual effect of the collapse in imports which followed the baht's devaluation in 1997 and helped the currency on the way to recovery. 

 Imports may now be rising, but economists interpret the narrowing of the surplus positively, saying greater demand for imports is a crucial sign of economic recovery. 


   Economy Emerging From Recession



"Thailand is clearly coming out of recession," says Neil Saker,
regional economist at SG Securities in Singapore. "Production is picking
up, banks are restructuring and recapitalizing, and bankers are prepared
to lend to good companies."



Other foreign analysts agree.



"Thailand's economic contraction was over by the end of the second
quarter of 1998. By the fourth quarter, the economy was growing again,"
says Adrian Foster, South East Asian economist at Nomura International
in Hong Kong, forecasting economic growth of 2.5% for this year.



The message has not been lost on investors. The decisions this week by
both Moody's Investor Service and Standard & Poor's to lift their
outlook for the Kingdom's sovereign credit rating merely confirmed the
belief of many that Thailand, the first Asian country to descend into
crisis, would be among the first to emerge.



Smoothing the path to recovery have been massive monetary easings
which have seen baht interest rates collapse to levels close to U.S.
dollar rates. Faced with dismal returns on deposits, Thai savers have
turned instead to the local stock market, driving the Stock Exchange of
Thailand's benchmark index up by 40% since the beginning of April.



Foreign investors have not been slow to catch the trend. Over recent
weeks offshore fund managers have been pouring money into the Thailand
at an ever accelerating pace, driving the baht sharply higher.



And according to some analysts, there is no obvious reason why the
baht's appreciation should stop in the near term. According to Foster at
Nomura, one of the major risks that has so far deterred foreign
investors - the high proportion of non-performing loans in the banking
sector - may have been greatly exaggerated.



According to the Bank of Thailand, 47% of all loans were
non-performing at the end of February. Foster, however, says the real
picture may be far less serious. A large proportion of the loans
classified as non-performing Foster describes as "strategic NPLs" which
borrowers have stopped servicing simply because the opportunity arose,
even if they are in fact capable of making payments.



   Bad Loan Levels Seen Dropping Rapidly



"To think that half a country's bank loans are bad is inconceivable,"
he says, arguing that with the erection of a sounder legal framework,
payments on many loans will resume and the level of NPLs will fall off
rapidly.



Less bad debt will mean more lending, brisker economic activity,
higher credit ratings, and more inward investment driving the baht
higher, say economists. And despite protests from Thai exporters, there
is little the central bank can do to slow the appreciation.


Intervention would be one potential option, but buying dollars would
inject even more liquidity into the domestic market, further fueling the
stock market rally and attracting more foreign funds, adding to the
upward pressure on the baht.



In any case, say central bank watchers, resistance to direct
intervention remains high within the Bank of Thailand, after a series of
futile actions to defend the baht bought the central bank to its knees
two years ago.



"What we are seeing now is a 180 degree turn around in the policy
dilemma - a complete reversal," says Saker at SG.



The authorities could attempt to slow the baht's rise by tightening
either fiscal or monetary policy to take some of the steam out of the
stock market, but either course would put upward pressure on interest
rates, something policy-makers are keen to avoid.



"There is a feeling that if they raise interest rates they risk
sucking in hot money," says Saker, "but lower interest rates will suck
money into the stock market."



The only answer, not only for Thailand but for other Asian countries
facing a similar dilemma, suggests Saker, may well prove to be capital
controls modeled on those adopted in Chile, which permitted longer term
investment, while penalizing short term capital flows.

title: FX  Asia: Regional  Currencies  Seen Nearing Top Of Bull Run
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian regional currencies are unlikely to keep pace with an extended run-up in the yen, as market players fret that local central banks will step in to brake, or block entirely, any further appreciation. 

 A sell-off in the U.S. dollar against the yen overnight Tuesday and early Wednesday in Asia drove a sharp rally in the regional currencies. The Singapore dollar, for example, gained 1.5% against the U.S. currency as offshore players were forced out of their long U.S. dollar positions by the yen-induced rise of the local currency. 

 But although dealers in Asia expect renewed selling to drag the U.S. dollar as low as Y118 when European markets open later in the day, market participants believe that the U.S. currency is close to finding a bottom against its Asian regional counterparts. 

 "Regional central banks have made it clear that they don't want their currencies to strengthen, so you can expect intervention to stand in the way," warns Ron Leven, Asian markets strategist at J.P. Morgan in Singapore. 

 As investor funds pouring into Asia in recent weeks have boosted local currencies, regional markets have seen a barrage of dollar-supportive verbal intervention from monetary authority and finance ministry officials from around the region. In Taiwan and South Korea, the authorities have actually entered the local markets, buying U.S. dollars in an attempt to forestall the rise of the New Taiwan dollar and the won. 

 "Asian governments don't want their currencies to strengthen dramatically. Given that the recovery in regional economies is uncertain and by no means entrenched, they still want to have competitive currencies," explains Thio Chin Loo, foreign exchange strategist at Banque Paribas in Singapore. 

 Technical Analysts See Dollar Nearing Bottom 

 While fear of intervention is a major factor, it is not the only reason traders and analysts believe the Asian currencies are approaching the top of their run. 

 The U.S. dollar is fast approaching key technical support levels against the regional currencies, which dealers think are extremely unlikely to be breached. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, many dealers are eying the U.S. currency's 200-day moving average at S$1.6925, a level they say should provide solid support for the U.S. dollar. And even if that is breached, they believe the market will certainly balk at pushing the U.S. dollar below its long term upward trend line at S$1.6870, given the slow pace of economic recovery the island is thought likely to see. 

 The U.S. currency's floor against the Thai baht (THB) is more difficult to call, especially in the short term. With Thai markets closed for much of this week, trading in the baht is likely to be thin and whippy, warn dealers. 

 Nevertheless, Wednesday morning saw the U.S. dollar bottom out at THB37.5100, as traders shied away from pushing the U.S. currency down through the THB37.5000 level at which the Bank of Thailand intervened to support the dollar in March. 

 If the central bank declines to defend that level, however, traders and analysts agree that the authorities would have little hesitation in entering the market to buy U.S. dollars if the U.S. currency threatened to drop below the THB37.00 mark. 

 Similarly, market participants believe the U.S. dollar's potential losses against the Philippine peso are limited, after the U.S. currency dropped to a low of PHP38.060 on Wednesday morning from PHP38.295 at the close of trading the previous day. 

 "The Philippine government has clearly indicated that it is not comfortable with the peso stronger than PHP38.00" to the U.S. dollar, says Cliff Tan, foreign exchange and interest rate strategist at Warburg Dillon Read in Singapore. "The authorities don't want the external sector, which has been the economy's only piston of growth, to fall into recession." 

 North Asian currencies also have little scope to strengthen further from current levels over the short term, according to analysts and traders. 

 Although the South Korean won rose more than 0.5% Wednesday morning, with the U.S. dollar hitting a low of KRW1,215.00, dealers say the U.S. currency is likely to encounter solid support at levels between KRW1,200 to KRW1,210. 

 Government-directed buying of U.S. dollars by the state-run Export-Import Bank, coupled with forthcoming repayments of foreign currency debt obligations, will draw a line under the U.S. currency's decline at KRW1,200, agree analysts and traders. 

 In Taiwan, market participants believe the central bank is likely to support the U.S. dollar at NT$37.75, and subsequently at NT$37.50, should fund inflows force a retreat from the first level. Beyond that, however, the central bank would be "very unhappy indeed" according to one trader. 

 Few analysts are attempting to pick levels for the dollar against the Indonesian rupiah (IDR), however. With the dollar barely straying beyond an IDR8,000 to IDR9,000 band this year, and little capital flowing either in or out of the country, there are no trends to whet the market's appetite. Although some market observers predict the rupiah may fall in advance of Indonesia's June 7 parliamentary elections, others argue that the central bank's reserves are more than sufficient to offset any likely outflows.

title: Thai c.bank says no baht  intervention .
text:
BANGKOK, April 9 (Reuters) - Thailand's central bank governor, Chatu Mongol Sonakul, said on Friday his bank has not intervened in the forex market to support the weak baht. 

 The baht briefly slid past the key 38 per dollar level in early Friday dealings and has been hovering just below that level for most of the day. On Thursday, the currency was quoted late at 37.79/37.80. 

 "We have not entered the foreign exchange market to guide the baht movement because it weakened only five to 10 satangs. I think no central bank should intervene (because of the small drop)," Chatu Mongol told reporters. 

 The governor said the central bank had not intervened in the foreign exchange market since the baht was at 35.80, which was some months ago. 

 He said baht weakness was psychological as there was market expectation that the baht should fall further to help Thai exporters. There has been a debate in past weeks in Thailand between the government and private businesses over whether the baht should be allowed to weaken to help sagging exports. 

 The government is not in favour of such a proposal and has said market forces should dictate the baht's level. 

 The governor reiterated his belief that a weaker baht would not likely help exports. He urged exporters to boost their competitiveness by improving productivity. 

 The baht hit its six-month low of 38.02 to the dollar briefly on Friday morning before bouncing back to trade at 37.96/38.00 in mid-afternoon. 

 Dealers said the baht's setback was capped by Thai exporters taking profit by unwinding their dollar positions when the Thai currency eased to about 38.00.

title: Thai Finance Minister Reaffirms Market-Driven Baht Policy
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Thai Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanhaeminda late Wednesday said that the country's financial authorities would continue to let the market set the exchange rate for the baht (THB) currency. 

 Tarrin told delegates of a World Bank conference on Asian corporate recovery that an appropriate exchange rate had to consider more than just export competitiveness. 

 The interests of importers and debtors also had to be taken into account, he said. The Bank of Thailand has a policy of intervening only to stem volatility, not to fight market trends. 

 At the close of Asian spot trading Wednesday, the dollar was at THB37.64, down from THB37.68 late the previous day. 

 The government is ensuring that there is enough liquidity for exporters to continue operating, so there is no credit crunch in the sector, Tarrin said. 

 "We suffer more from lower prices" due to slack demand in global markets, he said. 

 Appropriate measures to improve competitiveness included improvements in product quality and production standards, mutual assistance within regional organizations, and development of trade with neighboring countries and southern China, he said. 

 "We will try our very best to achieve our 4% export growth target," Tarrin said. 

 Thailand is the eighth-largest exporter in the world, and the export sector accounts for 45% of gross domestic product. If the baht weakens a bit, it will account for 50% of GDP, Tarrin said. Export growth of 4% should result in GDP growth of about 1%, given that the import component of Thai exports is about 50%, he said. 

 The government target for 1999 is for 1% GDP growth. 


On Tuesday, the Bank of Thailand said export growth was behind the
target. If the trend continues, the central bank said, the government
will need to take additional measures to stimulate the economy, beyond a
THB130 billion package of tax cuts and spending programs announced the
same day.

title: Thai  central bank  says won't move to support baht.
text:
BANGKOK, Feb 22 (Reuters) - The Bank of Thailand said on Monday it would not intervene in the foreign exchange market to support the baht. 

 Thai assistant central bank governor Kiettisak Meecharoen told reporters the baht had fallen recently due to external factors. 

 "We can not resist external factors. The baht weakness is in line with regional currencies. We have no plan to enter into the market to help shore up the baht," Kiettisak told reporters. 

 By 0920 GMT on Monday, the baht had fallen to around 37.70/37.75 to the dollar compared with 37.45/37.50 late on Friday after the Japanese yen fell under 122 yen per dollar. 

 Kiettisak said the yen fall was due to disappointment the G7 meeting over the weekend did not specifically address the recent yen weakness. 

 He said Thai economic fundamentals were unchanged but rising demand for the baht had helped boost short-term Thai interest rates. 

 The central bank's one-day repurchase rate closed at 5.875 on Monday morning, against 2.75 percent at the open. 

 Kiettisak said the central bank was considering whether it would keep some of its forward contracts to buy Thai baht for cashflow management. 

 He expected the central bank's onshore swap forward commitments to decline to no more than $2.5 billion by the end of the year from $5.3 billion on February 12.

title: Thai Govt/Econ Bills-4: Govt To Maintain Most Current Policy
text:
Tarrin said the Dec. 2 letter was the only other document sent to the IMF, outside of the published letters of intent, in which the passage of the economic legislation is mentioned, contrary to the claims of the opposition in the censure debate last week. 

 He said the undisclosed side letters covered, for example, how the Bank of Thailand intervened in the foreign exchange market when there was excess volatility between late 1997 and early 1998. The baht sank to a low of more than THB56 to the dollar in January 1998. 

 Some of the documents explained how the central bank intervened in the money market last year when commercial banks were competing for deposits by jacking up fixed-term deposit account interest rates and extending few new loans. 

 These practical measures could not be publicized as it would interfere with vital regulatory operations, he said. 

 Tarrin said he could not say specifically when the seventh letter of intent, currently being drafted in consultation with the IMF, would be ready for cabinet approval. Talks with the IMF each quarter usually take about two weeks. The team arrived from Washington late last week. 

 The seventh letter of intent is likely to be shorter than previous letters, he said, because much of the policy measures outlined in the previous letter will be continued. 

 In the sixth letter, the government said it hoped to secure passage of the bankruptcy bill and related legislation by the end of the current parliamentary session March 22. 

 Observers think it's unlikely that the entire package of 11 economic reform bills will be passed in this session. 

 The government's bill to amend to the existing Bankruptcy Act has been passed by the House and is being scrutinized by a Senate committee. 

 If changes in committee alter the substance of the bill, and the changes are accepted by the full Senate, a joint House-Senate committee must work out a compromise for both houses to consider again. 

 The House has the power to enact the original version of the bill without Senate approval if no acceptable compromise can be agreed upon, but the government would rather win support for the controversial legislation.

 Kiettisak said the Bank of Thailand would track the baht's movement for one or two more days and monitor the impact from jitters over a possible yuan devaluation which, he said, had returned on Sunday.

title: Thai  central bank  says won't  intervene  in baht.
text:
BANGKOK, Jan 20 (Reuters) - The Bank of Thailand on Wednesday reaffirmed its belief that market forces and economic fundamentals should dictate the value of the baht. 

 Its governor, Chatu Mongol Sonakul, told reporters the central bank had not intervened in the foreign exchange market to protect the value of the baht in the past seven months. 

 "In the past seven months since I came to office, the Bank of Thailand has not intervened in the market," he said. 

 "New economic theory seems to suggest that central banks and policy makers should not be too preoccupied with defending the value of the currency and should let it move in line with the economic fundamentals," he added. 

 Officials at the central bank have said that the bank has entered the market from time to time mostly to buy dollars to meet outstanding forward obligations rather than to intervene in the market. 

 But this has been disputed by some money market dealers who have in the past said that the central bank has intervened to stop the baht from sliding below a certain key level. 

 Usually central bank market intervention operations are secret and its officials can chose whether or not to publicly declare such actions.

 jobs data failed to drive it convincingly higher. 

     The yen's resilience and corresponding rises in regional 

currencies have sparked growing anxiety among Asian central 

 banks about a loss of export competitiveness. 

     The Bank of Korea stepped in to stem the won's rise last 

 week and Seoul dealers cited further signs of intervention on 

 Monday. 

Thailand's central bank is also believed to have bought 

 dollars against the baht in recent sessions. Manila currency

 dealers are beginning to expect officials to intervene to cap 

 the peso's rise. 

     Collapsing regional imports have taken the steam out of 

 Asia's much-touted export-led recovery. Regional governments 

 now fear an appreciation in their currencies might hamper it 

 further. 

     KOREAN WON SPOOKED BUT SEEN SUPPORTED 

     The Korean won was one of the few regional currencies to 

 lose ground as two state-run banks actively bought dollars, 

 absorbing sales by exporters and foreigners investing in the 

 stock market. 

     The won fell to a low of 1,183 per dollar from a high of 

 1,150 after the Export-Import Bank of Korea ploughed in with 

 hefty dollar bids, trading directly in the local market for the 

 first time. 

     Analysts said Seoul's efforts to slow the won's rise could 

 succeed, but any falls would also be limited. 

     "The government has announced measures to remove the issue 

 of international bonds in 1999 and has asked state enterprises 

 not to borrow and start repaying some loans. So that will 

 reduce the supply of U.S. dollars and cap the strength of the 

 won," said Irene Cheung, regional economist at CIBC in 

 Singapore. 

 "But fundamentally, I think there is support for the 

currency and I don't expect it to weaken much below 1,200 per 

 dollar in the first half of 1999," Cheung told Reuters 

 Television. 

 KOREA RAISES 1999 GROWTH FORECAST 

 The Bank of Korea raised its 1999 GDP forecast to 3.2 

 percent growth from a previous projection of one percent 

 growth, based largely on an expected surge in semiconductor 

 exports. 

     This compares with an expected contraction of five to six 

 percent for 1998. 

     The bullish outlook boosted the stock market, already up in 

 early trade on strong demand for newly listed Hanvit Bank. 

     Hanvit, the result of a merger between the Commercial Bank 

 of Korea and Hanil Bank, shot up to its daily limit high of 

 7,590 won at the opening bell. 

     PESO FIRMS BUT MARKET WARY 

     The Philippine peso rose in line with the yen, but the 

 37.50 per dollar level was expected to pose a stiff barrier. 

     Dealers were also wary after weekend press reports the 

 policy-making Monetary Board had permitted the central bank to 

 replenish its foreign reserves by buying dollars. 

     Manila stocks snapped an 11-day winning streak, but brokers 

 said any correction should be short-lived as interest in the 

 market remained strong. KL SHARES UPBEAT ON CABINET RESHUFFLE 

     Kuala Lumpur shares responded well to Prime Minister 

 Mahathir Mohamad's weekend cabinet reshuffle, which saw former 

 foreign minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi named Deputy Prime 

 Minister and Daim Zainuddin appointed Finance Minister. 

 Analysts said Abdullah's appointment reduced the likelihood 

 of a potentially damaging power struggle for the number two 

 post. 

     And the market-savvy Daim was expected to provide a steady 

 hand in charting Malaysia out of its recession. 

     The National Economic Action Council said concerns over the 

 government's ability to finance its 62 billion ringgit economic 

 recovery plan through 2000 were unfounded. 

     It said two-thirds of the funds would be sourced locally, 

 mainly through loans from the state pension fund and Petronas. 

     But data released on Monday showed the economy remained in 

 poor shape, with industrial output shrinking 11.5 percent 

 year-on-year in November after a 10.4 percent drop in October. 

     RUPIAH EDGES UP, CENTRAL BANK VOICES SUPPORT 

     The Indonesian rupiah was slightly firmer, but showed no 

 inclination to stray from its recent range near the 8,000 

 level. 

     Dealers expected rising dollar demand ahead of the Moslem 

 Eid al-Fitr celebrations on January 19/20. 

     Bank Indonesia governor Syahril Sabirin said the central 

 bank was prepared to step in if necessary. 

     "We are trying our best to make it stable. If some 

intervention is necessary we will do so. We do not want to see 

 the rate fluctuate in a wider band," he told Reuters Television 

 in Hong Kong ahead of a central bankers' meeting. 

 Sabirin said there was room for interest rates to ease 

 further and the rupiah strengthen, but added its current level 

 was all right. 

 TAIWAN, HONG KONG SHARES BUCK UPTREND 

 Most stock markets rode the Dow's gains, though Taipei 

 shares ended a shade softer on some late profit-taking. 

 Brokers saw stability in the near-term as the index has 

 held above the 10-year moving average at 6,300 for several 

 sessions. 

 Hong Kong stocks ended weak after a choppy day, as 

 investors vacillated between Friday's interest rate cuts and 

 news foreign creditors would not receive priority treatment in 

 the bankruptcy of Guangdong International Trust and Investment 

 Corp (GITIC).

title: ASIA MARKETS - Korea making the grade.
text:
HONG KONG Jan 5, (Reuters) - Asian share markets were 

 volatile in thin post-holiday trade on Tuesday, with Korea and 

Thailand leading gainers and Taiwan stumbling despite government 

intervention. 

     Regional currencies gained ground against the US dollar in 

 line with the Japanese yen's dramatic rally, although the 

 Singapore dollar defied the pull of the yen. 

     Sing dollar selling was said to be linked to purchases of 

 the Thai baht, as foreigners piled into the local stock market. 

     But volumes were very thin, and traders said there was 

 little in the way of fresh or significant factors to move the 

 market. 

     "There's no real volume going through," said a regional 

currency dealer at a European bank. 

     KOREAN STOCKS UP ON OUTLOOK UPGRADE 

     Korean shares moved ahead and spreads on outstanding U.S. 

 dollar bonds remained stiff after rising on the back of an 

 outlook upgrade from ratings agency Standard & Poor's. 

     During New York trading, S&P changed its outlook on South 

 Korea to "positive" from "stable" and affirmed the country's 

 local and foreign currency credit ratings. 

     The improved outlook "has already led to a 20 basis point 

 rise in benchmark spreads both in Korea five year and ten year 

 bonds" said Paul Marshall, associate director of credit trading 

 at Barclays Capital in Hong Kong told Reuters Television. 

 "I think that the factors that have led to the rally in 

 Asian bonds over the last three months or so are still in 

 place," he said. 

 Marshall cited three key points as supporting dollar bonds 

 of Asian sovereigns in the first part of 1999: a weaker US 

 dollar, positive current account positions of regional 

 economies, and lower domestic interest rates. 

 Shares jumped on the news in Seoul, after having rallied 

 sharply throughout the last quarter on expectations the country 

 would soon climb out of the "junk" investment grade acquired at 

 the height of the Asia crisis. 

     Foreign investors were seen picking up leading blue chips 

 KEPCO and Korea Telecom. 

     But a strategist looking at the KOSPI index in Hong Kong 

 said investing in the market at current levels, having tested 

 the 600 point level repeatedly in the last two sessions, was 

 more an act of hope than a fundamental strategy. 

 KOREAN WON KEEPS PACE WITH YEN, CENTRAL BANK TALKS IT DOWN 

 Among Asian currencies, the Korean won kept closest pace 

 with the mighty yen, trading in a 30 won range and finishing out 

 the day near its highs. 

 Foreign inflows of funds looking to catch the rising stock 

 market combined with exporter dollar sales orders to drive the 

 won's rise, but the currency met some resistance against the 

 dollar on verbal intervention from the Bank of Korea. 

 Dealers reported central bank checking of dollar positions 

 at foreign FX desks in Seoul, taking some wind out of the won's 

 sails. 

 But by the end of the day, it had kept pace with the yen, 

 gaining around the same amount as the Japanese currency against 

 the dollar. 

 THAI STOCKS LEAP AS FOREIGNERS RUSH IN 

 Foreign funds fueled a frantic rally in Thai stocks, with 

 turnover relatively high and speculative plays in banking and 

 property issues among the favoured plays of retail investors. 

 Brokers said bank stocks were attracting attention ahead of 

 a deadline on formalising recapitalisation plans between the 

central bank authorities and commercial banks chiefs on January 

 15th. 

 The market started the day in an upbeat mood after Thai 

 Military Bank Plc announced last night it was cutting prime 

 rates by 50 basis points to 12 percent. 

     Expectations of further reductions in prime rates were seen 

 helping property shares head higher as well. 

     TAIWAN SHARES SELL DOWN AGAINST GOVERNMENT SUPPORT 

     Despite continued government support of Taiwan's asset 

 markets, stock investors sold the main index down sharply, 

 albeit in light volume. 

     The weighted index found itself at fresh 29-month lows at 

 the close, on its first day of trade in 1999. 

     Market turnover was described as "blah" by a Hong Kong 

 institutional sales trader, only reaching T$43.97 billion on 

 Tuesday against T$51.74 billion on December 31. 

     The trader said initial selling pressure began after falls 

 on Tokyo's Nikkei index and gathered steam in the latter part of 

 the session. 

     INDONESIA BUDGET SHOCKS NOBODY, MARKET SHRUGS BUT MOVES 

 AHEAD 

     Indonesian stocks gained toward the close after having 

 traded in lacklustre ranges through most of the session. 

     At midday, the market had a look at the country's draft 

 budget for 1999/2000, but was not inspired by the slow recovery 

 projections. 

     "It is not really a surprise," Sri Mulyani Indrawati, an 

 economist at the University of Indonesia in Jakarta, told 

 Reuters Television. 

     "This budget is not really functioning to stimulate the 

 economy," she said, suggesting the already battered financial 

 structure and devastated social networks still needed acute 

 attention. 

 By the close of business the Jakarta stock exchange had 

 moved higher in the post-holiday thin conditions by more than 

 3.6 percent.

title: SE Asian  Currencies  Little Changed Early; Mkt Fears Ctrl Bks
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--In early trading Friday morning, most Southeast Asian currencies are little changed from levels seen late in Asian hours the previous day, despite the overnight slide in the U.S. dollar against the yen. Only the Philippine peso (PHP) has strengthened significantly, rising to retest Thursday's highs against the U.S. currency. 

 For the most part, traders attribute the relative heaviness of the Singapore dollar and the baht to the threat of central bank intervention to forestall excessive local-currency appreciation. 

 "There was huge (U.S. dollar) selling in the baht (market) yesterday," said a senior trader at a Thai bank. "Several hundred (million) dollars were sold, but the Bank of Thailand was on on the bid, buying and buying." 

 With the threat of Bank of Thailand intervention still overshadowing the market, participants are wary of pushing the local currency rapidly higher. 

 At 0130 GMT (8:30 p.m. Thursday EST), the U.S. dollar is quoted against the baht (THB) at THB35.9200, down a little from THB35.9400 late Thursday in Asia. 

 Fears that the Monetary Authority of Singapore will also enter the market to buy U.S. dollars at levels around S$1.6400 are weighing on the Singapore dollar. 

 At present, the U.S. dollar is trading at S$1.6450, virtually unchanged from S$1.6449 late Thursday. 

 Still sidelined by most participants, the rupiah (IDR) is also barely moved, with the U.S. dollar quoted at IDR7,547, compared with IDR7,559 late Thursday. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System, however, the U.S. dollar is at PHP38.77, up from its earlier low at PHP38.72, but down from PHP38.80 at Thursday's close.

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Regionals shed gains, peso slides.
text:
0925 GMT - Asian regional currencies drifted lower as the 

 yen gave up the bulk of its gains after a U.S. investment house 

 came in to cover dollars it sold in the morning. 

     But the dollar's rise was limited by concerns about Latin 

 America and jittery U.S. stock prices. 

     The Dow was hurt by concerns over the situation in Brazil 

 where the stock market sank 8.8 percent. 

     *** The Korean won gained one percent on the day and 

 dealers are looking for a break of the 1,200 per dollar barrier 

 soon. 

     Dealers will watch the outcome of negotiations between 

 Korea and the IMF on the scheduled repayment of IMF aid loans. 

     The government, which is barred by the IMF from directly 

 stepping into the market, might seek an eased stance over 

intervention in return for repaying the maturing loans. 

     *** The Taiwan dollar rose to eight-month highs, boosted by 

 the yen, but dealers said the central bank had short-covered 

 U.S. dollars to stabilise the Taiwan dollar before Saturday's 

 elections. 

 The three-way contest has in reality been a two-horse race 

 from the start, with polls showing incumbent Chen Shui-bian of 

 the opposition Democratic Progressive Party running neck and 

 neck with ruling Nationalist Party challenger Ma Ying-jeou. 

 *** The Thai baht was steady amid caution about possible 

central bank dollar purchases after Thursday's apparent 

intervention. 

Thailand's improved outlook has generated a lot of demand 

 for baht, especially ahead of the December 15 auction of failed 

 finance firms' assets, worth over 370 billion baht. 

 The Financial Restructuring Authority said it would proceed 

 with the auction on schedule despite the resignation of FRA 

 Secretary General Vichit-Vadakan. 

 *** The Philippine peso reversed its recent gains, sliding 

 through the 39 per dollar level on speculation the central bank

 was buying dollars. 

 Manila markets were hit by a sharp 11.2 percent 

 year-on-year rise in November inflation, well up from the 10.2 

 percent seen in October. 

 It was the highest annual inflation recorded in a single 

 month during the year and brought the per month average for the 

 11 months to 9.7 percent. 

 *** A senior Malaysian Finance Ministry official said the 

 ringgit's fixed exchange rate at 3.80 per dollar is 

 "competitive and not overvalued". 

 Secretary General Aris Othman said the government expects 

 the economy to begin recording a positive annualised rate of 

 growth by the third quarter of 1999 at the latest, if external 

 demand remains stable or improves.

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Regionals firmer with yen but quiet.
text:
0030 GMT - The regional currencies were firmer in early 

 business alongside the higher yen but end week volume was 

 light. 

     The yen is benefiting from a softer dollar which is being 

 hurt by the Dow's slippage. The Dow is being hurt by concerns 

 over the situation in Brazil where the stock market sank 8.8 

 percent. 

     A surprise round of European rate cuts had no real impact 

 in Asia. 

     *** Taiwan markets are likely to be quiet today with 

 investors taking a pace back ahead of Saturday's parliamentary, 

 mayoral and city council elections. 

     The three-way contest has in reality been a two-horse race 

 from the start, with polls showing incumbent Chen Shui-bian of 

 the opposition Democratic Progressive Party running neck and 

 neck with ruling Nationalist Party challenger Ma Ying-jeou. 

     *** The won got off to a flying start and has now put on 

 around eight percent since the middle of last month. 

     There is still speculation that the central bank might step 

 in with actual or verbal intervention if the authorities think 

 the won's rally will start to impact on exports. 

     *** The Thai baht was still firm but not making a lot of 

 headway after the central bank's apparent dollar buying 

intervention on Thursday. 

Thailand's improved outlook has generated a lot of demand 

 for baht, especially ahead of the December 15 auction of failed 

 finance firms' assets, worth over 370 billion baht. 

     Thai Foreign Minister Surin Pitsuwan's comment that a 

 dollar/baht rate of 34 to 35 was appropriate gave offshore 

 players yet another reason to dump dollars. 

     Dealers said the central bank's dollar purchases seemed 

 aimed at steadying the baht and more of the same is expected 

 today. 

     *** The Philippine peso continues to sparkle, thanks to the 

 stronger yen and overseas workers' remittances. 

     Corporate dollar inflows from the recent sale of stakes in 

 Nestle Philippines and Philippine Long Distance Telephone are 

 also boosting the peso. 

     The World Bank yesterday approved loans worth a total of 

 $600 million for the Philippines, part of $1 billion in credits 

 promised by World Bank President James Wolfensohn earlier this 

 year. 

 The money will be used to strengthen the banking system, 

 help companies cope with credit shortages and ease poverty in 

 rural areas. 

 *** In Pakistan, S&P cut its long term foreign currency

 sovereign and senior unsecured rates to double C from triple C 

 minus. 

 The downgrade follows the government's having missed a 

 US$13 million interest payment due Nov. 30, 1998, on its US$300 

 million FRN due 2001. The bond indenture allows for a 10-day 

 grace period. 

 Ratings in both the double-'C' and triple-'C' category 

 signal that an obligor is currently vulnerable and is dependent 

 on favorable external conditions to meet debt service. Obligors 

 rated double-'C' face imminent debt service problems. Change on

text:
As trading in the local market ended late Wednesday, the U.S. dollar was quoted at PHP39.020, down from PHP39.355 at the previous close. 

 Elsewhere in Southeast Asia, regional currencies lacked the peso's buoyancy. The Thai baht (THB), so frequently the star of recent sessions, crabbed sideways in a tight trading range throughout the Asian hours. 

 While most investors and traders retain a positive outlook for the baht, many are nervous of buying into the rally at this late stage. They are afraid that the Bank of Thailand will intervene in the market should the dollar fall below THB36.00, selling down the baht to take the pressure off local exporters. 

 Although Bank of Thailand Governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul declared on Wednesday that the central bank wasn't attempting to prop up the U.S. currency at the THB36.00 level, he admitted that the bank had been buying dollars in the market.  Late in Asian trading Wednesday, the U.S. dollar was quoted at THB36.0300, down slightly from THB36.0650 late the previous day. 

 In general, however, most offshore investors are relatively bullish on the baht. Many are predicting further gains in December, with the Financial Sector Restructuring Authority's planned Dec. 15 auction of $1 billion worth of defunct financial companies assets attracting considerable foreign interest.

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Regionals steady as dlr drifts lower.
text:
0920 GMT - Asian currencies were little changed but off 

 their lows in late trade as the dollar lost some of its shine 

 against the yen and mark. 

     The dollar's failure to break convincingly above 124 yen 

 overnight limited its rise, but dealers said its base was 

 supported by news that a mid-sized Japanese general contractor 

 JDC Corp had filed for bankruptcy protection. 

 *** Malaysian Second Finance Minister Mustapa Mohamed said 

 the government may tap overseas funds to help in the 

 restructuring and recapitalisation of domestic banks. 

 Bank Negara governor Ali Abul Hassan Sulaiman said the 

central bank would continue to promote bank mergers and would 

 soon launch a plan to chart the industry's direction over the 

 next two decades. 

 He also said Malaysia would not resort to printing money to 

 fund the fiscal deficit and would keep the fiscal shortfall at 

 six percent of GNP. 

 The IMF praised Malaysia's open trade regime as exceptional 

 by regional standards, but said the country's capital controls 

 could backfire, leaving the country vulnerable if its export 

 markets begin to dry up. 

 *** The rupiah was a bit lower but still doing well as the 

 conversion of aid dollars into the local currency continued to 

 provide support. 

 Bank Indonesia governor Syahril Sabirin said there was room 

 for the rupiah to strengthen to a level just below 7,000 or to 

 6,500, while interest rates could slide towards 20-30 percent

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Regionals hold up as Moody's hits yen.
text:
0435 GMT - Most Asian regional currencies held their ground 

 despite the yen's losses after Moody's Investors Service 

 downgraded Japan's sovereign debt rating. 

     Moody's lowered Japan's yen-denominated debt and 

 foreign-currency debt ratings to Aa1 from Aaa, citing weakness 

 in the country's fiscal standing and financial system. 

     Active short-covering after the Moody's move pushed the 

 dollar as high as 122.35 yen, up over two yen from its early 

 lows, but dealers said further gains were capped by caution 

 ahead of the Federal Reserve's policy meeting tonight. 

 Most market participants are looking for a quarter point 

 cut in the Fed funds rate, and this has kept Asian currency and 

 stock markets well supported in recent sessions. 

 But some dealers felt the Fed might decide to hold off for 

 analysisthe time being as the U.S. economy has been looking 

 fairly healthy. 

 "It depends on what they think is most important now. If 

 they want to keep the recovery in emerging markets going, they 

 should cut rates," said a European bank dealer in Singapore. 

     *** The impact of the Moody's move was also cushioned by 

 the fact that it had been widely expected for some time. 

     "The ratings agencies are always behind the curve...They 

 should have done this when Japan went into recession. Now 

 things are turning for the better and they cut the ratings," 

 the dealer said. 

 He said substantially reduced speculative activity and 

 year-end position squaring were also tempering the impact of 

 any bad news for regional currencies. 

 *** The Thai baht extended its recent gains despite news 

 the country's largest refiner, Thai Oil, had defaulted on 

 interest as well as principle payments on $1.85 billion worth 

 of debt. 

 Some dealers attributed the baht's resilience to demand 

 from foreigners ahead of the government's December 2 auction of 

 401 billion baht of defunct finance company assets. 

 But the baht's rise was limited by fears the central bank

 might intervene to prevent too sharp an appreciation, which 

 could hurt Thailand's export competitiveness. 

 *** The Singapore dollar was again worst hit by the yen's 

 fall, with dealers increasingly convinced that local 

 authorities were not in favour of it strengthening beyond the 

 1.62 level. 

 *** The Philippine peso remained on a firm footing after 

 climbing above the 40 per dollar level in early trade, buoyed 

 by hopes of a U.S. rate cut and remittances by Filipinos 

 working abroad. 

      Dollar bids from interbank players were expected to block 

 the peso's rally near the 39.50 level. 

     The Philippines posted a $332 million merchandise trade 

 surplus in September compared with a deficit of $619 million 

 the year before. Exports rose 19 percent year-on-year while 

 imports fell nearly 17 percent. 

 *** U.S. Vice President Al Gore played on Malaysian 

 sensitivities again by repeating that democracy and freedom 

 were essential for economic reform. 

 Gore, who is representing President Bill Clinton at the 

 APEC summit in Kuala Lumpur, infuriated Malaysia on Monday by 

 saluting the "brave people" supporting an anti-government 

 movement started by detained former deputy prime minister Anwar 

 Ibrahim. 

 His blunt words, later backed by Clinton, drew swift and 

 biting condemnation from Malaysian officials and business 

 leaders. 

 Malaysia's discomfiture was compounded when Philippine 

 President Joseph Estrada met Anwar's wife in a show of support 

 for the sacked minister and a rebuke to Mahathir. 

 *** The U.S. and Japan unveiled a $10 billion aid plan for 

 Asia at the APEC meeting. The package comprises a combined $5 

 billion from Japan, the Asian Development Bank and the World 

 Bank. With a further $5 billion from the U.S. through Export 

 Import Bank trade financing and Overseas Private Investment 

 Corp programmes. 

     In addition the U.S. will provide an additional $1 billion 

 in trade financing each to Indonesia, Thailand and South Korea. 

     A senior Japanese official said the $10 billion aid plan 

 was separate from Japan's $30 billion Miyazawa plan for Asia, 

 although some of the ideas were similar and overlapped.

 could hurt Thailand's export competitiveness.

 slow as imports of raw materials to produce export goods were 

 falling.

 sidelined by a growing diplomatic row between the U.S. and

 on the region.

title: Thai Baht Ends Down; Dollar Recoups Support At THB36.50
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht ended lower against the U.S. dollar for the first time in seven trading days in Asian spot trade as 36.50 baht (THB) remained a support for the dollar, local dealers said. 

 They said foreign banks bought the dollar as it dropped below THB36.50. 

 Some overseas traders said the Bank of Thailand has stepped in to prevent the dollar falling below the THB35.00 level. 

Central bank officials said they were trading in foreign currencies for the bank's own need to settle its forward currency contracts. The Bank of Thailand has never publicly admitted it was intervening in the market. 

 At the close, the dollar was at THB36.60, up from Thursday's close of THB36.42. The dollar had dropped to a low of THB36.36 during the intraday trade. 

 As of Friday, the baht has dropped 29.3% since the Thai government abandoned its fixed foreign exchange system July 2, 1997. The baht is now hitting 12-month highs against the dollar. 

 The baht strength is being supported by capital inflows due to a current account surplus, foreign direct investment and asset sales. 

 The Bank of Thailand set its reference rate at THB36.442 to the dollar Friday, down from THB36.575 Thursday. The reference rate is a weighted average of rates charged by Thai commercial banks in the previous trading day. It serves as a benchmark for domestic currency trading.

Most resilient of the Southeast Asian currencies to any renewed sell-off will be the Thai baht, say analysts, applauding the Bangkok government's progress towards economic and financial restructuring.

title: Thailand  says won't  intervene  to move baht.
text:
BANGKOK, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Thai Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai said on Friday the central bank would not intervene to affect the level of the baht. 

 Chuan told reporters his government did not have a specific view on the appropriate level for the currency, which has risen strongly against the U.S. dollar in recent days. He said the level of the baht would be set by the market. 

 "It is difficult to tell if the baht at this level is appropriate," Chuan said, adding that the market should decide the level of the currency. 

 "We cannot oblige calls by some exporters for government intervention (to sell baht) as it would distort the market. The baht should find its own market level," Chuan said. 

 "The baht's rally has not been due to central bank intervention but it's moved in line with market forces," he said. 

 The prime minister said the recent strength of the baht was mostly due to inflows of funds into the country. 

 The baht stood at 36.70/36.80 to the dollar at 0515 GMT on Friday, not far off the 12-month high of 36.66 that was traded on Thursday. 

 The currency was devalued from around 25 to the dollar in July last year and fell to an all-time low of 56.90 in January before beginning to rally. 

 The Bank of Thailand has bought dollars for baht at least once this week but the action may have only been to mop up cheap dollars to clear forward currency swap obligations, currency dealers say. 

Central Bank governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul said on Wednesday that the Bank of Thailand's net forward swap obligations had fallen in recent days, a change which dealers attribute to buying of dollars for baht. 

 Chuan said there was no clear-cut impact of the stronger baht on the country's export sector. 

 "The baht's gains do not affect Thai exports (much) because other regional currencies have also appreciated. We may lose some of the U.S. market because of the dollar weakness."

title: FOCUS-Thai markets jump on recovery hopes.
text:
BANGKOK, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Thai financial markets surged on Thursday amid a wave of speculative buying on hopes that the beleaguered economy might be on the brink of recovery. 

 The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) saw its busiest day for eight months with more than 12 billion baht ($326 million) of deals as the benchmark SET composite index rose almost 4.5 percent. 

 Trade was dominated by small investors, but their enthusiasm was bolstered by increasing interest from international funds. 

 The baht traded at new 12-month highs under 36.70 to the dollar and looked set to test resistance at 36.50 before the Bank of Thailand intervened to buy dollars late in the Asian afternoon, dealers said. 

 Analysts said action on the stock market was mostly driven by speculative trade. 

 About 70-80 percent of the liquidity was provided by hundreds of retail investors, speculators anxious to cash in on a rally that has pushed the share market up by almost a third in just two months, they said. 

 But behind these small buyers were the big guns of the international funds, who have been reweighting Thailand in the light of a series of macroeconomic improvements. 

 "A lot of this rally is based on buying by small investors and may not last," said Jeff Earhart, senior analyst at Seamico Securities in Bangkok. 

 "But important things are happening in the economy. Interest rates are coming down fast, the baht is rising, and, as the debt burden of Thai companies eases, a lot of the valuations of local companies are beginning to look too low," he said. 

 By Thursday's close, the SET composite share index was up 14.62 points, or 4.42 percent, at 345.07. The local Thai banking sector index rose 11.96 percent, the finance index was up 11.45 percent while the property index jumped 12.62 percent. 

 The banking sector was led by state majority-owned Krung Thai Bank and by Bank of Ayudhya, which jumped 1.75 and 2.00 baht to 14.75 and 13.50 respectively. 

 Burdened by heavy foreign debt, many Thai companies have become technically bankrupt over the last year as rapid economic growth has given way to recession. 

 The Thai economy is expected to contract by at least seven percent this year, after a 0.4 percent decline in 1997, and will do well to stabilise in 1999, analysts say. 

 But economists say investors are right to look again at Thai stocks. Interest rates have now fallen a long way from their peak in mid-August as liquidity in the money market has risen. 

 Overnight money market rates fell to just 4.00 percent on Thursday, down from 5.00 percent on Wednesday and a high of 11.50 percent two months ago. 

 Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda said on Wednesday the lower trend was "permanent" and the country's biggest bank, Bangkok Bank, announced on Thursday it would cut its minimum lending rates to 13.25 percent from 13.75 percent in November. 

 All this has helped the Thai baht strengthen steadily from its low of around 56 to the dollar in January. 

 The baht has risen 13 percent over the last two months and traded at a 12-month high of 36.66 to the dollar on Thursday before central bank buying pushed it back down to 36.80. 

 The stronger the baht, the smaller the foreign currency debt burden on Thai corporates, analysts say, and the baht still looks set for further gains. 

 "Technically I would say we might see Thai baht getting much stronger - maybe heading for 35," said Satian Tantanasarit, senior vice president for treasury at Thai Danu Bank. 

 "I would say Thai baht can get much stronger." 

 ($1 = 36.8 baht).

title: Thai Baht Stronger Mid-Morning On Continuing Dlr Weakness
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--The Thai baht (THB) is stronger in mid-morning Asian trade Thursday, with gains expected to continue but at a slower pace than Wednesday, dealers say. 

 At 0255 GMT (9:55 p.m. EST Wednesday), the dollar traded at THB36.665, down from Wednesday's close of THB36.85. The dollar last closed below THB36.70 Oct. 16, 1997. 

 General dollar weakness remains the primary factor behind the baht's rise, dealers say. The dollar has been under pressure around the world this week on worries over Brazil's economy, because of heavy U.S. investment exposure there. 

 A local market factor pushing down the dollar is the Bank of Thailand's order to Thai commercial banks earlier this month to reduce their foreign-currency asset holdings to 15% of Tier 1 capital, from 20%, effective November. 

 "It's a good reason for banks to sell U.S. dollars right now," says a dealer at Bangkok Bank in Singapore. 

 A dealer at a French bank in Bangkok says Thai Farmers Bank, the nation's third largest commercial bank, started selling dollars last week to comply with the central bank order.

title: EMERGING MARKETS  FX  - S.E. Asia surges.
text:
LONDON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - South east Asian currencies surged on Tuesday, boosted largely by local inflows, but the yen's steady softening against the dollar pulled the South Korean won down in its wake, analysts said. 

 The major central European units remained solid, with the Czech crown maintaining its strength despite Monday's larger than expected interest rate cut. 

 The Philippine peso led the Asian winners, with dollar/peso dropping nearly two percent from New York closing levels. 

 Analysts said the currency was lifted mainly by seasonal inflows as Philippine workers overseas remitted their earnings, as well as local press reports that the central bank would not move immediately to cap the peso rise. 

 Indonesia's volatile rupiah notched up a further strong gain, supported by expectations of another disbursement next month from the International Monetary Fund, analysts added. 

 The baht also continued to firm as Thailand remained a favourite with investors cautiously eyeing a return to Asia. 

 "The Thai central bank has been trying to no avail to prevent the baht from appreciating as sentiment remains positive," analysts at Standard Chartered said in a note to clients. 

 The Bank of Thailand recently intervened in the market to buy dollars, in an effort to stabilise the baht's ascent. 

 Taiwan's dollar eased back slightly from a seven-month high of 32.565 against the dollar, seen during the Asian day, and analysts said strong foreign interest in Taiwanese stocks was underpinning demand for the currency. 

 But the South Korean won, which like most Asian currencies has seen a run of strength this month on the back of the yen's sudden rise against the dollar, lost ground as dollar/yen edged further towards 120. 

 Analysts said South Korea's fundamentals remained shaky, with unconvincing talk that its dominant business empires would be restructured, and a weakening yen would eat into the country's export competitiveness. 

 "Domestically they're in a real mess," said Graham Neilson, an Asia economist at Banque Paribas in London. "The won needs to go weaker against the dollar and everything else, to see at least some benefit to the export sector." 

 The Czech crown held onto the gains it made after Monday's interest rate cuts, when the central bank sliced 100 basis points off the key two-week repo rate. 

 "(The cut) was much more than the market was looking for and the crown firmed on the back of it, which is amazingly counterintuitive," said Jake Moore, an emerging markets analyst at Barclays Capital in London. 

 "But it's got to be good news for the economy and good news for investment, so it has remained fairly stable." 

 The zloty firmed slightly ahead of a meeting on Wednesday of the central bank's Monetary Policy Council, amid expectations that the decision-making body might cut Polish interest rates. 

 "It still remains the most attractive Eastern European currency in terms of yield, so investors are still looking to buy up Treasury bills and short-term interest rate instruments," Moore said. 

 Hungary's forint, normally the most fragile of the main central European currency trio, rose sharply against its currency basket as foreign investors bought into Hungarian stocks and other assets. 

 By the end of morning trade in Budapest the currency was 1.2 percent below basket parity compared with 1.6 percent below at Monday's close, well within the central bank's 4.5 percent wide intervention band.

title: ASIA MARKETS - Stocks jumpy, central banks active.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 22 (Reuters) - Major Asian stock markets cheered up on Tuesday after Wall Street shrugged off the global airing of U.S. President Bill Clinton's grand jury testimony. But traders said Asia's markets were still jumpy, especially over the implications of Japan's protracted financial crisis. Regional currencies were hurt by yen weakness, and some saw central bank intervention. 

 HONG KONG STOCKS CLIMB WHILE MANILA SINKS 

 Hong Kong shares saw big early gains on thin volume, prompted by Wall Street's positive response to the political developments surrounding Clinton's testimony. 

 Bell-wether stocks HSBC Holdings, Hong Kong Telecom, China Telecom and Hutchison Whampoa were heavily traded. 

 But dealers declined to attribute the buying to genuine interest and said sellers were "backing off". 

 Philippine shares were the biggest losers on Tuesday, closing 3.5 percent lower as the reality of economic malaise hit home. 

 The country is coming to grips with an increasingly bleak economic outlook, economists said. 

 The stock market was hurt by confusion over leading blue chips Philippine Long Distance Telephone, rumoured to be a foreign takeover target, and Philippine Airlines (PAL), the national airline which is set to formally close on Wednesday. 

 Most market watchers felt PAL would not be forced into liquidation and was engaged in brinkmanship with the government, which has shown reluctance to bail out the airline. 

 CENTRAL BANKS IN THE FOREX MARKET 

 Limited central bank activity was seen in some currency markets, with fears of yen-induced falls pushing a few of the regional currencies through what were seen as key levels. 

 The yen was quoted around 135 to the dollar at 0950 GMT. 

 Korean central bank authorities were seen in the foreign exchange markets, after the won threatened to fall through 1,400 to the dollar on the back of the weak yen. 

 Speculative positions built up early on the dollar's recovery sparked verbal intervention by the Bank of Korea, dealers said. 

Thailand's central bank appeared to be looking for dollars on Tuesday as the baht weakened against the greenback, dealers said. 

 The government is still cleaning up remaining long baht positions taken in the forward market by the Bank of Thailand in the past year, traders said. 

 The Singapore dollar was supported by firmer short-term interest rates, but some said the rise was odd given the twin political concerns of Malaysia and Indonesia.

title: ASIA FOCUS - Chronology of Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 3 (Reuters) - The following is a chronology of Asia's financial crisis. 

 1997 

 Jan 23 - Leading South Korean steel maker Hanbo Steel Corp defaults on loans, the first of a string of major corporate failures in 1997. 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency comes under attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 The Philippines is affected. The central bank raises the overnight rate to 13 percent and dumps dollars. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thai finance minister. Resignation has immediate impact in the Philippines, where the overnight deposit rate rises to 15 percent. 

 June 27 - Thai central bank suspends operations of 16 cash-strapped finance companies and orders them to submit merger or consolidation plans. 

 June 30 - Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh assures the nation in a televised address there will be no devaluation of the baht. 

 July 2 - After a failed defence of the Thai baht, Bangkok floats its currency and calls on the IMF for "technical assistance". 

 The baht is effectively devalued by about 15-20 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah starts to crumble. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support. 

 July 24 - Asian currency meltdown. The rupiah, baht, ringgit and peso slump as confidence in the region deteriorates. 

 August 11 - In Tokyo, the IMF unveils a rescue package for Thailand including loans of $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of a managed exchange rate. The rupiah plunges. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. Brunei later adds $500 million to the bail-out package, bringing it to $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 20 - Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad tells delegates of IMF/World Bank conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Around this time the South Korean won also begins to slump in value. 

 Oct 27 - Asian jitters spill over on to world stock markets. The Dow plunges 554 points, its largest single-day point loss ever. 

 Oct 31 - Indonesia's IMF package is unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although the front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 Nov 1 - Indonesia shuts down 16 troubled banks. 

 Nov 5 - IMF approves a $10 billion loan for Indonesia as part of the massive international package. 

 Nov 17 - Korea abandons its defence of the won, which rapidly falls to 1,000 to the dollar. 

 Dec 4 - IMF approves a $21 billion loan for South Korea, part of a bail-out package that will total nearly $60 billion. 

 Dec 8 - Thailand closes 56 of 58 previously suspended finance companies. 

 1998 

 Jan 8 - Representatives of the IMF and South Korea agree to a 90-day rollover of short-term debt. 

 Jan 12 - Peregrine, one of Asia's largest independent investment banks, collapses under a mountain of bad loans to Indonesian borrowers. Shares fall sharply in Hong Kong, China and Singapore. 

 Jan 15 - IMF managing director Michel Camdessus and President Suharto sign an agreement strengthening economic reforms. 

 Jan 22 - The rupiah collapses. It is dealt at 17,000 to the dollar at one stage. Bank Indonesia intervenes and drives the currency back to end at 11,800. 

 Jan 27 - Indonesia announces a temporary freeze on debt servicing. 

 Jan 28 - International creditor banks and the South Korean government say they have agreed on a plan to exchange $24 billion of short-term debt for new loans maturing in one, two and three years. 

 Jan 30 - U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warns Asia's financial crisis could spread. 

 Feb 14 - The IMF threatens to cut off the bail-out fund for Indonesia over its plans to introduce a currency board. 

 Feb 26 - Indonesia's borrowers and lenders begin negotiations on rescheduling at least $70 billion in private off-shore debt. 

 March 1 - Indonesian President Suharto says reforms prescribed by the IMF have not worked. 

 March 4 - The IMF approves release of the third tranche payment from Thailand's package and commends the Thai government for its economic reforms. 

 March 6 - IMF says its board will not discuss Indonesia's economic reform programme before April, effectively delaying a $3 billion payment initially expected by March 15. 

 March 23 - Indonesia nearly doubles interest rates to boost the rupiah and control inflation. 

 April 1 - Japan begins steps aimed at liberalising its financial markets to make them "free, fair and global" by 2001. Tokyo share prices fall, the yen dips and Japan's central bank governor pronounces every economic indicator bad. 

 April 2 - The chairman of electronics giant Sony, Norio Ohga, says the Japanese economy is on the verge of collapse. 

 April 3 - U.S. ratings agency Moody's lowers its outlook on Japan's sovereign debt to negative from stable. Asian currencies fall sharply on the news. 

 May 7 - Fears that riots in the Indonesian city of Medan will spill over into a wider social crisis send regional stocks into retreat. 

 May 11 - India stuns the world with announcement of three underground nuclear tests. Pakistan stocks tumble 3.52 percent while India's National Stock Exchange index slides 2.55 percent. 

 May 13 - The United States imposes economic sanctions on India and Japan suspends some loans. 

 May 14 - Mobs rampage through Jakarta and students demand Suharto's resignation. Indonesia's worsening crisis takes centre-stage for Asian markets, several of which suffer sharp losses. 

 May 15 - Suharto returns home from a Group of 15 summit in Egypt amid signs he is losing his 32-year grip on power. 

 May 21 - Suharto steps down under strong pressure and is succeeded by former deputy president B.J. Habibie. Markets enjoy a limited rally. Jakarta stocks surge more than three percent. 

 May 25 - South Korean shares plummet 6.78 percent despite a lifting of foreign ownership limits on stocks. Most other Asian markets shrug off Seoul's fall. 

 May 26 - Seoul's KOSPI share index continues to dive, losing a further six percent, hurt by a looming recession and labour unrest. 

 May 27 - Asian markets are hammered as the yen falls against the dollar and amid mounting fears of economic recession. Hong Kong stocks plunge more than five percent after Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa warns of possible recession. 

 May 28 - Pakistan conducts nuclear tests. 

 May 29 - The dollar rockets to a seven-year high of 139 yen on fears of a possible nuclear arms race in Asia and after news that Japan's unemployment rate hit 4.1 percent in April, its highest level since the end of World War Two. 

 Recession looms in much of Asia. Hong Kong reports that its gross domestic product contracted two percent in first quarter of 1998. About the same time Indonesia and Malaysia also report their economies contracted in the first quarter. 

 June 1 - Pakistani stocks plunge 12.38 percent as traders get their first chance to react to sanctions imposed after the country's nuclear tests. Asian markets are hit as nuclear tension adds to a cocktail of domestic problems. 

 June 5 - International lenders and Indonesian companies reach a deal to reschedule the country's massive corporate debt. 

 June 8 - The yen falls past 140 to the dollar, sending a shudder through Asian markets. Signs that Japan and other leading economies are unlikely to intervene to support the unit sap confidence further. 

 June 10 - China's central bank governor warns that the weak yen is having a severe impact on Beijing's foreign trade, raising fears that China may devalue its yuan currency. Markets across Asia tumble, led by a near five percent fall on Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index. 

 In Taiwan, the local dollar hits new 11-year lows and the Australian dollar plummets past 59 U.S. cents. 

 June 11 - U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin all but rules out the possibility of joint intervention by major industrial powers to bolster the yen. He says the weak yen reflects the state of the Japanese economy. 

 June 12 - Economic Planning Agency says Japan's gross domestic product fell by an annualised rate of 5.3 percent in the first quarter, signalling recession. The yen dives towards 145 to the dollar as hopes fade of official intervention. 

 June 17 - The U.S. joins Japan in selling the dollar in favour of the yen. 

 The action takes markets by surprise and the yen rises to a high of around 134 at one stage from a level of some 142.50 prior to the intervention. 

 June 19 - U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin tells Reuters he is not expecting high level meetings in Tokyo to produce specific new action plans on the economy. His statements put further pressure on the yen. 

 June 20 - Top finance officials from the Group of Seven meet in Tokyo and vow to cooperate as appropriate in the currency markets. 

 June 23 - IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus calls the yen fall a "crisis within the crisis". 

 June 25 - Indonesia and the IMF sign another letter of intent - the fourth. The letter says that Indonesian GDP is expected to contract by at least 10 percent in 1998 and says the rupiah will stabilise at around 10,000 by the last quarter of 1998. 

 June 26 - Malaysia cuts bank statutory reserve requirements to eight percent from 10 percent. 

 June 29 - For the first time, South Korea closes banks, shutting five ailing operations in a major step towards meeting the mandate of the massive IMF rescue package. 

 July 2 - World Bank approves $1 billion loan disbursement to Indonesia, another $6 billion to arrive from international donors. 

 Japan Prime Minister Hashimoto and the ruling Liberal Democratic Party agree to adopt bridge bank system to tackle the country's massive bad loans. 

 July 4 - Foreign Minister Keizo Obuchi hints at permanent tax cuts. 

 July 8 - Hashimoto vows to seek permanent tax cuts and an overhaul of the tax system, but reveals no details. 

 July 9 - South Korea announces its intention to double this year's budget deficit in a bid to stimulate the economy. 

 July 12 - The ruling LDP is trounced in Upper House elections, winning only 44 seats, well short of a majority and 17 less than the 61 it had held prior to the election. 

 South Korea's Financial Supervisory Commission imposes involuntary restructuring on conglomerates, or chaebols, directing eight banks to pick about 16 chaebols for the exercise. 

 July 13 - PM Hashimoto announces his resignation and cancels planned official visits to France and the United States. 

 July 14 - Tens of thousands of South Korean workers down tools to protest against wage cuts and layoffs, part of the massive corporate restructuring programme. 

 July 15 - IMF approves immediate $1 billion loan payment to Indonesia. 

 July 16 - Striking Korean workers return to work, but warn of further protests if necessary. 

 Indonesia revises 98/99 budget to reflect the deteriorating economy, assuming a rupiah/dlr rate of 10,600. 

 Foreign governments announce their agreement to reschedule the country's $54.4 billion in sovereign debt. 

 July 20 - Protests begin at Hyundai's factory in Ulsan, striking workers pitch tents. 

 July 23 - Record 7.0 percent unemployment in South Korea, with more than 1.5 million unemployed. 

 July 24 - Obuchi wins 225 votes out of 411 in LDP voting to become LDP president and, almost certainly, prime minister. 

 July 29 - Moody's Investors Service warned that it may downgrade credit ratings of Thai banks due to poor results. 

 July 30 - Parliament formally names Obuchi prime minister; he then announces his new cabinet. 

 August 3 - Thailand unveils 25 point plan to salvage its economy at the start of two weeks of talks with the IMF. The plan includes measures to create jobs and stimulate the economy, and is later endorsed by the IMF. 

 Indonesia launches debt rescheduling agency to aid the country's debt-ridden companies. 

 August 6 - New Japanese prime minister Obuchi announces a plan to vary tax cuts according to existing tax brackets, and says he will ask parliament to approve cuts worth more than six trillion yen ($41.3 billion). 

 August 14 - The Hong Kong government intervenes in the local stock market, buying stocks to squeeze out investors accused of playing the currency and interest rates against the stock market. The Hang Seng Index soars 8.47 percent. 

 August 17 - Russia effectively devalues the rouble and declares a 90-day moratorium on some foreign debt. The next day, Asian markets slide. 

 Thousands of Hyundai Motor workers rally near the South Korean company's main factory complex in Ulsan, suspending production in protest over layoffs. Police stand ready for action. 

 August 25 - Hyundai workers return to work after a union-brokered agreement to limit number of layoffs. 

 August 26 - IMF approves $1 billion loan to Indonesia. 

 August 31 - Wall Street suffers its second-largest point loss in history, plunging 6.37 percent and sparking another series of stock market routs in Asia. 

 IMF approves $900 million loan payment to South Korea. 

 Sept 1 - Malaysia imposes new foreign exchange controls to contain speculation and restrict capital flows. The IMF warns that the move may undermine investor confidence. 

 Sept 2 - Malaysia announces that the ringgit will be fixed at 3.80 to the dollar indefinitely. 

 Wall Street stages its second-largest comeback in history, sparking off a rally in Asian markets. 

 Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim is sacked. Police state that Anwar is under investigation over allegations made in a banned book, "Fifty Reasons Why Anwar Cannot Become Prime Minister". 

 Sept 3 - South Korean riot police storm plants owned by Mando Machinery Corp., the country's largest auto-parts producer, to end a strike over planned mass layoffs.
