title: Thai baht tumbles to record lowcontagion, stocks s.
text:
BANGKOK, Jan 6 (Reuters) - Thailand's embattled baht tumbled to another record low on Tuesday hammered by a stampede for dollars against most regional currencies, dealers and analysts said. 

 But the stock market index, lingering now near nine-year-lows, stabilised at 367.44 at 0415 GMT, up 1.26 points after an early drop in thin, lacklustre trading. 

 The baht dived below 52.00 to the dollar early on Tuesday. It was quoted around 52.10/52.40 at 0330 GMT in the onshore market compared with 50.00/50.20 late on Monday. 

 Offshore, the baht plunged even further, to a day low of 54.40 versus 49.85/50.35 in the previous session. 

 To avert further falls in the baht, Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda said the cabinet would issue a statement to urge Thais and exporters with dollars to sell them for baht to help boost the currency. 

 "Today at the cabinet meeting, I will propose the government issue a statement calling on people and exporters who have dollars to sell them into the market...This will help the baht," he told reporters before the start of the weekly meeting. 

 The finance ministry and the central bank were looking into additional measures to fend off currency speculation, he said. 

 Dealers and analysts said the plunge in regional currencies, especially the strong Singapore dollar and Malaysian ringgit, signalled a sustained, massive capital outflow from the troubled Asian region. 

 This would make it tougher for crisis-hit Thailand, which is weathering its worst economic crisis in decades, to tackle its currency and other economic problems, they told Reuters. 

 The dollar's relentless march against the yen also made matters worse, they said. 

 "Regional factors drove the baht this low. The ringgit, rupiah, won were all hit. This is a disturbing sign, of money flowing out of the region, not just Thailand," said a dealer with a major European bank. 

 "Corporates rushed to buy dollars, fearing that if they did not cover positions now, their foreign debt burden could swell further," she said. 

 Traders suspected the Bank of Thailand may have intervened but said any kind of defence would not provide much support for the baht if the sell-off in regional currencies continued. 

 The market was still digesting the news that the Thai government would seek to review the terms of its $17.2 multilateral bail-out package arranged for it by the International Monetary Fund, they added. 

 "It is a sensible move and the fact that IMF package is a flexible one which is reviewed every three months gives some hope that some of the conditions could be adjusted to suit the changing environment," said Satien Tantanasarit, vice president of Thai Danu Bank. 

 But others cautioned the move to review the package could backfire. 

 "It is also a delicate issue which could develop into a negative factor if not properly handled," said one dealer. 

 The dollar buying squeezed liquidity in the money market, sending the overnight interbank rate soaring to 25-26 percent among major local banks. But some foreign banks were said to be quoting rates as low as 17-18 percent. 

 While most investors stayed on the sidelines in the stock market because of the baht's steep fall, some bought cheap bank shares which helped the index post modest gains, brokers said. 

 "It's mixed. Some still look to buy counters that have minimal foreign exchange exposure and those in the export sector which benefit from the weak baht," said one broker from a major local house. 

 "But other negative factors, the baht, the swelling debt, weighed on sentiment. Moreover, no one believes that the market has already bottomed out," he said.

title: Thailand /Ctrl Bank/ Intervention  -3: Probe By Crime-Buster
text:
Duangmanee, the central bank spokeswoman, said the central bank was increasing its inspections of currency transactions at commercial banks. 

 She declined to say how many transactions had been scrutinized or whether any violations had been found. 

 Thai and foreign bankers said they had seen no additional scrutiny. 

 'There's information submitted every day by commercial banks to the Bank of Thailand,' said James Roe, a treasury manager at Chase Manhattan Bank in Bangkok. 

 'It's normal practice to give information at the end of the day, and for the Bank of Thailand to ask about certain transactions. There hasn't been an unusual number of inquiries from the bank recently.' 

 Thai officials have frequently attributed trouble in the country's financial markets to foreign mischief, usually by currency or stock market speculators. 

 In July, Thai police raided the offices of two securities houses, ABM-AMRO Hoare Govett Asia Investment Research Ltd. and Capital Nomura PCL, amid rumors five Thai banks were about to fail. The raids resulted in no prosecutions. 

 On Wednesday, the Bangkok Post newspaper said the country's top crime-buster, Police Lt.-Gen. Seri Temiyavej, was investigating companies suspected of having caused the baht's steep fall this week. Seri couldn't be reached for comment. 

Currency dealers said the baht's slump this week was the result simply of a rush by Thai corporations to repay an estimated $6 billion foreign-currency debt due in December. 

 'What's driving the exchange rate is a general need by customers to hedge their exposure,' Roe of Chase Manhattan said. 'That typically comes to a crescendo at the end of the year.'

 Duangmanee declined to say whether Peregrine was formally under investigation, and a top Peregrine executive declined to comment.

 The baht has since fallen 45% against the dollar, putting many debt-ridden Thai corporations on the brink of insolvency. 

 The forward commitments have been a steady drain on the country's foreign reserves, which have been stabilized only by regular cash infusions by the IMF. 

 In the last two weeks of November, the Bank of Thailand repaid $2.1 billion of its forward commitments, bringing reserves down to a three-month low of $26.3 billion. 

 Under an agreement with the IMF, which provided a $17.2 billion bailout for Thailand, the country must maintain reserves of at least $23 billion this year. 

 That has restricted the central bank's ability to intervene in currency markets, bankers said. 

 But the central bank still retains other means of control, including anti-speculation regulations and tough talk, or 'moral suasion,' bankers said. 

 In May, to fight currency speculators, the Bank of Thailand ordered Thai commercial banks to stop selling baht to foreigners unless they could prove the currency wouldn't be used for speculation.

title: Thailand  Ctrl Bank Uses Verbal  Intervention  To Boost Baht
text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--Thailand's central bank, having nearly exhausted its war chest of foreign-currency reserves to prop up the baht this year, has begun to use a cheaper defense, bankers say: the threat of prosecution. 

 The Bank of Thailand said Wednesday it increased its vigilance of currency transactions to stamp out speculation that may have caused the baht to fall to a historic low this week. A spokeswoman said the bank had toughened enforcement of regulations imposed in May to curb speculators. 

 'We're asking for more information on foreign exchange transactions, and why they're needed,' said the spokeswoman, Duangmanee Vonpradhip. 'We'll warn them first (if regulations are violated) and try to get their cooperation. After that we have to take legal action.' 

 But several Thai and foreign bankers said they had detected no additional scrutiny from the central bank or from other regulators. They deemed the announcement a 'psychological ploy' to help stabilize the baht, which fell Tuesday to an all-time low of 49.50 to the dollar. The baht recovered to finish Wednesday at 46.90 to the dollar in domestic spot trading. 

 The baht may not have needed much help from regulators Wednesday. Although many currency dealers said the central bank's tough talk contributed slightly to its rise, they said most of the boost was provided by the yen's surge against the U.S. dollar. The dollar slumped late Wednesday to 126.85 yen from 130.80 yen earlier in the day, boosting many Asian currencies as it fell. 

 'The Bank of Thailand's use of verbal intervention is probably the first time it has used an opportunity created by the weakness of the dollar to apply psychological pressure to boost the baht,' said Ananda Bhaumik, a treasury consultant at Thailand's Laem Thong Bank PCL.

title: Thailand Baht Ends At New Low After Testing 49.50 To Dlr
text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--The Thai baht slumped to an all-time low of 49.50 to the dollar in intraday trading in the domestic spot market Tuesday, although it perked up slightly at the close of trading after intervention by the Thai central bank, dealers said. 

 The Thai currency was mixed in the swap market, where investors make agreements to buy and sell baht at fixed prices at fixed times in the future. One- and six-month premiums were down, although the two-month premium rose. 

 At the close of trading Tuesday, the dollar was 48.35 baht in the domestic spot market, up from 47.50 baht late Monday. At that level, the Thai baht is down 46.5% against the dollar since July 2, when the country abandoned its fixed exchange rate system. In offshore trading, the dollar closed at 47.15 baht, unchanged from late Monday. 

 Dealers attributed the slump to growing fears that the government will decree a halt to all repayment of public and private sector debt. The Thai government has said it is not considering a debt moratorium because Thai corporations so far have been able to refinance most of their debt. 

 But currency dealers said Thai corporations remain panicky about the dollar's ascent and are scrambling to buy dollars to repay foreign currency debts. That, in turn, has driven the baht lower. 

 Already many Thai corporations have been pushed to the brink of insolvency by the baht's slide. 'There's a big fear of defaults,' a dealer at the Bank of Tokyo said. 

 He said, however, that central bank intervention helped stabilize the currency. The Bank of Thailand sold dollars to foreign banks to strengthen the Thai currency. A spokeswoman for the central bank couldn't be reached for comment.

title: Thai baht firmer late after  central bank  action.
text:
BANGKOK, Dec 16 (Reuters) - The Thai baht firmed in early evening trade on Tuesday as central bank intervention helped bolster the currency, dealers said. 

 The Bank of Thailand's action sparked some profit taking, and a mild rebound in regional currencies following the Indonesian central bank's support for the rupiah earlier, also helped steel the baht in late trade, they added. 

 After a see saw day the baht was quoted late at 47.60/48.10 per dollar. It had opened this morning at an all time low of 48.45/48.95 and weakened further to trade at an all-time low of 49.35 in mid-morning before dealers said they believed the Bank of Thailand stepped in. 

 "It was very volatile, up and down. At first I thought it was demand from corporates that pushed the baht weaker and then after it broke the 49 level, I think exporters came to sell U.S. dollars and the central bank intervened in the market," said a dealer at a local bank. 

 "That pushed the baht much stronger, to a low for today of about 47.40. After that I think some corporates were buying back and pushed the rate back again," he said. 

 A recovery in regionals and some profit-taking helped pare late losses and may give the baht a steadier tone on Wednesday, dealers said. 

 The volatility helped many players end the day with square positions, dealers said. They said central bank intervention may have amounted to $10 million with a moderate overall volumes. 

 Locally one month forward swap rates quoted at 38/43 satang per dollar against 39/44 earlier. The baht also firmed to 46.90/47.20 per dollar offshore from 47.30/47.50 this morning.

title: Thai baht in free fall, hit by Asia  currency  woes.
text:
BANGKOK, Dec 12 (Reuters) - The Thai baht extended its free fall late on Friday tumbling to its all-time low of 45.60 to the dollar depressed by the battered Korean won and the Indonesian rupiah, dealers said. 

 Spot baht onshore was quoted at an all-time low of 45.50/45.80 to the dollar late on Friday against a 44.30/44.60 range early and 43.50/43.60 on Thursday afternoon. 

 "It traded at 45.60 in the late afternoon. Anything can happen to the baht if the (Korean) won and (Indonesian) rupiah are still under attack next week. There's not much Thailand can do to stop it," said a money market dealer at a foreign bank. 

 Dealers said they could not detect any signs of intervention by the Bank of Thailand to defend the baht. 

 Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai and Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda said the baht's big setback on Friday was influenced solely by offshore factors. 

 "The heavy impact from South Korea and Indonesia is being felt widely throughout the region. We must accept the fact that this is unavoidable," Chuan told reporters. 

 The rupiah fell to 5,255/5,325 to the dollar late on Friday from an opening of 4,640/4,680. 

 The won, facing heavy beating for the fifth day this week, recovered after active intervention by the Korean government which sent the currency to close Friday at 1,710 to the dollar against 1,719.8 on Thursday. 

 Chuan appealed for public calm, saying his government was determined to stabilise the baht through consistent economic policies. 

 Tarrin pledged he would focus on adopting sound economic measures that would boost market confidence. He said short-term Thai interest rates may have to stay high temporarily to help slow the baht's slide. 

 He told reporters he regarded the baht's early stability as more vital and urgent than easing heavy financing burdens faced by Thai businesses. 

 "On interest rates, we will keep them temporarily high to help ease domestic problems. Stability of our exchange rate is more important," he said. 

Central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulswadsi said: "At a time like this, we are hard pressed to resist the trend but we will try to slow down any rapid slide of the baht. We should not be panicked by news reports." 

 Dealers said the Bank of Thailand, in a move to slow market flight to dollars, raised its one-day bond repurchase rate to 22.00 percent at the close from 20.75 at opening. 

 They said the baht would have little chance of escaping the fallout of the regional debacle despite recent signs of improvement in Thailand's economic fundamentals. 

 "Our economic indicators have started to improve slowly but under the current circumstances, they don't mean anything in terms of helping the baht," a currency dealer said. 

 Thai stocks, languishing near their nine-year lows, remained weak on Friday in the wake of the regional crisis but managed to end the day with only mild losses, brokers said. 

 The SET Index closed down 3.12 points, or 0.84 percent, to 368.39 on moderate 3.82 billion baht turnover partly boosted by a second consecutive day of big lot transactions, brokers said.

title: FOCUS-Thai baht dives, little sign of BOT support.
text:
BANGKOK, Dec 12 (Reuters) - Thai leaders said on Friday the battered baht was hard pressed to resist sustained regional currency turmoil but dealers said they did not detect any clear signs of central bank intervention. 

 The baht hit its all-time low of 45.30 to the dollar at around 0500 GMT, after it opened at 44.30/44.60 and against 43.50/43.60 late on Thursday. 

Central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulswadsi said: "At a time like this, we are hard pressed to resist the trend but we will try to slow down any rapid slide of the baht. We should not be panicked by news reports." 

Foreign exchange dealers were divided on whether or not  the Bank of Thailand (BOT) had intervened on behalf of the baht. 

 A senior currency dealer at Bank of Asia Plc, said the central bank might have stepped in when the baht fell to nearly 45.00 to the dollar in late morning. But any such intervention was small as the currency resumed its slide shortly after, she said. 

 The baht stabilised at 44.65/44.95 by 0749 GMT. 

 "Some dollar bids were quickly liquidated. The central bank may have intervened but the amount must have been small, likely not more than $20 million. The authorities have indicated they have no intention to use too much money to do this," she said. 

 Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai on Friday appealed for public calm and said his government was determined to stabilise the currency through consistent economic measures. 

 Chuan said he and Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda closely monitored regional currency markets but his government would not take any action that could aggravate the baht's weakness. 

 Chuan blamed the baht's new low on heavy fresh setbacks of the South Korean won and the Indonesian rupiah on Friday. 

 "The heavy impact from South Korea and Indonesia is being felt widely throughout the region. We must accept the fact that this is unavoidable," the prime minister said. 

 A dealer at a foreign bank said some U.S. bank branches were active dollar bidders, partly induced by sustained tumbling of the won and rupiah. 

 Another trader at Bank of Ayudhya Plc, said the baht would look quite defenceless if the rupiah retreated below 5,000 to the dollar. 

 Later the rupiah did pierce that level and at 0742 GMT was quoted at 5,015/5,065 to the dollar. 

 A trader at Bank of America said year-end commercial dollar demand was evident on Friday in Thailand with foreign oil firms among major bidders. 

 He expected the baht to consolidate at about 45.00 if the regional currency crisis did not intensify next week. 

 Finance Minister Tarrin said on Friday Thailand needed to keep short-term domestic interest rates high to help slow a sustained slide of the baht. 

 Tarrin told reporters he regarded the baht's early stability as more vital and urgent than easing heavy financing burdens faced by Thai businesses. 

 "On interest rates, we will keep them temporarily high to help ease domestic problems. Stability of our exchange rate is more important," he said.

title: Thai markets await govt decision on finance firms.
text:
BANGKOK, Dec 7 (Reuters) - Thai financial markets are expected to steady this week as focus turns a government announcement expected on Monday on the fate of 58 suspended financial firms, analysts said. 

 Last week the battered stock market hovered near nine-year-lows while the baht plunged to an all-time low of 42.90/43.10 on December 3 on mainly regional concerns. 

 The markets recovered slightly toward the end of the week as South Korea struck a deal for a $57 billion bail-out package with the International Monetary Fund and the Bank of Thailand intervened to support the baht, dealers said. 

 "Investors are waiting for a government decision on the fate of 58 suspended finance companies which will be announced on Monday," said Thanadech Mahapokai, first assistant vice president of Book Club Finance and Securities. 

 "They also want to know how foreign creditors of the suspended firms would get their money back," he told Reuters. 

 Analysts said the government must find ways to solve the problems of the suspended firms' foreign loans estimated at $16 billion. 

 Monday's announcement by Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda set for 0130 GMT was expected to build confidence in Thailand's ability to handle its worst economic crisis in decades, analysts said. 

 If tough action was taken against the firms, it would underline the government's commitment toward restoring the tired Thai economy under a rehabilitation plan agreed with the IMF, which brokered for the country a $17.2 billion bail-out fund. 

 The IMF has said most of the debt-ridden firms -- seen as largely responsible for Thailand's crisis -- were insolvent and should be shut permanently. Its director-general Michel Camdessus said last Friday he believed Thailand would make a bold decision on the firms. 

 Analysts expect less than 10 of the 58 suspended firms to reopen. Total assets of the suspended firms are put by industry sources at 800 billion baht ($190.5 billion) while their loans outstanding amount to about half their assets. 

 Singapore-based financial consultancy I.D.E.A. said in a report that market expectations that only three of the suspended finance firms would be allowed to reopen had helped support the baht last week. 

 The central bank had lent the firms over 430 billion baht to tide them over during their liquidity problems. 

 The Financial Restructuring Agency (FRA), which has recommended action against the finance firms, will separate their good assets from bad ones after the key announcement. The Asset Management Corp (AMC) will manage bad assets. 

 The FRA and AMC were set up by decree. 

 Analysts said the Thai stock index, which finished at 388.77 on Thursday, the last trading day of last week, would possibly make a more significant recovery in the latter part of the first quarter of 1998. 

 The upcoming holiday season coupled with Thailand's current slump would keep most investors sidelined from the market. 

 "The country's economy is expected to show signs of improvement in the second quarter of next year and I think it would be the best time for investment on the market during the first quarter," Thanadech said. 

 Overall stock prices are valued at less than 20 percent of prices posted in mid-1996, he added. 

 "Any recovery in the market will require solid convincing evidence of an economic turnaround with renewed monetary expansion accompanied by lower interest rates," said Barry Yates, head of regional research at Seamico Securities. 

 High interest rates have risen further recently with major banks raising key ledning rates by 50 basis points. The minimum lending rate now stands at 15.25 percent, choking businesses. 

 The baht has lost almost 40 percent of its value since it was floated on July 2, causing heavy foreign exchange losses for many companies. 

 "Looking ahead, the underlying (baht) sentiment has not changed. Market trades are thin and confidence is weak. However, we may be able to enjoy mild relief so long as no major blow up occurs this month," I.D.E.A. said.

title: Thai baht slide ebbs late on  central bank  defence.
text:
BANGKOK, Dec 3 (Reuters) - The Bank of Thailand intervened in the spot market in the afternoon session on Wednesday and succeeded in halting a slide in the Thai baht after it tumbled to a record low against the dollar, dealers said. 

 The intervention helped the baht to recover and be quoted at 42.58/42.68 per dollar in late afternoon against a record low earlier in the day of 42.90/43.10 per dollar in the onshore market. The day's low was recorded at 42.95 

 "I think in the afternoon the baht is stronger because the central bank intervened in the market," said a dealer at a local bank. 

 Dealers at other banks said they suspected some limited central bank intervention in the spot market was responsible for the baht's late resurgence. 

Central bank Governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi had earlier urged the market to remain calm as the South Korean won's problems sent regional currencies into a tailspin and Thai corporates bought dollars to service foreign debt repayments falling due, dealers said. 

 "I think some corporates were panicked by the market because the baht slipped so fast and they are thinking about covering their positions in case the baht weakens again to 45 or 50," said the local bank dealer. 

 "There are internal and external problems for the Thai baht. Externally there is the Korean merchant banks and that might be asked to close. That has affected the won, the ringgit and the Thai baht," he added. 

 Internally there were concerns about a government announcement due on Monday regarding the fate of 58 suspended finance companies, dealers added. 

 A decision on the firms' future is due on Monday. 

 The central bank intervention should encourage some profit taking on Thursday and help neutralise dollar demand ahead of a bank holiday weekend, dealers said. 

 In the offshore market the baht quoted late at 42.38/42.58 per dollar, off an intraday low of 42.75. 

 The domestic one month swap premium edged up to 32/37 satang per dollar against 30.5/35 in the morning. 

 Large local banks quoted the interbank overnight rate at 22 percent, unchanged from the morning, dealers said.

title: FOCUS- Central bank  lifts Thai baht from slump.
text:
BANGKOK, Dec 3 (Reuters) - Thailand's embattled baht dived into uncharted territory on Wednesday, but the central bank managed to pull the currency out of the doldrums by intervening in the market, dealers said. 

 Analysts, however, predicted the baht would tumble further in the near term with no bottom in sight as long as an Asian currency and financial crisis spooked the region. 

Central bank intervention helped the baht recover to be quoted at 42.58/42.68 per dollar in late afternoon against a record low earlier in the day of 42.90/43.10. The day's traded low was 42.95. 

 "I think in the afternoon the baht is stronger because the central bank intervened in the market," said a dealer at a local bank. Other dealers said they also saw Bank of Thailand intervention prop up the beleaguered currency. 

 Dealers said the Thai unit was driven to record lows by dollar buying from companies which need to meet year-end debt repayments and on worries over South Korea's financial crisis and the battered won currency. 

 Historic lows reached by the Malaysian ringgit and the Indonesian rupiah added to its woes. 

 Earlier on Wednesday, Thailand's central bank governor appealed for calm after the baht's plunge. 

 Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi told a news conference the central bank was monitoring the sliding Thai unit closely and would use its limited resources prudently to stabilise the currency. 

 Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda also tried to talk up the baht by saying its plunge was caused by regional fallout rather than local issues, and there was not much Thailand could do because of limited financial resources. 

 "It is more of a regional problem than local. Won and worries over regional economic crisis depressed the baht," he said. 

 The weak baht dampened sentiment in the stock market but the index closed with only a small loss of 0.76 points at 377.38 as bargain hunters returned to an oversold market, brokers said. 

 Dealers and analysts told Reuters they had expected the baht to break the 43.00 per dollar level on Wednesday and possibly head toward the 45.00-level in coming months if Asia's financial problems lingered. 

 The baht has been dogged by misfortune and has lost almost 40 percent of its value since it was floated in July when the currency was at about 26.00 to the dollar. 

 Thailand is struggling with its worst economic crisis in decades and has accepted a $17.2 billion multilateral bail-out package arranged by the International Monetary Fund (IMF). 

 The finance sector is in trouble with 58 debt-ridden firms suspended by the authorities and a final decision on their fate expected on December 7. Businesses are closing and unemployment is on the rise. 

 "The Thai baht has been lacking in depreciation recently alongside with other regional currencies and today's weakness is a catch up," said Andy Tan, general manager overseeing regional currencies at Standard and Poor's-MMS Singapore. 

 "Sentiment was also affected by Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai's comments that the economy was in worse shape than he had imagined." 

 Chuan was quoted by the International Herald Tribune as saying in an interview that "in truth there are deep down problems that are much worse than what the people perceive". 

 Speaking to Reuters, Tan said: "We are in uncharted territory. The regional crisis is showing no signs of abating." 

 "A lot hinges on how the Korean situation turns out. As long as there are uncertainties, dollar-baht will continue to slide. 

 "No real bottom is seen for now, hopefully we will get new direction and sentiment will change in the new year," he said. 

 Satian Tantanasarit, vice president at the Thai Danu Bank's treasury department, said he was surprised the baht had fallen so sharply in the onshore market. 

 "We are all surprised by the fall and that the baht should behave like this in the onshore market. People are all just following...it should cap at 43.00 per dollar today and in three to four months, if things continue like now, we could hit 45.00," he said.

title: Key dates in Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 21 (Reuters) - South Korea said on Friday it was talking to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) about emergency loans. 

 This was the latest development in a string of financial crises across Asia. 

 The following are key dates: 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency is hit by a massive attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thailand's finance minister. 

 July 2 - The Bank of Thailand announces a managed float of the baht and calls on the International Monetary Fund for "technical assistance". 

 The announcement effectively devalues the baht by 15-20 percent. It ends at a record low of 28.80 to the dollar. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central bank Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. The intervention works and the currency hits a high of 2.5100/10 after a low of 2.5240/50. 

 July 11 - The Philippine central bank says in a statement it will allow the peso to move in a wider range against the dollar. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah is starting to be affected. In a surprise move, Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support under fast-track regulations drawn up after the 1995 Mexican crisis. 

 July 24 - Currency meltdown. 

 The ringgit hits a 38-month low of 2.6530 to the dollar. Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad launches bitter attack on "rogue speculators". 

 The Hong Kong dollar remains steady, but territory later reveals US$1 billion was spent on intervention during a period of two hours on an unspecified day in July. 

 August 5 - Thailand unveils an austerity plan and complete revamp of its finance sector as part of IMF-suggested policies for a rescue package. 

 August 11 - The IMF unveils in Tokyo a rescue package for Thailand including loans totalling $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 13 - The rupiah begins to come under severe pressure. It hits an historic low of 2,682 to the dollar before ending at 2,655. The central bank actively intervenes in its defence. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of managing the exchange rate through the use of a band. The rupiah plunges to 2,755. 

 August 19 - The South Korean won hits an all time low of 901 to the dollar. The currency has been sliding gradually during the year. On January 1 it stood at 842. 

 August 20 - The IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. The package now totals $16.7 billion. Brunei later adds $500 million to the bailout package, bringing it to a total of $17.2 billion. 

 Oct 2 - Won slips to 913.50 on news Ssangbang Wool faces a debt default. Corporate defaults have been one of the reasons for the won's fall. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 28 - The won's fall accelerates. It ends at 953 despite central bank intervention. 

 Oct 30 - The won -- which has a 2.25 percent daily trading band -- hits its lowest permitted level of 984.70. 

 Oct 31 - The IMF package for Indonesia is unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although the front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 Nov 1 - The won will "never, never, never" breach the psychologically important 1000 barrier a Korean central bank official says. 

 Nov 2 - Indonesia announces the liquidation of 16 unhealthy banks under the IMF economic reform programme. 

 Nov 4 - Thailand's government collapses as Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh resigns. The baht rises to 38.75 from 40.95 on the unpopular premier's departure. 

 Nov 7 - The markets are now openly speculating Seoul will have to go to the IMF to help defend the won. The won ends at 979.90 and traders are targetting the 1000 barrier. 

 In Thailand, opposition Democrat leader Chuan Leekpai says he will form the new government. 

 Nov 9 - Chuan is appointed new Thai premier. 

 Nov 10 - The won closes at 999.00 to the dollar. 

 Nov 17 - South Korea cracks. The central bank announces it will no longer defend the 986 level to the dollar. The won immediately falls its daily limit down to 1008.60. 

 Nov 18 - The Korean central bank suggests to the finance ministry that Korea should seek an IMF bailout loan. The won is at its 1012.80 daily limit low. 

 Nov 19 - Korean finance minister Kang Kyong-shik resigns to take responsibility for the financial turmoil. South Korea also widens its daily band limit on the won to 10 percent. 

 Nov 21 - Finance ministry official announces that Seoul is discussing details of a bailout package with the IMF.

title: Bank Of Thailand/Exporters -2: Must Help Stabilize Market
text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--The governor of Thailand's central bank on Wednesday urged Thai exporters to sell dollars they have been hoarding, saying their help was necessary to help stabilize the Thai currency. 

 The call from Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi came as the U.S. dollar rose above 40 baht for the first time in two weeks amid a rush by Thai corporations to repay foreign-currency debt. Dealers said demand for dollars was intensified by the slump of the South Korean won, which has sparked worries that that country may also need a bailout by the International Monetary Fund. 

Thailand's central bank, once vigorously interventionist in defense of its currency, now only occasionally expresses public disapproval of movements in the Thai currency market. 

 Around 0632 GMT (1:32 a.m. EST), the dollar was at 40.30 baht in the domestic spot market, up from 39.875 baht at the close of trading Friday. 

 Thai economists have said the country, now in recession for the first time in more than a decade, cannot afford to have the dollar above 40 baht for any length of time. Chaiyawat said exporters had been hoarding dollars on expectations that the U.S. currency will continue to rise against the baht. They should do their part to help strengthen the currency, he said. 

 'This is important to stabilize the markets,' he said. 

 -By Joe Rebello; 662 267-9883

title: FOCUS-Asian  currencies  uninspired as dollar drops.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies softened on Thursday while the Indonesian rupiah found itself torn between its central bank and companies seeking dollars. 

 Dealers said IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus's calming words about Southeast Asia's efforts to pull out of months of economic turmoil were largely ignored by the market. 

 Camdessus, on a tour of Southeast Asia, said he believed Asia would quickly rebound from its current crisis and should be able to return to high rates of economic growth. 

 He said Thailand had passed its first IMF review while Hong Kong and Malaysian banks were unlikely to face a crisis. 

 He also said Malaysia was in solid economic condition, though its current account gap was still on "the higher side". 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah was pushed to a high of 3,355 to the dollar in early trade on talk Bank Indonesia had sold dollars above the 3,400 level in Jakarta and Singapore markets. 

 But there was no official confirmation of the intervention and no clear sign the central banks of Japan and Singapore were involved in the operation, as was the case twice last week. 

 The rupiah drifted lower on dollar demand from offshore parties, especially Japanese companies, in afternoon trade. It was quoted at 3,400/10 to the dollar at 1010 GMT amid vague talk Bank Indonesia had checked rates above the 3,400 level again. 

 "We heard BI had been checking rates for the third time but I'm not sure if they actually sold dollars," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 "I don't think BI coming in alone would scare the market. It's unlikely they'll have that much effect unless they come in with the Bank of Japan (BOJ) and Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)," she added. 

 The Japanese finance ministry and the MAS declined to comment on whether the BOJ had taken part in the intervention. 

 Other Asian currencies looked soft but dealers said the market lacked energy as many players were winding down for the end of the year and the dollar's abrupt drop against the yen on talk of BOJ intervention also dominated interest. 

 In Thailand, the baht was steady but weak at 38.70/80 to the dollar against 38.55/65 late on Wednesday. The offshore rate was at 38.30/31 against 37.999/00. 

 Dealers said the market was awaiting the announcement of Thai Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai's new cabinet. Chuan was due to present his cabinet list for approval to King Bhumibol Adulyadej later on Thursday. 

 Dealers said the baht did not react to comments by the IMF's Camdessus that the Fund had no plans to make changes to Thailand's economic programme. 

 In Bangkok, Supachai Panitchpakdi, expected to be named deputy premier in charge of economic affairs in the new cabinet, appeared to echo the IMF chief's statements. 

 He said Thailand did not intend to renegotiate the terms of the IMF-led $17.2 billion economic bailout package. 

 The Singapore dollar eased to 1.5795/10 to the U.S. dollar against 1.5746/66 on Wednesday on buying of the Malaysian ringgit/Singapore dollar cross. 

 "There's been some ringgit/Sing buying going through. There's talk that the cross might go to 50 cents but I think it has to break 48.20 first," a European bank dealer said. 

 The ringgit was at 47.70/89 Singapore cents at 1010 GMT. 

 Across the border, the ringgit showed little sign of stirring out of the range it has established against the U.S. dollar in recent sessions, hovering around 3.3000/100. 

 The Philippine peso ended lower at 33.93 per dollar against a previous close of 33.43 on dollar short-covering and offshore dollar demand. 

 Dealers said the central bank intervened to sell about $4 million at 33.98 pesos in late trade, but further falls were expected to be capped by inflows from overseas contract workers. 

 In north Asia, the Korean won ended up at 986.70 to the dollar as the central bank kept to its staunch defence, selling dollars at 988.00 won in opening trade while repeating its daily words of support. 

 "Our stance to maintain the won steadily stronger has not changed," said Lee Eung-baek, chief of the central bank's foreign exchange division. 

 The Bank of Korea has moved its defence line up by one won to the dollar for each of the last two days, steering the embattled currency away from the 1,000 level eyed by the market. 

 But its actions have taken their toll on the money market where the overnight call loan rate hit a yearly high of 14.90 percent on Thursday. 

 Seoul traders said the market was awaiting a government package of measures to stabilise financial markets. 

 The Taiwan dollar slid to T$31.105 against its previous T$30.992 close on jitters about the weak yen and won. 

 After the market close, the central bank said there was no change in its monetary policy for the time being and it reserved the right to intervene in forex market when needed. 

 The Hong Kong dollar ended lower at 7.7320/40 to the U.S. dollar from Wednesday's 7.7300/10 close as interest rates eased. 

 Dealers said liquidity improved after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) clarified its rules on borrowing from its discount window. 

 On October 23, the HKMA had said it would levy penal rates on "repeated borrowers" at the window, making banks wary of tapping the facility and leading to a liquidity crunch.

title: Thai  Currency  Woes May Lead IMF To Revise Terms Of Aid Package
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- As its currency reaches new depths, Thailand could be forced to renegotiate the terms of its $17.2 billion loan agreement with the International Monetary Fund, economists said Friday. But the new terms may prove even more onerous for the country. 

 Three months after the IMF launched its biggest economic rescue program since the 1995 bailout of Mexico, many analysts say it has little to show for its efforts in Thailand. The baht reached a historic low Friday of 41.30 to the dollar and stock prices tested new eight-year lows. Still, Thai policymakers continue to dither over economic reform. 

 "People who used to think that the baht wouldn't go as low as 40 became very nervous and scrambled to sell the baht as a result," said one dealer at Thai Danu Bank PCL. "Many of those people, unfortunately, were Thai companies who have a lot of foreign debts to repay." 

 Thai corporations are dumping the baht for dollars on fears their debt obligations will grow larger as the baht continues to lose its value against the U.S. dollar. Thailand's private sector owes some $80 billion to foreign creditors, $37 billion of which is due in the next 12 months. 

 As the baht continued its free fall, the Bank of Thailand said it has intervened to prop up the currency, but declined to specify. Its action, however, did little to help the currency, dealers said. Any dollar selling in the next sessions will be a result of profit-taking by Thai exporters who earned their income mostly in the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 Experts say the currency's persistent decline suggests Thailand will eventually need to ask the IMF for additional cash to shore up its foreign reserves amid accelerating capital flight. The IMF, for its part, will have to revise performance targets based on what most economists agree are wildly optimistic economic-growth forecasts of 2.5% economic growth in 1997 and 3.5% in 1998. Many economists predict outright recession in 1998. 

 "Given such a weak baht, it seems the targets are going to be unachievable," said Maya Pinto, a regional economist with Independent Economic Analysis in Singapore. "The targets have to be made realistic. They need to be renegotiated." Many economists expect the IMF's growth targets to be lowered once the agency completes its first review of Thailand's economic performance Nov. 30. 

 The IMF by then is scheduled to provide the second tranche of credit to Thailand, and analysts say it may insist on stringent new policy measures in return for its largesse. It may ask for a second increase in Thailand's value-added tax, said Christa Marti, an economist with UBS Securities in Singapore. The tax was increased to 10% from 7.5% in August at the IMF's urging. 

 Thailand's financial slide has been even worse than economists expected, causing some to draw comparisons to the Mexican peso debacle. "Mexico, three months into its crisis, had its act together," said Bernhard Eschweiler, of J.P. Morgan Inc. in Singapore. Thailand's government, by contrast, has deepened the crisis by fumbling and backtracking on key economic-reform policies, many economists say. 

 Friday, the Thai central bank released data indicating just how great the cost of delay has been. Manufacturing activity in August fell 5.1% after rising 3.8% year-on-year in July, marking the first contraction in six years. Net capital outflows in August alone totaled 144.9 billion baht, up from 53.1 billion baht in July. In the eight months to August, the Bank of Thailand said, outflows totaled 229.3 billion baht. 

 Amid the outflows, only frequent drawdowns on the $17.2 billion IMF credit line has kept the country's foreign reserves from shrinking, experts say. The central bank had used up $5 billion of that credit line, including $600 million in October. Thailand's foreign reserves stood at $30.7 billion as of Oct. 15, up from $29.6 billion at the end of September. 

 The capital outflows reflect a fear among investors that the Thai government won't act decisively to fix the economy for several months, thus permitting the baht to slide further. Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, who revoked a cabinet decision to raise oil taxes this month rather than inflame his constituents, could face a general election in January. In the interim, the Thai government will be loath to make unpopular economic decisions, analysts say. 

 Under the terms of its agreement with the IMF, Thailand has to maintain foreign reserves of $23 billion in 1997 and $25 billion in 1998. It must keep inflation below 9.5% in 1997 and 5% in 1998, and maintain a budget surplus equal to 1.6% of gross domestic product in 1997 and 1% of GDP in 1998. 

 If the baht continues to decline, most economists said, most of those targets will become unattainable. "If it falls further, it will simply be disastrous," said Chalongphob Sussangkarn, a leading Thai economist who heads the Thailand Development Research Institute (TDRI). The country could reach the point of a "debt moratorium" in which the private sector is simply unable to repay its debts. Thailand, at that point, may have to rely on foreign reserves to to pay its bills. 

 Thai stock prices closed mixed Friday as investors bought selected shares on the back of relatively better trade figures released by the central bank, dealers said. But concerns over the plunging value of the baht still overshadowed the market. 

 The Stock Exchange of Thailand index closed 2.12 points higher at 447.21, compared with Thursday's close of 445.09. At Friday's close, the SET index was 46% lower than 1996's year-end close of 831.57.

title: Battered Thai baht, stocks plunge to record lows.
text:
BANGKOK, Oct 30 (Reuters) - The reeling Thai baht plunged further to an all-time low on Thursday, pulling Bangkok share prices down to their lowest close in more than eight years. 

 The baht punched through the psychological barrier of 40 to the dollar in late onshore market dealings amid active buying of safe-haven U.S. dollars, dealers said. 

 The currency has steadily declined since it was floated on July 2, plummeting 35 percent from its flotation level. 

 The bearish domestic and regional economic outlook also drove corporates and foreign funds to dump baht for dollars to raise funds to repay foreign debts or repatriate profits, they added. 

 The Bank of Thailand intervened in the market earlier in the day to prop up the sliding baht but the move had only a temporary impact and was largely ignored by market players. 

 At 1050 GMT, the baht was trading at 40.05 per dollar onshore. 

 Surprisingly, in the offshore market, which usually sees heavy speculation in the baht but was quiet due to a public holiday, the currency only hit a day low of 39.70 per dollar. 

 "People gave all kinds of reasons for the baht's fall. But the fact is we (Thailand) have $21 billion (in short term debt) due between now and the end of this year," said a senior dealer at a foreign bank. 

 "Some of that is being paid now. And if the debtors refused to roll over, it could be worse. And political and economic concerns could cause just that," he added. 

 Chatri Sophonpanich, chairman of Bangkok Bank also blamed the baht's plunge on a lack of confidence. 

 "Corporates and importers rushed to buy the greenback because they believed the baht would drop below 40 and that panicked the market," he said. 

 Dealers said they expected the baht to remain under pressure at current record-low levels unless some good news emerged. "But we don't see any good news on the horizon," said a dealer. 

 Thailand is facing its worst economic crisis in decades with big troubles in its debt-ridden finance and property sectors. The authorities have suspended 58 finance companies and set up a Financial Restructuring Agency as part of sweeping reforms to revive, merge or liquidate the firms. 

 In August, the government accepted a $17.2 billion bailout package brokered by the International Monetary Fund to help beat a liquidity crunch and put its battered economy on an even keel. 

 But investors have expressed concern that Thailand's implementation of financial reforms may be riddled with political interference or may be slower than expected. 

 A media report, later denied by the government, that Thailand might renegotiate the IMF bailout package was viewed by the markets as a sign of political interference, analysts said. 

 Compounding investor worries were political uncertainties as embattled Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh faced intra-party bickering in his six-party ruling coalition. 

 His administration, which is preparing the passage of electoral laws in parliament to set the stage for a house dissolution and fresh election early next year, is now viewed by analysts as a lame-duck, caretaker government. 

 As the baht staggered into uncharted territory, nervous stock market investors dumped shares, dragging the index down 2.64 percent or 12.07 points to 445.09. The closing level was the lowest since April 3, 1989, when it ended at 443.71. 

 "I think the big story for the stock market was that the dollar was weakening against just about everything else but the baht," said a local analyst. 

 Brokers said the market's near term future also hinged on the direction Wall Street would take on Friday and the quality of the latest leading monthly economic indicators due to be released by the central bank on Friday. 

 "I think a lot tomorrow will depend on the Dow Jones tonight and tomorrow's foreign reserves numbers, though we don't expect much," said a trader.

title: FOCUS-Thais not renegotiating IMF aid, baht dives.
text:
BANGKOK, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Thailand said on Thursday that it was not seeking to renegotiate the $17.2-billion bailout package arranged for it by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) as the baht plunged to a record low of 39.95 per dollar. 

 "It is not our intention at all to renegotiate the package. We cannot talk about renegotiation. I reaffirm that we will stick to the letter of the agreement with the IMF," Deputy Finance Minister Surasak Nananukul told Reuters. 

 He was commenting on a report in the International Herald Tribune on Thursday that said Thailand was seeking to renegotiate with the IMF. 

 The newspaper said Thai officials wanted to ease strict budget constraints and extend Thailand's borrowing limits in renegotiations early next week. 

 The baht's plunge, as Thailand weathers its worst economic crisis in decades, forced the Bank of Thailand to intervene in the forex market, a senior central bank official said. 

 After the central bank intervention, the embattled baht stabilised somewhat in the onshore market, dealers said, noting the unit had plummeted on strong demand for dollars from corporates to pay foreign debts or repatriate profits. 

 Surasak said an IMF team was in Bangkok to review the progress of Thai government steps to meet conditions in the IMF bailout package, but not for renegotiations. 

 He added that the IMF team was satisfied so far with the government's moves to cut its budget, and that Thailand had appointed a new head for its key Financial Restructuring Agency to revive, merge or liquidate 58 suspended Thai finance firms. 

 Major troubles in Thailand's debt-ridden finance and property sectors forced the country to take the IMF package in August to steady its tottering economy. 

 The government has taken painful measures, such as slashing 159 billion baht ($4.0 billion) in planned spending from its 1997/98 (October-September) budget and raising taxes on some imported goods, to meet IMF austerity requirements. 

 Separately, another deputy finance minister Chaturon Chaisang told reporters that his ministry proposed a further 18 billion baht cut in the budget. 

 The plan, to be discussed by the cabinet next Tuesday, would be an effort to try to offset revenue shortfalls that would result from recent government withdrawal of a controversial oil excise tax hike earlier this month, he said. 

 The government scrapped the unpopular one baht per litre excise tax increase on oil, which was a part of IMF austerity measures, after a major public outcry. 

 Finance Minister Kosit Panpiemras told reporters on Thursday that civil servants need not fear their salaries would be cut as part of austerity measures. But cuts would be made in spending by state enterprises. 

 "There will be no oil tax increase and no salary cuts for civil servants. But there will be some cutting in the administrations of state enterprises," he said. 

 The IMF is also requiring Thailand to come up with a cash surplus of one percent of gross domestic product, equivalent to 69.8 billion baht, in its 1997/98 fiscal year. 

 Finance Minister Kosit Panpiemras said that while Thailand would be able to meet the one-percent requirement, he was unsure if the numerical value of 69.8 billion baht could be met as the level of GDP growth was now uncertain. 

 To uplift the country's ailing export sector, the central bank said on Thursday that it had raised the value of export credits to 33 billion baht from 26 billion baht. 

 The private sector would also chip in another 33 billion baht to uplift the sector which has been stung by a major liquidity crunch and a slowdown in exports growth, assistant governor Kiartisak Meechareon said. 

 Kosit said on Wednesday that Thailand proposed to cap its foreign debt at $4.0 billion, of which $2.0 billion could be used to boost liquidity in the exports sector.

title: Bank of  Thailand intervenes  to prop up baht.
text:
BANGKOK, Oct 30 (Reuters) - The Bank of Thailand started to intervene in the foreign exchange market on Thursday to prop up the baht as the unit was seen as too low, a senior central bank official said. 

 Kiartisak Meechareon, central bank assistant governor, said the baht had "overshot" but declined to elaborate further or give details of the intervention. 

 The baht plunged to 39.95 to the dollar at 0730 GMT before firming to 39.77 baht. 

 Dealers said the baht dropped sharply on strong demand for dollars from corporates which either sought to pay foreign debt or repatriate funds home. 

 "We have to intervene because the baht seemed to have overshot. There is no central bank in the world that is not concerned about its currency," Kiartisak said. 

 "The government also uses other long term measures to support the baht, such as the credit expansion to boost the export industry. Once the exports improve, the baht will be more stabilised," he said. 

 The government on Thursday increased the credit to the export sector to 33 billion baht ($846 million) from 26 billion baht. ($1 = 39 baht)

title: Thailand  Baht/Ends -2:  Intervention  Helps Only Briefly
text:
The Bank of Thailand, which has said it would stop intervening to defend the currency after a futile battle against speculators this year, on Thursday said it resumed intervention.  'There's no central bank that is not concerned about the currency level,' said Kiettisak Meecharoen, an assistant governor at the bank who announced the intervention. He declined to provide details of the nature of the intervention. 

 The Bank of Thailand set its reference rate for the dollar at 39.293 baht Thursday, up from 39.003 baht Wednesday. The reference rate is a weighted average of rates charged by Thai commercial banks the previous day. It serves as a benchmark for domestic currency trading.

title: Key dates in Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 24 (Reuters) - A dramatic week on the Hong Kong stock market, with a savage fall followed by a partial recovery, is the latest development in a string of financial crises across East Asia. 

 The following are key dates: 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency is hit by a massive attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 The Philippines is affected. The central bank raises the overnight rate 1-3/4 percentage points to 13 percent and dumps dollars. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thailand's finance minister. 

 The resignation has immediate financial impact in the Philippines, where the overnight rate rises to 15 percent. 

 June 27 - The Thai central bank suspends operations of 16 cash-strapped finance companies and orders them to submit merger or consolidation plans. 

 June 30 - Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yonchaiyudh assures the nation in a televised address there will be no devaluation of the baht. 

 July 2 - The Bank of Thailand announces a managed float of the baht and calls on the International Monetary Fund for "technical assistance". 

 The announcement effectively devalues the baht by about 15-20 percent. It ends at a record low of 28.80 to the dollar. 

 In Manila, the central bank is forced to intervene heavily to defend the peso. 

 July 3 - The Philippine central bank raises the overnight lending rate to 24 percent from 15 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central bank Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. The intervention works and the currency hits a high of 2.5100/10 after a low of 2.5240/50. 

 July 11 - The Philippine central bank says in a statement it will allow the peso to move in a wider range against the dollar. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah is starting to be affected. In a surprise move, Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support under fast-track regulations drawn up after the 1995 Mexican crisis. 

 July 24 - Currency meltdown. 

 The ringgit hits 38-month low of 2.6530 to the dollar. Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad launches bitter attack on "rogue speculators". 

 The Hong Kong dollar remains steady, but territory later reveals US$1 billion was spent on intervention during a period of two hours on an unspecified day in July. 

 July 26 - Mahathir names hedge fund manager George Soros as the man responsible for the attack on the ringgit. He later brands Soros a "moron". 

 August 5 - Thailand unveils austerity plan and complete revamp of finance sector as part of IMF suggested policies for a rescue package. Central bank suspends 48 finance firms. 

 August 11 - The IMF unveils in Tokyo a rescue package for Thailand including loans totalling $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 13 - The rupiah begins to come under severe pressure. It hits a historic low of 2,682 to the dollar before ending at 2,655. The central bank actively intervenes in its defence. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of managing the exchange rate through the use of a band. The rupiah plunges to 2,755. 

 August 16 - An unnamed Beijing source tells a local Hong Kong newspaper that China is prepared to use US$50 billion to defend the Hong Kong dollar. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. The package now totals $16.7 billion. Brunei later adds $500 to the bailout package, bringing it to a total of $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 4 - Carnage in the Philippine peso continues. It falls to a record low of 32.43 to the dollar before central bank intervention helps it up slightly to end at 32.38. 

 Ringgit breaks through 3.0000 to the dollar barrier. 

 Mahathir delays several multi-billion dollar construction projects. 

 Sept 16 - Indonesia says it will postpone projects worth 39 trillion rupiah in an attempt to slash the budget shortfall. 

 Sept 20 - Mahathir tells delegates to the IMF/World Bank annual conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral and should be stopped. 

 Sept 21 - Soros says "Dr Mahathir is a menace to his own country". 

 Oct 1 - Mahathir repeats his siren call for tighter regulation, or a total ban, on forex trading. The currency falls four percent in less than two hours to a low of 3.4080. 

 Oct 6 - The rupiah hits a low of 3,845. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 14 - Vietnam, bowing to months of pressure on its dong currency, doubles the permitted trading range to 10 percent either side of the daily official rate. 

 Oct 17 - Malaysia presents a belt-tightening budget to try to stop the economy sliding into recession. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. The Hang Seng index plunges 23.34 percent to 10,426.30 by Thursday's close, after 13,601.01 the previous Friday. 

 The Hong Kong dollar is linked to the U.S. dollar at an official rate of 7.8 to one. After the turmoil in Southeast Asian markets, the heat is on the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Oct 24 - The Hong Kong stock market makes a partial recovery, climbing 6.89 percent to 11,144.34, but this still leaves the market 25 percent weaker than it was at the start of October.

 July 3 - The Philippine central bank raises the overnight lending rate to 24 percent from 15 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central bank Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. The intervention works and the currency hits a high of 2.5100/10 after a low of 2.5240/50. 

 July 11 - The Philippine central bank says in a statement it will allow the peso to move in a wider range against the dollar. The IMF backs the move and Managing Director Camdessus says he would recommend the IMF board approve the Philippines' request for an extension of its Extended Fund Facility (EFF). 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah is starting to be affected. In a surprise move, Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support under fast-track regulations drawn up after the 1995 Mexican crisis. 

 July 24 - Currency meltdown. 

 The ringgit hits 38-month low of 2.6530 to the dollar. Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad launches bitter attack on "rogue speculators". 

 The Singapore dollar hits 32-month low of 1.4738 to the dollar. 

 The Hong Kong dollar remains steady, but territory later reveals US$1 billion was spent on intervention during a period of two hours on an unspecified day in July. 

 July 26 - Mahathir names hedge fund manager George Soros as the man responsible for the attack on the ringgit. He later brands Soros a "moron". 

 August 5 - Thailand unveils austerity plan and complete revamp of finance sector as part of IMF suggested policies for a rescue package. Central bank suspends 48 finance firms. 

 August 11 - The IMF unveils in Tokyo a rescue package for Thailand including loans totalling $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 13 - The rupiah begins to come under severe pressure. It hits a historic low of 2,682 to the dollar before ending at 2,655. The central bank actively intervenes in its defence. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of managing the exchange rate through the use of a band. The rupiah plunges to 2,755. 

 August 16 - An unnamed Beijing source tells a local Hong Kong newspaper that China is prepared to use US$50 billion to defend the Hong Kong dollar. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. The package now totals $16.7 billion. 

 August 27 - Brunei adds $500 million more to Thailand's bailout package, bringing it to a total of $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 2 - A falling equity market helps push the Philippine peso to a record low of 30.90 to the dollar. 

 In Jakarta, the rupiah ends at 3,045. 

 Sept 3 - Indonesia announces measures to revive investor confidence in the country, including scrapping a 49 percent limit on foreign purchases of shares at initial public offerings and a hike in luxury taxes. 

 The package has little impact on the rupiah. 

 Sept 4 - Carnage in the Philippine peso continues. It falls to a record low of 32.43 to the dollar before central bank intervention helps it up slightly to end at 32.38. 

 Ringgit breaks through 3.0000 to the dollar barrier. 

 Mahathir delays several multi-billion dollar construction projects. A controversial measure to ban short selling in 100 key stocks will also be withdrawn. 

 Sept 16 - Indonesia says it will postpone projects worth 39 trillion rupiah in an attempt to slash the budget shortfall. 

 Sept 20 - Mahathir tells delegates to the IMF/World Bank annual conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral and should be stopped. 

 Sept 21 - Soros says "Dr Mahathir is a menace to his own country". 

 Sept 22 - The forex market gives its answer to Mahathir. The ringgit tumbles more than two percent to end at 3.1220 to the dollar. 

 Sept 30 - Ringgit fall continues. Mahathir says in Chile that 1998 Malaysian economic growth would slow due to the falling ringgit. It hits a low of 3.2150.

title: Asian cooperation on  currencies  a way off-analysts.
text:
BANGKOK, Sept 17 - This week's meeting of seven ASEAN finance ministers in Bangkok will not specifically address cooperation on currencies, which analysts said on Wednesday would be years in the making. 

 "There is no topic, it will be an informal meeting," said Somkid Jatusipitak, adviser to Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya. 

 Ministers from seven Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) will hold talks on Thursday, one day ahead of the Asia Europe Meeting (ASEM) of finance ministers. 

 When asked about local newspaper reports that the ministers had decided to delay talks on how to deal with the currency crisis, he said: "No, I said they would discuss cooperation in general. We don't want to have any set position ahead of the ASEM meeting." 

 His reaction came as no surprise to analysts who said the region's macro-economic house had first to be put in order before any solid plans could be laid down to cooperate on currencies. 

 And that, they said, could take years. 

 "Currency cooperation requires coordination of economic policy formulation," said P.K. Basu, regional economist at UBS Securities in Singapore. 

 "If a country's economic policies don't gain the confidence of its neighbours then those neighbours will be somewhat less willing to cooperate to defend it's currency. Currency cooperation is easier said than done." 

 While reserves around the Asian region are substantial, analysts said it is not a simple matter of countries banding together with coordinated intervention should a currency come under pressure. 

 As May's Thai baht debacle showed, such a cooperation could turn out to be a bottomless pit and analysts doubt cash-rich countries would be willing to take the risk. 

 "It's fine to talk about cooperation in markets but I can't see the richer nations signing up to such a deal when there are major economic problems still to be solved," said one Singapore-based analyst who preferred not to be named. 

 "I mean Thailand has already spent billions defending the baht and to no avail, I can't see other countries signing up to any agreement on currencies until the economic situation settles down." 

 Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya has said baht intervention will deplete Thailand's reserves by six to 14 billion dollars over the next year. The International Monetary Fund is spearheading a $17.2 billion international bailout package aimed at rebuilding Thailand's reserves situation. 

 There is also the background problem of the baht devaluation itself. Analysts said it was far from clear whether Thailand's neighbours were warned about the devaluation and that could well have raised a few hackles. 

 "The devaluation had a big impact on the rest of Southeast Asia and on that there was much less evidence of coordination and cooperation than there was in May during the initial attack on the currency," UBS's Basu said. 

 There is already a repo agreement in place which is designed to help countries with foreign exchange problems, but this is designed to help with liquidity rather than providing asset power to try to stop any decline in a currency. 

 The system works by allowing a country to place its holding of U.S. Treasury bonds with another central bank for dollars on the spot market. The system simply allows a country to get hold of U.S. dollars quickly, and at attractive rates, using their U.S. Treasury paper as collateral. 

 "For any rock-solid agreement on currency cooperation you need to have similar monetary conditions in each country," said Chiang Yao Chye, Head of Asia Pacific Research at CIBC in Singapore. "Otherwise who is to determine at what rate a currency should be and why should one country spend its reserves to prop up another when it could be overvalued?"

title: Thailand /Baht Ends -2: Despite  Central Bank 's  Intervention
text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--The Thai baht slumped to a new record low in domestic spot trading Wednesday, hurt by brisk dollar-buying by Thai corporations nervous about the continued depreciation of the baht, dealers said. 

 The central bank's move to prop up the baht later in the session Wednesday - by aggressive dollar-selling - failed to take the heat off the Thai currency, dealers said. Investors, in fact, rushed to buy dollars from the Bank of Thailand to take advantage of the attractive exchange rate, dealers said. 

 At the close of trading Wednesday, the dollar was at 37.85 baht in the domestic spot market - the level dealers said was the highest in history. At that rate, the dollar was 7.7% above its closing level of 35.15 baht Tuesday. 

 The U.S. currency also closed at a historic high in the offshore market, at 35.55 baht Wednesday from 34.60 baht Tuesday. 

 Dealers attributed the scramble for dollars to investor fears of a further baht fall. Since the Bank of Thailand abandoned the fixed-exchange rate regime, the baht has lost 32% of its value against the dollar. 

 'Many people decided to dump the baht as soon as the dollar broke above 35 baht,' a dealer at Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corp. Ltd said. 'They were afraid that the dollar will rise to as high as 40 baht.' 

 The Bank of Thailand, moving to prop up the baht, offered to sell dollars to commercial banks between 36.00 and 36.50 baht in the afternoon, dealers said. However, the central bank's effort proved futile as investors continued to dump the baht in favor of the U.S. currency, dealers said. 

 'The central bank just rolled the ball into investors' court,' said a dealer at a Japanese bank in Bangkok. 'People were happy to buy dollars from the central bank because they got it cheaper than the market's rate.'

title: Thailand  Central Bank  Sells Dlrs To Prop Up Baht - Dealers
text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--Thailand's central bank on Wednesday sold dollars in the domestic spot market to prop up the weakening baht after the Thai currency hit a historic low against the dollar, dealers said. 

 Dealers weren't able to specify the amount of the Bank of Thailand's intervention. However, a dealer at a U.S. bank in Bangkok said the central bank's move helped pull the dollar off its record high of 37.50 baht reached around 0630 GMT (2:30 a.m. EDT). 

 At 0800 GMT (4:00 a.m. EDT), the dollar is at 36.75 baht, up from 35.15 baht at the close of trading Tuesday. A central bank spokesman wasn't available for comment. Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi, governor of the Bank of Thailand, declined to confirm or deny an intervention. 

 Dealers attributed the baht's slide to Thai corporations' worries about their foreign debt exposure. Thai corporations owed around $73 billion in foreign debts, most of which is unhedged. Since the Bank of Thailand abandoned its fixed exchange-rate system July 2, the baht has fallen more than 28%. 

 'Many people decided to dump the baht as soon as the dollar broke above 35 baht, which is the level never seen before in history,' said a dealer at Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corp Ltd. 'They were afraid that the dollar will rise to as high as 40 baht.' 

 Some dealers also attributed the dollar's retreat from its historic high partly to profit-taking after the dollar rose 4% since Friday. 

 'Some investors sold the dollar at 37 baht and waited to buy it back when it fell below that level,' said a dealer at Citibank in Bangkok. 'There's definitely profit-taking going on.'

title: FOCUS-More pain as Asian  currencies  plumb depths.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 3 (Reuter) - The agonisingly persistent weakening of Asian regional currencies continued with gusto on Wednesday with the Thai baht, Philippine peso and Malaysian ringgit all sagging to fresh record lows. 

 A lack of confidence in the Asian region as a whole in the wake of the Thai crisis continues to be the main driving factor and a perky U.S. dollar is not helping matters, analysts said on Wednesday. 

 The dramatic slide on most Asian stock markets reversed itself on the back of a record daily gain on Wall Street but this did nothing for the currencies. 

 The baht lost seven percent of its value in the domestic market, sinking to 37.60 per dollar in the onshore market from a previous record low of 35.15 on Tuesday evening. 

 In Malaysia, the ringgit sank as low as 2.9860 to the dollar from 2.9360/410 at Tuesday's close while the peso touched 31.83 compared with the previous 30.89 close. 

 Analysts said the action proves the slide in stocks and currencies are not directly linked, although they have both recently been falling for similar reasons. 

 Wednesday's moves reflected a belief that administrations around the region were ready to allow currencies to go even lower, they said. 

 "I think this reflects a realisation that the central banks will stop fighting so hard to defend the currencies," said James Mitchell, a strategist at Salomon Brothers in Singapore. 

 Such a stance would allow monetary policy to be relaxed, something which would help stocks but obviously hinder the currencies. 

 This was graphically displayed by the move in the Malaysian stock market, which slumped five percent while Thai and Philippine stocks rallied. 

 Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad appeared on television on Tuesday night vowing to continue to defend the currency. 

 He also announced a government proposal to spend 60 billion ringgit to buy back shares --- but said locals who wished to sell would get premium prices, while foreigners would get market prices. 

 Malaysian shares were the only ones to decline throughout the session although Thai stocks did give up early gains. 

 In the Philippines the central bank actually cut its liquidity reserves for banks to six percent from eight percent on a staggered basis, an effective, albeit mild, monetary easing. 

 Thailand said was considering similar measures. Deputy Prime Minister Virabongsa Ramangkura said he had asked the Bank of Thailand to consider relaxing a rule that commercial banks and offshore banking units set aside seven percent of imported short-term foreign funds as reserves at the central bank. 

 Ramangkura said he was also keen to see the central bank shorten a maximum 180-day period that Thai exporters can keep their dollar or foreign-currency denominated export earnings before converting them into baht. 

 Meanwhile, in Indonesia there was much talk that the recent sharp rise in central bank certificate rates, or SIBs, will be brought back down and currency intervention by Thailand was shrugged aside. 

 Even though the Thai central bank actually intervened in the market today, analysts do not believe the International Monetary Fund (IMF) -- which after providing its bail-out package does have some influence on policy -- will allow an aggressive defence of the currency. 

 Analysts also said there was little Asian governments and central banks could do to contain the sell-off in regional currencies. 

 "The danger with intervention or very tough rhetoric is you increase the chance of market players trying to test the limits. I believe the best thing would be to let what's going on run its course," said Chan Chia Lin, head of economic research at ABN-Amro Bank. 

 While recent controls on non-trade currency deals have stopped opportunist speculators from jumping on the bandwagon, currencies are still vulnerable. 

 "The imposition of controls only potentially limits the amount of short-selling of your currency by foreign players," Chan said. "But it doesn't protect you from demand for U.S. dollars from domestic corporates who have sizeable unhedged external exposure," she said.

title: Thai baht dips to new low despite  intervention .
text:
BANGKOK, Sept 3 (Reuter) - The Thai baht plunged to new lows in late trade on Wednesday in the domestic market despite intervention by the central bank to stall the baht's slide, dealers said. 

 "The central bank stepped in the market in early afternoon. But the baht continued to fall further after the dollar selling by the central bank had dried up," said one senior dealer at a foreign bank. 

 The baht dropped to new low of 37.60/37.90 near the close onshore after the Bank of Thailand's intervention pushed the baht up to 35.50/35.60 in early afternoon trade. 

 The baht was traded at around 35.70/35.90 in early morning. 

 Dealers said most importers and borrowers of foreign loans were bidding wildly for the dollar today on fear of the baht's further weakness. 

Central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi said on Wednesday the market should not panic over the baht's sharp slide, saying its setback was temporary before the currency regained its stability. 

 "(The market) should not over react to the baht's slide. The authorities would move to prevent market panic and stop its sharp fall," Chaiyawat told a news conference. 

 The governor declined to indicate the level at which the central bank would intervene to defend the baht, saying it should be determined by the market. 

 Chaiyawat said the baht's Wednesday record low was partly due to the dollar's strong rally against most currencies. He said the baht's latest decline was proportionately smaller than those sustained by other Southeast Asian currencies. 

 In the offshore market, the baht was quoted at 35.35/35.65 late compared with 34.88/34.98 in early morning trade. 

 The one-month baht/dollar swap premium was quoted at 40/50 satangs late in the onshore market and 37/47 offshore. 

 The overnight interbank rate jumped to 24 percent in late trade from 20 percent early as heavy dollar buying squeezed liquidity in the banking system, dealers said.
