title: Thai  central bank intervenes  to halt baht slide.
text:
BANGKOK, Sept 3 (Reuter) - The central bank intervened through primary local banks to halt a rapid slide in the baht on Wednesday, dealers said. 

 The baht, which had briefly hit 37.00 per dollar around midday, was being quoted at 35.50/36.00 per dollar at 0644 GMT. 

 "I see no other reason for the baht to come back to this level but intervention by the Bank of Thailand through the primary local banks," said a dealer at a local bank. 

 The central bank earlier said the baht's rapid slide on Wednesday took the currency to a level inconsistent with Thailand's economic fundamentals. 

 The baht slipped to 36.50/37.50 per dollar from 35.15/35.25 late on Tuesday as corporates continued buying dollars in anticipation of the baht's further weakness and refusal of Thai exporters to liquidate dollar holdings, dealers said. 

 Dealers said thin volumes increased market volatility. Some players said they believed the baht's sell-off looked over-extended at 37.00. 

 "The highest bid was around 37.20 but I think that's a bit overdone," said a spot dealer at a large foreign bank in Bangkok. 

 "This morning the corporates were taking any quote they could get thinking it was going to go lower but exporters were holding back. Volumes were pretty thin so it's not taking much to move market 50 satang or so," he said.

text:
Dealers said the worries over capital increases were aggravated after Siam City Bank PCL said Wednesday it was doubling its registered capital to 12 billion baht to help finance a merger between its affiliated finance companies. Investors worried that there will be more to come in the banking sector, dealers said. 

 Meanwhile, the Bank of Thailand's latest economic indicators offered little relief. Analysts said the figures mostly weighed in as expected. 

 Under its new commitment to release foreign reserves figures every two weeks, the central bank said that as of Aug. 15, its foreign reserves were at $27.9 billion baht. This is a three-year low, and investors took it as a sign that the central bank will see more declines in its foreign reserves resulting from its failed attempt to defend the Thai currency from speculative attack. This market, where investors agree to buy and sell baht at set rates at given times in the future, was the Bank of Thailand's preferred way of intervening in the currency markets. As these forward contracts become due, analysts fear Thailand's foreign reserves could fall as low as $10 billion. title: S.E.Asian  currencies  crumble as ringgit slumps.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 28 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies crumbled on Thursday as the Malaysian ringgit threw off all remnants of poise and slumped to historic lows. 

 The Thai baht, the usually sturdy Singapore dollar, the Indonesian rupiah and the Philippine peso all followed the ringgit's descent. 

 Dealers said the ringgit was hit by mounting worries about a possible trade deficit in July and investor panic triggered by the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange's unexpected move late on Wednesday to stop short-selling of major stocks. 

 The ringgit, which has now lost five percent in the past week, opened weak and ploughed through a series of historic lows, hitting 2.8920 to the dollar in late afternoon trade. 

 The Kuala Lumpur stock index fell 8.31 percent to a four-year low of 777.46 before recovering to close at 812.18. 

 "People are just liquidating their ringgit holdings. They don't want to play the market now that they've changed the rules," the head of foreign exchange at a Singapore bank said. 

 The ringgit was at 2.8840/90 to the dollar at 0930 GMT against 2.8230/80 late on Wednesday. 

 Dealers said the market was now targetting the 2.90 level for the ringgit, though the stampede was slowed somewhat by fears of intervention by Bank Negara. 

 "We think Negara might be up there near the 2.89 level. And on the swaps, every time we reach a certain level, they get pulled down," the Singapore dealer said. The central bank does not ordinarily comment on its market interventions. 

 In Thailand, the baht tumbled to a new low of 34.40 to the dollar in early trade on worries about domestic politics and declining foreign reserves. 

 Market interest was focused on a parliamentary economic debate seen as an effort to head of an opposition no-confidence motion and players showed little reaction to monthly economic data as it was braced for poor numbers. 

 Nor did Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya cause significant ripples by saying Thailand's forward swap contracts could deplete reserves by $6-14 billion over the next year. 

 "Thailand has already realised losses of $3 billion and for every day that the baht doesn't improve, they're going to lose a couple of hundred million dollars," a dealer said. 

 Thanong told parliament the expected foreign reserve loss would be covered by a $17.2 billion finance package arranged by the International Monetary Fund. 

 The baht was at 34.00/15 to the dollar onshore against 33.90/34.00 late on Wednesday. It was at 34.10/25 offshore. 

 The Singapore dollar fell to a low of 1.5185 to the U.S. dollar, dragged down by the ringgit. It was at 1.5178/88 against 1.5030/40 on Wednesday. 

 The Indonesian rupiah headed back down towards the 3,000 to the dollar level, again largely because of the ringgit's fall. 

 "It's mainly the regional factor again. The ringgit was hit overnight in London and New York which drove the Singapore dollar lower and spilled over later to Indonesia," a U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said. 

 The Philippine peso recovered from opening lows after the central bank intervened to sell dollars at the 30.30 peso level. 

 It was at 30.00/15 to the dollar against its opening 30.25. 

 The peso fell to a record low of 30.45 on Wednesday, partly on fears of funds fleeing the battered stock market. The central bank then sold $1 million and raised liquidity reserves by three percentage points. 

 The Manila share index lost 9.28 percent, its biggest drop in a decade, to end at 2,071.97 on Thursday following the release of lower first half economic growth figures. 

 The South Korean won was propped up by the central bank's repeated intervention, which triggered stop-loss dollar sales, lifting the won to 901.60 against Wednesday's close at 902.80. 

 The Taiwan dollar also ended firmer at T$28.688 as investors unloaded U.S. dollars in the face of the central bank's stubborn defence of the T$28.727 level for more than two weeks. 

 After the market close, central bank deputy governor Hsu Chia-tung said the currency had no reason to fall further and the bank would hold firm in its defence of the T$28.727 level.

title: Thai baht resumes fall, drags down other  currencies .
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 22 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies showed renewed signs of weakness on Friday as falls of the Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah infected the others. 

 The Thai baht hit a record low of 33.30 in domestic markets on heavy commercial demand for dollars and nagging concerns about the country's economic and political outlook. 

 "Some corporates might buy dollars to pay back foreign loans coming due. The volume (of dollar purchases) is quite substantial," a Bangkok dealer said. 

 The baht was at 33.13/32 to the dollar at 0410 GMT against 32.65/75 late on Thursday. The offshore rate followed suit, sliding to 32.80/33.00 against 32.30/50. 

 "With 33 being broken, the sky's the limit. It's in uncharted territory," the head of Asian currencies at a European bank in Singapore said. 

 He said the baht looked set to hit 35 to the dollar and the central Bank of Thailand (BOT) was unlikely to intervene to stop the slide. 

 "The central bank is very tied up with the IMF (International Monetary Fund) package. And as long as they're able to maintain the two-tier regime, the market will not dare to push the baht in a big way because there's not much liquidity," he said. 

 On Thursday, BOT Governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi said Thailand would receive $1.6 billion in loans immediately as the first installment of the IMF's $3.9 billion loan package.He also pledged to meet the IMF's economic goals to receive further aid. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah weakened anew as players covered short dollar positions ahead of the weekend and local companies sought to hedge their positions. 

 "The funds are buying the dollar again after liquidating their positions above the 2,900 level," the Singapore dealer said. Sentiment was also depressed by Standard and Poor's announcement on Thursday that it had revised the ratings outlook on Indonesian banks to negative from stable, he added. 

 Reports of a run on deposits at one of Indonesia's banks were also affecting the market, he said. 

 Spot rupiah was at 2,735/45 at 0410 GMT against 2,675/75 late on Thursday. 

 A Japanese bank dealer in Jakarta said the rupiah showed scope to strengthen through the 2,700 level again as the outlook for liquidity remained tight. 

 "Liquidity is still the main concern. Operators are also preparing for Monday because the previous central bank forward intervention will mature," the dealer said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit surrendered early gains and fell sharply on spillover from the rupiah and baht, though thin volumes and wide spreads continued to exaggerate activity. 

 The ringgit was at 2.7700/20 to the dollar after reaching a high of 2.7430 earlier, against 2.7650/700 late on Thursday. 

 The Singapore dollar slid back through the 1.50 to the U.S. dollar level and dealers said a breach of 1.5040 could trigger fresh buying of the U.S. dollar. 

 "But the pace will be slower as the market is looking more favourably at the Singapore dollar than the other regionals," a dealer said, citing strong Singapore export figures announced on Wednesday and an upward revision of its 1997 growth forecast. 

 The Philippine peso recovered from a weak start as exporters and other companies converted foreign currency deposits to pesos following recent central bank moves to tighten liquidity. 

 The peso was at 29.79/85 to the dollar against Thursday's close of 29.885. 

 In Taiwan, the central bank's prolonged defence of the T$28.727 level in the face of offshore speculative pressure finally dampened demand for U.S. dollars. 

 The Taiwan dollar showed a firm bias and was quoted at T$28.724/726 against Thursday's T$28.724 close. 

 Taipei dealers said inflows of foreign equity funds to the recovering stock market also helped the recovery.

title: Thailand has $23.4 bln fwd swap contracts-BOT.
text:
BANGKOK, Aug 21 (Reuter) - Thailand has $23.4 billion in forward swap contracts, which come due over the next 12 months, Bank of Thailand governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi said on Thursday. 

 Chaiyawat said $8.6 billion of the contracts are onshore and $14.8 billion are offshore. 

 He said the onshore contracts would not have much impact on foreign reserves as they would be rolled over. He said if the offshore contracts were rolled over they would not affect foreign reserves. 

 The Bank of Thailand intervened actively in defence of the baht when it was attacked by speculators in mid-May. Most three-month forward currency contracts used by foreign hedge funds during the attacks either matured or were rolled over early this week. 

 Chaiyawat said the central bank took the $8.6 billion onshore forward swap contracts as part of its normal job of maintaining short-term domestic liquidity. 

 He said Thailand would only feel a gradual impact on its foreign reserves over the next 12 months when the $14.8 billion offshore forward contracts mature without being rolled over. 

 The governor said future lower Thai foreign reserves would be replenished by loans obtained from the IMF-sponsored package.

title: Thailand/ Central Bank  Gov -3: BIS Provides 'Bridge' Credit
text:
Investors in the swap markets make agreements to buy and sell baht for a fixed price at a specified time in the future. During a series of speculative attacks on the Thai baht this year, the Bank of Thailand said it 'intervened' in those markets by borrowing the U.S. currency, although it never said how much. 

 The interventions thwarted speculators and shored up the country's foreign reserves in the short term. But because the reserves data didn't reflect the bank's swap commitments, investors began to lose faith in the published reserve numbers, analysts said. Continued intervention eventually became unaffordable, forcing the central bank on July 2 to abandon its fixed-exchange rate system, letting the baht drop 20% in value against the dollar. 

 Analysts have said the $16.7 billion aid package organized by the IMF will protect the country against a drain in foreign reserves. The IMF alone has contributed $4 billion in a 34-month standby credit agreement with Thailand. Other countries and international agencies, including Japan, China, and the Asian Development Bank, have also contributed.

title: Profit taking pushes S.E Asian  currencies  higher.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 1 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies, rocked by weeks of turmoil, firmed on Friday morning as players cashed in some of their gains on the dollar ahead of the weekend. 

 Dealers said players were reluctant to establish new positions ahead of the release of Thailand's economic rescue plan, due by August 5, which is expected to include assistance from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). 

 "Everybody wants to see what the IMF will do in Thailand on the fifth because that will indirectly affect all the other regional currencies," a Singapore-based trader said. 

 Vague rumours of an impending military coup in Thailand hit New York markets overnight, causing sales of dollar/baht and a rise in swap premiums. But the rumours had been around for weeks and little credence was attached to them, dealers said. 

 One said there was talk the Bank of Thailand had intervened to sell the dollar around 32.10 baht in Singapore markets on Friday. No confirmation was available. 

 The baht slipped back a notch from morning highs after Standard & Poor's Corp placed Thailand's "A" long-term foreign currency rating on creditwatch. 

 That was further bad news for the Thai economy, implying greater than expected loan losses in the crisis-torn financial sector. 

 The baht was quoted at 31.85/31.95 to the dollar onshore at 0435 GMT against 31.700/9500 late on Thursday. The offshore rate was at 31.80/32.00. 

 In Malaysia, the ringgit showed little immediate reaction to news Bank Negara Malaysia had asked banks to hold their base lending rates steady. 

 Banking sources in Kuala Lumpur said the central bank had asked them to hold their base lending rates at 9.67 percent despite a recent spike up in interbank rates. 

 The ringgit was at 2.6245/95 to the dollar after firming through the 2.63 level earlier on profit-taking in the dollar by funds. 

 Dealers said the dollar looked firm against the ringgit, but talk of large orders to sell the dollar at the 2.6400 level was likely to limit its rise. 

 The market was awaiting Malaysia's trade data for June, expected next week, amid talk of a 1.5 billion ringgit deficit after May's surplus of 157 million ringgit. 

 The Singapore dollar rose through the key 1.47 level to the U.S. dollar but dealers said its rise was likely to be capped around 1.4650. 

 "This is probably just profit-taking. I'm still looking at a higher dollar/Sing," a dealer said, adding that the market continued to expect the Sing to drop to around 1.50. 

 Trade in the Indonesian rupiah was slow, dominated by covering of short dollar positions for the weekend. Spot rupiah was at 2,605/15 against an opening of 2,613/23. 

 The Philippine peso was firmer as banks scrambled to meet a deadline to cut long dollar positions after the central bank slashed the long dollar limit of banks to five percent of capital from 10 percent, or 10 million, whichever is lower. 

 Newspapers quoted central bank governor Gabriel Singson as saying he expected banks to unload $200 million due to the new ruling. The peso was at 28.960/29.060 against its previous close at 29. 

 The Taiwan dollar slipped back from an early high of T$28.590, inspired by the central bank's move to raise two key interest rates after the market's close on Thursday. 

 The central bank raised the rediscount rate to 5.25 percent from 5.00 percent and accomodations against secured loans to 5.625 percent from 5.375 percent, effective from Friday. 

Central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong said the rate hikes were aimed at maintaining stability in the forex market. 

 The Taiwan dollar was at T$28.653/660 against Thursday's close at T$28.70, its weakest finish since 1988.

title: Thailand June Econ Data -2: Forward Positions Erode Reserves
text:
Thailand's economic slowdown, however, is expected to have a beneficial effect on two indicators that once alarmed economists - the trade and current-account deficits. The consensus forecast calls for the current-account deficit to shrink to 21.38 billion baht in May from 38 billion baht in April. The trade deficit is expected to have shrunk to 22.4 billion baht in May from 41 billion baht in April. 

 'The data will be what everybody expected to see,' said an economist at a European brokerage in Hong Kong, who asked not to be named. 'The economy is going to weaken further, and the reserves are going to contract. But the question is by how much.' Under the circumstances, he said, the Thai stock market isn't likely to be ruffled. The bad news, the economist said, 'is already priced into the market.' 

 Analysts attributed the sharp drop in foreign reserves in June to a 'snowball effect' that began in May with the worst speculative attack on the Thai baht in 14 years. That attack caused the central bank to spend $4 billion of its reserves to defend the currency in May. 

 That drop in reserves, announced in late June, caused foreign investors in Thailand to panic, resulting in big outflows of capital and obligating the central bank to spend yet more of its reserves in a vain attempt to defend the baht peg - eventually abandoned July 2. 

 Since then, the baht has dropped about 18% based on onshore market quotes, with the Bank of Thailand seen intervening occasionally to maintain at least a modicum of currency stability. 

 Arporn Chewakrengkai, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Securities (Thailand) Ltd., said the loss of reserves reflected a crisis of confidence among both domestic and foreign investors. 'That isn't anything the Bank of Thailand can control,' she said. 

 Economists expect Thailand's reserves to continue to drop for the rest of the year, because of the forward positions taken by the Bank of Thailand in May during its attempts to defend the baht. 

 The Union Bank of Switzerland predicts that reserves could drop to $15 billion by year end. By law, Thailand is required to maintain reserves of at least $8 billion to back up the currency.

title: Thailand gets new bank chief as IMF aid sought.
text:
BANGKOK, July 29 (Reuter) - Thailand named a new central bank governor on Tuesday after political pressure forced the abrupt resignation of Bank of Thailand veteran Rerngchai Marakanond. 

 Financial markets applauded the appointment of Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi to the top central bank job and focused on the prospect of greater intervention by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Thailand's troubled economy. 

 Chaiyawat, like Rerngchai, is another 24-year central bank veteran. 

 The IMF, enlisted by the Thai government after initial reluctance, was expected to override the central bank and call the shots in running the economy in coming months, analysts said. 

 They said Chaiyawat, 50, would have his job shaped mostly by monetary and fiscal disciplines imposed by the IMF in the aftermath of Thailand's de facto devaluation of the local baht currency. 

 On Monday Thailand confirmed that it was seeking IMF advice to put its economy back on even keel and could possibly seek a credit line from the world body. 

 That decision overshadowed any impact that would normally arise from a change of its central bank governor, analysts said. 

 "It makes no difference who will be Rerngchai's successor in terms of policy. I would say for the next six months, the new governor would not have much choice but to walk the IMF line. His job would be made easier," said Kitti Limsakul, economics lecturer at Chulalongkorn University. 

 Few analysts were surprised by Rerngchai's resignation. 

 They said he had previously hinted he may quit. He was also seen as being closely associated with ex-Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan in resisting a baht devaluation. 

 Amnuay quit in June partly over policy conflicts with other cabinet ministers. Thailand let the baht float on July 2 and the currency has subsequently lost nearly 20 percent of its value. 

 "His resignation is a product of changing circumstances," Kitti said. 

 But Rerngchai did not leave without giving the government a parting shot. 

 "Like any human being...who is discouraged by sarcastic remarks and in order to protect my integrity and that of the Bank of Thailand, I would like to show my spirit by resigning from the governorship," Rerngchai said in a statement. 

 "My job so far has been strongly criticised and I faced consistent political pressure for me to leave office," he said. 

 Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh declined to say much about Rerngchai's departure after the cabinet meeting in northern Chiang Rai town. 

 "I am moved. He is an example of a man who worked for the good of the country," he said. "The transfers and removals are to create unity within the country's economic framework. If anything happens, I will be solely responsible." 

 Rerngchai's stout defence of his position confirmed market views that he was pressured to leave so Chavalit's government could forge ahead with its own agenda and appointees to fix an economy stumbling through its worst slump in over a decade. 

 "It's a pity that Rerngchai had to go but the government needed to clear the decks so it can make a fresh start now that it has sought IMF assistance," said a foreign debt analyst. 

 Rerngchai was blamed for the baht's disastrous showing following the managed float. 

 He also faced criticism for his handling of the troubled financial sector, which has been hit by a liquidity crunch and overexposure to depressed property firms. 

 "The politicians were taking some unfair shots at the man (Rerngchai) but they also had reasonable criticisms of him, like he waited too long to float the baht and spent a lot of national reserves in defending it," said another analyst at a foreign brokerage firm. 

 An IMF austerity package that could be adopted by Thailand would include tough measures aimed at improving the current account and balance of payments. 

 Kitti of Chulalongkorn University said that with Rerngchai and Amnuay gone, the pressure on shoring up the battered economy would rest on Prime Minister Chavalit and his new Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya. 

 "Chavalit could not keep passing the buck. If the economy failed to show signs of bottoming out soon, the prime minister would also have to take the heat, politically," he said. 

 The economist said Chavalit and politicians in his six-party coalition would need agree to additional serious budget cuts which would likely be recommended by the IMF.

title: Asia-Pacific Central Bk -2: Different Views On  Forex
text:
'There was the usual rhetoric about speculators,' the official said. 'But the point was made a world full of mobile capital is a difficult and dangerous world for central banks that intervene.' 

 The Bank of Japan officials argued against intervention to defend the currency in all cases - arguing that its experience of intervening in the markets showed that the best policy is to let the currency find a bottom and only then give it a boost when it's already headed higher. 

 An official in the Bank of Japan's international department confirmed that is the BOJ attitude - based on its past experience, it's better to let the currency find a bottom or a ceiling rather than try to pinpoint a certain level via intervention, he said. 

 Despite heavy intervention to stem speculative pressures, Thailand, the Philippines and Malaysia have all been forced this month to abandon efforts to support their currencies

 If created, the EMEAP fund would likely be of greatest immediate interest to Thailand and the Philippines, both struggling with the aftermath of the decisions to float their currencies. Thailand announced this week it will seek help from the IMF to right its economy after the plunge of the baht. The Philippines has already stepped up its borrowings from the IMF to rebuild reserves that were depleted in defending the peso. 

 But such an EMEAP fund would likely come with strings attached, according to the central bank official. 

 Japan in particular insisted at the meeting that any EMEAP money wouldn't be used to fight currency speculators. It would only be used to further IMF-inspired economic adjustments - though that was loosely defined at the meeting, according to the official. 

 The money, which would likely go into reserve accounts at the central bank, could be used to fund a budget deficit or provide funds for the banking sector. 

 Bank of Japan governor Yasuo Matsushita led the Japanese delegation. After the meeting, BOJ executive director Takashi Anzai told reporters that EMEAP had only agreed to 'study' the issue of extra funding for countries in difficulty. 

 But the central bank official who attended the meeting said there was a 'reasonably strong presumption' among Southeast Asian central banks that some kind of EMEAP loan fund would emerge.

title: S.E. Asian  currencies  plumb new depths.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 24 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies plumbed new depths on Thursday and could fall further as speculative attacks give way to hedging, analysts said. 

 The Thai baht, which led the decline, recovered from lows of around 32.70 to the dollar, but continued to look vulnerable against a backdrop of bad financial sector news. 

 The relatively resilient Singapore dollar caved in to mounting pressure, falling through the psychological 1.47 level against the U.S. dollar on stop-loss sales. 

 And the Malaysian ringgit crashed to an early low of 2.6540 to the dollar on spillover weakness and continued to look depressed. 

 "It's a brave man who speculates in these markets now," said Tim Lucas, treasury manager at Bank of Bermuda in Hong Kong. "What's happening now is genuine portfolio hedging and genuine concern as opposed to having a speculative play." 

 The baht suffered again after only seven of 18 finance and securities firms reporting half year results made a profit. The sector's losses totalled a depressing 3.5 billion baht (US$108 million). 

 There was talk the central Bank of Thailand (BOT) had intervened to sell dollars above the 32.60 baht level, helping the baht stage a mild recovery. A BOT official declined to confirm or deny the market talk. 

 The baht was at 31.950/32.020 to the dollar onshore at 0955 GMT and 31.930/32.030 offshore. 

 Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said he would announce a major economic package within two weeks that would help stabilise the baht and bring down Thai interest rates. 

 Dealers attributed the Singapore dollar's sharp drop to Finance Minister Richard Hu's comments about Singapore's competitiveness not being hurt by the recent tumble of other Southeast Asian currencies. 

 Hu told parliament on Wednesday Singapore's exchange rate was determined by market demand and it would continue to be managed on a trade-weighted basis with a medium-term perspective. 

 The Singapore dollar fell to a 32-month low of 1.4785 and was quoted at 1.4770/75 at 1000 GMT. 

 "It was mainly interbank stop-losses being triggered and we've broken out of all the highs for the last few years," said the regional currency chief at a European bank. 

 The U.S. dollar could reach S$1.50 within a month if regional turmoil persisted, he said. 

 Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's call for cooperation among Southeast Asian countries to fight currency speculators gave the ringgit market brief pause, dealers said. 

 But the ringgit soon succumbed to selling again as players shrugged the comments off as just a suggestion. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was back below the 2,600 level to the dollar in late trade but its decline was relatively muted, partly due to signs the central bank had been intervened. 

 "The rupiah is moving in a steady mode compared to the rest. So they're not that alarmed. I think they're just trying to smooth the flow," one dealer said. 

 The rupiah was at 2,613/23 against an opening at 2,575/85. 

 The Philippine peso ended steady at 28.500/550 to the dollar against its previous 28.5. 

 Hong Kong dollar forwards remained near their highs despite talk of heavy intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority. 

 Dealers said funds were buying the U.S. dollar forward, anticipating a fall in the Hong Kong dollar, which is pegged at HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals weak in late trade.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 23 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies remained on slippery ground in late Wednesday trade after coming under renewed pressure as the Thai baht slid to new lows, forex dealers said. 

 Poor market liquidity and wide spreads added to market volatility as players turned increasingly nervous ahead of an Asian central bankers meeting in Shanghai on Friday. 

 Expectations the meeting might result in some form of coordinated intervention to counter the speculative onslaught on the region's currencies kept the dollar well bid, dealers said. 

 "The big issue for the market at the moment is this meeting in Shanghai as there is the possibility of concerted intervention or a statement that they are willing to join hands to support currencies," said Chiang Yao Chye, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in Singapore. 

 In Thailand, the central bank intervened to stem the baht's slide as the currency was pulled down by heavy commercial demand for dollars in the domestic market. 

 "We noticed the central bank intervened to stop the baht's fall at around the 32.50/32.60 to the dollar level," a senior dealer at a local bank in Bangkok said. 

 The baht hit a record low earlier with some dealers reporting transactions at as low as 32.60 to the dollar. At 1050 GMT, it was quoted at 32.250/32.550 onshore and 31.500/31.550 offshore. 

 Dealers attributed the sharp plunge in the onshore market maqinly to sales by importers seeking dollars to pay their bills and by corporations needing the dollar to repay foreign loans. 

 They said the central bank did not need to sell large amounts of dollars to curb the baht's fall because the pressure on the currency was mainly from local players trading in small amounts. 

 A senior Thai central bank official attributed the baht's weak tone to poor first-half earnings reported by local banks and finance companies. 

 The Singapore dollar succumbed to fresh selling after comments by Finance Minister Richard Hu which players treated as yet another signal to buy the U.S. dollar. 

 Hu told parliament Singapore dollar's exchange rate was determined by market forces and its recent appreciation against its neighbours, especially the baht and Indonesian rupiah, did not pose a significant threat to its competitiveness. 

 "Our exchange rate policy should not be guided by short-term expediency considerations. We always focus on managing the exchange rate of the Singapore dollar on a trade-weighted basis with a medium-term perspective," Hu said. 

 The Singapore dollar fell to a low of around 1.4690 to the U.S. dollar after the comments, compared with 1.4645 earlier. 

 The Malaysian ringgit was hit by fresh waves of selling by offshore U.S. banks despite talk that Bank Negara Malaysia had intervened to sell dollars around 2.6350/70 ringgit. 

 The ringgit was quoted at 2.6355/85 to the dollar against a morning low of 2.6230. 

 "We are not sure if there is any intervention at all. The said banks could be taking their own positions," a dealer at a Malaysian bank in Kuala Lumpur said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah remained weak after being dragged down by the slump in the baht. Spot rupiah was at 2,587/97 against an opening of 2,570/80. 

 "We saw some central bank intervention at the 2,580 level which helped boost the rupiah to 2,540 level in late morning, but uncertainty in Thailand kept the dollar tone biddish," a U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said. 

 "If the rupiah could break the 2,500 resistance level, then there is potential for a strong comeback. But if it falls below the 2,600 level, speculators would launch an attack to test the band again," a local bank dealer said. 

 The Philippine peso fell on commercial demand for dollars, closing at 28.50 to the dollar against 28.15 previously. 

 Manila traders said there was no sign of central bank intervention and the peso remained under pressure despite new rulings aimed at encouraging dollar sales and curbing speculation.

title: FOCUS - Thai baht dives to record low,  intervention .
text:
BANGKOK, July 23 (Reuter) - Thailand's beleaguered baht plunged to a record low in the local market on Wednesday, forcing central bank intervention to arrest the currency's worst slide since it went into a managed float on July 2. 

 Dealers said the baht's dive in the thinly traded onshore market was mainly due to a scramble for dollars by local importers seeking the U.S. unit to pay bills and by corporates needing the greenback to repay foreign loans. 

 Some dealers reported baht/dollar deals done at a level as low as 32.60 to the dollar before the Bank of Thailand's defence of the currency through dollar sales. 

 "We noticed the central bank intervened to stop the baht's fall at around the 32.50/32.60 (bid/ask) to the dollar level," a senior dealer with a local bank told Reuters. 

 Others said the central bank did not have to sell many dollars to curb the baht's fall. 

 This was because pressure on the currency was mainly from local players trading in relatively small amounts and the currency's movement was exaggerated in a thin market. 

 After the intervention by around 0925 GMT, the baht steadied and was quoted at around 32.21/32.41 against the dollar in the domestic market and stronger at 31.45/31.55 in the offshore market. 

 Thai central bank officials were not available for comment on the reported intervention. 

Thailand's stock market plummeted more than four percent, in part due to worries about the baht, brokers said. It closed down 28.50 points to 631.28. 

 The baht's tumble comes as Thailand goes through its worst economic slump in more than a decade and its financial sector faces numerous troubles. 

 The baht was released into a managed float by Thailand after being pegged for 13 years to a trade-weighted basket of currencies dominated by the dollar. 

 Since the flotation, the baht has undergone a de facto devaluation of about 20 percent. 

 Dealers and a senior Thai central bank official also attributed poor baht sentiment to weak first-half earnings results reported by local banks and finance firms this week. 

 "I think this is mainly a result of the bank's results we saw yesterday and that knocked the fragile confidence that had crept back in," said one Singapore based analyst. 

 "If you look at the results of the banks there are some horror stories in terms of earnings per share." 

 With the corporate market still squeezed there was still a cash-flow problem. That, on top of the bad balance sheet issue made worse by the devaluation of offshore liabilities, had led to a scramble for dollars in short supply, he said. 

 Thanasak Chantarovat, deputy director of the central bank's banking department, said the baht could also have been hurt by negative expectations about data on the level of non-performing loans of financial institutions due to be released soon. 

 The data is due to be announced through the stock exchange on Thursday, a local banker said. 

 Financial markets have been waiting nervously to gauge the level of non-performing loans by banks and finance firms, which are overexposed with billions of dollars in sour loans to the depressed and cash-strapped property sector. 

 Some dealers said they saw an appropriate level for the baht at between 30.50-31.50 to the dollar in the near term, given current concerns over the Thai economy and problems in the financial sector.

title: Thai baht quoted at new record low against dollar.
text:
BANGKOK, July 23 (Reuter) - The Thai baht was quoted on Wednesday at a new record low of 32.15/32.50 against the dollar as players sought refuge in the greenback, dealers said. 

 Some foreign and local banks onshore were quoting the baht at new lows to test the resolve of the Bank of Thailand and see if it would intervene in the market to stabilise the sliding currency, they added. "There is so far no sign of any central bank intervention," a dealer with a local bank told Reuters. 

 In the offshore market, the baht was quoted higher at 31.20/31.40 to the dollar. 

 The Thai central bank said on July 2, after it freed the baht from its peg to a trade-weighted basket of currencies dominated by the dollar and allowed it into a managed float, that it would intervene if the baht fell to an "appropriate level". 

 When the baht hit around 30 to the dollar last week, a top central bank official said it had fallen low enough. 

 Earlier on Wednesday, the baht fell to its previous record low of 31.60 on talk that commercial demand for dollars had dampened baht sentiment in a thin market. 

Central bank officials declined to comment on any plans to intervene to prop the baht up. 

 But one official said the baht's drop was exaggerated because of the thinness of trade in the market. 

 Thanasak Chantarovat, deputy director of the central bank's banking department, told reporters that the baht slide on Wednesday was aggravated by poor first-half earnings of commercial banks and finance companies. 

 He said the weak bank earnings stemmed from their required higher reserves for doubtful loans but he added that the increased provisions would strengthen banks in the long run. 

 The official said sentiment on the baht could also be hurt by expectations that data on the level of non-performing loans of financial institutions would be released soon to the stock market. 

 "They could have negative psychological effect if the figures are high but I don't think they would be that bad," he said.

title: Thailand Baht Ends In All-Time Low On Strong Dlr Buying
text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--The Thai baht plunged to its all-time low against the dollar Wednesday, hurt by brisk dollar buying by Thai corporations nervous about the continued depreciation of the baht, dealers said. 

 The Thai currency, however, strengthened in the swap market, where investors make agreements to buy and sell baht at specified times in the future. Swap premiums dropped. 

 At the close of Asian trading Wednesday, the dollar was at 32.30 baht in the domestic market - believed to be a historic closing high for the U.S. currency. However, this was still below the afternoon high of 32.50 baht, which was the all-time high. 

 The dollar closed at 31.00 baht Tuesday. In the offshore market, the dollar closed at 31.55 baht, up from 30.60 baht Tuesday. 

 Dealers attributed the baht's historical decline to a scramble for dollars among Thai corporations, which have an estimated $45 billion in short-term loans. 

 'Demand for dollars was purely commercial,' said a dealer at a U.S. bank in Bangkok. 'Thai companies still owe a lot of money to foreign lenders, and importers still need dollars to pay for their imports.' 

 At the closing level, the dollar was well above the 30-baht range at which the Bank of Thailand has said it would intervene to defend the baht. Even so, the Bank of Thailand did little to prop up the baht Wednesday, dealers said. 

 'There was some intervention through Thai banks, but I don't think it was to reverse the trend,' said a dealer at a Hong Kong bank in Bangkok. 'I think the (central) bank just wanted to keep the baht from falling too sharply against the dollar.' 

 The Bank of Thailand set its reference rate for the dollar at 30.842 baht, up from 30.370 baht Tuesday. The reference rate is a weighted average of rates charged by Thai commercial banks the previous day. It serves as a benchmark for domestic currency trading.

title: Thailand not seeking IMF loans, officials say.
text:
BANGKOK, July 16 (Reuter) - Bank of Thailand and finance ministry officials said on Wednesday that Thailand has not considered seeking loans from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to help ease its liquidity and economic problems. 

Central bank spokeswoman Duangmanee Wongprateep said Thailand had not asked for financial assistance from an IMF team now visiting the country. The team is in Thailand to help assess government measures for bailing out cash-strapped or troubled financial institutions. 

 "In theory, (an IMF loan) is an option open to us but we have not moved to consider seeking one from them," she told Reuters. 

Central bank officials said a separate IMF team has visited Thailand to provide technical advice on how to implement the baht's managed float policy. The baht was floated on July 2. 

 Thailand let its baht depreciate sharply early this month after the currency faced speculative pressure for several weeks. 

 Finance ministry sources said an IMF loan was still not required despite Thailand's current economic downturn, the worst in over a decade. 

 "No move has been made (on borrowing from the IMF). Such a need would arise if our foreign reserves were greatly depleted but it is premature to say our reserves have plunged because of central bank intervention (to defend the baht)," a finance ministry official said. 

 He said some of the forward baht/dollar positions taken by the Bank of Thailand in May in defence of the baht had still not matured, making it difficult to determine how much foreign exchange the central bank would use in its intervention. 

 "Borrowing from the IMF would subject Thailand to certain austerity conditions and we should consider them first," he said. 

 However, analysts said that while Thailand may not need IMF financial assistance it could benefit from loans by the agency because these would be viewed by the financial market as a stamp of approval of the country's economic adjustment policies. 

 The Thai stock market rallied sharply on Wednesday as regional funds moved into the bourse on hopes that the IMF may be preparing to step in and help the economy. 

 Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya and Bank of Thailand Governor Rerngchai Marakanond go to Tokyo on Wednesday night for talks with their Japanese counterparts on the country's economic situation. 

 Japan appears to have linked financial aid for Thailand's ailing economy to IMF involvement in its economic management.

title: Thai c.bank confirms  intervention  to help baht.
text:
BANGKOK, July 14 (Reuter) - Bank of Thailand governor Rerngchai Marakanond on Monday confirmed market talk and said the central bank had intervened by selling dollars to help stem the baht's fall against the U.S. currency. 

 "We intervened in the market, but in a very small way. This caused the baht to stabilise in the afternoon," Rerngchai told reporters. 

 Rerngchai also said the central bank planned to keep the two-tier foreign exchange market and its current strict capital controls to prevent any further attack on the baht. 

 Rerngchai was speaking after meeting Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, former finance minister Amnuay Viravan and senior officials from the government's think-tank, the National Economic and Social Development Board (NESDB). 

 The governor said the foreign exchange market, which has been jolted by the crisis in other regional currencies, was expected to return to normal in the next one to two days. 

 "The baht is at very low level and will stay at around 30 baht for some time. But the market should calm down in the next one to two days," Rerngchai said. 

 The baht fell sharply to new record low of 30.80 to the dollar on Monday morning on a spillover effect of speculative attacks on other regional currencies, dealers said. 

 The baht recovered ground in the afternoon, to trade at around 29.85/30.00 in mid-afternoon in the onshore market compared with 30.30/30.75 in early dealings. 

 The baht was also buoyed by the central bank deputy governor Chaiyawat Wilbulsawasdi's statement earlier that the baht had fallen to a level that was low enough and the bank would take action to stabilise the currency and stop wild fluctuations. 

 NESDB's secretary general Wirat Wattanasirtham said preliminary figures showed Thailand's gross domestic product would grow at a mere 4.6 percent this year if the baht were to fall by 10 percent. 

 He said the current account deficit would be at about 5.0-5.5 percent of GDP if the baht dropped 10 percent. 

 The Bank of Thailand said on Monday the baht had fallen about 15 percent since it switched to a managed float on July 2 from the previous system of pegging it to a basket of currencies.

title: Southeast Asian  currencies  under siege.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 14 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies were hit by waves of selling on Monday as uncertainty following the Philippine peso's effective devaluation last week spread like wildfire through the region. 

 In Malaysia, the ringgit fell to a 16-month low of 2.5500 to the dollar in early trade amid Bank Negara Malaysia's failure to intervene aggressively, dealers said. 

 The ringgit was quoted at 2.5375/95 to the dollar at 0400 GMT against 2.5042/52 at its Kuala Lumpur close on Friday. 

 "It's crazy," a European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 "Because of the story of the Philippine peso, which they devalued last week, the market is expecting the ringgit and rupiah to follow suit," she added. 

 Another European bank dealer in Singapore said Bank Negara was heard to have sold dollars around the 2.5500 ringgit level. "But I think Negara was in just to slow down the fall rather than stop the flow," he said. 

 Dealers said the market was still long of dollars, leaving room for the ringgit to head lower. 

 They said Bank Negara may be allowing market forces to dictate the spot's value rather than defending the ringgit aggressively in the face of heavy selling interest. 

 Dealers estimate the Malaysian central bank spent over $1 billion to support the ringgit last week. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah rebounded from its early lows as offshore players began unloading dollars. 

 Dealers said offshore players seemed to be trying to cash out from the market after they drove the rupiah to a low of 2,469.0 on Monday morning. 

 "I think some feel that the rupiah is low enough for a buy back, reversing the market trend," a local bank dealer in Jakarta said. 

 But another local bank dealer said the rupiah buying was initiated by some state banks and followed through by offshore players, driving the rupiah to a high of 2,445 before operators bought some dollars back. 

 The rupiah was quoted at 2,453.0/58.0 at 0400 GMT against an opening 2,451.0/55.0. 

 "Bank Indonesia (BI)'s band widening last week is not helping to strengthen the rupiah. With BI having the lowest reserves, the rupiah will be the next currency to attack," a Singapore-based dealer said. 

 The central bank widened its intervention band to 12 percent from eight percent last Friday, in what was seen as a move to pre-empt possible turbulence in the rupiah after speculative attacks on the peso and baht. 

 In the Philippines, the peso fell to a low of 29.75 to the dollar in thin trade as banks remained wary after the central bank's move on Friday to allow the peso-dollar rate to trade within a wider band. 

 Volume was a light nine million dollars after two-and-a-half hours of trading on Monday. 

 The central Bank of Thailand (BOT) intervened to stem the baht's fall in domestic markets, selling dollars at the 30.75-30.80 baht level, dealers said. 

 "The central bank intervened through a small local bank by selling the dollar at around 30.75-30.80," a European bank dealer in Bangkok said. 

 A BOT spokeswoman declined to say whether the central bank had intervened in the market. 

 Commercial dollar demand and lingering jitters from the peso slide pushed the baht to new lows. The currency was quoted at 30.500/30.800 to the dollar in the domestic market at 0400 GMT, after the intervention, against 30.00/30.60 late on Friday. 

 "The amount of intervention was insignificant. But it capped the baht at around 30.80," the dealer said.

title: Thai baht seen fragile despite  intervention .
text:
BANGKOK, July 14 (Reuter) - The Thai baht is likely to hit new lows in coming months despite the Bank of Thailand's insistence that the currency has sunk far enough, analysts said on Monday. 

 The central bank's vow on Monday to support the baht would not be enough to withstand an erosion of foreign investor confidence in regional currencies following the de facto devaluation of the Philippine peso and the Thai baht in recent weeks, analysts said. 

 "The baht will remain fragile in the short term. It's largely due to uncertainty across the region as a lot of people are taking (funds) out of the region," Jimmy Koh at Singapore-based research house I.D.E.A. told Reuters. 

 "By the end of this year, I expect the baht to be around 31-32 to the dollar," Koh said. 

 Thailand's worst economic downturn in over a decade and near crisis in the finance sector would add pressure on the currency, analysts said. 

 "It will take time for the economy to pick up and the financial crisis to be resolved. In the short term, the pressure on the baht will still persist," said Ali Seng at MMS International. 

 Seng said the baht was expected to fall to about 31-33 baht per dollar by the end of this year, echoing expectations of a number of other analysts. 

 Analysts said there were also worries about the quality of assets owned by financial institutions after the baht's de facto devaluation and their overexposure to cash-strapped property firms. 

 Deputy Bank of Thailand Governor Chaiyawat Wibulsawasdi said on Monday he believed the baht's current level of 30 to the dollar was low enough. 

 The central bank would take action to stabilise the currency and stop more wild fluctuations, he added. 

 "It is our direct responsibility to take measures to do anything that will help stabilise the foreign exchange rate and ease volatility in the market," he said. 

Central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond on Monday confirmed the bank had intervened to stem the baht's slide against the U.S. dollar. 

 "We intervened in the market, but in a very small way. This caused the baht to stabilise in the afternoon," Rerngchai told reporters. 

 This is the first time since the adoption of the managed float foreign exchange system for the baht on July 2 that the central bank has intervened to defend the currency. 

 Dealers said the Bank of Thailand, via a small local bank, intervened in the domestic market and sold dollars at the record low level of 30.75-30.80 per dollar. 

 The baht was quoted at a record low of around 30.30/30.80 per dollar early on Monday in the domestic market compared with 30.00/30.60 late on Friday. 

 After the central bank's intervention and statement, the baht recovered significantly to trade at around 29.70/30.20 in late afternoon.

title: Thai baht plunges, spurs  intervention , stocks fall.
text:
BANGKOK, July 14 (Reuter) - Jittery regional currencies drove Thailand's newly floated baht to a record low against the dollar on Monday, spurring central bank intervention and causing shivers in the local bourse. 

 For the first time since announcing a surprise, de facto devaluation on July 2, the Bank of Thailand intervened in the market to stem the baht's steep fall against the dollar. 

Central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond confirmed market talk of an intervention and said the bank had sold dollars to help stabilise the Thai currency. 

 "We intervened in the market, but in a very small way," Rerngchai told reporters. "This caused the tumbling baht to stabilise in the afternoon." 

 The baht fell sharply to a record low of 30.80 to the dollar in morning trade on a spillover effect of speculative attacks on other regional currencies, dealers said. It recovered ground late to trade around 29.25/29.75 bid/ask offshore and 29.90/30.00 in domestic markets. 

 Rergnchai said he thought the currency market had been jolted by regional currencies and said it should stabilise in the next day or two. 

 The central bank's deputy governor, Chaiyawat Wibulsawasdi, said the Bank of Thailand decided the baht had fallen low enough when it dived over 30 baht to the dollar. 

 When it announced a change to a managed float from its 13-year-old regime of pegging the baht to a basket of currencies, the Bank of Thailand said it would intervene as required to keep the baht at an appropriate level. 

 Chaiyawat said the currency had dropped 15 percent, in terms of the average daily interbank rate, since the float was implemented on July 2. 

 But the central bank's determination to stick to its policy of "managing" the float failed to convince equities punters. 

 The bourse, which lost more than four percent of its value last week, dropped 2.65 percent on Monday in thin dealings as investors unloaded large capitalised stocks on fears the baht would lose more ground, brokers and analysts said. 

 The Stock Exchange of Thailand's key index ended down 16.64 at 611.91 points in thin turnover of 3.4 billion baht. 

 "Investors believe that the baht isn't yet stable and will slip further from today," said one broker. "They think it's risky to hold baht at present." 

 Several major Thai companies face huge exchange losses this year, analysts said. At 30 baht per dollar Siam Cement Plc, the country's largest conglomerate, faces exchange losses of 9.9 billion baht on its unhedged foreign loans. 

 "Every bit the baht goes down makes a lot of these companies lose more and more," said one analyst. 

 Analysts said they needed to see more concrete signs that the Thai economy -- growing at its slowest pace in a decade -- was on the road to recovery before the stock market would pick up. 

 A finance ministry official said on Monday Thailand would not rule out seeking financial assistance from the International Monetary Fund to help solve its economic problems. 

 Analysts said any such borrowing would be accompanied by painful conditions but it was necessary for Thailand to have a credit life-line.

title: Thailand Economic Planning Agency Sees '97 GDP Up 4.6%
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Thailand's economy will grow 4.6% in 1997, assuming the Thai currency can be kept from depreciating more than 10%, the government's main economic planning agency said Monday. 

 The preliminary forecast by the National Economic & Social Development Board is the government's first since the currency was implicitly devalued July 2. Previously the central bank forecast growth of 5.9%, down from 6.4% in 1996. The forecast was presented Monday to Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh and his advisors. 

 Wirat Wattansiritham, the NESDB's secretary-general, did not explain why the government had assumed a currency depreciation of 10%. Since July 2, the baht has depreciated 14% against the dollar in domestic markets, and more offshore. 

 The central bank's reference rate was 29.945 baht to the dollar Monday, up from 29.155 baht Friday. The Bank of Thailand said it would intervene to prevent the dollar from rising above 30 baht, but some economists say they expect the dollar to climb to 33 baht by the end of the year. 

 The NESDB said inflation should rise to 6 to 6.1% in 1997 from 5.8% in 1996, assuming a 10% baht depreciation. Under the same assumptions, it said, exports should grow 9.7% in 1997 after a 0.2% decline in 1996. It said the current-account deficit should shrink to 5 to 5.5% of the gross domestic product, down from 6% in 1996.

text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--Thailand's foreign reserves could dwindle by more than 50% to $15 billion by the end of the year as a result of continued central-bank intervention to prop the Thai baht, the Union Bank of Switzerland has predicted. 

 The bank said in a report obtained by Dow Jones Monday that the U.S. dollar could rise as high as 33 baht by the end of the year, up from about 30 baht now. The Bank of Thailand said Monday it would intervene by selling dollars to prevent the U.S. currency from rising above 30 baht. 

 'The demand for foreign currency will be large over the next 12 to 24 months...,' UBS said. Without a resumption of strong capital inflows, 'the baht will come under renewed strong pressure - something the (Bank of Thailand) can only temporarily offset through intervention.' 

 By law, Thailand needs at least $8 billion in reserves to back up its currency. Its reserves stood at $33.3 billion at the end of May, a two-year low. UBS has estimated Thailand will need to borrow between $20 billion and $40 billion from international lenders such as the International Monetary Fund to shore up reserves and stabilize cash-strapped financial institutions. 

 UBS said Thailand has outstanding short-term debt of $42 billion to $45 billion, most of it owed by the private sector. 'As the credit standing of Thai firms deteriorates, there will be added pressure to resort to onshore borrowing as offshore credit sources dry up,' UBS said. It said Thailand also has $8 billion to $12 billion in long-term debt that matures in the next year. In the same period, the bank said, the country will also need $8 billion to finance its current account deficit.

title: Thai banker sees permanent two-tier baht regime.
text:
BANGKOK, July 4 (Reuter) - A leading Thai banker said on Friday Thailand may follow Singapore in making its control of offshore currency supply permanent to help ward off future speculative attacks on the baht. 

 Olarn Chaipravat, president of the Thai Bankers Association, said the two-tier baht exchange system, put in place by the central bank since mid-May to block access of baht for offshore speculators, should be institutionalised with some minor adjustments. 

 "The two-tier system, with some changes...for 90 percent separation of the markets, will probably be the end-scenario between offshore and onshore foreign exchange markets. 

 "If it is closed 90 percent and open 10 percent, it can be the system like the one that Singapore has used for a long, long time. Singapore never allows speculators to attack the Singapore dollar from offshore sources," the banker said. 

 Heavy market attacks on the baht in May forced Thailand to switch this week from its long-standing practice of fixing the baht against a dollar-dominated basket of currencies to a new managed float. 

 The de facto devaluation sent the baht falling to 28.700 to the dollar in late Friday trading from 25.800 early this week. 

 Olarn, chief executive of the Siam Commercial Bank Plc, had been opposed to a baht devaluation. 

 The banker and economist, who had turned down past government offers of a finance ministerial job, said the weaker baht would give only a limited boost to Thai exports which, with an average 42 percent import content, would carry higher production costs. 

 "(The devaluation) is like flood water reaching town, getting everybody wet. Only those who sought protection by hedging their dollar exposure managed to stay dry but even that would only be temporary," he said. 

 Olarn told reporters he believed the optimal baht rate in the next three to six months would be 27.50 to the dollar. 

 "The devaluation was not meant to be a cure-all remedy for the Thai economy. It is a painful thing that we have to live with, to allow private sector participants to adjust by increasing competitiveness and improving productivity of companies and industries so that they can compete effectively in a globalised world market." 

 The banker said with the baht's new floating system, private business would need to closely monitor future signals of when the Bank of Thailand would intervene in defence of the currency. 

 He declined to estimate the devaluation impact on economic growth and inflation, saying it would be determined by the extent of the future loss in the baht's value.

title: FOCUS-Thailand floats baht, investors applaud.
text:
BANGKOK, July 2 (Reuter) - Thailand floated the baht on Wednesday in a bold move which jolted its stock exchange out of the doldrums and sent shock waves through Southeast Asian markets. 

 The baht plunged by 15-20 percent in offshore markets despite a bid to offset the blow by the central Bank of Thailand, which raised its lending rate by two percentage points to 12.5 percent. 

 But Thailand's stock market gave a hearty thumbs-up to the news, with the bourse index soaring by nearly eight percent to 568.79 by the close of trade as foreign firms bought heavily. 

 Analysts said the tough measures may breathe fresh life into Thailand's ailing economy, which is grappling with a swollen current account, a troubled financial sector and the slowest rate of growth in a decade. 

 "This is a victory for economic pragmatism over vested political and business interests. The Bank of Thailand finally did the right thing when it had its back to the wall," said Mike Stead of Union Securities Plc in Bangkok. 

 In offshore currency markets, the baht sank to record lows of around 28.80/29.60 to the dollar from 24.25 ahead of the announcement. 

 Reaction was mixed around the region, with the Philippine peso and shares falling sharply while the yen surged to 114.15 against the dollar from 114.92 on its perceived safe-haven status. 

 Analysts saw the managed float as a de facto devaluation allowing the central bank to avoid costly intervention, but said it remained to be seen how far the baht would be allowed to fall. 

 "The value of the baht will be determined by market forces to reflect fundamental economic forces," finance minister Thanong Bidaya said in an early morning statement. 

 "The Ministry of Finance and the Bank of Thailand believe the managed float system will benefit Thailand's overall economic development," he said. 

 Commercial banks would not quote overnight lending rates and exchange trade ground to a virtual halt as markets waited for the central bank to announce its new baht reference rate. 

 The Bank of Thailand said it would replace its previous peg for the baht, which was set against a basket of currencies, with a daily reference rate based on the previous day's trading levels. 

 The level will be set at 0130 GMT daily. The Bank of Thailand said it had "an appropriate rate" in mind within which it expected the baht to move, but gave no details. 

 "However, if the baht goes beyond the appropriate rate the central bank will intervene in the market," central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulsawasdi told a news conference. 

 The Thai Bankers Association said local banks had agreed to set a baht trading range among themselves of 75 satangs below and above the baht-dollar reference rate to stem volatility when domestic markets re-open on Thursday. 

 Analysts said there was a question-mark over how far and how fast the central bank would allow the baht to fall, but they expected it to bring the currency down gradually. 

 In the near term, higher interest rates would hurt Thailand's economy, but there was scope for them to fall in coming months if the tough measures did ultimately restore confidence. 

 "There was a tremendous buildup of funds that were waiting to go into the market if there was a devaluation or, as it happened, a flotation," George Morgan, country manager for ABN Amro Hoare Govett, told Reuters Financial Television. 

 The flotation will allow the Bank of Thailand to avoid intervening to support the baht, after using between four and five billion dollars of its foreign reserves in May to defend the currency from a heavy speculative attack. 

 This cut the country's foreign reserves to a two-year low of $33.3 billion at the end of May from around $37.3 billion a month earlier 

 "I think these measures are aimed at boosting confidence," said Kobus van der Wath, Regional Head of Treasury and Economics at Standard Chartered in Singapore. 

 "But fixing a reference point for the baht allows them to set the pace," he said. 

 Analysts had expected renewed near-term speculation against the baht because of negative sentiment over the Thai economy and recent moves to rescue its beleaguered financial institutions. 

 "Under the new system, movements in the exchange rate are expected to be quite large at the initial stage. However, relative stability should be attained after a brief adjustment period," Bidaya said. 

 Some bankers and analysts warned that Thai corporates with high unhedged foreign loan exposure were likely to face severe repayment problems as exchange costs soared. 

 Thai corporates have around $60-80 billion or the equivalent outstanding in foreign currency loans, with many unhedged against currency fluctuations after years when the baht was virtually fixed, they said. 

 "Are Thai companies going to be able to repay their dollar loans is the next big question," one senior European analyst said. 

 "And if they can't, then the banks are going to have to take a big hit." 

 Financial authorities have pledged to help businesses hit by the baht's flotation, but there are fears they can do little to help. 

 With the International Monetary Fund, the Bank of Japan and other central banks also pledging assistance to Thailand, analysts said the future for hard hit Thai firms may come down to the willingness and speed of these agencies to help.

title: Thailand rocks markets with baht flotation.
text:
BANGKOK, July 2 (Reuter) - Thailand floated the baht and raised its key lending rate by two percentage points on Wednesday in a desperate attempt to put the fire back in its battered economy. 

 But currency analysts, who initially interpreted the move as a de facto devaluation which would allow the central bank to avoid costly intervention, said they would wait and see how far the baht would be allowed to fall. 

 The news, which sent shock waves through Southeast Asian markets, knocked 20 percent off the value of the baht and sent the currency to a record quoted low of 29.25 to the dollar, from 24.25 earlier. 

 At 0800 GMT the baht was trading at 28.30/90 to the dollar. Analysts said the currency could weaken further to 30.00 to the dollar. 

 The baht flotation caused the Japanese yen to rise against the U.S. dollar on safe-haven buying to a day's high of 114.15 yen, but the dollar later trimmed its losses and was quoted at about 114.50 yen at 0805 GMT. 

 "The value of the baht will be determined by market forces to reflect fundamental economic forces," finance minister Thanong Bidaya said in an early morning statement. 

 "The Ministry of Finance and the Bank of Thailand believe the managed float system will benefit Thailand's overall economic development," he said. 

 Thailand's stock market gave a hearty thumbs-up to the news, and investors boosted the index for the bourse by nearly eight percent in busy trade. Business was dominated by foreign institutions. 

 "There was a tremendous buildup of funds that were waiting to go into the market if there was a devaluation or, as it happened, a flotation," George Morgan, country manager for ABN Amro Hoare Govett, told Reuters Financial Television. 

 In a bid to keep the baht from a meltdown, the Bank of Thailand simultaneously raised its key commercial bank lending rate by two percentage points to 12.5 percent. 

 But commercial banks would not quote overnight lending rates and exchange trade ground to a virtual halt as markets waited for the central bank to announce its new baht reference rate, due at around 1000 GMT. 

 The rate will replace the previous daily peg, which was fixed against a trade-weighted basket of currencies dominated by the U.S. dollar. 

 The Bank of Thailand said it had "an appropriate rate" in mind in which it expected the baht to move, but gave no details. 

 "However, if the baht goes beyond the approriate rate the central bank will intervene in the market," central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulsawasdi told a news conference. 

 Analysts said there was a question-mark over how far and how fast the central would allow the baht to fall, but they expected it to bring the currency down gradually. 

 They said that in the near-term, higher interest rates would hurt Thailand's economy, which is still grappling with a swollen current account deficit, slowing growth, and a troubled financial sector. 

 But analysts said that if the new measures did ultimately restore confidence, there would be scope for Thai interest rates to fall in the coming months. 

 The flotation will also allow the Bank of Thailand to avoid intervening to support the baht. The bank used up to five billion dollars of its foreign reserves in May to defend the currency after it came under heavy attack. 

 This cut the country's foreign reserves to a two-year low of $33.3 billion at the end of May from around $37.3 billion a month earlier 

 "Clearly their backs were to the wall given the speculative attack on the baht and I think these measures are aimed at boosting confidence," said Kobus van der Watch, Regional Head of Treasury and Economics at Standard Chartered in Singapore. 

 "But fixing a reference point for the bath allows them to set the pace," he said. 

 Analysts had expected renewed near-term speculation against the baht because of negative sentiment over the Thai economy and recent moves to rescue its beleaguered financial institutions. 

 "Under the new system movements in the exchange rate are expected to be quite large at the initial stage. However, relative stability should be attained after a brief adjustment period," Bidaya said. 

 The news hit regional stock and money markets, with several governments reacting quickly to offset any negative impact. 

 The Philippines sold hundreds of millions of dollars and forced up interest rates to shield its currency. Manila stocks fell to close nearly two percent lower on Wednesday as stock market investors took fright. 

 For the first time in years, Bank Negara Malaysia used its own name to intervene in the foreign exchange market as it sold dollars early on Wednesday. 

 The Indonesian rupiah also slipped lower, while in Japan, the yen gained against major currencies on its safe-haven status in the region. 

 The Bank of Japan welcomed the decision and said the baht's flotation increased the scope for cooperation among central banks. 

 In Australia, the Reserve Bank confirmed it had been asked to provide technical advice to the Bank of Thailand for the managed float, but gave no details. 

 Thailand said it had also asked the International Monetary Fund for technical help.

title: Thailand floats baht - details summary.
text:
BANGKOK, July 2 (Reuter) - Here are details on the managed float of the baht announced by Thai financial authorities on Wednesday. 

 - The value of the baht would be set by market forces but the flotation would be managed by the authorities. 

 - The baht's peg against a basket of currencies would be discontinued. 

 Since 1984, the baht's midrate against the dollar has been fixed on a daily basis by the central bank based on a trade-weighted basket of currencies denominated by the dollar. 

 - The Bank of Thailand said it was raising its key bank rate to 12.5 percent from 10.5 percent, effective immediately. 

 The bank rate is the rate the central bank charges on loans to commercial banks. 

 - The Bank of Thailand said a baht-dollar reference rate would be set daily at the close of trade following the baht flotation. 

 The reference rate would be based on the baht's trading average the day before. 

 - The Bank of Thailand said it had an "appropriate rate" in mind to which it expected the baht to move. 

 If the rate went beyond the appropriate level the central bank said it would intervene in the market. 

 - Central bank officials said that under the new baht system they would be following the Singapore model of managing the currency, without elaborating. 

 - Bank of Thailand Governor Rerngchai Marakanond said Thailand had sought technical assistance from the International Monetary Fund and the Reserve Bank of Australia. The RBA has since agreed to provide technical advice to the Bank of Thailand in the managed float. 

 - A two-tier baht market - one offshore and another onshore - that has been in place since the last speculative attack on the baht in May when the central bank imposed currency controls would remain for now but its future would be reviewed. 

 - The Bank of Thailand said it expected the baht to remain volatile in the short term after the flotation, but said the public need not panic. 

 _ The Bank of Thailand said it would intervene in foreign exchange markets from time to time to achieve its baht flotation policy objectives and guard against excessive fluctuation. 

 - Thai financial authorities will give businesses affected by the baht's flotation and volatile soft loans help to allow them to meet foreign debt repayments. No details given yet. 

 - The Bank of Thailand said foreigners and non-resident bank clients were banned from buying dollars for speculative purposes following the flotation. 

 - Foreigners failing to produce evidence of underlying business or investment transactions would not be allowed to buy dollars or raise dollar funds by selling short-term, baht-denominated money market instruments with less than six-month maturity. 

 - The Bank of Thailand said the restrictive measures were temporary.

title: FOCUS-Thailand floats baht, raises interest rates.
text:
BANGKOK, July 2 (Reuter) - Thailand sent shock waves through Asian currency markets on Wednesday by floating the battered baht, a move which analysts said was a de facto devaluation. 

 In a bid to keep the currency from spinning into a freefall the Bank of Thailand also raised its key commercial bank lending rate by two percentage points to 12.5 percent. 

 "In order to end uncertainty over Thailand's exchange rate policy, Thailand's exchange rate system will from 2 July 1997 be a managed float," finance minister Thanong Bidaya said. 

 "The value of the baht will be determined by market forces to reflect fundamental economic forces. The Ministry of Finance and the Bank of Thailand believe the managed float system will benefit Thailand's overall economic development," he said in a statement. 

 In offshore markets, the baht sank to 27.00/28.00 to the dollar from 24.25 on news of the float, which analysts said would allow the central bank to avoid intervening to support the ailing currency. 

 "It means they can stand away from intervention if they want to," said Chiang Yao Chye, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in Singapore. 

 Bankers estimate that the Bank of Thailand used up to five billion dollars of its foreign reserves in May to defend the baht after it came under heavy speculative attack. 

 This cut the country's foreign reserves to a two-year low of $33.3 billion at the end of May from around $37.3 billion a month earlier 

 Pressure was expected to mount again soon amid sustained bearish sentiment over the country's economy and moves to rescue its beleaguered financial institutions. 

 "Under the new system movements in the exchange rate are expected to be quite large at the initial stage. However, relative stability should be attained after a brief adjustment period," Bidaya said. 

 "The Bank of Thailand will intervene in the foreign exchange market from time to time to achieve policy objectives and guard against excessive baht fluctuations." 

 The statement gave no details on the exact way in which the managed float would work, but the central bank said later a baht-dollar reference would be set daily, based on the baht's trading average the day before. 

 The Bank of Thailand said it had "an appropriate rate" in mind in which it expected the baht to move, but gave no details. 

 "However, if the baht goes beyond the approriate rate the central bank will intervene in the market," central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulsawasdi told a news conference. 

 Dealers said they would not be surprised if the baht tested 30.00 to the dollar. Thai overnight interbank rates were unqoted on Wednesday because banks were unwilling to lend until the market settled down. In the Philippines, the peso was hit by ripples from the Thai announcement, and the Philippines central bank raised interest rates to counter speculative attacks. 

 The Indonesian rupiah and Malaysian ringitt were also jolted by the news. 

 Bidaya said domestic confidence in Thailand's foreign exchange rate system had remained shaky despite the fact that the central bank had successfully defended the baht in May. 

 "This is a de facto devaluation, but we need to know about the onshore/offshore trading system before we know if the speculators have won," a European currency trader based in Singapore said. 

 Thailand has a two-tier exchange rate system which limits offshore trading of the baht. 

 Before the float, it was fixed on a daily basis against a basket of currencies dominated by the U.S. dollar. 

 Analysts said higher lending rates would not help Thailand's economy, which is burdened with a swollen current account deficit and financial market woes. 

 "The economy's already slowing down, interest rates should be coming down not going up," a senior foreign exchange trader at a European bank in Singapore said.
