title: FULL TEXT-Bank of Thailand statement on baht.
text:
BANGKOK, July 2 (Reuter) - Following is the full text of the statement by the Bank of Thailand on Wednesday on changes to the country's foreign exchange policy. 

 1. The Minister of Finance, upon the recommendation of the Bank of Thailand, on 2 July 1997 issued a Notification determining that the value of the baht would henceforth be set by market forces. 

 2. As from 2 November 1984, the baht value had been set in reference to a basket of currencies of Thailand's major trading partners. The exchange rate of the baht against the United States dollar was announced daily by the Exchange Equalization Fund, which stood ready to buy and sell US dollars with commercial banks at determined rates. This system resulted in the baht becoming one of the most stable currencies in the world and supported Thailand's rapid growth over the years. 

 3. The tight monetary policy followed by the Bank of Thailand since 1995 in order to contain incipient pressures on inflation and the current account have had the desired effect on economic stability. However, the coincidental sharp slowdown of exports and capital inflows in 1996, together with problems in financial institutions resulted in a rapid deceleration of investment and growth. Calls for a relaxation of monetary policy evoked widespread speculation that exchange rate policy might be adjusted to allow for reductions in interest rates. While the authorities' interventions were successful in containing speculative pressure in foreign exchange markets, the confidence of domestic businesses in the authorities' exchange rate policy continued to weaken in the wake of widespread speculation and criticisms. 

 4. In order to end uncertainty over Thailand's exchange rate policy, Thailand's exchange rate system will from 2 July 1997 be a managed float, whereby the value of the baht will be determined by market forces to reflect economic fundamentals. 

 5. Under the new system, movements in the exchange rate are expected to be quite large at the initial stage. However, relative stability should be attained after a brief adjustment period. The Bank of Thailand will intervence in foreign exchange markets from time to time to achieve policy objectives and guard against excessive fiuctuations. 

 6. To support the new foreign exchange regime, a cautious monetary policy stance will continue to be followed. Effective today, the Bank of Thailand has raised the bank rate from 10.5 to 12.5 percent. In due course, the Bank will allow market forces to adjust interest rates downward in the context of a stable or strengthening baht. In the longer run, the managed float system will enable the authorities to implement monetary policy consistent with domestic policy objectives and support healthy capital inflows. 

 7. Some slowdown in economic activity must be accepted in the wake of the new exchange rate regime. However, this will lay the groundwork for growth with stability in the years ahead. In the short run, so as to alleviate any negative effect on debt servicing and prices that may result from an adjustment in the baht value, the authorities are prepared to consider implementing supplementary measures, particularly those related to prices of goods considered as necessities, tax deduction for businesses suffering exchange losses, and financing facilities for priority economic sectors. 

 8. The Ministry of Finance and the Bank of Thailand believe that the managed float system will benefit Thailand's overall economic development. The new system will provide sufficient flexibility to accommodate developments in Thailand's economy and respond to the situation in financial and foreign exchange markets. 

 ---------------- Notification of the Ministry of Finance

 By virtue of the power conferred upon him under section 8 Paragraph Three of the Currency Act, B.E. 2501, as amended by The Currency Act (No.4) B.E. 2516. 

 The Minister of Finance, upon the recommendation of the Bank of Thailand, hereby issues this notification as follows; 

 1. The Notification of the Ministry of Finance dated 2 November B.E. 2527 Re; Change of Foreign Exchange System is hereby repealed. 

 2. The foreign exchange system shall be such that the value of the Baht is set by conditions in foreign exchange markets. 

 3. The Bank of Thailand shall engage in buying and selling of foreign currency for the purpose of maintaining the stability of the Baht under the system mentioned in 2. 

 4. The Bank of Thailand shall from time to time as deemed necessary, publish the exchange rates between the Baht and foreign currencies for use as a reference rate in conversion of foreign currencies into Baht. 

 (c) Reuters Limited 1997

title: Thailand/Floats Baht/Amplifier -4: Recession Likely In '97
text:
The floating of the baht is likely to result in deep cuts in forecasts for economic growth, including those of the Bank of Thailand. Rerngchai said the central bank will cut its forecast for 5.9% growth this year. Saker of SocGen-Crosby said he expects the Thai economy to shrink in the half of 1997, fulfilling the standard definition of a recession. For the full year, he said economic growth will be 1%. Thailand hasn't had a recession in 30 years. 

 The Bank of Thailand acknowledged a slowdown is inevitable, although it said nothing of recession. In a statement it said: 'The authorities are prepared to consider implementing supplementary measures, particularly those related to prices of goods considered necessities, tax deductions for businesses suffering exchange losses, and financing facilities for priority economic sectors.' 

 The Thai stock market, however, is likely to benefit. Thailand's benchmark stock index had fallen 36% since the start of the year to 527.28 points before the currency float. That's the amount Mexico's index fell in reaction to the peso devaluation. Because Thailand's stock market anticipated the baht's fall, stock prices are now likely to move up, analysts said. The Stock Exchange of Thailand index Wednesday registered its biggest single-day gain in nine months, climbing 41.51 points to 568.79 points. 

 Under the new currency system, the Bank of Thailand said it will intervene to defend the baht only 'from time to time to achieve policy objectives and guard against excessive fluctuations.' 

 That means scrapping the trading band that obligated the central bank to intervene whenever the dollar moved more than 0.08% in one day. It also means scrapping the currency basket -consisting of the dollar, the Deutsche mark and the Japanese yen- to which the baht had been pegged since 1984. 

 -James Hookway and Warangkana Tempati of Dow Jones Newswires contributed to this article.

title: Thailand Baht Ends Stable Despite Shutdown Of 16 Fincl Cos
text:

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals calm, baht awaits data.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 26 (Reuter) - The Thai baht was steady on Thursday ahead of the release of central bank monthly economic data expected later in the session, dealers said. 

 Sentiment was cautious as the market waits to see the extent to which Thailand's foreign reserve declined after central bank intervention to defend the baht from speculation last month. 

 The Bank of Thailand will announce April and May economic data at 0800 GMT. 

 Traders said a sharp fall in reserves would put downward pressure on the baht. 

 Prime Minister Chavalit Yonchaiyudh has said he does not want to devalue the currency. 

 The baht was quoted at 25.840/870 at 0430 GMT to the dollar against 25.820/850 late on Wednesday. 

 But trade was relatively quiet in the onshore market, with comments from former Thai Prime Minister Chatichai Choonhavan in New Delhi having little affect on activity, dealers said. 

 Chatichai said the Bank of Thailand estimates that gross domestic product (GDP) will grow by 5.9 percent in 1997, down from 6.4 percent last year. He also said the government would strongly defend the value of the baht. 

 The Bank of Thailand kept the baht/dollar midrate unchanged at 25.77. Offshore, the baht was barely changed at 25.400/500 against 25.300/25.400 on Wednesday. 

 The Malaysian ringgit recovered as dollar gains were capped on the topside near the level where dealers felt the central bank would intervene at 2.5240. 

 The dollar was well bid in the offshore market but failed to trek beyond 2.5250, which continues to keep ringgit defensive. 

 "People are still trying to buy the dollar/Malay. There is commericial demand for the dollar before June 30, but market is still long dollars offshore," a European brokerage dealer said. 

 He said dollar demand was prompted by mid-year book closing and some window-dressing activities. 

 At 0430 GMT, the ringgit was quoted at 2.5200/100, up from 2.5232/42 at its close in Kuala Lumpur on Wednesday. 

 Malaysian dealers said there was also some caution as the system could turn tight. Some two billion ringgit from a Bank Negara lending maturity is said to leave the market on Thursday. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah was stable against the dollar on sufficient liquidity, with short-term swaps easing. 

 Dealers said there were few market-moving factors and the dollar/rupiah looked trapped within current narrow ranges. 

 Some selling activity was sighted in short-term swaps early in the session, dampened by ample liquidity. 

 The central bank, Bank Indonesia, supplied some 262 billion rupiah temporarily in the market.

title: Thai  currency  defense seen relying on attrition.
text:
NEW YORK, June 23 (Reuter) - The standoff between the Thai government and currency speculators is likely to extend over the next four to six weeks in a brutal war of attrition, U.S. trader and hedge fund managers said. 

 In the forward market, the Thai government stands to suffer heavy reserve losses if the baht is devalued before the large positions which it has put on to stem speculative pressure are closed, they said. 

 The Bank of Thailand has spent about $2 billion to $3 billion in interventions on the spot market, but its contingent liabilities in the forward market are several times larger, estimated a fund manager. 

 "We are half way through the crisis," he said. "I don't think the central bank would cave in at this point." 

 Most of the aggressive selling by international hedge funds in April and early May involved contracts over 60-day and 90-day baht forward rates, which eventually prompted the Thai government to impose a two-tier exchange rate system. 

 Hedge funds under the control of George Soros were reported to have $4 billion in forward currency contracts due in August, according to The Nation newspaper published in Thailand on Monday. A spokesman from Soros Funds in New York, citing company policy, declined comments on the report. 

 The pressure in the next 30 to 45 days is reflected in volatility of the baht forward rates.  Traders quoted one-month rate at 86.8 percent of the spot bid and 96.6 offered. Two-month was bid 50 percent, six-month 31 percent and 12-month 24 percent. 

 In the latest round of baht selling on Finance Minister Amnuay's resignation last week, Thai corporations joined the fray and the battleground was mostly in the spot market, traders said. 

 David Rolley, a portfolio manager at Loomis Sayles in Boston, compared the situation to Mexican corporations selling pesos before the the devaluation in 1994. 

 "It was not just speculators who bet on an overvalued baht," he said, adding that "selling also came from legitimate corporate hedging against their dollar liabilities." 

 The Thai private sector owes $66 billion in foreign currency debt, of which the bulk is due in one year or less, he said. 

 Currnecy traders said concerted intervention by Southeast Asian central banks stablized the baht at about 25.00 per U.S. dollar and the level appeared to be holding. 

 The forward market, in contrast, was eerily slow, they said. 

 "The central bank has the upper hand right now," said a trader, noting that quite a few hedge funds were groaning because they were trapped in the market by the exchange control. 

 "It is the most vindictive system we have seen," said an analyst, who asked not to be named. 

 To be sure, hedge funds have mounted some unsuccessful currency attacks in the past, such as the assault on the French franc, but they could liquidate their positions in the open market and reclaim some value, whereas in Thailand's current two-tier exchange rate system, the speculators had no way out, he said. 

 "When it is over, I doubt anyone would ever try to attack the baht again," the analyst said.

title: Singapore pledges to continue to defend Thai baht.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 19 (Reuter) - Finance Minister Richard Hu said on Thursday Singapore would continue to help Thailand defend its baht against speculators. 

 "We will continue with what we have been doing, which is to collaborate with the Thai central bank, but as you have seen so far the Thai authorities have managed quite a lot," Hu told reporters on the sidelines of a conference on project financing. 

 "I think there is no doubt that the present glitch (in Thailand) is a temporary one," he said following the resignation of Thai counterpart Amnuay Viravan. 

 On May 14, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said it had intervened jointly with the Bank of Thailand in the foreign exchange market to defend the baht against speculators. 

 MAS, effectively Singapore's central bank, rarely admits intervention in the market. 

 MAS deputy managing director Koh Beng Seng told reporters two days after the intervention that the move to defend the baht against speculators was effective. 

 But Amnuay's resignation on Thursday triggered another tumble of the baht in Asia, triggering a wave of hedging against other regionals, dealers said. 

 Some dealers said news that Thai Commerce Minister Narongchai Akrasanee also planned to resign would prompt more selling of baht. 

 The baht was pushed down to 26.300 against the dollar in late morning, but revived to 25.150/659 at midday. 

 Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh said a new finance minister would be appointed on Friday but kept financial markets guessing as to who it might be.

title: Malaysia offered to defend baht, says Thai minister.
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, June 6 (Reuter) - Malaysia offered to defend the baht during a recent speculative attack on the Thai currency, Thailand's Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan revealed on Friday. 

 "There have been offers from countries (of the region), including Malaysia, but we have not used the facilities," he told a news conference. 

 Malaysia's central bank, Bank Negara Malaysia, has not commented on whether the Thai government had sought its help to defend the baht during a sharp attack on the currency in mid-May. 

 But the Monetary Authority of Singapore said it intervened in the market, along with the Bank of Thailand, to help the baht during the recent assault on the currency. 

 Central banks in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) have an ongoing pact to defend each other's currrencies in times of such crises. 

 "There has been some manipulation, some attack on our currency," said Amnuay, visiting Kuala Lumpur on the invitation of Malaysia's acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. 

 "The situation has calmed down and stabilised," he said. 

 Amnuay said Malaysia had gone through a similar currency turmoil in 1993 and "we can learn from experiences of Malaysia". 

 Since the assault on its currency, Thailand has introduced capital controls which have decreased foreign investors' access to the baht. 

 But Amnuay declined to give any details of the situation or how long the controls, under which overseas currency swaps have been stopped, will remain in place. 

 "It is not the place or time to discuss our plans," he said when asked if the country would formalise an exchange policy with other countries in the region.

title: Thailand: Shrs End Dn As Foreigners Sell Stk For Baht
text:
BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Thai stock prices finished 3.2% lower Friday - an eight-year low - after foreign investors sold off banking stocks to scrape together Thai baht to pay their debts in the foreign exchange market, dealers said. 

 The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index closed 17.43 points lower at 530.62, compared with Thursday's close of 548.05. 

 Around 170.6 million shares valued at 5.19 billion baht changed hands, compared with 98.0 million shares worth 2.80 billion baht Thursday. 

 The select SET 50 index was 1.79 points down at 37.76. 

 Declining shares hammered advances 204 to 96, excluding foreign shares. At the close of Friday's session, the SET index was 36% down on 1996's year-end close of 831.57. 

 Overseas players dominated trading, with the foreign- registered banking stocks soaking up much of the trading volume. Dealers reckoned the selling was sparked by demand for Thai baht in the overseas foreign exchange market. 

 'To get hold of Thai currency, some investors are borrowing baht to buy stock. They then sell the stock to get cash in hand to pay off their obligations in the foreign exchange market,' said a dealer with Securities One PCL. 

Forex investors were still scrambling for baht after Thailand's central bank staged a massive intervention in late May to defend the currency from its heaviest speculative attack in years. 

 Foreign-registered shares of Bangkok Bank PCL fell 4 baht to 210, with Thai Farmers Bank PCL foreign shares down 4 baht to 118. Siam Commercial Bank PCL's foreign shares fell 12 baht to 115.

text:
BANGKOK, May 30 (Reuter) - The baht rallied strongly against the dollar in the offshore currency market on Friday as the currency's surging foreign rate sharply widened its gap with that quoted in the domestic market, dealers said. 

 Dealers said the baht firmed to an intraday high of 24.840 to the dollar in offshore markets before it retreated to about 25.120/25.220 at 0748 GMT. The rate compared with a domestic low of 25.830 quoted by Thai-based dealers. 

 A two-tier offshore and onshore baht market has been in place since mid-May, after speculative attacks on the currency, when the central bank imposed capital controls to cut off baht supplies at local rates to offshore players. 

 Dealers said the stronger offshore baht reflected higher foreign demand for the currency, most likely from speculators, seeking to cover their short-baht positions taken earlier after their failed attacks on the currency. The Bank of Thailand also ordered local banks to quote higher baht rates to foreign players.

title: Thailand/Data/Amplifier -2: May Data Could Be Bleaker
text:
Thailand pegs its baht to a dollar-denominated basket of currencies and doesn't allow the currency fluctuate by more than 0.16% each day. When the dollar moves outside that range, the central bank is obligated to buy or sell U.S. currency at below-market rates to rein it in. 

 To maintain the system, the central bank has to keep interest rates high even when the economy stalls. Prominent Thai government officials, such as Commerce Minister Narongchai Akrasanee, say the system stifled the Thai economy after 1995. Most economists agree that the currency peg is unsustainable in the long run. 

 As Thailand's economy cooled to its slowest rate in a decade last year, currency speculators began to bet the peg wasn't sustainable in the short term either. As a result, the baht has been attacked at least three times in the last 10 months, and the attacks have become progressively more severe. 

 In the most recent attack, in May, the Bank of Thailand got unprecedented aid from Southeast Asian central banks. The Monetary Authority of Singapore openly intervened in Thailand's defense, and other regional central banks, including the Bank of Japan, made supportive statements. But the Thai central bnak ultimately had to resort to informal capital controls to quell the attack, effectively shutting down the overseas forward market for baht. 

 The central bank's data for April portend worse news for May, analysts said. Given the ferocity of the currency attack this month, the balance of payments deficit for May could exceed 26.6 billion baht, said Dominique Maire, an economist with UBS Securities (East Asia) Ltd. in Bangkok. He said foreign reserves will decline further, signaling growing weakness in Thailand's currency defenses.

title: Thailand, China sign securities repo agreement.
text:
BANGKOK, May 27 (Reuter) - The central banks of China and Thailand banks have signed a bilateral repurchase agreement as part of regional cooperation among Asian countries to stabilise their currencies during emergencies. 

 A central bank statement said the pact allows one central bank to borrow U.S. dollars from the other needed for intervention in foreign exchange markets in order to help stabilise its currency. 

 It said the U.S. dollar borrowing would be backed by U.S. government securities as collateral. 

 The Thai central bank said the agreement was similar to earlier repo pacts it signed with Japan, Malaysia, Indonesia, Australia, Hong Kong, Singapore and the Philippines. 

 It did not reveal the ceiling of U.S. dollar borrowing provided by the agreement but said earlier that each bilateral pact has a $500 million limit.

title: Thailand/Computer Breakdown/SET -3: Reality Not Clear
text:
The reality on Monday wasn't so clear cut as some investors would have hoped. Instead of cutting the discount rate, the central bank said it was changing the way the minimum retail rate is calculated. This means the MRR will be freed up from bank deposit rates, a Bank of Thailand spokeswoman said, allowing the retail rate to move independently from the prime rate. 

 But there's one exception. The retail rate won't be allowed to rise more than 4 percentage points over the prime rate, which stands at 13% in Thailand. Analysts said the move allows banks to charge their retail clients more, freeing up funds to ease rates to commercial borrowers. 

 A dim signal it may have been, but it was enough to spark some reaction among leading commercial banks. 'There was some good news out there,' said Songyos Kulvichien, first vice president at Securities One PCL. 'Thai Farmers Bank cut its minimum lending rate, and this could spark some buying.' 

 Thai Farmers Bank PCL (P.TFB) reduced its minimum lending rate by 25 basis points to 12.75%. Bangkok Bank PCL (P.BBK), the country's largest, was fast on its heels, announcing a planned minimum lending rate cut of 25 basis points to 12.75% this week too. 

 'I think we'll have to cut the rate within this week. Other banks are doing this too,' said Executive Vice President Piti Sithi-Amnuai. He said Bangkok Bank's minimum lending rate would to fall 25 basis points to 12.75%. 

 But the central bank's policy move could suggest difficulties in getting interest rates down further, analysts said. 

 'They're trying to bring the rates down without affecting the baht,' said Sriyan Pietersz, market strategist at Capital Nomura Securites PCL. He said it would be difficult for the central bank to bring rates down further because of the need to protect the baht from further attacks in the foreign exchange market. Last week, the Bank of Thailand successfully fended off an attack from speculators through massive intervention in the foreign exchange market.

title: Thailand/SEC/Short-Selling -2: Can't Do Anything Legally
text:
Massive intervention from the Bank of Thailand and other Southeast Asian central banks brought the dollar down to a six-month low by the end of last week. Speculators were burned as they found themselves unable to unwind their positions because they couldn't get their hands on baht. Some observers estimate they lost up to $300 million. 

 But unlike the Bank of Thailand in the forex market, there's nothing the SEC can legally do to counter short-selling as it takes place outside its jurisdiction. 

 Prasarn declined to comment on whether the SEC action is being taken independently of the central bank. But analysts are concerned.

 Observers said the Thai regulators could be sending a warning to foreign investors short-selling in offshore markets that they're being watched. But that situation may not last for long. title: FOCUS - Thai markets end frenzied week on calmer note.
text:
BANGKOK, May 16 (Reuter) - Thai investors heaved a sigh of relief on Friday as the country's stock and money markets finished a frenetic week on a slightly calmer note. 

 After nearly three weeks of seemingly endless declines and a seven percent drop in the past five trading days, the Stock Exchange of Thailand's key index nudged up slightly to end 3.32 points higher at 561.19. 

 Afternoon bargain-hunting helped boost the index, brokers said. 

 Traders and analysts said the bourse was buoyed by feelings that the latest currency crisis was over, and belief that the Thai baht was not going to be devalued in the near term. 

 "The foreigners are coming in, picking up cheap stocks. Once it became clear that the baht was not going to be devalued, at least during this current round, on valuations there are cheap stocks here," said a foreign trader. 

 The baht, which was hammered on Wednesday and Thursday amid rumours of an imminent devaluation, remained relatively steady throughout the day. It was quoted at 25.775/25.865 bid/ask to the dollar in late deals after falling as low as 26.330/26.430 late on Wednesday when speculators aggressively dumped the baht. 

 The central bank said on Friday that speculative attacks on the baht had ended and the situation for the embattled currency was returning to normal. 

 "Since yesterday, there has been no speculation (in the baht). If there is any speculation, we will do our duty (and intervene)," said Bank of Thailand deputy governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi. 

 The Bank of Thailand teamed with several regional central banks this week and intervened in foreign exchange markets to successfully defend the baht. It also asked local banks not to buy dollars from offshore parties in another attempt to fend off speculation in the baht. 

 Analysts cautioned that although markets had stabilised on Friday, the fundamental problem behind the crisis -- a slowing economy and a lack of confidence that the government's current measures will be able to cure it -- still remains. 

 "I think it is a victory but not the end of the war," said George Morgan, country manager for ABM-AMRO Hoare Govett. "It's not backed up by any improvement in economic outlook. Speculators will be back again." 

 Thai authorities said they would announce on Monday some support measures to try and help the battered stock market, which is at eight-year lows. 

 Those measures include the issue of 5.0 billion baht ($192 million) bonds by Securities Finance Corp (SFC), which will use the funds to buy margin loans from securities companies, central bank assistant governor Siri Ganjarerndee said on Friday. 

 Traders and analysts said a slew of first quarter corporate results released on Friday were generally negative, but said a decline in earnings had already been widely anticipated. Most results came in above worst case forecasts, they said. 

 "They were almost all poor, very poor, but predictably so," said an analyst at a leading European broker.

title: Thai stocks in doldrums despite baht defence.
text:
BANGKOK, May 16 (Reuter) - Currency speculators retreated to nurse their wounds after Asian central banks fended off attacks on the Thai baht this week, but there was little sign of relief for the country's frail stock market, analysts said on Friday. 

 Analysts said the Thai bourse, rated the worst performer among more than 50 stock exchanges in recent months, may get a brief lift from Thailand's success in defending its currency from speculative attacks. But few expected the prolonged downtrend in stocks to bottom soon. 

 "We finally got some good news that the Bank of Thailand succeeded in defending the baht, but most people feel Thailand just won the battle but not the war," said Mike Stead, chief analyst at Union Securities Co Ltd. 

 He said Thai stocks may, at best, stage a small technical rebound in line with the baht. The composite SET Index was down 6.56 points, or 1.18 percent, to 551.31 at 0800 GMT on Friday. 

 At 0800 GMT, the baht was quoted at 25.800/850 to the dollar against 25.300/340 late on Thursday. The Bank of Thailand said attacks on the currency had ended following heavy intervention from Thai and other regional central banks this week. 

 The baht's losses earlier this week sparked a fall in the country's stocks to near eight-year lows. 

 The SET Index has lost 35 percent in 1996 and 33.7 percent so far this year, including a 16.6 percent setback this month. 

 Analysts said weak economic fundamentals, blamed for hurting market sentiment and helping fuel rumours of policy conflicts in the government this week, remained largely unchanged. 

 The Thai economy is projected to grow at five to six percent this year, its slowest pace in a decade. The country's troubled property sector has sharply weakened bank earnings and pushed some over-exposed finance companies to near bankruptcy. 

 Economist Somjai Phagaphasvivat of Thammasat University said the government was walking an economic tight-rope. 

 "Thailand's dilemma is it could not lower high domestic interest rates to help revive the economy and stock market because doing it now would further weaken the baht and trigger a massive capital flight," he said. 

 Somjai said the central bank had few options but to maintain its high interest rate and baht fixing policies until money and stock markets gained more stability. 

 The Bank of Thailand said on Friday that measures would be announced on Monday to help support the stock market, including a bond issue to raise funds to purchase margin loans from securities companies. 

 Analysts said the market's mood remained cautious and reflected lingering jitters about the economy and the disastrous first quarter earnings of most listed firms. 

 "We don't know if some more bad news (is) lurking around the corner," a foreign analyst said. 

 Stead of Union Securities said Thai energy stocks and some electronics issues stood out as the best bargains for investors still with the nerves to return to the market. 

 He said Electricity Generating Plc, Cogeneration Plc, and Banpu Plc enjoyed strong earnings potential and could quickly rebound from their recent steep losses tied to the bearish market. 

 "I am not particularly optimistic on banks and especially finance companies. Any bank rebound will be limited," he said. 

 The bank and finance sectors, hurt by bad loans to property developers, have tumbled 31.5 and 58.5 percent so far this year. In March, the government ordered a revamp of the finance sector.

title: FOCUS - Thai  central bank  says baht returning to normal.
text:
BANGKOK, May 16 (Reuter) - Thailand's central bank said on Friday that speculative attacks on the baht had ended and the situation for the embattled currency was returning to normal. 

 "Since yesterday there has been no speculation (in the baht). If there is any speculation we will do our duty (intervene)," Bank of Thailand deputy governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi said. 

 "The speculation in the baht has stopped, judging from the level the baht is trading against the dollar in the market compared with the midrate," Chaiyawat said. 

 "Investor thinking is now on the reverse side. They are now buying the baht because they know it is not worth speculating," he added. 

 Attacks on the baht by foreign speculators this week forced swap rates to soar, sparked heavy Thai and other regional central bank intervention to keep the currency from sliding and sent shockwaves through the Thai stock market, which fell to near eight-year lows. 

 However, forex dealers said on Friday that they had noted selling of dollars for the baht in the spot market by those seeking to ease their tight baht liquidity. 

 At 0543 GMT, the baht was weaker at 25.800/900 against 25.300/340 late on Thursday. The central bank fixed the midrate at 25.82 versus the dollar. 

 Chaiyawat also made clear that foreign speculators who sold the baht heavily for U.S. dollars would have to pay a high price for their action by buying back the baht from the more expensive swap market to square outstanding positions. 

 "We separate local investors from outside speculators in terms of liquidity supply. The outside speculators cannot buy baht back to meet obligations through regular channels. For Thai business, everything will be normal," he said. 

 "The speculators must pay the price. Because of their speculative move, the swap premiums soared. If they intend to buy from the forward market like that, they must buy through the swap market," he added. 

 Local foreign exchange dealers confirmed that the central bank had told them not to buy dollars from offshore punters to fight against further speculation. 

 "We were informally informed (by the central bank) not to buy dollars from offshore players," said a dealer. 

 Chaiyawat said he expected liquidity and the overnight interbank rate in the local money market to be tight on Friday but added that the central bank was ready to help ease and calm the situation. 

 "Today liquidity will be tight. But the Bank of Thailand will ensure that those with liquidity problems will be helped," he added. 

 The local interbank rate jumped to 20-22 percent early on Friday from 14-15 percent late on Thursday as liquidity tightened while demand for baht rose and the baht/dollar swap premiums rocketed to around 70-100 satangs, dealers said. 

 Thailand has been dogged by investor jitters because of its sluggish economy which is expected to grow at just over five percent this year -- the lowest in a decade.

title: Thailand ready to fight new baht attacks - report.
text:
BANGKOK, May 16 (Reuter) - Thailand will be alert against any fresh speculative attacks on the ailing baht after its effective defence of the currency this week, central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond said. 

 Rerngchai told the Nation newspaper in an interview on Thursday that his bank was prepared to intervene in foreign exchange markets and would seek cooperation, if necessary, from other regional central banks to do the job. 

 "The baht volatility has been going on for several days, but we decided to fight the battle in the foreign exchange markets so that we did not have to defend the baht at home," he said. 

 Rerngchai said: "If necessary, we'll also ask for cooperation from other countries. You've got to understand that the speculators follow no ethical codes...in the foreign exchange markets there is no world police." 

 "Now the foreign exchange rates fall within the band which we try to maintain, but we cannot be careless," he said. 

 The governor declined to say how much Thailand had used to defend the baht on Wednesday but dealers estimated the country spent billions of dollars to shore up its currency. 

 The baht fell to 26.330/26.440 to the dollar early on Wednesday before the Thai central bank intervention which helped the currency close sharply firmer at 25.910/25.940. 

 At 0341 GMT on Friday it was quoted at 25.450/25.650. 

 Rerngchai said currency speculators had underestimated a joint defence mechanism that Thailand has with 11 regional countries. "We have informed the speculators all along that this cooperation exists, but they say the cooperation is only on paper." 

Thailand said it defended the baht on Wednesday through concerted intervention carried out with the Monetary Authority of Singapore. Other regional banks were also suspected to have been buying the Thai currency.-- Bangkok newsroom (662)-6520642

TOKYO (AP-Dow Jones)--The Bank of Japan has no comment on whether the government of Thailand has approached Japan with a request to intervene in currency market to support the baht, a senior Bank of Japan official said Thursday. 

 Speaking on condition of anonymity, the official also denied an earlier report that the central bank had suggested such a request was made. Earlier Thursday, one foreign newswire in Tokyo reported that a BOJ official confirmed such a request had been made. 

 The BOJ official said that the central bank is 'relieved' over the baht's movements in the currency markets Thursday and said 'It looks like market sentiment regarding the baht is stabilizing, even improving already.' 

 After a sharp selloff earlier, the Thai baht rose amid central bank baht buying in Bangkok and Singapore Thursday. The baht had plunged to a seven-year low Wednesday. 

 The dollar is currently quoted at 25.30 baht. 

 The official said the Bank of Japan is currently taking a wait-and-see stance and closely watching further steps on economic and financial policy that may be taken by the Thai government. 

 He noted that the BOJ and the Thai central bank remain in close contact. 

 Earlier Thursday, a Thai official said Thailand will seek Japanese assistance to combat a speculative attack on the baht. 

 'We will ask our major trading partners, like Singapore and Japan, to spend some money to defend the baht,' Poosana Premanoch, Chavalit's deputy secretary-general told reporters. Singapore's central bank has already intervened to defend the baht in concert with the Bank of Thailand.

title: Thailand/ Central Bank /Speculators-2: 'They've Given Up'
text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--Speculators who on Wednesday launched one of the most severe attacks on the Thai currency in years are now selling dollars frantically, having been stung by central-bank intervention, a senior offical at the Bank of Thailand said Thursday. 

 'I think speculators have unwound their positions,' said the official, who is familiar with the bank's money-market operations, told Dow Jones Newswires. 'It means they've given up. They're probably selling dollars now, which is why the baht is trading so high.' 

 The dollar, which closed Wednesday 0.46 baht outside the upper limit of the central bank's trading range, is now trading 0.14 baht outside the lower limit of the range. The range is 25.79 baht to 25.83 baht. Around 0757 GMT (3:57 EDT), the dollar is trading at 25.65 baht. 

 When the baht is outside the upper limit of the range, it means the central bank is selling dollars to defend the currency. When it is outside the lower limit, it means the central bank has to buy dollars to defend the currency. 

 The central bank official said, however, that the Bank of Thailand doesn't want the baht to be outside the lower limit of the range, either. 'I'm very concerned about this, he said. He declined to say, however, whether he expects the currency to return within the band by Friday.

title: Thailand:  Central Bank  Rules Out Baht Devaluation
text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--Thailand's central bank on Thursday ruled out a baht devaluation or any change in the country's exchange-rate system and urged Thai companies and investors not to lose confidence in the system. 

 'The bank would like to ask the private sector to remain confident in the authority's policy and to ignore rumors because it will only support the action of speculators who want to sabotage the confidence and the security of the country,' the central bank said in a statement. 

 The Thai currency has been under attack by speculators since Wednesday, although interventions by the Bank of Thailand and the Monetary Authority of Singapore have helped forestall further decline in the currency. 

 The baht fell Wednesday to its lowest point in more than seven years, as the dollar closed at 26.30 baht.

title: Thailand Shares Lower At Midday; SET Down 4.2% Or 23.99 Pts
text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--The Thai stock market's main barometer is 4.2% lower midday Thursday as investors bail out of the market amid continued selling of the Thai currency on concern over the health of the economy, dealers say. 

 At 0530 GMT (1:30 a.m. EDT), the Stock Exchange of Thailand index is down 23.99 points to 547.31, after ranging from a high of 565.52 and a low of 544.10 points. 

 The SET 50 Index is 2.08 points lower at 39.54. 

 At midday, declining shares outnumber advances 268 to 31 on trading volume of 84.4 million shares worth 2.89 billion baht. 

 'Sentiment in the stock market is very bad,' one dealer said. 'There's a lot of pressure still weighing on the baht, and there's a lot of uncertainty about what will happen.' 

 The Thai baht suffered more selling in the foreign exchange market Thursday morning after it sank to a low of 26.25 baht to the dollar Thursday. But by midday, the baht was stabilizing after reports of intervention from the Bank of Thailand in overseas markets. At 0534 GMT (1:34 a.m. EDT), the dollar was trading at 25.70 baht. 

 The selling was sparked by concerns over the Thai government's ability to handle the country's slowing economy. 

 But despite the central bank intervention, the anxious mood at the SET isn't lifting. Dealers said investors were selling across the board, and foreigners were dumping blue-chip stocks. 

 Bangkok Bank PCL is 7 baht lower at 149, with Thai Farmers Bank PCL down 2.50 baht to 97.50. Advanced Info Service PCL is 1 baht down at 154, with industrial conglomerate Siam Cement PCL 54 baht lower at 504.

title: Thai baht rallies late as rates hit speculators.
text:
BANGKOK, May 15 (Reuter) - The Thai baht rallied in late trade on Thursday as the central bank allowed banks to quote Friday for Monday delivery deals for overseas clients at high financing costs, dealers said. 

 The high baht rates foiled speculators, severely tightened liquidity and renewed interest in the baht, they added. 

 The baht strengthened to 25.300/25.340 per dollar at 1022 GMT from 25.910/25.940 early, dealers said. The Bank of Thailand fixed the mid-rate at 25.81 a dollar against 25.85 on Wednesday. "The spot market was quite calm down today with more dollar being offered in the market," said a dealer at a foreign bank. 

 The Bank of Thailand stressed on Thursday it would maintain high interest rates to defend against speculative attacks on the currency. 

 The offshore players also found it difficult to borrow funds for speculation in the baht as the central bank was earlier said to inform banks in Thailand not quote to offshore parties for tom/next activities, dealers said. 

 However, the central bank in the afternoon allowed banks to resume quoting tom/next to non-resident clients. 

 "We are allowed to resume quoting tom/next (for Friday dollar/baht deals and Monday delivery) for overseas clients but at about two baht," said one broker at a foreign bank. said. 

 The authorities made it clear that local banks would have to offer funds at high financing costs to discourage speculation against the baht, she added. 

 Most players were also wary of pushing the baht down further amid worries about another intervention by Bank of Thailand and its regional counterparts to defend the currency, dealers said. 

 Central banks of Thailand and Singapore on Wednesday jointly intervened in the Singapore market to stabilise the battered baht. 

 The Bank of Japan said on Thursday it may join hands with other Asian central banks and intervene in foreign exchange markets to help support the baht if asked to do so by Thailand. 

 But forward premiums were shooting up further due to a severe shortage of funds after recent buying of the dollar by speculators, dealers said. 

 The one-month baht/dollar swap premium jumped to 15.00/16.00 satangs per dollar late from 12.00/13.00 in early morning, dealers said. 

 The overnight interbank rate eased to 14.00-15.00 percent late from 18.00-20.00 percent early, dealers said. 

 "Most banks had done nothing today. But I heard the rate of 14.00-15.00 was being done in the market in the afternoon," said one money market dealer.

title: BOJ may help support Thai baht, but not yet - dealers.
text:
TOKYO, May 15 (Reuter) - Japan's central bank said on Thursday it may join hands with other Asian central banks and intervene in foreign exchange markets to help support the crumbling Thai baht if asked to do so by Thailand. 

 Any such moves would be part of the Asian currency safety net agreement reached between Asian monetary authorities in 1996, an official at the Bank of Japan (BOJ) told Reuters. 

 "The agreement is there, although it is not a thing we would activate unless we were asked by Thailand," he said. 

 "We have an agreement, and if we want to use it, we certainly will. But it's not a question of our making the first move," he added. 

 Last year, Japan agreed with the monetary authorities of Australia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand to establish bilateral repurchase agreements to provide liquidity in times of currency crisis. 

 Such "repo" pacts give participants instant access to cash -- for use to defend their currencies against excessive volatility -- by virtue of them selling their holdings in U.S. government securities to partners with a promise to buy them back later. 

 On Wednesday, in the first use of this agreement, the Thai central bank and the Monetary Authority of Singapore jointly intervened in the foreign exchange market to defend the baht. 

 Malaysia's central bank and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority were also said to have bought the Thai currency after it fell to 26.250-26.300 to the dollar, though there was no confirmation. 

 Rising concerns about the slowing Thai economy and rumours of political turmoil in the cabinet that could lead to the possible resignation of Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan triggered heavy baht sales for the dollar on Wednesday. 

 Amnuay, who has repeatedly denied he will quit, reiterated on Thursday that Thailand will defend its currency against attacks in the market by currency speculators. 

 "We have been successful and we will be successful," he said, adding: "We have support from all our friends." 

 But Tokyo dealers said it may well take time before the BOJ joins any future moves, saying the Japanese central bank's main concern at this point is the dollar's volatile moves against the yen. The greenback has plunged more than 10 yen in the past two weeks, and some fear even more slides lie ahead. 

 "Right now the BOJ has its hands completely full just trying to deal with the dollar and yen. This isn't the time for it to think about other things," said one Asian currency dealer at a major Japanese bank. 

 He said, and others agreed, that if the Japanese central bank did agree to take part in joint intervention, the impact definitely would be stronger. 

 "But they would have to be very careful how they did it because to see the BOJ selling dollars, even against an Asian currency, risks sending a strange signal to the market and could accelerate the dollar's fall against the yen," he added. 

 A dealer with a long-term credit bank, citing the weak Thai economy, said he was concerned by the possibility that not all of Wednesday's sales were speculative. 

 "There's the worry that the flow of capital out of the country may be starting to pick up speed, meaning the weak currency situation could drag on for a long time and diminish the impact of any intervention," he said. 

 But most dealers said they felt it was unlikely the BOJ would refrain from taking part in future joint moves should the baht depreciate seriously, owing to the need to maintain favourable ties among other Asian nations and its huge financial involvement in the region. 

 "Totally aside from the question of its investment in Thailand, which of course is one concern, Japan has made a big deal about its cooperative ties with other Asian nations. So if the baht falls further, and the Bank of Thailand asks it to intervene, they will most likely take part," the credit-bank dealer said.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Baht recovers but still vulnerable.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 15 (Reuter) - The Thai baht recovered some ground on Thursday as players turned wary of selling it down after the previous day's joint intervention by the central banks of Thailand and Singapore. 

 "The hedge funds are still buying the rumours the same as yesterday but the force is lesser now since the Bank of Thailand and other banks came in," a Siam Commercial Bank dealer in Bangkok said. 

 Dealers said activity had subsided in the spot baht market but forwards were shooting up due to a severe shortage of funds after Wednesday's aggressive baht sales by speculative funds. 

 The baht was quoted at 25.790-25.840 to the dollar at 0415 GMT against 25.910/25.940 earlier and 26.330-26/430 late on Wednesday. The Bank of Thailand (BOT) set the mid-rate at 25.81. 

 "Everybody's hitting the forwards. I think they're just squeezing the short-term liquidity. Tom/next is at 65/100 -- it's like trading the one-year," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 Dealers said there had been no signs of central bank intervention on Thursday. 

 "They (the BOT) have informed banks in Thailand not to quote to offshore parties for tom/next. There's no need for them to intervene," another Singapore-based dealer said. 

 "Everybody's just trying to fight for survival, they're just scrambling for funds," he added. 

 Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said on Thursday that Thailand had been and would continue to be successful in defending the baht. 

 "We have support from all our friends," he told reporters as he left a seminar in Tokyo. 

 The BOT and Singapore's de facto central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), said in a statement on Wednesday that they had taken joint action to stem excessive speculative activities in the baht. 

 It was the first joint action confirmed by the two central banks. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah remained under pressure after being aggressively sold overnight on false rumours of unrest in Jakarta during the campaign for the May 29 election. 

 Spot rupiah was at 2,438.50/39.50 at 0415 GMT after finding some support at the 2,439.0 level, compared with an opening of 2,433.0/44.0. 

 Swap rates rose broadly on foreign buying, dealers said. 

 They said a carry-forward effect from Wednesday, coupled with the ongoing jitters in the Thai market, hit the rupiah, triggering more stop-loss dollar buying. 

 The rupiah tumbled to a low of 2,445 in London overnight on false rumours of violence and arson at a police station in Jakarta, but it later recovered to 2,435. 

 Dealers said stop-loss limits were triggered in Singapore and London late on Wednesday after the rupiah was hit by the rumours. 

 One major local bank dealer said swap points jumped in early Thursday trading as offshore operators were squeezed on the forward side. 

 "Offshore players going long on dollars have to buy swaps for hedging or to get the rupiah financing, driving swap rates up across the board," the dealer said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit staged a partial recovery but continued to look vulnerable after foreign funds dumped the currency on Wednesday due to spillover fears over Thailand. 

 "Today the market is caught a bit long so they're selling dollars but it looks supported around 2.5160," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 He said players would also be wary of pushing the ringgit down again after Bank Negara's aggressive intervention in London markets overnight. 

 "Negara was in aggressively around the 2.5250 level yesterday in London. They probably sold more than $1 billion," he said. 

 A European bank dealer in Singapore pegged the amount sold by the Malaysian central bank at around $700 million. 

 The ringgit was at 2.5176/86 to the dollar at 0415 GMT against 2.5240/50 at close of Kuala Lumpur on Wednesday. It had fallen to as low as 2.5260, its lowest level since January 3. 

 The Singapore dollar was firm in the face of its neighbours' woes, but dealers said potential "safe-haven" flows to the currency were being dampened by fears of MAS intervention. 

 "The MAS has been supporting the (U.S) dollar at the 1.4320 level. I don't know why they want to hold it here since the dollar/yen has come off so much," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 -- Syed Azman in Kuala Lumpur (603-206 2323), Mantik Kusjanto in Jakarta (6221-384-6364), James Mclean in Bangkok (662-652-0642) and Sonali Desai in Singapore

title: FOCUS - Thai baht adjustment inevitable, analysts say.
text:
BANGKOK, May 15 (Reuter) - Reform of the Thai currency system is inevitable after this week's stinging speculator attacks on the baht, analysts said on Thursday. 

 But they ruled out devaluation as a way of appeasing currency predators, saying it was likely to result in more grief than joy for the government and economy. 

 "The fixed exchanged rate, capital mobility and effective monetary policy cannot coexist," said an analyst from a U.S. brokerage firm. 

 "It is not the question of whether the Bank of Thailand has enough resources to defend the currency. I'm sure it does. But why allow the inflexible baht to be a constant irritation to the monetary policy?" 

 Analysts said Thailand could not afford to allow interest rates to come down in order to boost the sagging economy -- projected by private analysts to grow at a decade-low of less than six percent this year -- without letting go of the baht. 

 Most analysts declined to speculate on a time frame for any adjustment but some felt it could happen in six to 12 months. 

 Offshore speculators attacked the baht this week despite its high-yielding rates, forcing the currency to swing widely out of the four-satang band within which the Bank of Thailand now allows it to fluctuate. 

 The attacks forced the central bank to intervene heavily in the market along with other regional central banks and issue repeated denials of a devaluation or any currency adjustment. 

 The baht is now pegged to a basket of currencies, which is confidential, but believed to heavily weight the dollar. The dollar's weight was increased to about 80 percent in 1986 when it was clear that the dollar was trending down at a rapid pace, economists said. 

 The basket peg was suitable for Thailand during 1985-1995 as a long decline in the dollar kept the baht undervalued and Thai exports competitive, analysts said. 

 The system also made the baht one of the most stable currencies in the region and an easy target for interest rate arbitraging. 

 But the peg also attracted speculative attacks on the baht when the dollar jumped in February, resulting in considerable disruption in the domestic money market. 

 The Bank of Thailand has kept interest rates high to defend the baht against attacks, but this week its strategy came under pressure again as more attacks set in. 

 "If you allowed the baht to reflect market sentiment by making it more flexible, then you don't have to worry about interest rates," said Song Seng Wun of ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett in Singapore. 

 The Bank of Thailand intervened heavily to support the baht and pushed up the implied overnight interbank rate to punish speculators. The action did calm the market somewhat on Thursday as the baht was quoted at 25.790-25.890 against 26.330-26.430 late on Wednesday. 

 "There's blood on the streets. The speculators are being burned," said the head of trading at a European bank of the central bank action. 

 Chia Woon Khien, regional economist of Singapore-based Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken, speculated that the Bank of Thailand was likely to adjust the basket of currencies first. 

 The central bank could do so by gradually reducing the weight of the strengthening dollar in the basket and widening the trading band later when economic conditions stabilised. 

 "Between a re-balancing of the currency basket and a widening of the trading band, the (central bank) is likely to adopt the former first, given that the first is more discretionary and reversible," she said. 

 But the timing for any such adjustment was crucial, said Supavud Saicheua of Phatra Reseach. 

 A belief that the dollar was on the rise, concern about poor Thai export prospects and a still large current account deficit would be compelling reasons for people to believe that a more flexible baht could result in a weaker baht, he added. 

 "But we believe that a more flexible baht need not imply short-term disruption or induce damaging speculation if appropriately timed," he said in a report.

title: FOCUS-Thai  currency  firms after  intervention .
text:
BANGKOK, May 15 (Reuter) - Thailand successfully defended its embattled currency on Thursday with central bank intervention, a squeeze on liquidity and reassurances that there were no plans to devalue. 

 Several Asian central banks cooperated with Thailand by jointly intervening to defend the embattled baht against speculative attacks, Thai deputy central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi said. 

 The baht was quoted sharply firmer at 25.250/25.350 late on Thursday against 25.910/25.940 early in the morning and 26.330/26.430 late on Wednesday. 

 "The central bank would like to ask the private sector to have confidence in the government policy and not to listen to the rumours," the Bank of Thailand said earlier in a statement. 

 "The central bank wishes to stress that there would be no devaluation or changes in the currency exchange mechanism which were mentioned by rumours," it said. 

 In Singapore, dealers said the Thai central bank had ordered local banks not to quote tomorrow/next rates in the baht to offshore parties, effectively cutting off a source of short-term borrowing to fund speculation. 

 Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan on Thursday also repeated the government's determination to guard the currency against speculative attacks. He said in Tokyo the government's defence of the baht has been, and will be, successful. 

 Rising concerns about the slowing Thai economy and rumours of political turmoil in the cabinet that could lead to Amnuay's possible resignation triggered heavy baht sales for the dollar on Wednesday. Amnuay has repeatedly denied he would quit. 

 "(On Wednesday) there was fierce speculation on the baht in the overseas market," the central bank statement said. "At present the situation has eased to a certain degree." 

 The central bank and the Monetary Authority of Singapore jointly intervened in the foreign exchange market on Wednesday to defend the baht. Malaysia's central bank and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority also bought the Thai currency, trade sources said, although their intervention was not confirmed. 

 The Bank of Japan said on Thursday that, if asked, it may intervene in the market to help support the baht under a 1996 Asian currency safety net agreement. 

 Last year monetary authorities of Australia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand agreed to establish bilateral repurchase agreements to provide liquidity in times of currency crisis. 

 Amnuay said that Thailand has support "from all our friends" in its currency defence. He also moved to soothe fears about the deterioration in the Thai economy, saying the country was "in a process of recovery." 

 The economy had gone through its worst, he said, adding he was pleased with a sharp decline in the current account deficit and inflation, and expectations that exports were improving. 

 The market rumours also hit the Thai bourse on Thursday, causing the market to drop to near eight-year lows. The main index closed at 557.87 points, a fall of 2.35 percent. 

 Thailand's currency woes have unnerved other markets in the region with the Philippine peso, the Malaysian ringgit and the Indonesian rupiah also suffering heavy selling. 

 The statement, which came after heavy speculative attacks on the baht this week and a plunge in the stock market index to near eight-year-lows, said the premier's office also provided reassurance that the Thai economic situation remained stable. 

 To fight baht speculators, the central bank intervened heavily in the local and foreign markets, especially on Wednesday when the run on the currency heightened. 

 It also sought assistance from regional counterparts to fight speculators and received support from them, a senior central bank official said. 

 The statemet said inflation had decreased from seven percent last year to 4.4 percent and the forecasted current account deficit was expected to be six percent of gross domestic product at the end of this year compared to over eight percent last year, it added. 

 The structure of the long term debt had risen to 60 percent from 50 percent, it added. 

 "Next week Mr. Amnuay Viravan and the Governor of the Bank of Thailand are also preparing to announce additional measures to promote confidence in the Thai economy and financial institutions as well as measures to increase its liquidity," the statement said. 

 "As a result there are no reasons whatsoever to devalue the baht currency," it added. 

 The baht rallied late on Thursday supported by regional central bank intervention and was quoted at 25.300/400 against the dollar compared with 26.330/430 late on Wednesday.

title: FOCUS-Thai stocks at eight-year-low but jitters ease.
text:
BANGKOK, May 15 (Reuter) - The Thai bourse suffered more losses to approach new eight-year lows on Thursday but analysts said the mood was less frantic as the baht stabilised and fears of an imminent currency devalution eased. 

 After nearly three weeks of declines, the battered Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) key index shed another 2.35 percent to close at 557.87 points -- the lowest finish since May 1989. 

 The market had dropped as low as 544.10 before late fund buying pared losses, brokers said. 

 Talk of a possible baht devaluation over the past few days had battered the stock market and the currency. But the baht rallied late on Thursday following intervention and assurances by Thai authorities that it would not devalue the currency. 

 The Thai currency was quoted at 25.350/25.450 to the dollar in late dealings, compared with 26.330/26.430 late on Wednesday when it was hammered by speculators. 

 The Bank of Thailand on Thursday reassured investors it had no plans to devalue the currency. 

 "The central bank wishes to stress that there would be no devaluation or changes in the currency exchange mechanism which were mentioned by rumours," it said in a statement. 

 Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan also repeated the government's determination to guard the currency against speculative attacks. He said the government's defence of the baht has been, and will be, successful. 

 Analysts said the reassurances and intervention by the Bank of Thailand and other central banks helped stabilise the baht and, in turn, the stock market. 

 The central bank and the Monetary Authority of Singapore jointly intervened in foreign exchange markets on Wednesday, and other regional central banks were said to have done the same, although it was not confirmed. 

 The Bank of Japan said it would be prepared to intervene to support the baht if asked to do so.

title: Economists rule out Thai baht devaluation. [Corrected 5:57 gmt]
text:
SINGAPORE, May 15 (Reuter) - There is no reason why the Thai baht should be devalued, economists said on Thursday as the currency recovered in Asia after Wednesday's sell-off. 

 "The economic fundamentals are with the Bank of Thailand. The current account deficit is collapsing. There's no reason for a devaluation," Desmond Supple, Asia currency economist (corrects title) at BZW in Singapore told Reuters. 

 Lawrence Hathaway, Chief Economist East Asia at UBS Securities in Singapore agreed. "There are sound reasons that devaluation is not unambiguously good for the economy." 

 At 0322 gmt the baht was quoted against the dollar at 25.80/90. Traders said there was little activity because of the huge dealing spread. 

 On Wednesday, the baht hit a low around 26.26, prompting joint intervention to support the currency from the Bank of Thailand and the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

 Market talk also had it that other Asian central banks, such as the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, also interevened to defend the baht, but there was no confirmation. 

 The baht has come under speculative pressure in the last couple of days on growing concern about the slowing Thai economy and rumours of political turmoil within the Thai cabinet. 

 There were also rumours that Finance Minister Amnay Viravan could resign, although he has denied this. 

 BZW's Supple said the Bank of Thailand was fighting the speculators by pushing short-term rates sharply higher. "The implied overnight rate is at 150 percent right now. They're making the speculators pay," he said. 

 By boosting short-term interest rates central banks can make it hugely expensive for speculators to short a currency. 

 "The Bank of Thailand's economic policies are working, but the market is trying them on," Supple said. 

 He said Thailand had been very successful in reducing the current account deficit. The deficit was now around six percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), compared with 8.2 percent last year, he said. 

 "If you look at the three month moving average the current account deficit was 18 billion baht in February compared with 37 billion in February last year," Supple said. 

 "The people forecasting devaluation are assuming the current account deficit will not come down and that's just not the case," he said. 

 Hathaway of UBS commented; "The Thai central bank is very committed to maintaining the current baht peg. There's been no wavering at the political level." 

 As Hathaway spoke to Reuters, Amnuay was in Tokyo telling an international conference, "We are determined to fight speculation. I repeat we are determined to fight speculation." 

 The Bank of Thailand also told investors in a statement not to listen to rumours of a devaluation. It said its intervention was meant to protect against speculation on the currency. 

 Hathaway said that to protect the economy, "The Thai central bank will be reluctant to boost interest rates for a prolonged period of time." 

 But with short-term rates moving up so sharply, "It underscores how expensive it is to short the currency." 

 The head of foreign currency trading at a European bank in Singapore agreed. 

 Referring to the rise in short-term rates, he said, "They are not going to devalue the baht and they'll go to any lengths to avoid it."

title: Thailand to fight  currency  speculation -- Amnuay.
text:
TOKYO, May 15 (Reuter) - Thailand will defend its currency against attacks in the market by currency speculators, Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said on Thursday. 

 "We are determined to fight speculation," Amnuay told an international conference on Asia, in response to a question about speculative moves in the Thai currency. 

 On Wednesday, the Bank of Thailand and the Monetary Authority of Singapore intervened in the Singapore market to stabilise the baht after the Thai currency fell to 26.250-26.300 to the U.S. dollar. 

 Amnuay also told the conference that the Thai economy is in a process of recovery. 

 "We are in a process of recovery," he said. "We are through the worst, but there is much left to do," he added. 

 The Thai economy is in its worst shape in 10 years, with gross domestic product projected to expand about five to six percent this year, after 6.7 percent in 1996 and 8.6 percent in 1995. 

 Amnuay also dismissed questions about a possible devaluation of the currency. "That's a silly question," he said. 

 He said that currency instability was due partly to dollar/yen fluctuations and partly to speculators trying to take advantage of such moves. 

 "We are determined to fight speculation. I repeat we are determined to fight speculation," he said. 

 Referring to the Thai economy, he said the economy had gone through its worst, but much was still to be done. "You can't solve economic ills in a few weeks or months." 

 He said he was pleased with many economic indicators, especially the drastic decline in the current account deficit and the decline in inflation, adding that exports looked to be improving. 

 "We have had some financial sector problems that would make the recovery process perhaps slow," he said. 

 "We believe some measures we have launched have had some positive effects and we will be able to resolve the problems in the near future."

title: C/A deficits take toll on some emerging  currencies .
text:
LONDON, May 15 (Reuter) - Exotic currencies from Thailand and the Czech Republic, countries with high current account deficits, came in to the firing line on Thursday and analysts said heavy selling would persist. 

 Concerns about higher interest rates, both in Japan and the United States, have alarmed investors and has led to heavy selling in Thailand and the Czech Republic as the international cost of funding investments in these countries would rise. 

 "I don't think it's an attack on the Czech Republic or Thailand per se, but the reality is investors who have been running yield positions are closing them out," said Chris Tinker, chief economist at Standard Chartered in London. 

 Market analysts explained that yield hungry investors have funded their positions via cheap yen borrowings over the past year. 

 A rise in the Japanese discount rate, currently at 0.5 percent, would raise the cost of funding these positions and would trigger an unwinding of investments in these countries. 

 Analysts said that, if borrowing costs rise in the United States and Japan, investors would become reluctant to finance investments where high currents account deficits are being run, because of their greater dependence of speculative foreign capital. 

 Thailand and the Czech Republic were two obvious candidates where large current account deficits have led to a flight in capital, which resulted in big drops in the baht and and crown today. 

 As a result, the Bank of Thailand, with several Asian central banks, and the Czech Central Bank (CNB), intervened earlier today to defend their respective currencies against further speculative attacks. 

 The Thai baht was quoted sharply firmer at 25.250/25.350 late on Thursday following the intervention against 25.910/25.940 early in the morning and 26.330/26.430 late on Wednesday. 

 The Czech crown fell one full percentage point in early Thursday trading to hit a record low five percent weaker than its central target rate against a basket of dollars and marks. It later rebounded to minus 3.4 percent following the intervention. 

 "What is happening in Thailand and the Czech Republic, in two very different parts of the world, is that current accounts are no longer being forgiven in financial markets and Brazil is vulnerable," said Richard Gray, emerging market analyst at BankAmerica in London. 

 "The spillover effect is being transmitted around the world by fear of current accounts. I do think you may see some knock-on consequences from the Thai baht into the Czech Crown and independently into Brazil," he added.

To shore up its defenses of the baht, Thailand in the last year has been signing agreements with the central banks of several countries. It has currency-cooperation agreements with Australia, Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia, the Philippines and Japan. As of Wednesday, however, only Singapore had openly come to Thailand's defense. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore made no comment on its decision beyond a joint statement released with the Bank of Thailand. That statement said: 'This concerted operation is aimed at stemming excessive speculative activities, which may lead to disorderly conditions in the Thai and regional financial markets. Other appropriate measures will be taken as necessary.' 

 The attack on the baht also sparked a sell-off in the Malysian ringgit and the Indonesian rupiah Wednesday. 

 But some currency dealers in Singapore said the authority's intervention had been modest. 'We're not sure how much the authorities bought but the way the intervention is being done doesn't seem to be effective,' said the chief of regional currencies at a Japanese bank in Singapore. 'It seems the market is having the upper hand.' 

 If the market continues to enjoy the upper hand over several days, many analysts said, Thailand could be forced to submit to a policy change. Thailand's foreign reserves - $38.1 billion in March - are ample, but experts say a sustained attack could drain even that amount. 


'From a pure fundamental point of view, there's no need for Thailand
to do something immediately on the currency,' said Bernhard Eschweiler,
an economist with J.P. Morgan Inc. in Singapore. 'But from a market
point of view Thailand is clearly vulnerable.' Wednesday's attack on the

title: Thailand  Currency  Frailty Shows In Baht Attack -Amplifier
text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--Jolted by an attack on the baht that sent shudders through other Southeast Asian currency markets Wednesday, Thailand's central bank received aid from Singapore for the first time in defense of the currency. 

 The attack on the baht, in which foreign institutional investors dumped baht for dollars to test Thailand's bank's ability to maintain its fixed exchange-rate system, pushed the dollar to its highest level in more than seven years against the baht. 

 In the panic that followed, Thai stock prices plunged to a six-and-a-half-year low as the benchmark Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index fell 28.94 points to 571.30. Interbank rates surged to 20%, a three-month high. Swap rates soared. 

 The Bank of Thailand, scrambling to defend a currency system that has been the foundation of Thai economic policy for 13 years, found succor in an unusual quarter. The Monetary Authority of Singapore, usually loath to enter the currency struggles of other countries, intervened jointly with the Bank of Thailand to defend the baht. Central-bank officials said it was the first time the two banks had acted in concert. 

 But the intervention was less successful than previous attempts to defend the currency - a sign, analysts said, not only of Thailand's reduced economic circumstances, but also of the growing difficulty of keeping the baht pegged to a dollar-dominated basket of currencies. 

 Despite the intervention, the dollar closed at 26.30 baht - 0.42 baht outside the upper limit of the band in which the central bank allows it to trade versus the baht. The dollar Tuesday closed at 25.915 baht.

title: Baht hit by finance portfolio rumour, economy woes.
text:
BANGKOK, May 14 (Reuter) - Thailand intervened on Wednesday to defend the baht against fresh market attacks, and its central bank warned of taking more actions to counter market pressure on the currency. 

 The Bank of Thailand said it teamed up with the Monetary Authority of Singapore to intervene in the Singapore market to stabilise the baht. 

 Analysts said the intervention, the first joint action confirmed by the two central banks, came after the baht fell to 26.250-26.300 to the dollar. 

 The Thai currency recovered to 26.030-26.080 after the central bank action, but it was quoted sharply weaker at 26.550-26.750 during off-hour trading late on Wednesday. 

 "I don't know if the baht would see a calmer market tomorrow. It still looks weak and fragile after intervention," a dealer at a foreign bank said. 

 But another currency trader at Thai Military Bank Plc said she expected speculators to lie low on Thursday after the central bank showed its determination to back the currency. 

 The Bank of Thailand said: "This concerted operation is aimed at stemming excessive speculative activities which may lead to disorderly conditions in the Thai and regional financial markets. Other appropriate measures will be taken as necessary." 

 The baht's woes were partly triggered by suggestions last weekend by members in Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's coalition for Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan to resign and take responsibility for Thailand's mounting economic problems. 

 Amnuay told Reuters in Tokyo, after attending a meeting of the Asian Development Bank in the Japanese city of Fukuoka, that he was confident of his future as finance minister. 

 He said Thailand was committed to maintaining baht stability and its central bank would succeed in turning back any further market attacks on the currency. 

 Chavalit on Tuesday voiced his full backing for Amnuay. The prime minister also ruled out any plan to devalue the baht. 

 The Thai economy is in its worst shape in 10 years with gross domestic product projected to expand about five to six percent, against 6.7 percent in 1996 and 8.6 percent in 1995. 

 The attacks on the baht sent more shock waves through the ailing stock market, where the Composite Index plunged 4.82 percent to a near eight-year low of 571.30 points on Wednesday. The index has lost 13.6 percent this month. 

 Finance ministry officials and some private bankers said the damage from a baht devaluation would outweigh benefits for the Thai economy. 

 They said a devaluation would not substantially help Thai exports as more than 75 percent were industrial products with high import contents. The officials said a devalued baht would instead sharply raise the financing costs of Thailand's estimated $90 billion foreign debt. 

 "Efforts to dampen speculation on Amnuay's future were not helped by his absence," a dealer at Hongkong and Shanghai Bank said. Amnuay is not due back in Bangkok until Saturday. 

 Assistant central bank governor Siri Ganjarerndee attributed the attack on the baht to negative market perception of the Thai economy and to rumours of possible economic policy and finance portfolio changes. 

 He told reporters the rumours prompted a market flight to the dollar from baht, a move sharply tightening short-term domestic liquidity.
