title: Thai markets hit by economy, political worries.
text:
BANGKOK, May 14 (Reuter) - Thai markets took another pounding on Wednesday as foreign investors took flight from the baht and sold stocks on fears over the economy and the political situation. 

 Stocks in Bangkok tumbled 4.35 percent by the lunch break as foreign investors led renewed selling of blue-chip stocks on concern about the sluggish economy and market pressure on the baht, brokers said. 

 The SET index plunged 26.11 points to 574.13 on moderate 2.09 billion baht trade. The SET-50 index retreated 2.36 points to 41.94. The main composite index hovered at its lowest level since mid-June 1989. 

 "We got a lot of selling orders from foreign clients who partly reacted to the currency market's shift to the dollar from the baht," said a foreign broker. 

 An analyst at Chao Phaya Finance and Securities said expected weak first quarter earnings of most telecommunication companies also prompted morning selling. 

 Brokers said investors are still concerned about the sluggish economy which is expected to grow less than six percent this year. 

 Some currency dealers said they believed the Bank of Thailand had intervened to defend the baht in the Singapore market during midday on Wednesday but the central bank did not confirm it. 

 The baht fell to 26.250-26.300 to the dollar before it recovered to 26.030-26.080 at 0656 GMT. The central bank fixed the baht/dollar midrate at 25.86 on Wednesday against 25.88 on Tuesday. 

 "I heard that the central bank intervened, otherwise the baht could not stage such a comeback," a Thai bank dealer. 

 Dealers said their Singapore counterparts quoted baht selling offers in big $100 million lots against $10-30 million deals in normal market conditions. 

 Rising concerns about the slowing Thai economy and rumours of political turmoil within the cabinet, seen hampering effective monetary policy, triggered baht sales for the dollar. 

 Dealers said the Bank of Thailand fixing the mid-rate at 25.86 did not prevent the rate slipping to 26.03. 

 "There was a lot of stop-loss and panic-selling which caused the market to trade 20 satangs above the fixing," a dealer with a U.S. bank in Singapore said. 

 "The demand for the dollar is much stronger today. Players in Hong Kong and Singapore were heavily bidding the dollar (by selling baht)," said one dealer at a local bank in Bangkok. 

 Thai prime minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh reiterated on Tuesday there would be no change in economic ministers and Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan will continue in his post and maintain authority. 

 "Amnuay will still have authority in economic affairs and there will be no change in the economic ministers," Chavalit said after the weekly cabinet meeting. 

 His comments come during renewed rumours that Amnuay was due to resign following a conflict with a major partner in Chavalit's coalition. 

 On Monday, Amnuay had also dismissed market speculation that the Chart Pattana Party, a major coalition party in the government, was unhappy with his performance during the administration's six months in office. 

 Some members in Chavalit's government suggested late last week that Amnuay could help halt the Thai economic slowdown and a prolonged stock market decline by stepping down.

text:
SINGAPORE, May 9 (Reuter) - The Thai baht recovered from Friday morning lows by midday after the Bank of Thailand (BOT) denied market rumours of a band widening and intervened in spot and forward markets to stem the currency's decline. 

 Dealers said the rumours, that the BOT planned to widen the dollar/baht trading band, emerged in London markets overnight and prompted a sell-off in the baht. 

 The baht was quoted at 26.013/26.018 to the dollar at 0510 GMT after the BOT intervened in Singapore forex markets to sell the dollar at 26.025 baht, dealers said. The Thai unit fell to to a low of 26.090 in early trade. 

 Paiboon Kittisrikangwan, the central bank's division chief in charge of money and foreign exchange markets, told Reuters the Bank of Thailand had no plan to change the exchange rate mechanism. 

 "A lot of U.S. investment houses were trying to attack the baht and buy dollars yesterday and it's been quite hectic today as well," said a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore. 

 Dealers said the dollar's sharp drop against the majors on Friday also helped the baht rebound, but it was still trading well above the central bank's mid-rate of 25.99. 

 "People were reluctant to take many long dollar positions due to a weakening of the U.S. unit abroad and the central bank's intervention in the Singapore market," a dealer in Bangkok said. 

 But sentiment remained bearish and dealers said the baht could be vulnerable to further declines against the backdrop of continued weakness on the stock market and worries about the stability of the finance sector. 

 Elsewhere, regional currencies benefitted from the dollar's sharp fall against the yen as fears of a rate hike in Japan gained ground while the likelihood of a further U.S. tightening appeared to recede. 

 A speech by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan late on Thursday was viewed as signalling that the U.S. central bank might hold back from further rate hikes for the time being. 

 Greenspan said he expected economic growth to slow later this year and next, but that the central bank would need to act if that did not prove to be the case. 

 "People took it as a sign that there won't be any immediate rate hike. That's why the market sold dollars and it has also turned quite bearish recently," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The dollar was quoted at 122.75/85 yen at 0510 GMT in Tokyo against its opening 123.15/18. 

 The rupiah rose amid steady money market liquidity though overall activity remained slow. 

 A U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said the rupiah maintained a bid tone after strengthening to a high of 2,427.0 on Thursday in Singapore and New York while Jakarta was closed for a holiday. 

 Spot rupiah was traded at 2,428.50/29.50 at 0510 GMT against an opening of 2,429.0/30.0. 

 A local bank dealer said the dollar briefly touched an early high of 2,430.0 before it was sold down on weakness in major offshore markets, where players brushed aside the heated campaign for Indonesia's general elections on May 29.

 "Ringgit sentiment for the short-term has changed due to weak dollar/majors," a dealer with a Malaysian bank said. "A lot of dollar selling is expected at above 2.5100." 

 Dealers said the ringgit's upside could, however, be limited due to political concerns after Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said he would grant full powers to his deputy Anwar Ibrahim and go overseas for two months later in May.

 "Dollar/Sing could come off to 1.4380 depending on how far dollar/yen comes off. The market is still long dollar/Sing and ringgit/Sing," the U.S. bank dealer said.

title: Amnuay says  central bank  not propping up baht.
text:
BANGKOK, May 9 (Reuter) - Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said on Friday the baht rallied against a weakening U.S. dollar in line with market forces and he believed the central bank had not intervened to artificially prop up the Thai unit. 

 Amnuay said the official baht/dollar midrate fixed by the Bank of Thailand at 25.99 on Friday, against 26.05 on Thursday, reflected the U.S. dollar's movement in major markets.

title: Thailand's SET index breaks through 600-pt level.
text:
BANGKOK, May 9 (Reuter) - Thailand's SET index broke through the key psychological level of 600 late on Friday morning as economic and currency concerns saw continued sales of bank and finance stocks by foreign investors, traders said. 

 The SET Index dropped 14.07 points, or 2.29 percent, to 599.97 by 0429 GMT. The SET 50 fell 01.10 points, or 2.44 percent to 43.29. Turnover was 950 million baht. 

 Renewed market speculation on Thailand's baht fixing practice after reports of central bank intervention in Singapore this morning and worries about economic fundamentals undermined sentiment, brokers said. 

 "Foreigners are still selling banks as they have been most of the week. We are checking on the intervention rumours but the currency is a worry again," said a trader at a brokerage firm affiliated with Thai Farmers Bank. 

 Weak economic growth, export and corporate earnings outlooks, as well as liquidity and asset quality problems in the finance sector weighed on sentiment, analysts said. 

 Texas Instruments Inc 's attribution of Thai economic problems as a factor for its withdrawal from joint ventures with Alphatec Electronics Plc was a further negative factor, traders said. 

 Alphatec was limit down 6.50 baht to 59.50, Asia Credit dropped 7.50 to a year low of 76.50, TISCO also hit limit low, falling 5.25 to 48.75.

title: Bank of  Thailand intervenes  to sell dollars.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 9 (Reuter) - The Bank of Thailand intervened in Singapore foreign exchange markets on Friday to sell dollars at 26.025 baht after the Thai unit came under intense pressure on rumours it denied of a band widening, dealers said. 

 The baht was quoted at 26.012/26.017 to the dollar at 0330 GMT after falling as low as 26.090 earlier, dealers said. 

 They said the Thai central bank had also intervened earlier in the swap market, offering the six-month and one-year swaps. 

 The rumours, that the Thai central bank planned to widen the dollar/baht trading band, emerged in London markets overnight and prompted a sell-off in the baht. 

 "A lot of U.S. investment houses were trying to attack the baht and buy dollars yesterday and it's been quite hectic today as well," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 Dealers said the baht had calmed down somewhat after the central bank's denial of the rumour and its intervention. But the currency was still trading well above Friday's mid-rate of 25.99 per dollar. 

 "We should trade between 26.000 and 26.030 for the rest of the day," another dealer said. 

 Paiboon Kittisrikangwan, the central bank's division chief in charge of money and foreign exchange markets, told Reuters the Bank of Thailand had no plan to change the exchange rate mechanism. 

 "Rumours about any change in the exchange rate mechanism, including band-widening, are utter nonsense," he said.

title: Thailand Baht Slightly Higher Late Despite Dollar-Buying
text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--The Thai baht closed marginally higher against the dollar in Asian spot trading Wednesday, despite a late round of dollar-buying from investors covering their short-term positions, dealers said. 

 Meanwhile, the baht was little changed in the swap market where investors agree to buy and sell dollars at specified times in the future. 

 In the spot market, the dollar closed at 26.085 baht compared with 26.086 baht Tuesday. At this level, the Thai currency was just outside the range in which the central bank allows it to trade against the greenback, indicating strong dollar-buying. That band was set at 26.04 baht to 26.08 baht Wednesday, but it was unknown whether the Bank of Thailand intervened in the market to support the baht. 

 The central bank set its dollar-baht midrate at 26.06 baht, down from 26.10 baht Tuesday. 

 'Investors bought dollars to support their short-term positions after the central bank lowered its midrate by four satang,' one dealer said. But he added that the buying wasn't enough increase the value of the dollar as the U.S. currency continued to fall against the Japanese yen. 

 The Thai baht is pegged to a basket of currencies dominated by the dollar but also including the yen and the German mark. When the dollar falls against its major counterparts, the baht tends to gain. 

 Interbank rates were unchanged. Both the overnight and call rates closed at 9%-9.5%

title: Thailand Baht Ends Higher As U.S. Dollar Falls Vs Yen
text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--The Thai baht advanced against the U.S. dollar in Asian spot trading Monday, gaining as the U.S. currency fell in value against the Japanese yen and German mark. 

 The Thai currency, however, weakened in the swap market where investors agree to buy and sell dollars at specified times in the future. Dealers said premiums on baht rose on expectations that liquidity in the money system would tighten. 

 'The Bank of Thailand issued 30 billion baht in bonds on Friday, and this money started flowing out of the system,' a dealer at a U.S. bank. 

 At the close of spot trading Monday, the dollar was at 25.979 baht, down from 25.982 baht Friday. At that rate, the dollar was within the Thai central bank's intervention band of 25.95 baht to 25.97 baht. If the dollar falls outside of the range, the Bank of Thailand is obliged to intervene in the market. 

 The central bank set its dollar-baht fixing rate at 25.97 baht Monday. 

 Dealers said the baht gained in the swap market because of the decline of the dollar against the yen. The baht is pegged to a basket of currencies including the dollar, the yen and the mark. When the dollar falls against its major counterparts, the baht tends to gain in value.

title: Thai Jan exports rise, other trade indicators weak.
text:
BANGKOK, March 26 (Reuter) - Thai January exports posted moderate year-on-year growth for the first time since last May but trade and current account deficits widened during the month, a finance ministry source said on Wednesday. 

 The source said Thailand's balance of payments also moved to an estimated 26.6 billion baht ($1.02 billion) deficit in February from a 24.7 billion baht surplus in January due to market attacks on the baht in the first half of last month. 

 The senior ministry official said January exports rose about 5.1 percent year-on-year to 115.9 billion baht after falling for seven consecutive months. 

 Exports declined by 0.2 percent for the whole of 1996 after rising 23.6 percent in 1995. 

 The official said more Thai canned seafood, shoes, electrical appliances and furniture were shipped out in January but agricultural commodity exports slowed down. 

 January imports also surged to about 154.9 billion baht as factory demand for petroleum and industrial raw materials escalated, from 139.3 billion baht in December. 

 January imports were at their highest monthly level since May 1996. 

 He said the January trade deficit widened sharply to a higher than expected 39.0 billion baht, a high since April 1996 and against 22.3 billion in December. 

 But the current account deficit, moderated by seasonally higher tourism revenue, widened only slightly to 22.5 billion baht in January from 19.1 billion in December. 

 Thailand's service account, covering mainly tourist and shipping industries, posted a 16.5 billion baht surplus in January, higher than the 3.2 billion baht surplus in December. 

 The official said press reports of a review by Moody's Investors Service of long-term Thai debt ratings and market attacks on the baht emerged during the first half of February, prompting the Bank of Thailand to intervene in defence of the currency. 

 He said the baht attacks sharply tightened money market liquidity with short-term interbank rates ranging 10-30 percent during February 1-14. 

 The source said, however, that the central bank's tough stand shored up market sentiment on the baht in the second half of last month, helping the high overnight interbank rate to ease to 8.50-26.00 percent. 

 He said the battered export sector showed no early recovery signs in January with the manufacturing production index estimated to grow only four percent year-on-year, its weakest rate in about 10 years.

title: Thai Baht Ends Up After Suspected  Intervention  By Ctrl Bk
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended up slightly against the U.S. dollar Monday on speculation that the Thai central bank intervened in the market after the currency hit its lowest level in almost three and a half years in early trading. 

 Renewed strength in regional currencies led by Indonesia's rupiah, which rallied in anticipation of the imminent removal of President Abdurrahman Wahid also supported the baht, traders said. Indonesia's National Assembly voted after the market's close to oust Wahid and appoint Vice-President Megawati Sukarnoputri in his place. 

 The dollar was quoted in late trade at 45.76 baht, marginally down from THB45.775 at the Asian close Friday. 

 Dealers said the dollar reached THB45.97 in early Sydney trade, in line with weakness in most regional currencies after emergency impeachment proceedings against Wahid began. 

 The dollar opened in Bangkok around THB45.85-THB45.87 but heavy offers by Singapore dealers pushed the dollar back down to an intraday low of THB45.72. Traders said the move appeared to originate from institutions that usually acted on behalf of the Bank of Thailand. 

 "The rumor on central bank intervention spread all over the market, encouraging exporters to unload their dollars," a dealer at a local bank said. 

 However, central bank governor Pridiyathorn Devakula told reporters that the intervention talk was "just a rumor" and pure speculation. He added that the baht's fall early Monday was very brief, and was prompted by the uncertainty surrounding political developments in Indonesia. 

 Renewed strength in most Asian currencies, particularly the Singapore dollar during the day, also helped support local currencies, dealers said. 

 Pridiyathorn said the new foreign exchange reporting forms should be ready before end-July, in line with previous expectations. 

 The new forms, which were to extend existing reporting rules for foreign exchange transactions to nonresident accounts, have been under review since last month. 


Dealers expect the dollar to trade Tuesday in a THB45.70-THB45.90
range, depending on the political situation in Indonesia.

title: Emerging  FX  - Rupiah gets a boost but yen drags.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 23 (Reuters) - Asian currencies parted ways late on Monday, with Taiwan and Korea wary of the yen and Southeast Asia spellbound by the Indonesian rupiah. 

 The rupiah climbed by over ten percent from late Friday levels around 11,138 as parliament geared itself to sack President Abdurrahman Wahid. 

 Still, the currency's gains were capped given the country's poor economic fundamentals, and its impact on the other regional currencies was muted as the rupiah market is limited to onshore. 

 Indonesian importers were also keen to take advantage of the cheaper dollar and helped cap further rupiah gains. 

 Falls in Japanese stocks to 16 year lows and weak economic data overshadowed lingering doubts over U.S. President George W. Bush's committment to the strong dollar policy. The yen found itself mired in the day's lows. 

 The yen's wobble sent shivers through North Asian currencies, with the Taiwan dollar facing data that provided more evidence of the island's slowing economy. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah jumped to a four-month high of 10,100 after foreign and local banks rushed to sell dollars as the country's political crisis headed towards a climax. 

 The Supreme Court ruled President Wahid's decree of a state of emergency was illegal and he could not disband the top assembly, which almost unanimously rejected his declaration. 

 The assembly's two main parties recommended the president be sacked, bringing his political demise one step closer. 

 But dealers said the rupiah's rise was exaggerated by thin volumes and analysts doubted if the gains were sustainable as political and economic uncertainty linger. 

 Charts showed the dollar was massively oversold with a 14-day relative strength index reading at 3.8, suggesting scope for consolidation or correction. 

 Bank Indonesia said it expected the rupiah to strengthen through 10,000 on expectations of improving political conditions. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht dipped to 45.97 - a whisker away from its 40-month low of 46.00 - before talk of central bank intervention and a firmer rupiah lifted the currency out of its trough. 

 Offshore parties, especially Australian names, bought the dollar/baht actively in early trade as some investors use the baht as a hedging proxy for the less liquid rupiah. 

 A Japanese bank, which recently acted on behalf of central bank, sold dollars soon after the baht hit its intraday low, sparking talk of intervention. 

 Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula denied having intervened in the market, and market sources close to the deal said the Japanese bank's dollar sales were for customers and the amount was only around $20 million. 

 Pridiyathorn also said the authorities expected to finalise details of forex reporting rules for non-residents before the end of July. The comment is likely to hold the market back from aggressively building up dollar positions for now. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar sank to 1.8310 before recouping lost ground on talk of central bank intervention and gains in the rupiah. 

 The currency was also supported by tight liquidity in the money market, with the overnight rate remaining firm at around 3.50-4.00 percent. 

 Dealers said the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) was suspected to have been draining liquidity in the market to cap the Sing dollar's losses by not sterilising its intervention. 

 But the currency is likely to keep its bearish tone in the near-term given underlying domestic fundamentals. 

 "The off-budget package to be announced this week will ease the pain of the downturn, but it will not materially impact on the economic growth this year," said a DBS report. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso bowed slightly to local corporate dollar demand, but wariness over possible central bank intervention ahead of President Gloria Arroyo's State of the Nation speech held speculators back. 

 Manila dealers said most players were acting on behalf of their corporate clients. Dollar sales in the afternoon session around 53.40 by foreign banks renewed talk that the central bank was intervening in the market. 

 The government said it was working on issuing dollar-linked peso note with the aim of stabilising the local currency. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won tracked the yen lower, hovering around the day's low of 1,310.30 near the close. Sentiment was also dampened by sharp losses in local stocks. 

 Korea's benchmark KOSPI hit fresh three-month lows after dismal U.S. corporate results and forecasts. 

 Dealers said news of the government planning an economic stimulus package in the second half of this year to help ensure growth provided only mild support for the won as the amount is likely to be limited. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar braved through dismal economic data and downtrodden local stocks as players unwound their dollar longs in a market that has been long on dollar since July 5. 

 Singapore dealers said the bad economic news had already been priced into the market. June export orders dropped by 19.92 percent on year while industrial output fell by 11.27 percent. 

 The unemployment rate set a new record in June, rising by 4.51 percent.

title: Emerging  FX  - Stuck in ranges, trade cautious.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 13 (Reuters) - Asian currencies lingered within familiar ranges early Friday in what is expected to be a cautious session ahead of the weekend. 

 Gains in U.S. stocks will help lend some support but surprisingly high weekly unemployment data and Argentina's financial woes will continue to cap any gains. 

 The debt crisis in Argentina, Latin America's third largest economy, has raised fears of emerging market contagion spreading to Asia. 

 Those concerns have however aided the yen against the dollar as investors unwinded carry trades in which they use the low-yield yen to invest in higher-yielding emerging market assets. 

 The yen was off its overnight 2-= week high against the dollar at the start of Tokyo trade but was still around 124, far from last week's lows around 126. 

 With nothing major on the local events calendar, players will focus on June U.S. retail sales and producer prices both due 1230 GMT and a consumer sentiment report from University of Michigan at 1300 GMT. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR The Sing dollar edged back to 1.8340 having hit 11-year lows of 1.8398 on Thursday after the MAS shifted its stance to neutral from tightening to counter the economic downturn. 

 Dealers said local banks were offering U.S. dollars around 1.8350, stirring speculation they were acting on behalf of the authorities. They suspected the authorities have sold around $200 million when the Sing dollar spiked up on Thursday. 

 They added players were likely to square positions ahead of the weekend but U.S. funds were looking to buy dollars on dips from 1.8320-40. 

 The MAS said on Thursday it was ready to intervene to dampen excessive volatility but said it does not normally comment on its market operations. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO The peso was likely to come under pressure having hit fresh 5 1/2 month lows of 53.40 on Thursday. 

 Manila dealers said robust corporate demand from importers and jitters over possible spill-over damage from Argentina's financial turmoil would hurt sentiment. 

Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said the bank did not intervene in the market. 

 THAI BAHT The baht was pinned just below 45.60, torn between importer dollar demand and fears of possible intervention. 

 Bangkok dealers said oil companies were looking to buy dollars around 45.50 but players are wary the Bank of Thailand might intervene around 45.85, 37-month lows hit on April 9. 

 The central bank said it was committed to keeping the baht stable and said it was prepared to intervene occasionally to do so. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won edged down on continued equity-related outflows and on uncertainty over the yen's direction. 

 Dealers in Singapore said gains in major U.S. tech companies after they raised revenue forecasts was likely to help overall sentiment. 

 But the upside was seen limited on an uncertain economic outlook at home and concerns about Argentina. 

 The won is still within an overall uptrend against the dollar since April 4, when it touched a low of 1,365.30 but has failed to strengthen past the 1,290 level since June 12. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar was steady just a shade off the 35 mark on hopes the Nasdaq's overnight gains will boost equity-related inflows. 

 However, players looking at the worsening economic outlook and an easier central bank exchange rate stance on would continue to probe weaker levels for the Taiwan dollar. 

 With parliamentary election due December 1, analysts expect the central bank to allow a gradual exchange rate depreciation to help sagging growth and exports. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah kept within its well-worn range around 11,360 amid fading trading interest ahead of August impeachment hearings against President Abdurrahman Wahid. 

 Dealers said even the usually dollar-starved local corporates were keeping a low profile to avoid getting caught long or short in the run up to the special parliament session which will start the impeachment process. 

 Security concerns were heightened after at least 80 armed policemen and two armoured cars moved in on Thursday apparently to resist arrest of their rebel chief as ordered by President Wahid.

title: Thai PM: No Plan To Change Repo Rate; Money Mkt Works
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said Wednesday that there is no plan to change the 14-day repurchase rate after it was hiked by 100 basis points in early June. 

 Thaksin denied rumors that the central bank's monetary policy board was planning to raise rates again. 

 "Prior to the repo rate hike, market mechanisms had been distorted. Now, market mechanisms are working well," Thaksin told reporters. 

 The monetary policy board will meet Thursday for a preliminary discussion ahead of its policy-setting meeting scheduled for July 19. 

 Thaksin said the central bank's aim in monitoring the baht is to ensure that the Thai unit moves in line with the region's currencies and that volatility is limited. 

 A volatile baht could hurt exporters and importers and would also prompt currency speculation, he said. 

 The baht has been fairly stable on fears of central bank intervention, after Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula admitted that the central bank had entered the market in recent days to control liquidity as part of its regular operations. Pridiyathorn has said the bank will manage the baht's float more actively.

title: Emerging  FX  - Depressed as outlook worsens.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 10 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were easier late on Tuesday with the Singapore dollar and Taiwan dollar hitting new multi-year lows, depressed by poor economic data. 

 The yen also gave up some of its gains, but still managed to keep its distance from late Friday lows around 126. 

 But that was not enough for Asian currencies battered by slowing economies at home and abroad, and with little to suggest the slowdown had hit bottom. 

 The Sing dollar saw new 11-year lows after the government slashed its 2001 growth forecast as the economy shrank for the second straight quarter raising fears of a full-blown recession. 

 The Taiwan dollar fell to 34-month lows as second quarter export and import declines hit record levels. 

 Analysts said the poor data had raised fears Singapore may announce a radical shift in its monetary policy at a review due Thursday, which would have consequences for other regionals especially the baht, rupiah and the peso. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar sank to fresh 11-year lows beyond 1.8370 on disappointing growth numbers. 

 Advance second quarter GDP data showed falls of 0.8 percent on-year and 10.1 percent on an annualised quarter-on-quarter basis, leaving Singapore in a technical recession. 

 The government slashed its 2001 growth forecast to 0.5-1.5 percent from 3.5-5.5 percent, adding to the gloom. 

 Dealers said European banks and U.S. investment banks were early sellers of the Sing dollar, with a further selloff by local banks pushed it to levels not seen since July 1990. 

 They cited sporadic corporate U.S. dollar offers at around 1.8370 but said players were looking to buy dollars on dips. 

 Analysts said the dismal GDP data raised the prospect of the MAS shifting its bias to neutral from tightening at its mid-year policy review on Thursday. 

 Dealers also focused on a parliamentary sitting on Wednesday when the government might raise the prospect of fiscal stimulus to counter the downturn. PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso came under pressure from weaker regional currencies, but avoided a damaging break of 53.10, 5-= month lows hit last week. 

 Manila dealers said telecom companies bought dollars near 52.85 with scattered dollar bids by importers lining up around 52.90 in otherwise thin trading. 

Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said he did not expect the peso to deteriorate to between 55 and 60 in the next several months as predicted by some investment banks. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht held on to levels around 45.50 amid fears of central bankintervention but the regional weakness, especially the Singapore dollar's fall kept the dollar well bid around 45.40. 

 Dealers in Singapore said foreign players were trimming dollar longs while local corporates and importers were bidding for dollars. 

 But caution prevailed after the Bank of Thailand confirmed on Monday it had intervened last week to shore up the baht. 

 Dealers said speculation about Thailand's commitment to a managed float had also kept foreign players cautious, despite repeated assurances by Thai officials they would stick to the current regime. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar touched a low of 34.759 with bearish trade data cementing views the authorities would guide the exchange rate lower to cushion the ailing economy. 

 Dealers said the central bank gave up its defence of the 34.50 level late Monday and had since only conducted smoothing operations to slow the pace of the Taiwan dollar's decline. 

 June trade numbers showed exports shrinking 16.6 percent on the year, slightly better than market forecasts while imports contracted by a worse than expected 25.2 percent. 

 For the second quarter exports declined 17 percent and imports were down 22.8 percent on the year. Both were record quarterly declines. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won gave up its early gains as the yen came under pressure and as foreign investors continued to offload local stocks, raising concerns some of the sale proceeds may be converted into dollars. 

 Foreign investors sold a net 81.6 billion won worth of shares on Tuesday after sales of 285 billion in the past two sessions. 

 Dealers said the falling Taiwan dollar and Singapore dollar also pressured the won. Taiwan and Singapore compete with Korea in several export sectors including electronics. 

 The won has failed to strengthen past the 1,290 level since June 12 but hopes of heavy investment flows in the second half have kept it in an overall uptrend since April 4, when it touched a low of 1,365.30.

 Political and economic worries continued to cloud the outlook, with the market shrugging off news Jakarta had reached agreement on almost all fronts with a visiting IMF mission. 

 Chief economics minister Burhannudin Abdullah said talks on controversial changes to central bank laws, the main sticking point in negotiations, had been deferred as sufficient compromise had been reached before the mission's arrival last Thursday. 

 Chartists said the rupiah could be headed for further losses if the dollar broke out of a constricting triangle dating back to early April on the weekly chart, and continued its uptrend.

title: Emerging  FX  - Mixed but economic worries weigh.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 10 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were a mixed bag on Tuesday with some winning a brief reprieve from a steadier yen but others weighed down by the grim economic outlook. 

 In early Tokyo trade, the yen drifted away from Friday's lows around 126.15 as the dollar came under pressure from better-than-expected European and Japanese economic numbers. 

 Germany showed exports up by a surprising 16.5 percent on the year in April while Japanese machinery orders were down in May but not to troughs the market was expecting. 

 Meanwhile, Federal Reserve said U.S. consumers in May borrowed at their slowest pace since the end of last year, indicating consumer spending was slowing. 

 Another reminder of a depressing economic outlook came from Singapore which slashed its growth outlook after weak advanced second quarter growth estimates. 

 With the Taiwan central bank out of the market, the Taiwan dollar slipped to fresh 34-month lows. Analysts believe the central bank was engineering an exchange rate decline to help boost sagging growth and exports. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR The Sing dollar lapsed to a fresh 11-year low below 1.8310 after advance GDP figures released a flood of selling by interbank players. 

 Advance GDP growth for the second quarter fell 0.8 percent year-on-year. On an annualised quarter-on-quarter basis, it fell 10.1 percent, making a technical recession. 

 The government also cut its 2001 growth target to 0.5-1.5 percent from 3.5-5.5 percent. It said growth will remain weak in the third quarter, and only slow recovery will be seen in the fourth quarter. 

 Dealers said European banks and U.S. investment houses bought U.S. dollars from 1.8280, but fears of possible intervention encouraged them to take profits at around 1.8300-10. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore is to announce its mid-year policy review on Thursday. Market views is divided over whether the MAS would shift its bias to neutral from tightening. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO The peso was pinned near 52.83 in thin morning trading, staying within striking distance from 5-= month lows of 53.10 hit last Wednesday. 

 Dealers said volume has thinned since the central bank asked banks and corporates to use the non-deliverable forward market to cover future dollar needs. 

 They added any bounce in the peso would be met by fresh selling given the sluggish outlook for the domestic economy, a view shared by the IMF which said the Philippine was facing a challenging economic situation. 

 The IMF also said the country was vulnerable in its fiscal and banking sectors as well as externally. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht held onto around 45.45 but sentiment soured on the stumbling Sing dollar. 

 Bangkok dealers said oil and machinery importers are looking to buy dollars at around 45.40, but such bids are running into offers by players who fear possible intervention, especially after the Bank of Thailand confirmed it had intervened to support the baht last week, when it hit 10-week lows of 45.70. Dealers have estimated the bank had sold at least $100 million. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won edged higher in line with the yen and on hopes foreign equity investors may halt their sale of local stocks after the Nasdaq's overnight gains. 

 However, dealers said settlement of stocks sold by foreign investors in recent sessions would cap any significant gains. 

 Foreign investors have sold a net 285 billion won worth of local shares in the past two sessions. 

 Bank of Korea will release June import and export prices at 0300 GMT. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar fell to fresh 34-month lows as the central bank pulled out of the market indicating it will allow the currency to settle in a weaker band. 

 The Taiwan dollar hit 34.70, seen in early September 1998, before exporters came in prompting other players to book profits on the U.S. dollar's gains. 

 Charts also suggest the U.S. dollar was due for some profit-taking, with the 14-day relative strength index showing a reading of 83.19. 

 The central bank had defended the 34.50 level for the past six weeks after engineering its fall from around the 33 level in May. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah edged down to 11,350 as local corporates were back with fresh dollar orders after most of them had covered their rupiah requirements for tax payments. 

 A survey showed business sentiment has slipped further in April-May due to grim economic outlook and shaky politics. 

 A bi-monthly survey by state brokerage Danareksa showed its business sentiment index - which incorporates conditions for the present situation and six months ahead - dropped to 110.1 from 113.8 in February-March and 115.3 in January-February. 

 A reading above 100 denotes positive responses outnumbered negative ones.

title: Asia Markets - Stocks suffer, no solace for  currencies .
text:
SINGAPORE, July 9 (Reuters) - Asian equities suffered a 

 downbeat session on Monday as investor unease over corporate 

 earnings soured the market's already rampant pessimism about 

 the economic outlook. 


    In Tokyo, the benchmark Nikkei average         fell more



than two percent at one stage, hit by concerns about high-tech



earnings.



    But it trimmed losses in the afternoon after Japan's core



private-sector machinery orders fell a less-than-expected 2.1



percent in May from a month ago, giving a crumb of comfort to



the market.



    "I would hesitate to describe it as a source of optimism,"



ING Barings economist Richard Jerram said.



    "My concern in general is that profits drive machinery



orders and profits are clearly taking a beating at the



moment... So I view it as more of a temporary respite more than



anything."



    Japanese government bonds (JGBs) also headed south as



investors bet banks would cover equity losses by selling bonds



to window-dress their half-year bookclosings in September.



    So yields on the benchmark 232nd 10-year cash JGBs



 rose 10 basis points to 1.345 percent, the



highest level since April 26, before paring gains.



    The market was also wary the government might have to



implement a supplementary budget to support the economy, which



it would need to fund by issuing extra bonds with the budget



deep in the red.



    The yen        was taking a breather at 125.54 having



buckled to three-month troughs of 126.15 late on Friday.



    SING DOLLAR IN THROES



    The yen's latest spasm left a scar on regional currencies,



with the Singapore dollar a major casualty.



    It kept a softer tone at 1.8280 per dollar, within striking



distance of 1.8290, the fresh 11-year low hit late on Friday.



    Dealers warned of more pain ahead for the Sing dollar as



the evidence of a slowing economy is emerging at an alarming



pace.



    The government releases second-quarter growth figures on



Tuesday, which analysts said could contain the seeds for a



further decline.



    The Monetary Authority of Singapore is due to announce its



mid-year policy review on Wednesday, as some argue the need for



an easier stance to weather the slowdown.



    But the market view is still divided over whether the MAS



would actually shift its tightening bias to neutral, guiding



the Sing dollar to weaken on a trade-weighted basis.



    "Monetary policy is aimed very much at trade-weighted



(targets), which means even if they keep to their modest



appreciation stance, the dollar/Sing can still head higher,"



Philip Wee, regional markets and treasury strategist at DBS



Bank, told Reuters television.



    Wee said the Sing dollar's weakness was in line with other



regional currencies and domestic interest rates are low.



    "So you don't really need to see any change in the stance."



    Wee expected the Sing dollar to reach 1.83 to 1.84 if the



yen slips further to 135 or 140.



    BAHT WINS REPRIEVE



    The baht        has settled around 45.44 but failed to



stretch higher even after baht funding costs in the offshore



market eased.



    The one-month forward rate edged down to 25/45 satang per



dollar having shot up to 40/60 earlier from around 12 a week



ago.



    Bangkok dealers said the baht was torn between dollar



buying demand by importers and fears of possible intervention.



    Anxiety about possible intervention intensified after Bank



of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula confirmed the bank



had intervened to support the baht last week to keep the


currency stable.



    Dealers have estimated the bank had sold at least $100



million last Thursday when it hit 10-week lows of 45.70.



    Analysts said uncertainties surrounding forex reporting



rules would support the baht, but they saw it was unlikely to



pop up above 45 as underlying concerns about the economy would



weigh on the currency.

title: Emerging  FX  - Easier amid doubts on US, yen.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 9 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were easier late on Monday amid doubts over the yen's firmer tone and on dampened hopes of a quick recovery in the U.S. economy. 

 The yen briefly poked above 125.50 from Friday's lows beyond 126 on profit-taking in dollars, but most players remained bearish given Japan's grim economic outlook. 

 Weak U.S. jobs data on Friday weighed more on regional currencies than the dollar as it raised concerns about a much awaited revival in Asia's biggest export market. 

 The data showed 114,000 non-farm jobs lost in June, more than double the forecast, and the jobless rate rising to 4.5 percent from 4.4 percent in May. 

 Speculation some of Asia's central banks, pressured by poor economic numbers and the uncertain outlook, may allow their currencies to settle in weaker ranges also favoured the dollar. 

 No aggressive intervention was seen when the Taiwan dollar hit fresh 34-month lows and the Singapore dollar headed back towards 11-year troughs near 1.8290. 

 Sharp losses in the region's major equity indices, tracking overnight falls in U.S. stock markets, also weighed. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar took a hit as the central bank stepped back from its six-week defence of the 34.50 level, letting it reach lows of 34.65, last seen in early September 1998. 

 It was also weighed by losses in Taipei shares , which closed at fresh six-month lows as investors focused on Wall Street's performance instead of recent state moves to boost market liquidity. 

 Analysts said the next big target for the Taiwan dollar was at 35.00, but the central bank was expected to slow the pace of its decline. 

 Technical signals also suggested the Taiwan dollar might be in for a breather as the U.S. dollar was back in overbought territory with a 14-day relative strength index reading of 77.9. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar lingered close to 11-year lows around 1.8290 hit late Friday ahead of Tuesday's second quarter preliminary gross domestic product estimates, which are expected to show continued weakness. 

 Dealers said it was also weighed by players betting the central bank would hint at a softening of its monetary bias in a policy review statement, due on Wednesday. 

 But most players were reluctant to take aggressive positions due to fears of intervention. With the market already long on U.S. dollars, players were also cautious of profit-taking if the scheduled events deliver what the market is expecting. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht bumped against 45.50 as its borrowing costs eased offshore, allowing players to beef up their dollar longs. 

 But wariness over central bank intervention checked the baht's decline while local banks and corporates capped its upside at around 45.30. 

 Bank of Thailand governor Pridiyathorn Devakula confirmed the central bank had intervened to support the baht last week. Dealers suspected the BOT had sold at least $100 million to shore up the baht when it hit lows of 45.70 last Thursday. 

 Pridiyathorn said the central bank had intervened to quell volatility in the currency market but would not resist the regional trend. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah firmed slightly on a lack of demand for the dollar from local corporates, some of whom were instead seen buying rupiah for tax payments. 

 However, dealers in Jakarta said its upside was capped with interbank players bidding for dollars around 11,320 levels. 

 The political outlook remained grim as President Abdurrahman Wahid gave his opponents a deadline of July 20 to back off from efforts to oust him or said he would declare a state of emergency. Impeachment hearings are set to begin on August 1. 

 Wahid says parliament's plans to consider impeaching him were illegal and a threat to the nation. 

 The announcement came after political leaders, including vice president Megawati Sukarnoputri, failed to attend a meeting called by Wahid to resolve the issue. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won revisited recent lows of 1,298 per dollar as Korean shares fell to 10-week troughs on worries about the prospects for vital tech exports, following a spate of earnings warnings by major U.S. and European tech firms. The expected settlement of share sales by foreign investors also weighed on the won. Foreign investors sold a net 181.2 billion won on the Korean stock market on Monday, after selling a net 103.8 billion won on Friday. 

 After a two-month uptrend dating back to April 4, the won has run into some resistance in the past month, failing to strengthen past the 1,290 level since June 12 as the yen weakened against the dollar. But hopes of foreign investment flows have kept it from weakening past 1,310. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso ended onshore trade slightly higher as corporates stayed out of the market and interbank players booked profit on dollar longs amid fears the central bank may intervene. 

 Dealers in Manila said the speculation was sparked by governor Rafael Buenaventura's comment on Sunday that the peso should be "better than 53 this week". 

 Dealers said the market was also cautious after President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo said she would announce plans to fix economic problems this week. 

 But the dollar remained overbought with a 14-day RSI reading of 82.14. It has been above the overbought level of 70 since mid-June, reaching a peak of 95 when it hit 5-= month highs of 53.10 pesos last week, according to Reuters data.

title: Thai c.bank confirms  intervention  on baht.
text:
BANGKOK, July 9 (Reuters) - Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula confirmed on Monday the central bank had intervened to support the baht last week. 

 He told reporters that the central bank aimed to keep the currency stable but would not try to resist the regional trend. Pridiyathorn said the central bank had intervened last Thursday in support of the baht. 

 He said the bank's intervention was not abnormal. 

 "It is not unusual. We would not resist the market and will move in line with the regional trend. Baht trading should not be too volatile," he said.

title: Thai Baht Ends Up Amid Talk Of Ctrl Bk  Intervention
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended slightly higher against the U.S. dollar Thursday as rumors of intervention by the Bank of Thailand triggered heavy dollar selling in the afternoon session, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 45.45 baht, slightly down from THB45.48 at the Asian close Wednesday. 

 The U.S. unit rose to a high of THB45.67 in early trade as the yen weakened. 

 "In early afternoon, there was dollar selling pressure which started offshore. The market suspected that there might have been some kind of intervention from the central bank, though there's no confirmation from the authorities," said a dealer at a major local bank. 

 The central bank was rumored to have sold a total of $100 million to $200 million via Thai banks and brokers in Bangkok and a Japanese bank in Singapore, dealers in Singapore said. 

 A dealer at a local bank said the central bank was suspected of intervention to soak up liquidity in offshore swap markets, driving up implied yields and forcing investors to rush to cover short-baht positions. 

 Dollar buying on dips by local corporates, however, helped bring the U.S. currency off a low of THB45.42, dealers said. 

Central bank assistant governor Chettavee Charoenpitaks declined to comment on speculation that the central bank had intervened in the foreign exchange market Thursday. 

 Chetthavee said Thursday that the bank wasn't concerned by the baht's recent weakness, as it was in line with the trend in regional currencies and the yen's decline. 

 But the central bank will be closely monitoring the market for any irregular movements, he said. 

 Chettavee said the central bank will speed up its review of new transaction reporting requirements, which the central bank uses to monitor capital flows and compliance with restrictions on baht outflows, but he declined to say when it might be completed. 

Central bank governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said earlier this week that the review will be completed by the end of July. Many investors remained sidelined by the ongoing uncertainty over the central bank's intentions. 

 The dollar is expected to open Monday in a range of THB45.40-THB45.70. 

 Thai markets will be closed Friday for a public Buddhist holiday. 

 Government bond yields closed mixed Thursday, as investors continued to buy very short-term issues, while selling pressure slightly outweighed buying in the longer issues, dealers said. 

 The issue due December 2008 closed at 5.43%, up from a last deal Wednesday of 5.42%, while the October 2003 issue finished at 3.95%, down from 4.01%, said the Thai Bond Dealing Center in its daily report. Yields move in the opposite direction to prices. 

 Sentiment remains fragile, because although the finance ministry has said it won't issue government bonds in the current quarter, new supply could be very heavy once issuance resumes. 

 Overnight money market interest rates rose on demand for cash ahead of the long weekend and pressure from implied yields in the onshore foreign exchange swap market, which rose due to recent weakness in the baht. 

 Longer rates were mostly stable amid generally flush liquidity.

title: Thai economist favours flexible baht regime.
text:
BANGKOK, July 4 (Reuters) - A key economic adviser to Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said on Wednesday he favoured a managed but flexible regime for the Thai baht, a position in line with the policy pursued by the Thai authorities. Former Thai Finance Minister Virabongsa Ramangkula told a seminar he believed the Bank of Thailand should adopt a policy on the baht that would neither be based on a fixed exchange rate nor on a full free float. 

 "The appropriate exchange rate should be based on any regime that is not pegged to a particular currency, nor should it be a 100 percent free float. It should be a managed float regime," he said. 

 Virabongsa surprised financial markets earlier this week by telling a local newspaper in an interview that Thailand should consider pegging the baht to a basket of currencies as a means of stabilising its currency. 

 Thai language daily Krungthep Thurakij on Tuesday quoted Virabongsa as calling on the central bank to devise a new system to manage the currency to avoid the volatility of recent months. 

 He told the paper that the new system would be a balance between the current "managed float" regime, under which the Bank of Thailand (BOT) lets the currency float freely but intervenes to slow big movements, and a fixed rate system. 

 The suggestion was quickly dismissed by Thai authorities with both BOT Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula and Thai Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak saying the baht level should be set by market forces and they would stick to their current policy of a "managed float" for the currency. 

 Virabongsa said on Wednesday a fixed rate for the baht would pit Thailand against market forces, while a complete free float would expose Thai businesses to increased foreign exchange risks and erode their competitiveness. 

 "There should be (foreign exchange rate) management but not under a set, inflexible regime," the economist said. 

 The Thai baht stood at around 45.50 per dollar on Wednesday afternoon, down from around 43 at the beginning of the year.

title: Asia Markets-Grim economy offsets gains on the Dow.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 3 (Reuters) - Key Asian equity markets were 

 marginally higher, aided by U.S. blue chips, but others fell 

 due to the underlying gloomy sentiment about the economy. 

     In Japan, the benchmark Nikkei average closed in positive 

 territory. But the mood was still sour after the Bank of 

 Japan's tankan business sentiment survey on Monday reinforced 

 fears about the faltering economy. 

     "The market was nursing a hangover from the tankan 

 yesterday," an equity analyst in Tokyo said. 

     Dealers said volume was thin and trading would remain 

 rangebound ahead of the Upper House election on July 29. 

     The leading Liberal Democratic Party must perform well in 

 the election in order for Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi to 

 press ahead with reform plans he has pledged to deliver. 

     Public support for Koizumi is sky-high at 84 percent, 

 according to a recent newspaper survey. 

     The yen held firm at around 123.80 from 124.30 late in New 

 York on Monday. 

     PESO SUFFERS 

     The steadier yen helped most regional currencies to trim 

 their recent losses. 

     But the peso suffered home-grown afflictions, slipping to 

 fresh 5-=   month lows of 52.97 per dollar as corporates rushed 

 to hedge their dollar requirements for the second half of 2001. 

     The central bank repeated that it had not intervened in the 

 market on Tuesday. But governor Rafael Buenaventura said the 

 bank was ready to do so if necessary. 

     But dealers were suspicious about the impact of 

intervention, given the bank's tiny forex reserves. 

     Official Philippine figures show gross international 

 reserves at the end of May stood at $14.44 billion. 

     Barclays Capital estimates about $7.2 billion of forex

 reserves are held in securities. Only $5 billion are in 

currency or deposits, compared with Korea's $10.5 billion and 

 Indonesia's $6 billion. 

 "...the amount of unencumbered and liquid forex reserves is 

 likely to be much smaller than implied by the official reserve 

 assets number of $14.4 billion on its own," Barclays said in a 

 research note. 

 Analysts believe the worst is still not over for the peso. 

 "The Philippines is the risky place. Political risk was 

 very high towards the end of last year and that is giving very 

 high economic risk and security risk now," Bhanu Baweja, 

 regional economist at IDEAglobal in Singapore told Reuters 

 Television. 

 "All currency strategists, traders, economists will have to 

 factor in a certain amount of security risk. So you will see a 

 weakening currency here." 

 BAHT UNCERTAIN 

 The baht was another currency unable to benefit from the 

 steadier yen, hitting one-month lows of 45.45 per dollar. 

     But traders were reluctant to bid the dollar up further on 

 fears of possible intervention by the Bank of Thailand (BOT). 

     They also turned cautious after the BOT and the government 

 said they had no plans to abandon the current managed float 

 regime for the baht and would intervene to stem any volatility. 

     Under new the central bank governor, Pridiyathorn Devakula, 

 the BOT's policy focus has shifted from inflation targeting to 

 keeping forex reserves strong and deterring capital outflows.

 going down to attack the cause of the disease," he said. 

     "Without taking on corporate reforms, without taking on 

 banking reforms, ...this kind of restricted regime is actually 

 going to mean that the flight of capital from Asia continues."

title: UPDATE 1-Thailand says no plans to peg  currency .
text:
BANGKOK, July 3 (Reuters) - Thailand's central bank governor and finance minister on Tuesday brushed aside speculation the country might follow the advice of an influential economist who says the baht should be pegged to a basket of currencies. 

 Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula and Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said the authorities had no plans to abandon the current managed float regime for the baht. 

 Somkid told reporters the Thai authorities would focus on maintaining baht stability without changing the exchange rate policy. 

 Pridiyathorn said the central bank would be ready to intervene if the baht was too volatile, but that the country would retain a managed float system. 

 Dealers said recent statements by Pridiyathorn and Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra that the baht should move in line with regional currencies had prompted baht selling. 

 The baht retreated on Tuesday, standing at around 45.37 per dollar at 0626 GMT against 45.29 late on Monday. 

 In his Tuesday comments Pridiyathorn said the central bank would this month finalise changes in rules on reporting foreign exchange deals. He said the changes would not create an excessive back office burden for banks handling such transactions. 

 Speculation Thaksin's government was considering some kind of capital controls has mounted in recent months but has been repeatedly denied by the authorities. 

 ADVISER CALLS FOR PEGGED BAHT 

 Former Finance Minister Virabongsa Ramangkula, an economist and a top adviser to Thaksin, was quoted on Tuesday in Thai-language daily Krungthep Thurakij as saying Thailand should devise a new system to manage the currency to avoid the volatility of recent months. 

 The new system would be a balance between the current "managed float" regime, under which the Bank of Thailand lets the currency float freely but intervenes to slow big movements, and a fixed rate system. 

 "It might not be appropriate for Thailand to return to the old fixed rate system as it would expose us to market attacks like in the past. But at the same time, insisting on maintaining a managed float regime would restrict our economic growth," he said. 

 "The solution is for Thailand to find a new exchange rate system that would be a balance between a managed float and a fixed exchange rate." 

 He said that under this proposal, the Thai central bank would allow the baht to fluctuate within a band of perhaps 10 percent. 

 The exact size of this band would be kept confidential, to avoid offering currency speculators a target, he said. 

 "This is to keep the exchange rate stable and help the private sector save the cost of managing currency risks," he said. 

 Until mid-1997, Thailand operated a system of bands against the dollar. The system was abandoned on July 2, 1997 after sustained selling pressure by foreign exchange dealers. 

 Dealers said the baht, based on its real effective exchange rate (REER) that measures its trade weighted competitiveness relative to currencies of other developing countries, should head lower against the dollar after recent falls in other currencies. 

 A senior dealer at a foreign bank said comments by the governor and finance minister had assured the market the baht exchange rate policy would remain unchanged in the short term.

title: Top Thai economist wants baht pegged - paper.
text:
BANGKOK, July 3 (Reuters) - An influential Thai economist is urging Thailand to consider pegging the baht to a basket of currencies as a means of stabilising the Thai currency, a Thai newspaper reported on Tuesday. 

 Former Finance Minister Virabongsa Ramangkula, a top adviser to Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, told Thai language daily Krungthep Thurakij that Thailand should devise a new system to manage the currency to avoid the volatility of recent months. 

 The new system would be a balance between the current "managed float" regime, under which the Bank of Thailand lets the currency float freely but intervenes to slow big movements, and a fixed rate system. 

 Virabongsa told Krungthep Thurakij in the interview: 

 "It might not appropriate for Thailand to return to the old fixed rate system as it would expose us to market attacks like in the past. But at the same time, insisting on maintaining a managed float regime would restrict our economic growth. 

 "The solution is for Thailand to find a new exchange rate system that would be a balance between a managed float and a fixed exchange rate," he said. 

 Virabongsa said an alternative regime which the Asian Development Bank had considered would be for the baht to be pegged against a basket of currencies of regional and major trading partners, not just against the U.S. dollar like in the past. 

 He said that under this proposal, the Thai central bank would allow the baht to fluctuate within a band of perhaps 10 percent. 

 The exact size of this band would be kept confidential, to avoid offering currency speculators a target, he said. 

 "This is to keep the exchange rate stable and help the private sector save the cost of managing currency risks," he said. 

 Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said on Tuesday he had no plans to return the baht to a fixed exchange rate regime but his bank would be ready to enter the market to stabilise the baht. 

 Until mid-1997, Thailand operated a system of bands against the U.S. dollar. The system was abandoned on July 2, 1997 after sustained selling pressure by foreign exchange dealers. 

 Thailand's decision to allow the baht to float helped trigger the Asian financial crisis.

title: POLL-Thai baht seen slightly lower by end-2001.
text:
BANGKOK, July 2 (Reuters) - The baht	  will track an



expected softer yen and regional currencies in the second half


 of 2001, edging lower to 46 per dollar by the end of 2001 from 

 around 45.45 now, according to a Reuters poll. 

 The end-2001 forecast marks a downward revision in 

 analysts' projections. The last Reuters poll in January saw an 

 end-year forecast of 43.71. 

 Ten economists polled by Reuters predicted a steady to 

 slightly firmer baht in the first half of 2002. They expected 

 the currency to trade at an average 45.79 per dollar in 

 mid-2002. 

Currency analyst Hui-Chin Chong at JP Morgan Chase said: 

 "The baht would probably bottom out in September at around 

 47.50, which should be the most bearish in line with the yen. 

 It would also not be helped by a generally bearish outlook for 

 the overall Thai economy." 

 Usara Wilaipich of Standard Chartered Bank said pending 

 changes to Thai forex reporting rules and the Bank of 

Thailand's signal of its readiness to intervene to stabilise 

 the baht had kept the currency stable for most of the past 

 month. 

 "For a one-month forecast, we don't think the baht would go 

 anywhere. It would be rangebound at around 45.50. There's a lot 

 of confusion over the FX rules and central bank policy. People 

 therefore prefer to stay on the sidelines than to take a 

 position," she said. 

 Suvit Patangkaro of the SCB Research Institute said the 

 baht should strengthen slightly in the first half of 2002, with 

 expected higher Thai interest rates helping stem capital 

 outflows.

title: Emerging  FX -Snug in ranges as dollar/yen stable.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 7 (Reuters) - Asian currencies endured another rangebound session on Thursday, as the dollar and yen played tug-of-war over a small bit of turf. 

 Local developments also failed to generate much excitement. As widely expected, the Bank of Korea held its overnight call rate steady at five percent while investors in Manila shrugged off the Philippine central bank's decision to also hold off on further rate cuts. 

 Poor trade data failed to ruffle the Taiwan dollar. And the Thai baht saw relatively tame trading in a market wary of the Bank of Thailand's next move. 

 For now, the yen had the upper hand against the dollar as it gained on the sterling ahead of the British general election. Investors were banking on a victory by the ruling Labour Party, which is expected to hold a referendum on joining the euro and engineer a much more competitive exchange rate before conversion. 

 But both the dollar and yen were facing negative factors, with the yen suffering from economic uncertainty and the dollar upset by a letter from U.S. trade groups to Treasury Secretary Paul O'Neill complaining about the strong dollar. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht was strait-jacketed in a narrow 45.14-45.34 range as dollar sales by funds and interbank players were countered by fears of central bank dollar-buying intervention. 

 Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula confirmed on Thursday that the authorities had intervened in the market on Wednesday, but declined to elaborate. 

 There were rumours in the market on Wednesday that the BOT spent $100-200 million to buy the dollar from 44.80 to curb the baht's rapid rise and to build up its foreign reserves. 

 "The message is that the central bank will do what it needs to keep the baht stable. And they bought the dollar at pretty good levels. So they managed to slow down the baht's rise which could hurt exports and replenish their reserves at the same time," said a Bangkok dealer. 

 Singapore dealers said the baht's downside was likely to be limited at around 45.50 in the near-term as foreign funds who were long of dollars sought to trim their positions, believed to be in the billions. 

 Baht liquidity remained flush in the short-end, with the one-month forward rate quoted at 3/5 satang per dollar offshore and -2.5/0 satang onshore. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won ended nearly flat from Tuesday's close of 1,286.7. Seoul markets were closed on Wednesday for a public holiday. 

 Singapore dealers said trading was light, and the market ignored a widely expected decision by the Bank of Korea to hold its overnight call rate steady at five percent due to concerns over rising inflation. 

 Charts showed the dollar/won has been on a downtrend since it hit a high of 1,265.3 on April 4, coinciding with the dollar/yen's move lower. 

 But dealers said the won's gains were capped around 1,280, with importers interested in buying dollars around that area. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar did not stray far from a tidy range of 34.031-34.080 despite grim economic data. 

 The Ministry of Finance said earlier May exports fell by 22.6 percent on year, while imports fell by 29.6 percent on year. Both figures were much worse than expected. 

 But Singapore dealers said activity was dull as the central bank had been spotted on both sides of the market. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah shuffled around the 11,200 mark, enjoying a spell of stability, but its gains were capped near 11,000 as local corporates continued to snatch up dollars on dips. 

 Charts showed the dollar/rupiah staying within a range of 10,800-11,450 as fears of political violence died down after parliament voted to convene a special session to decide whether to impeach President Abdurrahman Wahid. 

 Analysts say while the rupiah may climb if Wahid is deposed in a peaceful manner, its rise would be short-lived given Indonesia's huge economic problems. 

 Meanwhile, the government insisted on a parliamentary debate over controversial central bank amendments, which have impeded negotiations with the IMF over the resumption of lending. 

 Chief economic minister Rizal Ramli said it would be difficult for the government to keep 2001 inflation below 10 percent following its decision to raise prices in key sectors. The government's proposed budget revisions to parliament have assumed inflation this year would hit 9.3 percent. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar was slightly firmer in quiet trade, keeping well within its 1.80-1.82 range of the past three weeks. 

 Dealers said the market was still looking to buy the U.S. dollar on dips to around 1.8060 - its Wednesday low - due to the weak economic outlook for Singapore and the region. 

 "The U.S dollar/Sing dollar is expected to remain in the 1.80-1.82 trading range, barring a major weakening of the regional currencies. We expect a year-end level of around 1.78," said a DBS report. 

 DBS based its year-end forecast on an assumption that the economy would turn around in the last quarter, with growth picking up to around 3.6 percent on the year in the fourth quarter from 1.8 percent expected in the third quarter. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The Philippine market was locked in a tight 50.50-50.78 range in what dealers described as an "uneventful" market. 

 "Little has happened in the market today. There are no strong leads, and only around $83 million was transacted compared with around $143 million yesterday," said a Manila dealer, adding that the second quarter was normally a slow period for trade. 

 The rebel saga weighed on sentiment, but did not move the market much as investors expected it to be a protracted story. 

 The central bank left its key overnight rates unchanged, saying it would prefer to wait for more economic data before taking action. The borrowing rate is at 9.0 percent and the lending rate at 11.25 percent.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Gov Confirms It  Intervened  In  Forex  Mkt
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thai central bank Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula confirmed Thursday that the Bank of Thailand intervened in the foreign exchange market Wednesday to cap the baht's rise. 

 Pridiyathorn told reporters that the move was in line with the central bank's managed float system aimed at keeping the currency stable. 

 The baht had strengthened to below 44.80 baht to the dollar early Wednesday over confusion surrounding the central bank's new foreign exchange requirement rules which were to go into effect July 2. 


The new reporting forms were later withdrawn for a review. The baht
retreated back above THB45.00 to the dollar after the move.
- - 07/06/01 06-22G



"We want to stabilize the market which will facilitate business
activity," Pridiyathorn said.



He said the central bank's policy to raise interbank interest rates is
aimed at slowing down debt repayment by the private sector and also
slowdown the debt conversion from the U.S. dollar to the Thai baht.



Pridiyathorn said that the impact of higher rates on the bond market -
where yields rose sharply on the rate hike expectations - will be short
lived and only a one-time effect.



Pridiyathorn said that the losses the bond market is suffering from
now are "quite small compared to the gains it has posted so far on the
back of low interest rates.
- - 07/06/01 07-04G



"In business there is an equal chance that you earn or lose, that
makes it fun," Pridiyathorn said.



He said the move by some private companies to postpone planned
debenture issues was a "good move", proving that his policy is
effective.



"The higher rate will make the issuance too costly for them," he said.



Property developer Central Pattana PCL (H.CPT) and Khanom Electricity
Generating Co. earlier this week postponed issues worth 1.5 billion baht
($1=THB45.020) and THB7.5 billion, respectively, waiting instead for
better market conditions.



Responding to the question about the impact of higher rates on the
central bank's Financial Institutions Development Fund, or FIDF, which
is the largest borrower in the interbank and repurchase markets,
Pridiyathorn said the central bank can handle the impact.



The higher interbank rates are expected to raise FIDF's interest
costs. The higher burden could then turn on tax payers as the government
is required to give full support to the fund.



"I know what I have done. I do it with full consciousness. It (the
policy) may create some damage, but I look for greater returns later,"
he said.

suttinee.yuvejwattana@dowjones.com

BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Thailand needs low interest rates for at least
another two to three quarters to allow the new state asset management
agency and additional fiscal measures work their way through the
economy, Citibank economist Anusorn Tamajai said Thursday.



Anusorn, a respected economist known to be close to current Finance
Minister Somkid Jatusripitak, called on the government to quickly
clarify its stance on interest rates as recent confusing signals might
hurt confidence and the recovery process.



"If they are against high rates, they have to send clear signals,"
Anusorn said, referring to a recent comment by the authorities that
domestic deposit rates were currently too low.



Anusorn told a press briefing that he agreed with the new central bank
Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula that interbank rates should be higher
than deposit rates, but he added that moves in that direction would have
to be made carefully to avoid pushing up deposit rates.



"And, at this point, banks couldn't carry higher deposit rates without
increasing lending rates, which would go against what the economy
needs," he said.



"The net effect is that I cannot see how (higher deposit rates) could
help the economy in the short-term," he said.



Pridiyathorn replaced Chatu Mongol Sonakul who was sacked last week
following a dispute with the government over the suitability of the low
interest rate policy.



The new governor said higher interest rates will help stem capital
outflows and slow early debt repayment.



   Econ, Export Growth Forecasts Cut



Anusorn said that Citibank had revised its forecast for Thailand's
gross domestic product growth this year to 3.1%, from 3.6% previously,
and has cut its export growth forecast to 0.5%, from 6% earlier.



He said the cuts had been made due to worries over some local policy
factors and the continued impact of external factors, despite an upward
adjustment in Citibank's forecast for the U.S. economic growth from 1.6%
to 1.9%.



In that situation, a rather weak baht is still needed to help exports,
he said. But, he added, it's more important that the government increase
fiscal stimulus to boost domestic consumption - something higher rates
couldn't achieve.



"Higher deposit rates wouldn't benefit the public in general as most
deposits are concentrated in the hands of a minority. That would also go
against several other policies of the new government, which targets a
better income distribution to a larger number of people," he said.



Anusorn noted that the confusion over the interest rate policy has
already had a severe effect on the bond market, which has almost stopped
functioning, and is also harming the equities market.



"This goes against the need to build up these two markets to avoid an
excessive reliance of the economy on the banking sector," he said.



Among the few positive results higher rates could have is the
strengthening of the baht, Anusorn said. He warned, however, this could
be short-lived as the exchange rate system is still a flexible managed
float system.



Pridiyathorn has said he wants to keep the baht stable and maintain
foreign exchange reserves above $30 billion.



Anusorn said the central bank shouldn't focus on foreign
exchange-reserve targeting but should maintain its focus on the
inflation targeting system, devised under the previous governor.



He said a policy of price stability and is most appropriate for the
managed float system.
