title: Thai Baht Ends Lower; Upcoming  Forex  Rules Support
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht finished slightly lower Friday as importers took the currency's recent gains on concerns over possible changes in Thai central bank policy as an opportunity to buy U.S. dollars on weakness, traders said. 

 The dollar ended at 45.36 baht, slightly up from THB45.33 at the Asian close Thursday. 

 Intraday weakness in the Japanese yen also weighed on the baht, but the Thai currency ended off a late low of THB45.50 to the dollar on jitters related to a meeting between the Thai central bank and financial institutions. 

 The Bank of Thailand met bank officials Friday to explain new reporting requirements for transactions involving nonresident accounts, which will be implemented July 2. 

 The tightened reporting requirements are to improve the ability of the central bank to monitor capital flows and compliance with existing controls on baht outflows. 

 Concerns that current limited capital controls will be tightened have heightened since incoming central bank Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula, who is expected to take office next week, said late Wednesday that he is mulling a package of measures to limit capital outflows. 

Central bank officials declined to comment on any changes in policy or organization which might occur after reviews conducted by the new governor. 

 Uncertainty supported the baht Friday, and should continue to do so until Pridiyathorn's intentions are clearer. 

 Comments from Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak Friday injected more uncertainty into the situation. He said monetary and fiscal policy won't be changed. 

 He also added that balance of payment deficits should be prevented and that the government's economic policy would focus on stability rather than growth. The latter comments could signal an increase in interest rates or a further tightening of capital controls. 

 Dealers expect the baht to open in a range of THB45.30-THB45.60 per dollar Monday. 

 Thai government bond yields dropped 10 to 30 basis points Friday as continued buying by the central bank finally convinced the market to participate in a partial recovery after the 90- to 100-basis point increases seen early in the week, dealers said. Yields move in the opposite direction to prices. 

 Ongoing uncertainty over the intentions of Pridiyathorn on interest rates should limit any further gains until he completes a review of monetary policy. 

 The incoming governor has scheduled a press conference for 0400 GMT Monday (12:00 a.m. Monday EDT), but he isn't expected to provide explicit guidance on interest rates. Officials have said rates controlled by the central bank will remain low, but may rise slightly. 

 The yield on the government bond due December 2008 dropped to 5.37% from 5.65%, after rising sharply Thursday, while the issue due December 2006 finished at 4.90%, down from 5.17%, the Thai Bond Dealing Center said in its daily report. 

 Bank of Thailand intervention helped to set a yield for the bond due April 2002 at 2.50%, after the market failed to close a deal on the issue Thursday. 

 The overnight interbank interest rate continued to decline from the highs they reached earlier in the week after the news of the central bank governor's replacement broke Monday, as the central bank continued to inject funds through the repurchase market. Other money market rates were mostly flat.

title: Asia Markets-Dented by Wall Street, China B-shares buck trend.
text:
HONG KONG, May 31 (Reuters) - Asian asset prices were 

 pressured on Thursday by a technology-led sell-off on Wall 

 Street which dented stocks and left investors mulling the 

 potential for more gloom ahead in the region's export oriented 

 economies. 


    South Korea	   and Hong Kong	  equities were



hardest hit in the region with benchmark indices falling 2.6



and 1.8 percent respectively.



    Japan's bellwether Nikkei 225	   was shaken down 1.7



percent by a tumble on the U.S. Nasdaq and a bout of



investment ratings downgrades of high-profile telecoms and



high-tech firms.



    The euro lurched lower to around 101.39 yen	     in



late afternoon trade, compared with around 103.00 in morning



trade, and its weakness translated into dollar strength in the



yen , which climbed to 119.16 against the greenback.



    TECH WOES HIT STOCKS



    Hong Kong blue chips were led lower by China Mobile



 as investors feared further profit warnings from U.S.



tech firms.



    Turnover stood at HK$15.98 billion (US$2.05 billion), the



highest in more than a month. Declines outnumbered advances 325



to 192, with 233 stocks unchanged.



    Earnings warnings from U.S. tech companies sent the Nasdaq



spiralling down more than four percent overnight.



    China Mobile, the top mainland cellular carrier and the



Hang Seng's second largest constituent, ended 2.83 percent



lower.



    South Korean shares closed more than two percent lower as



investors eschewed tech stocks, beating down chip maker Samsung



Electronics to a two-week low.



    CHINA B-SHARES BUCK TREND



    China's hard currency B-shares bucked the faltering trend,



bolstered by investors banking on another wave of liquidity



flowing into the markets with the end of a ban on using foreign



exchange deposited since February 19 to buy shares.



Some analysts estimated $2-$3 billion in deposits -



amounting to 10 to 15 percent of the overall market



capitalisation - could flow into B shares over the next month



after the restriction is lifted on June 1.



The Shanghai B share index closed up 2.61 percent



at 239.731 points after touching a record high of 241.305 in



late trade. Turnover rose to a huge $582.03 million from an



already heavy $493.17 million on Wednesday. Shanghai's B-share



index is up 168 percent so far this year.



Shenzhen's B index inched up 0.50 percent to



425.51. Turnover rose to HK$2.23 billion from a heavy HK$2.18



billion.



"Most of these stocks can potentially double...the existing



valuation gap is about 42 percent and I see a lot of B-share



prices exceeding their A-share prices," Joe Zhang, head of



China research at UBS Warburg in Hong Kong, told Reuters



Television.



The government opened the formerly foreigners-only B share



markets to Chinese investors in late February, but in a bid to



exclude black market money it barred the use of hard currency


deposited after February 19.


THAILAND NOT INTERVENING


Deputy Bank of Thailand Governor Pakorn Malakul na



Ayutthaya said the central bank had not intervened to support



the baht, which has gained against the dollar this week.



Pakorn said the BOT injected about 20 billion baht into the



repo market in the past two days in order to prevent sharp



volatility of short-term interest rates after the government



fired central bank governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul on Tuesday.



He said the local money market had tightened this week as



reflected by a sharp rise in government bond yields. But



analysts say the baht's recovery could be short-lived.



"In the long run you simply cannot have interest rates



lower than the U.S. interest rate and have a strong currency,"



Steven Xu, senior economist at SG Securities in Hong Kong told



Reuters.



Xu said steepening the yield curve to help recapitalisation



of banks badly mauled by Asia's financial crisis had negative



implications for the baht and asset prices in Thailand.



"We could see a period of artificial strength of the baht,



but then something has to give and that means you're going to



see greater inflation coming through in the economy and you're



going to see lower stock/asset valuations," Xu said. The baht



was quoted at 45.30 to the U.S. dollar in late Asian trade. It



has appreciated about 0.9 percent after hitting a low of 45.64



on Tuesday.

The Indonesian rupiah gained over one percent with



the market relieved over the absence of serious violence after



parliament voted to hold a special session to decide whether to



impeach President Abdurrahman Wahid.



The currency ended off an intra-day high of 10,925, but was



still firm as players unwound dollar longs, triggering



stop-loss dollar sales around 11,100.

peaceful transition of power, but it would soon run aground due



to Indonesia's mountain of foreign debt.



"Probably before August we are going to see political



clarity, we are going to see strong leadership coming through



in Jakarta. That's going to boost market confidence and I



wouldn't be surprised if the Indonesian rupiah strengthened to



somewhere between 9,000 and 10,000 in the short term," SG's Xu

title: Thai Baht Ends Up On Stronger Yen, Caution On Rate Review
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht finished slightly higher against the U.S. dollar Thursday on a stronger yen and caution ahead of a central bank review of monetary policy intended to limit capital outflows, dealers said. 

 The dollar ended at 45.330 baht, down from THB45.375 at the Asian close Wednesday. 

 The dollar rose to THB45.400 after Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said the country would maintain a low-interest rate policy, dealers said. 

 But Thaksin didn't rule out the possibility that an upcoming review of monetary policy will result in a hike in interest rates, so some players unloaded dollars and dragged the pair off its high. 

 Most investors were sidelined pending a central bank meeting with onshore bank treasurers Friday to explain new central bank reporting requirements for foreign exchange and other transactions, to be implemented July 2. 

 The tightened reporting requirements are to improve the ability of the central bank to monitor capital flows and compliance with existing controls on baht outflows. 

 Incoming Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said he will conduct a review of monetary policy with the central bank after his appointment is formally confirmed. The confirmation should take place late this week. 

 Pridiyathorn said he was considering changes to limit capital outflows, but any changes in interest rates, capital controls or other elements of monetary policy would be introduced as a package. 

 Pridiyathorn and government officials have said interest rates have stayed too low for too long, resulting in undesirable capital outflows. 

 Outgoing Governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul maintained that low interest rates were essential to support recovery in the economy and the financial sector, and that outflows were positive, as they were mostly to repay foreign debt. 

 A slightly worse-than-expected trade deficit in April of $134 million announced Thursday had little effect on the baht, as the market had known the figures would be disappointing. 

 Dealers expect the baht to open Friday in a range of THB45.350-THB45.500, subject to movements of other regional currencies against the dollar, with limited participation from offshore players ahead of the implementation of the new reporting requirements. 

 Yields on long-term Thai government bonds stabilized following 90-to-100 basis point increases in the previous two days. However, yields on selected short-term issues continued to rise, in spite of central bank buying in three- and four-year bonds, dealers said. 

 Late selling by mutual funds - to prepare cash for redemption by bond-fund unit holders - pushed up the yield on the illiquid government bond due October 2003 to around 4.00%, from a last deal Wednesday of 3.39%, dealers said. Yields move in the opposite direction to prices. 

 The yield on government bonds due December 2008 finished flat from the previous close, however, around 5.50%, off a high of 5.60%. 

 HSBC Treasurer Mark Boyne said Thursday he expects volatility in a range of about 20 basis points from current levels until the incoming central bank governor clarifies whether or not he intends to hike short-term interest rates. 

 The Bank of Thailand released Thursday a schedule for weekly Treasury bill auctions in June, beginning Monday, of very small THB1 billion tranches of both 28-day and 91-day T-bills. 

 The small offerings should enable the authorities to keep T-bill yields down despite the uncertainty, possibly by ordering state banks to bid near the average yields accepted at this week's auctions, around 1.61% for the 28-day and 1.735% for the 91-day T-bills. 

 The June schedule for Tuesday auctions of Financial Institution Development Fund, or FIDF, bonds was also released Thursday. The first auction on June 5 will be of THB2 billion in two-year bonds and THB3 billion in five-year bonds. 

 Small closing deals in certain FIDF bonds recorded Wednesday at sub-market level yields indicated that state agencies might also be ordered to submit low-yield bids at auctions. 

 A schedule for weekly government bond auctions to be held on Wednesdays in June hasn't been released yet. 

 The fragile government bond market wasn't ready to absorb any news about new supply, said a dealer at a foreign bank. 

 If the central bank can restore stability in the market and recover some of the losses seen since Monday, however, next week's auction should proceed as usual, the dealer said. 

 Money market interest rates fell from the highs set Wednesday and today on expectations that the incoming central bank governor will raise short-term interest rates it controls, due to central bank intervention in the repurchase market. 

 The Bank of Thailand said it injected THB20 billion worth of liquidity through repurchase market lending and bought between THB6 billion and THB8 billion worth of government bonds during Tuesday and Wednesday combined. 

 Dealers said intervention in the markets continued Thursday. Repurchase market interest rates for terms of one-, two- and three-months came off highs or returned from periods of inactivity to close at last week's historic lows. 

 The overnight interbank rate closed around 2.25%-2.50%, down from a close Wednesday of 3.00%-3.25% and a high earlier that day at 3.75%.

title: Thai Baht Ends Up Slightly, Shadowing Yen's Movements
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht finished up slightly Tuesday, tracking the Japanese yen higher against the dollar, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 45.60 baht, down slightly from THB45.63 late Monday, but off an earlier low of THB45.52. 

 The yen's gains overnight pushed the U.S. unit down early, and local exporter dollar sales added to the pressure. 

 Volume was minimal, however. The dollar recovered slightly against the baht in the afternoon, shadowing its movements against the yen. 

 Offshore investors were sidelined ahead of the central bank's clarification on new foreign exchange transaction reporting requirements to be implemented July 2. 

 "No one wants to take positions. Everyone is waiting for the meeting of the central bank (with onshore bank treasury departments) June 1 to clarify how the new requirements will work," a dealer at a foreign bank said. 

 The baht is expected to trade in a narrow range until then, barring any regional volatility. The dollar is expected to open Wednesday between THB45.50 and THB45.70. 

 The reporting requirements will improve the central bank's ability to monitor baht outflows and identify banks and clients involved in circumventing limits on those flows. 

 Bank of Thailand limits the supply of baht to offshore foreign exchange swap markets making it more expensive for speculators to short-sell the baht. 

 Restrictions on baht outflows and detailed reporting requirements have virtually eliminated speculative volumes, thereby limiting volatility and keeping the baht's depreciation in line with other regional currencies. 


The baht is expected to continue to weaken in the medium-term due to
the dollar's bullish prospects against regional currencies, domestic
political uncertainty, economic weakness, and fragile global demand for
exports.
- - 22/05/01 11-18G



Government bond prices ended slightly lower, but confidence that the
central bank will continue to intervene and to keep interest rates low -
despite government calls for a review of monetary policy - kept losses
to a minimum in low volume.



Yields of long-term government bonds rose two-to-three basis points.



Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said Tuesday he had asked the
central bank to review monetary policy and to report to the Cabinet next
week.



Several of Thaksin's advisers have criticized the central bank's low
interest-rate policy, saying that it reduces public income from deposits
and contributes to capital outflows, as companies are encouraged to
refinance foreign debt at low domestic rates.



Dealers said the bond market was unaffected, as investors don't
believe central bank Governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul will alter the low
interest rate policy.



The central bank encourages local refinancing of foreign debt, and
maintains low interest rates to support economic recovery and
restructuring of corporate and public sector debt.



The central bank's Monetary Policy Board will meet Thursday. It is
expected to maintain the policy-signal 14-day repurchase market interest
rate at 1.5%.



However, Bank of Thailand intervened in the market Tuesday to keep
yields from rising amid the uncertainty. The central bank bought
one-month and three-month Treasury bills, and three-year and 10-year
government bonds, dealers said.



The three-year bond closed at 2.80%, compared with a last deal of
2.85% Monday, while the 10-year finished at 5.20%, down from 5.202%. But
the December 2008 issue closed at 4.68%, up from 4.65% Monday, the Thai
Bond Dealing Center said in its daily report.



The market was subdued ahead of an auction Wednesday of THB3.5 billion
of nine-year government bonds and THB1.46 billion of a 20-year issue.



Dealers said the nine-year government bond traded Tuesday in a
bid-offer range of 5.27% to 5.23%, around a last deal Monday of 5.2425%.



The average accepted yield for the nine-year government bond is
expected to be close to secondary market levels, between 5.22% and
5.30%, a dealer at a foreign bank said.



The 20-year bond average accepted yield should be around 6.90% to
6.96%. Secondary market bids were around 6.96% Tuesday, but offers were
scarce, the dealer said.



An auction Tuesday of government-guaranteed bonds issued by the state
Financial Institutions Development Fund, or FIDF, resulted in premiums
of just over 40 basis points on the government bond yield curve, as
expected.



The central bank sold THB2 billion of a two-year FIDF bond at a
weighted-average of 3.012%, and THB2 billion of a five-year FIDF bond at
an average of 4.1146%. The two-year bond closed in the secondary market
at 3.00%, but the five-year issue was untraded.



Investors began to show renewed interest in higher-yielding state
enterprise and corporate bonds, dealers said.



An issue by Advanced Info Service due March 2006 was traded at 4.76%,
but closed at 4.78%, unchanged from Monday.



Money market interest rates were mostly flat amid flush liquidity.

title: Thai Baht Ends Slightly Up, Tracks Singapore Dlr Move Up
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended slightly higher against the U.S. dollar Wednesday, tracking the Singapore dollar's move up during the day, traders said. 

 The dollar closed at 45.50 baht, down a touch from THB45.555 at the Asian close Friday. Thai markets were closed Monday and Tuesday for a public holiday. 

 Dealers said trade was relatively thin, with the U.S. dollar moving in a narrow range as most investors were sidelined in the absence of fresh, market moving news. 

 "It seems like most investors are still in holiday mood," said a dealer at a foreign bank. 

 The Thai baht hit an early intraday low of THB45.62 against the U.S. dollar after the Singapore dollar touched its intraday low of $1.8250. 

 However, the baht later regained ground in line with the Singapore dollar's recovery due to fears of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Thailand. 

 Exporter dollar selling in the afternoon also helped support the local currency, they said. 

 The U.S. dollar is expected to open in a range of THB45.40 and THB45.60 Thursday. 

 Analysts said trade is likely to continue its slowing trend during the rest of the week as most investors await the U.S. Federal Reserves' Open Market Committee rate setting meeting May 15. 

 The FOMC is widely expected to further cut interest rates by 50 basis points to facilitate a soft-landing of the U.S. economy. Such expectations should give the Asian currencies a boost in the short-term, analysts said. 


Investors were also monitoring Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra's key
speech at the Fortune Global Forum in Hong Kong late Wednesday. He is
expected to give the right message to foreign investors in a bid to
dispel thier fears created by his speech last month, suggesting Thailand
may close its markets to foreigners.
- - 09/05/01 10-36G



Thai government bond prices ended down in sluggish trade, following a
disappointing auction of nine-year government bonds earlier in the day,
traders said.



The yield on the THB3 billion nine-year issue came at the higher end
of expectations at 5.1475%, significantly up from 5.0828% at the
previous auction.



"The nine-year is seen as a trendsetter for the secondary market. Its
higher yields in the auction triggered selling in other close tenors,"
said a dealer at local bank.



In the secondary market, the yield on the April 2010 issue closed at
5.17%, jumping from 5.07% at the previous close.



The yields on most medium-term bonds also rose after the auction by
five to six basis points.



Among the most active issues, the bond maturing December 2006 closed
at 3.95%, compared with 3.91% Friday. The July 2007 issue closed at
4.16%, compared with 4.10%, while the December 2008 issue finished at
4.60%, compared with 4.54%.



Thai markets were closed Monday and Tuesday for a religious holiday.



A longer-term THB1.5 billion 20-year bond was sold at 6.9400% at the
same Wednesday auction, however, unchanged from the last auction, with
substantial demand from long-term investors such as insurance companies.



The central bank will auction THB2 billion each of two-year and
five-year government bonds, guaranteed by the state's Financial
Institutions Development Fund, or FIDF, Thursday.



Dealers said despite strong interest for short-term instruments,
yields on both FIDF issues may move up by 5 to 10 basis points, compared

title: Thailand  has no plan to  intervene  to lift baht-PM.
text:
BANGKOK, April 18 (Reuters) - Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said on Wednesday the government would not intervene to support the baht, which usually follows the movement of other regional currencies. 

 "We have to look at the whole region, we can't just intervene to make the baht unusally stronger than other regional currencies," he told reporters. 

 He said he would rather say little about the baht and let the central bank monitor its movement. 

 "I understand the market mechanism of the baht and will not do anything that is against the nature (of the baht movement)," he said. 

 The baht has tumbled to three-year lows in recent weeks but has been stable this week at around 45.40 to the dollar.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk: Situation In External Economies Worsens
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thailand's central bank said Thursday the situation in external economies has worsened more than expected since the monetary policy board's last policy meeting in early March. 

 Thirachai Phuvanatnaranubala, central bank assistant governor for monetary policy, said after a preparatory meeting for the next policy meeting April 19, that exports from Thailand and the region have been hurt by the economic slowdown in the U.S. and Japan. 


The board reviewed Thai and regional data for January and February,
but it won't discuss what the trends mean for Thai monetary policy until
next week's meeting, he said.
- - 12/04/01 11-23G



Thai exports in the first two months of the year dropped 3.4% from the
same period last year, while Taiwan and Japan suffered declines of 4.4%
and 4.5% over the period. Exports from Hong Kong and the Philippines
continued to grow but at a sharply reduced rate from last year.



"In reaction to the slowdown, some countries have cut interest rates,
including Hong Kong - due to its currency's ties to the U.S. dollar -
but also Taiwan and the Philippines. Other countries took fiscal steps,"
Thirachai said.



He gave no indication how the monetary policy board would react,
saying it would be considered on April 19.



No change is expected in the policy-signal 1.5% 14-day repurchase
market interest rate, although some research houses believe a 25 basis
point cut is possible.



One of the factors the board will consider is the expected addition of
14.6 billion baht ($1=THB45.34) to liquidity during the fiscal year to
Sept. 30 through stimulus measures planned by the Thai government, he
said.



Next fiscal year, planned policies will bring THB70 billion into the
system, and the following year THB26 billion.



Another factor to be considered by the board will be the fall of the
baht and other regional currencies due to the decline of the yen,
Thirachai said.



He gave no indications of the central bank's view on foreign exchange
rate movements.



Bank of Thailand acknowledged intervening in foreign exchange markets
two weeks ago when the baht hit a 37-month low of 45.45 baht to the
dollar.



A rebound in the yen and concern about possible intervention by
regional central banks have prompted investors to unwind long-dollar
positions against the baht and other regional currencies.



The dollar closed Thursday ahead of a four-day weekend at THB45.34,
down from a new 37-month high of THB45.85 earlier in the week.

title: Thai PM: Weak THB No Worry As Ctrl Bk Monitoring Mkt
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said Tuesday he isn't concerned about the recent weakness in the baht because the central bank is closely monitoring the market. 

 Thaksin said local exporters were taking the opportunity to boost exports while the baht is weak. 

 The dollar had dropped from around 45.65 baht to the dollar at the Asian open Tuesday to around THB45.50, after the Thai central bank was said to have joined a selling spree triggered by the U.S. currency's early slide against the Japanese yen. 

 The market took Thaksin's midday comments as a reaffirmation that the government favors a weak baht policy to boost exports and pushed the dollar up to test THB45.60. 

 Dealers expect a range of THB45.50 to THB45.65 to hold Tuesday, however, because the central bank controls foreign exchange policy, and it has confirmed intervention around these levels last week. 

 Bank of Thailand is believed to be comfortable with a gradual depreciation in line with movement of regional currencies against the dollar, but it closely monitors trade for speculative activity. 

 Restrictions on baht outflows are used to limit supply offshore, raising the cost of borrowing baht to cover short positions to punishing levels whenever speculators gang up on the currency.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk: Baht Volatility Mostly On Dollar-Yen Moves
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thailand's central bank said Monday that recent volatility in the baht was mostly due to the movement of the U.S. dollar against the Japanese yen. 

 Chettavee Charoenpitaks, Bank of Thailand assistant governor for financial markets operations, told reporters that the authorities are closely monitoring baht trade in foreign exchange markets. 


In response to questions about a local newspaper article alleging that
the central bank would develop new capital controls, Chettavee said he
wasn't aware of any such plans.
- - 09/04/01 05-38G



Chettavee said that Thai foreign exchange policies leave the market
well controlled and that there is no need for any new measures.



Bank of Thailand restricts the flow of baht to offshore markets in
order to raise the cost of covering short-baht positions by borrowing in
offshore foreign exchange swap markets.



Local dealers are required to name parties and define the purpose of
all foreign exchange transactions, helping the central bank to monitor
capital flows and compliance.



Bank of Thailand intervened in the offshore spot, forward and swap
markets last week to further dry up liquidity and slow the baht's
decline.



But officials have said repeatedly that most of the recent volatility
was due to the dollar's rise against the yen and other regional
currencies, and that there has been no abnormal speculative activity.



Chettavee said the baht has also received some support from the
country's economic fundamentals.



If domestic confidence is good, the baht shouldn't weaken much
further, Chettavee said, without specifying how far the baht might
weaken or which aspects of the domestic economy were supportive.



Analysts expect the baht to weaken slowly until U.S. and global demand
for Thai exports begins to recover later in the year.



At midday Monday, the dollar was trading at 37-month highs between
THB45.80 and THB45.83, up from a range of THB45.60 to THB45.65 late
Friday in Asian trade.

title: Thai Finance Minister: No Need To Alter Interest Rates
text:
KUALA LUMPUR -(Dow Jones)- Thailand won't alter interest rates to shore up its currency, and the volatility of the baht is a short-term problem, Thai Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said Sunday, on the fringes of a finance ministers meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. 

 "No need," Somkid said in response to a question on changing interest rates. 

 "I believe in my country's fundamentals. Currency volatility is short-term, if we prepare in advance, nothing (negative) will happen," he added. 

Thailand's central bank intervened in the market last week to support the baht.

title: Asia Markets - Nasdaq gives stocks some lift,  currencies  glum.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 6 (Reuters) - Asian stocks danced to the 

 Nasdaq's upbeat tune on Friday in early trade, but lost some 

 energy as the day wore on and doubts developed about whether 

 U.S. gains would be sustained. 

     Most closed firmer but well off their highs. 

     Regional currencies stumbled alongside the yen after 

 euphoria surrounding a new Japanese economic package quickly 

 fizzled out. 

     Tech-heavy Korean and Taiwan markets rose after the Nasdaq 

 jumped 8.92 percent or 146.20 points to close at 1,785.00 

 overnight -- its biggest percentage gains ever. 

     U.S. market sentiment had been boosted by news Dell 

 Computer Corp stood by its first-quarter targets. 

     The Korean Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) ended 2.54 

 percent or 12.53 points higher at 506.22. Taiwan's TAIEX gained 

 2.02 percent on the Nasdaq's rally and signs of easing 

 U.S.-China tensions. 

 Japan's stocks closed off their intraday's high after a 

 long-awaited emergency economic package designed to boost the 

 country's growth and stock market came in short on detail. 

 "The package looks fairly solid - it just left too many 

 questions unanswered to warrant a broad-based advance," said 

 Nobuaki Kurisu, chief fund manager at Sumisei Global Investment 

 Trust Management. 

 The next event for market focus is the all-important U.S. 

 job report to be released later in the day, for a clue to U.S. 

 economic health and the prospect of further rate cuts by the 

 Federal Reserve. 

 Economists polled by Reuters expected the March jobs report 

 to reveal a higher unemployment rate, up to 4.3 percent from 

 the current 4.2 percent rate where it has been lodged all year. 

CURRENCIES SINKS, INFLATION FEARED 

 Asian currencies buckled under the yen's renewed weakness, 

 with the Indonesian rupiah leading the losers due to persistent 

 corporate dollar demand. 

 But central bank intervention underpinned some of the 

currencies. Dealers said the Korean central bank sold the 

 dollar through state banks while Bank Indonesia was spotted 

 selling the U.S. currency directly to cap the rupiah's fall at 

 10,930. 

 The move came after the Monetary Authority of Singapore was 

 rumoured to have intervened in the market on Monday and the 

 Bank of Thailand suggested earlier this week that it had been 

 in the market to stave off baht volatility. 

 Analysts expressed concerns sustained declines in these 

currencies could worsen the already bleak growth prospect of 

 the region as they increased risk of inflation. 

 "This stops people from placing a one-way bet on the 

 direction of inflation and interest rates in the region," said 

 David Fernandez, head of Asian sovereign research at JP Morgan 

 Chase. 

 "The market right now is taking currency weakness seriously 

 and it's time to be cautious as hopes that central banks would 

 continue to cut rates to boost the economy will have to be put 

 on pause," he said. 

 WEAK YEN COULD HIT PEGS 

 There has been concern in the market that the yen's 

 sustained weakness could raise the spectre of competitive 

 devaluation among Asian pegged currencies such as the Malaysian 

 ringgit, Chinese yuan and Hong Kong dollar. 

 The yen has depreciated by around 10 percent year this 

 year. While other free-floated currencies can fall in tandem 

 with the yen, these pegged currencies have not, making them 

 look overvalued. 

 "There has been yet again rhetoric about pressure on the 

 Hong Kong economy via price and output adjustments witnessed in 

 1998, and about how the Chinese renminbi peg stands in the face 

 of persistent yen weakness," said Lian Chia Liang, analyst at 

 Merrill Lynch. 

 China managed to hold the yuan steady against the dollar 

 despite Asian financial crisis which saw the yen falling past 

 140 in summer 1998. Investors are questioning if the country 

 would be able to do the same this time. 

     Yan Haiwang, deputy governor of the People's Bank of China, 

 said on Friday that a devaluation of the yuan was impossible. 

     "I have never thought about devaluing the yuan and it is 

 quite impossible for that to happen," he told an economic forum 

 attended by finance and central bank officials from Japan and 

 China.

title: PRESS DIGEST - Asian Wall Street Journal - April 6.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 6 (Reuters) - The following stories were reported in Friday's electronic version of The Asian Wall Street Journal: 

 * Japan's currency rose nearly two yen per dollar, regaining ground after recent steep declines. The increase happened after Tokyo leaders criticised "excessive" movements in the yen. 

 * Regional Wireless intends to bid on MobileOne, Singapore's number two cellular provider, possibly to counteract last month's unveiling of Singapore Telecommunicatikon bid for Cable & Wireless Optus . 

 * The United States and China held "intensive" talks on the release of the U.S. crew involved in a collision with a Chinese jet fighter. China repeated its demand for an apology, which Washington has ruled out. 

 * Indonesia adopted the IMF's new suggestions for its restructuring plans. But Texmaco's debt-workout accord seems to violate the new guidelines. 

 * Indian investigators blamed the pilots in the July 17 crash of an Alliance Air jet that killed 61, according to a report by the aviation ministry. 

 * Japan's ruling party set the date for a presidential election to choose a successor to Mori, after the prime minister declared his intent to resign. 

 * Mitsubishi Tokyo Financial said three of its banks expect to post combined net losses of $1.09 billion for the fiscal year, blaming large disposals of bad loans. 

 * Thai Central Bank governor Chatu Mongol confirmed the Bank of Thailand intervened in currency markets on Wednesday to slow - but not stop - the baht's weakening pace. The baht slid to a 37-month low against the dollar Wednesday. 

 * Taiwan President Chen Shui-bian met for the first time with the Dalai Lama in a long-anticipated session of friendly exchanges that underscored their common differences with China. 

 * Muslim rebels in the Philippines backed off a threat to behead a U.S. hostage in response to a last-minute appeal from his mother to let the captive go. 

 * Thaksin Shinawatra acknowledged that he could be found guilty of financial wrongdoing and forced to resign as Thailand's prime minister. 

 * Hitachi and Kawasaki Heavy teamed up in hopes that their railway expertise will help them win overseas orders as the Japanese market shrinks (From Nikkei Net Interactive).

title: Emerging  FX  - Bounce back as yen jawboning helps.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 5 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were steadier in late trade on Thursday with a rebound in the yen providing some breathing space. 

 The yen traded at its highest level this week, hovering around 124.00 per dollar after Japanese officials made concerted efforts to talk it up. 

 It hit a two-and-a-half year low of 126.84 per dollar on Monday and brought down with it regional currencies amid concerns Japan's political and policy gridlock would make it difficult to snap out of its economic troubles. 

 Some analysts said recent declines in the regional currencies were excessive and there should be some dollar correction soon, although a meaningful turnaround might not take place until the second half of this year. 

 "(The decline) in March had been overdone and obviously was precipitated by the dollar/yen effects," said Arthur Woo, economist at HSBC. 

 "But our house's view is that this will eventually reverse probably not immediately but toward the second half of the year when the relief will come for most of the currencies in the region," he said. 

 The fact that recent hefty losses in regional currencies have raised the hackles of Asian central banks also dampened dollar demand a bit. 

 Korea said aggressive measures were needed to stabilise currency markets, Thailand implicitly confirmed it did intervene to stave off baht volatility and the Philippines said the peso would not drop to 52 per dollar. 

 Markets in Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong were closed for a one-day holiday, keeping overall activity rather subdued. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH The rupiah got little solace, hovering at just above three-week lows of 10,710 in relatively thin trading. 

 Jakarta dealers attributed the fall to solid corporate demand for the U.S. dollar with auto manufacturing companies, chemical and oil firms and state-owned enterprises snapping up an estimated $30 million in total. 

 Dealers said Bank Indonesia offered cold comfort to bears as its sales of around $10-15 million in the morning from 10,700 to 10,680 failed to support the downside. They added the rupiah should breach immediate support of 10,710 in the not too distant future as companies and banks have more appetite for the U.S. dollar. 

 Analysts said the higher SBI rates at the central bank's weekly auction reflected the authorities' effort to drain liquidity from the market and hence indirectly discourage the dollar buying. The rate on one-month SBIs rose to 15.79 percent from 15.58 percent at Wednesday's auction. 

 They added hopes for the IMF to approve Indonesia's reform programme and disburse a stalled $400 million loan would remove a key risk element for the rupiah. 

 A mission from the IMF will visit Jakarta as early as next week to review Indonesia's programme, a Japanese government official said. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht trod water cautiously, caught between strong corporate demand for the dollar and fears of central bank intervention. 

 The central bank said it had dealt with the baht's recent weakness, using both spot and forward market mechanisms. 

 The currency also drew mild support from news Thailand had posted a trade surplus of about $700 million in March. 

 "But in the immediate term, the baht's direction would depend largely on the yen. If the yen moves toward 122-123, for example, the baht's upmove could be steep because the market is excessively long of the dollar," said a Singapore dealer. 

 Baht funding costs offshore eased, with the one-month forward rate dipping to 35/65 satang per dollar from 60/70 satang in the morning. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR The Sing dollar tracked the higher yen and hit session highs of 1.8060, repairing most of the damage done by Monday's fall to decade lows of 1.8230. 

 Some cited speculation of capital inflows on talk a planned sale of Singapore's number two cellular operator Mobile One was attracting foreign operators. 

 Industry sources said companies expressing interest in M1 included Britain's Vodafone Group and Australia's Telestra Corp . 

 They estimate M1, a mobile phone arm of Keppel Telecommunications and Transportation , could be valued at between S$2-3 billion. 

 But dealers said the rise would be short-lived as banks and companies were looking to buy dollars on dips at around 1.8050. Analysts are also less sanguine about the outlook of the Sing dollar given slowing electronics exports and the deteriorating economic situation overall. 

 Salomon Smith Barney cut its three-month Sing dollar forecast to S$1.83 from S$1.74. 

 The government is due to release a revised forecast for growth in 2001 and a preliminary first quarter growth figure on April 10. The government currently estimates the economy would grow 5-7 percent in 2001. 

 Salomon downgraded Singapore's growth forecast for 2001 to 5.0 percent from 5.3 percent. Analysts said lower-than-expected figures would certainly bring the dollar/Sing back to above 1.8150. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso touched a low of 50.29 before finishing onshore trading little changed from its Wednesday close of 50.16. 

 Dealers in Manila said the peso traded in a tight range for most of the day helped by a steadier baht and a firmer yen. But the upside was capped by reluctance to unwind dollar longs on wariness about the near-term regional outlook. 

 The central bank said it was not in the market to support the peso and predicted the currency would not fall to 52 per dollar, though it saw volatility for the next two to three months. 

 It central bank decided not to cut overnight interest rates at its weekly policy meeting despite flat inflation growth from February to March. March inflation was an expected 6.7 percent. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 No trading was reported in the Taiwan dollar offshore non-deliverable forward market with financial markets in Taipei closed for the Ching Ming holiday. Trade will resume on Friday. 

 Dealers in Singapore said one-month NDFs were steady at 0.130/150 and three-month at 0.330/375. 

 The Taiwan dollar on Wednesday closed at a 13-week low of 32.979 against the U.S. dollar, from Tuesday's 32.90. 

 Dealers said the Taiwan dollar's direction on Friday would depend on overnight movements in the yen and U.S. equity markets. 

 Any turn of events in the continuing row between China and the U.S. over a U.S. spy plane and its detained air crew would also have an impact on sentiment. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The Korean won was bid higher in thin offshore markets with Korea's financial markets closed for a holiday. 

 Offshore dealers expected the won to recoup some lost ground when the market reopened due to a stronger yen and the central bank's remarks. 

 The central bank said in a statement on Thursday that aggressive measures were needed to stabilise the won. 

 The currency ended at a fresh 30-month low of 1,365.20 per dollar on Wednesday.

title: Thai  Central Bank  Confirms  Intervention  to Slow Baht's Slide
text:
Dow Jones Newswires 

 BANGKOK, Thailand -- Central Bank Gov. Chatu Mongol Sonakul confirmed Thursday that the Bank of Thailand intervened in the offshore market to control the baht's movement. 

 Mr. Chatu Mongol told reporters that the central bank sold "not a big amount" of dollars to slow the baht's weakening pace but not stop it. He said the move took place in the foreign exchange spot, swap and forward markets. He said the central bank also adjusted its already tight foreign-exchange trading regulations to stem speculation against the currency. He didn't elaborate. 

 "The intervention was aimed to limit the baht's volatility," Mr. Chatu Mongol said. 

 The baht slid to a 37-month low of 45.50 baht to the dollar Wednesday after central-bank officials declined to confirm market speculation that an intervention had taken place. Late Thursday in Asia, it was trading at 45.325 baht to the dollar. 

 Mr. Chatu Mongol said the central bank will continue to monitor the baht's movement and will take further action if necessary. He said that Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra also had expressed his concern over the baht's weakness and wanted it to stabilize. The government has said in the past that it's not worried by the baht's slide as it has been in line with regional weakness and would help boost slowing export growth. 

 Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak denied Wednesday that the central bank had intervened in the foreign exchange market, adding that there was no reason to worry for the baht's weakness. 

 But traders said there had been speculation in the market that the central bank sold dollars in London trading late Tuesday after the baht hit a low of 45.45 and probably again Wednesday when it hit its new 37-month low of 45.50. 

 The central bank also appeared to tighten liquidity in the offshore market where implied foreign exchange swap rates shot up to over 20%. 

 Mr. Chatu Mongol didn't appear concerned over the impact of the intervention on the central bank's foreign exchange reserves as the amount sold was small. He said that in the past, the central bank had taken advantage of a stronger baht to buy dollars for debt repayment purposes, including payments to the International Monetary Fund. The central bank repaid $400 million to the IMF in the first quarter of 2001. Its foreign-exchange reserves stood at $32.6 billion as of March 23. 

 Separately, Mr. Chatu Mongol said that commercial banks should make efforts to lower their operating cost in order to reduce lending rates and narrow the wide margin between lending and deposit rates. 

 Banks have been maintaining a wide margin of over five percentage points to compensate for the high cost of provisioning against nonperforming loans. "Once banks manage to lower their cost, lending rates should go down, but it's going to take time," Mr. Chatu Mongol said. 

 He said he would like nonperforming loans to drop to below 10% of total lending in the financial system, from 17.8% at the end of February, for commercial banks to run their business cost-effectively. 

 The government has initiated plans to set up a state asset management company that will buy 1.1 trillion baht worth of bad debt from state-owned banks and up to 250 billion baht from private sector banks.

title: Thai finmin says no c.bank baht  intervention .
text:
BANGKOK, April 4 (Reuters) - Thai Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said on Wednesday the Bank of Thailand had not intervened to support the baht. 

 "(There has been) no intervention. The central bank is already monitoring it closely and there should not be any worry," Somkid told reporters. 

 "The baht's weakness has been caused by external factors faced by the whole region. It does not suggest the Thai economy is not sound." 

 Earlier, the central bank said it could not comment on talk it intervened on Tuesday, but said it was ready to act to combat excessive baht volatility. 

 The currency has dropped to three-year lows and was quoted at 45.39/49 to the dollar at 0700 GMT.

title: Emerging  FX -Stumble on weak yen, U.S.-China woes.
text:
SINGAPORE, April 4 (Reuters) - Asian currencies buckled under a heap of negative factors, ranging from a weaker yen, U.S.-China tensions over a U.S. spy plane, and increased risk aversion towards the region as the global economy cooled on Wednesday. 

 Analysts said the dollar remained a preferred currency despite sustained losses in U.S. equities, a sharp decline in U.S. interest rates, and easing oil prices. 

 "Longer-term structural optimism for the U.S. economy triumphs for now over shorter-term cyclical pessimism with respect to the value of dollar," said a Salomon Smith Barney report. 

 It suggested that investors continue to stay long of dollars against the regional currencies. 

 The yen retained its bearish tone after a much-hyped package of emergency measures for Japan's ailing economy was delayed. Dealers said the dollar might consolidate briefly around this level before moving higher toward 127 yen. 

 The standoff between Washington and Beijing over a U.S. spy plane and its crew also kept the market nervous. 

 China has adopted a hardline, blaming the U.S. for Sunday's mid-air collision between the spy plane and a Chinese fighter over the South China Sea, demanding an apology and holding on to the 24 crew. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR The Sing dollar trailed off to lows of 1.8158 in quiet afternoon trade, with sporadic U.S. dollar bids countered by unwinding of long positions. 

 There was renewed talk of Singapore's Changi airport looking to buy Sydney Airport after the Australian government said last week it would complete the sale in the second half of 2001. The Sydney Airports Corp has said its book value is A$3.25 billion. Dealers said prospects of further capital outflows related to more M&A activities were handicapping the Sing dollar. 

 A disappointing 1.2 point dip in Singapore's Purchasing Manager's Index in March reinforced concerns about the slowing economy, analysts said. The figure represented the second month of contraction since January 1999. 

 However, one currency strategist said the downside was well supported at 1.8180 and then 1.8230, levels where she said the Monetary Authority of Singapore had intervened in London on Monday, when the Sing dollar fell to decade lows. 

 She said her calculation showed the Sing dollar nominal exchange rate was bobbing out of the policy band, which the MAS uses to manage the economy. 

 "Bears think they can pressurise the Sing forever, but stop and think about it. This is way out of the band," she said. 

 "I think the MAS is waiting for a big jump (in dollar/Sing) to intervene in the market again." 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won slid to a fresh 30-month closing low of 1,365.2 as the yen stumbled past 126, despite the Korean government's pledges to introduce measures aimed at stabilising the currency. 

 Dealers said trading was initially cautious as the market remained wary over central bank intervention. The Bank of Korea was rumoured to have intervened via state banks on Tuesday. 

 However, the won later succumbed as the dollar gained more ground on the yen and foreign investors sold a net 177.4 billion won worth of stocks. 

 Authorities said earlier they were working on a package of measures to stabilise the market. They also repeated warnings that they were watching the market closely. 

 On the offshore non-deliverable forward market, one-month dollar/won was at 1,358.5/59.5 against 1,344.5/45.5 late Tuesday and the three-month was at 1,362.5/64.5 against 1,347.3/48.3. 

 THAI BAHT The baht turned tail to hit fresh three-year lows of 45.47, despite official efforts to talk it up. 

 Local banks joined a selling spree with banks in Singapore and foreign banks in Bangkok, dealers said. 

 The market had been wary about possible intervention by the Bank of Thailand after talk circulated authorities sold U.S. dollars via a Singapore-based bank at 45.40 late on Tuesday. 

 But bears regained confidence in trouncing the baht after Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said the BOT had not intervened to support the baht. 

 He said the baht's weakness was caused by external factors and it did not suggest the Thai economy was not sound. The central bank said the baht has been too volatile versus regional currencies and that it was ready to act. 

 "They are trying to find ways to slow the pace of the decline," a currency analyst said. "They don't mind the decline. They mind the pace of the decline." 

 He said firmer offshore baht funding costs provided the only solace for the baht. The one-month forward rate stood at 50/70 satang per dollar against 50/60 earlier. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah hit a three-week low of 10,600 as demand for dollars from local corporates spiked despite sporadic intervention by Bank Indonesia. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said with an increase in the flow of bad news from the economic front, in addition to currency weakness across the region, most corporates were staying long of dollars. 

 A dealer at a European bank said the central bank pumped in about $25 million and finally succeeded in defending the 10,600 mark and propping it up to 10,560. 

 The dealer said early intervention had little impact as the bank sold dollars in small amounts, at different levels. 

 Governor Sjahril Sabirin said BI would continue intervening as the rupiah would get worse without the intervention. 

 Meanwhile chief economics minister Rizal Ramli warned the 2001 budget deficit could overshoot the target of 3.2 percent of gross domestic product to slightly over five percent. 

 The defence minister said violence could get worse if political tensions do not ease. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso eased to a low of 50.17, not seen since mid-January, as importers chased the dollar up expecting more pressure from other regional currencies in the coming days. 

 Dealers in Manila said most exporters were holding back their earnings while importers were trying to lock in their dollar needs before the peso slipped lower with the regional downturn. 

 A dealer at a U.S. bank said support for the peso was likely to come in at around 50.20 while its upside was capped at 49.80. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar tripped over the weaker yen, but resisted the 33 level thanks to wariness over central bank intervention. 

 Dealers in Singapore said the central bank was speculated to be selling dollars when the Taiwan dollar edged to 32.995. But they added the market was expected to test that level again, especially if the yen showed further weakness. 

 Outflows from foreign investors also hobbled sentiment towards the local dollar as Taiwan stocks closed lower for the fourth straight session. Foreign investors sold a net T$5.132 billion in Taiwan shares on Tuesday. 

 Taiwan was also coping with anxiety over the stand-off between the U.S. and China over a U.S. surveillance plane. China regards Taiwan as a renegade province and has been perturbed by the Bush administration's more openly pro-Taiwan stance and possible U.S. arms sales to Taiwan.

title: Thai Baht Hits New 37-Mo Low As  Intervention  Fears Ease
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht hit a fresh 37-month low against the U.S. dollar in Asian spot trade Wednesday on continued corporate dollar buying, following an easing of concerns about possible central bank intervention, traders said. 

 The U.S. dollar finished at 45.465 baht, up from THB45.285 at the Asian close Tuesday. 

 Dealers said the dollar tested THB45.50 in late afternoon trade before retreating slightly on profit-taking. 

 The U.S. unit had dropped as low as THB45.11 in London after the Asian close Tuesday, and dealers had believed it was Bank of Thailandintervening through an offshore bank. 

 After trading around THB45.20 to THB45.30 most of the morning, market participants returned to buy dollars again in the afternoon after contradictory statements by the central bank and finance minister eased fears of any central bank intervention. 

 Assistant central bank Governor Bandid Nijathavorn wouldn't comment on the reported intervention, but said the authorities stood ready to intervene if the baht weakened excessively, and that the central bank was concerned about day-to-day volatility. 

 Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak, however, said the central bank hadn't intervened in foreign exchange markets and that there was no reason to worry. 

 "The government showed that they have no clear policy on how to protect the baht. That's why the baht resumed its downward journey again in the afternoon," a local bank dealer said. 

 The current government was formed in February, and officials have yet to polish coordination of public statements with the central bank, which has long-standing monetary and foreign exchange policies and fairly well-established ways of communicating its intentions to the market. 

 Dealers expect the dollar to open between THB45.20 and THB45.60 Thursday, as profit-taking and tight liquidity in offshore foreign exchange swap markets should cap the dollar's gains. 

 Bandid reminded markets of the central bank's ability to monitor and punish violations of its restrictions on the flow of baht to offshore markets, which make it too expensive for speculators to cover short-baht positions by borrowing in offshore swap markets. 

 Dealers said the dollar will eventually resume climbing to test THB46 level due to the combined impact of regional dollar strength, a sluggish local economy, and other negative regional and local factors. 

 An ongoing Constitutional Court hearing on an anti-corruption commission's indictment of Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra for failure to disclose assets heightened market uncertainties, although resolution of the case isn't expected until late this year at the earliest. 

 Thai government bond prices ended mostly flat Wednesday as the market waited for clearer direction in long-term yields, dealers said. 

 Late selling in the December 2006 issue pushed the bid-offer range to 4.42%-4.37%, from a close Tuesday of 4.355%, but most issues closed flat. 

 The issue due December 2008 closed at a bid-offer of 4.99%-4.85%, around a last deal Tuesday of 4.88%. Wide spreads meant volume was thin. 

 Bank of Thailand canceled a 1.46 billion baht ($1=THB45.161) offering Wednesday of 20-year government bonds, and accepted only 1.33 billion baht ($1=THB45.161) in bids in a THB3 billion offering of nine-year bonds. 

 The weighted-average accepted yield for the issue maturing April 9, 2010, was 5.26%, with a bid coverage ratio of only 2.67 times. 

 The accepted yield range was 5.15% to 5.32%, in line with expectations that the central bank would reject bids to cap the range below the 5.33% secondary market closing Tuesday of the government bond due March 2011. 

 Dealers had expected insurance companies to come up with sufficient bids for the 20-year issue, but based on extrapolations from the government bond yield curve, they had also expected the central bank to reject bids if yields were closer to 7.5% than 7.0%. 

 Wednesday's auction was to be the first for the 20-year issue, so the cancellation deprived the secondary market of any guidance on the extended yield curve. The issue due 2015 was bid at 6.35% late Wednesday with no offers, compared with a last deal Tuesday of 6.20%. 

 A dealer said the market has to decide how soon it thinks the Thai economy will recover. 

 "If you assume that next year the economy will begin to recover, then banks will begin to lend again and interest rates can go higher, and people should park their money in short-term instruments," he said. Higher yields mean lower prices. 

 "But if people think, like I do, that the economy will still be sluggish next year, then rates should stay flat, excess liquidity will remain in the market and should return to long-term bonds" for higher interest earnings, he said. 

 Overnight money market interest rates dropped on increasing liquidity, which rose due to the flow of funds into short-term markets, and retention of baht in nonresident accounts as foreign net selling continues on the Thai bourse.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk  Intervention  Reported; Baht Mkt Cautious
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thailand-based dealers said Wednesday they believe the central bank sold dollars offshore at the Asian close Tuesday, to convince offshore analysts and local companies that they will oppose a weakening of the baht in excess of the regional trend. 

 A bank treasurer said the sharp movement in the dollar from its 37-month high of 45.40 baht late Tuesday to THB45.15 within 45 minutes, was due to dollar selling by an offshore bank that was probably acting on behalf of the Bank of Thailand. 

Central bank officials weren't immediately available for comment. They usually refuse to comment on alleged interventions. 

 If the authorities did act, the treasurer said, the intervention was smart, small and well-timed, complementing controls on baht outflows which restrict liquidity in offshore markets and driving the dollar to a low of of THB45.11 in London overnight. 

 "Fear that the central bank could come back in the market at that level (THB45.40) will be a good excuse for profit-taking," whenever the dollar tests resistance on Wednesday, the treasurer said. 

 The central bank has sufficient reserves - $32.6 billion as of March 23 - for limited, well-timed interventions to further tighten offshore liquidity and punish speculative excesses. 

 The bigger threat to speculators is the close monitoring of foreign exchange transactions of local banks, which enables the central bank to enforce outflow restrictions and choke off baht supply to offshore foreign exchange swap markets. 

 Whenever the baht begins to fall, demand for baht to cover short positions quickly pushes up the cost of borrowing baht in swap markets, forcing investors to buy baht directly in foreign exchange spot markets. 

 Implied annual interest rates to borrow baht through offshore swaps have been around 20% or more in recent days, making speculative trades against the currency unprofitable. 

 The U.S. dollar was trading Wednesday morning in a range of THB45.20 to THB45.30, after profit-taking reversed an early test of THB45.35. 


Dealers expect the dollar to remain in a range of THB45.10 to THB45.40
Wednesday, unless the U.S. unit begins to climb again against the
Japanese yen and the Singapore dollar.
- - 04/04/01 05-02G



Assistant central bank governor Bandid Nijathavorn told reporters
later Wednesday that the authorities stand ready to intervene if the
baht weakens inappropriately.



The central bank is concerned about day-to-day baht volatility, and
direct intervention in the market is one of the tools available to
authorities, he said. He refused to comment on the reports of
intervention late Tuesday.



Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said separately that the central
bank didn't intervene, and that he wasn't concerned about the baht.



Analysts said the central bank's alleged actions and authorities'
verbal interventions this week are designed to slow the slide in the
baht, rather than reverse it, because Thailand needs to maintain export
competitiveness with regional neighbors.



"We doubt all the (verbal intervention) signals an interest in
arresting the baht's slow slide, but rather to keep the pace measured
and deliberate," given the declining level of exports recently from last
year's levels, IDEAglobal said in a daily report Wednesday.



Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra's recent comment that the baht
shouldn't fall much further may be aimed more at restoring the
confidence of Thai exporters and importers, than at scaring away
speculators.



Since the dollar began rising sharply last month from below THB43,
Thai companies began shifting the timing of impending foreign exchange
transactions, analysts said.



"I think it's safe to say that exporters were holding back their
revenues," Kim Eng head of research Richard Henderson told Dow Jones
Newswires.



While dollar sales were delayed, importers and debtors expedited
dollar purchases to meet upcoming obligations, he said.



Bank of Thailand requires a lot of paperwork from local companies and
dealers involved in foreign exchange transactions, but a shift in the
timing of authorized deals can have a significant effect.



Firms expedited dollar sales and delayed purchases in January, after
the overwhelming victory of Thaksin's Thai Rak Thai Party in the general
elections sharply reduced political uncertainty and restored a relative
measure of confidence in economic prospects.



The dollar fell from around THB44 in December to almost THB42 in
February.
- - 04/04/01 07-19G



Analysts say exporters' failure to repatriate earnings shows up in
"errors and omissions" in the balance of payments.



Last year, exporters contributed to errors which showed up as outflows
- but were mostly inflows in the trade balance which didn't materialize
- of several hundred million dollars a month, they said.



In January, an inflow under errors and omissions was recorded at $916
million, nearly balancing outflows in the capital account of $946
million.



Henderson said corporate repatriation of dollars held offshore last
year may represent a significant percentage of those January inflows.



Capital account and error flows for March won't be reported until the
end of May, but Henderson expects to see a significant reversal to
outflows under the error category.



Meanwhile, capital account outflows to repay foreign debt will
continue to absorb current account and trade balance inflows, as
corporates issue local bonds to refinance and restructure debt burdens,
he said.



After Somkid's comments mid-afternoon Wednesday, the dollar rose
briefly to a new 37-month high of THB45.48 amid renewed local corporate
demand, before falling back to a range of THB45.40 to THB45.45.

title: Asia  Central Bank  Watch: Thailand May Opt For Weak Baht
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column 

 BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Bank of Thailand has sent a strong message to the markets with its new foreign exchange transactions reporting requirements, signaling that it won't let the Thai baht become a speculative target. 

 But it stopped short of imposing stricter rules that would dry out offshore trading in tandem with Malaysia and more recently Indonesia, as many in the market had feared. 

 The central bank's stance served a double purpose, observers say: the Bank of Thailand isn't necessarily against a weaker baht but it's excessive volatility that it wants to avoid. In fact, the central bank may be even willing to tolerate a weaker exchange rate to help stimulate the economy which is showing signs of weakness following a spate of negative data. 

 "I would expect the central bank to show more latitude from now on in dollar/baht appreciation," Simon Flint, currency strategist at the Bank of America in Singapore, said. "There seems to be less moral outcry against people selling the baht now, than there was before." 

 News that Thailand drifted to a trade deficit for the first time in 11 months in January after a 3.9% drop in exports, stirred worries that the impact of the global economic slowdown on the country would be felt earlier than expected. The government has since tried to ease such fears, promptly leaking data showing that the trend won't continue into February. 

 But Thailand's fragile economic recovery still remains vulnerable to external risks, leading analysts to believe that the central bank won't stand in the way of a weaker baht. 

 Barclays Capital notes in its latest comment that the weakening Japanese yen will increase the likelihood of Asian exports contracting for the first time since early 1999. 

 This could be particularly felt in Thailand, where "any further softening of exports is likely to result in an extension of the current ultra-loose monetary policy, whereby real deposit rates are tending to zero," Barclays said. It added that the weak yen makes the bank's year-end target for the baht of THB48 to the dollar look conservative. 

 The central bank refrained from cutting its already low 1.5% 14-day benchmark repurchase rate at its latest monetary policy board meeting earlier this month, despite fueling market expectations it might do so to stimulate growth. But it has signaled its desire to keep bond yields low by frequently intervening in the market to support bond prices that have come under pressure on increased supply. 


   Further Tightening Depends On Market's Response



The baht has slipped from about 43 baht to the dollar since March 1 -
when the central bank introduced its new disclosure regulations - to
THB43.60 to the dollar Tuesday, weighed by January's weak trade data and
the recent slide of the Japanese yen and the Indonesian rupiah.



Effective March 1, the Bank of Thailand introduced detailed disclosure
requirements on foreign exchange transactions. Banks must reveal more
details on their foreign exchange dealings such as the names of their
customers and specify the purpose of each transaction.



The new requirements were initially received with caution, briefly
curtailing trading, but soon traders worked out ways to bypass the
stringent rules by simply declaring trading as their main purpose of the
transaction, a practice that the central bank appears to allow for now.



"It's been about two weeks that the measures have been in effect and
the market appears to understand them and accept them," Bandid
Nijathaworn, central bank assistant governor, told Dow Jones Newswires.



He said that a further tightening of regulations would depend on the
market's response to the new requirements. "We'll have to give it some
more time to be able to fully assess the response of the market," he
said.



"The Bank of Thailand will let the baht move according to the market
mechanisms," Anusorn Tamajai, executive vice president at Citibank in
Thailand said. "A weaker baht is better for the economy."



Anusorn expects the baht to slide toward THB45 to the dollar over the
next three to six months, driven mainly by regional rather than domestic
factors.



The central bank so far appears comfortable with the baht's gradual
slide and feels no need to intervene. Bank of Thailand senior director,
Atchana Waiquamdee, Tuesday said that the baht has weakened on external
factors only and has been rather stable compared to other regional
currencies.



"We have no need to intervene in the market," she said.



   Domestic Risks Could Pressure The Baht



To be sure, the baht has been fairly resilient in recent days despite
volatility across the region. High expectations about the new
government's policies which is moving fast to fulfill promises to set up
a state asset management company that will bail out banks from costly
bad debt, have helped support the local currency despite adverse market
conditions.



But market participants are still concerned that the central bank
could opt for tighter foreign exchange regulations if pressure on the
baht mounted, as reflected in the recent spike of foreign exchange swap
rates.



Analysts warn that there are still risks in the domestic front that
could test the central bank's tolerance levels in the months ahead. The
new government's policies haven't been tested yet and disappointment may
follow the initial optimism if results fall below expectations.



Political uncertainty may also play a role next month when the
Constitutional Court opens a hearing against Prime Minister Thaksin
Shinawatra on charges of attempting to conceal his wealth. If found
guilty, Thaksin will be banned from politics for five years.



"There are still domestic risk factors that could lead to a 2% to 3%
appreciation of the dollar against the baht in coming months," Flint
said. "But I wouldn't expect the central bank to impose stiffer
regulations as a result of that."



-By Jenny Paris, Dow Jones Newswires; 662-266 0744;
jenny.paris@dowjones.com

title: Thai PM: Govt Not To  Intervene  In  Forex  Mkt
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thailand's Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra reiterated Thursday that the government won't intervene in the foreign exchange market to defend the baht following the release of unfavorable economic data. 

 "We cannot intervene, because if we entered the market we would lose our credibility. At this point the exchange rate is not in a dangerous situation," he told reporters. 

 He added that the recent economic data "show there is a problem that we must work hard to address and correct urgently. We are not overconfident but there is no reason to panic." 

 According to data released by the central bank Wednesday, Thai exports slipped 3.9% in January while imports surged 31.3% to drive the monthly trade balance into a $282 million deficit, the first in 11 months. 

 Thaksin added that by the middle of next month, the government will release data showing the economic situation of the country, in particular the investment situation. 

 The government is currently in the process of gathering and reviewing all the data to ensure its assessments are correct, he said. 

 The objective of the data release will be to explain to the people what the actual situation is, how it compares with the established targets and to serve as the base of coordinated government action, he added.
