title: UPDATE 1-Thai govt says will not interfere in  forex  policy.
text:
BANGKOK, Feb 26 (Reuters) - Thai Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said on Monday the new government of Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra had no policy of interfering in the central bank's exchange rate policy. 

 "The exchange rate policy is just part of the overall economic policy ... and the government has no intention of intervening," Somkid said during a parliamentary debate. 

 "This government will encourage the Bank of Thailand to apply its monetary policies and the foreign exchange policy, along with government policies to achieve the national development strategies." 

 Somkid was responding to criticism from opposition politicians that the government's policy on the exchange rate was ambiguous. 

 Thaksin told parliament his government would "pursue a foreign exchange policy that accommodates income generation for people at all levels, that benefits overall economic recovery, and that increases competitiveness of the high-local-content manufacturing sector". 

 Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda, finance minister in the previous government led by Chuan Leekpai, accused the government of ignoring market mechanisms in pursuing its foreign exchange policy. 

 "The way the forex policy is written makes it seem that this government would intervene in the Bank of Thailand's foreign exchange policy, not giving priority to market forces," Tarrin told parliament. 

 The two-day government policy debate will end on Tuesday.

title: Emerging  FX  - On higher ground, but risks lurking.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 27 (Reuters) - Asian currencies regained their footing in subdued trading late Monday, helped by Nasdaq-inspired gains in regional equities markets. 

 But analysts say consistently high oil prices, slowing external demand, still vulnerable technology stocks, and political turmoil continued to haunt regional markets. 

 A stronger Thai baht gave Southeast Asian currencies, especially the Singapore dollar, a leg up. The baht got a boost from lingering concerns over tight offshore baht liquidity and the approval of Thai Petrochemical Industry's debt restructuring plan. 

 Moves by the Bank of Thailand which amounted to indirect intervention also kept the baht firm. 

 The bank said commercial banks would have to sell to the authorities at a discount dollars obtained from one-day non-commercial dollar/baht deals made with offshore or non-resident parties. 

 Meanwhile, the yen was trying to stay above the 111 level and the euro was propped up by wariness over possible central bank intervention. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht is likely to hold its ground in the near-term after the Bank of Thailand announced it would impose a penalty on banks which extended non-commercial baht credits to offshore parties beyond the limit of 50 million baht. 

 The central bank said on Monday commercial banks would have to sell to the authorities at a discount dollars obtained from one-day non-commercial dollar/baht deals made with non-resident parties. 

 It said the instruction would be effective for November 27-29. During this period, commercial banks would have to sell to the Bank of Thailand the dollars bought through such deals at a discount of 1.20 baht per dollar. 

 "This translates roughly into a borrowing cost of around 1,000 percent per year," said a dealer in Singapore. 

 Even before the central bank made the announcement, talk of such a move had been swirling in the market all day, keeping dollar bulls at bay. 

 "But the baht retreated a bit at one point in the afternoon due to real commercial demand for dollars. However, I don't think the dollar will go far in the immediate term given the cost of carrying long dollar/baht positions now," said another dealer at a European bank in Bangkok. 

 News of creditors approving a $3.8 billion debt-restructuring plan for the country's biggest corporate defaulter Thai Petrochemical Industry barely cheered the market as its management vowed to appeal against the vote. 

 The case is seen by foreign investors as a test case for Thailand's efforts to tackle its crushing bad loans burden. 

 One-month forward rates eased marginally to 6.0/16.0 satang per dollar offshore and -13.00/-11.50. The overnight interbank rate also nudged lower to 2.75-3.00 percent. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso was buoyed by dollar remittances from Filipinos working abroad, but most investors were cautious on the eve of a Senate hearing on whether to push ahead with the impeachment trial of President Joseph Estrada or dismiss the case. 

 The government put thousands of troops on high alert on Monday to quash any violent protests that might take place. 

 "The inflows remained a key driver of the market today. But from tomorrow, politics is likely to take centrestage again," said a dealer at a U.S. bank in Singapore. 

 "Players are very cautious judging from offshore trading volumes which were fairly thin," he said. 

 But Philippine central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said on Monday he expected the peso to stabilise due to a growing belief the political problems would be resolved constitutionally. 

 The government said its external financing requirement for 2001 would total about $1.9 billion, covering an expected budget deficit of 85 billion pesos as well as other government debt servicing needs. 

 One-month non-deliverable forward peso was quoted at 49.80/49.95 per dollar while six-month NDFs were quoted at 52.60/53.20. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar slipped past 1.7600 in early trading, but later bounced back above that level as players took profit on the U.S. dollar's gains. 

 Dealers had been expecting the Monetary Authority of Singapore to cap the U.S. dollar's rise at 1.76. However, the MAS was not spotted in the market on Monday, and dealers were nonchalant about any possible intervention by the authority. 

 Dealers blamed the early weakness in the Sing dollar on the wilting yen. They later said the Sing dollar strengthened in line with the baht. 

 The Sing dollar is managed against an undisclosed trade-weighted basket of currencies, and is vulnerable to moves in regional currencies. 

 Dealers said support for the U.S. dollar was seen at 1.7550, as there was congestion around that area during mid to late October. Resistance for the U.S. dollar was expected at 1.7620, which was the intraday high on November 24. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won managed to hold onto most of its gains, though dealers said volume was thin in the wake of the currency's slump to a 13-month intraday low last week. 

 Foreign investors buying some 206.7 billion won worth of shares on Monday lifted the currency. However, the won's rise was capped around 1,180, as oil importers and offshore players were buying dollars around that level. 

 Despite Monday's gains, analysts say the won will see further losses in the longer term due to softer economic growth, weaker currencies of its main competitors Japan and Taiwan, and anxieties over government-led corporate reforms. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar barely moved from Friday's close of 32.875, ending at 32.878. 

 Dealers said month-end U.S. dollar selling by exporters kept the Taiwan dollar buoyed. However concerns over the island's slowing economy, the unresolved issue of increasing bad loans, and ongoing political turmoil were still damping sentiment. 

 As further evidence of Taiwan's economic slowdown, the top economic planning agency said the index of leading business indicators fell further in October due to the anxiety reigning in local financial markets. 

 Dealers said the market needed fresh incentives and the central bank was expected to continue defending the 33 level, if it came under fire again this week. 

 But given the dimmer economic prospects for Taiwan, analysts said the bank would have to allow more weakening in the currency. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah was steady in a thin market, with trade in some local banks cut short as Muslim dealers observed the first day of the fasting month. 

 The unit was underpinned by the firmer baht and Singapore dollar, dealers said. 

 "There is not much going on onshore. The rupiah moved in a narrow range and took its cue from the regionals," said a dealer at a European bank in Jakarta. 

 The saga over the recapitalisation and board reshuffle at the central bank remained in focus, with players awaiting parliamentary approval of changes to laws governing the bank. 

 Analysts said uncertainty over the central bank's role and leadership would only undermine the rupiah if it persisted.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Dn Late; Won,Taiwan Dlr Worst Hit
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies sagged late Thursday, with the South Korean won extending its recent inexorable decline as the market grew immune to the central bank's hackneyed verbal mediation, dealers said. 

 The New Taiwan dollar also lost some ground, falling for the ninth consecutive session to a fresh 19-month low. 

 In Southeast Asia, the Philippine peso and the Thai baht were weaker, while the Singapore dollar and the Indonesian rupiah were slightly firmer. 

 Analysts said the South Korean won and the New Taiwan dollar will continue to be undermined by the cloudy outlook for the semiconductor sector, which their economies depend on, and easing demand from the U.S., which is slowing the pace of these countries' exports. 

 And as they compete for shrinking demand for their exports, both currencies will also weaken in sync with the Japanese yen. The yen is widely expected to languish against the dollar, after Japan's political disarray drove it through the key Y110 support, analysts added. 

 "The three economies compete in exports to third markets," said Chi Lo, a senior economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Hong Kong. 

 Domestically, political uncertainties in Taipei and hiccups in South Korea's restructuring efforts will drive away foreign investors, who have already turned skittish toward emerging markets in recent months, said Lo. 

 "I do see further weakness in the short term for both the New Taiwan dollar and the Korean won," he added. "The domestic and external factors are turning against the two currencies." 

 Lo said the U.S. dollar will likely strengthen further to NT$34 against the New Taiwan dollar and 1,200 won within the next three to six months, although the South Korean currency will be more volatile. 

 Leading the descent, the won lost 1.4% to hit its lowest level in more than a year due to local and offshore dollar demand, despite market rumors of central bank intervention, which subsequently appeared unfounded, and the trite verbal mediation, dealers said. 

 The dollar finished at 1,193 won, its highest close since Nov. 2, 1999, when it ended at KRW1,193.30. The dollar closed Wednesday at KRW1,176.90. 

 Dealers were impervious to the all-too-familiar comments by the authorities about their concern over the recent fall in the won and their threat to adopt measures, if necessary, to slow down the decline. 

 "They're just giving lip service...there's no real action," said a dealer at a U.S. bank in Seoul. 

 "The only thing that will stop the won from weakening to KRW1,200, and beyond to KRW1,250, is the central bank coming in aggressively to defend the currency, but they're not doing it right now," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, a currency strategist at UBS Warburg. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency closed at a new 19-month high of NT$32.931, up from NT$32.870 Wednesday, as foreign equity funds spooked by domestic political uncertainties and a slowing economy flowed out Taipei. 

 Although the benchmark local stock index edged up 0.3% Thursday, foreign investors sold a net NT$1.40 billion on the Taiwan Stock Exchange, dealers said. 

 Reversing from its recent gains, the Philippine peso retreated Thursday on expectations that the central bank will cut its policy rates as early as Friday, during its board meeting, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 49.380 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from Wednesday's close of PHP49.120. 

 The central bank has said it is too early to reduce overnight rates right now, but if stability in the peso continues, as the Philippine Senate begins the impeachment process against President Joseph Estrada over corruption allegations, a cut may happen sooner than later. 

 The central bank hiked overnight rates by four percentage points in mid-October to support the peso, which plunged to historic lows following allegations that President Joseph Estrada took millions of dollars in payoffs from illegal gambling syndicates and provincial tax revenues. Estrada has denied the charges. 

 After rebounding sharply in New York trading hours Wednesday, the Thai baht lost ground as tight liquidity in the forward market eased, dealers said. 

 Around 0915 GMT, the dollar was at 43.855 baht, up from the overnight low of THB43.35 Thursday. 

 Higher offshore swap premiums, which raises short-term funding costs, had recently prompted offshore players to cover their short baht positions, fueling the currency's gains. 

 Thai central bank Governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul said Thursday Bank of Thailand reserves the right to intervene in the market, but will do so as little as possible, implying that the central bank will likely tolerate the baht's current levels. 

 Bucking the region's weakness, the Indonesian rupiah was slightly higher on dollar long-liquidation, dealers said. 

 The dollar slipped to 9,410 rupiah from IDR9,450 late Wednesday. 

 Thanks to the rupiah, the Singapore dollar was firmer at S$1.7548 against its U.S. counterpart, compared with S$1.7564 late Wednesday.

 BANGKOK (Dow Jones)--Thai central bank Governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul told reporters Thursday that Bank of Thailand reserves the right to intervene on behalf of the baht, but will do so as little as possible. 

 Chatu Mongol wouldn't comment on whether the central bank has been active recently, but Deputy Governor Pakorn Malakul Na Ayudhya said Wednesday that there has been no intervention during the baht's recovery in recent days. 

 Chatu Mongol said that the central bank will keep its tight regulations against foreign exchange movements to fend off possible speculation against the baht. 

 "We tighten regulations every day and we'll keep monitoring the market for unusual movements," he said, without elaborating whether tighter controls were being considered. 

 Speaking earlier at a business luncheon, Chatu Mongol called on the next government to ensure the central bank's independence in conducting monetary policy. 

 He said that unless the central bank was granted full independence and reported to parliament and not the government, its ability to stabilize the economy would be restricted. 

 "The role of the central bank in helping to keep the economy stable will no longer be possible soon," he warned. 

 He said independence wouldn't mean that monetary policy would be in contrast with the government's economic policies. 

 "These two policies must be intertwined," he said. 

 A bill on the central bank's independence is pending parliamentary approval and will have to be examined by the new parliament that will emerge from general elections Jan. 6.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Mum On Reports Of Suspected  Intervention
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thailand's central bank Thursday declined to comment whether it intervened in the foreign exchange market to support the weakening baht. 

 In response to Dow Jones Newswires' question on reports that central bank intervention was suspected late Wednesday, Assistant Governor Bandid Nijtavorn said: "It is the Bank of Thailand policy that we don't comment on currency on a daily basis. We also never comment on our operations." 

 The Bangkok Post, a Thai daily, Thursday reported there has been market speculation of "heavy intervention" by the central bank, which might have been behind the baht's significant rebound against the dollar in late trading Wednesday after the local market closed. 

 The baht hit a high at THB43.35 to the dollar in New York overnight, compared with THB43.78 at the Asian close Wednesday. It was a sharp recovery from a 32-month low at THB44.34 to the dollar reached Monday. 

 Dealers said the baht's sudden rebound was due to an offshore baht liquidity squeeze, which pushed offshore swap premiums higher, thus making it costlier to hold the dollar. 

 Bandid noted that the central bank maintains its current regulations on foreign exchange trading, and refused to say whether it planned to tighten its regulations further or ban offshore baht trading, as reported in the Bangkok Post. 

 Effective Nov. 1, the central bank has required investors to submit detailed information on foreign exchange transactions.

title: Emerging  FX  - Regionals drift within weak ranges.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were a mixed 

 bag late on Wednesday, mostly holding their ground within 

 recent weak trading ranges. 

     Dealers said fear of intervention in Thailand and Korea and 

 a holiday in Indonesia and an off-day in Singapore on Thursday 

 kept activity and movement in the region's foreign exchange

 markets subdued. 

 But the peso plumbed a new all-time low as the political 

 turmoil amid impeachment proceedings against President Joseph 

 Estrada kept sentiment bearish. 

 Analysts said lingering worries about U.S. tech stocks, an 

 expected slow down in global growth and high oil prices were 

 likely to keep regionals under pressure. 

 "Even if there is a soft landing in the U.S. and the Fed 

 keeps interest rates unchanged till the end of the year, there 

 will be problems," a currency analyst at a European bank said. 

 He said global growth was likely to peak, Japan's growth 

 was likely to remain positive but weak and Europe was likely to 

 raise interest rates to stem inflation and defend the euro. 

     He said oil prices would eventually come down but not 

 before the middle of next year. 

     "The scenario represents a bearish outlook for growth and 

 exports and further easing of most of the currencies in the 

 region," he said. 


    The euro	  fell to a record low against the dollar as



the market overcame its fears of intervention in the absence



of



supportive statements from the Group of 20 meeting in Canada.



The yen slipped after a firm Tokyo start on a



statement from U.S. Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers



reiterating long-standing U.S. support for a strong dollar.



Oil prices were firmly entrenched above $33 a barrel as key



U.S. oil data increased the fear of a crunch in winter heating



oil supplies.



THAI BAHT



The baht see-sawed as the market was caught in a tug of war



between Bangkok-based players taking profit on the dollar's



recent gains and Singapore-based dealers squaring their



positions before a holiday on Thursday.



A dealer at a local bank in Singapore said there was heavy



dollar-selling at the beginning of the session, but that turned



around when the dollar was deemed as being oversold. "We still



prefer to go long on dollars," he said.



Dealers in Bangkok said the market generally ignored



comments by the Thai Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai and local



banks were spotted taking profit on the dollar around 43.70.



The prime minister told Reuters earlier the level of the



baht should be determined by the market. Separately, he said he



wasn't too concerned with the recent baht weakness and still



expected strong exports growth.



     Analysts say the economy may actually benefit from a



weaker baht as it is a boon for exports.



    While the dollar has been finding it difficult to



convincingly break the 44 baht level - a technically



significant level - many analysts and dealers expect it to hit



44.50 in the next month. Investors view the baht as a proxy for



the less liquid rupiah and peso. Moreover, the low interest



rates in Thailand make the baht an attractive funding play for



offshore investors.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah barely budged as markets in Jakarta were closed



due to a public holiday.



Given Indonesia's changeable politics, local companies have



been dominating that market, as offshore players with little



appetite for risk continue to avoid it.



Volumes in both the offshore and onshore markets have been



razor-thin and with little bullish news coming out of



Indonesia, most analysts forecast further downside for the



rupiah.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso slipped to a record low of 49.80 to the dollar as



political uncertainty surrounding the impeachment proceedings



against Estrada kept sentiments bearish.


Central bank governor, Rafael Buenaventura, confirmed the



bank intervened to support the currency, but he declined to



provide details.



    Dealers said the central bank started selling dollars soon



after the peso slipped in early trade.



    A currency analyst said Buenaventura's statement on Tuesday



that the central bank did not plan a rate hike for now could



have contributed to the early fall.



    KOREAN WON	   -2



    The won traded within a tight range in thin trading on the



back of remarks by Finance Minister Jin Nyum that the



government would limit the downside of the currency.



    But dealers said the impact of the central bank's verbal


intervention to smooth the won's slide would not work for long.



    They said worries about the Nasdaq coming off, fears of



escalation in the Middle East tension pushing up oil prices and



the outflow of foreign funds from equities was likely to hamper



the recovery of the won.



    The benchmark KOSPI	   closed 0.50 percent lower at



542.33.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR	



    The Taiwan dollar was softer against the dollar, as the



U.S. currency found favour in the spot and non deliverable



forward (NDF) market.



    Mohktar Hassan, a currency analyst at research house IFR



Asian Eye said the Taiwan dollar's trading trend has been to



open strong and end soft against the dollar with opening levels



supported by central bank selling of dollars.



    A 1.78-percent rise in the key Taiwan stock index on



Wednesday did little to support the Taiwan dollar.



    Instead, active buying of the U.S. dollar in the NDF market



and demand for the U.S. dollar for debt repayments pushed the



Taiwan dollar lower.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The baht stole the limelight away from the Singapore



dollar, which shuffled along a narrow range in quiet trading,



dealers said.



    A dealer at a European bank noted that activity only picked



up in the afternoon, when London-based players bought U.S.



dollars around S$1.7525/30.



    The Sing dollar has followed regional currencies lower in



the past few sessions, hurt by regional sentiment.



    Moreover, the Sing dollar is managed in a trade-weighted



basket so it is affected by weakness in the euro and yen, which



carry greater weightage in that basket.



    Dealers also said weakness in the euro would drag down the



Sing dollar in overnight trading.

title: Thai Baht Ends Up; Profit-Taking After Baht Support Holds
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended higher against the dollar Tuesday as investors took profits and unwound long-dollar positions after failing to breach resistance at 44.20 baht, and the central bank verbally intervened in support of the baht, dealers said. 

 The dollar finished at 43.845 baht, down from THB43.99 late in offshore Asian trade Monday. Thai markets were closed for a public holiday Monday. 

 Offshore investors took advantage of the central bank's absence Monday to push the dollar past THB44 for the first time since June 1998, but when a test of resistance failed at a high of THB44.17 Tuesday, long-dollar investors took profits and local exporters joined in the selling. 

 A dealer at a foreign bank said the dollar is still very strong against global currencies generally, but the current market exchange rate already reflects many of the negative factors weighing on the baht - from political uncertainty ahead of general elections expected between Dec. 16 and Jan. 6, to constraints on growth from high oil prices and slow progress in restructuring nonperforming loans. 

 The dollar should open Wednesday in a range of THB43.60 to THB44, but key support and resistance will be THB43.50 and THB44.20, respectively, he said. 

 Bandid Nijathaworn, Bank of Thailand's spokesman, said he was "concerned" by baht weakness, although it was due mainly to dollar strength. 

 He said the central bank was monitoring the market and it had noticed active volume offshore, especially in short-term transactions. 

 Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda and his deputy Pisit Leeahtam said separately Tuesday that the central bank should continue to monitor the market and act to reduce speculative or unusual activity if possible. 

 Dealers said they suspected rumors that the central bank was active in the market near the high were untrue. They believed that the intervention was purely verbal. 

 Analysts say Bank of Thailand is very unlikely to waste any of its reserves fighting the market, but it can - at relatively low cost - engineer short-term shortages of baht in offshore swap markets, which can hurt speculators by raising the costs of covering or maintaining long-dollar positions. 

 Government bond prices ended lower in light volume Tuesday, compared with closing prices Friday, dealers said. 

 A few foreign banks and funds did some panic selling early Tuesday when the market reopened after the Monday holiday, due to the baht's fall over the long weekend. 

 Buying by local banks in the afternoon helped bring prices off lows in thin volume. 

 The issue due 2006 closed at a yield of 4.57%, off a high of 4.60% but up from 4.52% last week. Yields move in the opposite direction to prices. 

 The 2008 issue closed at 5.43%, off a high of 5.45% but up from 5.36% Friday. The 2011 issue finished at 6.13%, off a high of 6.16% but up from 6.07%. 

 Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda said the government will issue THB20 billion worth of savings bonds to the public, of which THB10 billion will be issued this quarter. This is to help finance a planned budget deficit of THB105 billion in the year to Sept. 30, 2001. 

 Dealers said foreign banks won't be returning to buy in the bond market until they know more about the government's issuance plans, and about who will be running the finance ministry after elections expected in December or January. 

 They believe that at least THB50 billion worth of regular government bonds should be issued to help finance the deficit, in addition to the savings bonds. 

 The finance ministry hasn't announced its plans yet, but another THB200 billion could be issued to cover losses of the state rescue fund, the Financial Institutions Development Fund, and another THB100 billion to refinance maturing issues. 

 The overnight interbank interest rate closed slightly higher as banks withheld funds at the beginning of a new biweekly reserve period, seeking higher yields. 

 Flush liquidity kept the implied tomorrow-next yield in the onshore swap market relatively flat at around 3%. 

 The overnight repurchase market rate closed down slightly from the Friday close, which was abnormally high due to demand from a foreign bank which was caught short late in the day when volume was very thin.

title: Offshore players push Thai baht near key support.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 23 (Reuters) - The Thai baht slid in thin offshore trade on Monday and dealers said the market appeared to be trying to test the key support level of 44.00 to the dollar, which has not been seen since June 1998. 

 Thai financial markets were closed for a holiday on Monday, limiting volume in the baht but also making offshore players bolder about pushing the currency lower. 

 "As the onshore markets are closed, offshore players are trying to speculate. They may try to push it beyond 44 some time later today," a dealer in Singapore said. 

 The baht was quoted at 43.77/82 per dollar at 0451 GMT in Singapore against levels of around 43.48 late on Friday. It hit a low of 43.90 on Wednesday. 

 The dealer said most offshore players had stayed on the sidelines on Friday after the Thai central bank said it was prepared to intervene if the market became too volatile. 

 But Bank of Thailand Assistant Governor Chettavee Charoenpitaks also said on Thursday he did not expect the baht to fall to 44 per dollar. Dealers said this had given the market a target. 

 Technically, the dollar is also expected to struggle near 44.00 as it has not firmed above that level since March 1998, when it was in a steep downtrend from an all-time high of 56.90 baht in January 1998. 

 Dealers said the central bank comments and stop-loss dollar orders linked to the expiry on Thursday of dollar/baht option positions helped keep some pressure off the baht on Friday. 

 But offshore players were spotted buying dollars at 43.60 baht before the central bank comments. 

 "Some of the offshore players were buying dollars at 43.60 which shows a lot of pent-up demand is there and probably that's what is happening today," the dealer said. 

 Mokhtar Hassan, regional currency analyst at IFR Asia Eye, said Thai authorities were unlikely to defend the baht at current levels, given the weakness of other Asian currencies including the yen, against the dollar. 

 "Technically the baht can fall to 44.40, but baht liquidity in the offshore forwards will be squeezed today because of the dollar buying and the baht should find some support due to the liquidity adjustment," Hassan said. 

 One-month offshore forwards were last quoted at -4.0/-2.5 satang/dollar against -6.0/-3.0 satang/dollar late on Friday. 

 Investors have tended to short the baht as a proxy for less liquid Asian currencies like the Philippine peso and Indonesian rupiah as Thailand's low interest rates make it a prime funding vehicle.

title: Thai  central bank  says ready to  intervene  on baht.
text:
BANGKOK, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Bank of Thailand Governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul said on Friday the central bank was ready to intervene in foreign exchange markets if the Thai baht became too volatile. 

 Chatu Mongol told reporters the current level of the baht was acceptable and made Thai businesses competitive. He said part of the reason for recent falls in the baht was speculation against the currency. 

 "If the exchange rate changes too rapidly we are ready to intervene in the market," he said. 

 The baht has been under heavy pressure in recent weeks and fell to a 28-month low of 43.90 per dollar on Wednesday. on Friday at 0410 GMT, the baht stood at 43.24/34. 

 Chatu Mongol said the central bank would keep a close eye on the baht.

 BANGKOK, Oct 20 (Reuters) - The Thai baht erased early gains and resumed its downward momentum in late Asian trade on Friday due to dollar demand from corporates and offshore parties amid the uncertainty over the Thai economic and political outlook. 

 Comments by Thailand's central bank governor about a possible intervention in the market gave short-term support to the baht, leading it up as high as 43.26 per dollar midday. 

 But by 1110 GMT, the baht was trading at 43.67/72 per dollar compared with 43.31/36 in early Asian trade. 

 Bank of Thailand Governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul said his bank was ready to intervene if the exchange rate became too volatile. He said part of the reason for recent falls in the baht was speculation against the currency. 

 "Corporates were very active in afternoon trade while offshore parties were back to buy dollars after unwinding some positions after the (central bank) comments," said a dealer at a major local bank. 

 Some dealers reported a market rumour that the central bank had intervened in the foreign exchange markets by buying baht at 43.40 but most dealers shared the view that the central bank had not yet entered the market. 

 "I didn't see any intervention in the market," said a dealer at a European bank. He added that the recent rebound was due to dollar stop-loss orders linked to an expiry on Thursday of dollar/baht options. 

 "There were some dollar sales left over from Thursday. After the options expired, there was no reason to hold dollars," the dealer said. 

 They said a foreign entity had previously hedged against investment in Thailand by buying a call option to buy dollars and sell baht at a strike price of 44 baht per dollar. 

 Dealers said the market was more cautious about trading after the verbal intervention by the central bank and before a long three-day weekend holiday in Thailand.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Monetary News Conference Delayed To 1000 GMT
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thailand's central bank said Tuesday it will delay a news conference scheduled to follow a monetary policy board meeting to 1000 GMT (6:00 a.m. EDT), after the close of local markets, to avoid any unnecessary impact on intraday prices. 

 The news conference was originally scheduled for early afternoon. 

 Analysts expect no immediate change in the central bank's low interest rate policy - which is reflected by the 1.5% 14-day repurchase market rate. 

 On Monday, Bank of Thailand reaffirmed its commitment to keeping rates low by intervening in the secondary bond market to drive the government bond yield curve lower. 

 The monetary policy board's forecast ranges for inflation are expected to rise, however, due to weakness in the baht currency and high oil prices. 

 Officials didn't give details of the meeting's results, saying only that they wanted to avoid any impact on markets. 

 Only general indications of the policy meeting's results are expected later Tuesday. 

 The new quarterly Inflation Report, containing a full range of forecasts under various scenarios and slated for approval at Tuesday's meeting, is to be released in full Oct. 24.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Tightens Its Grip As Baht Hits New Lows
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai central bank has stood idle through most of the baht's woes in recent months, at times even encouraging its slippery ride. 

 But as the currency moved to hit fresh lows, exceeding even the most bearish estimates, the Bank of Thailand appears to tighten its grip for the first time, indicating it is ready to step in and defend the baht. 

 Soon after the baht hit a 28-month low of 43.68 baht to the dollar early Friday, assistant governor Chetthavee Charoenpitaks acknowledged for the first time there could be some speculative activity in the foreign exchange market. 

 Chetthavee declined to comment whether the central bank would intervene in the market but did indicate that THB42 to the dollar was a fair value for the baht. He said that at THB43.00 to the dollar "the baht was too weak". 

 "The Bank of Thailand has the ability to intervene and it should if volatility continues," said Anusorn Tamajai, economist at Citibank in Bangkok. "For now, the baht's weakness may be still acceptable as other regional currencies are also weak, but if the baht goes beyond THB44 to the dollar, the central bank should act." 

 Anusorn said that beyond that level, the baht would trigger serious inflationary pressure. 

 However, Supavud Saicheua, economist at Merrill Lynch, said the central bank could do little other than "just talk up the baht". 

 "The intervention has began in effect but they won't do anything drastic as long as uncertainties both domestically and in the region continue," Supavud said. 

 The dollar was at THB43.55 late Friday as a political turmoil in the Philippines coupled with tension in the Middle East and rising oil prices. 

 Chetthavee said the baht shouldn't be linked with the peso since the two countries differed " both politically and economically." 


   Active Intervention Unlikely For Now



But much of the baht's weakness has little to do with regional
concerns. It is rather political uncertainty at home over general
elections expected by early January and the impact of a fresh surge in
oil prices on Thailand's fragile economic recovery that have sustained
pressure on the currency.



"Oil prices will definitely slow down economic activity, probably even
more than we anticipated, while elections keep investors on a
wait-and-see stance," Anusorn said.



Citibank already revised its 2000 gross domestic product growth
forecast to 4.2% from 4.5% previously.



Anusorn warned that the central bank should find other ways to support
the baht than raise interest rates, a move that would dampen growth
further.



Among possible actions would be either to intervene directly in the
foreign exchange market, or tighten controls for short-term speculative
capital and non-resident baht accounts, he said.



"The Philippine central bank raised rates 400 basis points and the
peso continued to slide," Anusorn said, referring to the Banko Sentral
ng Pilipinas' move Thursday to hike rates after the peso hit an all-time
low of PHP48.50 to the dollar.



The Bank of Thailand has been reluctant so far to either raise rates
or intervene in the foreign exchange market. Foreign exchange reserves
stand at a healthy US$32.1 billion but may not be sufficient if the baht
continues to weaken.



The central bank apparently wants to avoid a repeat of the futile
attempt to support the currency in the 1997 financial crisis when it
depleted its foreign exchange reserves, but did not prevent a sharp
devaluation.



For now, it has been limited to verbal intervention and stricter
regulations for foreign exchange movements. In a circular to commercial
banks, publicized Friday, the central bank said it will seek more
information on foreign exchange transactions, effective November 1.
Banks will have to provide detailed information on the purpose of the
transactions and the type of business they concern.



"Any attempt to actively support the baht would be futile," Merrill
Lynch's Supavud said. "There is no sense to do something when
uncertainties will remain unresolved even after they take action.
They'll just continue to talk up the baht."

title: Thai Baht Ends Down On Middle East Fears, Global Dlr Gains
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended sharply lower against the dollar Friday on the dollar's surge against regional and global currencies as renewed turmoil in the Middle East shattered hopes of an easing in oil prices, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 43.575 baht, up from THB43.29 at the Asian close Thursday, but off a 28-month high of THB43.70, they said. 

 The U.S. currency rose early on news of Thursday's events in the Middle East and fears that violence there could disrupt global oil supplies. 

 The dollar fell back to a low of THB43.37 around midday, however, on news that Thailand should be able to sell two more nationalized banks and after comments by a central bank official raised the prospect of intervention on behalf of the baht. 

 But a sell-off in government bonds and renewed weakness in global markets pushed the dollar higher again in the afternoon. 

 Chetthavee Charoenpitaks, assistant central bank governor, said there are signs of speculation against the baht in the foreign exchange market. 

 Bank of Thailand has a long-standing policy of intervening only to damp volatility or to raise funding costs for speculators. 

 Chetthavee declined to comment on whether the central bank plans to intervene to support the baht. 

 After the close of Bangkok markets, however, the new Bank of Thailand spokesman, Bandid Nijathaworn, said there have been no unusual movements in the foreign exchange market. 

 The baht has weakened due to concerns about the strength of the domestic economy and to the regional strength of the dollar, he said. 

 But the central bank said it will step up monitoring of foreign exchange markets by requiring new forms supplying additional information on each transaction effective Nov. 1. 

 Analysts don't expect the central bank to waste its reserves fighting the market, but the authorities may look for ways to raise funding costs by tightening liquidity offshore, without affecting a domestic low-interest rate policy. Low domestic rates are viewed as essential to support economic recovery, debt restructuring, bank earnings and recapitalization. 

 The dollar is expected to rise to the THB44 to THB45 range amid political uncertainty ahead of general elections, expected between mid-December and early January, but the country's finances are in good shape, and there are no concerns about a recurrence of the 1997 currency crisis. 

 Meanwhile, the finance ministry said HSBC Holdings Ltd. of the U.K. has agreed to terms for the sale of 75% stake in the nationalized Bangkok Metropolitan Bank. The deal should be approved by Cabinet Oct. 17. 

 A Thai group of businesses has also made a new offer for Siam City Bank PCL, and a similar deal should be arranged within two months. 

 The sales will be positive for the baht, but the good news was overwhelmed by negative sentiment. 

 Government bond prices plummeted Friday on oil prices, baht weakness and mutual fund selling to cover redemptions, dealers said. 

 A lack of bids and wide spreads between bids and offers pushed cash trading volume in government, state enterprise and corporate bonds down to about THB3.5 billion, from THB5.45 billion Thursday, dealers estimated. 

 Most yields closed 20-to-45 basis points higher.

title: Asian  currency intervention  threat remains alive.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 26 (Reuters) - Concerted intervention by leading industrialised nations to boost the ailing euro last week is giving Asian central banks a break, but analysts said it might be a matter of time before they feel the need to act on their currencies. 

 There have been signs recently, explicit or subtle, that some regional central banks might be wringing their hands over high oil prices and sliding currencies. 

Currencies across the region, which trended downward for several weeks on concerns over the impact of oil prices and the euro, rebounded slightly following Friday's surprise intervention by the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations. 

 But analysts dismissed the market reaction as knee-jerk. With sentiment for the dollar remaining strong and more people betting against Asian currencies due to political and economic uncertainty, they could soon head towards levels that would prompt the authorities to react. 

 "They might not need to be in the market at this point. But I would not rule out the possibility," said Chia Woon-Khien, chief analyst at SEB Merchant Banking in Singapore. 

 "Normally, there are three conditions that prompt central banks to act - when currencies drop below certain target levels, when the pace is out of synch with others in the region, and when domestic factors lead to speculative actions. These risks are still very prominent," she said. 

 TAIWAN AND THE PHILIPPINES 

 Taiwan's central bank, frequently in the market for smoothing operations, has been particularly vigilant in the past few weeks to support the currency which is hurt by outflows and poor sentiment brought about by uncertainty over the tech sector. 

 Last Monday alone, dealers estimated its intervention accounted for a third of the day's $689 million turnover. 

Forex dealers in the Philippines said the central bank might have spent around $250 million to $300 million during the first half of this month to defend the peso. 

 The bank says it has not been in the market since last week, but adds it does not rule out the possibility in the future. 

 BAHT'S MIXED SIGNALS 

 In Thailand, government officials have sent mixed signals to the market recently on currency intervention. 

 While one minister said the authorities might resort to short-term market intervention if excessive volatility in the baht hurt the economy, another senior minister said there was no need to prop it up. 

 Contradicting remarks notwithstanding, there have been signs the authorities are growing concerned about the macro picture. 

 Some economists forecast that if the baht fell below 43 per dollar, the government's inflation target of 2.5-3.0 percent for this year could be breached. 

 "Last week, the central bank was in the market to check for rates and monitor who's involved in major transactions. I think they were quite edgy," said a European bank dealer in Bangkok. 

 "I don't pay attention to what officials say. Before the central bank intervened in May when the baht was around 39, they had said the same thing. With political uncertainty intensifying, the intervention risk is very much there," he said. 

Thailand is expected to hold an election later this year. 

 The Bank of Thailand has adopted a hands-off policy on the baht since floating it in July 1997. But it has intervened in the market occasionally to smooth out volatility. 

 SINGAPORE'S IMPORTED INFLATION 

 Worries about potential intervention kept the Sing dollar above the key psychological 1.7500 level after briefly dipping below that mark on Friday for the first time since July 24. 

 Singapore manages its dollar against a trade-weighted basket of currencies, using the exchange rate as a tool to fight inflation in its open economy. 

 With inflation as measured by price of imported manufactured goods surging to nearly 10 percent, some analysts reckon the government might soon act to curb inflation before it reaches consumer prices. 

 "These are rates which have triggered policy actions on the currency in the past," said David Carbon, strategist at Pacific Asset Management. 

 "Authorities in recent weeks have begun reminding the public and financial markets that pre-crisis currency policies remain the order of the day, and fighting inflation with currency appreciation will be pursued as and when the need arises," Carbon said in a recent report.

title: Thai baht down, pressured by corporate dlr demand.
text:
BANGKOK, Sept 25 (Reuters) - The Thai baht came under pressure again in late Asian trade on Monday due to persistent dollar demand from corporates for debt repayment, but was still managing to hold above last week's 27-month lows. 

 Dealers said the baht's downside was limited as the market remained cautious about any possible intervention by the central bank, even though the Bank of Thailand repeated it would only intervene if the currency faced sharp volatility. 

 Assistant central bank governor Chetthavee Charoenpitaks said the baht's early gains could be attributed to the appreciation of the euro and a decision by the United States to draw on its national oil reserves. 

 Having hit a day high of 42.45 earlier on offshore dollar profit-taking, the baht was quoted at 42.65/70 to dollar at 1050 GMT. 

 "After an early rebound, corporates are bidding for dollars at every level. This is real demand as some companies are due to repay their foreign debt ahead of the end of the accounting year this month," said a dealer at major local bank. 

 Assistant central bank governor Thirachai Phuvanat naranubala said the bank's easy monetary policy had not hurt domestic consumer spending or triggered unusual capital outflows. 

 Despite mounting pressure to reconsider its low interest rate policy, Thirachai said state-owned banks would be asked to play a leading role in cutting loan rates to support the central bank's policy of lower lending rates.

title: Thai Baht Ends At New Low; Dlr Likely To Break THB43
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht fell to a fresh 27-month low against the dollar Friday as onshore corporate dollar buying persisted through rounds of offshore buying and profit-taking, and regional markets plunged on fears of a slowdown in global demand for computer chips, traders said. 

 The dollar finished near the day's highs at 42.935 baht, up from THB42.67 at the Asian close Thursday. 

 Traders said the dollar is likely to break through THB43.00 after the Bangkok close, but they expect THB43.20 to be much tougher to crack. 

 Resistance at THB43.20 should still be in place when the market reopens for the Asian day Monday, they said. 

 The Stock Exchange of Thailand Index of Thai stocks dropped 3.2% to 274.14 points, amid a regional selloff in countries with strong representation in the electronics sector. 

 Some dealers said a warning of lower third-quarter gross margins by Intel Corp. (INTC) of the U.S. may be due to company-specific problems, rather than signifying a drop in global demand for chips. 

 But the gloom in equities only boosted the strength of the dollar's rise against regional currencies. 

 Almost all analysts expect the dollar to reach at least THB43.80, and possibly push past THB44 in the coming months, but many expect the baht to stage a recovery next year after the formation of a new government. Thai general elections are expected sometime between late November and January. 

 Foreign debt repayment by Thai state enterprises and corporates ahead of the end of the fiscal year and the Japanese half-year has stoked dollar demand, along with frantic hedging against further depreciation in the baht as the dollar threatens to continue climbing against all regional currencies. 

 Thailand's fiscal year ends Sept. 30. 

 The government expects the situation to improve somewhat next month, when the pace of debt repayment eases, but investment inflows aren't expected to resume in strength until investors get a look at the new government. 

Central bank Governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul said Friday, however, that an agreement should be signed with the U.K.'s HSBC Holdings for the sale of the nationalized Bangkok Metropolitan Bank after he returns from abroad Oct. 6. 

 Bank of Thailand and other officials have begun verbally intervening in the foreign exchange market, but the central bank isn't expected to spend any foreign reserves unless the dollar reaches THB44, or begins to move too quickly on any given day. 

 Money market interest rates and implied yields in foreign exchange swap markets were flat or even eased slightly, amid flush liquidity both onshore and offshore. 

 The baht's weakness did cause offshore cross-currency interest rate swaps to firm slightly, however, and they are expected to rise about 10 basis points next week.

title: FX  Asia:Thai Baht Gets No Support In Slippery Road Ahead
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht has hit a fresh bout of weakness in recent days as worries over high oil prices peak and many analysts anticipate a further downside ahead as little support is offered from authorities. 

 Thailand's high exposure in oil prices and growing uncertainty over the coming general elections have been behind the latest move that led the baht to a fresh 25-month low early Tuesday of 42.33 baht to the dollar. 

 The dollar's strength and the markets' risk aversion as they are looking to hedge against a further rise in oil prices have taken their toll on most regional currencies. But the baht appears to have taken the worst beating recently, outweighing even such turbulent peers as Indonesia's rupiah and the Philippine peso. 

 "The market is now betting that the baht will continue to weaken and could soon break the next support level which is at THB42.50," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, currency strategist at UBS Warburg in Singapore. 

 Most analysts see the dollar around THB42 to THB43 by year end, although some expect the dollar to break the THB43 level as early as next week. Dollar buying by local importers for debt repayment and position squaring by Japanese players at the end of their six-month accounting period at the end of September will be the trigger, traders said. 

 But analysts feel it's more "than just the external debt story" behind the baht's weakness." 

 A number of factors are working against the embattled currency. Thailand's economy has a large exposure in oil prices, the baht's interest rate differential to the dollar is larger than in the rest of the region and signals over the outcome of upcoming general elections haven't been positive so far. The currency's offshore liquidity also offers scope for speculation. 


   Markets Puzzled By Authorities Stance



Authorities have done little to help the baht recover, often appearing
to encourage its weakness.



"The central bank has been giving out conflicting signals as to what
its intentions are," Mohi-uddin said. "The markets look to the central
bank for direction and get confusion."



The Bank of Thailand has so far refrained from intervention,
indicating it's comfortable with the current baht levels. However,
central bank governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul recently gave his first hint
that action might be on the cards, saying that "the central bank
reserved the right to intervene."



The government has been equally puzzling. Days after saying that the
"baht's weakness was a concern" that needed to be discussed with the
central bank, deputy prime minister Supachai Panitchpakdi changed his
tune. He said Tuesday that intervention was unnecessary as the baht
shouldn't be stronger than its regional peers. He said the weak baht
would benefit exports, still the country's main engine for economic
growth.



However, the market believes that authorities would be uncomfortable
with the baht around THB42.50 to the dollar which could prove a
significant psychological barrier.



"I don't expect the dollar to go easily past THB42.50 in the short
term," said Mark Boyne, Treasurer at Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp.
in Bangkok.



Boyne said that elections will determine the currency's course in the
longer run but refused to speculate on the baht's levels after the vote
takes place, probably late this year.



"It will depend not only on the election outcome, but also how
smoothly the election process will go," he said.



Barclays Capital believes that its year-end target of THB43 to the
dollar might be overshot and is looking for the dollar to soar to THB48
in 2001 as high oil prices will start trimming economic growth.



The market shrugged off better-than-expected gross domestic product
data for the second quarter released Monday as GDP growth is still
expected to slow in the second half of the year due to the oil prices
and the elections, making the government's 5% target optimistic.



"Thailand is vulnerable to higher oil prices... and political risk is
growing ahead of general elections," Barclays said in its latest report.



It said that with the opposition Thai Rak Thai party looking more and
more certain to win the vote, fiscal loosening seems unavoidable. The
new government could also find itself at odds with the central bank,
should it want to increase a maximum 3.5% core inflation target, as Thai
Rak Thai has indicated.



"Either way, the election period is baht-negative," Barclays said.

title: Thai Baht Ends At 25-Month Low On Regional Woes
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht finished at a new 25-month low Monday as the dollar climbed against regional and global emerging market currencies, dealers said. 

 Local importers and debtors joined offshore speculators in buying dollars, pushing the greenback past psychological resistance of 42 baht to finish at THB42.22, up from THB41.90 at Friday's Asian close. 

 News of higher-than-expected second-quarter gross domestic product growth of 6.6% on year, well above a consensus forecast of 5.5%, had no effect on the market amid the overwhelmingly negative sentiment in regional markets. 

 Bank of America said in a daily note that it expects the dollar to hit THB42.50 in the near term. 

 But a foreign bank dealer said heavy local dollar buying over the last two weeks is beginning to effect short-term interest rates and liquidity. 

 Unless there are major moves in other regional markets, therefore, the dollar should be capped at THB42.30 on Tuesday, he said, with support at THB42.00. 

 Deputy Premier Supachai Panitchpakdi said Monday that baht weakness is cyclical rather than structural, due to U.S. dollar strength and Thai foreign debt repayment. 

 Many research houses agree, forecasting a recovery in the baht next year after hitting a low later this year of THB43 or THB44, when investment inflows return after a new government is formed following elections expected late this year. 

 The National Economic & Social Development Board, or NESDB, which released the GDP data, said it believes the central bank will be forced to intervene if the dollar reaches THB43. 

 Bank of Thailand said Friday it reserves the right to intervene, but saw no need as of last week's levels. 

 Meanwhile, short-term money market interest rates rose due to heavy local dollar buying, but only slightly, given generally flush liquidity. 

 The overnight repurchase market interest fell off highs in the afternoon session, reportedly on central bank intervention. 

 Implied interest rates in the onshore swap market rose for terms of up to three months, but longer terms were inactive. 

 Several commercial banks joined a continuing round of interest rate cuts, in line with central bank calls for lower lending rates. 

 But Supachai warned that low deposit rates were hurting domestic consumption. Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda said economic ministers would consider the commercial bank interest rate spread and several related issues next week.

text:

title: Thai Baht Ends Up On Indonesian Rupiah Strength
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended higher Thursday as the Indonesian rupiah's surge to a two-month high outweighed news of the conviction of a key Thai ruling party member on corruption charges, traders said. 

 "There is a very strong correlation between the baht and the rupiah, otherwise we could have seen pressure on the baht today," one trader said. 

 The rupiah rose as Indonesian President Abdurrahman Wahid moved to appease the hostile Indonesian parliament by handing day-to-day operations to Vice President Megawati Sukarnoputri. 

 News the constitutional court Thursday found former interior minister Sanan Kachornprasart, secretary-general of the ruling Democrat Party, guilty of concealing his wealth and barred him from office for five years hurt stock prices.  Traders said Sanan's conviction could prove harmful for the Democrats ahead of national elections by the end of the year. The conviction could push the dollar back above the key psychological barrier of THB41.00, they added. 

 However, central bank governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul said in an interview with Dow Jones Newswires Thursday he is comfortable with the baht's current trading range as the currency's recent weakness is helping high export growth rates. 

 Sonakul said the central bank will keep its low interest rate policy to boost growth and accelerate debt restructuring although he acknowledged the pace of bad loan reduction has been slow. 

 He dismissed recent media reports that the Bank of Thailand intervened in the foreign exchange market to prop up the baht from a 10-year low in late July but didn't rule out intervention in the future, if necessary. 

 Short-term money market rates were flat to lower led by slightly lower onshore swap rates and flush liquidity, traders said.

title: WEEK AHEAD-Bearish baht, Nasdaq woes bode ill for Thai stocks.
text:
BANGKOK, July 30 (Reuters) - Thai stocks hobbling along at 

 21-month lows can expect little help from the country's 

 battered currency this week, especially after the Nasdaq's 

 recent losses, analysts said. 

     Baht bearishness returned on Friday, driving the unit 

 towards fresh 10-month lows of around 41.40 to the dollar after 

 the central bank said it would intervene in the market only in 

 cases of excessive volatility. 

     "The policy of the Bank of Thailand since we started the 

 float is to leave the exchange rate to the market to 

 determine," said Bank of Thailand deputy governor Tanya 

 Sirivedhin. 

     "We would not intervene unless there were signs that there 

 is really some excessive volatility taking place," she said on 

 the margins of a regional central bank conference in Singapore. 

Currency dealers took that, and other recent official 

 comments, as signs the government favoured a softer baht and 

 low interest-rates to help boost Thailand's export-led 

 recovery. 

     That spelt bad news for equities, with foreign investors 

 seen likely to withdraw yet more money from the Thai market to 

 protect the hard-currency value of portfolios, analysts said. 

     SOME IMPACT LIKELY FROM NASDAQ 

     Added to this, some analysts said investors were likely to 

 sell high-tech stocks after the technology-packed Nasdaq 

 composite index plunged 4.66 percent on Friday to 3,663, as 

 news of strong U.S. economic growth raised the odds of interest 

 rate increases. For the week, the Nasdaq fell 10.5 percent. 

     "The sharp fall in Nasdaq will impact our market, there 

 could be some selling in high-tech and telecoms stocks," said 

 Thanawat Patchimkul, strategist for DBS Thai Danu Securities. 

     "The impact would be more of sentiment driven rather than 

 anything direct," he added. 

     The benchmark composite SET index ended Friday down 2.62 

 points or 0.89 percent at 291.60, marking a loss of 4.6 percent 

 on the week. The index has fallen sharply from a year high of 

 499.52. 

     Friday turnover was a tiny 1.5 billion baht ($36.4 million) 

 with the index in territory last seen in October 1998. 

     "On the technical side the market is also heading down and 

 therefore we have put a zero weighting on the Thai market along 

 with Indonesia and Philippines," said Kenneth Ng, head of 

 research at ING Barings Securities. 

 Ng said the zero weighting in ING's regional portfolio was 

 because Thailand's macro-economic fundamentals were not too 

 good, causing the house to cut its forecast for gross domestic 

 product growth to 5.5 percent from 5.7 percent. 

 FOREIGN FUNDS PULL OUT 

 "I see the market drifting (this) week as funds continue to 

 pull out," Ng added. 

 Foreign investors have sold a net 29.67 billion baht of 

 stocks so far this year against 3.13 billion for the whole of 

 1999. 

     Those same investors sold a net 705 million baht last week 

 against 679 million for the week ending July 21. 

     SET's breach of key psychological support of 300 points 

 last week had dealers talking of further falls ahead. 

     They put the next support at 270 with resistance at 300 and 

 then 305. 

     "The market trend is damp and I expect the market to slide 

 further, with the next rebound at around 270 points," said 

 Aekpittaya Lemkongaek, technical analyst at Capital Nomura 

 Securities. 

 Technically, the Thai market is trading in oversold 

 territory with the 14-day relative strength index of the 

 composite index standing at 14. An RSI under 30 is usually 

 considered a sign the market is oversold. 

 Market watchers said economic data due on Monday was 

 unlikely to have much impact although it might highlight the 

 overall trend for economic recovery. 

 "The economic data will show that the recovery of the Thai 

 economy is not in jeopardy," said David Loomis, head of 

 research at Nava Vickers Ballas Securities. 

 He said the market was being dragged lower by worries about 

 non-performing loans in the financial sector and the baht's 

 fall.

title: Thai baht weak, c.bank buying report doubted.
text:
BANGKOK, July 28 (Reuters) - The Thai baht erased the previous day's recovery in early Asian trade on Friday, testing 41.20 as dealers poured cold water on a newspaper report of central bank intervention to prop up the currency. 

 The baht traded at 41.11/41.16 per dollar at 0320 GMT, down from 40.94/40.99 late on Thursday, with dealers reporting a resumption of offshore dollar buying. 

 The baht has fallen from near 40 to the dollar in a little over a week. 

 Dealers were generally sceptical of a local newspaper report saying the Bank of Thailand had intervened in London's foreign exchange market late on Wednesday to support the rapidly depreciating currency. 

 Most dealers said there was no sign of intervention despite The Nation's report of central bank buying as the unit hit a 10-month low of 41.36. 

 "I don't think the central bank intervened in the market as we did not see any irregular volume," said a dealer at major state bank. 

 Another dealer said: "There has been no sign of speculative trading in the market. The transactions are mostly from real demand from importers and exporters. I don't think the central bank will use foreign reserves to do such things". 

 However, Standard and Poor's MMS in Singapore said in its report there was market talk that the central bank had sold modest amounts of dollars at that level on Wednesday via a bank out of Singapore. 

 "The rumour has prompted most players be more cautious and help slow down the downtrend of the baht to 42," said another dealer at major local bank. 

Central bank officials were not immediately available for comment. 

 Dealers said exporters were holding off their dollar liquidation due to anticipation that the unit might fall further. 

 Increasing the chances of the baht hitting 42 was market thinking the Thai government and the central bank preferred a weaker baht to help boost exports and economic recovery. 

 But some dealers said they expected short-term support at 41.20. 

 One-month dollar/baht offshore forwards eased slightly to -6.0/-4.0 satang/dollar versus -5.0/-4.0 late on while onshore forwards were unchanged at -12.50/-11.50 satang/dollar. 

 One-day interbank rates were steady at 2.0 percent and the central bank's one-day repo rate was at 1.25 percent early compared with 1.0 percent late.

title: Asia Markets-Chilled by Nasdaq, Nikkei breaches 16,000.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 28 (Reuters) - Hefty losses on the U.S. 

 Nasdaq overnight took a toll across most Asian stock markets on 

 Friday. 

     The exception was Taiwan, boosted by state fund buying. 

     Shares in Tokyo fell sharply with the benchmark Nikkei 

 average ending below key 16,000 support for the first 

 time since May 1999 as major tech issues were bruised. 

     Finance Minister Kiichi Miyazawa said he was not worried 

 about movements in the Japanese stock market but declined to 

 comment on the Nikkei's drop under 16,000. 

     Economic Planning Minister Taichi Sakaiya, however, said 

 the Bank of Japan should take into account recent falls in 

 stock prices when deciding whether it should end its zero-rate 

 policy. 

     In South Korea, the KOSPI suffered a near five percent drop 

 as foreign selling rocked blue chips SK Telecom and 

 Samsung Electronics . 

     Most Asian currencies failed to cling to Thursday's gains 

 as players opted to cover their dollar positions ahead of the 

 weekend. 

     SING DOLLAR UPSIDE LIMITED 

     The Singapore dollar was rescued from 22-month lows after 

 an official from the Monetary Authority of Singapore said on 

 Thursday it was prepared to allow a gradual appreciation of the 

currency given the country's strong fundamentals. 

     It traded comfortably off a 1.7515 trough hit on Monday but 

 analysts said the rebound was not likely to last too long. 

     Chartists said the Sing dollar could breach 1.7300 

 convincingly next week, with 1.7240 seen as a strong 

 resistance. 

     "In the immediate term, dollar/Sing is going down as charts 

 indicate it's under a downward correction here," said Eric 

 Chong, technical analyst at Standard Chartered in Singapore. 

     "But the recent (dollar/Sing) fall is a bit overdone. 

 Therefore, on a longer term view, the dollar is still on the 

 uptrend," he added. 

     On the fundamental front, any gains will be hampered by 

 lingering political uncertainty in the region, especially ahead 

 of the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR) in Indonesia where 

 President Abdurrahman Wahid will be called on to account for 

 his turbulent first year in office. 

 THAI BAHT BEARISH 

 Despite the Sing dollar's rebound, which has helped other 

 regionals, the embattled Thai baht came under renewed pressure 

 after the central bank said it would only intervene to support 

 the currency in case of excess volatility. 

 Bank of Thailand (BOT) deputy governor Tanya Sirivedhin 

 said: "We would not intervene unless there were signs that 

 there is really some excessive volatility taking place". 

 The baht erased most of Thursday's gains in early trade as 

 dealers poured cold water on a local press report the BOT had 

intervened in London markets to support it. 

     Bangkok newspaper The Nation said the central bank had 

 bought dollars as the baht hit a 10-month low of 41.36. 

     On the sidelines of a regional central bank conference in 

 Singapore, Tanya told Reuters she was unaware of any 

intervention as reported by the Nation. 

     "I've been here in Singapore so I don't know if anything 

 like that took place," she said, but added that she would be 

 rather surprised if it had. 

     The baht now looked poised to test the 41.36 level hit on 

 Wednesday as the the authorities seemed to have given a green 

 light for it to weaken further, analysts said. 

     KOREA REFORM 

     Analysts are upbeat on South Korea's economic recovery on 

 the back of strong exports and the booming high-tech sector, 

 but there are still concerns over debt-laden financial firms 

 and slowing restructuring among major conglomerates. 

 The Finance Ministry said it would ask creditors of the 

 country's second largest conglomerate Daewoo Group to 

 draw up final plans by September for reforming or selling off 

 its 12 core affiliates. 

 In a statement issued after a meeting of economic-related 

 ministers, the ministry said creditors would be asked for final 

 reform plans for dozens of non-Daewoo firms also under debt 

 workouts by the end of the year. 

 Analysts warned of the risks of slowing reform but pointed 

 out that a possible slowdown in the U.S. economy would prod the 

 government to be more aggressive. 

 "I think there's definitely a reform fatigue going on right 

 now. It's coming through because there's slight amount of 

 complacency due to the fact that the economy is so strong," 

 said Dilip Shahani, senior treasury economist at HSBC Markets 

 in Hong Kong. 

 "We believe that as the U.S. economy slows down, this 

 reform fatigue will turn into an urgency. As that urgency comes 

 up, the government will be able to push through the final 

 phases," he said.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Expected Lower Next Week
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mixed late Friday, with the Thai baht and the Philippine peso resuming their recent downtrend, heralding more weakness for these Southeast Asian units. 

 The dollar had rebounded above the 41 baht psychological resistance level, to trade at 41.225 baht around 0815 GMT, up from THB40.925 late Thursday. 

 Against the peso, the dollar had risen to PHP44.980 earlier Friday, but retreated to PHP44.860 late in the day, little changed from Thursday's close of PHP44.865. 

 The Singapore dollar continued its upward move after Thursday's strong gains, which were spurred by the Monetary Authority of Singapore's comments suggesting the local currency may be allowed to appreciate. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was marginally firmer, although it remained stuck within its recent trading range. Despite heightened political uncertainty ahead of the country's National Assembly next month, investors are hesitant to push the currency lower, with the central bank having stepped up its vigilance to deter speculation against the rupiah. 

 A 4.8% plunge in the South Korean stock market stung the won, while month-end U.S. dollar-demand from local importers helped support the New Taiwan dollar, dealers said. 

 Political uncertainties in several Southeast Asian countries, the dollar's strength against the Japanese yen and strong local corporate demand for the U.S. currency will continue to pressure Asian currencies next week, analysts said. 

 "Asian currencies will still maintain their weak tone," said Thio Chin Loo, a foreign exchange strategist at BNP Paribas. 

 Meanwhile, market participants are awaiting the release of U.S. second-quarter gross domestic product data due later Friday. "Tonight's GDP will probably put to rest fears of a hard landing," said Thio. 

 The Thai baht's rebound Thursday proved to be short-lived when the beleaguered currency - the latest target for Southeast Asian bears - fell back below the THB41 support level Friday, on dollar-demand from local corporates and offshore dollar-buying, dealers said. The Thai baht, which had been under heavy pressure since the start of the week, was pushed to a 10-month low Wednesday. 

 Amid political uncertainty ahead of Thailand's general elections later this year, many analysts expect the baht to weaken beyond THB42 to the dollar in the next few months. 

 In fact, a slide toward THB41.50 could come as early as next week, a dealer at an Asian bank said. 

 The Thai authorities' apparent tolerance for a weak baht had provided the catalyst for offshore investors to push down the baht, dealers said. 

 A Bank of Thailand official Friday denied a report that the central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market in London trading hours this week to defend the baht against speculative trade. 

 The baht's weakness is expected to continue dragging down the Philippine peso, which is already undermined by domestic political uncertainties and concerns over the government's yawning fiscal deficit. 

 In other Southeast Asian currency markets, the movements of the rupiah and the Singapore dollar were tame. 

 The dollar was at 8,935 rupiah, down slightly from IDR8,963 late Thursday. Keen dollar demand around IDR8,900 will likely keep the U.S. currency buoyed, while Indonesian state banks and offshore participants are expected to sell dollars around IDR9,150, a dealer at a U.K. bank said. 

 Against its Singapore counterpart, the U.S. currency was at S$1.7322, down from S$1.7350. Participants are still smarting from the de facto central bank's unexpected announcement Thursday it was prepared to allow a modest appreciation of the Singapore dollar in relation to the currencies of its major trading partners. 

 Elsewhere, foreign fund equity outflows on the local stock market and dollar-buying in the non-deliverable forward market dented the South Korean won, dealers said. 

 The dollar finished at 1,116.60 won, up from Thursday's close of KRW1,113.40. 

 The won, which has been outperforming its other ailing Asian counterparts in recent months, could weaken further next week with the yen's weakness and as the stock market is pressured by concerns over the health of the country's conglomerates, said Thio at BNP Paribas. If the dollar breaks KRW1,120, it is set to strengthen to KRW1,130 thereafter, she added. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency was at NT$31.050, barely changed from Thursday's close of NT$31.052.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk: Baht Down On Strong Dlr; No Abnormal Trade
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thailand's central bank reiterated Tuesday that the baht's fall to new nine-month lows is caused mainly by the U.S. dollar's rise against regional currencies, and that it hasn't seen any unreasonably speculative or abnormal activity in foreign exchange market. 

 Deputy Governor Pakorn Malakul Na Ayudhya told reporters that the baht's losses are also partly due to private sector repayment of foreign debt, which is normal at a time when the cost of funds in the domestic market is lower than in overseas markets. 

 Pakorn's comment that the central bank hasn't found any abnormal or speculative trade indicates that Bank of Thailand won't be intervening in foreign exchange markets. 

 Dealers said offshore trade in the foreign exchange spot market Tuesday may be largely speculative, but that there is no evidence in swap and forward markets of rising demand for baht to leverage the ability to set up speculative long-dollar positions. 

 Implied interest rates in offshore and onshore swap markets are flat to lower, they said. 

 At 0548 GMT (1:48 a.m. EDT), the dollar was quoted at 40.90 baht, up sharply from THB40.77 at the Asian close Monday. 

 Dealers expect an advance to THB41 Tuesday or Wednesday and possibly THB41.50 next week, amid uncertainty about the continuity of economic policies and reform efforts ahead of elections expected in the fourth quarter. 

 In support of the baht, Pakorn said the Thai currency continues to benefit from capital inflows for asset acquisition and investment in corporate recapitalizations. 

 Thailand is also running a current account surplus, although it has narrowed from a rate last year of about $1 billion a month. 

 Pakorn said U.S. authorities are unlikely to raise interest rates further, after hiking key rates six times. He said the effect of previous increases will take time, and there are indications that the U.S. economy is already slowing. 

 He didn't specify the effects expected on the Thai economy under any scenario, but the central bank has confirmed that it will maintain a low interest rate structure to support economic recovery. 

 -By Phisanu Phromchanya, Dow Jones Newswires; 662-266-0744; phisanu.phromchanya@dowjones.com

title: Thai Fin Min: Baht Weakness In Line With Yen, Regionals
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thai Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda said the baht currency's decline against the U.S. dollar Monday is line with weakness in the Japanese yen and other regional currencies. 

 Tarrin told reporters that the central bank informed him there were no irregular capital flows in and out of the country, nor any abnormal speculative activity in offshore markets. 

 Bank of Thailand has a policy of intervening in foreign exchange markets only if there are excessive or irrational speculative flows. 

 Tarrin said the selling of Thai stocks was in line with losses on the U.S. Nasdaq market Friday and regional bourses Monday. 

 Asian markets are going through a period of adjustment to the slowdown in the U.S. economy, he said. 

 As the Stock Exchange of Thailand reopens for afternoon trade, the SET Index is down 10.10 points, or 3.3%, at 295.56 points.

 Dealers expect a temporary correction back to THB40.50 before the dollar rises to THB41, possibly this week. 

 Aside from regional political uncertainty and foreign exchange market trends, the baht is weighed down by outflows of funds for repayment of foreign debt and political uncertainty ahead of elections expected in the fourth quarter.
