title: Thai Ctrl Bk: Baht Weakness Due To Regional Dlr Strength
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thailand's central bank said Tuesday recent movements in the baht exchange rate were due mainly to the strength of the dollar against regional currencies, although outflows for repayment of foreign debt and political uncertainty also contributed to weakness in the local currency. 

 Pakorn Malakul Na Ayudhya, Bank of Thailand's deputy governor for monetary policy, told a news conference that political uncertainty in Indonesia and the Philippines contributed to the regional currency weakness. 

 A "wait and see" attitude, normal among investors ahead of general elections expected in Thailand in the fourth quarter, was also contributing to the baht's weakness, he said. 

 The central bank observed "nothing abnormal" in capital outflows, much of it for repayment of foreign debt, Pakorn said. 

 Bank of Thailand has a policy to intervene in foreign exchange markets only to counter what it terms speculative, abnormal or irrational capital flows. 

 Reduction of foreign debt will be positive for the country and the currency in the long term, he added. 

 Pakorn was speaking after a meeting of the central bank's Monetary Policy Board, at which the board decided to maintain a low interest rate environment, as expected.

title: UPDATE 2-Baht wilts to 9-month lows on c.bank comments.
text:
BANGKOK, July 12 (Reuters) - The Thai baht plumbed new nine-month lows on Wednesday as the government and central bank signalled they were prepared to tolerate a sliding currency to boost exports and economic growth. 

 The embattled currency recovered some ground in afternoon trade on offshore dollar profit-taking after it managed to avoid breaking through the 40.20 level against the dollar, and a rebound in the Philippine peso also helped. 

 But analysts said the outlook was for further weakness. 

 The currency was hit in early trade after central bank governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul said the current level of the baht was acceptable and the Bank of Thailand would not intervene to prop up the currency. 

 Chatu Mongol said the Bank of Thailand would maintain its low interest rate policy, and added that the weak baht would be good for exporters. 

 By 1100 GMT, the baht was quoted at 40.03/08 to the dollar after dropping as low as 40.17 earlier. It was at its lowest levels since October 11, 1999, when it had traded at 40.30. 

 Deputy Prime Minister Supachai Panitchpakdi also said he was unconcerned about the baht's fall, adding that it would be beneficial for agricultural exports. 

 The baht breached the psychological level of 40 to the dollar on Tuesday on bearish sentiment spilling over from other regional units. The peso sank to a 30-month low on Tuesday, and the weaker tone of the rupiah also weighed on the Thai currency. 

 The baht has fallen six percent since the start of April, compared with a 21 percent decline for the rupiah and eight percent for the peso. 

 Supachai said he did not expect the baht to fall further because it was supported by strong economic fundamentals, and this gave the currency some support later in the day. 

 "There is nothing new in the central bank's policy to keep interest rates low. But Suphachai's comment on the limited downside of the baht helped boost sentiment," said a dealer at major Thai bank. 

 DOWNSIDE RISK REMAINS 

 Analysts said there were fundamental domestic factors to suggest more downside risk for the baht, however, with short-term support at 40.40/50 seen as the next target. 

 "The baht could fall beyond our 39 baht/dollar (average) forecast for the next 12 months," Merrill Lynch Phatra Securities said in its Wednesday daily note. 

 The brokerage said a recent 25-basis point cut in domestic interest rates was one factor driving the unit down, as the cut would accelerate capital outflows to repay private foreign debt. 

 The Bank of Thailand recently said Thailand's private sector owed an extra $20 billion, raising its net debt position to $56 billion from $35 billion. 

 "We understand that the BOT will tolerate a baht at 41-42 before it feels that the 3.5 percent inflation target will be breached. Given the anaemic economic recovery, the chances of inflation picking up during the next 6-12 months remain small," Merrill said.

title: Baht shouldn't fall further - Thai deputy finmin.
text:
BANGKOK, July 12 (Reuters) - Thai Deputy Finance Minister Pisit Leeahtam said on Wednesday the embattled baht should not weaken further as it was underpinned by improving fundamentals. 

 "I can assure you that the baht should not weaken further because our economic fundamentals have strengthened over the past two years. Our foreign debt has declined a lot," Pisit told reporters before speaking at a seminar. 

 He said the Ministry of Finance would not put any pressure on the central bank to intervene, despite the baht's drop to nine-month lows. "We would not ask them to do anything against the market mechanism," he said. 

 Earlier on Wednesday, Deputy Prime Minister Supachai Panitchpakdi also said the baht should not fall further.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Gov:Draft Law Delays Won't Hinder  Operations
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thai central bank Governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul said Wednesday that delays in Parliamentary approval of draft laws governing the Bank of Thailand until next year won't hinder operations. 

 Chatu Mongol told reporters on the sidelines of a seminar that the central bank is already conducting monetary policy under the framework of the draft Bank of Thailand Act. 

 Meanwhile, the combination of central bank accounts under a separate draft Currency Act won't hinder money and foreign exchange market operations, because the authorities don't have a policy to intervene aggressively, he said. 

 The current Bank of Thailand act calls for a fixed exchange rate, which was overwhelmed by market forces and scrapped in 1997. 

 The new law balances the power of the governor with the creation of a Monetary Policy Board to set policy under a flexible inflation-targeting framework, aiming for low inflation and stable financial institutions. 

 The board will hold its second meeting July 18, to consider forecasts for the economy, foreign exchange rates and the effects of high oil prices over the next two years. 

 At its first meeting last month, the board set a target range of 0% to 3.5% for core inflation, defined as consumer price index inflation minus volatile food and energy prices. 

 Under the current Currency Act, reserves backing notes and coins in circulation are kept separate from other accounts, and aren't available for other essential monetary operations. 

 Chatu Mongol said that until the draft act to modernize the central bank's accounting is approved, the central bank will have to be very careful about any decision to intervene aggressively in markets. 

 Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai said Tuesday that the Currency Act won't be placed on the Parliament's agenda during the current term, so that the government can pursue more vital legislation in the limited time remaining. 

 More than 100 opposition members of Parliament have resigned in a bid to force the government to dissolve the lower house early and hold new elections. 

 But the government has said it must first pass electoral reforms and a budget for the year beginning Oct. 1. 

 The government was under pressure from certain social and political groups to scrap the Currency Act due to a clause viewed as a bailout of rich bankers, which provides for a one-time transfer from reserves of THB132 billion plus interest to the state's rescue fund for financial institutions. 

 The fund is expected to realize losses of around THB1 trillion in the next five to ten years, which must otherwise be borne by taxpayers.

title: Thai Baht Ends Down In Line With Rupiah,Regionals; Rates  Down
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended a touch lower Thursday in line with the Indonesian rupiah, the Philippine peso and other Southeast Asian currencies, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 39.550 baht, up marginally from THB39.545 at the Asian close Wednesday. 

 Falling regional currencies were the main factor behind the baht's weakness. 

 The baht touched a new intraday low for the year at THB39.680 early Thursday before the Bangkok opening, due in part to a false report of Thai central bank comments by a news agency late Wednesday. 

 The baht regained ground in afternoon trade as offshore investors squared positions to take profit on the dollar's strength. 

 "There is no fresh market-moving news, so investors decided to take short-term profit before setting new positions," said a dealer at local bank. 

 Bank of Thailand said late Thursday that recent weakness was in line with regional currencies, and that no intervention was necessary. 

 The political situation in Thailand did contribute to baht weakness, the central bank said without elaboration. 

 Thailand's government is attempting to push electoral reforms and a budget for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1 through Parliament before calling new elections for the lower house, probably in the fourth quarter.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Flat; Likely To Be Range-Bound
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies are mostly steady early Monday, and will likely remain within tight trading bands amid caution ahead of the U.S. Federal Reserve's two-day policy meeting beginning Tuesday, dealers said. 

 While the Fed is widely anticipated to leave interest rates unchanged, some market participants have already priced in the possibility of a 25-basis-point hike, dealers said. 

 The Japanese yen's stability, after the Liberal Democratic Party-led coalition retained power in elections for Parliament's lower house Sunday, has provided little incentive for Asian currencies to snap out of their recent trading ranges, dealers said. 

 Trading in Asian currencies is expected to remain subdued as market participants are hesitant to open up new positions as the end of the half-year ends, dealers said. 

 "They will unwind or maintain what they have," a dealer at an Asian bank said. 

 The dollar's failure last week to convincingly breach key resistance levels of some Asian currencies may also push the U.S. currency to the lower end of the recent trading range in the short term, dealers said. 

 Against the Indonesian rupiah, the dollar has slipped to 8,645 rupiah around 0115 GMT (9:15 p.m. EDT), from IDR8,660 late Friday, after failing to stay above IDR8,700 late last week. The dollar will likely trade in the IDR8,600-IDR8,700 range for the rest of the day, dealers said. 

 The U.S. currency is at S$1.7323 against the Singapore dollar, up marginally from S$1.7311 late Friday, but well within its recent trading band of S$1.7300-S$1.7370. 

 The U.S. dollar is expected to trade within a narrow range of S$1.7300-S$1.7340 Monday, following unconfirmed rumors the Monetary Authority of Singapore might have intervened around S$1.7340 last Friday, dealers said.

title: Merrill sees Thai cenbank tolerating weaker baht.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 16 (Reuters) - Despite its recent rumoured interventions, Thailand's central bank is unlikely to be overly concerned about the baht's weakness as long as inflation does not overshoot its targets, Merrill Lynch said. 

 The Bank of Thailand has projected a 2.5-3.0 percent inflation rate for 2000 against 0.3 percent in 1999. 

 "Our baht forecast rests mainly on domestic inflation," said Suvavud Saicheua, head of Thailand economics at Merrill Lynch in a note to clients. 

 "As long as inflation does not exceed four percent, we believe that the Bank of Thailand can tolerate some baht weakness," he said. 

 The report said the central bank is likely to leave interest rates unchanged for the next 12 months to keep Thailand's economic recovery on track despite growing prospects for more aggressive interest rate increases in the U.S. 

 This means it will have to be more tolerant of a weaker baht. 

 "Recent Bank of Thailand intervention to push the baht back below 39 per dollar does not imply a baht target in our view. Rather, it suggests that the BOT would like to increase the cost of speculation against the baht," Supavud said. 

 "The three percent baht depreciation from 1999 would push inflation up by only 1.0-1.5 percent in our estimation...," he said, citing factors including declining food prices. 

 The baht was quoted at 39.26/31 per dollar at 0527 GMT, down some 4.6 percent from its end-1999 level of 37.45, based on Reuters Graphics data. 

 Merrill said it was sticking to its recently revised forecast of 39 baht per dollar for the fourth quarter and the rest of 2001, although occasional weakness beyond this level could not be ruled out. 

 Merrill lowered the forecast earlier this month from a previous projection of 38.00 per dollar.

title: Thai baht recovers late, outlook negative.
text:
BANGKOK, May 12 (Reuters) - The Thai baht recovered from its lowest levels in five months on Friday on dollar profit-taking by offshore parties and onshore banks. 

 But dealers said the outlook for the baht remained negative due to dollar strength against regional units amid an expectation of a possible rate hike in the U.S. on Tuesday. 

 The baht was traded at 38.83/38.86 per dollar late after having earlier hit an intraday low of 39.03. The Thai unit fell through support at 39 to hit a five-month low at 39.07 on Thursday. 

 Against the euro, the baht was at 35.0531/35.1009 late against 35.1524/35.2170 early. 

 "After the baht hit the day low of 39.03, offshore players unloaded the dollar to take profit from recent gains," said a dealer at a local bank. "They probably want to square positions ahead of the weekend." 

 Dealers said market was convinced the Bank of Thailand intervened to shore up the baht on Thursday by buying the currency at 39 to the dollar in the offshore market. 

 Tasana Rachatapo, director of the central bank's banking department, declined comment when asked whether the central bank had intervened. 

 She said the weakness of the baht was due to on a halt in dollar sales by exporters amid persistent demand from oil firms. 

 Some dealers said a decline in foreign reserves and forward currency swap contracts last week could be connected to intervention. 

 The Bank of Thailand said on Friday foreign reserves stood at $31.8 billion on May 4 against $32.1 billion on April 28. It said it had net forward foreign exchange contracts to buy Thai baht of $2.5 billion on May 4 against $2.6 billion on April 28. 

 "The central bank did not confirm or deny," said a dealer at a foreign bank. "It's obvious they did something yesterday but I do not see any such action today." 

 Dealers said a hike in global oil prices and expectations of a 50 basis point increase in U.S. rates put more pressure on local oil companies to accelerate dollar buying in recent days. 

 They said the rise in the main Thai stock index on Friday after fours days of losses gave some psychological boost to the baht despite an uncertain outlook for the equity market. 

 On Friday, the composite SET index closed up 2.71 percent at 345.67 due to a technical rebound, but it was down 9.9 percent on the week. 

 Dealers said short-term offshore swap rates declined in late trade, reflecting easing demand for the dollar, after jumping almost 30 percent on an annualised basis due to recent weakness of the baht.

 One-month dollar/baht offshore forward premiums were unchanged at 10/13 satang per dollar late and onshore at a discount of -12.50/-11.75 satang.

title: Thai Baht Ends Flat As Dollar Rally Loses Steam
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- The Thai baht ended flat in Asian spot trade Friday as the dollar's rally against regional currencies ran out of steam ahead of the weekend, dealers said. 

 Rumors that Bank of Thailand had intervened earlier in the week helped to support the baht, but dealers said they saw no signs of any direct central bank sales this week. 

 The dollar closed at 38.845 baht in Asian trading Friday, unchanged from Thursday. 

 At 0953 GMT (5:53 a.m. EDT), the dollar was slightly higher at THB38.885 in continuing London trade, but well within the THB38.75-THB39.00 range anticipated over the weekend. 

 The baht has weakened this week in line with most other regional currencies, in anticipation of a 50 basis point increase in key U.S. interest rates next week. 

 Dealers said that under the circumstances, it was extremely unlikely that the central bank would abandon a policy of nonintervention to support the baht. 

 "Do you think the central bank wants the baht stronger? I don't think so. With the yen and the Indonesian rupiah so much weaker, it would hurt the country's export competitiveness," a local dealer said. 

 He said Bank of Thailand may have acted at times, however, to help bring about the short squeezes in offshore swap markets seen this week whenever the baht started to drop too quickly. 

 Higher premiums in swap markets make it more expensive for speculators to set up or maintain long-dollar positions. 

 The central bank limits the supply of baht in offshore swap markets through controls on baht outflows. 

 Dealers said purchase of dollars with baht obtained from settlements of the sale of Thai equities helped to push the U.S. currency up during the day, but the Stock Exchange of Thailand Index recovered 2.7% to 345.67 points Friday after heavy losses earlier in the week. 

 The dollar rose briefly to a high of THB39.045, but couldn't sustain those levels. 

 Money market rates were flat to lower, in line with low onshore swap rates. 

 The central bank is able maintains high liquidity and low interest rates in domestic markets because of its controls on baht outflows.

title: Asia Markets-Pummelled by rate-driven exodus.
text:
SINGAPORE, May 11 (Reuters) - Asian markets were pummelled 

 on Thursday as expectations of an aggressive tightening in U.S. 

 interest rates continued to spin a vicious cycle, driving 

 regional stocks and currencies lower. 

     "Besides the theme of higher U.S. interest rates, the focus 

 for Asian markets right now is also very bad equity market 

 performance that's leading to portfolio outflows out of Asian 

 countries," said Thio Chin Loo, strategist at BNP Paribas 

 Group. 

     "That's putting a dampener on Asian currencies," she told 

 Reuters Television. 

     The glum sentiment also depressed bond markets, kicking 

 Asian bond spreads wider as investors fled to save-haven U.S. 

 Treasuries. 

     All regional stock markets were lower, taking their cue 

 from weaker U.S. markets overnight that saw a sell-off in tech 

 shares spill over to more interest-rate sensitive sectors like 

 banks and brokers. 

 Losses were led by Tokyo's benchmark Nikkei average which 

 tumbled more than 4.5 percent, finishing below 17,000 for the 

 first time since September. 

 Traders blamed fears of more volatility in U.S. stocks in 

 coming sessions ahead of Tuesday's rate-setting meeting of the 

 U.S. Federal Open Market Committee. 

     Spared the potential damage were Hong Kong and South Korea, 

 both closed for public holidays. 

     REGIONAL CURRENCIES SHUNNED 

     Increased hedging activity and pre-payment of foreign loans 

 by Asian companies wary of further dollar strength were also 

 weighing on regional currencies, BNP-Paribas' Thio said. 

     The dollar rallied to two-month highs above 110 yen in late 

 Asian trade, helped by the Nikkei's descent. 

     Regional currencies, some already plagued by domestic 

 concerns, were defenceless against the dollar, prompting some 

 central banks to step in. 

     A stream of dollar bids from offshore and corporate players 

 dragged the Indonesian rupiah to 8,420, its lowest level since 

 September 29. 

     Although talk of central bank intervention and sporadic 

 dollar profit-taking lifted the unit from its day low, the 

 market remained bearish. 

     The Sing dollar managed only a mild rebound amid market 

 rumours that the central bank had intervened to defend it from 

 a 13-month low. 

     THAI BAHT'S WOES PERSIST 

     Bangkok dealers said the Bank of Thailand also intervened

 in offshore foreign exchange markets to support the baht after 

 it fell through 39.00 per dollar. 

     But despite the unconfirmed action, the baht remained 

 around five-month lows, with some dealers forecasting it would 

 slip again to test next support at 39.20. 

     The 39.20 per dollar level marks the 50 percent Fibonacci 

 retracement of the dollar's September 28 to January 3 decline, 

 chartists said. 

     "There is no good reason for corporates to shoulder rising 

 costs as a result of a widening gap in global interest rates. 

 The hike in U.S. interest rates put pressure on Thai corporates 

 to rush to repay foreign debts," Anusorn Tamjai, macroeconomist 

 at Citibank in Bangkok said. 

 Dealers said denial by the Thai central bank and finance 

 minister that financial authorities intended to impose capital 

 controls gave psychological support. 

 Thai Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda and the Bank 

 of Thailand on Thursday denied rumours that they planned to 

 impose capital controls to help prevent further falls for the 

 baht. 

 KOREA SEES SCANT INFLATION THREAT 

 Korea's Finance Minister Lee Hun-jai attempted to calm 

 fears of an overheating economy, saying inflationary pressure 

 was largely absent despite expectations GDP growth would exceed 

 an originally forecast six percent this year. 

 "We are now looking for a solid real GDP growth this year, 

 most likely higher than the originally expected six percent," 

 Lee told an annual meeting of the Asia Society in Shanghai. 

     "Better still, we see no clear signs of overheating while 

 significant inflationary pressure is largely absent," he said. 

     South Korea's GDP grew 10.7 percent in 1999, which had 

 sparked market worries of a pick-up in inflation. 

     Lee said inflation this year would be within the originally 

 estimated three percent, while a strong export performance 

 would yield a continued trade surplus. 

     But worries for the economy seemed far from over as local 

 media reported the country may need an additional 42 trillion 

 won to complete financial sector restructuring by the end of 

 this year. 

 Maeil Business Newspaper quoted state-funded Korea 

 Institute of Finance as saying South Korea had already spent 86 

 trillion won since the 1997 economic crisis to clean up the 

 financial sector.

title: UPDATE 2-Dealers say Thai cenbank props up baht.
text:
BANGKOK, May 11 (Reuters) - Currency dealers said the Bank of Thailand had intervened to prop up the weakening baht on Thursday, while the stock market continued its week-long decline. 

 Dealers said baht buying by the central bank at 39 to the dollar pushed the unit back above the key support level, and by late Asian trade it had recovered to 38.88/93. 

 But it remained at five-month lows and dealers said the intervention might have only a limited impact. Several forecast the baht could slip back again to test its next support at 39.20. 

Central bank assistant governor Chetthavee Charoenpitak said he had not been told of any intervention but three dealers at major Thai banks confirmed they had seen the bank in the market. 

 "Despite the intervention, there is an attempt by offshore parties to drag the baht down and test support of 39 again," said a dealer at major Thai bank. 

 "Some exporters entered market to check the rate but most of them are waiting to take profit from recent gains of dollar at above 39." 

 Satian Tantanasarit, chief dealer at DBS Thai Danu Bank, said he expected the volatility of the baht to be reduced next week, when the U.S. Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates 50 basis points. 

 Dealers said the baht weakness was due to sustained dollar buying by offshore parties and corporates amid concerns about fund outflows and the possible U.S. rate hike. 

 RUMOUR DENIALS PROVIDE PSYCHOLOGICAL SUPPORT 

 Dealers said a denial by the Bank of Thailand and Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda that the authorities intended to impose capital controls gave psychological support. 

 Asked about the rumours, Tarrin replied: "They are wrong." 

Central bank assistant governor Chetthavee Charoenpitak told reporters the baht's weakness was in line with movements in other regional currencies and due to external factors and the stock market. 

 It was another gloomy day for stocks as investors sold telecoms, media and technology, as well as banks. 

 The benchmark composite SET index ended down 6.99 points, or 2.03 percent, at 336.54, its lowest close for 14 months. It closed at 333.28 on March 10, 1999. 

 This week alone, the SET has lost 11.43 percent, in an average daily turnover of 2.33 billion baht. 

 Dealers said continued volatility in nearly all regional and global markets had helped erode the confidence of Thai retail investors, who have joined foreign investors as sellers. 

 A stock analyst at Merrill Lynch said Thailand was now referred to as one of the "TIP" countries - Thailand, Indonesia and Philippines. "It's a sector in which there is very little interest from foreign investors," he said. 

 Its reform process needed to be speeded up if it was to get back on to the radar screens of institutional investors, he said. 

 Chartists said the next target for dollar/baht was the 39.20 level, a 50 percent Fibonacci retracement of the dollar's September 28 to January 3 decline on the daily chart. 

 "39.20 is actually the dollar resistance. It's not at this level (39.00)," said a baht trader. 

 A break beyond 39.20 would put the dollar on track for a further rise towards 39.80 baht. 

 Dealers were bearish towards the Thai unit near-term, given expectations of persistent corporate dollar demand to accelerate debt repayment ahead of the Tuesday Fed meeting. 

 "It is a story of fund movements," said Anusorn Tamjai, macro economist at Citibank in Bangkok. "Foreigners are moving their money out of the Thai market as other global markets yield more attractive returns.

 which hit their 2000 lows as flustered importers and corporate 

 players scurried to buy dollars. 

     Central banks in Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand were 

 heard intervening in the market to prop up their sliding 

currencies, but no official confirmation was available. 

     "Regional currency sales were broad-based. There's talk 

 that central banks were in the market today - Singapore, 

 Indonesia and Thailand," said Philip Wee, treasury economist at 

 Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore. 

     "The dollar offers were mostly done through offshore banks. 

 But there's no confirmation on this," he said. 

     Analysts said Asian currencies would retain their weak tone 

 in the near-term against a backdrop of continued dollar 

 strength. 


    The dollar briefly rose above the 110 yen	  barrier as



a sharp fall in Tokyo shares overshadowed confidence in Japan's



economic recovery.



    The benchmark Nikkei	   closed 4.63 percent off on



Thursday, ending below 17,000 points for the first time since



September 27, 1999.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



    A stream of dollar bids from offshore and corporate players



sent the rupiah reeling to 8,420 -- its lowest level since



September 29.



    Although talk of central bank intervention and sporadic



dollar profit-taking lifted the unit from its day low, market



sentiment remained glum.



    Dealers said any rebound could be temporary as corporate



dollar demand remained high and exporters were opting to park



their dollar receivables offshore amid political and economic



uncertainties.



THAI BAHT



The baht struggled to stand above the key 39.00 level where



the central bank was rumoured to have intervened.



Dealers said it was likely to slip back below the level



again soon due to sustained dollar demand from both offshore



and corporate players.



"If the central bank declares that it had indeed intervened


and that it hates to see the baht below 39, then market

title: UPDATE 1-Thai  central bank intervenes  to prop up baht.
text:
BANGKOK, May 11 (Reuters) - The Bank of Thailand intervened in offshore foreign exchange market to support the baht on Thursday after the Thai unit broke down through support at 39 to the dollar, dealers said. 

 The action pushed the baht back up through 39 and by 0720 GMT the currency had recovered to 38.82/85 per dollar, but was still around five-month lows near a level last seen in early December. 

 But dealers said the intervention might have only a limited impact and several forecast the Thai unit could slip back again to test next support at 39.20 per dollar. 

 "The baht bounced back within 5-10 minutes after falling to the 39. It is obvious that there must be someone intervening in the offshore market...We assume it is the central bank," said a dealer at major Thai bank. 

Central bank officials were not immediately available for comment but three other dealers at major Thai banks confirmed they had seen the central bank in the market. 

 Dealers said the baht breached key support at 39 due to sustained dollar buying by offshore parties and corporates amid concerns over fund outflows and a possible U.S. rate hike. 

 Dealers said a denial by the Thai central bank and finance minister that financial authorities intended to impose capital controls gave psychological support to the Thai unit. 

 Thai finance minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda and the Bank of Thailand on Thursday denied rumours that they planned to impose capital controls to help prevent further falls of the baht. 

Central bank assistant governor Chetthavee Charoenpitak told reporters the baht weakness, which was in line with the movements of other regional units, was due to external factors and the selling of shares in the stock market. 

 FURTHER DECLINES SEEN 

 Chartists said the next target for dollar/baht was the 39.20 level, which marked a 50 percent Fibonacci retracement of the dollar's September 28 to January 3 decline on the daily chart. 

 "39.20 is actually the dollar resistance. It's not at this level (39.00)," said a baht trader. 

 A break beyond 39.20 would put the dollar on track for a further rise towards 39.80 baht, the 62.8 percent Fibonacci retracement of its September-January dollar decline. 

 Dealers said they remained bearish on the Thai unit on expectations of persistent dollar demand from corporates to accelerate debt repayment ahead of a U.S. central bank meeting on monetary policy on Tuesday. 

 The Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise key U.S. interest rates by 50 basis points. 

 "It is a story of fund movements. Foreigners now are moving their money out of the Thai market as other global markets yield more attractive returns," said Anusorn Tamjai, macro economist at Citibank in Bangkok. 

 "There is no good reason for corporates to shoulder rising costs as a result of a widening gap in global interest rates. The hike in U.S. interest rates put pressure on Thai corporates to rush to repay foreign debts," he said. 

 Anusorn said he expected the baht to move in range of 39.00-39.50 in one-to-three month period. 

 Dealers said declines in the Thai equity market had dampened sentiment and dragged the baht lower as the market expected foreigners to continue to unload Thai shares and sell the baht. 

 Thailand's composite SET stock index closed down 1.67 percent at 337.81 at midday on Thursday, having fallen more than two percent at the opening. 

 Foreign investors have sold a net of 23.14 billion baht worth of Thai shares so far this year against net sales of 3.13 billion for the whole 1999, stock exchange data show.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk Reiterates  Forex  Non- Intervention  Policy
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thailand's central bank Thursday reiterated its policy of letting the market set the baht's level, despite continued weakness in the local unit. 

 At 0540 GMT (1:40 a.m. EDT), the dollar was at THB39.065, much higher than THB38.765 earlier Thursday. The baht hasn't closed below THB39 to the dollar for six months. 

 Despite the weakness, the central bank will continue its laissez-faire approach to the market, Chetthavee Charoenpitaks, an assistant governor, told reporters. 

 Bank of Thailand only intervenes in the market to moderate huge speculative movements in the baht, which it feels doesn't have an underlying link to real capital flows. 

 Weakness in regional currencies, notably Indonesia's rupiah, were helping pull the baht lower, Chetthavee said. 

 Offshore investors are moving quickly midday Thursday to take long dollar positions, amid concerns that the U.S. will raise rates next week, further hurting Asian currencies. 

 Thailand's lingering economic problems, including a stubbornly high level of nonperforming loans, are also hurting investor sentiment, causing a huge outflow of foreign funds from the local stock market, which is at 14-month lows.

title: Thai c. bank says no baht  intervention .
text:
BANGKOK, May 4 (Reuters) - A senior Thai central bank official said on Thursday the Bank of Thailand has not intervened in the market to shore up the baht despite the currency's setbacks this week. 

 Thirachai Phuvanat-naranubala, assistant central bank governor, told reporters the Bank of Thailand closely watched the baht's movement but it had not made any efforts to halt its retreat against the dollar. 

 "The baht has eased along with the weaker euro and yen...we have not seen any unusual foreign exchange transactions. The Bank of Thailand has not stepped in to intervene but we are closely monitoring them," he said. 

 The baht, tracking most bearish regional currencies, fell to near a five-month low of around 38.52 per dollar on Thursday from around 38.05 late last week. 

 Thirachai said Thai market players chose to retain their dollar positions this week partly in anticipation of rate hikes by the U.S. Federal Reserves later this month.

title: Thai Ctrl Bk: Won't  Intervene  In Baht Despite Weakness
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thailand's central bank said Thursday it won't intervene to support the baht despite the currency's recent weakness. 

 Teerachai Phuvanatnaranubala, a Bank of Thailand assistant governor, confirmed the central bank's policy to let the market set the baht's level. 

 "As long as the baht moves on market demand, the central bank won't intervene in the market," he told reporters. 

 Bank of Thailand only intervenes when it sees huge speculative money movements distorting fundamental capital flows. 

 In late trade, offshore investors pushed the dollar through resistance at THB38.50, its lowest level in five months. 

 The baht's weakness is due to offshore investors speculating that the U.S. Federal Reserve will hike interest rates at its next meeting May 16, Teerachai said. 

 Higher rates in the U.S. could attract funds out of Asian currencies into dollar assets, analysts say. However, most analysts see the baht higher by the year end on a strong current account surplus and rising foreign direct investment.

title: Thai Dep PM: Exports To Drive Economic Growth In 2000
text:
BANGKOK -(Dow Jones)- Thai Deputy Prime Minister Supachai Panitchpakdi said Monday that exports will remain a major driver of economic growth in 2000, but that public sector spending will cease to be much of a factor after September. 

 Supachai told a news conference after a meeting of economic ministers that it will be difficult to continue deficit fiscal spending to stimulate the economy once the current fiscal year has ended on Sept. 30, because it would cause too much of an increase in public sector debt. 

 Thailand's public sector debt rose to 36.8% of GDP as of the end of September 1999, from 15.3% three years earlier. 

 The Government Spokesman's Office said in a statement issued at the news conference that the country's total foreign debt dropped to $74.6 billion at the end of 1999 from $86.2 billion the previous year, however, as the private sector continued to pay down foreign debt. 

 Supachai said the Export-Import Bank of Thailand will continue to increase the availability of packing credits to exporters, and the government will help the private sector accelerate debt restructuring to encourage investment. 

 Economic ministers received a report Monday on previously-released gross domestic product growth estimates for 1999 and 2000, of 4.0% for both years from Bank of Thailand, and of 4.1% and 4.4%, respectively, from a state planning agency. 

 The central bank said exports grew 7% in U.S. dollar terms in 1999, and are forecast to grow 7.4% this year. 

 Supachai said economic ministers were informed that the country's trade surplus could fall to around between $3 billion and $4 billion in 2000, from around $8.5 billion last year and $10.2 billion in 1998, and that a trade deficit is possible in 2001. 

 If the trade balance is still in deficit in 2002, and public sector debt remains high, it could have a negative effect on the economy, he said. 

 Therefore, Bank of Thailand will keep a close eye on the foreign exchange rate, because if the baht gets too strong it could hurt the country's exports, he said. 

 The central bank has intervened in the foreign exchange market to keep the baht currency from getting too strong, but it hasn't distorted the market, Supachai said. 

 He gave no details, nor did he mention in what time period the intervention took place. 

 Bank of Thailand has a policy to buy dollars on weakness to boost foreign reserves and to prevent any excessive volatility. 

 Foreign reserves rose $800 million between Dec. 24 to Dec. 30, 1999, of which $500 million was accounted for by transactions with local financial institutions in foreign exchange swap markets, to boost baht liquidity in case of excess foreign demand over the New Year. 

 Bank of Thailand may have purchased up to $300 million dollars in the spot market over the period, but it normally doesn't comment on its market transactions. 

 Supachai, who is also commerce minister and is responsible for export promotion, has consistently expressed more concern about the possible negative effects of a strong baht than Finance Ministry and central bank officials. 

 -By Nitsara Srihanam; 662-266-0744; nitsara.srihanam@dowjones.com 

 Thailand's Government House confirmed in a statement released after the economic ministers meeting that the National Economic & Social Development Board's forecast trade surplus for 2000 is $6.3 billion, down from a preliminary estimate of $9.6 billion in 1999.

title: Thailand: Baht Ends Higher In Spot Mkt As Dlr Slips Vs Yen
text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--The Thai baht perked up against the dollar in spot trading Monday, buoyed by the U.S. currency's decline against the Japanese yen and the Deutsche mark. 

 The Thai currency also rose in the swap market, where investors make agreements to buy and sell dollars at specified times in the future. Swap premiums dropped amid brisk dollar-selling, dealers said. 

 'Funds are coming in, and the baht is more stable,' a dealer at the Bank of America said. 'Traders feel more confidence in the currency.' 

 At the close of trading Monday, the dollar was at 25.945 baht, down from 25.962 baht at the close of trading Friday. That indicates the central bank was buying dollars at below-market rates from Thai commercial banks, since the dollar finished outside the Bank of Thailand's intervention band of 25.95 to 25.99 baht Monday. 

 The central bank's midrate for the dollar was 25.97 baht Monday, unchanged from Friday. 

 The baht is pegged to a basket of currencies dominated by the dollar, the mark and the yen. It tends to rise whenever the U.S. currency falls against the yen and the mark. At the close of trading in Bangkok Monday, the dollar was at 123.40 yen, down from 123.45 yen in New York late Friday. The dollar was at 1.6878 marks, down from 1.6950 marks in New York late Friday. 

 Interbank rates, meanwhile, declined amid the dollar-selling. The overnight and call interbank rates closed at 9.5%, down from 10% to 10.5% Friday.

title: Thailand: Baht Ends Lower In Spot Mkt As Dlr Gains Vs Yen
text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--The Thai baht slipped against the U.S. dollar in spot trading Monday, hurt by the dollar's rise against the Japanese yen late Friday - which drove the central bank's intervention band higher. 

 But the Thai currency strengthened in the swap market, where investors make agreements to buy and sell dollars at specified times in the future. Swap premiums declined amid dollar-buying, dealers said.

title: Thailand shows Asia needs banking upgrade - experts.
text:
HONG KONG, March 7 (Reuter) - Thailand's banking sector crisis brought repeated calls for an upgrade of Asia's immature financial infrastructure at an International Monetary Fund-Hong Kong Monetary Authority meeting on Friday. 

 "Asia needs a stronger, more dynamic financial infrastructure," IMF managing director Michel Camdessus told the conference on financial integration in Asia. 

 The region's banking system has not kept pace with its economic development, and the speedy pace of economic reform has created an urgent need for an overhaul, delegates said. 

 "In many countries, in Asia and elsewhere, prudential regulation and supervision have not kept pace with the new complexities of the banking business," Camdessus said. 

 "If left unaddressed, this gap could pose dangers for domestic and external stability. Indeed, all countries must be vigilant about the strength of their banking systems, so that the monetary authorities can tighten policy when needed, without fear of aggravating banking sector problems." 

 Asset quality problems forced Thailand to intervene earlier this week to demand better provisioning by its banks. Thailand was hampered in dealing with the situation by its monetary policy. Its currency, the baht, is pegged to a basket of currencies dominated by the dollar, but was under pressure from speculators who were encouraged by Thailand's poor economic picture and weak financial sector. 

 Lower rates would have eased liquidity -- but would also have lowered the cost of borrowing for currency speculators. 

 Higher interest rates to ward off the speculators would have increased the cost of borrowing for the cash-strapped banks. 

 While most speakers stopped short of calling for regional banking regulation and supervision to prevent the same situation occurring elsewhere -- an idea mooted by Australia recently -- some experts recommended frequent and regular gatherings of central bankers and finance ministers. 

 "Most countries need to take steps to strengthen the official supervisory oversight of financial institutions and markets," said Gerald Corrigan, managing director at Goldman Sachs and a former president of the New York and member of the Federal Open Market Committee. 

 Key to the debate are capital inflows, which have widened current account deficits across Asia with serious implications for external balances and interest rates. 

 Corrigan warned that while many Asian nations with wide current account deficits have taken comfort from large foreign exchange reserves, the capital inflows responsible for much of their foreign exchange can evaporate overnight. 

 "Deregulation has also led to a greater exposure of credit and foreign exchange risk, and increased the danger of banks being inadequately capitalised with consequent incentives to offer above-market interest rates and engage in less prudent lending," said Mahmood Pradhan, a senior economist with the IMF. 

 The situation is becoming more urgent as more and more nations in the region seek financing for the sort of huge infrastructure projects on which their future depends, he said. 

 "The challenge is for many of these countries to address their infrastructure needs, including environmental requirements, without putting undue strains on public finances or on external positions," Pradhan said. 

 Although many Asian nations have successfully raised capital through privatisations, the amount of capital raised through privatisation in Asia was relatively small compared with Latin America, he said.

title: Thailand: Baht Ends Down In Spot Mkt On  Central-Bank  Turmoil
text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--The Thai baht slipped against the U.S. dollar in spot trading Thursday as investors rushed to buy the U.S. currency on reports of political turmoil within the Bank of Thailand. 

 But the Thai currency finished mixed in the swap market, where investors make agreements to buy and sell dollars at specified times in the future. One-month and one-year premiums declined, but three-month premiums rose. 

 At the close of trading Thursday, the dollar was at 25.953 baht, up from 25.948 baht at the close of trading Wednesday. The Bank of Thailand set its mid-rate for the dollar at 25.93 baht, down from 25.94 baht Wednesday. 

 The dollar's level indicated interventions by the Bank of Thailand, since the currency opened and finished outside the central bank's intervention range. That obligated the Bank of Thailand to sell dollars at below-market rates to Thai commercial banks. The intervention band Thursday was 25.91 baht to 25.95 baht. 

 Dealers attributed the dollar-buying partly to the government's decision Wednesday to suspend a deputy central-bank governor, Jaroong Nookhwun, accusing him of bungling efforts to prosecute a former president of the scandal-tainted Bangkok Bank of Commerce PCL. That sparked rumors that Rerngchai Marakanonda, the central-bank governor had resigned. The Bank of Thailand denied the rumors. 

 Rerngchai called a press conference Thursday to assure investors that the central bank's independence hadn't been compromised. 'Our monetary policy and financial-institutions supervision remain unchanged regardless of the suspension order,' although he said central bank employees had been demoralized by the government's decision.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Baht eases on dollar gains.
text:
* Thai baht eases on dollar's overnight gains versus majors. Positive economic data underpins currency, keeping it below central bank's mid-rate. 

 * Singapore dollar remains soft but subdued after overnight sales on news of Brunei finance minister's resignation. 

 * Malaysian ringgit under pressure from dollar's rise. 

 * Indonesian rupiah driven by liquidity conditions. 

 SINGAPORE, Feb 27 (Reuter) - The Thai baht subsided in line with the dollar's overnight gains versus the majors following comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan suggesting a U.S. interest rate hike might be in the offing. 

 The baht was quoted at 25.893-25.898 to the dollar at 0405 GMT against 25.842/25.852 late on Wednesday. 

 But dealers said it remained below the central bank's daily fixing of 25.91 for most of Thursday's morning session after the Finance Ministry leaked relatively positive economic data on Wednesday. 

 "I believe the baht is now returning to its normal footing, tracking the dollar/majors. The data yesterday might be viewed by some as still depressing. But if you put it into context, it showed a positive trend," said a UK bank dealer in Bangkok. 

 The data showed Thailand's December trade deficit narrowed to 22.3 billion baht from 24.2 billion baht in November. 

 The Finance Ministry said exports growth for 1996 contracted 0.2 percent compared with a 0.1 percent contraction forecast by the Bank of Thailand earlier. 

 An SBC Warburg analyst said the chance that investors might be moved into a baht selling spree again was minimal after the ministry's release of the data. 

 The central bank is due to officialy release its key economic indicators on Thursday at 0800 GMT. 

 "I see this as an improvement. Of course, some investors might want to see the trade deficit narrow because of strong improvement in exports rather than of the substantial drop in imports. But at the end of the day, it is the trade balance figure that affects the currency." he said. 

 "And I don't think any speculator who recently took losses from the Bank of Thailand's intervention will have more risk appetite to speculate on baht devaluation again soon," he said. 

 Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar remained under pressure after reaching an overnight low of 1.4280 to the U.S. dollar. 

 Dealers said funds had sold the Sing dollar following news that Brunei's Finance Minister had resigned and been replaced by his brother, the Sultan of the tiny oil kingdom. 

 The news spurred speculation Brunei might want to weaken its currency or de-link it from the Singapore dollar, dealers said. 

 "There were rumours Brunei wanted to bring up its non-oil exports. One way to do that would be to weaken the Brunei dollar, which is pegged against the Sing dollar," said a local bank dealer. 

 He said there was some buying of dollar/Sing by interbank players in the morning but it looked capped near its overnight highs. "There's no real interest from customers. They're probably all speculative buys," he said. 

 Dealers said the dollar/Sing was likely to trade a 1.4240-1.4290 range for the day. It was quoted at 1.4267/77 at 0405 GMT. 

 In Malaysia, the ringgit remained under pressure from the dollar's overnight rise but dealers said strong dollar selling interest around the 2.4925 level would limit the ringgit's fall. 

 The ringgit was quoted at 2.4833/43 to the dollar at 0405 GMT against 2.4810/20 at its Kuala Lumpur close on Wednesday. 

 "Dollar/ringgit's looking biddish after last night. But it'll probably trade a 2.4840-2.4900 range today," said a Singapore-based dealer. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was easier as the market continued to focus on liquidity conditions in the absence of other leads. 

 Spot rupiah was at 2,391.5/92.0 at 0405 GMT, compared with an opening of 2,391.0/92.0. 

 Dealers said short-term swaps fell, while longer-term rates were stable, suggesting the temporary nature of the current ample conditions. 

 Bank Indonesia kept its intervention band at 2,381/2,573 and the conversion band 2,381/2,429 on Wednesday after raising them by one point on Tuesday.

title: Financial markets await key Thai trade figures.
text:
BANGKOK, Feb 25 (Reuter) - Thailand's troublesome trade deficit should show some improvement in December when the central bank releases key economic indicators this week because of an anticipated slowdown in imports, analysts said on Tuesday. 

 Another key indicator that would be closely watched was the January level of foreign reserves to get some idea how much of Thailand's war chest might have been used to counter recent speculative attacks on the baht, they told Reuters. 

 If the trade figure worsened, the Bank of Thailand could almost certainly expect another bout of offshore attacks on the baht, the analysts said. 

 Thailand's fragile baht was the target of speculative attacks as it dived to new lows against a rising dollar from late last year. However, a weakening of the dollar and firm official statements ruling out devaluation have steadied it. 

 The Bank of Thailand will on Thursday release latest trade and current account figures for December and other leading economic indicators for January. 

 "The trade figure will be watched by everybody because it is the key driver for any economic turnaround," said Wong Yit Fan, Standard Chartered Bank's chief economist for Southeast Asia and Indochina. 

 "The domestic economy is going to continue in a slow mode because the interest rates are held high...The key thing for the economic turnaround is actually export growth," said Wong, who forecast marginal improvement on December exports. 

 Analysts believed that any improvement in the trade deficit would come from a reduction in imports as Thai demand turned sluggish in line with a slowing economy. 

 Arporn Chewakrengkai, chief economist of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, expected the December trade deficit to narrow to 22 billion baht ($85 million) from 24 billion baht in November. 

 "It's not that exports will improve much. Actually, the exports figure is likely to fall month-on-month. It's the much slower imports that could narrow the deficit," she said. 

 Thailand expects total exports growth in 1996 to contract by 0.1 percent against nearly 24 percent growth posted in 1995. A modest 7.7 percent growth is forecast by officials this year. 

 Some analysts doubted that January foreign reserves figures would show clear signs of the Bank of Thailand's massive currency intervention in the market to defend the baht. 

 SBC Warburg said in a report that the extent of any reserves drawdown might not become apparent for several months if the Bank of Thailand funded its spot intervention through currency swaps in the forward market. 

 "This kind of intervention delays the drawdown of reserves when the currency is under attack and thus mitigates the negative impact of falling reserves market sentiment," it said. 

 Thailand's foreign reserves were recorded at $38.7 billion in December, down from $39.6 billion in November. 

Foreign exchange dealers estimate that the central bank may have used between $3-10 billion to defend the currency since late last year when devaluation rumours plagued the baht. 

 Analysts expect the December current account deficit to remain high, but said the figures could be instrumental in bringing the overall 1996 deficit to below the central bank's forecast of 8.2 percent of gross domestic product.

text:
Industry executives reckon that the retail market for dark and 'white' distilled spirits is at least 50 billion baht, but the market for the products made by Charoen's distilleries has plateaued in recent years, as beer and imported whiskey have increased in popularity among Thais. 

 And Charoen may not dominate that market for much longer. Thailand's bureaucracy and past administrations have pledged to liberalize the liquor industry when the concessions end in 1999, making it likely that Charoen will lose at least part of his liquor empire. 

 Still, many believe that his grip on the distilling industry is so strong that he stands a good chance of retaining a significant portion of the business. 

 Some industry executives speculate, for example, that Charoen may try to persuade the Thai government now under another long-time Charoen pal, Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh to renew his monopoly to distill cheap but potent white spirits by arguing that opening that market could lead to abuses by less-experienced distillers. 

 Charoen's concessions now give his group 100% of the white liquor market and about 70% of the brown, or dark, liquor market. 

 Charoen's nonliquor investments have occasionally stirred controversy as well. Take his forays into banking, for example. In 1986, with the struggle over liquor concessions still unresolved, Charoen surprised Bangkok's financial community by buying into First Bangkok City Bank, or FBCB. 

 The bank was struggling with bad property loans, foreign exchange losses and management irregularities that eventually led the Bank of Thailand to intervene with a financial rescue package. Despite his big liquor debts at the time, Charoen won Finance Ministry approval to begin buying FBCB stock from the bank's key shareholder at a heavily discounted price just before the central bank intervened. 

 Charoen and his associates have since accumulated about 35% of FBCB's equity, taking control of the bank, now Thailand's seventh largest, with assets of about $8.7 billion at the end of 1995. 

 FBCB, which is listed on the Stock Exchange of Thailand, is profitable, with annual earnings growth averaging almost 30% from 1993 through 1996. But the bank isn't known for innovation its loan, deposit and trade-finance businesses have been slow to automate.

title: Thailand Baht Falls To 14-Month Low On Grim Economic Data

title: Plans for free floating baht needed now - KTT.
text:
BANGKOK, Nov 20 (Reuter) - Thailand's fixed exchange rate would be inappropriate and probably unsustainable in a more liberalised financial environment, Krungthai Thanakit said its November economic report released on Wednesday. 

 The finance and securities firm said a fixed baht may be appropriate given current conditions, but preparing to freely float the currency and planning monetary policies under floating rate conditions must now be a priority. 

 At present the central bank sets the Thai baht's exchange value each day against a basket of international currencies largely weighted to the U.S. dollar. 

 The Bank of Thailand indirectly intervenes if trading threatens to take the currency more than two satang either side of this set rate. "Now is the time to consider fully not only what should follow the baht basket ... The first-order answer has to be a floating exchange rate," said Krungthai Thanakit. 

 The report said that the fixed baht has caused some policy conflicts, and monetary management this year may have been easier under a freely-floated regime. 

 "Monetary growth in 1996 could have been very much smoother had the BOT (Bank of Thailand) not commiitted to a fixed baht exchange rate," it said. "Once the constraint of a fixed exchange rate has gone, what will the monetary policy of the central bank be, how will it be imposed, and how will it be monitiored?" 

 Recent pressure on the baht, sparked by slowing exports and a large current account deficit, required direct central bank intervention in overseas swap markets for the first time. 

 Krungthai Thanakit's call for plans to float the baht support comments made in Hong Kong yesterday by Narongchai Akrasanee, the chief of General Finance and possible economic advisor to the new Thai government.

title: FUND VIEW - Stocks in Thailand, Korea swing wildly.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 8 (Reuter) - Thailand is about to assume Korea's position as the worst-performing stock market in Asia. 

 After months of bullish words but little buying, fund managers started pouring money into Korean stocks last week, lifting the KOSPI off a 35-month low. But in Thailand, the pendulum swung stocks in the opposite direction. 

 A series of political and economic woes hammered Thailand's SET index down to three digits on Friday for the first time in three years. It rose back above key support at 1,000 after a private sector rescue fund rushed to buy, and closed at 1007.51. 

Thailand's central bank intervened with billions of dollars on the foreign exchange market on Friday after denying rumors, started in Singapore, of a looming devaluation. Meanwhile, rumors of brokerages being hit by client defaults on margin loans battered Thai stocks, prompting the 15.7 billion baht ($US628 million) rescue by the private sector rescue fund. 

 "If sentiment deteriorates even further, not even 10 rescue funds will save the market," warned Stephen Leung, chief investment officer at BZW Asia. 

 There are few signs Korea is benefitting at Thailand's expense, apart from changes to Morgan Stanley Capital International's indices. Most Asian markets were required to give ground to make way for Korea, whose Asian index weighting doubled to eight percent from four percent, and Taiwan, which was included for the first time effective September 2. 

 Fund managers said foreigners have funnelled US$3.5 billion into Korean stocks so far, but an 18-percent limit on foreign investment disguised their market presence until buying became particularly pronounced last week. 

 "We've suddenly seen very strong foreign money come in," said Abihijit Chakrabortti, regional strategist with Lehman Brothers. 

 A 35-month low close of 753.35 on August 28 stimulated serious interest on August 29, helping to bounce South Korean stocks back to end Friday at 784.05. 

 Asian market experts have been watching for a market bottom in Korea for weeks, as a slowing economy, poor half-year corporate earnings, political uncertainties and a widening trade deficit kept investors sidelined. 

 The jury is still out on whether last week's recovery is sustainable, partly because domestic investors continue to shun equities in favour of higher-yielding corporate paper. 

 "We think it's been overplayed, and on a relative valuation basis, Korea looks like one of the cheaper markets in Asia," said Chakrabortti. "But some of that value could be in doubt because there could still be more earnings disappointment." 

 Fund managers now seem to be playing the waiting game in Thailand, which was hit by a downgrade of its sovereign short-term debt rating by Moody's Investors Service Inc. 

 As forecast in an ING Barings report one week ago, the rating downgrade prompted rumours of a baht devaluation, requiring more official denials and central bank intervention. 

 Once again, the Asian view of the situation differed from that offered by North American experts. 

 "The central bank has handled the situation extremely effectively and in a more far-reaching manner than the aftermath of the peso crisis," ING Barings said, rejecting non-Asian comparisons to Mexico's 1994 cash and currency crisis. 

 Leung said consumer goods accounted for 80 percent of Mexico's imports prior to the 1994 crisis, while 70 percent of Thailand's imports are investment related and backed by substantial foreign reserves. 

 Foreign fund managers said the market will take its cue from a no-confidence vote in the prime minister on September 18, but the market could gyrate wildly beforehand. 

 If the no-confidence vote succeeds, parliament will have to be dissolved an a general election called, which would prompt a sudden rally in stocks and lower interest rate yields, ING Barings said.

 "The BOT intervened in the swap markets in Singapore and Hong Kong on Thursday morning," BOT governor Rerngchai Marakanond told a news conference. 

 "There were positive results from the intervention as swap interest rates dropped by about five percentage points," Rerngchai said. 

 The intervention was one of three measures announced on Thursday that aim to solve the current tight money supply. 

 The governor said it was the first time the central bank had intervened in a swap market abroad. Rerngchai said the decision was taken because the bank's recent injection of funds into the system was not working. 

 Thai money markets have been hit by tight liquidity over the past few days, with interbank rates soaring to new 18-month highs. 

 The BOT on Thursday also injected 10 billion baht ($400 million) into the system through the bond repurchase markets. 

 Another measure announced on Thursday was the decision to allow finance firms and banks to borrow funds from the central bank through guaranteed instruments. 

 Under the plan, which is effective immediately, commercial banks, finance companies and finance and securities firms can use bills of exchange and promissory notes with a maturity of no more than six months to borrow funds from the central bank. 

 After the measures were announced on Thursday, the interbank rate eased to 13-15 percent from 25-26 percent early. 

 Dealers said the tight liquidity has been due to a heavy outflow of foreign funds and large amounts of dollar buying which was triggered by rumours of a possible baht devaluation. The BOT has denied it plans to devalue the baht. 

 From July 1-18, foreign funds showed a net inflow of $219 million, but they were expected to show a net outflow for the whole month because of the heavy dollar buying in the last week triggered by the baht devaluation rumour. 

 Rergnchai also said high swap premiums compounded the tight liquidity by hindering inflows of foreign funds. 

 The governor said the BOT intervention was aimed at resolving the tight liquidity situation as soon as possible. 

 The BOT rarely intervenes directly in local foreign exchange and money markets. The bank controls the foreign exchange market through the fixing of the mid-rate and the money markets through the bond repurchase markets. 

 The bank will continue to intervene in the swap market as long as it is necessary, Rergnchai said.

title: Bank Of  Thailand /Repo Market-2: Growing  Intervention
text:
BANGKOK (AP-Dow Jones)--Thailand's central bank pumped 15 billion baht into the country's repurchase (repo) market Wednesday in a move to lower interbank rates that had reached a 19-month high, a top official said. 

 The amount was disclosed to reporters by Siri Ganjarerndee, an assistant governor at the Bank of Thailand. It reflects the central bank's growing intervention in currency and money markets that were jolted by devaluation rumors this week. 

 The Bank of Thailand on Monday sold dollars worth $340 million and injected 4 billion baht into the repurchase market to defend the baht and to lower interbank rates that had risen because of the rumors.

title: Bank Of Thailand/Exchange-Rate-3: Baht Moves Very Little
text:
The Thai baht is a pegged currency, its value determined from a 'basket' of currencies that includes the dollar, the yen and the Deutsche mark. It has had a history of extraordinary stability, analysts say: in the last three years the dollar has traded in a range of 24.50 baht to 25.50 baht. 

 'If you looked at a chart of the dollar versus the baht over the last few years, you'd see just a flat line,' said Kevin Chan, an economist with Salomon Brothers in Hong Kong. 

 Analysts credit the Bank of Thailand for that stability. Each morning, it sets a band within which it wants the baht to trade. The exact width of the band is seldom disclosed, analysts say, but its dimensions may be guaged by the 'mid-rate' set by the central bank each morning. Typically, analysts say, if the Thai currency moves outside a range of 1 baht, the Bank of Thailand intervenes by buying or selling dollars. 

 The frequency of intervention is high, and the rewards usually are considerable: a stable baht attracts foreign investors, promotes Thai exports and generally helps the economy grow. As a result, analysts say, the Bank of Thailand has been loath to consider any change in the system. 

 'The bank has been saying the baht is sacrosanct,' said Sriyan Pietersz, an analyst with Capital Nomura Securities PCL. 'They've been saying the system will not change as long as we have a current-account deficit.'

title: Thailand  Interbank Rates Fall; Mkt Cool To  Interventions
text:
BANGKOK (AP-DJ)--Thai interbank rates continued to sink Friday, apparently cool to attempts by the Bank of Thailand to tighten the money supply through a big sale of bonds this week. 

 The overnight interbank rate is at 6%-6.5%, down from 7%-7.25% Thursday. The call rate is at 6.5%, down from 7.5% Thursday. 

 Repurchase rates are also declining. The one-day rate is at 7.75%, down from 7.875% Thursday. The seven-day rate is 7.875, down from 8% Thursday. 

 Foreign capital inflows, which totaled $653 million in the first two weeks of January alone, have dragged down interbank rates sharply so far. That has brought down deposit rates, and even lending rates, at some banks. 

 The Bank of Thailand, anxious to stop rates from coming down too far, this week tried to drain money out of the repurchase market by selling bonds. The central bank sold 8 billion baht worth of bonds this week, its deputy governor, Rerngchai Marakanond, told reporters Thursday. 

 He also said that commercial banks, in a bout of dollar-selling this week, sold about $580 million to the Bank of Thailand, which had been offering a higher rate for the U.S. currency than was available on the spot market. 

 'There's been some intervention,' said a dealer at the Bank of Tokyo. 'The bank didn't want commercial banks to bring their rates down too much.' 

 But the intervention hasn't had much effect, said another dealer at the Bank of America. 'They can't absorb all the liquidity because it's simply too much,' she said. 

 Dealers said they were aware of no interventions by the central bank Friday. Rerngchai couldn't be reached for comment.

title: Asia  Currency  Scare/Thailand -3: Bank Of Thailand Praised
text:
Despite the system's flaws, the Bank of Thailand gets high marks for its handling of the crisis, all agree. Sensing the liquidity shortage, it set up a currency swap facility on Jan. 13 that poured funds back into the market by letting banks borrow baht at between 9.5% and 10%, instead of at the higher interbank rates. The central bank also kept its daily foreign exchange fixing reassuringly steady, and took pains to keep dealers and reporters informed of its policies. 

 The steps were effective. Within 24 hours, as the baht's sturdiness grew apparent, some banks actually reversed course and put funds back into the market, notes a Hong Kong dealer. 

 The Bank of Thailand acknowledges structural problems exist and says it is taking steps to remedy them. But it insists major reforms aren't needed. For example, there's no plan to change settlement rules to allow two-day payment. 

 But since the crisis, the bank has proposed several measures that many believe would help prevent a similar liquidity squeeze in the future. To boost liquidity in the repurchase market, the central bank plans to accept more types of securities, including bonds not backed by the government but issued by state-owned banks such as the Industrial Finance Corp. of Thailand, the Government Housing Bank and the Bank for Agriculture and Agricultural Cooperatives. Now, only the limited supply of government bonds or government-backed bonds of state enterprises are eligible to trade in the repurchase market. 

 The central bank also is considering a plan to designate a number of primary dealers through which it could intervene in Thailand's still-small secondary bond market.
